# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Age of Ailean (An Aois Ailein)

# Part One: The Grove and the Hill

# Chapter One: Of the Seven Nights

*GE 1*


> *Chaidh e dhan doire na ghille, is thill e na rìgh.*
> He went into the grove a lad, and he came back a king.
>
> — said of Ailean Mòr, as the reciters of Dùn ìseal keep it

## I. Of the Fires under the Oaks

*Coinneach mac Shuibhne tells this, in the years before he grew grey, and Clann na Ceiste have kept his words whole, changing nothing, for they say a true thing need not be improved.*

Coinneach was three years younger than his brother, a lad of one-and-twenty that summer, and he had followed him north with a sack of oatcake and a skin of buttermilk that his brother would not eat. He did not know, when he set out, that he would not be let nearer than the edge of the trees.

Ailean had been gone the better part of a year, carrying his six pots on a pole across his shoulders, each with its lid of turf, feeding six fires that had never before burned in one place. Their father asked no questions of him before he went, and none of the household did either, for it was known in Clann na Ceiste, as it had been known since the mason's day, that the coals were not a thing to be asked about. Coinneach had watched him go with the same silence the others kept, had held it two seasons, and then could hold it no longer. He told no one where he was walking, and simply went, north and further north, by the roads his brother must have taken, until on an evening in high summer he came out of birch scrub onto a rise above a stand of oaks and saw smoke going up through the leaves in six colours, and knew he had found him.

He came down through the trees meaning to walk straight in, and got no further than the first oaks.

It was not a hand that stopped him, nor a word, though a word came soon enough. It was the ground itself, or the air over it, which changed the way water changes when it goes suddenly from a stream's cold to a spring's warmth, so that a man's skin knows it before his eyes have found any reason. Coinneach stood with one foot already lifted to the next step and could not set it down inside the ring of oaks. He looked and there was Ailean, sitting cross-legged in a clearing with six low fires around him each burning in its own colour, gold and white and a red so dark it looked nearly black, and copper-red, and a fire like beaten silver, and a sixth with no more colour to it than any hearth-flame has, though it stood straighter than any hearth-flame ought to stand. In the middle of the six, on the bare earth, lay a small stone burning with a low light of no colour he could name, for it was every colour at once and none of them would hold still.

His brother sat with his head unturned, and it was the shape beside him that spoke, tall as a standing man and made of the same grey as the smoke that went up past it without disturbing it at all.

"That is close enough," it said, not loudly, and yet Coinneach heard it as clearly as if it had been at his shoulder. "Go back to the trees. Camp there if you will. Come no nearer while the fires burn."

"I am his brother," said Coinneach, because it seemed a thing that ought to be said to whatever this was.

"I know whose brother you are," said the shape, and there was no unkindness in it, only the flat certainty of a being that had watched a very great deal and found little of it needed explaining twice. "That is why you are let stand where you stand, and not sent further off than that. Go back to the trees."

Ailean turned his head then, once, and looked at him across the fires, and Coinneach saw that his brother's face in that light was the same face he had grown up beside, and yet lit from some place behind the eyes as well as in front of them, the way a horn lantern is lit from within, and not merely warmed on the outside by a fire someone else has made. He did not speak. He lifted one hand a little way from his knee, which Coinneach took, rightly, for all the greeting he was going to get, and then his brother's eyes went back to the fires and did not come to him again that night.

Coinneach went back to the trees. He was one-and-twenty years old and he had walked the length of the island on a road with no end that he had been told of, and he sat down under a birch with his sack of oatcake between his knees and did not eat any of it, because eating in front of a fast felt to him like a kind of theft.

He had grown up three years behind his brother in the same house, under the same low roof, and had thought, until that summer, that there was little enough about Ailean he did not already know: which shoulder he favoured carrying a lamb, which songs he sang badly and on purpose to make the younger children laugh, how long he could hold his breath under the mill-pool. Their father had said nothing when Ailean took up the coals; he had only watched him go with the flat, unsurprised look of a man watching a debt come due that he had long known was owed, and had said nothing either when Coinneach, two seasons on, packed a sack of his own and went after him without leave asked or given. What sent Coinneach north, in truth, was simpler than disobedience: a year is a long time for a house to sit waiting on news of one son, and Coinneach had never in his life been good at waiting. He did not know, sitting there, that this was the first of seven nights, or that he would keep every one of them awake, or that the deeds he watched from outside a ring of trees that summer would be the only true account any teller after him would ever have of what was done inside it. He knew only that his brother's face had changed, and that he meant to be there when it changed back, if it ever did.

## II. Of the Seven Nights

*The vigil within the ring belongs to Sloinneadh a' Chlachair to tell, for Coinneach was never let see it; they keep it word for word, as it has come down from the grove itself, and it is set here as they set it, against what Coinneach watched from the trees.*

Ailean sat among the seven fires (the seventh, the stone in the ring's centre, had taken light at dusk when the shape called Coimhdeach na Fine stooped over it, and burned after that with no colour that could be named, being every colour, and none of them still), and Coimhdeach na Fine stood over him and told him how the watch must be kept.

"Stay with them until they are cold," it said. "Do not leave them, do not sleep far from them, and eat nothing while they burn."

"Why?" said Ailean.

"So that the spirits, being merged, may know one keeper, and the fire go into no hand but the hand that did not leave it."

"And after me?" said Ailean. "Will my children have it?"

Coimhdeach na Fine was a long while answering. The six fires and the seventh burned on between them without a sound, and the smoke of them stood up straight through windless air.

"It will be yours," it said at last, "and no one's after you. Your children will have a little of it, and their children less, as a hearthstone keeps the heat a while when the fire is out; and then your line will not have it, and will forget that it ever had, and the island will call you a tale. But hear this, and keep it. When strangers hold this island, the fire will wake again in your line."

"What strangers?"

"That is not given to me to say."

Then Coimhdeach na Fine went from him, or ceased to be seen, which Sloinneadh a' Chlachair does not tell apart, and Ailean was left alone among the fires to keep his watch.

He kept it as he had been told. He did not leave the ring, and did not sleep far from it, and ate nothing while the seven fires burned, though he drank from the grove's own spring on the nights the fires stood steady enough to be left a while. The first two nights the hunger in him was a plain, animal thing, no different from any hunger he had carried on any long ride before; by the third it had gone quiet, the way pain goes quiet in a wound that will either mend or kill and has stopped asking a man's opinion on which. On the fifth night he thought he heard voices in the fires, low under the sound the flames made, saying the same words over that he could never afterward recall, only as a rhythm, the way a chant is remembered by its beat after its language is lost; and on the seventh he could not have said, waking or not waking, whether he had slept at all, for the fires gave the same light and the same warmth at the black heart of that night as they had at the first evening's dusk, unspent, unlessened, as if the passing of six nights meant no more to them than the passing of six breaths.

Outside the ring, under his birch, Coinneach kept a watch of his own, with no gods to answer his questions and no fires to warm him and no lid of turf to hold his hunger down. Through the first night he lay on his back and watched the light of the seven fires stand and shift between the trunks, colours he had no names for laid over colours he did, gold on birch-bark, the black-red flickering against a stone he could not see round, and told himself he would sleep an hour and did not sleep at all. By the second night the hunger had settled into a duller ache than hunger, a low ache he had stopped arguing with, and he found he could watch the coloured light for longer stretches without his mind wandering off after food or home or his father's face when he learned where his younger son had gone. By the third and fourth he had stopped counting the nights as nights and begun counting them as fires, one fire more burned down toward whatever it was burning down toward, though from where he lay none of the seven ever seemed to burn down at all.

It was on the fifth night that he first heard the voices.

He was not sure, after, that he had heard anything, and he never claimed more than that he had. They came from the direction of the ring, under the light and the smoke-smell and the small settling sounds any fire makes, two voices or three, pitched too low for words, one of them — he would say this only once, near the end of his own life, to the woman who wrote it down — sounding almost as if it were his brother's, though shaped into a rhythm Ailean had never used in speech, more like a man saying the same word over and over to hold a thing steady in his mind. Coinneach sat up under the birch and listened until the muscles of his neck ached with listening, and heard nothing more he could swear to, and lay back down with the hunger and the cold and the sense, new to him that night, that a thing was happening within the ring of oaks that had no plain edges to it, that could not be watched the way a fight or a birth or a burial could be watched, only felt at, the way a man feels at a wall in the dark.

He did not go nearer. He had been told to keep to the trees, and he kept to them, and that is the whole of what Coinneach mac Shuibhne did for seven nights: he kept to the trees, and did not eat, though no one had forbidden him to, and did not sleep, though no one had asked that of him either, and watched colours he could not name go up through leaves he could, until he no longer knew which watch was his brother's and which was his own.

## III. Of the Eighth Night

*Here the two tellings run together, for on the eighth night there was a thing that both saw, though neither saw the same thing, and Clann na Ceiste keep both accounts and do not choose between them.*

On the seventh night Ailean could not afterward say whether he had slept. The fires had not burned low in seven nights, had shown him no more fuel spent than on the first evening, and had not needed his hand at any of them; and on the eighth night, without warning and without sound, they went out. All seven together. He came to himself, or woke, Sloinneadh a' Chlachair will not say which, and found the ring of oaks entirely dark, the pots and the pale stone lying grey and cold on the trodden leaves, and himself colder than he had been in any of the nights before, as if the fires had been lending him their own warmth all along and had just then called the loan due.

Outside the trees, at the same hour by whatever reckoning either of them kept afterward, Coinneach saw the dark come down over the grove and felt some weight go out of the night with it, some pressure he had not known was on him until it lifted. He got to his feet. More than once in seven nights he had meant to walk in regardless of what stood there and see for himself what had become of his brother, and each time some pull in the air of the place had turned him back before he had gone three steps. Now, with the fires dead and the grove black as any wood at midnight, he found his feet would carry him no better than before. Standing at the edge of the oaks with his hand on a trunk, he felt the bark shiver, very faintly, the way a held breath shivers a man's chest, and then the grove filled with light.

It did not come up from the ground as the seven fires had, and it was not the colour of any fire he had seen in his life. It came in among the trees the way people come into a hall, many at once, talking low, and it moved. Coinneach saw shapes crossing between the trunks that his mind, afterward, could give no better name than shapes: a big one that laughed without a sound reaching him, one small and quick that he took, for no reason he could give, to be carrying fire in her own two hands, one bent low as though listening at the ground. He never named them, all his life, though others named them for him later out of Aithris a' Chruthachaidh, and he would not say they were wrong, only that he had not known, standing at the edge of the trees with his hand shaking on the bark, which name went with which shape.

He tried to go in, setting his foot forward the way he had tried every night before it, and his foot would not carry him; this time it was not only the ground that refused him, for his whole body stood at the edge of that light the way a man stands at the edge of a cliff in the dark, knowing the ground is there and not trusting his legs to find it. Once he called his brother's name. Nothing in the light answered him, and after a while the light began to thin, the shapes going from many to few to none, until only the grey stillness of an ordinary wood before dawn was left among the oaks, and Coinneach sat down where he stood, because his legs had at last stopped holding him up, and waited for the sky to go from black to grey in its own time, the way skies do whether gods have walked a wood that night or not.

## IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

*What was done to Ailean between the fires going out and the light coming in, no one now living was let see; what was said to him, and by whom, and what he answered, Clann na Ceiste keep as it was given them, and it is not this telling's place to add to it or take from it.*

Dawn found Coinneach still sitting at the edge of the trees with his back against an oak, and the sun perhaps a hand's width up when a figure came out of the grove toward him, walking easily, as a man walks who has slept well and eaten and has nowhere urgent to be. It was a little while before Coinneach's eyes, sore with a week of watching, made the figure into his brother, and longer still before he trusted the making.

He got up. His legs had gone stiff with a night's sitting and he stumbled the first step, and Ailean put out an arm and caught him, the ordinary way an older brother catches a younger one who has stumbled, and it was that arm, closing on his own, that told Coinneach the truth of the night before any word did. It was warm. Not warm as a living arm is warm, blood-warm, the warmth a man carries without noticing it in himself and only feels in another when the morning is cold; this was warm the way a hearthstone is warm long after the fire has gone out and been swept, a warmth with weight to it, that seemed to come up out of the bone rather than lie on the skin. Coinneach had held his brother's arm a thousand times in one-and-twenty years and he had never felt anything like it, and he did not let go at once, though he knew, holding it, that he ought to.

"You're cold," Ailean said, as if that were the only strange thing about the morning.

Coinneach found he could not, for a space, make any words come. When they came they were not the ones he had spent seven nights preparing. "What happened to you," he said, "in there," and even as he said it he heard how small a question it was for what he had watched from outside the ring.

Ailean looked at him a while before he answered, and something crossed his face that Coinneach, in all the years he told this tale afterward, could never settle on a single word for: not joy, though there was joy in it; not fear, though there was fear in it too; nearer, he came to think in his old age, to the look of a man newly returned from a country whose language he has learned well enough to think in, and cannot just then remember how to render into the one his own people speak.

"They named me king," he said.

That was all. Who had named him, he did not say, though Coinneach, standing there with his brother's warm arm still half in his grip, thought he knew well enough without being told, having watched shapes cross a lit grove all night from the wrong side of its trees. What a king was king of, on an island that had never had one, went unsaid too, and what had been put into him, or taken from him; nor did he ask his brother to swear any silence about it, for he seemed to know already, in some way Coinneach could not follow, that there was no danger of Coinneach's telling more than he had seen, since Coinneach had seen almost nothing at all.

They went back into the ring together, Ailean walking as if the ground of it held no more weight for him than any other ground now, and Coinneach following a half-step behind, still not wholly easy in himself about crossing that line of oaks even with the fires long out and his brother's hand on his shoulder. The six pots lay where they had stood for seven nights, empty and cold, their turf lids scattered where the wind or something less than wind had thrown them; the pale stone that had held the seventh fire lay among them, small and grey and giving off no more warmth to the eye than any stone off any hillside, though when Coinneach at last made himself touch it, near midday, it was warm too, in the same deep hearthstone way his brother's arm had been. Ailean gathered the six pots onto his shoulder-pole without a word, as though he meant to carry them on somewhere, though he never lit any of the six fires in them again in all his life, and left the seventh stone lying where it lay, uncovered, among the leaves.

They did not go home. Coinneach asked once, that first morning, whether they were for their father's hearth, and Ailean said only that they were going south, and began walking, and Coinneach, having followed him a year's worth of roads already, followed him down this one too.

He did not stop at Na Glinn Àrda, where the households of Clann na Ceiste kept their herds about the crack in the ground that no one living could remember the naming of, though he had kin enough there to have stopped a season among them and been fed and questioned and made much of; and some of those kin, seeing him go by without turning aside, left their own hearths and their own herds and walked out onto the road after him without being asked, the way men will follow a fire seen at night across open country before they have decided in their own minds to go anywhere at all. By the time the grove was three days behind them there were eleven of them walking south with Ailean and his brother, kin near and kin distant, none of them able afterward to say clearly why he had left byre or field to do it, only that the sight of Ailean walking past his own people's gates without stopping had seemed a thing that could not be let go by unfollowed.

## V. Of the Kin Who Followed

*This part of the road Coinneach told plainly, having been on it himself and needing no fires and no Coimhdeach na Fine to tell it by.*

They were an odd company to look at from any rise above the road: a king who had been a king nine days, walking at no great pace and carrying six empty pots on a pole across his shoulder as though they still held cargo worth the carrying; his brother a half-step behind him, hollow-eyed from a week without food or sleep and saying little; and behind the two of them, by the time Na Glinn Àrda were a day's walk gone, eleven more, none of whom had set out that morning meaning to leave home at all.

A woman with a baby on her hip had been driving geese in from a field when Ailean passed her gate; she left the geese to find their own way back and simply fell in on the road, the baby asleep against her shoulder before the first mile was out and no more roused by the change in her life than by any other jolt of the walking. An old man who had buried two wives and outlived a third said, when his daughter asked him where he thought he was going at his age, only that he had a feeling in his chest he had not had since he was a boy and did not intend to argue with it. There was a boy of nine who came because his older cousin came, and a stooped-shouldered woman with a limp who kept pace with the rest of them without complaint or explanation the whole way south, and would not be persuaded home again even when the going grew hard. None of the eleven, asked afterward, could give a better account of why he or she had come than the old man's: a feeling in the chest, not to be argued with.

Ailean spoke little to any of them on the road, and to Coinneach hardly more, though he let his brother walk always at his shoulder and never once told him to turn back, which Coinneach, in the years he had left to think on it, came to count for more than any number of words would have been worth. Twice they slept in the open under no roof at all, and both nights it was noticed, though not spoken of loudly, that the ground near where Ailean lay was warmer by morning than the ground a little further off, warm enough that the heavy dew that greyed the rest of the field left a bare, dark ring around him the size of a sleeping man, as though the ground itself remembered him from the night before it had ever been asked to.

They did not hurry. Ailean walked as a man walks who knows the road will still be there whether he covers it in ten days or twenty, and stopped where there was water and shelter and went on again when he chose and not before, and slowly, day by day, the sack Coinneach had carried north with such care went from full to half-full to empty, shared out among a company that had grown too large for one man's forethought to feed, and nobody starved, and nobody afterward could quite say how that had been managed either.

Coinneach walked among them the whole way south, and told none of them what he had watched from outside the ring of oaks. He had sworn no oath of silence; he had simply found, trying the words over to himself on the road, that they came out smaller than the thing they were meant to carry, the way a bucket of well-water looks like less once it is out of the well than it did going down for it. He kept the telling instead, turning it over through the long days of walking, fitting it to itself the way a man fits a stone to a gap in a dry wall, testing each piece against what he had truly seen and setting aside what he had only half seen or wholly imagined in the dark under the birch; and it was in this way, walking south behind his brother down a road that had no name yet because there had been no one before them to walk it and give it one, that the first account of the seven nights and the eighth was made, by a man of one-and-twenty who had been let see none of it, and who therefore, of all who ever told it after, was the most careful never to say more than he knew.

# Chapter Two: Of the Knapper's Son

*GE 1 – 2*

*At the flint-pit below Dùn ìseal, where the ground is still pocked with old workings, the spear-makers tell this among themselves, and have told it to their sons.*

## I. Of the Watch on the Lip of the Hill

The lad's father worked flint in a pit behind the houses, and had worked it there since before the lad was born, so that the boy grew up knowing the smell of struck stone the way another child knows the smell of bread. He was thirteen that summer, old enough to be set to watching and too young for much else, and it was his turn, with three others no older, to sit on the lip of the hill and watch the valley road for cattle-thieves and for worse.

The hill had no name then but the hill. It stood over the meeting of two streams, with byres and forty-some houses scattered along its shoulder and no bank round any of it, for the valleys had never needed one; the worst that came up that road in most summers was a hard bargain over grazing, or a drunk man from the next household with a grievance three years old. The lad sat with his knees drawn up and a spear across them that had been his father's, and had been his father's father's before that, and watched the road go down into the haze where the valley bent west.

He saw them a long way off: a string of figures on the track below the ford, twelve of them by his later count, walking without haste and without the shuffle of people driving beasts. No dust rose with them, for there had been rain three days before, and no baggage showed on any back that he could see. He watched a while longer than he should have, the way a boy watches something he cannot name a fear for, and then he ran.

He came down through the houses shouting that there were strangers on the road, twelve strangers walking, and by the time he reached the gate of his own house half the hill had heard him and were coming out with whatever lay nearest the door. His father came out of the pit still holding the antler tool he worked with, and looked at his son and then down the road, and said nothing, which the lad took worse than if he had shouted.

The holders of the hill gathered every spear they owned, which came to some sixty, old and new, well-made and poor, and stood in a crowd on the steepest part of the slope, where anyone climbing would have the ground against him. The lad stood among the men with his father's second-best spear, for the best had gone to his uncle, who had a longer reach. He was not told to stand there. No one told him to go home either, and by the time anyone thought of it the twelve had reached the foot of the hill, and it was too late to send a boy anywhere without being seen to do it.

## II. Of the Twelve at the Foot of the Slope

The twelve stopped where the ground began to rise, all but one of them, a man the lad's eye kept sliding past and back to, for he stood taller than the rest by a head and something more, though nothing else about him marked him out: no gold, no fine cloth, nothing in his hands. He came on alone, up the grass, at the pace of a man walking to his own door.

The lad said afterward, when he was old and had told the tale more times than he could count, that every man on that slope had meant to throw. He had meant to throw himself, and had thought about the throw the way his father had taught him, weight back, elbow up, and had been glad of the practice. The man came up within a long cast, and then well within an easy one, and the lad did not throw, and could not afterward say why not; only that somewhere between one breath and the next a warmth had come onto his face, as though a door had opened on a kiln a field away, and his arm, which had been ready, simply did not do what he had told it.

Nor was he alone in it. Beside him the eldest of the hill's holders, a man who had led them through two bad winters and a feud with the next valley and had never in the lad's knowing been slow to act, let the point of his spear down into the grass, and then let the shaft go after it, and sat down where he stood with his face in his hands, as a man sits down who has been struck somewhere no wound shows. One by one the rest did something of the kind: let their spears fall, or turned and went back down into the houses without a word to anyone, walking the way a man walks from a hearth he has just been told is not his any longer.

The tall man walked through the middle of them as a man walks through standing barley, touching nothing, looking at no one long enough to be looked back at, and went on up to the crown of the hill, and stood there turning slowly, taking in the valleys on every side as though he were counting them. After a while he called down the slope, in a voice that carried without being raised, for someone to bring him water.

No one moved. The lad found that his legs, which had failed him in one way a few minutes before, were willing enough now, and he went up the hill with the water-skin his mother kept filled by the door, because it was nearer to hand than thinking twice, and because a boy of thirteen does not weigh the same things a grown man weighs.

## III. Of the Water and the Spear

Up close the man was less strange and more so both together. His face was a young man's face, unweathered in a way that did not fit a life spent walking hill roads, and the lad, who had an eye for ages from watching his father's customers come and go, put him at four-and-twenty and never once, in all the years he knew him after, found cause to change the guess. His eyes, when they came round to the boy, were patient in a way the lad had no word for then and only found one for much later, when he was old himself and had watched enough patient men. He took the skin and drank, unhurried, and handed it back, and looked at the boy properly for the first time.

"What is your name?"

The lad gave it.

"Is that your father's spear?"

"His second-best," the lad said, before he had decided to say anything at all. "The best went to my uncle."

The man looked at the spear a moment, not long, the way a man who knows tools looks at one that is neither good nor bad. "Take it back to him," he said. "Tell him I shall want a great many more."

That was the whole of it. He turned from the boy and looked out again over the valleys, north and south and along the line of the streams, and the lad went back down the hill with the water-skin empty and the spear heavy in his hand in a way it had not been an hour before, though nothing about the spear had changed.

The houses talked that night as the lad had never heard them talk, in low voices round hearths where the doors were shut earlier than usual, and every household had its own account of the moment its spears had gone down, none quite agreeing with its neighbour's, and none of them, the lad noticed even at thirteen, willing to say plainly that they had been afraid. His father sat a long while turning the spear over in his hands after the boy gave him the king's word, saying nothing, and at last hung it back on its pegs over the door and told his son to bank the fire and go to bed, in the same voice he used on any ordinary night, though the lad lay awake past the last of the talk outside and heard his father still sitting by the hearth when he finally slept.

## IV. Of the Households Coming In

What came after was slower than the taking, and stranger in its own way for being slow. Through that first summer and into the next, the households of the valleys about the hill came in to the tall man one after another, a family at a time, like water finding its level with no one to drive it there. No word went out that the lad ever heard of; they simply came, walking up with whatever they thought a king should be given, which varied enormously, for none of them had ever given anything to a king before. Some brought hides. One old woman brought a pot of her own making and nothing else, and the man took it and thanked her by name, though no one had told him her name, and she went home and told everyone who would listen that he had known her before she spoke.

They told him where their grazing ran and asked him to hold the telling of it, for a valley that had quarrelled every spring past memory of the oldest man living had begun, within a season of his coming, to want someone outside every household to say where one man's grass ended and the next man's began. They brought their quarrels too, old ones some of them, older than the lad, disputes over a strip of ground or a dead man's cattle that had gone unsettled so long that both sides had half forgotten what had started them and kept them running out of habit more than grievance.

He heard the first of these on the open ground below the crown of the hill, where the grass was already beaten thin from the households' coming and going, and the lad was there among a crowd of forty or fifty who had come to watch, for there was nothing else that summer worth leaving off work for.

## V. Of the First Judgement

The two households in it held land on either side of a strip of pasture between two becks, and each swore the strip for its own, and each brought an old man to say so, and the old men disagreed with each other in exactly the words their fathers were said to have used, so that the lad, listening, had the strange feeling of hearing an argument that had never once changed in forty years.

The king, for so the hill had begun to call him among themselves though no one had heard him claim the word, let both sides finish. He asked one question only, of the elder of the two old men: which household's cattle grazed the strip the summer the boundary stone at the beck's mouth had last been moved. The old man answered without thinking, the way a man answers a question he has never once considered might matter, and in the answering gave away the case he had come to argue, for his own memory put the other household's cattle on the ground in that year, before the stone was moved.

"Then it is theirs," the king said, "and has been since before either of you were troubling your fathers about it. Move the stone back and be done."

That was the whole of the judgement, said as a man says which way the wind is, and it left both households standing where they were for a moment as though a wall they had leaned on all their lives had been taken away without warning. The one that lost the strip went home saying nothing worse than that the old fool had talked himself out of his own land, which was true and did not comfort him. The one that won it went home quieter than a household should go home from a victory, and the lad's father said, that night, that he had never in his life seen men so glad to be told what to do, nor so frightened of the man who had told them.

Other judgements followed through that year and the next, on smaller matters mostly, a stolen calf, a well two families both claimed to have dug, a marriage promised and not kept, and each was settled in the same handful of words, without appeal and, so far as the lad ever heard, without a single household going back afterward to argue the finding a second time. The valley people began to say among themselves, half in complaint and half in something nearer relief, that a man could no longer nurse a grudge on that hill the way his father had nursed his, for there was somewhere now to take it and be rid of it in an afternoon.

## VI. Of the Warmth with No Fire

It was in that first winter, when the snow lay longer on the hill than the oldest people could remember it lying, that the thing happened which the hearths of Dùn ìseal still tell before any other, though the lad himself did not see it and had it only at second hand, from a girl a year or two older than himself who swore to it all her life and was believed.

She had gone out past the houses one clear, bitter night to see to a beast that had strayed near the king's own fire, which he kept apart from the rest and let no one tend, and found herself standing nearer him than she had ever stood, closer than she had meant to come. She told it that she had expected to feel the cold worse there, in the open, away from any hearth of her own; instead she felt warm through, as a person feels warm sitting close by a good fire banked high, though there was no fire near her at all, only the king standing with his back half to her, looking at nothing she could see. Neither of them spoke a word. She stood there long enough to grow uneasy at her own staying, and went back to the beast and the byre, and was warm, she said, the whole walk back, though the night did not warm around her; only she did.

She told it once to her mother and was told to keep it to herself, and did, mostly, until she was old and telling it cost her nothing anyone could use against her. By then half the hill had a story like it, of standing near him on a cold night, or a hot one, and coming away changed in temperature without a fire to blame; and no one who told such a story could say why they had never thought, at the time, to ask him about it.

## VII. Of the Pit and the Word Kept

The word the king had sent back with the lad's spear was not forgotten on either side. Through that autumn the flint-pit behind the houses worked longer hours than it had in the lad's memory, his father and his uncle and two men taken on from a household that had come in late, cutting and knapping spearheads by the score where before they had made them a few at a time, as they were needed and no faster.

The lad was set to help before the leaves were fully down: fetching stone from the outcrop above the pit, sorting the good nodules from the flawed, learning under his father's hand the strike that split a piece clean and the strike that shattered it for nothing. He was not good at it that first year, and his father told him so without unkindness, the way a man tells a boy a true thing he expects him to outgrow. What the lad was good at, from the start, was watching: he had watched the taking of the hill from close enough to remember every part of it, and he watched now, at his father's elbow, the way a spearhead came out of a piece of stone the way a fish comes out of water, all at once and not at all by accident.

Word came up from the king's own steward, before the first snow, of how many heads the pit was to have ready by the turning of the year, and the number was larger than the lad's father had ever cut for one order, larger by a good deal than the whole hill had needed for its own use in a generation. His father took the order without complaint and without haste either, and set to teaching his son faster than he might otherwise have done, for there was more work now than two men and two hired hands could easily carry, and a third pair of hands that could be trusted, even a clumsy pair, was worth the teaching of it.

By the depth of that winter the lad could strike a passable head three times in five, which his father allowed was better than most boys managed in a year, and the lad understood, without being told in so many words, that the pit behind his father's house had become, in the space of one summer and one autumn, the place spears came from for a king who had said he would want a great many more, and had meant it.

## VIII. Of the Ring Pegged in the Snow

The bank was begun in that same hard winter, which surprised the hill more than the king's coming had, for no one builds earthworks in frost if it can be helped, and the ground on the hill's crown was iron by the turning of the year. Yet it was in the snow, not after it, that the king walked the crown of the hill with a bundle of pegs cut from ash and set them himself, one after another, pacing out a line that took in the old byres and left room, he said, for houses that were not built yet.

The households worked it in shifts through the worst of that winter, breaking frozen turf with mattocks that blunted faster than they could be sharpened, and the lad's father sent flint scrapers up to the diggers when the antler picks gave out, so that for a stretch of days the bank of Dùn ìseal was cut as much with worked stone as with anything else, an oddness the old people of the hill still mention when the bank is spoken of at all. The lad went up himself on the days his father could spare him, and stood in the line passing frozen clods hand to hand along the ditch, and remembered afterward mostly the cold in his fingers and the steam that stood over sixty or eighty people working close together in the freeze, so that from a little way off the whole crown of the hill seemed to smoke like a fire banked for the night.

The king worked among them on the days he was there, which were not all of them, for he was already riding out to valleys beyond the first ring of them and coming back only every so often; but on the days he set his own hand to the ditch the work went faster, not because anyone slacked when he was gone, the lad's father always said, but because no one wanted to be the one found idle when he came back unlooked-for. By the time the frost broke, the line of the ditch ran round the crown of the hill, a raw scar in the turf a spade deep, marking room, when the last house should be fitted into it, for some forty households. It was a scar and no more. The bank itself, raised to a man's height and closed at its gate, was eight more summers in the building, for the households dug when the grazing and the harvest let them and not otherwise; but the lad always said that the ring was made that winter, in the snow, and that the rest was only earth.

## IX. Of Those Who Were Brought Down

It was in the first days after the frost broke that a small company came down out of Na Glinn Àrda to the north, where no one on the hill had thought to look for anyone belonging to the king, for he had never spoken of a household of his own, and the hill had half decided, in the way a hill will decide things without anyone saying them aloud, that he had none. It learned afterward that he had gone north himself in the first autumn, on one of the ridings it had taken for the bringing-in of further valleys, and stayed a month in Na Glinn Àrda with his own, and come back alone to the digging.

There was a woman among them, somewhere in her middle years, with the bearing of someone used to being minded rather than minding, and a girl of some seven or eight years walking close beside her with a child's face set hard the way a child's face sets when it has learned to be careful; and there were others with them, kin and a few hands to carry what little they brought, for they had come a long way and light. The lad, who was at the gap in the new ditch that day mending a hurdle, watched them come up the same track the twelve had come up the summer before, though slower, and with none of the twelve's stillness; the woman looked about her at the new-cut ditch and the raw turf as a person looks at a place they have been told of and find smaller, or larger, or simply other than the telling.

Word went round the hill before the company had reached the gate that this was the king's own wife and his daughter, brought down at last from wherever he had left them before ever he walked south with eleven others and a name the grove had given him; and by evening it was known, the way such things become known on a hill where everyone's business is everyone's, that the woman was called Muireall, and the girl Gormshuil, and that there was a child not yet born who would be born on the hill itself before the year turned again, the first child of the king's blood, it was already being said, to draw breath inside the new ring.

The lad did not speak to any of them that day, nor for some while after, for a knapper's son and a king's wife had little enough cause to cross paths on a hill of forty houses. But he remembered, all his life, the particular quiet that fell over the crown of the hill as the small company passed through the gap left for a gate and the households stood back to let them by, the same quiet, though no one on the hill ever said so aloud, that had fallen on the slope the summer before when sixty spears had come down together without a hand raising one of them; as though the hill had learned, in less than a year, to know a thing worth being quiet for when it saw one coming up the road.

The child came before the summer was out, a son, born inside the new ring as it had been said he would be, and the hill took it for a settled thing after that, the way a household takes a roof for settled once the last thatch is laid: that the king had come to stay among them, and had brought what a man brings when he means to stay, a wife, a daughter, and now a son born on the ground he had taken. The lad's father cut a spearhead that week finer than any he had cut that year, for no order and no payment, and gave it to a neighbour to carry up to the king's fire, and would not say afterward why, only that it had seemed to him a thing that wanted doing. Whether it ever reached the king's hand, or what he made of it if it did, the lad never learned; but he kept, until he was an old man teaching the strike to his own grandsons, the plain conviction that some things are given because the giving is owed, and not because anyone is waiting to be thanked for them.

# Chapter Three: Of Gormshuil at the Gate

*GE 2 – 106*

## I. Of the Watching Child

She was eight when the ditch was pegged round the crown of the hill, old enough to be given a task and trusted to see it through, which on Dùn ìseal in those years meant standing at the gate in the gap of the new ditch and counting who came and went, so that her father, who had never asked for a gatekeeper and had never needed one before the ditch was dug, would have someone to tell him at evening whether the day had brought anything worth his hearing.

Gormshuil took to the work the way some children take to a thing before anyone has decided whether it suits them: without being asked twice, and without complaint, and with a memory for faces that her mother said was not natural in a girl her age and was, all the same, glad of. She knew every household on the hill by the second summer, knew which dog belonged to which byre, knew the traders who came up from the valley with hides and the ones who came with nothing to trade and everything to ask. She stood at the gate in all weathers, wrapped in a plaid too big for her that had been her mother's, and watched the ditch deepen under the diggers' mattocks summer by summer, and the raw earth of the bank rise and harden until, in her fifteenth year, it closed at its gate and no longer looked like a wound in the hill.

Her father she saw less than the diggers saw the ditch. He rode out most mornings with a handful of men and came back most evenings, and some months he did not come back at all, and word of him arrived instead by whoever had last seen him, three valleys off or five, settling a quarrel or riding through country that had not yet troubled itself to send word of quarrels to anyone. When he was on the hill he sat at the crown of it in the low turf-roofed house that had been built for him and was already too small, and heard whoever came to be heard, and Gormshuil, who by nine had worked out that the gate and the hearing-house stood in a line she could watch both from, took to sitting on the bank between the two of them with her knees drawn up, watching her father the way she watched everyone else who came and went, as though he too were someone she had not yet finished learning.

It was in her twenty-fourth year that word came up from the west, carried by a trader with salt fish who had it from a trader with wool who had it from further off still, that a woman called Beathag Ruadh held a hill on the shore of the great lake, a red hill, he said, though no one on Dùn ìseal had seen it, and that she held it of her own right and not of any king's. Gormshuil, sitting on the bank with the fish-trader's words going round the hearing-house like smoke finding a draught, asked her father that evening whether the red hill's woman meant trouble for them. Her father said that a hill a long way off with its own line of holders was no trouble to anyone, and that trouble, when it came, came from nearer at hand and was easier to see coming than a woman on a lake shore three weeks' walk west. She did not understand then what he meant by it. She understood later, when she had learned that her father rarely answered a question with less in it than the question itself had carried.

## II. Of Her Mother's Dying

Muireall had never taken to the hill the way her daughter had. She had come to it already a grown woman, with a way of holding herself that the hill's own women, used to going where the work was and standing where it put them, found hard to place. It read as pride to those who did not know her. The truer word for it was the bearing of someone who had once expected her days to be minded by others and had found herself, past the middle of her life, minding her own, and her husband's besides, in a country she had not chosen. She kept the king's house as well as it could be kept with what the hill afforded, bore him two sons on the crown of it after Gormshuil, Dòmhnall in the second year of the bank and Fearchar some years after, and grew, through all of it, thinner and greyer at a pace that her daughter, watching everyone from the gate as she watched everyone, was the first on the hill to notice and the last to say aloud.

Muireall died in the twenty-fourth year of the hill, in an autumn that brought nothing else worth remembering, of no sickness anyone could name and no hurt anyone had seen taken. Gormshuil, thirty that year and past the age where a mother's dying is a child's grief only, sat with her the last two nights and heard nothing from her that the hill later thought fit to keep as a saying, only the ordinary things a dying woman says to a daughter who has sat up with her: where a particular comb had come from, whom a particular debt was owed to, that the youngest boy, Fearchar, was to be watched, for he had a temper his brother lacked and would want checking before it found him trouble he could not talk his way out of.

The king came in from the valleys two days after she was put in the ground, and stood by the mound a long while without anyone daring to go near him, and then went into the hearing-house and heard three cases that had been waiting on him and gave judgement on all three before dark, and never, in all the years his daughter afterward kept the gate and watched him come and go, spoke Muireall's name again where anyone could hear it. Gormshuil, who had expected grief from him and got instead the ordinary business of the hill taken up exactly where it had been left, understood only much later, when she had watched him bury more of his own than any one person should have to bury and go on burying them in the same fashion, what the going-back-to-work truly was: the whole shape grief took in a man who could not be seen to carry it the way other men carried theirs. Other men, in time, stopped carrying it. He never would.

## III. Of the Hard Winter and the Warm Ground

Two winters later came the hardest anyone then living on the hill had seen, snow lying from before Samhain until past the turn of the year, deep enough in the high folds of the valley to bury a standing sheep to the back, and the byres on the crown of the hill, never built for more than an ordinary cold, began by midwinter to empty of their own accord: not to wolves, for the wolves that year kept as much to shelter as the cattle did, but to the cold itself, working on beasts that had nowhere warm enough to stand and nothing left under the snow worth pawing for.

The king was in the north that winter, three valleys off and more, holding some quarrel down that had waited three seasons for him and would not wait a fourth, and no word could be got to him and back again before the herds were finished. It was Gormshuil, thirty-three that year and holding the hill for her father as she had by then held it more times than either of them troubled to count, who gave the order to drive what stock still stood down off the crown of the hill and along the frozen valley floor to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, where the earth steams the year round and the snow, however hard it falls, does not lie.

It was two days' driving, though the springs lie no more than a morning's walk below the hill in summer, through drifts that in places stood higher than the beasts themselves, with men and dogs both worked past what either would ordinarily be asked, and one night spent in the open on ground too cold for anyone to sleep sound, and Gormshuil walked the whole of it on her own feet at the head of the drive rather than ride, for a rider's beast, she said, ate what a walking man's did not, and every mouthful of fodder they carried was owed to the herd and not to anyone's comfort. They came down onto the warm ground on the second morning with the steam rising off the wet grass into air still hard with frost, and the cattle, smelling it before the drovers had done more than see it, went down the last slope at a run that no amount of driving had got out of them in two days of snow.

She lost none. It was said afterward, and is said still wherever the hill's own reciters keep the tale, that no herd of Dùn ìseal's had ever gone into a hard winter and come out the other side of it whole, and that no herd did again for a long while after; and it is said too, by those who keep the harder telling alongside the easier one, that Gormshuil came off that drive with two fingers on her left hand that never afterward bent all the way, and never spoke of them, and wore, from that winter to the end of her life, a glove on that hand in company and bare skin only among her own household, where no one thought to remark on it because everyone had always known.

## IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

Her father married again in her thirty-sixth year, a woman of the valleys called Sorcha, younger than Gormshuil herself by a dozen years and more, which the hill noted and did not remark on aloud, for it had by then grown used to noting things about the king's household that it did not remark on aloud. Sorcha kept the house with less of Muireall's stiffness and more of the valley's easy give-and-take, and bore him two sons in turn, Somhairle first and Iain Dubh some years after, and Gormshuil, who might by rights have resented a stepmother younger than herself keeping the house she had half kept herself since her own mother died, found instead that she liked the woman, and that the liking cost her nothing, for by then she had other things pressing on her that a stepmother's presence did nothing to change one way or the other.

What pressed on her was the gate, and had pressed on her since she was eight, and did not let up now that she was a woman grown with a household and children of her own coming on. Her father rode out each spring with the thaw and came back each autumn with the first hard frost, as regular in it as the seasons themselves, and every year that passed, it seemed to Gormshuil watching from the bank where she had once sat as a child, he came back looking less like a man who had spent a winter riding through weather that aged other men, and more, if anything, like the same young man who had walked south so many summers before with a name the grove had given him and nothing else anyone could point to.

She did not speak of it to him, not in those years, for there was no way to raise the matter that did not sound like an accusation of something neither of them had chosen, and she was not, whatever else she was, a woman who raised what could not be answered. She spoke of it once to Coinneach, her father's brother, who had followed him north those first seven nights with food he would not eat and had stayed by him ever after, growing old in the ordinary way while his brother did not, teaching whoever would learn it Sloinneadh a' Chlachair as Coimhdeach na Fine had given it to Ailean in the grove, word for word, changing nothing, for he held, and taught Gormshuil to hold after him, that a true thing needed no improving.

"He does not age," she said to Coinneach, on the bank one autumn evening with her father not yet three days back from the valleys and the light going long and gold across the crown of the hill. "I have watched him thirty years since the grove and he does not age, and I am beginning to."

Coinneach, who by then had gone the colour of ash himself and moved more slowly than he once had, looked at her a long while before he gave her the nearest thing to an answer he ever would. "I was there the night the fires went out," he said. "What came into the grove, I saw. What it cost him, he has never told me, and I have never asked. Between the two of us, niece, that is a fair division of the matter: he keeps what went into him, and I keep from asking. Take the same division for yourself, if you can bear it."

She bore it, because there was nothing else to be done with it, and because Coinneach himself, who had borne it longer than she had and would not live to see how much longer it went on, seemed to think it bearable. He died the winter she turned sixty-one, an old man by then in every particular, the first teller of her father's deeds and the last of those who had stood outside the grove on the first night and could say what the waiting had been like from the near side of it; and Gormshuil, who took Sloinneadh a' Chlachair from him whole in his last winter, the way he had taken it whole from no one but his own memory of the grove, found that she had, without quite meaning to, become the second person on the hill after her father to carry the whole of it in her head.

## V. Of the Grandchildren Who Took Him for Her Son

By her sixtieth year Gormshuil's own hair had gone from the black it had been to a grey that no longer surprised anyone who looked at her, and her back, which had straightened proudly enough through her middle years, had begun to take on the particular stoop of a woman who has spent forty summers standing at a gate in every weather the hill could send. Her children by then had children of their own running loose about the crown of the hill, a generation that had never known a Dùn ìseal without its bank and ditch and took the shape of the place for as given as the hill itself; and it was among these grandchildren, more than anyone older and wiser ought to have allowed, that the confusion first took root that would trouble Clann na Ceiste's tellers for as long as they kept the tale.

The king came in at the gate each autumn a young man, unchanged from the young man who had ridden out each spring, and his daughter who met him there was by then old enough to be anyone's grandmother; and the children, who saw the two of them together perhaps a dozen days in a year and had no memory of a time before Gormshuil was old, took the young man at the gate for her son and not her father, and called him so among themselves, and were not, when the mistake was pointed out to them by an elder who had known both from the start, greatly inclined to unlearn it, for the mistake fit what they saw with their own eyes a good deal better than the truth did.

Gormshuil herself never corrected them past the first few times. It was, she told her eldest granddaughter once, easier to let a child believe a small wrong thing that harmed no one than to make her carry a large true one before she had the years to hold it; and besides, she said, and this she said only the once, and only to the girl, and never again to anyone, there were mornings now when she looked at the young man coming up the gate-track with the autumn light behind him and found the mistake easier to bear herself than the truth was, for a mother growing old beside a son who stayed young is only the ordinary sorrow of the world running backward, while a daughter doing the same beside her father has no shape that the world has a name for yet.

## VI. Of the Last Autumn

She was eighty-one the autumn she died, an old woman by every measure the hill kept, bent nearly double by then and blind in one eye from a cataract no one on Dùn ìseal had the skill to lift, and she had asked, some months before, to be carried to the gate one last time to see the year's herds brought up off the summer grazing, for she said she had watched every herd come up that track for near seventy years and did not care to break the habit on the strength of dying.

Her father was on the hill that autumn, having come in early, before the frost, as though he had known, though no one afterward could say how a man might know such a thing, or whether he had known it at all, or only chanced to be there. He sat with her the last two nights of her life in the low house where she had lived since her children grew and left it to her, and those who kept watch outside said only that no voice was raised in it, and no weeping either, only the ordinary small sounds of two people sitting together with a great deal between them and very little of it needing to be said aloud after so long.

It was on the second night, near dawn, that she asked him the thing she had carried since the evening on the bank with Coinneach, more than twenty years dead by then, and had never asked her father himself in all that time, for there had never seemed to be a right hour for it and now, she judged, there would be no other hour at all.

"Does it hurt," she said, "to stay young?"

He did not answer her. Those who were near enough to hear said afterward that he sat a long while with her hand in his, the hand with the two fingers that had never bent right since the winter of the warm ground. What he gave her instead, when at last he spoke, was her name, said once, in the way a man says a name he does not expect to have cause to say again. Whether that was answer enough for her, or no answer at all, or something a daughter and a father had settled between themselves long before that night without either needing the words for it, none of those keeping watch outside the house could say, and none of them ever claimed to know.

She died before the light came up fully over the crown of the hill. The king sat by her a night and a day after that, through the whole of the following day and into the second night, and spoke to no one who came to the door, and ate nothing that was brought to him, and when he came out at last it was to see her put into the ground with his own hands helping to lift the turf, which he had done for no one since Muireall and would do, in na Bliadhnachan Fada that followed, for very few others; and he never, from that day to the last day anyone on the hill saw him, spoke his eldest daughter's name aloud again where another ear could catch it, any more than he had spoken her mother's.

It was then, and not before, that the hill understood in full what its own eyes had been telling it for seventy years and its tongue had been too careful, or too frightened, to say plainly: that na Bliadhnachan Fada the king carried were the grove's alone, given once and given whole to the fires that burned in it, and that they did not pass by blood to a child got before the grove was ever lit, however much of the king's own bearing and will such a child might carry in every other particular. Gormshuil had carried his stubbornness, his stillness under a question he did not mean to answer, and something in the set of her shoulders at the gate that anyone who had watched him stand at the door of the hearing-house would have known at a glance for his; she had not carried the fire, and would not, and the hill, watching her go into the ground an old bent woman beside a father who looked her grandson's age, understood at last what it would mean for every child of his get after her, and for every child not yet got, and fell, for a season, unusually quiet on the matter, the way a hill falls quiet over a thing too large to be talked through in an evening.

## VII. Of Dòmhnall Taking the Hill

Dòmhnall was seventy-four that year, the eldest of the king's children born after the grove and the first child of his blood to draw breath inside the new bank, and he had none of his half-sister's stoop nor any grey in him at all, for he carried what she had not: a young man's face on a man three-quarters of a century old, and a young man's back besides, straight as a stripped sapling, so that those who saw him take up the seat in the hearing-house that his sister had held for near five decades saw, or thought they saw, no change at all, only the same shape of authority moving from one body to another in a manner too smooth to properly mark as a passing.

It was not, for all that, taken lightly on the hill. Dòmhnall had grown up under his sister's watch as much as under either parent's, for she had kept the gate through the whole of his childhood and a fair part of his manhood besides, and he stood at her grave-mound the morning after the turf was laid with an expression that those who knew him best said they had never seen on him before and rarely saw again, and said, to no one in particular, that he supposed he had better learn to count who came and went, since no one else on the hill seemed inclined to teach him and there was no one left alive who had learned it from the very start the way she had.

He took up the hearing-house within the month, for the hill's business did not wait on grief any more than it had waited on the king's grief for Muireall fifty years before, and the reciters, setting his name down after his sister's in the eldest of the spoken lists, called him third of Rìghrean na Cloiche and left the gap between his naming and hers, eighty years and more by the tellers' later count, standing in the record exactly as long as it had stood in the life of the hill, for that, the reciters held, was itself a kind of truth-telling, and no one who came after them ever thought to shorten it.

# Chapter Four: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch

*GE 107 – 227*

*At Dùn ìseal the boundary stones still stand in the grass below the bank, and the holders of the valley tell this against their own name, for it is a telling that gives them no credit.*

## I. Of the Setting of the Stones

Dòmhnall Clachach had held the hill a little over thirty years when he first thought of the stones, and he thought of them the way a man thinks of a thing he has put off too long, for the idea was old with him already, and it was the quarrels that brought it back each spring, wearing at last through his patience, that gave it a shape worth acting on. He was a son born after the grove, and though he did not yet look it, he had crossed a hundred years, and something in a hundred years of hearing the same two households swear the same strip of grazing to different fences had taught him that a king's word settled a dispute for exactly as long as it took the disputants to forget who had lost.

He came to it standing over Gormshuil's grave one morning in early summer, which he did more often than he told anyone, for she had held the hill before him and he had loved her as a man loves an elder sister who dies old while he stays young, a grief that has no clean place to sit. Two households of the eastern slope were at their fences again that week, the third time in four years, over a strip of poor grass between two becks that neither side wanted badly enough to fight for and neither would give up for pride. He judged it as his father judged such things, in a sentence, and watched both households go home no gladder than they had come; and it came to him, walking back up to the bank in the last of the light, that his father settled quarrels one at a time because there was always a father to settle the next one, but that a valley needed something that did not depend on a man being there to ask.

He set the stones himself, that summer and into the one after, walking the boundary of every household's grazing with two men to carry and a third to dig, and setting into the ground, at every place the old men of both sides could agree the line had always run, a stone too heavy for one man to shift without help and too plain to be mistaken for anything but what it was. The stones he chose with care, flat-topped things from the outcrop above the flint-pit, and had each one cut with a single mark, not a name, for he did not want the stones to belong to anyone; he wanted them to belong to the ground. It was slow work, for every stone needed both sides' word before it went into the earth, and there were places where the old men could not agree even standing on the very ground, pointing at tussocks that had shifted a hand's width in forty years of frost and thaw and swearing each tussock had been exactly there since before their fathers were born.

By the end of the second summer there was a line of grey stone down the whole of the eastern slope and along the beck to the ford, and Dòmhnall stood at the last of them with turf still fresh at its foot and believed, for perhaps a season, that he had done something that would hold.

## II. Of What the Stones Did Not Settle

What the stones did was move the argument, not end it. Within a year the eastern households had stopped quarrelling over where the grazing lay, for that was written now in stone that did not forget and could not be argued with by an old man's memory; but they had begun instead to quarrel over the stones themselves, whether a stone stood a pace to the wrong side of where it should, whether a beck had moved its bed since the setting and left a stone stranded on the wrong bank of its own line, whether a man's grandfather had truly agreed to a boundary his grandson now swore had been forced on a bad year when the household was too weak to argue.

Dòmhnall judged the first of these himself, in the ninth year of the stones, standing over a marker two households both claimed had been moved in the night, though neither could say by whom, and both swore the beck ran different from where it had run at the setting. He walked the ground a long while before he spoke, and when he did it was to say a thing he had not planned to say: that the stone stood where it had been set, that he remembered setting it himself with his own hands and could point to the exact tussock it had gone down beside, and that the beck, not the stone, had moved.

It was true, and both households knew it was true the moment he said it, for a man with na Bliadhnachan Fada does not forget where he put a stone the way an ordinary man forgets, and there was no arguing memory against a man who did not age between the setting and the asking. But he saw, walking home from that judgement, that he had settled the quarrel by being the sort of witness no one else on the hill could ever be, and that when he was gone north, as his father sometimes was, or gone into the ground, as his father was not, the eastern slope would have only the stones themselves to argue with, and stones, unlike a king, cannot be asked which of two stories is true.

He said as much to no one, then. It sat in him the whole of that year, the plain fact that he had traded one kind of quarrel for another and called it a settling because the second kind was quieter and took longer to come round. He kept the stones. He never told the hill that he doubted them.

## III. Of the Wars of the Valleys

His father was, in those years, seldom on the hill at all. Rìoghachd Chlann nan Dè that had begun as forty houses inside a single bank had by Dòmhnall's thirtieth year on the hill grown to take in valleys three and four days' walk from Dùn ìseal, brought in, for the most part, by the same warmth that had stilled sixty spears on the first slope; yet not every valley came in warm. There were households in the folds of land north and west that had heard what had happened at Dùn ìseal and did not believe it, or believed it and resented it the more for believing, and among those the king rode with few, for he never took a great host anywhere, and what fighting there was, the reciters afterward called Cogaidhean nan Gleann, though it was nothing any teller of true wars would recognise: a burnt byre here, a dozen spears crossed there, three men dead in one valley and none in the next, and everywhere, in the end, the same silence that had fallen on the first hill, sooner or later, in every household the king came to himself.

Dòmhnall did not ride with him in those years, for the hill needed holding and someone of the blood needed to hold it, and it fell to him as it had fallen to Gormshuil before him. He heard Cogaidhean nan Gleann the way the hill heard them, in the words of traders and the sons of households that had come in, garbled a little in the telling, so that the same skirmish might reach Dùn ìseal in three different shapes within a season, each one sworn true by the man who brought it. He learned to listen for what stayed the same under the different tellings, which was always the small thing and never the large: a name, a place, the colour of a wound, and from those he built for himself a truer picture than any single teller gave him, though he never told anyone he did it, being a man who kept his methods to himself the way his father kept his fires.

It was in the eighty-second year of the stones, when Dòmhnall himself had begun to notice that the eastern slope's grandsons called him uncle without knowing quite why, that word came down from the north-west of trouble in a valley whose name he had heard only twice before, where a household under a hard old man called Griogar had turned back two of the king's riders with spears and no words at all. The king went himself with a dozen men, no more, for he never took more than a dozen anywhere he rode himself; and it was there, in a fight Dòmhnall never saw and heard of only after, in the hundred and thirteenth year of his own holding of the hill, that his younger brother Fearchar took a spear through the leg that never healed straight.

## IV. Of Fearchar Lamed

Dòmhnall was not at Griogar's valley, and no telling that reached him afterward agreed on whether the king himself had been within reach of the blow that laid Fearchar down, though most said he had not, that he had been elsewhere in the fight when it happened and came to his son only after, and knelt by him a while on the trampled ground, and said nothing that anyone standing near enough to hear could afterward report. What is certain, and what Dòmhnall heard from Fearchar's own mouth years later, sitting by him at Dùn ìseal with the birch chair already built and Fearchar's leg already a thing he no longer troubled to hide the shape of, was that the wound should by any ordinary reckoning have killed him, for it took him in the thigh and bled a long while before anyone could stop it, and that it did not kill him, and did not heal straight either, so that he walked the whole long remainder of his years, however many they proved to be, on a leg that bent wrong at every step.

"I asked him once," Fearchar told Dòmhnall, the two of them sitting outside the bank in the last of an autumn evening with the fires being lit below them one by one, "why he let it set crooked, when he can do what he did for you and me both, na Bliadhnachan Fada and all the rest of it, and my leg wanted only a little of the same mending to be as good as it ever was."

"What did he say?"

"Nothing. You know how he answers a question he does not mean to answer." Fearchar shifted his weight off the bad leg, the way Dòmhnall would watch him do ten thousand times more before either of them was done with the world. "I have thought since that he cannot mend a thing that is already done, only keep a thing from being undone. Whether that is true I could not swear to you. He never offered, and I never asked him twice."

Dòmhnall said nothing to that either, for he had wondered the same of na Bliadhnachan Fada in himself, whether they were a mending or only a keeping, and found no more of an answer in himself than his brother had found in their father.

## V. Of the Storm

The first named storm came in Dòmhnall's seventy-first year on the hill, in a season that had given no more warning than any other autumn, and it broke on Dùn ìseal in the dark of one night with a wind that took the thatch off six houses and laid a seventh flat to its footings, and did not slacken until the second day was well begun. Dòmhnall spent that night going from house to house within the bank with what men he could gather, holding roofs down with ropes and bodies both, and lost no one, which he counted afterward the one mercy the storm allowed him, though he lost, besides the houses, most of the summer's cut hay and two of the flint-pit's best sheds.

The name the hill gave the storm that night, in the fright of it, was lost within a generation, the way such names are, for a storm remembered by its fear rather than by what it did rarely keeps the word fear gave it; but the memory of the naming outlived the name, so that the oldest tellers of the hill still say, when a bad wind comes up, that it is nearly as bad as the one they named and forgot, without any of them able to say what they had called it.

It was traders coming up from the west that winter, driven off their usual road by flooded fords, who brought word that the storm had done worse on the coast than it had done at Dùn ìseal: that the shell causeway the Seann-Dhaoine had built long before any of the hill-folk's grandfathers were born, out at Seann Warr, was broken through in three places and the marsh behind it standing full of lake water that should have been kept out of it, and that the Seann-Dhaoine themselves, whose causeway it was and whose land it flooded, had not come out to mend it. Dòmhnall asked the trader twice whether he had that right, for it seemed to him a strange thing for any people to let stand broken, a causeway being the kind of work a people mends before the frost sets a second time; and the trader, who had walked the broken ends himself and touched the old stone with his own hand, said only that the Seann-Dhaoine had watched him do it from a little way off and said nothing and done nothing, and that he had not liked to ask them why.

Dòmhnall thought about that longer than the news seemed to deserve. He had grown up on tellings of the Seann-Dhaoine as a people who built well and kept what they built, the shell roads and the stone landings older and truer than anything the hill-folk had yet raised for themselves; and a broken thing of theirs left broken sat oddly with him; but he was sixty miles and more from Seann Warr with a hill of his own needing him, and he let it go, as a man lets go a strange thing that is not his to mend.

## VI. Of the Household That Stood

There was a household on the western slope, some three years after the storm, that Dòmhnall came, in his own mind, to think of afterward as the first true test of the stones, for it was the first quarrel in his time that was not, at bottom, about grass or a fence-line at all. The household was old on that ground, older than the bank, and its elder, a broad grey man named Labhrainn who had never in his life been asked to give an account of himself to anyone, took it into his head that year that a boundary stone set on his own western fence marked less grazing than his household had always held, and refused outright to stand by the line Dòmhnall had walked forty years before.

It was not, Dòmhnall came to understand over the course of that summer, truly about the ground at all, though Labhrainn argued the ground with more heat each time they spoke of it.
