It was that Labhrainn had watched, over the forty years since the stones went in, the hill's judgements settle themselves more and more by the stone and less and less by the elder men of each household standing on the ground and arguing their memory against each other, the way it had always been done before Dòmhnall's father took to writing boundaries in rock; and he had come, slowly and without ever quite saying it to himself, to resent a settling that no longer needed his own word to stand.

Dòmhnall judged against him in the end, for the stone was where the stone had always been and Labhrainn's own father had stood by its setting with his own hand on the digging-bar; but he judged it gently, and afterward, rather than let the matter close the way most of his judgements closed, with both sides going home and neither speaking of it again, he rode out himself to Labhrainn's byre the following spring and sat with the old man a whole evening over nothing more than a jug of the household's own brewing, and asked him about the ground itself and what it had carried in his grandfather's time and what it carried now, and let him talk himself through most of an evening about a thing no one had asked him to account for in years.

It did not mend everything between them. Labhrainn never again spoke warmly of the boundary stones, and told his own sons, dying, that a king who needed rock to remember a man's word was a king who did not trust the man; but he never again brought a quarrel against the line itself, and Dòmhnall understood, turning it over on the ride home, that he had not won the old man over so much as given him back, in an evening's listening, a little of what the stone had quietly taken from him.

## VII. Of Somhairle Who Took No Share

It was in that same stretch of years that word came up to Dòmhnall of his youngest half-brother, Somhairle, son of Sorcha, who had by then seen some hundred and sixty years and looked, by every account that reached the hill, no more than a boy of fifteen summers, slight and quiet and given to standing at the edge of any gathering rather than in the middle of it. Somhairle had asked their father, so the telling went, not for a share of anything, neither land nor herds nor a place among the holders, but only leave to go and live among the households of Na Glinn Àrda, where Clann na Ceiste kept their herds about the crack in the ground that none of them could name the naming of, and to be counted there as nothing more than one more mouth at one more hearth.

Their father had granted it without, so far as anyone heard, a single word of argument, which struck Dòmhnall, when he heard of it, as stranger than the asking itself, for their father argued little about anything but rarely gave leave so quickly to a son who wanted nothing in return for the giving. Dòmhnall rode up himself, the following autumn, to see his brother settled among Na Glinn Àrda, and found him living in a hearth no larger than any other, tending goats with a household that treated him, as far as Dòmhnall could tell in three days among them, as an odd, quiet, useful boy and nothing more, none of them seeming to know, or to care to know, whose son he was.

"You could have had the hill from me one day," Dòmhnall said to him, the evening before he rode back south, the two of them sitting outside the byre with the smoke of the household's fire between them and the crack in the ground somewhere off in the dark, silent as it had been silent as long as either of them had heard tell of it. "Or land of your own, wherever you asked for it. Why this?"

Somhairle was quiet long enough that Dòmhnall thought he would not answer, which was a thing, he was coming to notice, that ran in their father's blood more than any of the rest of it. "Someone has to remember," Somhairle said at last, "who everyone is, and whose son follows whose, once there are enough of us that no one hearth can hold the whole of it in one old man's head. I do not want a share, because a man who holds land judges his own kin a little differently than a man who holds nothing but names. I want only to be believed, when I say who someone's grandfather was."

Dòmhnall thought of the stones then, though he did not say so, and of Labhrainn, and of the plain fact that he himself had traded one kind of memory for another and never been sure, since, that he had traded up. He said only that he hoped his brother would be believed, and rode home the next morning turning the thought over the whole way, that his father's line seemed to be filling itself, generation by scant generation, with sons who wanted no share of anything, as though the getting of land had already, this early, begun to seem to some of them a smaller thing than the keeping of a true account.

## VIII. Of the Chair of Birch and the Riding North

Fearchar's leg never straightened, and by the thirtieth year after Griogar's valley he had stopped pretending it might, and the household carpenters of Dùn ìseal built him, without being asked, a chair of woven birch with long poles fore and aft so that four men could carry him to the gatherings he would no longer walk to, and he took to it without complaint and, Dòmhnall thought, with something almost like relief, for a man who has hidden a limp for thirty years finds a certain ease in being carried openly instead.

It was at one of those gatherings, in the hundred and fifty-first year of Dòmhnall's holding, with Fearchar set down in his chair at the edge of the crowd and the fires of the bank burning behind them, that Dòmhnall went to his father and asked him for more than the hill.

He had thought long about how to put it, and put it plainly in the end, the way his father answered best. He said that the hill was settled now as settled as stone and habit could make it, that its quarrels had grown smaller than the quarrels of a valley twelve days north where the king's word had never yet reached in any lasting way, and that he, Dòmhnall, had held one hill for a hundred and fifty years and wanted, before his own years grew heavier than they yet felt, to hold ground that was not yet settled at all.

His father heard him out without moving, in the way that had stilled sixty spears on a slope more than two hundred years before, and when Dòmhnall had finished he was quiet long enough that Dòmhnall began to wonder whether he had asked wrongly, or asked for a thing that was not his to ask for.

"The north is not held," his father said at last. "Griogar's valley and the ones like it took a spear of your brother's and gave me nothing back but a name I do not trust yet. Go and hold what has been won there, and what has not been won yet, and do it your own way; I will not tell you the stones you should set."

It was, Dòmhnall understood even as he heard it, both more and less than he had asked for: more ground, and no guidance at all in how to keep it, which was, he came slowly to see over the years that followed, the only kind of gift his father ever gave any of them. He left Dùn ìseal that same season, with a company no larger than the twelve his father had once walked south with, and Fearchar, from the chair of birch, watched him go with the flat, unsurprised look of a man who has already begun to understand that he himself will hold this hill a long while yet, on a leg that never healed and a patience that, unlike the leg, would have to.

The hill took Fearchar for its holder without a word of dispute, for he had sat at its judgements at his brother's side since his wounding and the households knew his voice as well as they had known Dòmhnall's; and the boundary stones of the eastern slope, which Dòmhnall had set with his own hands in the thirty-first and thirty-second years of his holding, stood on into a rule that was not his, arguing, in their own plain way, long after he had ridden north, the case he had made for them before he was sure himself that he believed it.

# Chapter Five: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice

*GE 227 – 312*

*On An Cnoc Ruadh they still tell this against no one, for it is the telling that gave them their own list, and a list is a thing worth the trouble of a fire.*

## I. Of the Hill by the Lake

Uilleam Faire was born on An Cnoc Ruadh in the twelfth year of Uisdean Mòr's holding, and grew up believing, as every child on that hill believed, that the water below it had always belonged to his own people and to no one else's. It was an old line, older than any telling the hill-folk of Dùn ìseal kept of themselves, and it did not reckon its years from a grove or a crowning or any king's coming, but from a woman named Beathag Ruadh who had held the hill before any of them were born and had never been anybody's but her own. The tellers of the western lake shore spoke of Dùn ìseal, when they spoke of it at all, the way a man speaks of weather coming up from a quarter he does not much like the look of: something that would arrive whether he watched it or not, and was not yet his trouble.

Uisdean Mòr had held the hill since he was five-and-twenty, a broad, slow-spoken man with a temper that took a long while to rouse and longer to cool, and he was the second name on An Cnoc Ruadh's own list, which the hill kept apart from any other and recited apart from any other. He had grown into the holding the way a man grows into a coat cut a little large for him, filling it out year by year until, by the time Uilleam was old enough to notice such things, no one on the lake shore could any longer picture the hill without him standing on it. It was in the seventeenth year of his holding, when Uilleam was not yet five, that Uisdean set his mind to the ditch.

The neck of the hill was its one weakness, a low saddle of ground where the rise from the lake met the rise from the inland side and a man on foot could walk up either slope without troubling to draw breath. Uisdean had watched that saddle for years the way another man watches a loose tooth, and in the spring of his own son's birth he set every household on the hill to digging it out, a ditch as deep as a tall man and as wide as three men lying end to end, and when the ditch was done he set a palisade of oak along the spoil bank behind it, trunk after trunk driven upright and lashed and packed with clay, until the neck of the hill stood higher and harder than any part of it the lake or the land had made on their own.

Uilleam remembered the finishing of it only as a child remembers a thing too large for him to hold whole: the smell of the sap where the axes had been, the noise the households made when the last trunk went into its socket, his own father lifting him onto a shoulder to see over the heads of the crowd. He did not remember understanding, that day, what the wall was for. He came to understand it slowly, the way a boy comes to understand most of what his elders already know and have stopped explaining: that An Cnoc Ruadh answered to no one, and that a wall was the shape a people gave to that answer when they meant it to hold.

## II. Of Growing to the Watch

The years after the wall went up were quiet ones on the lake, quiet enough that Uilleam, growing through them, came to think of quiet as the hill's natural weather and trouble as the thing that came from elsewhere, the way his grandmother had once told him trouble always did. He learned to fish the reed shallows below the western slope, learned the lake's moods from a boat before he learned them from the shore, and learned, from his father, who had helped dig the ditch and never tired of saying so, the two things a man of An Cnoc Ruadh was born owing: a debt to the water, which fed them, and a debt to the wall, which kept them theirs.

He came to the watch at sixteen, as most of the hill's young men did, standing his turns along the palisade in the grey hour before dawn and the grey hour after dusk, when the light off the lake made every shape along the far shore worth a second look before a man let it go. It was dull work more often than not, and Uilleam, in those first years, sometimes let his mind wander from the wall to the water and back without ever quite deciding which bored him less. He was not a clever man, by his own account, given to him late in life and never once disputed by anyone who had known him; but he was a careful one, and carefulness, on a watch, outlasts cleverness more often than either is given credit for.

It was on the watch, in his twentieth year, that he first heard the full telling of why the wall stood where it stood and swore to no one but itself, and he heard it from Uisdean's own mouth, for the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh still walked the wall himself some nights, unable, it seemed, to trust entirely to younger legs a thing he had dug with his own hands. Word had come up from the east, Uisdean said, standing beside him in the cold with his breath showing white, that the king of the hill-folk, the one the reciters called Ailean Mòr, had brought in valley after valley to the south and east of Dùn ìseal, not always by asking, and that his blood held na Bliadhnachan Fada and did not age as other men's did, and that no one who had sworn to him seemed to find a way afterward of unswearing.

"And are we to swear to him," Uilleam had asked, young enough still to ask a question so plainly, "when he comes?"

"He has not come," said Uisdean, and would say no more of it that night, though Uilleam came, turning the night over as an old man, to think his holder had not answered the question so much as set it aside, the way a man sets aside a debt he means to pay but has not yet decided how.

## III. Of the Two Hundred Spears

The king came in the thirty-ninth year of Uisdean's holding, at the end of a summer, and he came the way a change in weather comes: seen a long way off, and unhurried about arriving.

Word ran up the lake shore three days ahead of him, carried by a trader who had passed his company on the inland road and could not say, when pressed, how many spears he had counted, only that he had stopped counting. He came at last along the shore itself in the low light of an evening, some two hundred men on foot behind him, no more armed, Uilleam thought, watching from the wall with the rest of the watch crowded along it, than any company that size would carry as a matter of course; but two hundred men are two hundred men, and the hill had never in Uilleam's lifetime seen so many strangers standing on its own shingle at once.

They camped below the hill, between the water and the rise, and lit their fires, and did what any company of two hundred does at the end of a day's march: ate, and settled their gear, and set their own watch, which Uilleam noted with a watchman's interest was neither larger nor smaller than seemed reasonable for a company expecting no trouble that night. What they did not do was send up any word to the hill at all. No herald came to the ditch to ask leave, or make demand, or say so much as a name. The king's fires burned below them the whole evening, and the hill's own fires burned above, and between the two the neck of the ditch lay dark and empty and, Uilleam thought, watching it, strangely loud with the things neither side was saying.

Uisdean stood on the wall a long while that evening, further along from where Uilleam kept his own post, and said little to anyone who came near him. Uilleam heard afterward, more than once and always secondhand, that his holder had been asked by one of the elder men whether they should send down and ask the strangers' business, and had answered that a man who wanted to be asked his business generally opened with it himself, and that he would not go chasing after an answer nobody below had troubled to offer.

The night held fair and still until well past midnight, and Uilleam, on the last watch before dawn, was among those who saw the fire start.

He said afterward, and said it the same way every time he was asked, for the rest of his life, that he had been looking straight at the palisade when it took, and had seen no torch, no spark carried on the wind, nothing thrown from below or dropped from above. The wood simply began to burn, along its whole length at once rather than from any one place outward, and the flame it made was low and did not leap the way a fire leaps when it is fed, and it was the wrong colour, a dark shining thing more like the last coal of a hearth banked for the night than like any blaze Uilleam had ever put a name to. He shouted the alarm before he had finished looking at it, and the hill came awake around him in the space it takes a dog to bark twice.

They fought the fire with what they had, lake water carried up in skins and pots and whatever else came to hand, and green hides thrown over the worst of it to smother rather than douse, and by the grey edge of morning the palisade stood black and smoking and mostly whole, for the low strange fire, whatever it had been, had burned slow enough to be beaten, this first time, before it took the timber through. No one came up from the camp below while they fought it, and no one from the hill went down to ask why. When full light came the two hundred spears were still on the shore exactly where they had camped, breaking their fast over their own fires as though nothing along the hill's rim had happened in the night at all.

## IV. Of the Long Waiting

Uisdean rebuilt through what remained of that autumn and on into the winter, and he rebuilt, against the plain word of every carpenter on the hill, with green oak.

Uilleam had asked him once, hauling timber up the inland slope with a dozen others in the wet cold of that season, why a man who had just watched seasoned wood burn to the ground chose to set up wood that was worse for burning in its place, and Uisdean had given him an answer that satisfied him at the time and satisfied him less each time he turned it over afterward: that seasoned oak took years to grow seasoned and he did not have years to spare before the frost, and that green oak, whatever its faults, was oak that stood on his own hill and had not been begged, borrowed, or bought from anyone camped on his shingle. It was not, Uilleam came to think, an answer about timber at all.

Below the hill the king's company neither struck camp nor pressed any nearer. They fished the shallows, and mended their gear, and by the second month of that winter had begun trading, in a small and wary way, with households of the hill who found it easier to sell a little salted fish downhill than to carry the same fish a day's walk round the lake to anyone else who might buy it. Uilleam himself sold two baskets of eels that winter to a spearman who paid him fairly and asked no questions he did not want answered, and came away from the transaction unsure, as he said afterward, whether he had done a small treason or nothing at all.

He saw the king twice that winter, at a distance both times, and remembered afterward that there had been nothing about the man, seen from the wall on a grey afternoon, that marked him out from any of the two hundred around him, save that the others moved out of his way without seeming to notice they had done it, the way water moves round a stone in a stream without the stream troubling to remark on the stone. Once he was mending a boat drawn up on the shingle, working the caulking with his own hands like any boatwright's man. Once he was simply sitting, near the water, doing nothing that Uilleam could make out from that distance at all, for the better part of an afternoon, while his company went about their business around him and left him to it.

"He is waiting us out," Uisdean said, the one time Uilleam heard him speak of it plainly, standing on the half-finished wall with the green timber sweating sap in the cold. "He thinks a wall that burns twice is a wall that will not be rebuilt a third time, and he means to be here to see whether he is right."

"And is he?"

Uisdean did not answer that either. He set the last of the green oak into its socket himself, with his own hands, in the worst of that winter's frosts, and the hill took it, watching him do it, as an answer of a kind.

## V. Of the King's Frost

Spring came late that year and cold, and by the time the flint-pits were opened again for the season the palisade stood finished, dark green wood weeping sap along every joint, and the households of An Cnoc Ruadh had begun, cautiously, to speak of the whole matter as a thing that had passed. The king's company still camped below, for they had never once struck their tents through the winter, but two hundred men who fish and mend and ask nothing come, after enough months, to seem less like a siege and more like a second, smaller, oddly patient village that had grown up on the shingle without anyone's leave.

It was in the early days of an t-Ògmhios, when the year should by every reckoning the hill kept have been well past any frost, that the cold came down out of a clear sky in a single night and put a white rime on the grass along the whole shore, the kind of frost no one living on the lake had ever known to fall so late in the turning year. The hill's own old women called it, from that morning on, Reothadh an Rìgh, and kept the name whether or not anyone could say with certainty it was fair, for it seemed to them a thing too strange to be weather and not strange enough to be anything they had a better word for.

Uilleam was on the wall again that night, as he had been on the night of the first burning, and he said afterward that he knew, the moment the frost's cold reached him through his plaid, that it was not a night like other nights, though he could not have said, if pressed, what told him so beyond the wrongness of the season itself. He kept his eyes on the palisade the whole watch through, the way a man keeps his eyes on a wound he expects to open again, and so he was looking straight at the green oak, for the second time in his life, when it took.

It went the way Teine a' Chlachair had gone and worse, the whole wall alight at once in the same low, dark, shining flame, but the green wood, which should by every carpenter's word have resisted longer than the seasoned timber had, burned instead in what Uilleam swore, to the end of his days, was less time than it takes to say a man's name twice over. He was the first to reach it with water, running the whole length of the wall with a hide-skin held before him, and he threw what he carried into the heart of the worst of it before three other men had so much as reached the ditch; and he said afterward, when asked, and he was asked more times over the rest of his life than he ever tired of answering, that he had done it without thinking at all, the way a man's hand goes to a burn before his mind has finished deciding it is burned.

It did no good. The fire took the new wall as it had taken nothing else that year, and by the time the rest of the households reached the wall with what water and hides they could gather, there was nothing left standing worth throwing water at. Uilleam stood at the ditch's edge afterward with the empty skin still in his hand and watched the last of the low dark flame die down into ordinary embers, ordinary at last, the strangeness gone out of it the moment there was nothing left for it to burn, and he never once, from that night to the end of his life, could say for certain whose doing it had been. He had thrown the water himself, with his own two hands, at a fire he could not name and could not explain and could not, in the end, put out; and he carried that half-answered night with him the rest of his years the way another man might carry an old wound that aches before rain, without ever being wholly sure the ache and the weather were truly bound to one another at all.

## VI. Of Uisdean Going Down

In the morning Uisdean Mòr came down from An Cnoc Ruadh alone.

He gave no order that any man should follow him, and Uilleam, who stood near enough at the gap in the ditch to hear him say it, remembered the words plainly: that this was his own debt and he would carry it down himself, and that the wall, or what was left standing of it, would want every hand that was not his own for the clearing. He went down the inland path rather than the shore path, which struck Uilleam even then as a strange choice for a man walking to a reckoning, until he understood, watching from the wall with the rest of the households crowded along it in the smoking wreck of the morning, that Uisdean had wanted the longer way, the way that gave a man time to decide, step by step, what he meant to say before he arrived at having to say it.

From the wall the distance was too great for Uilleam to hear a word of what passed on the shingle below, and he was honest about that for the rest of his life, never once claiming, as certain other tellers of the tale were happy enough to claim on his behalf, to have caught so much as a syllable of it. What he saw, and swore to, was this: Uisdean coming down onto the stones and stopping twice on the way, as a man stops who is arguing with himself and losing; the king not rising from where he sat on a stone by the water, mending, by Uilleam's guess from the shape of it, some small thing held in his hands; the two of them a long while, neither moving, close enough that their shadows on the shingle nearly touched and did not; and then Uisdean going down on one knee on the wet stones, slowly, the way a heavy man goes down when his own weight has finally decided the matter for him, and putting his two hands out, and the king taking them in his own.

They sat together afterward, the two of them, a good while on the shingle with the wrecked wall smoking above them, and were seen, by those close enough on the shore to see it and not so close as to be sent away, to share out something between them that might have been food and might, from that distance, have been anything at all. Uilleam did not go down. He stood his place on the wall, as he had been told to, and watched his holder eat with the man whose two hundred spears had camped below their hill through a whole winter without once being asked to, and understood, without anyone troubling to explain it to him, that whatever An Cnoc Ruadh had been before that morning, it was going to be a different thing after it.

## VII. Of the Two Lists

Uisdean came back up the hill by evening, tired in the way a man is tired after a thing decided rather than a thing done, and called the households together at what was left of the gap in the wall to tell them, in as few words as he ever used for anything, that An Cnoc Ruadh had sworn to the king, and that the king had taken the oath as freely given and asked nothing further of it that day. He did not say, and Uilleam noticed the absence of it even then, that An Cnoc Ruadh had sworn to Dùn ìseal, or to the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche, or to any name but the king's own; and it was some years before Uilleam came to understand that the distinction, small as it sounded on the evening it was made, was the whole of what his holder had gone down to the shingle to settle.

The palisade was rebuilt a third time, that summer and the next, with seasoned oak at last, for there was no longer any king's company camped below to hurry the choosing of the timber; and it never burned again in Uilleam's lifetime nor, so far as An Cnoc Ruadh's own list has ever had cause to record, in anyone else's. The king's company struck their tents within the month and went east, back the way they had come, and did not return; and the lake shore, which had spent a whole winter watching two hundred strangers fish its shallows and mend its boats, found the quiet afterward stranger, for a season or two, than the company itself had ever been.

An Cnoc Ruadh kept its own list after that, as it always had, and the list said what the hill wanted said and no more: that Uisdean Mòr, second of the list, had built the wall, and lost it twice, and sworn to the king on the third morning of trying. It did not name the fire, or its colour, or the frost that came too late in the year to be trusted, or the man who had thrown the water and never once, in all the tellings he was asked to give, found a way of saying more than he had truly seen. Dùn ìseal's own reciters, when word of the swearing reached them, told the tale fuller, and stranger, and An Cnoc Ruadh never once quarrelled with their telling, which struck Uilleam, hearing both versions set side by side in his own old age, as the strangest part of the whole business: that a hill so careful of its own list should let another hill's tellers keep the truer half of its own story, and never ask for it back.

Uisdean held An Cnoc Ruadh two-and-twenty years after the swearing, until his eighty-seventh year, and died on the hill in his own bed, an old man by any ordinary reckoning, having outlived the fire and the frost and the two hundred spears by a longer stretch than any of them had lasted. Uilleam stood the watch on the wall until he himself was an old man, and told the tale of the burning, when he was asked for it, exactly the same way every time, changing nothing, adding nothing, and ending it always at the same place: that he had thrown the water with his own hands, and did not know, to his dying day, whose fire it was that he had failed to put out.

# Chapter Six: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones

*GE 290 – 388*

*At Seann Chwen the salters still point out the flat stone under the fourth boat-shed and say a hill man once wept over it, though none of them now living saw him do it, and the telling has grown shorter with every hearth it has passed through.*

## I. Of the Road by Gesture

Dùghall was nine years old the summer his father first let him come the whole way down to the shore rather than turning him back at the last ridge with the pack-ponies to mind, and he remembered afterward, better than he remembered most of that year, the smell of the place before he saw it: salt and rot and woodsmoke, and under those a fourth smell he had no word for and never found one, which he came in time to think of simply as the smell of the Seann-Dhaoine, the way a byre has its own smell and a smokehouse its own, and no more to be explained than either.

His father carried hides down that road, cured goat and deer hide from the high pastures where Dùghall's people wintered their herds, and hill cheese pressed hard enough to travel a week without spoiling, and he had carried both for longer than Dùghall had been alive, walking a track that ran three days from the pastures to the coast and three days back, by way of a ford and a wood and a long turn round a bog that swallowed a cart to the axle if a man forgot to keep to the causeway of laid brush. He carried them to trade, and what he traded them for, over a lifetime of the road, was whatever the shore had that the pastures did not: strings of pale shell, salted fish packed in baskets lined with kelp, and hooks and awls of whalebone worked finer than any hill craft could match, though no one on the hill had ever learned how the working was done, only that the Seann-Dhaoine traded them and would trade nothing else half so willingly.

There was no tongue between them. Dùghall's father had walked the road forty years and could no more speak a word of what the Seann-Dhaoine spoke among themselves than Dùghall, watching him that first summer, could speak it himself; and it seemed to Dùghall, young as he was, a strange thing that two peoples could trade across the same stretch of shingle for two generations and never once trouble to learn each other's words for the things they were trading, until he grew older and understood that his father had tried, once, as a young man, and had been met with a courtesy so complete and so unyielding that he had never tried again. The Seann-Dhaoine would take a hide from his hand and turn it over and weigh it with their eyes, and hold up so many fingers for so many strings of shell, and if the count did not please him he could shake his head and hold up fewer fingers of his own until it did; but if he pointed to his own mouth and then to theirs, meaning what word do you call this, they only looked at him, not unkindly, the way a man looks at a child asking something he has decided not to answer, and went on with the weighing.

"They are not unwilling," his father told him, the first night they camped within sound of the sea, with the ponies hobbled and the fire built low against a wind that smelled of nothing Dùghall knew. "I used to think they were unwilling. They are not. They simply do not mean to be understood, and there is a difference between a door shut against you and a door that was never built to open at all."

Dùghall asked him, because he was nine, and had not yet learned the questions a boy holds back from a man three days from home with the whole evening free for talk, whether the Seann-Dhaoine had a king of their own, the way the hill had one, and whether that king was old the way his own king was said to be old and yet not old at all. His father was quiet long enough that Dùghall thought he would not answer, and then said only that no hill man had ever seen anything among the Seann-Dhaoine that looked like a king, or like a hearing-house, or like a bank round a hill; that they lived in stone houses set low against the wind, with roofs of turf grown so thick and so old that from a distance the houses looked like the ground itself had swelled; and that whatever held them together, if anything held them together at all beyond the shore and the boats and the middens at the backs of their houses, no hill man who had traded with them for two lifetimes had ever come close enough to it to say.

They traded that first summer as they had traded every summer before it, Dùghall standing a little behind his father with the ponies' lead-ropes in his fist and his eyes going everywhere at once: at the low houses with their smoke rising thin and grey from holes in the turf rather than any chimney; at the boats drawn up on the shingle, sewn from planks in a manner no hill boat used, without a single dug timber in them that he could see; at the Seann-Dhaoine themselves, who were neither taller nor shorter than hill folk, and dressed in skins sewn close against the wet, and moved about their work with an unhurried economy that made his father's brisk hill way of doing things look, by comparison, almost wasteful. Nothing about that first summer told him anything was different from the fifty summers that had come before it, or the fifty that his father told him, without much interest, would likely come after.

## II. Of the Marks at the Midden's Edge

It was some years later, in the eighteenth summer of Dùghall's own carrying, that he first noticed the stones.

He was seven-and-twenty that year, walking the road on his own for the first time with a string of ponies that was his in all but the naming of it, his father having grown too heavy in the knees for three days of bog-causeway and having handed the road to his son the way a man hands on a thing he is glad to be rid of and sorry to be rid of in the same breath. Dùghall knew the shore by then as well as he knew the high pastures, knew which household traded fairly and which wanted watching, knew the particular stretch of shingle where the whalebone was always best worked and the particular household, three houses back from the water, whose midden ran along the whole eastern side of their turf-roofed house in a long grey ridge of shell and ash and broken bone, taller each year than it had been the year before, the way a midden grows behind any household that has lived long in one place.

What he had not noticed before, or had noticed without troubling to ask himself why it should be noticed at all, was that flat stones stood set on their edges at intervals along that ridge, driven into the ground like small grey teeth, and that each one, when the light fell right across it, showed a mark cut into its face: a single stroke, deep enough to hold shadow, and nothing else. Some stones showed one stroke. A few, further along the ridge, showed two, cut close together as though by the same hand at the same sitting. None showed more than two.

He asked his father about it that autumn, back on the hill with the season's trading told over and counted, and his father said he had seen the stones himself, years back, and had asked a Seann-Dhaoine once, by pointing and by the beginnings of a question he could not finish in gesture, what they were for, and had got nothing for his asking but the same courteous, unyielding look that met every question of that kind. "I stopped asking," his father said. "A man who trades on a shore for forty years learns which of his questions the shore means to answer and which it does not, and he does himself no good going on asking the second kind."

Dùghall went on asking, though only of himself, and the stones stayed in the back of his thought the way a half-heard word stays in the back of a man's thought until he happens on the rest of it. He began, without much deciding to, to count them on each visit, and to notice that the count grew, slowly, by no more than a stone or two in a summer, but steadily, the ridge lengthening a little further each year along the side of the low turf house, and the household living beside it going on with its fishing and its weaving and its unhurried work as though the growing ridge of stones were no more worth remarking on than the growing midden it stood beside.

It was in his six-and-thirtieth summer that he stood longer than he meant to before the ridge of stones and worked out, counting on his fingers the way a boy counts, that there were now eleven of them where nine summers before there had been six, and that no one in the household beside the midden had ever, in all his visits, set a new stone while he was there to see it done. He asked himself, standing on that shingle with his ponies shifting behind him and the tide starting to turn, what manner of thing was counted five at a time in some years and not at all in others, cut once and left, never added to, never changed once cut.

He had no answer that summer, or the next, and he told himself, the way his father had told himself before him, that it was a question the shore did not mean to answer, and went on with his trading.

## III. Of the Stroke Cut After a Burial

The answer, when it came, came to him unasked, in the way such things most often do.

He was seven-and-sixty that summer, an old man by any hill reckoning, with sons of his own long grown and one of them now carrying the greater share of the packs at his shoulder, and grey enough all through, not only at the temple, that the household by the midden, who had never once in his lifetime of visiting given any sign of marking one hill trader from another, seemed to him, for the first time, to greet him as something other than a stranger, and did it wordlessly, there being still no words between them, in a kind of settled ease, an old woman of the house handing him dried fish before he had finished unpacking, as though the handing were no longer a trade freshly struck but a thing already agreed between them long before, renewed rather than made.

It was on the third morning of that visit, with the mist not yet burned off the water and the household's boats still drawn up rather than launched, that Dùghall woke in the lean-to he was given to sleep in and heard, through the turf wall, a sound he had not heard on that shore before: low voices, several together, rising and falling in a way no ordinary talk of a household's morning work ever took, something with a shape to it, a beginning and a middle he could feel coming though he understood not one word of it, the way a man who cannot read music can still feel a tune reaching for its close.

He did not go out while it lasted, for something in the sound itself told him not to, the same instinct that would have kept him from walking into a hill household's grief before he was asked. It went on the better part of the morning, and when it ended he heard, instead, a single low note, held a long while and let go, and then nothing, and then the ordinary sounds of a household returning to itself: a pot set on a fire, a child's voice, the drag of a boat's keel over shingle as the men of the house at last put out to fish, later than they had ever put out on any morning of Dùghall's eight-and-fifty summers of visiting.

He went out then, and found the old woman who had handed him the fish, sitting alone at the door of the house with her hands still in her lap, and he did not ask her anything, for he had long since learned there was nothing to ask that she would answer; but he looked, without meaning to make a study of it, toward the ridge of stones along the midden's edge, and saw that the newest of them, the twelfth, cut some years before and standing bare since, now carried, beneath its single old stroke, a second stroke, fresh enough that pale stone still showed raw in the groove of it, not yet weathered to the grey of the stroke above.

He stood a long while looking at that stone, the fresh cut and the old one side by side on the same grey face, and it came to him, all at once and entire, the way a thing comes to a man only after his mind has been carrying the pieces of it separately for twenty years without knowing they belonged together: the low voices in the turf house that morning, the single held note let go at the end of it, the boats kept ashore past their hour, and now the fresh stroke cut beneath the old. His own mother's grave-mound came to him then, on the hill, and the stone his father had set at its head with her name scratched into it by a hand that had never learned to cut letters cleanly; and he understood, standing on that shingle with the mist still not fully burned away, that he was looking at the same thing in another people's hand: a household marking, one stroke at a time, the going of its own dead.

A word the hill had begun to use of the king came to him too, though he said nothing of it that day to anyone: something quietly said among those old enough to have watched three holders of Dùn ìseal come and go while the man who crowned each of them stayed exactly as he had always been, that the king did not count his dead the way other men counted theirs, for he had never yet been given cause to stop counting and start remembering instead. Dùghall was no teller and made nothing of the thought beyond turning it once in his own mind and setting it down again, but it stayed with him longer than most of what he carried home from that shore.

He counted the whole ridge again that morning, slower than he had ever counted it before, and found that every household along that stretch of shore kept its own stones the same way, one ridge to a house, and that some stones bore a single stroke only and some bore two or three, cut close together as brothers might be cut close together, and a very few, at the old ends of the oldest ridges, bore strokes enough that he lost the count and had to begin again. He did not ask the old woman anything that day, or any day after, for he understood now, as clearly as his father had ever understood it without being told, that this was one of the things the shore did not mean to answer by gesture, because it had never been a question that gesture could hold; but he carried the understanding home with him at the season's end the way another man might carry a wound, quietly, and told it, since there was no one living he could tell it to who would understand it better, at his father's grave-mound on the hill, his father being many years in the ground.

His father had told him once, long before, that the shore did not answer that kind of question. Standing at the grave, Dùghall thought his father had been right, and that the shore had answered it all the same, and that the answer was of a kind a man is sorrier to have than to go without.

## IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

Dùghall walked that road another four summers after the morning of the fresh stroke, through years in which the hill itself grew busier behind him than it had ever been in his father's time, a king's blood settling deeper into valleys that had known no king at all when Dùghall was a boy, though little enough of that reached him on a road that ran, each summer, the same three days to the same stretch of shingle and the same three days home. He carried the stones with him after that morning the way a man carries a thing he has decided not to speak of past the one telling it needs; he did not mention them again to his sons as they grew old enough to walk the road at his shoulder, for a thing seen once with such plainness needs no repeating, whatever wish a man might have to spare his sons the seeing of it, and he judged that each of them, in his own year, would see the ridges for himself, the way he had, and he judged rightly.

He was one-and-seventy, and had not carried the whole road himself in some summers, when he took his eldest son's boy down to the shore for what both of them understood, without either saying so, was likely to be the old man's last visit to it. The boy was near enough grown to carry his own share of the packs and had been down the road twice before at his father's side, but never yet with his grandfather, and Dùghall had asked for the going the way a man asks for a thing he means to have, plainly, and had been given it without argument by a household that had learned long since not to argue with him over which of his own wants were worth the arguing.

They came down to the shore on a grey morning with rain not far behind them, and Dùghall, walking the last stretch more slowly than he remembered ever walking it, past the ford and the wood and the long turn round the bog, found the shore quieter than he had ever found it in two-and-sixty years of coming to it. Two of the turf houses nearest the water stood roofless, their thatch long fallen in and not renewed, the walls softening back into the shape of the ground the way an old grave-mound softens; and where he counted, from long habit, the smoke rising from the houses further back, he found himself counting on fewer fingers than the count had ever taken before, four threads of smoke where a man his age remembered counting nine, and no boats drawn up before two houses that he remembered, in his father's day, as always having a boat.

He led his grandson along the shore to the ridge of stones by the household that had first shown him the fresh stroke, all those years before, and found the old woman gone, as he had known she must be gone, and a younger woman in her place who did not know him, or gave no sign of knowing him, though she took the hides from his hands with the same unhurried courtesy her mother, or her mother's mother, had shown his father before either of them was born. The ridge of stones had grown longer still, stone on stone further than Dùghall's eye could easily follow in one look, and near its older end, where the earliest stones stood weathered grey and soft-edged with age, he found gaps in the ground where stones must once have stood and stood no longer, fallen or taken or simply sunk, he could not tell which, into turf that had grown up round the place they had been.

"Count them," he told his grandson, not because the boy could make anything more of the count than Dùghall himself had ever made of it, but because he wanted the boy to have done it once, with his own hand and his own eye, before the old man who had first taught him to look at that ridge was no longer there to tell him to. The boy counted, moving along the stones with his lips working the numbers, and lost the count twice and began again, and came back to his grandfather at last to say that he could not be sure, past a certain point, whether he was counting stones the household still kept or stones that had simply fallen and lay half-buried among the ones still standing, and that either way the number was larger than any number he had learned to hold easily in his head at once.

Dùghall said only that he had found the same trouble himself, the first time and every time since, and that it was, he had come to think, no bad thing for a man to meet a count he could not finish, if the count itself was an honest one. He did not tell the boy, that day or after, all that he had come in two-and-sixty years to guess and never to know for certain: that the smoke he had counted thinner every visit these last ten summers, and the boats missing from before houses that had always kept a boat, and the roofless walls softening back into the ground where households he had traded with all his life no longer answered a knock, seemed to him, taken together with the lengthening ridges of stone, less like a shore that was simply quiet that year than like a shore that was, house by house and summer by summer, running out of itself; for it was not a thing he could prove by any count he knew how to keep, only a weight that had settled on him, walking that grey morning past the fallen roofs, that he had no gesture to put down and no one on that shore who would have understood the putting down if he had found one.

He traded what he had brought, that last visit, for less than he had once traded the same weight of hides for, though whether the shore itself had grown poorer or only that household had, he could not have said; and he walked home the three days with his grandson at his shoulder saying little, the boy carrying, without knowing he carried it, the whole of what his grandfather had carried down that road for two-and-sixty years and never once found a way to set down whole for anyone but himself. Dùghall died on the hill the following winter, an old man by any hill man's reckoning and older than most who walked that road before or after him, and it was his grandson, and not his son, who took up the packs the next summer and walked south alone to the shore, counting the stones at the midden's edge before he traded a single hide, the way the old man had taught him, on a morning grey enough, and quiet enough, that the boy stood a long while at the ridge before he could bring himself to begin.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone

*GE 389 – 590*

*Of the wall and the stone Somhairle set down only this, and Clann na Ceiste have kept his telling exactly as he gave it, word for word, adding nothing after it and taking nothing away.*

## I. Of the Road East

Somhairle was three hundred and fifty-one years old and looked a boy of seventeen when his father told him to come down from Na Glinn Àrda and walk the coast road with him.

He had been near two hundred years among Clann na Ceiste by then, long enough that the reciters no longer marked him out as the king's son so much as the one among them who forgot nothing, and set exact by exact into a boy's memory Sloinneadh a' Chlachair from the seven nights forward, the pots left cold under the oaks, the six households that came in first, the storm that broke the shell causeway at Seann Warr and was never mended. He had heard the causeway named a hundred times before he ever saw it, and had not thought, hearing it, that he would.

His father sent no reason with the summons, only a word carried up by a rider that the king rode east in three days and would have his son with him, and Somhairle came down off the slab where he had been sitting with old Aonghas going over the drowned years of the third generation, and walked south to the hill without asking why, for asking why was not a thing the king's messages generally rewarded.

They rode with a small company, no more than a dozen, along the road that ran below Dùn ìseal and out past the last of the valley households to the shore, a road Somhairle had walked in the telling many times and now walked with his own feet, noting as he went the things the telling left out: the smell of the bog before the bog was seen, a heron standing so still in a flooded ditch that two of the company took it at first for a grey stone, his father saying almost nothing the whole first day and then, on the second, telling a story about a horse he had once owned that would not cross running water after dark, which had nothing in it of kings or grooves or na Bliadhnachan Fada, and made the company laugh, and Somhairle understood, hearing it, that his father told such stories on purpose, the way a man puts a plain loaf on the table before a feast so that no one goes to the feast too hungry.

Seann Warr stood where the coast road ran out into shingle, a scatter of low turf-roofed houses set back from the water with their smoke going up thin and straight in the still morning, boats drawn up in a line along the strand, and beyond the houses, where the midden ground ran along the whole landward side of the settlement, Balla nan Stràc.

It was not tall. Somhairle had built it taller in his own mind from the telling, the way a boy builds most things he has only heard of, and found instead a course of flat stones no higher than a man's chest, running the length of two hundred paces or more along the midden's edge, each stone set on end and driven into older stones below it, so that the wall was not built so much as accumulated, one course laid on the last the way frost lays itself on a window a night at a time. He walked the whole length of it with his father before either of them spoke, and when he came near enough to see the faces of the stones he understood what he was looking at.

Every stone bore strokes. Some bore one, cut deep and old and softened at the edges with weather; some bore a dozen, cut close together in threes and fours the way a hand cuts fast when the hand does not want to stop; and near the wall's older end, where the stones stood furthest back and greyest, the strokes ran together into a texture Somhairle could no more count than he could count the grass of a whole field, thousands upon thousands, laid down one household's dead at a time over years past any hill man's reckoning.

"How long has it stood?" he asked, for it was the sort of question the Line trained a boy to ask.

"Longer than the wall at Dùn ìseal," his father said. "Longer, I think, than the grove." He said it without weight, the way he said most things, but he stood a while by the oldest of the stones with his hand resting flat against it, not moving, and Somhairle, watching him, thought for the first time that his father's stillness before a thing was itself a kind of answer, though he did not yet know what question it answered.

The households of Seann Warr, who were Seann-Dhaoine and had always been Seann-Dhaoine, went on about their morning as the king's company walked their midden's edge: mending nets, gutting fish on flat stones worn smooth with the work of it, a child carrying water up from the strand in a skin bag nearly as big as she was. None of them came near. None of them, so far as Somhairle could see, so much as turned to look, though he did not doubt they had marked every man of the company from the moment the dozen horses came over the last rise. His father had told him once, in Na Glinn Àrda, that the Seann-Dhaoine were not a people who could be asked anything and answered, and Somhairle had taken it then for one more line of the Line, learned and repeated and not much felt. He felt it now, standing at the wall's edge with a whole people's dead cut into stone at his shoulder and not one living soul among them near enough to name a single one.

He set the wall down that night in the words the reciters used, spare and dated and without ornament, the way Coinneach had taught the first of them to set things down: *at Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, some three thousand strokes in all, and the wall grows for many lifetimes.* It was the first thing of his own that Somhairle ever added to the Line, and he kept, all his life afterward, a particular carefulness about it, the way a man keeps a particular carefulness about the first thing he ever built with his own hands, whether or not it stood the straightest.

## II. Of Seann Tarr and the House over the Dead

Nine-and-thirty years went by before Somhairle saw the second of the three shores, and by then he had come into the years where a man of Clann na Ceiste was sent out on his own rather than at his father's stirrup, to keep the lines fresh at the edges of the kingdom where the reciters of Na Glinn Àrda seldom rode.

He went to Seann Tarr in the north-east on a grey errand that had nothing to do with the Seann-Dhaoine at all, a dispute between two hill households over a stretch of grazing that had crept, as such disputes did, further than either household could honestly remember it ever running, and it was only after he had settled the grazing, a half-day's work that left both sides sullen and neither satisfied, which the reciters counted a fair outcome, that he walked down to the shore to see for himself what the tellings said of that coast.

Seann Tarr was a smaller place than Seann Warr, a dozen households at most, set close along a narrow strand under cliffs that kept the worst of the north wind off the boats. Its dead lay under the living rather than apart from them at a midden's edge: a long low house near the shore's centre, older than the houses around it by the settling of its walls, its floor paved with slabs cut and dressed and laid edge to edge, and on each slab, worked into the stone itself rather than merely cut across it, strokes gathered in fives, four upright and a fifth laid across them, the way a boy ties a bundle of rushes.

The house was lived in. A family sat at its hearth when Somhairle came to the door, an old man mending a net, a woman working something at a low bench he could not make out, two children asleep in a corner on a heap of skins, and none of them rose or spoke or gave any sign that a stranger stood in their doorway, though the old man's eyes came up once, held Somhairle's a moment with neither welcome nor refusal in them, and went back to the net.

He did not go in. Standing at the threshold with the smell of peat smoke and fish oil thick in the low room, he understood that he was looking at a household that had built its home upon its own graves and gone on living there generation after generation, the dead underfoot and counted, the living overhead and continuing; no hill custom he had ever been taught by the Line had prepared him for a people who would choose, of their own accord, to keep so close a floor.

He asked no question, for he had learned that much from his father's stillness at Seann Warr. He stood a while at the door and then walked back up to the cliff path, and set the house down that night as he had set down the wall, spare and dated: *at Seann Tarr the counting comes in fives, cut into the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.*

## III. Of the Thickening

It was two-and-forty years further on, in his four hundred and thirty-second year, that Somhairle first heard from the coast road that something on the three shores had changed, and the word came, of all people, from an ordinary carrier of hides, a man he did not know, met by chance at a ford on the road south, who mentioned it the way a man mentions weather, in passing, to fill a silence while the horses drank.

"The stones are thick this year," the carrier said. "Thicker than I've seen them go in a season, and not at one shore only. I heard the same from a man who walks the Seann Tarr road, and another who does the southern coast. Three shores, all at once, and none of them saying why."

Somhairle rode to Seann Warr within the month, and found the wall grown by more courses in that one season than he remembered it growing across the whole of his own boyhood, fresh stone driven in among the old, strokes cut so close upon each other that in places a man could not set a fingertip between one groove and the next. He rode from there to Seann Tarr and found the floor of the house crowded past what its own slabs could easily hold, new stones laid at the room's edges where no stone had lain before, the family who kept it thinner by two than he remembered them, the old man who had mended the net gone from among them and no one at the hearth to say where.

He sent word to his father, less because the Line required it than because he did not know, that year, what else to do with a thing he could not yet set down as a plain dated fact; and the king came down himself, that summer, to Seann Warr, with no great company this time, only Somhairle and three others, and walked the wall's whole length alone while the rest of them waited at its far end.

Somhairle had seen his father stand still before a thing once, at that same wall, eighty years before. He had not seen him stand as he stood that day, a long while, longer than the walk of the wall itself could account for, one hand flat against the newest of the stones the way another man rests a hand on a sick child's brow, and the light off the water going from morning to nearly noon before he turned and came back down the strand to where his son waited.

"Athair," Somhairle said, for he had not called him father in the ordinary way of the hill since he was young enough to be carried on a shoulder, and the word came out of him now unasked, the way a boy's word comes out of a man when a thing has frightened him and he does not yet know it. "What did you see?"

His father looked at him a moment before he answered, and there was nothing in his face that Somhairle could afterward describe as grief, or fear, or any name a reciter might set down and have another reciter understand; only a stillness gone very deep, the warmth that other men felt from him when he took their hand banked low, like a hearth covered for the night rather than let go out.

"A people counting," he said.

He said nothing more of it that day, or, so far as Somhairle ever learned, to anyone else afterward. They rode back to Dùn ìseal at a walking pace, taking two days over a road they had come in one, for the king set an easy pace and did not press it, and Somhairle, riding at his side, understood without being told that his father would not be asked again, and did not ask.

He set the visit down that autumn in the fewest words the Line would bear him use: *the king comes to the wall at Seann Warr and stands a long while before it. Asked what he saw, he answers: a people counting.* He added nothing to explain it, for there was nothing in him that could explain it, and he had begun, by then, to learn from his father's own example that the plainest telling of a thing a man cannot understand is often the only honest one.

## IV. Of the Half-Cut Stone

Somhairle did not go south to the coast at Seann Chwen until his four hundred and seventy-fourth year, some forty years after the wall at Seann Warr thickened, and he went then only because a carrier's tale reached Na Glinn Àrda of a stone left unfinished, a strangeness even among strangenesses, and the reciters of Clann na Ceiste, who by then kept his three earlier tellings among the oldest of the new lines added since Coinneach's death, judged it a thing that wanted a witness rather than a third-hand telling.

Seann Chwen lay two days' ride to the south and west of Dùn ìseal, a larger settlement than either of the other two shores, its houses set close along a strand backed by low dunes, and Somhairle found it, coming down off the dune road in the low light of an evening, quieter than either Seann Warr or Seann Tarr had been at any season he had seen them: fewer boats drawn up than the strand had room for, fewer threads of smoke than the count of houses would account for, doors standing open on rooms he could see were empty from the road.

The midden's stones stood at the shore's southern end, a shorter ridge than the wall at Seann Warr but no less thick with strokes for its shortness, and it was near the ridge's newest end, where the stone should by every pattern Somhairle had learned from the other two shores have carried its freshest cut, that he found Clach nan Dà Stràc, the one the carrier's tale had named.

It stood no different from its neighbours to look at from a distance, flat, grey, driven into the ground at the same angle as the rest. Up close, the difference was plain. Two strokes ran clean and deep across its face, finished the way every other stroke on every other stone he had seen was finished, cut with a steady hand that knew where the groove would end before the tool ever touched the stone. The third stroke began beside them, cut perhaps a third of its length, the chisel's own marks still visible along the cut's floor where a practised hand had worked it, and then stopped, mid-groove, as cleanly as a man's voice stops mid-word when something reaches through a doorway and takes the rest of the sentence out of him.

Somhairle knelt by it a long while in the failing light, running a finger once, and only once, along the unfinished groove, though he had been taught by every teller before him that a hill man laid no hand on the Seann-Dhaoine's stones. He could not afterward say why he did it, only that the stone asked to be touched the way an open wound asks to be looked at, and he had never in four hundred and seventy-four years learned how to refuse a thing that asked so plainly.

No household stood near enough to the ridge that evening to be asked anything, had asking done any good, and Somhairle did not try. He slept that night in the lee of the dunes with his small company, and in the morning, before he rode north again, he walked the ridge once more from end to end and found no stone cut after the half-finished one, not there, and not, when he sent word in the following years to have the wall at Seann Warr and the house at Seann Tarr both checked again, at either of the other two shores.

He set it down as he had set down the rest, in the fewest words the fact would bear: *at Seann Chwen the last stone is left half-cut, two strokes finished and a third begun and forsaken, the chisel marks stopping in the midst of the cut.*

## V. Of the Silence

The last smoke any hill man saw rising from Seann Tarr was seen by the carrier who had first told him of the thickening years before, now grown old on the same road, who came up to Na Glinn Àrda that autumn with a tale of finding the house over the dead standing open, its hearth cold, its net-mending bench bare, and no one, living or otherwise, anywhere along that narrow strand to say where the household had gone.

Somhairle rode down himself the following spring and found the man had told it true. The house stood as the carrier had found it, its roof not yet fallen, its door not yet fallen from its hinges, everything in it left as a household leaves a thing it means to come back to and does not; and along the whole shore, in the dozen houses that had stood there in his own remembering, no smoke rose at all, from any hearth, on a morning cold enough that smoke would have shown a mile off had there been any to show.

There was no need to go that year to Seann Warr or Seann Chwen, for word had already reached him from both that the same quiet had come to each in its own season, in no cause a hill man could point to and name, within the span of a few years of each other, until by his five hundred and thirteenth year, when he set the matter down for what he judged would be the last time, there was no shore on the eastern coast, the north-east, or the south where the Seann-Dhaoine still kept a fire.

He rode the coast road himself that last year, alone, from Seann Warr to Seann Tarr and down again to Seann Chwen, three shores in one long circuit no reciter before him had ever made in a single season, and found at each the same stillness: middens grown over at their edges where no new stone had been cut to keep the ground bare, boats left to rot on their keels or gone entirely, the low turf houses softening back, roof by roof, into the shape of the ground they had been raised from. No one at any of the three could tell him where a household had gone, for the households who might have told him were themselves gone, and the hill-folk who had traded that coast for generations had, by then, mostly given over walking to shores that no longer answered a knock.

He set down the silence in the same spare hand he had used for the wall and the house and the stone, and it was the shortest of his four tellings: *after Clach nan Dà Stràc no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their strokes are cut no more. How they ended, this telling does not know.* Nothing was put before that last sentence that pretended to know more than it did, though he was asked, more than once in the years that followed, by reciters younger than himself who wanted a fuller answer than the Line was willing to give them. He told them what his father had told him without ever quite saying it in words: that some questions the world does not mean to answer, and a teller does himself no honour going on asking the second kind past the point where asking has anything left to find.

## VI. Of Cairistìona

It was in the ordinary run of things, and not by any turning the Line thought worth marking on its own account, that Somhairle came, in his five hundred and forty-second year, to marry.

She was Cairistìona, of a household in Na Glinn Àrda that had kept sheep on the same slopes since before the king ever rode north with the six pots, and Somhairle had known her the plain way a man of the valleys knows his neighbours, across a dozen ordinary years of gatherings and shearings and the small business of households that live near one another, before either of them thought to call the knowing anything more than that. She was not of Clann na Ceiste, and had no wish to be; she kept sheep, and mended, and sang, when the mood took her, in a low clear voice that Somhairle had once heard carry the whole length of a shearing pen without anyone in it troubling to hush for her, and she asked him, the autumn he finally asked her, why a man who could recite four generations of a stranger's dead without missing a name had taken so many years to find the one of his own worth the asking.

He had no good answer for her, then or later, beyond the true one, which was that the years did not press on him the way they pressed on other men, and that he had let himself believe, without ever quite deciding to believe it, that there would always be time enough later for the things that were not the Line.

They were married at the turn of the year, in Na Glinn Àrda, before the fires of both their households and what reciters of Clann na Ceiste could be spared from the slab, and it was, by every account that reached Dùn ìseal afterward, a plain wedding and a glad one, with nothing in it that wanted setting down for its own sake, and Somhairle set nothing of it down himself, for he had learned by then which of the things that happened to a man belonged to the Line and which belonged only to the man.

He did add, that same winter, one line more to the telling of the three shores, the last he ever added to it, for he judged, turning the matter over by his own hearth with Cairistìona asleep beside him, that a fact once told plainly needed no further ornament, whatever a man might privately go on wondering about it for the rest of his years. He wrote only that the coasts that had once answered a hill trader's knock now answered nothing at all, and that this was the whole of what any teller of the Line, king's son or otherwise, had ever truly seen, and set his hand to it, and added, beneath the last line, nothing more.

# Part Two: Salt and the Handful

# Chapter Eight: Of the Old Names

*GE 591 – 671*


*At Seann Skell the boat-menders still say a household came down the river before any of them had a boat to mend, and would not so much as lean a ladder on the old stones to reach their own roof.*

## I. Of the Word Seann

In the five hundred and ninety-first year of the hill, word went down every valley the king's blood had settled that a son had been born to Somhairle in the high pastures, a boy got on Cairistìona and named Beathan, and that Somhairle meant to keep him there among Clann na Ceiste rather than bring him down to the hill at all. It was carried by no messenger sent for the purpose, only by the ordinary traffic of drovers and salt-carriers who passed word along with everything else they carried, and it reached Iain mac Fhearchair's household on the middle reaches of the Abhainn naomh the same week as the shearing, so that the two things sat together afterward in the memory of that year: the wool piled white on the green, and the news that the long-lived line had another child in it who would, if the pattern held, still be a boy to look at when Iain's own grandchildren were old.

Iain's household had been settled on the river a generation, in a bend where the water ran slow enough for cattle to ford it without swimming, and they knew the coast only at second hand, from traders who came up with strings of shell and salted fish and went back down again with wool and hides, speaking of a shore two days further on where a people neither the king's nor any other's had once lived thick along every inlet and left their houses standing when they went. It was in Iain's father's day, or his father's father's, that the hill-folk settling those upper reaches had begun to call the old places by their old names with the plain word for *old* set in front, rather than trouble to make new names of their own or learn what the places had once been called in full: Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen for old places on coasts far off, Seann Skell for the harbour town, whose true name, if the Seann-Dhaoine who built it had ever spoken one aloud to a hill man, had not come down to anyone still living to speak it back. No one had decided this the way a judgement was decided on the hill. It had simply grown, the way a path grows across a field where enough feet have already gone, and by the time Iain was a grown man with a household of his own it was no more a choice to say *Seann Skell* than it was a choice to say *river* for the water running past his door.

"We keep their names and touch nothing else of theirs," Iain told his daughter Marsaili more than once, when she was young enough still to ask him why, "because a name costs nothing to keep and a great deal to make, and because I have never yet heard of any good coming to a man who took up a thing the Seann-Dhaoine left lying." He said this the way he said most things, without much weight behind it, a rule handed down the way a shape for cutting turf is handed down, useful and unexamined; and Marsaili, born the ninth year after Beathan and growing up on the same bend of river her father had grown up on, took the rule in with her milk and thought no more about it than she thought about the water's own habit of running downhill.

She grew up hearing the coast talked of at the fire the way distant, half-believed places are always talked of by people who have never gone there: the harbour with its old mole running out into the tide, long enough, the traders said, to shelter a dozen boats, though no hill boat had ever tied up along it in living memory; the low round houses set back from the water with roofs of turf grown so old and so thick they seemed part of the ground; and, standing apart from the houses nearer the harbour mouth, a tower of dry stone, squat and windowless but for a slit here and there, that no trader who had ever gone down that road claimed to have set foot inside, or wished to. Iain himself had seen it once, as a young man carrying wool down with his own father, and would say only that he had stood a while looking at it and had felt no wish at all to go nearer, a feeling he could put no better word to than the feeling a man gets standing at the edge of another household's grief, uninvited and better off staying that way.

Marsaili's grandmother, who had come up the river herself as a girl from a household further south and had once, as a young woman, gone the whole way down to trade at the harbour before any hill family lived within two days of it, told a different kind of tale of the coast, less awed than practical: that the Seann-Dhaoine's houses, whatever queerness clung to the tower, were built no differently in their bones from a hill house, stone and turf and a hearth in the middle, only rounder and lower and set closer to their neighbours than hill custom liked; that the smell of the place, salt and weed and the char of driftwood fires, was the whole of what she remembered as strange about it; and that she had stood once at the harbour mouth and counted eleven boats out on the water at once, drawn each toward a different reach of the tide with no more order to them than a scatter of gulls, and thought, young as she was, that she had never in her life seen so many hands at one work with no one among them giving orders. Marsaili turned that telling over more than the tower's, though she could not have said, even at the time, why one stayed with her longer than the other; only that it seemed to promise something the fireside talk of towers and silence did not: a shore that had once held ordinary lives as well as mystery, boats out at their ordinary work, a people who had risen in the morning to mend nets rather than to be spoken of forever after in a hushed voice by strangers who had never known them.

## II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

Marsaili was eight-and-twenty, married four years to Tearlach mac Ghilleonain and mother already to two children with a third on the way, when her father called the household together on an evening in the dark half of the year and told them, without any great preamble, that he meant to move it down to the coast before another winter turned.

The river bend had grown crowded in his lifetime, three households now grazing ground that had fed one comfortably in his father's day, and word had come up, as word always came, that the harbour at Seann Skell stood as empty of hill-folk as it had ever stood, a river-mouth with good landing and no one living close enough to use it. "The Seann-Dhaoine are gone from it entirely," he said, "and have been gone longer than any of us has lived, and I would rather my grandchildren grew up on a shore with fish in easy reach than go on quarrelling over this bend with my brother's sons for another forty years." No one argued the sense of it strongly enough to change his mind, though Marsaili's mother wept the first night over the grave of her own mother, which she would be leaving behind unvisited, and Tearlach said little, being a man who followed where his wife's father led and had long since made his peace with it.

They went down in the early spring of the six hundred and twenty-eighth year, eleven souls and what beasts and goods a scatter of ox-carts could carry, following the Abhainn naomh two days further than any of them had gone before, until the river widened between low banks and the air changed, carrying salt under the green smell of the water the way a distant fire carries smoke before it can be seen.
