They came out at last above the pool where the river met the tide and looked down on the harbour their traders had spoken of for three generations without any of them having stood where Marsaili now stood: houses roofless and grown over in green, the old mole running out from the shingle in its long low line of unmortared stone, its landward end still dry but its far foot already under the first of the flood tide, exactly as the traders had always said it would be; and set apart from the rest, nearer the harbour's mouth than any house had been built, the tower, grey and blind-walled, with gulls going in and out of the slits in its side as freely as if no one had ever built it and no one had ever left it.

Their first camp that night was pitched on the higher ground behind the old houses, not among them, though the roofless walls would have made a readier shelter than the carts and hides they slept under; and it was Iain who set the rule before anyone else could set it differently, walking the ground himself in the last of the light and marking with a line of stones where a household might build and where it must not, keeping every new wall a stone's throw and more from the nearest standing Seann-Dhaoine wall, and the whole camp further still from the tower.

"We will use what is already given to any hand that walks the shore," he told them, meaning the mole, the harbour, the fish that had gone uncaught in it for however many years it had stood empty, "and we will raise nothing of our own against what is theirs, and we will not go into that tower, not to shelter from rain, not to store grain, not for any reason a man can think of on a dry night that will not look a great deal smaller to him on a wet one." The hill kept no law in those years, only the king's own judgements given one at a time on his own hill, and no king's word had ever reached this shore at all. What held here was only Iain's rule for his own household, given the weight an old man's rule carries when no one troubles to test it, and it held, that first season, without a single soul asking why more than once.

They built their first houses that summer within sight of the old ones but never touching them, using timber carried down with the carts and turf cut fresh from the higher ground, and mended the landward stretch of the mole with stones gathered from the shore rather than lifted from the mole, a distinction Iain was careful to draw and careful that his sons and his sons-in-law drew after him: a man might lay a new stone beside an old one, he said, but he would not take an old stone up to make it new, for the taking felt to him a different thing entirely from the laying, though he could not have said in words exactly where the difference lay.

## III. Of the Storm and the Cracked Stone

Marsaili's third child, a daughter, was born that autumn in a house not yet a full season old, with the sound of the tide new enough in everyone's ears that her mother swore afterward the child had slept worse for it than either of her brothers had slept for anything in their own first winters; and it was in the deep of that same winter, in the first days of an Fhaoilleach with the year barely turned, that the first great storm out of the west found the harbour and put every soul in it to a test none of them had faced on the river.

It came in the night, as the worst of them do, a wind that rose from nothing in the space of an hour and drove the tide higher up the shingle than the eldest among them, who remembered storms enough from the river years, had ever seen water climb on open coast. Marsaili woke to hear the roof-tree groaning overhead and Tearlach already up and bracing the door with his own shoulder against a wind that seemed to want the whole house and not merely the roof of it, and she gathered her children into the one dry corner and sat with them through the worst of it not knowing, until daylight came grey and reluctant over a sea still heaving, whether the mole her father had set such store by mending would stand the night at all.

It had not stood whole. The seaward third of it, the oldest stretch and the part no hill hand had touched, lay broken where the worst of the sea had found a weakness the tide alone had never shown, great unmortared stones thrown down and scattered along the shingle like a wall a giant had kicked apart in passing, and the harbour that had sheltered nothing more than a handful of coracles through the autumn now lay open at its mouth to whatever the sea chose to send in.

There was argument that morning, the first real argument the household had had since the leaving of the river, for two of Iain's sons-in-law held that the broken stones, lying now scattered and half buried in shingle rather than set in their old order, were no longer truly the Seann-Dhaoine's wall at all but only stone, ready stone, lying where any hand might lift it and set it again to better purpose than the sea had left it; and Iain, old now and walking the wreck of the mole with a stick he had not needed on the river, heard them out and said no.

"They are broken," he told them, "but they are not ours for the breaking, and a thing does not become mine because the sea has done to it what I would not do myself. If the mole is to stand again it will stand on new stone laid by our own hands beside what is left of the old, the way it stood before the storm, and not built up out of what the storm knocked down." Tearlach, who had held his tongue through the whole of the argument as he generally did, said only, when it was over, that he thought the old man right, though he could no more have said why than Iain himself could, only that it seemed to him a shore a man had only lately come to was no place to start testing which of another people's rules could be broken and which could not, when the people themselves were no longer there to say.

They mended the mole that spring with fresh-quarried stone from the higher ground, a harder labour by far than reusing what lay ready to hand on the shingle, and the work went slower for it, so that it was two summers before the harbour stood sheltered end to end again; but no household on that shore, in all the years Marsaili afterward kept count of, ever again argued seriously for lifting a Seann-Dhaoine stone to lay it elsewhere, whatever state the sea or the years had left it in.

The quarrying taught them things the river had never had cause to teach: which of the higher slopes gave stone that split clean along a true face and which gave stone that shattered wherever it pleased, which carts could be trusted down the steep track to the shingle loaded and which would want a second pair of hands at the tail-rope on the last pitch. Marsaili, carrying her own weight in stone down that track through the whole of the second summer with her youngest strapped across her back, came to know the harbour's ground better in those two years of hauling than she ever came to know the river's, and said once, laughing, to Tearlach, that she had left her father's country to escape one kind of labour and found the sea had simply given her another; and Tearlach, who laughed rarely, laughed at that, and answered that at least the sea's labour ended somewhere a man could see it end, in a mended wall standing plain against the tide, whereas the river's quarrels over grazing ground had never in his lifetime ended at all, only paused between one dispute and the next.

## IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

It was in the six hundred and fortieth year, with the mole whole again and three more households come down from the river to join the first, that Tearlach and two of Iain's grandsons built the first boats the harbour had held since whatever craft the Seann-Dhaoine had once kept there, small round-sided hide boats of a kind the hill had always used on lake and river, never before trusted to open tide; and it was Marsaili, not any of the men who had built them, who insisted on being in the first that went out from the mended stone, on a morning calm enough that even Iain, watching from the shingle with the caution of a man who had buried nothing yet to the sea and meant to keep it that way as long as he could manage, allowed that the risk was a small one.

She remembered, all the years she lived after, less of the fishing, ordinary enough once the strangeness of open water under her had worn off in the first hour, than of looking back at the harbour from out past the mole's broken and mended length and seeing, for the first time from that angle, how the shape of the old landing had been made, centuries before any hill hand cut a single new stone for it, by people who had understood the set of the tide and the run of the current well enough that the household's own hurried mending had done little more than follow, stone for stone, a plan already laid down and only needing to be honoured rather than improved upon. She said as much to her father that evening, and Iain, who had spent forty years believing a stone left better than touched, only nodded and said that he had thought something of the kind more than once, standing on the mole at low water, and had never found a way of saying it that did not sound, even to his own ear, more like the Seann-Dhaoine's due than a hill man's.

The boats went out through that whole summer and the years after it, and the harbour that had stood empty across every hill man's lifetime before Iain's began, slowly, to keep the ordinary marks of a shore that was lived on: nets drying, a smokehouse raised for the first catch too large to eat fresh, children set to mind the coracles at low tide the way children on the river had once been set to mind cattle at the ford. It was in the six hundred and sixtieth year, with Iain himself eleven years dead and Marsaili holding the household in his place, that the sea took its first life from among them in earnest, a young man of Tearlach's own house drowned in a squall that came up faster than any boat then on that shore could outrun, and it fell to Marsaili to decide, with no custom of the river to guide her and none of the Seann-Dhaoine left to ask, how a household newly of the sea ought to bury one the sea had taken.

She chose, in the end, neither the river's cairn, which felt to her a landsman's answer to a thing the sea had done, nor any borrowing from what little could be guessed of the Seann-Dhaoine's own way with their dead, of which nothing certain had ever been carried up from that shore but rumour and the strokes on a midden stone two days' walk to the south; she chose instead to bury him on the higher ground behind the houses, within sound of the water but above its reach, with stones set at his head and feet in the plain hill fashion her own mother's grave on the river had worn, and told the household afterward, when one of the younger ones asked why they had not tried the sea itself, that a household new to a shore had no business inventing rites for it before it had lived there long enough to know what the shore would teach, and that the plain way, at least, wronged no one living or dead.

She held the harbour a further eleven years after that burial, long enough to see four more households come down the river to join the first four, long enough to see her own grandchildren born within sound of the tide who had never seen the river bend their grandfather had left, and long enough to have word reach her, once, of the king himself, riding the coast road in the company of no more than three men and stopping a night, not at her hearth, which never had that honour, but at a household two harbours further south that afterward told and retold the little he had said of Seann Skell: that he had heard the hill was settling an empty shore, and thought it a good thing, and would send no one to tell them how to hold it. It was the whole of what reached her, third-hand and thinner with every telling, and she made no more of it than the household two harbours south had made, save to say, when it was repeated to her at her own fire, that it sounded like a man content to let a shore be filled the way it wanted filling, and that she had never once, in forty-three years upon it, felt the want of any other kind of king.

In her last winter she took to sitting on the shingle of an evening with the mended mole running out dark before her into water gone the colour of the sky, and it was there her eldest daughter asked her once whether she missed the river, meaning the question kindly, as one asks an old woman a question already half answered by the asking of it. Marsaili said that she did not, and that she had come in the end to think of the harbour less as a thing the household had taken up empty than as a thing that had been waiting, stone by patient stone, for hands willing to use it without ever quite believing it was wholly theirs to use. She died in the six hundred and seventy-first year, the first of Iain's line to be buried within sight of the sea rather than beside the river her father had led them away from, and her household laid her, by her own wish given plainly enough beforehand that no one thought to argue it, on the same rise above the shingle where the young drowned man lay, within sound of water that had never, in all her years upon it, told her whether the Seann-Dhaoine had built their harbour for a people not their own to use, or for no reason a hill mind could ever hope to reach.

# Chapter Nine: Of Mòrag the Hard

*GE 672 – 719*

*At Dùn ìseal the reciters give her the one deed and no other, and say that one is enough to carry a name the length of the list.*

## I. Of the Hill Without Salt

Mòrag Chruaidh was eighteen years short of four hundred and had held the hill for her father the better part of a generation before she gave the household its first war. Dòmhnall Clachach had ridden north in the hundred and fifty-first year of his own holding to see what could be made of ground his people had only lately come to, and he had been gone, by the time Mòrag's tale properly begins, longer than most of the households below the bank could remember him being present; so that to the children born on the hill in those years the king's blood that sat in judgement there and settled the grazing and heard the quarrels was, from their first memory of it, a tall, dark-browed woman who never once let slip that the hill was not, in the fullest sense, her own.

It was not her own, and she knew it better than anyone said aloud. Dòmhnall held it of the king; she held it of Dòmhnall; and beneath all the holding, further back than any bank or ditch, the hill and the valleys round it were the king's, in the plain sense that he had taken them with his own hand and never once given the taking away. Mòrag judged, and levied, and rode out with a spear at her side when a spear was needed, and slept easier for knowing that whatever she failed to settle could, in the last account, be carried to a man whose years never told on him and whose memory held every name once given him. It was a good arrangement for a woman with the temper her father's line ran to, and she had never yet found the want in it.

The hill Mòrag held was not the hill her father had taken. The bank her father Dòmhnall had set the boundary stones for still ran round it, but three more rings of houses had grown up outside the first bank in the years since, and the valley road that had once ended at the gate now ran on south and west to a dozen daughter settlements that sent their grazing quarrels up to the hill the same as they had always done, only in greater number and with less patience for waiting their turn. Mòrag heard them in the same low stone hall her father had built, sitting the chair he had sat, and gave judgement in the plain, unhedging way the household had come, over three generations, to expect of anyone who sat it: a sentence, seldom more than a sentence, and the hearing closed. She had grown up watching her father do the same and had never once, as a child, imagined she would be doing it herself before he was dead, or even much aged; it was one of the small, unspoken strangenesses of a household of the king's blood that a holder might sit a chair for a hundred years and more and see her own grandchildren grow grey while she herself was only beginning to feel the first weight of the years in her knees of a cold morning.

She found the want the autumn the hill went without salt.

It was not the first such autumn. Salt was a thing the hill bought or bartered for, brought up from the southern shore by traders who kept the terms of the trade to themselves and raised the price a little each year the hill's herds grew and the hill's hunger for it grew with them; and there had been lean seasons before when a bad crossing or a bad harvest on the trading side left the hill's larders going into winter with meat that would not keep and no way to keep it. What was new that autumn was the manner of the going without. Three separate traders, in the space of one summer, had come up the valley road empty-handed and sworn, each in his own way, that the southern shore had stopped selling; that the folk who worked the salt-scrapes at Baile ghorm had grown proud of what they made and meant, this year, to keep the whole of it for themselves and their own kin along the coast, and had said as much, plainly, to any hill trader who came asking.

Mòrag heard the third of these traders out in the hall her father had built, a low stone room hung with the antlers of beasts long since hunted out of the near valleys, and said nothing for a while after he had finished, turning the matter the way she turned most matters that came to her, slowly and from more than one side before she let herself speak on it. "They have salt and no king," she said at last, half to the trader and half to herself. "We have a king and no salt. Between us that is no bargain at all, only two households that have not yet learned which one is the stronger."

She did not send to her father in the north before she decided what to do about it, and told herself afterward, when there was time to tell herself anything, that a season's riding would have brought his answer back too late to matter and that a holder who could not judge for herself in her holder's own absence was no holder at all; both of which were true, and neither of which was the whole of why she went. The whole of why she went she kept to herself, then and after, save that once, very old, she told a great-grandchild that she had wanted, that autumn, to know for certain whether the strength that had taken every valley the hill now held had come down to her at all, or had stopped somewhere short of her father's father and left her nothing but the name.

## II. Of the Shingle at Baile ghorm

She took eleven men south along a coast track the hill's herders used for driving beasts to the winter grazing, and came down on the salt-scrapes at Baile ghorm in the grey hour before a summer dawn, meaning, she told her own men more than once on the road, to take the salt and nothing more: no house burned, no beast lifted that was not already a working ox needed to carry the load away, no blood shed that the salt-folk did not themselves choose to shed defending it. It went otherwise, as such things generally do once the first spear leaves a man's hand rather than his intention.

Mòrag had never seen the sea before that road brought her to it, and she said afterward, to the one or two she ever spoke to plainly of that morning, that the first sight of it in the grey light, flat and enormous and giving off a smell like nothing the hill valleys had ever taught her to expect, had unsettled her more than the fighting that followed. Her men, drawn from households that drove beasts to the winter grazing within sound of that same shore, took the sight as no more than a familiar landmark reached at last, and it was one of them, a broad, unhurried man named Gilleonan who had made the drive a dozen times and never once thought to raid at the end of it, who first pointed out to her, in a whisper pitched not to carry, the low red glow strung along the strand ahead of them where the salt-hearths still burned through the last of the night, banked but not let die, exactly as a household bank a hearth-fire it means to want again before morning.

The salt was made in those years over open hearths set along the shingle above the tide line, shallow stone-lined pits kept burning through the drying months while women fed them driftwood and raked the crusting brine, work that blackened the hands and thickened the skin of the forearms in a way Mòrag noticed, afterward, on every salt-worker she ever after had cause to look closely at. The hearths could not be carried off. What could be carried off was what they had already made, heaped in baskets and skin bags under low turf shelters at the shingle's head, and it was these Mòrag's men went for, working fast in the half-light while she herself stood watch at the shelters' mouth with four spears about her and told herself the thing was nearly done.

It was not nearly done. Mòrag stood at the shelters' mouth in the last dark listening to her own men working the baskets free of the turf with a care that struck her, even at the time, as oddly gentle for men in the act of a raid, as though the habit of handling salt without wasting a grain of it had come over them the moment their hands closed on the baskets, whatever else was in their minds that morning. She had told them, on the road down, to take nothing they did not need to carry the taking off cleanly, and she watched them keep that word with a thoroughness that later struck her as almost comic beside what came after: men stepping carefully over a sleeping dog's blanket so as not to wake it, a basket set down and re-tied when its cord slipped, as though the whole enterprise were no more than an ill-mannered borrowing that decent men would see set right before they left.

A dog gave tongue somewhere up the strand before the last basket was clear of the shelters, and the salt-folk came down onto the shingle in twos and threes and then in a rush, men first and then, close behind them, women who had been raking the hearths since before light and came still holding the long wooden rakes they raked with, which proved, in the event, weapons enough at close quarters against men encumbered with baskets. Mòrag's people got the greater part of the salt away up the strand before the fighting closed round them properly, but the getting away cost seven lives on the hill's side before it was done: three cut down on the shingle itself, one taken by a rake-blow to the skull that no one on either side had thought could kill a man and did, two more overtaken on the track above the strand by salt-folk who knew the ground better than any hill man could in the dark, and the last, a boy not yet twenty summers who had begged Mòrag to let him come because his elder brother was already one of the eleven, drowned trying to swim a inlet he had judged, wrongly, narrower than it was.

Mòrag herself killed no one that morning, a fact she never afterward either claimed as mercy or denied as failure, saying only, when asked directly by one of her own grandchildren many years on, that she had spent the whole of the fighting getting her people and the salt clear of the strand and had had no leisure that morning to keep a tally of who fell to whose hand. What she did do, standing at the shingle's head with the last basket loaded and her own men falling back around her in a ragged line, was turn once, before the light was fully up, and look back down the strand at where her seven lay among stones already dark with more than seawater, and she made, in that turning, the one decision of the whole raid she never afterward doubted: that whatever the hill said of the salt, and whatever the king said when word of it reached him, the seven names would not be let go the way a lost beast or a broken tool is let go.

## III. Of the Bank Behind the Shingle

She kept that decision through four days' ride home with the salt on the hill's own carts and her dead carried the shorter way, by boat along the coast to the nearest point a cart track could meet them, and she kept it through the winter that followed, in which the hill ate salted meat again for the first time in two years and no one below the bank asked her too closely what the salt had cost to bring. At the turn of that winter, on the night the hill kept for its dead in the ordinary way, she stood at the fire her father had built the hall's hearth from and named all seven aloud, one after another, in the order they had fallen so far as anyone could tell it: Donnchadh Bàn first, her own father's oldest belted man, who had gone down under the first rush at the shelters' mouth; then the three of the strand; then the two of the track; then, last and youngest, the boy who had drowned asking to be let come. She named them again the winter after that, and the winter after that, until the naming was a thing the hill did every year at the same fire without anyone having to be told to do it, and the reciters keep it still, said each year now by households who know none of the seven by anything more than the name itself.

Word of what had answered her raid reached the hill more slowly, brought up by the same traders who had once brought salt and now, for a season, brought nothing at all. The salt-folk of Baile ghorm, it was told, had lost the raid's night but had not, in the reckoning that mattered to them, lost the salt itself, for salt is a thing the sea goes on making whether or not any given year's hearths stand. What they had lost, and set about mending within the same season, was the manner of keeping it safe: a fire that burns for a season burns in one place, tended by hands that must sleep sometime, and can be come at in the dark by anyone willing to risk the raking-women's rakes. Within two summers of Mòrag's raid the folk of Baile ghorm had raised a low bank of shingle and turf behind the tide line, and inside it had dug shallow clay-lined basins that needed no fire at all, only sun and wind and the slow work of months, the brine thickening on its own where no torch had to be kept burning to give a raider his mark in the dark. It was the first work of its kind the hill-folk had ever heard of, and it changed, within a lifetime, how salt was made the length of that shore; and though none of the tellers who carried the news up to Dùn ìseal ever said so in as many words, every one of them understood, and Mòrag understood best of all when she heard it, that the bank behind the shingle had been raised as much against her as against the sea.

## IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

Word of the raid reached the king before word of the bank did, carried, as such things were carried in those years, faster than any single messenger could have carried it, by the ordinary passing of the news from hearth to hearth along the roads Mòrag's own carts had used. He came to Dùn ìseal himself the spring after, riding down out of the north with no great company about him, and Mòrag met him at the gate the way she had met few enough kings' visits in her life, having held the hill so long under her father's long absence that she had half forgotten what it was to stand second to anyone on her own ground.

He heard the whole of it from her own mouth, sitting the evening through in the hall her father had built, and asked few questions, and made, when she had finished, no judgement at all in the sense she had braced herself to hear one. "The south is not mine yet," he said, when she pressed him at last for some word of blame or of praise, one or the other, so that she would know which way to carry the matter forward. "You took salt from a people who owe me nothing, and lost seven doing it, and they answered you well enough that you will not take salt from them that way again. I will not tell you that was rightly done, and I will not tell you it was wrongly done, because it was neither mine to forbid nor mine yet to avenge." He was warm where his arm brushed hers crossing the hall's threshold, warm the way a hearthstone is warm long after the fire has been let sink, a thing she noticed and did not remark on, having grown up hearing it remarked on by everyone older than herself until the remarking itself had worn thin.

What he did instead of judging was take her west with him, a week's riding and more along tracks that grew narrower and less certain the further they went from the hill's own valleys, through country Mòrag had never had cause to see, low wooded ridges giving way at last to open water that lay so still under the evening light she took it, the first hour she saw it, for a second sky fallen to earth. The king rode the whole way in no great haste and said little of where they went or why, and Mòrag, who had never before travelled at his side for longer than an evening's hearing, came in those days to understand something of what the household meant when it said, of him, that he was easier company on a road than in a hall: he asked after her father's health in the north, and after the boy who had drowned in the inlet, whose name he had already by heart though no one had told it him twice, and once, on the third evening, sang a verse of something in no tongue she recognised, low and to himself, that she never afterward heard him sing again and never once asked him what it had been.

They came at last to the lake shore where An Cnoc Ruadh stood, an old holding of its own line that had never once sworn to Dùn ìseal and never once needed to, owing the king directly and no one between. Seonag nic Uisdein held it then, of Uisdean Mòr's blood though born, the list already said of her, more than three hundred years after he died, and she met the king at her own gate with a worn leather bag at her belt that Mòrag took at first for nothing more than the ordinary purse a holder might carry to a meeting of consequence.

It was not a purse. Seonag opened it before the king without being asked and weighed it once, twice, in her open palm, her lips moving a little as she did, and said that the bag held one pebble for every household on the hill and along the shore below it, set in when a household was first counted and taken out again, without ceremony, the season a household failed or moved on or was absorbed into another; so that she needed no reciter and no written tally to know, at any hour a man cared to ask her, how many hearths answered to An Cnoc Ruadh, only the weight of a bag she had carried at her own belt since she was a girl learning the count from her mother. The king took the bag from her hands and weighed it himself, the same small motion, and gave it back, and said only that he was content; and it was the whole of the business between them, no more words spent on it than that, though Mòrag, watching, understood she had been brought the whole week's ride west to see it.

She turned the pebble bag over in her mind the length of the ride home, weighing it, she told herself more than once, the way Seonag weighed her own. Seonag held a shore that had never raised a bank against a raid because it had never given the sea's folk cause to raise one; held it, so far as Mòrag could see in the short days she spent at An Cnoc Ruadh's gate, by knowing exactly what she held and claiming not one pebble's weight beyond it. Mòrag had gone south with eleven spears to take what was not owed her and had come home with seven names to carry the rest of her life for the taking of it. She did not, in the years after, ever raise another raid, though she never once said, to anyone who asked her plainly why not, that the pebble bag was the reason.

## V. Of the Years That Followed

The years after the raid went the way most years on a settled hill go, told afterward less as a string of single days than as a handful of things a household remembered doing for the first time. Word came up from the south-west coast, in the seven hundred and fifth year, that households at Doire shean had begun firing clay pots in open bonfires, coil upon coil built up and baked hard in a single burning, a craft that within a few lifetimes spread the length of the southern shore and put an end, wherever it reached, to the older habit of carrying water and grain in skins that split and baskets that rotted; Mòrag heard of it from a trader glad, for once, to be carrying news rather than salt, and had two of the first pots brought up to the hill's own hearth, where they sat, chipped and much mended, longer than she herself sat the hill. Eleven years after that, at the landing on the green river now called, by the folk who used it, Cidhe Beag, a boat was hollowed whole from a single oak trunk, long enough to carry six men and their gear, and sunk at its mooring and left there, the first boat of its kind anyone then living had seen made in one unbroken piece rather than built up plank by lashed plank; and though it lay a long way from Mòrag's own hill and she never once saw it with her own eyes, the telling of it reached her all the same, as the telling of most new things on the island by then reached whoever held Dùn ìseal, sooner or later, by one road or another.

In the meantime the hill went on eating salt bought rather than salt taken, for the traders of Baile ghorm, whatever they thought privately of the household that had raided them, found within a few seasons that a bank of clay basins made more salt than seven hearths ever had, and that a hill with wool or hides to trade was worth more to them standing than raided. Mòrag herself never again sat across a bargaining fire from any of them, holding that a holder who had once taken by the spear had no business haggling afterward as though nothing had passed between the two households; she left the trading to men of her own who had not ridden south with her, and took what salt came up the valley road without asking too closely what price had been struck for it. It was, she told herself, no more than the ordinary distance a holder kept from the ordinary business of her own hill, though more than one of her own household noticed, without ever saying so where she could hear it, that she kept that particular distance more carefully than any other.

She held the hill forty-seven years in all, counting from the raid, and gave it up at last with her strength still whole in her, having judged, as she told the household plainly enough when she told them anything, that a hill was ill served by a holder who stayed past the age when she still had something to learn from it, and that the king's line, by then, had another of its own ready for the holding. The one who came after her was her father's own brother, Iain Dubh, a son of the king himself and older by every reckoning than she was, though he looked, that year, no more than a man in his middle strength beside her own face, which had begun, that year, to show its first lines; and it was Iain Dubh, taking the hill from her hand at the gate in the seven hundred and nineteenth year, who asked her the one question no one else in the household had thought, in all the years since, to put to her directly.

"How did you do it," he said, not naming the thing he meant, because there was only the one thing between them worth asking after, "with eleven spears against a whole shore, and come home with only seven lost?"

Mòrag looked at him a while before she answered, the way she had looked at most things worth the trouble of an answer, and said at last that she did not rightly know how she had done it, only that she had gone down meaning to take salt and had come home understanding that a household's strength was never so plainly its own as it liked to believe, and that the seven she had lost had bought her that understanding at a price she would not, if the choosing were given her again, judge worth paying twice. It was the whole of what she gave him, and the reciters, who kept little enough of her beyond the one deed, kept that answer with it, and no more.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Shingle at Baile ghorm

*GE 719 – 729*

*At Baile ghorm the salt-rakers still tell it as Màiri nan Làn told it, and add nothing to her telling and take nothing from it.*

## I. Of the Pans

Baile ghorm in those years was a scatter of huts behind a shingle bar, and the shingle bar was the reason for everything else. Behind it lay clay basins the salt-folk had dug with their own hands out of the mud a spring tide could no longer reach, and the sun and the slow fires under the basins did the rest, so that what came out at the end of a good week was salt enough to trade the length of the southern shore and some way past it. Màiri nan Làn had raked salt from the time she was old enough to be trusted with the wooden rake and not trusted with anything sharper, and she went on raking it the whole of her life after, and it was this, more than the year she is chiefly remembered for, that filled the greater part of her days: salt, and the sun on the pans, and the particular ache across the shoulders that came from drawing a rake through drying crystal from dawn until the light went.

The salt-folk of Baile ghorm did not then call themselves the king's, and had not, in Màiri's grandmother's time, so much as heard his name spoken with any certainty of what it meant. The hill lay a long way north and inland, a good many days' walking by the tracks they knew, and the southern shore had gone on making its own salt and keeping its own dead and marrying its own children into its own households without reference to any hill at all, the way a shore does when nothing has yet come down it hard enough to make reference necessary. Word had come, in the years before Màiri's birth, of a granddaughter of the hill's line who had ridden down with spears and carried off a season's salt in one raid, and lost seven of her own doing it, and the salt-folk had gone back to their pans afterward because there was no other place to go back to. Behind the shingle bar they had raised a low bank in the years just after, a slight thing that would slow a determined raid without ever quite stopping one, and had thought, most of them, that this settled the matter as well as it was likely to be settled.

Màiri's own mother had been a girl at the pans the year Mòrag Chruaidh came, old enough to remember the shapes of the running, though too young to be given a rake she might have to drop and run from, and she had passed the telling to Màiri the way the shore passed everything, at the fire, in pieces, over years, until the child no longer remembered a time before she had known it. Seven of the hill's men had died on the shingle and the track that morning, her mother said, and the salt-folk had counted them where they lay and let the hill carry them home; and Màiri grew up knowing that count as well as she knew her own kin's names, though she had never seen any of the seven living. It seemed to her, hearing it as a child, a settled story with a settled end, a raid that had happened once and would not happen twice, the bank behind the bar built and the account closed. She was thirty-seven before she understood how wrong a child's sense of an ending can be.

It was Iain Dubh who unsettled it again. Màiri knew him only as a name that meant trouble was owed and had not yet been paid, a hill man's name carried south on the same paths that carried salt north, and she was thirty-seven years old, with two grown sons of her own gone to households of their own and a third child still under her roof, on the morning she first saw him with her own eyes. She did not know, raking that morning, that she was seeing the last morning he would ever have.

## II. Of the Coming of Iain Dubh

He came the way the other one had come, from the north and inland, with spears enough behind him to make the salt-folk's low bank look exactly as inadequate as it was, and he came, as the first one had, for the salt. The salt-folk had had eight years since Iain Dubh took the hill from his father, eight years of hearing that he was harder even than the woman before him, or easier, or unlike her altogether, for such word travels a long road and grows a different shape at every hearth it passes, and none of it prepared them for the morning the spears actually stood on the ridge above the pans with the light behind them.

Tadhg Garbh was thirty-two that year, a big slow man who had never in Màiri's memory raised his voice at anything, married two years to a woman named Beathag who kept geese behind the huts and was, by every account but his own, a far quicker wit than he was. He had raked salt beside Màiri since they were children too small to be trusted with the rake, and she knew him the way the shore's people knew one another, by his walk before his face, by the particular slowness with which he came to any decision and the particular stubbornness with which he held it once come to. It was Tadhg who stood nearest the gap in the bank when the spears came down off the ridge in the grey hour before the light was fully up, thirty and more of them against the dozen or so men who had reached the gap before the rest of the shore was even roused, and it was Tadhg's spear, thrown last of all among a scatter of others and almost, men said afterward, as an afterthought, that took Iain Dubh through the throat before he had closed half the distance to the pans.

Màiri was not at the gap. She had been raking the pan nearest her own hut, further along the bar, and came up out of sleep-thick confusion at the first shout to find the whole shore already running, men snatching spears from where they leaned against the hut walls, women driving the smaller children back behind the salt-sheds, and she ran with the rake still in her hand for want of anything else to carry, useless as it was for fighting, because it was the thing nearest to hand when the shouting started and she had not thought to set it down. What she saw, coming up onto the higher ground behind the bank, was the fighting break apart the way a flock breaks when a stone is thrown into the middle of it, men running one way and then another, spears thrown and missing and a few finding their mark, and in among them a tall figure that had been walking, not running, at the head of the hill men, going suddenly down onto the wet clay of the nearest pan and not getting up again.

She did not know, in the confusion of that morning, whose fall it was. It was only when the fighting broke off as suddenly as it had begun, the hill men drawing back from the bank in a huddle around the fallen man rather than pressing on for the salt they had come for, and then lifting him between four of them and carrying him away north at a pace that could not honestly be called a retreat and could not honestly be called anything else, that the shore began to understand what had happened; and it was days later, when the first traders came south with the word already travelling ahead of them the way such word always travelled, that Baile ghorm learned the man on the clay had been the king's own son, holder of the hill these eight years past, and the first of Ailean Mòr's children, in all the generations already reckoned there, to die by a spear rather than by the slow ordinary dying that took everyone else.

Seven of the hill's men had died the first time Mòrag Chruaidh came down, and the hill kept their names. Only Tadhg Garbh's spear had found its mark this second time, and no one on Tràigh an t-Salainn died that day at all, which some of the older rakers afterward called a mercy and others called only luck, arguing at the winter fires for years over which word was truer and never settling it.

Iain Dubh had come to the hill at six hundred and seventy-four years old, by the count the reciters kept, a great age by any reckoning but the hill's own, where it made him no more than a man in the middle of his strength; he died at six hundred and eighty-two, on the clay of a pan he had never so much as touched with his own hand, and the list that had until then named only the taking of hills and the giving of judgements set down, for the first time, a year of death that was not also a year of some ordinary failing of the body.

## III. Of the Cairn on the Hill

What was done on the hill afterward, Màiri did not see and only heard, the way she heard most things from the hill, thinned by distance and by however many mouths a tale had passed through before it reached Tràigh an t-Salainn. It was told that they raised the cairn where Ailean Mòr's own eye had chosen the ground, and that Tormod, Iain Dubh's son, stood by it through the raising with a face that gave nothing away to anyone watching, which was thought remarkable in a young man not yet ninety years old whose father had just been carried home dead on a hide.

Tormod had held nothing yet in his own right; he was his father's eldest living son and no more than that, and the hill in those days gave nothing to a man for being a son, only for being chosen, so there was no certainty even at the cairn-side that Tormod would ever hold what his father had held. He was eighty-seven that year, a young man still by the reckoning of his blood, and stood the length of the raising without once being seen to weep, which the traders who carried the tale south thought worth remarking on, though Màiri, hearing it told and told again over the years, came to think it told them less about Tormod's grief than about how little the traders understood of a household that buried its dead expecting, in the ordinary run of things, centuries more of them to bury before its own turn came.

What was certain, and what the salt-folk heard clearly enough even at their distance, was that the king had not been on the hill when his son died, having been away in the north those same weeks settling some quarrel of grazing that no one on Tràigh an t-Salainn ever troubled to learn the particulars of, and that he came home to find the cairn already raised and his son already under it.

It was told that he stood by the cairn three days and spoke to no one the whole of that time, not to Tormod, not to Sorcha's other children, not to the reciters who stood ready, as reciters always stood ready, to add whatever words he cared to give them to the list. On the fourth day he walked off the hill alone, on foot, taking none of his household and no spears at all, and it was some while before anyone understood, from the direction he had gone, that he was walking south toward Tràigh an t-Salainn.

## IV. Of the Man on the Shingle

Màiri was raking the third pan from the bar's western end, in the heat of the day when the brine had gone thick and needed turning before it set, and she straightened once to ease her back, the way she straightened perhaps forty times in a working day without ever after remembering any of the other thirty-nine, and saw a man coming along the shingle from the west.

He was alone. That was the first thing she took in, and the strangest, for no one came to Baile ghorm alone who had any better choice, the coast track through the dunes being lonely enough that even traders went it in twos. He walked as a man walks who owns the ground he is walking on, not fast, not slow, and something in the set of his shoulders, though she had never in her life seen him before, told her plainly enough who he must be before any word had passed between them.

She dropped the rake and screamed for the men, and she was not ashamed afterward that she had screamed first and thought second, for it seemed to her the only thing a body could rightly do, seeing what she believed she was seeing come walking toward the pans where his son had died with a spear in his hand not a year past. The men came from the huts at a run, thirty of them and more, snatching up the same spears that had done for Iain Dubh, and made a line across the shingle between the king and the salt.

He came on. He did not slow for the line any more than he had slowed for the empty dunes behind him, and Màiri, standing back from the men with the rake still fallen where she had dropped it, noticed a thing she could never afterward explain to anyone who had not stood where she stood: that the wind coming in off the water was cold on her own face, as a sea wind is cold in that season, and yet the air seemed to sit warm around him the whole way he walked, as though he carried some part of a hearth along with him inside his clothes and none of it showed. She had heard the tale of the shingle raid told back to her often enough by then, in every version the shore's fires had made of it, and none of the tellings had thought to mention the warmth; it was hers alone, kept back the whole of her life for want of a way to say it that did not sound, even to her own ear, like a woman claiming more of the day than she had truly been given.

He wore no hardened hide and carried no spear of his own, only a plain travelling cloak gone dusty at the hem from the dunes, and there was nothing in his dress to mark him for a king rather than any herdsman come down off the hill roads, nothing but the walk and the warmth and the thing in his face that made thirty armed men draw into a line rather than simply stand aside and let a stranger pass.

Tadhg Garbh stood near the middle of the line. Màiri knew him well enough to know the exact look that came over his face as the king closed the distance, a look she had seen on him only once before, the morning Iain Dubh came down, and she understood without being told that Tadhg had raised his own spear to his shoulder and meant, or half meant, to throw it a second time. She watched his arm come level and hold, and hold, the muscle standing out along it until it shook with the holding, and then watched him lower it slowly and stand looking at the spear in his own hand as if someone else had put it there and he could no longer think why he was holding it at all.

No one else threw. The king walked into the line of them and stopped, close enough now that Màiri could see his face plainly, an ordinary face, she thought afterward, trying to find some grander word for it and never quite finding one that fit better than ordinary, tired about the eyes the way any man's face is tired who has walked a long way and slept little. He looked along the line, face by face, the whole thirty of them, and to each face he gave the same length of looking, no longer at Tadhg Garbh's than at any other, though every soul on that shingle knew by then whose spear it had been. He said nothing at all. The silence went on long enough that Màiri heard, under it, the ordinary small sounds of the shore going on regardless, water working at the shingle, a gull somewhere behind the huts, and thought it strange that the world had not stopped to match the stillness of the men.

## V. Of the Double Handful

It was old Mòr, eldest then among the salt-folk, who broke it. She went down on her knees on the wet shingle in front of him, an old woman kneeling before a man who looked, to any eye that did not know better, a full sixty years younger than she was, and she reached into the nearest pan and took up salt in both hands, a double handful, grey with the clay still in it and wet enough to run between her fingers, and held it up to him without a word.

He took it from her hands into his own. He ate a little of it, not much, no more than a man might taste from curiosity, and put the rest of it back into her cupped palms, closing her fingers over it with his own before he let go, so that she was left kneeling there holding salt he had given back to her rather than salt she had first given him.

Then he turned and walked back the way he had come, along the shingle toward the dunes, and no one moved to stop him and no one, Màiri said afterward more times than she could count, felt afterward that there had been any moment in the whole of it when stopping him had truly been a thing within their power.

By evening word had gone the length of the shore that the salt was the king's, though no one could afterward say which of them had first put it in those words, or whether it needed saying at all after what had been seen on the shingle. No blood had been shed that day, the first time in two raids that a day at Baile ghorm had ended with no new name to be kept among the dead, and no payment was ever asked or given for the blood that had been shed before it, not Iain Dubh's, not the seven of Mòrag Chruaidh's raid a generation before. The rakers argued it at their fires for the rest of that winter and on into others, some holding that a man who ate a stranger's salt and gave the rest back with his own hand had shown them the plainest mercy a conquered shore could hope for, and others, Tadhg Garbh loudest among them at first, though he grew quieter on the subject as the years went by, holding that a man who could walk unarmed through thirty raised spears and take nothing but a taste of what he might have taken whole had shown them something a good deal less comfortable than mercy, a proof of a power that made mercy beside the point.

Màiri herself never took either side of it strongly, though she was asked often enough, being the one whose scream had first brought the men running. What she said, when pressed, in the years she had left to be asked, was only that she had stood close enough to see his face when Mòr knelt to him, and that it had not been the face of a man deciding anything in that moment. It had been, she said, the face of a man for whom the thing had already been decided a long way further back than the shingle, perhaps as far back as the cairn on the hill, perhaps further, and that whatever word the rakers wanted to put to it, mercy or the other thing, the deciding of it had happened somewhere she had no way of following him to.

## VI. Of Tadhg Garbh's Boat

Tormod came down from the hill himself the following spring, the first time any of his father's blood had set foot on Tràigh an t-Salainn since the killing, and stood at the cairn the salt-folk raised of their own accord on the rise above the pans, a small thing beside the one on the hill but built with the same care, seven stones for the seven of Mòrag's raid worked in around its base though none of the seven had died in this second fight at all, only Iain Dubh, because the salt-folk had come by then to think of the two raids as one long account and wished the reckoning to sit together. He came with no more than four men, and asked, before he would let anyone lead him up to the cairn, to be shown the pan where his father had fallen, and stood on the clay there a while with his boots sinking into it, saying nothing that Màiri, watching from a little way off, could afterward report with any confidence. Tormod said little that anyone remembered word for word, being still careful with speech in a way his father had never troubled to be, but he swore Tràigh an t-Salainn's peace would hold from his own line as it had held from his father's since the king's coming, asked Tadhg Garbh's name and was given it without anyone thinking to soften the telling, looked a moment at the big slow man who had thrown the spear, and said only that a man defending his own pans with his own hand owed no account to anyone for it. Then he rode north again within the day, and it was the last any of Tràigh an t-Salainn saw of him for a great many years.

Tadhg Garbh lived a year longer, and it was not a year that sat easily on him. He raked salt as he had always raked it and spoke to his household as he had always spoken, but Màiri, working the pans beside him through that last year more often than either of them chose to remark on, saw a man turning something over that he could not set down and could not finish turning. In the spring of the year after the king's coming he took a boat out alone before first light, one of the small hide craft the shore used for the near fishing, and did not come back with the tide, nor with any tide after it. No storm was remembered that night worth the name, and no wreckage of the boat was ever found along that coast, and the salt-folk were left, as they had been left once before, without a settled word for what had happened, some saying the sea had simply taken a tired man home and others saying, more quietly, that a man who has held a spear against the king's own son and thrown it true does not always find it easy to go on living beside the shore where he did it, whatever mercy was shown him after.

Màiri outlived him more than fifty years, and raked salt at Baile ghorm the whole of that time, through summers when the pans ran thick and winters when they scarcely ran at all, and told the tale of the man on the shingle to her grandchildren and their children after her the same way each time, adding nothing and leaving nothing out, until it passed from her mouth into the shore's own keeping and needed no more telling from any one person at all. The bank behind the bar stood as it had always stood, no higher and no lower than the salt-folk had first raised it, and the pans went on giving up their grey harvest to the rake exactly as they had before any king's blood had ever bled onto the shingle beside them, salt drawn from salt water under the same sun, the shore's oldest and least remarkable labour, going on the same the year the king came as it went on every year before and every year after.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Sand on the Hearths and the Opened Ground

*GE 770 – 901*

*At the new houses above Cnoc chaol they still measure a child's growing by Seasaidh's own count: so many years since the sand, so many since the valley, so many since the stones.*

## I. Of the Sand

Seasaidh was seven years old the night the sea came into the house.

She had no memory afterward of hearing it come, only of being carried, wet and half asleep, in her mother's arms up a slope she did not know the household owned, while behind them a sound went on that she took at first, muddled with sleep, for wind in a bad season and only later, turning the night over and over across the rest of her life, understood to have been water moving where no water had ever moved in the memory of anyone then living. Cnoc chaol stood, in those years, low along a shingle rise a stone's throw back from the tide line, a scatter of houses no different from a dozen others on that coast, and the sea had kept, for as long as the oldest households could reckon, to a plain and honest habit of coming up the shingle at the flood and going back down it at the ebb, so that no one had thought to ask what the sea might do if it once forgot the habit.

It forgot it that night. There was no storm to give warning of it, no wind worth remarking, only a stillness some of the older folk said afterward they had felt before the water came, a stillness in the air that a few had remarked on at the time and none had known what to make of, and then the sea rose past every mark it had ever left and came in across the low ground faster than a grown man could run from it, taking two households whole and leaving, on every hearth it reached and did not carry away with it, a sheet of grey sand laid smooth as if a hand had smoothed it, a hand's depth thick, and threaded through with the broken shells of creatures no one on that shore had ever pulled up in a net, the shells of water deeper than any of them fished.

Seasaidh's father did not come up the slope with them. She learned this only in the grey hour after, standing in the ruin of what had been the lower houses with the sand already drying pale under the first sun and her mother's hand gripping hers hard enough to hurt, and she did not properly understand, at seven, what the word meant when her mother said it, only that a shape in her life that had always been there was now, without any ceremony to mark the change, not there, and that everyone around her had gone quiet in a particular way that told her not to ask more of it than she had already been told. Twelve of the coast's households were counted dead when the counting was done, a number that meant nothing to her at seven beyond the fact that among them was the shape that had been her father, and that her mother's face, in the days that followed, wore an expression Seasaidh had not seen on it before and would see again, at longer and longer intervals, for the whole of the rest of her mother's life.

The old folk, sifting through what the sand had left standing, found little worth the digging. A quern-stone, a scatter of the small clay counters children played at knuckle-games with, the charred end of a roof-beam still faintly warm where the sand had not quite smothered the last of a hearth-fire before it went out under the weight of the water. No one went back to rebuild on the same ground, though it was, as more than one of the older men said standing on it in the days after, as good a stretch of level shore as the coast offered and would offer again once the sand had settled and grassed over, which in time it did. But there was a fear laid into that low ground now that no amount of good level shore could talk a household out of, and the survivors of Cnoc chaol carried what could be carried up the slope behind the old site, to a shelf of higher ground looking down over the drowned houses, and began again there, in the first weeks with nothing more than what had been snatched up on the way out and what could be cut and carried in a hurry, and in the seasons after with houses built properly, walls of stone this time where the old houses had been turf and wattle, as if stone alone might argue the sea out of a second visit.

## II. Of the Slope

Seasaidh grew up on that slope, in a house her mother and her mother's brothers raised with their own hands in the first winter after the wave, and she grew up, as children do who lose a father too young to properly grieve him, with the loss folded into the ordinary shape of her days rather than standing apart from it: a story told at the fire on certain nights, a silence that fell over her mother at certain turns of the tide, a habit, which Seasaidh kept all her own life after without ever quite deciding to keep it, of counting the households on any shore she came to and reckoning, without meaning to, how far up the ground they stood from the water.

The new houses held. Seasaidh was thirteen, fourteen, old enough to help at the nets and the drying racks, before she stopped waking at every ordinary sound of a high tide working at the shingle below, and older than that again before she stopped, on the anniversary nights the household kept without ever naming them anniversaries, looking down from the new slope at the pale drowned ground below and feeling the particular cold that was not the sea's cold at all. The village above the old site never took a name of its own separate from the name the drowned ground had carried before it, for there seemed to the folk who built it no reason to call the new houses by any word but the word the coast had always used for that stretch of shore, so that Cnoc chaol came to mean, without anyone deciding it should, the slope and not the sand, the living houses and not the dead ones, though every soul who grew up there in Seasaidh's years knew exactly which ground the older word had first belonged to, and pointed it out to their children in turn, low ground, drowned ground, not to be built on.

It was on that slope, in her nineteenth year, that Seasaidh first met Pàl, a quiet, broad-shouldered young man come down with drovers from the inland valleys, wool to trade for salt fish, third son of a household that held grazing two days inland along a river Seasaidh had never seen and could not, that first year, well imagine, a country of grass and slow water and no tide at all to reckon anything by. He came back the following year, and the year after that with less excuse for coming than wool alone gave him, and by her twenty-second year Seasaidh had agreed, to her mother's mixed grief and relief, to go inland with him and take up a household on ground she had never set eyes on, a decision she thought little enough of at the time, being twenty-two and in that particular kind of love that makes distance feel like nothing more than a thing to be walked through, and understood a good deal better once she had lived some years on the ground she had gone to.

## III. Of the Valley

The valley Pàl's household held lay a long two days' walk from the coast by the tracks Seasaidh came to know well over the years that followed, a green trough between two low scarps with a stream running the length of its floor and grazing enough on either slope to hold three households in fair comfort, which was, in those years, as much land as any inland household thought to ask for. It had no name of its own beyond what its own folk called it among themselves, the valley, the long field, words that served well enough for people who rarely had cause to speak of it to anyone who did not already know which valley was meant, and Seasaidh, coming to it a coast woman with salt still in the creases of her hands, found it at first a strange, closed sort of country, hemmed in by its own slopes the way the coast was never hemmed, no horizon of open water to look to, only grass and more grass and the stream's steady, unhurried talking.

Love for it came slowly, the way love comes for a thing not chosen for oneself, first through Pàl and the children who came after him, four of them living past their first winters out of six born, and then through the valley's own quiet virtues: its shelter from the coast's winds, its grass holding green longer into a dry summer than any pasture she had known as a girl, its stream that never once, in all the years she kept house beside it, rose higher than a channel a child could jump. Seasaidh told her children more than once, meaning it kindly and meaning it, so far as she then knew, truly, that the valley was a safe country, dry-footed, its only weather the ordinary weather of wind and frost and the occasional hard winter that thinned the flocks but never the households.

She was fifty-seven years old, her hair more grey than not and her hands stiffening a little in the cold mornings the way hands do at that age, and her youngest grandchild not yet walking, when she woke one night in early autumn to a sound she had not heard in fifty years and had never expected to hear again on ground so far from any tide: a long, low groaning, felt through the floor of the house as much as heard, that went on, off and on, through the better part of that night and left, by morning, a crack running clean across the floor of the valley a little below the household's own byre, wide enough in places for a grown man to set his boot into and lose it to the darkness below, and running, as the light came up fully and Pàl and the neighbouring households walked the length of it, further than any of them cared to walk to find its end.

## IV. Of the Opened Ground

It was not, that first morning, a thing any of them had words ready for. A storm, a bad winter, even a fire, these were misfortunes the valley's folk had inherited a stock of sayings for, ready-made comfort passed down from households that had weathered the same before them; but no one living in that valley, nor any teller any of them could call to mind, had ever spoken of the ground itself coming open under a household's feet, and the strangeness of it sat on the valley folk for days afterward heavier, in its way, than the plain damage would have warranted on its own, for the crack had taken no life and thrown down no house, only opened, silently and for no cause any of them could name, across ground they had walked without a second thought every day of their lives.

Seasaidh, standing at the crack's edge that first morning with Pàl's hand hard on her arm holding her back from the loose lip of it, felt the old cold come up in her the way it had not come up in fifty years, the exact cold of the slope above Cnoc chaol looking down at drowned ground, and understood before anyone else in the valley said it aloud that this was, for her, the old fear come round again by a different road, the world's ground proving, a second time in one life, less solid underfoot than a person is raised to believe. She kept it from Pàl that morning, for there was, in the moment, no way to say it that would not have sounded, even to her own ear, a stranger claim than the crack itself: that she had felt this exact cold before, on a coast two days' walk away, over water and not over ground at all.

The spring that had, for as long as the household could remember, risen at the valley's upper end and run down along the near slope to join the stream below the byre, moved in the days after the ground opened, its old channel running dry by inches until within a season it ran altogether elsewhere, breaking out a hundred paces downhill in a new hollow none of them had marked before as ground a spring might choose, so that the valley folk found themselves, in the space of one autumn, relearning a stretch of ground they had thought as settled and as known as their own hands. No house stood near enough the crack to be lost to it, which the valley folk afterward counted a mercy plain enough not to need much saying, the byre nearest it standing a good long stone's throw off and no dwelling closer than that; but grazing was lost along the crack's whole run, sheep would not be driven near it and cattle liked it no better, and for a season and more the valley's folk went about their ordinary work with a wariness that had not been part of the valley's temper before, glancing at ground they had never before thought worth a glance.

Word of it went out along the drover roads the way word of anything went, carried by whoever next had reason to travel, and it was carried, that winter, all the way to the hill, though none of the valley's own folk had thought to send it there on purpose; a drover simply told it at a hearth where it was overheard by a man travelling on to the hill for other business, and he told it again where he next stopped, and so, by the slow accident of ordinary talk rather than by any deliberate asking, the king came to hear of a valley two days inland where the ground had opened and a spring had moved.

## V. Of the King at the Crack

He came in the spring following, on foot and with no more than two men behind him, word of his coming reaching the valley only a day ahead of the man himself, which gave the household barely time enough to be afraid of the honour before the honour was standing at their gate. Seasaidh was sixty that year, old enough by the valley's own reckoning to have earned a settled place at any gathering, and old enough, too, to remember plainly enough what a king's coming had meant on the coast in her own girlhood, though she herself, a child then, had never once seen him with her own eyes; and she stood that morning at the edge of the yard with her grown children about her and felt, watching him walk up the last stretch of track from the ford, the same thing every teller she had ever heard tell of him agreed on and that she had never, until that morning, quite believed simply for having heard it so often: a warmth on the air around him that had nothing to do with the season, felt at ten paces and at five and closer, as though the man carried some small part of a well-kept hearth folded into his ordinary clothes and none of it showed on the outside of him.

He asked to be shown the crack before he would take food or rest, and walked its length with Pàl and two of the valley's older men, Seasaidh a little behind them with the rest of the household, and said little as he walked, stopping twice to crouch at the lip of it and look down into the dark the way a man looks into a well he means to judge the depth of, though he let down nothing to measure it by, only looked. He asked how the spring had moved and was shown its new channel, and asked whether any beast or soul had gone into the crack in the season since it opened, and was told, truthfully, that none had, the valley folk having kept clear of it by instinct before anyone had thought to make a rule of keeping clear.

"You have done well enough on your own," he said at last, standing at the widest part of the crack with the two men who had walked it beside him and the rest of the household drawn up a little way off, "better than most would, coming on a strangeness with no one to tell them what it meant." He looked along the crack's run a last time, the way, Seasaidh thought, watching him from where she stood, a man looks at a thing he expects to see again rather than a thing he expects to be done with. "I'll not tell you to fill it in, nor to leave it. The ground will do as the ground does, here as anywhere else I've stood on it. Keep your beasts back, and your children, and build no house nearer it than you'd build to a drop of the same depth cut by a man's own hand, and you'll have done all that wants doing." He said nothing more of it, neither warning nor blessing beyond the plain sense of what he had already said, and Seasaidh, hearing it repeated at valley fires for years afterward in tellings that grew, as tellings do, a little grander with each retelling, thought privately, and said so to her own grandchildren when she was old enough to say what she liked, that the grandest thing in it had been how little he had made of a thing the valley had spent a whole season being afraid of.

He stayed the one night, eating at Pàl's own hearth without ceremony and sleeping, so far as anyone in the household could tell, an ordinary man's sleep, and was gone again by the next morning's light, walking back the way he had come with his two men and no more said of the crack than had already been said at its edge. Seasaidh never saw him again in the years left to her, though she heard, as everyone on that road heard sooner or later, of him at other gates, other gatherings, other years, always the same face, always the same warmth reported by whoever had stood near enough to feel it, while her own face, and Pàl's, and the faces of every soul she had grown up beside on the coast or married among in the valley, went on ageing the ordinary way faces age, so that by the time she herself was old she had long since stopped finding it strange and had come, instead, simply to expect it, the way a person comes to expect the tide.

## VI. Of the White Stones

The crack neither closed nor widened greatly in the years that followed, though it moved, by inches and by seasons, the way such ground moves, a little here after a hard frost, a little there after a wet spring, so that a line drawn along its edge in one year would not quite serve to mark it ten years on. The valley folk kept clear of it as they had from the first, by habit more than by any rule laid down, until Seasaidh, old now, her own children grown and settled with households of their own along the same valley, took it into her head, in the winter of her seventy-seventh year, that habit alone was a poor thing to trust a crack's whole length to, memory being shorter than a valley's life and children being born every year who had not stood, as she had, at the lip of the ground on the morning it first opened.

She began the stones herself, carrying the first of them up from the stream bed one at a time, more than her stiffening hands and her grown children thought wise for a woman of her years, and set them along the crack's outer edge a good stride back from the drop, white stones chosen for their whiteness rather than their size, so that even a child running in poor light might see the line of them and know, without needing to be told twice, where the safe ground ended. Her sons and daughters, seeing what she was at and unable to talk her out of it, took up the carrying themselves before she had done more than the first stretch, and grandchildren after them, so that the work, begun as one old woman's stubbornness, became within a season the whole valley's doing, households from both ends of the settled ground coming to add their own stones to the line until it ran the crack's full length, broken here and there where the ground itself had already made the danger plain enough without a stone to say so.

Pàl had died the winter before her seventy-fifth year, an ordinary death of an ordinary old age, and Seasaidh kept the house alone after him with a grandson's family settled near enough to see to her, a life she found, in the telling of it to those same grandchildren, no harder to bear than any other loss a long life brings, having by then buried a father, a mother, and a husband, and having come, in the slow way a person comes to such things, to hold that grief widened rather than emptied a person, leaving room, each time, for one more thing worth minding on behalf of those still to come after.

"The ground keeps its own counsel," Seasaidh was fond of saying to her grandchildren in those last years, over the white stones, "and a wise household keeps a stride back from it"; and the children of the valley grew up, in the years after, knowing the crack the way Seasaidh herself had once known the drowned ground below Cnoc chaol: a plain fact of the country they lived in, marked, minded, and left otherwise alone.

She died in her eighty-second year, in the same house Pàl had first brought her to sixty winters before, with her children and most of her grandchildren about her, and was buried on the near slope above the valley within sight, though not within a stone's throw, of the white line she had begun; and the valley folk, telling of her afterward at their own fires, told less often of the coast she had come from or the wave that had taken her father than of the stones themselves, so that within two generations more it was chiefly as the woman who had marked the crack that her name was kept at all, the sand and the drowning folded quietly into an older telling behind it. No house was raised, in all the years that valley folk afterward kept the ground, within a stone's throw of the crack on either side of it, and the white line, mended where frost or flood undid a stretch of it and never once let go entirely to grass, ran the whole visible length of the opened ground, still tended by hands that had never known Seasaidh living, when every soul who had stood at its edge the first morning was gone to the hill's own reckoning of the dead.

# Chapter Twelve: Of the Unlit Hearth and the Basket

*GE 902 – 1,070*

*At Achadh dhìreach the hearths still measure an gual dathach by the hand Anna nic Coinnich taught them, though most who measure it now could not say whose hand it was.*

## I. Of the Hearth Never Lit

Before there was a household at Achadh dhìreach that anyone now living could name, there was a hearth, and the hearth was never lit.

It stood a little back from where the stream bent under the first rise of ground, laid with the same care any hearth was laid in those years, stones set close and true and a clay lip built up round the fire-bed to hold the ash from spreading. Dry wood lay ready beside it, split fine for a first catching flame, and beside the wood, wrapped in a scrap of hide gone stiff with age, a single sliver of an gual dathach, no bigger than a child's thumb. Whoever laid that hearth had meant to light it.
