The wood was cut for lighting and the coal was set out for lighting and neither had been touched by fire in all the years anyone afterward dug down to look at them, so that the hearth-stones, when at last a spade turned up their edge in the nine hundred and second year of the king, came up out of the ground as clean of soot as the day they were laid.

No one at Achadh dhìreach in that year could say who had laid it, or why they had gone away before the striking, or where they had gone. The valley folk who found it were three brothers new to the ground, clearing a strip for barley their grandfather had marked out and never lived to break, and they stood over the buried hearth a long while before any of them would put a hand to the coal, for a coal so old and so untouched seemed to them a thing that had waited on purpose, and a man does not care to be the one who wakes what has chosen, for whatever reason of its own, to go on sleeping.

They left it dark. It is told that the eldest of the three, a man named Griogal, said only that the hearth had been left as it was for a reason a hearth-builder would have known and he did not, and that he would sooner leave a mystery standing than put a flame to one, and his brothers, who had less patience for mysteries generally, agreed with him in this one thing because neither of them wanted, any more than he did, to be the hand that lit a fire someone else had refused. They laid a flat stone over the coal and the wood, and built their own hearth a stone's throw off, in ground that had never held one before, and told their children, as their children told theirs, to leave the old stones be.

By the nine hundred and fifty-sixth year the buried hearth lay three yards down, covered by every season's turf and every year's midden and the slow gathering of a valley floor that never stopped rising under the feet of the people who lived on it, and only the oldest households still troubled to point out, to a child digging where a child ought not to dig, the exact spot where the ground held its secret. It became, in the way of such things, less a fact remembered than a habit kept: no one broke new ground there, though no one any longer troubled to ask why not, and the valley folk who farmed the good soil all round it did so without once feeling the want of the strip they left alone.

## II. Of the Measure Nowhere Written

The custom that Achadh dhìreach came at last to keep with an gual dathach did not begin at Achadh dhìreach, and no one there, when it reached them, could have said where it had begun, only that it had reached every hearth in Na Glinn Àrda within the space of a very few years, the way a plain sense sometimes travels faster than any single teller can be found to have carried it.

It is told that at a drovers' ford some days off, where beasts were rested on the road to the hill and travellers slept a night or two among strangers before going on, a household new to the ground had burnt more of the coal in one sitting than its neighbours thought wise, warming a sick child through a hard night, and had been watched doing it by three others who came the following winter to see for themselves what a fire fed too generously with an gual dathach would do. Nothing came of the watching that year, nor the year after; but the households of that ford, and then the households near them, and then households further off than any of them had ever traded with directly, took to measuring what they put on a fire by the width of a hand cupped and no wider, a full hand and no more, and kept to it without any one of them being able to say who had first said it aloud or when.

By the thousand and eleventh year, or near enough that no two households at Achadh dhìreach agreed on the count, a full hand had become the whole of the law that any of them knew regarding the coal, and it was law in the plain sense that a stranger travelling from the ford country to Na Glinn Àrda and back again would have found the same measure kept at every hearth along the road, though no king had proclaimed it and no holder of any hill had ever ridden out to enforce it. It sat alongside the old buried hearth in the valley's own reckoning of itself, two things neither explained nor questioned: a hearth once laid and never lit, and a measure everywhere kept and nowhere written, and it was the particular cast of that valley's mind, by the time Anna nic Coinnich was old enough to carry water to her mother's fire, to hold the two as somehow of a piece, as if the unlit hearth had been the first hand's warning and the measured hand the whole valley's late answer to it, though no one then living, and likely no one who had ever lived at Achadh dhìreach, could have said whether the two things touched each other at all outside a child's tidy way of making sense of what she was given.

Anna was born in the thousandth year of the king into a household two fields off from the buried hearth, the youngest of four, and grew up knowing the width of her own cupped hand the way she knew the sound of the stream under the first rise: a fact of the valley so plain it needed no more remarking than the shape of the hills. Her mother measured coal onto the fire from a clay jar kept high on a shelf, out of the smaller children's reach, and said the same words each time without seeming to notice she said them, *làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh*, a full hand and no more, until Anna herself said them without noticing, first to her own younger cousins and later, when she had a household of her own, to children who were hers.

## III. Of Achadh dhìreach

She married at nineteen a man named Aonghas, a byreward from the next valley over, and came to keep her own hearth within sight of the old buried one, close enough that on quiet evenings she could stand at her own door and see the flat stone the valley still pointed out to children, greyed now with a lifetime's weather and half sunk into ground that had risen round it a further hand's depth in her own lifetime alone. She raised four children of her own there and buried one, a boy of six years taken by a fever the winter she was thirty, and came in time to be one of the older women of that stretch of the valley, the kind whose hearth other households' children were sent to when their own mothers had no time to mind them, and whose word on the raising of children, and increasingly on other matters besides, carried further than her own household's fence.

The years between were ordinary years, and the valley's own telling of them kept little of their particulars beyond a bare handful: a dry summer that thinned the barley but did not fail it outright; a boundary quarrel between two households over a strip of grazing that Anna's own father, before his death, had helped settle by walking the ground with both parties and marking new stones where the old ones had shifted; a stranger through from the coast one autumn with salt to trade and news of a boat hollowed whole from a single oak, which the valley folk heard with the mild interest they gave most things that happened somewhere else. Achadh dhìreach in those years held some dozen households strung along the stream, no larger a place than it had ever been and in no hurry, so far as anyone there could tell, to become larger, its people keeping cattle and a little grain and the long patience of a valley that had never once, in any teller's memory, been visited by anything worse than weather.

Two households nearer the stream's bend than Anna's own belonged to a man named Eanraig Ruadh and his wife Beathag, who had come to that stretch of ground a generation before Anna's own birth and were, by the time this telling reaches them, well into the years a valley calls old without troubling to count them exactly. Eanraig had buried two wives before Beathag and outlived three of his own children, and had the name, among the younger households, of a man who kept his own counsel and his own hearth hotter than most, being of the kind, not uncommon at any age, who felt the cold in his bones before his neighbours felt it in theirs and would sooner burn a little more than shiver through a long evening. Careless he was not thought. His beasts were well kept, his roof well thatched, and his grandchildren, of whom there were by then a good many scattered among the valley's other households, were spoken of kindly wherever they went, a man careful, by every neighbour's account, in every particular save one. It was only the fire he kept generous, and it was a generosity the valley had grown used to seeing without remarking on it further than to say, now and again, that Eanraig liked his hearth warm.

## IV. Of the Basket

The summer of the year one thousand and sixty-six never properly came, the valley said afterward: a cold wet season with a north wind in it that killed two of Eanraig's own lambs before their first shearing and set every household along the stream burning peat in the middle of an t-Iuchar as though it were the wolf-month. Eanraig Ruadh, an old man past any count he still troubled to keep, felt that cold in joints that had troubled him little in warmer winters, and said to Beathag, more than once in the hearing of a grandchild who later told it, that a man his age had earned the right to sit warm through whatever was left to him, and that he did not propose to spend his last winters shivering for the sake of a measure some ford household three valleys off had thought up before either of them were born.

It is not told, and Anna herself, questioned on it by her own grandchildren once she had grown old, would never say she knew, whether Eanraig meant from the first to break the measure outright or only to stretch it a little further each night than the night before, the way a habit is broken most often, by inches too small for the breaker to notice breaking anything at all. What is told is that on a night early in an t-Iuchar, with the cold still hard on the valley and a wind come round to the north that found every gap in a poorly chinked wall, Eanraig set on his fire, in one going, very nearly the whole of a basket his eldest living son had carried up from the trading he alone regularly made along the ford road, a basket meant, by that son's own account given afterward, to see the household through the better part of the coming year measured out by handfuls and not spent in a single night by a man who had stopped, in his old age, quite believing that the measure applied to him.

Anna was wakened past midnight by a light in the sky the wrong colour for any fire she had ever seen a house burn, a light that stood up over the roofs of the nearer houses in a colour she groped afterward, telling it to her own children, for words to fit and never quite found, saying only that it ran shot through with something beneath the ordinary red-gold of a burning roof, a colour that seemed, she said, to come from further down in the fire than fire usually burned from. She was out of her own house and across two fields before Aonghas had his boots properly laced, and she was not the first there, for households nearer Eanraig's had wakened before her at the sound alone, a sound she never afterward tried to describe with any confidence, only that it was louder, and went on longer, than a roof-fire's ordinary crack and settle.

The house was past saving by the time enough hands had gathered to try. It had gone up whole, roof and walls together, in the time it takes a household to wake and dress and cross two fields, and what the valley folk stood back from, in the end, was a column of flame past any fighting with water carried in pails, the colour of nothing any of them had a word ready for, standing straight up in a windless patch of air though the wind blew hard everywhere else that night, and giving off a heat that drove them back a good ten paces further than an ordinary house-fire would have made them stand. Eanraig Ruadh did not come out of it, nor Beathag, nor a grandchild of six years named Ualan who had been left to sleep the night under their roof while his own mother tended a sick sister two houses off, and the valley folk who stood in the cold that night, watching a fire none of them had ever seen the like of and none of them could get near enough to fight, told each other afterward, in whatever words came to each of them, that they had known, standing there, that they were watching something answer a measure that had been broken, though not one of them, questioned closely by whoever came after to ask it of them, could say what they meant by the word *answer* beyond the plain fact of the fire's colour and its heat and the three lives it took with it.

The house burned to its stones before the light came up grey over the wet fields, and when the ash had cooled enough for hands to go into it, what the valley folk found at the heart of the ruin was the hearthstone itself split clean through from one edge to the other, a crack a finger's width across running the whole length of it, and the crack, where the ash had been swept back from it, ran with a colour none of the hands that first uncovered it wanted, at first, to put a name to, a slow seep of something neither quite liquid nor quite the ordinary black of a burnt-out fire, the colour, Anna said afterward more than once, of the light that had stood over the roof before any of them reached the house.

## V. Of the King's Hand

Word went up to the hill the following morning by the fastest rider the valley could put on the road, and it is not told, because the valley folk who sent him did not themselves know, what word he carried beyond the plain fact of three dead and a hearthstone that would not stop running colour a full day after the fire that cracked it had gone entirely cold. The king came down himself, and came quickly, by whatever road he judged quickest, with no more than two men riding behind him, and stood at Achadh dhìreach before the second evening was out, looking, to the valley folk gathered at a careful distance from the ruin, exactly as he had always looked to every valley he had ever come down to: a big man, plainly dressed, with a warmth about him that those nearest him felt on their faces like a hearth's own heat though the day was cold and he stood some way off from any fire, and no more years on him, so far as the oldest among them could judge, than he had carried the last time any of their grandparents had seen him, which for some of those standing there was longer ago than their own lifetimes reached.

He walked into the ruin alone, past the ring of ash and fallen roof-timber the valley folk had not yet found the heart to clear, and stood over the split hearthstone a long while without speaking, while behind him the whole of Achadh dhìreach that could walk that far stood in the cold and watched him do it. Anna, near the front of that watching, close enough to see plainly what the others further back could only half make out, saw him crouch at last and put his open hand flat on the stone where the crack ran widest, over the seep of colour that had not stopped running since the fire went out, and hold it there.

She said afterward, to whoever asked her in the years that followed, that she had expected some manner of struggle in it, a wrestling of some kind between a man's hand and whatever force had cracked a stone and burned a house to its footings in a single night, and that what she saw instead was stranger for being so plain: the king knelt with his hand on the stone the way any man might kneel to warm cold fingers at an ordinary fire, unhurried, his face giving away nothing she could afterward describe as effort, and the colour, under his open palm, went out of the crack the way colour goes out of a coal left to burn down past its last spark, fading first at the edges nearest his fingers and then, by degrees too slow for any single watcher to say exactly when the last of it went, along the whole visible length of the crack, until what was left under his hand, when at last he stood, was a stone greyed through and dead as any hearthstone that had never held more than an ordinary fire.

He turned to face the valley folk then, and it is this part of the telling that Achadh dhìreach kept whole, word for word as near as any single teller could manage it, long after the particulars of the fire itself had softened in the retelling. He did not ask, standing there, who among them had broken the measure, though there were those in that crowd, Anna among them, who believed he already knew it as plainly as if Eanraig himself stood before him to confess it, and he did not speak, either, of the three dead beyond a look toward the ruin that every witness afterward called grave without any of them agreeing on quite what in his face had made it look so.

"The full hand is a good custom," he said, and his voice, Anna said, carried no more weight in it than a man's voice carries saying any plain thing to a gathering of his own people, no raising, no anger she could point to, only a flatness that some of those who heard it took afterward for a kind of tiredness and others took for something nearer to grief. "Keep it. I will not make it a law, for I have made none, and I do not mean to begin with this one. But keep it, all the same, for your own sakes and not for mine, and teach it to whoever is too young yet to have learned why."

He said no more than that, and did not stay the night, though he sent his two men back some days later with grain enough to see the valley's poorer households through a year shortened by the loss of Eanraig's stored barley along with everything else the fire had taken, and he did not come again to Achadh dhìreach for a good many years after, so far as any teller there afterward troubled to remember, there being, in the plain course of things, no further occasion that called him.

The valley did not build a new house on the ground where Eanraig Ruadh's had stood. What they did, in the following spring, once the ground had settled and the last of the ash had been carried off, was raise a house a little to one side of the old footings, close enough that the greyed and cracked hearthstone still lay within an easy carrying, and set that same stone, whole as the king had left it, as the new house's own hearth rather than break it up for footing-stone or leave it where it lay to be grassed over the way the buried hearth of a hundred and sixty years before had been grassed over in its turn. It was Eanraig's eldest living son who raised that house and who chose, against some counsel that thought it an ill-omened stone to build a fire on, to keep it rather than quarry a fresh one, saying only that a stone the king himself had greyed with his own hand was as safe a hearth as any household in the valley was likely to keep, and safer, by his own reckoning, than one that had never been tested at all; and it was on that same stone, mended nowhere and cracked still, though the crack never widened nor ran with any colour again in all the years anyone at Achadh dhìreach afterward kept a fire on it, that his own children and his children's children, down a good many generations, laid their own fires and measured their own coal by the same full hand the whole valley had kept since before any of them were born.

Anna nic Coinnich lived a further fourteen years after that summer, long enough to see grandchildren of her own grown to households and to sit, in her last years, the same kind of hearth other households' children were sent to when their mothers had no time to mind them, as she herself had once kept for the valley in her middle years. She was asked, more than once by grandchildren too young to have any memory of the fire themselves, why the full hand mattered so much when a household's own fire seemed, to a child's eye, small trouble whichever way it was measured, and she answered them each time, so far as the valley's own telling of her preserves it, the same way and in the same few words, holding out one open palm, cupped, for the child to see the shape of it.

"Làn na glaice," she would say, "'s gun tuilleadh." A full hand, and no more. And when the child, as children mostly did, asked her why a hand and not some other measure, she would only close the hand slowly, as if weighing what it held though it held nothing at all, and tell them that a hand was the one measure every household owned alike, rich or poor, old or young, and that a custom kept because everyone owned the means to keep it was worth more, in her long experience of the valley's ordinary years, than any law a distant hill might have troubled to write down and send a rider to enforce.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of the Watchers of the Slab

*GE 1,071 – 1,174*

*In Na Glinn Àrda the keepers still say the first watch was kept by a man who did not need to sleep and sat it anyway, so that no one after him could claim the cold had been too much to ask.*

## I. Of the Line Kept in the Valleys

Na Glinn Àrda held no bank and no ditch and no hearing-house, and wanted none, for the households that lived there had never been households in the way the crown of Dùn ìseal understood the word: they did not gather grazing, and they did not marry outward more than they had to, and they kept, from father to son and from mother to daughter, a thing no other valley on the island troubled to keep at all, which was Sloinneadh a' Chlachair entire, every name of it, said the same way twice running or said again until it was. Somhairle had brought it up into the hills himself as a boy of a hundred and sixty who looked fifteen, taking no share of his father's kingdom and asking for none, and by the year this telling opens he had carried it the better part of a thousand years, in a memory that had by then grown old enough to hold more than any one household's business could have put into it.

The valleys knew him for that, and for little else. He was not a lord among them, for Clann na Ceiste had no lord; he was the one who came round at Bealltainn and at Samhain and sat by whatever fire would have him, and said the Line through from Ailean at the grove down to whoever in the house had been born that year, and let the house correct him if a name had slipped, though no house ever found one that had. He kept, besides the Line, the telling of the coal: how the mason had broken the vein at Tobar dhìreach and the lightning had fired it; how na Seachd Guail had been lit one by one down the generations, each by its own spirit; and how an gual dathach that ran through the rock under the hill country held all seven, though no one, not even Somhairle, who had asked his father once and been given no more of an answer than a look, could say what his father had carried out of the grove.

The slab lay above Tobar dhìreach on a shelf of ground that no household had ever built a byre against, a grey stone longer than a standing man, laid flat by the mason's own people over the broken vein when its fire had burned itself out, as the Line keeps it, with a stain at its lower edge the size of two cupped hands that had never, in all the years anyone kept count of such things, washed paler with any rain. Children were told, and told their own children after, that the stain was the mark of Teine a' Chlachair, which had burned in the vein beneath until there was nothing left in the break for it to burn; whether that telling was truer than any other telling of the stain, Somhairle himself would not say, holding, as he held of most things touching his father's blood, that a thing not given to him to know was not his to guess at aloud.

In the fifth year past Anna nic Coinnich's basket and her cupped hand at Achadh dhìreach, the ground a little below the slab's lower edge began, in a wet spring that brought down more of the hillside than any spring before it, to show a crack no wider than two fingers, running some yards toward the burn and then losing itself in turf that had not moved. It was nothing to trouble a herd over, and no house near it lost so much as a lamb into it in all the years it was watched; but it lay close enough under the slab's own stain that the valleys, who had learned by then to be careful of what the coal-marked ground did when it moved, set a line of white stones along it the way the coast had done at the crack Seasaidh's people knew, and left it at that for the better part of fifty years.

The handful had come up into Na Glinn Àrda the same road the tale of it had come, carried by traders and by Somhairle's own telling at the fires, and had taken there no differently than it had taken on the crown of the hill: a household that had never lost anyone to the coal took the custom on trust from households that had, and cupped its hand, and burned no more than the hand would hold, and asked no further questions of a rule that answered its own case well enough. Clann na Ceiste had, besides, more reason than most to keep the handful close, for they lived nearer the coal's own ground than any household of the lowlands did, in valleys where a herder turning peat for the winter fire might, on an unlucky day, turn up a vein no thicker than a finger running bright through ordinary black turf, and know, from the telling if from nothing else, to leave it exactly where it lay and cut his peat a spade's length further along.

## II. Of the First Turn

It was at Samhain in the eleven hundred and twentieth year that the households nearest the slab, gathered as they gathered every year at Samhain, fell to talking of the crack below the stain, and one among them, whose name the Line does not keep though the deed is kept in his stead, said that a thing close under the coal's own stone ought not to be left with no one minding it through the dark half of the year, the way a fire banked for the night is minded by whoever last built it up. No one could say what the minding was for, nor what it was minding against; but the thing was agreed the way most things were agreed in those valleys, by no one arguing hard enough against it to be worth outlasting, and it was settled that a household would sit by the slab from dusk to dusk, one household at a time, turn and turn again, from that Samhain until the light came back in the spring.

Beathan was among the first six to sit it, and no one thought it strange, for Beathan had by then lived among the herding households of Na Glinn Àrda the better part of five hundred years, looking, in all that time, no more than thirty, and had long since stopped being remarked on for it by anyone who had grown up seeing him about the fires. He was Somhairle's son and the king's grandson, and he took no more of a share than his father did, and he sat his turns the way any household sat them, wrapped in the same plaid, eating the same bannock, minding the same fire built low against the slab's foot so that its light would not run down the crack and its smoke would not hang where a watcher needed clear eyes.

The household whose turn followed his that first winter was a herding family from the shoulder of the hill above the burn, a man called Gilleonan and his wife Ìde, newly married that same autumn and glad enough, in the way of the newly married, of any night that put them alone together away from both their mothers' hearths, whatever the ground beneath them happened to be doing. Gilleonan had heard of Beathan the way every child of the valleys heard of him, as a fact of the place and not a wonder, the way a child hears that the burn runs cold even in summer; but he had never sat a night beside him until the two households' turns fell close enough together that autumn that Beathan, coming up early to see the fire well banked before he handed the watch on, found Gilleonan and Ìde already there ahead of their own hour, neither of them quite willing to say why, both of them glad of an excuse to sit a while longer by a fire that was, whatever else it was, warmer than their own hearth that first married winter.

The watch asked little of the body and a good deal of the patience. A household came up before dusk with peat enough for the night and food enough for two, built the fire low against the slab's own foot the way every watch before it had built it, and sat, turn and turn about within the turn, one waking while the other slept a little if the night allowed it, until the sky over the shoulder of the hill paled enough to call the thing done. There was talking, when the cold did not close a mouth too tight for it, and there was silence, and there was the ordinary work a hand can do sitting down, a distaff or a knife and a stick, and there was the slab, grey and close and no more talkative than any other stone, giving back the fire's low light along its stain and nothing else all night for year upon year. Six other households besides Beathan's and Gilleonan's stood in that first round, a shepherd's widow from above the ford of the burn, a household of basket-weavers who came up from lower in the glen only for their turn and grumbled at the walk every time, two brothers who split every watch between them rather than share it with wives who wanted no part of a cold night on a hillside, and a household so newly settled in the valleys that its turn, the first winter, fell to a woman who had not yet learned the names of half her neighbours and sat it, by her own later telling, more afraid of saying the wrong thing to Somhairle's son than of anything the ground might do. None of the six, in all the years the first round held, saw the crack do more than it had ever done, which was to lie there, unwidened, and let the frost silver its white stones along with everything else on the hillside; and it became, before the round was five years old, as ordinary a thing on a household's calendar as a lambing or a peat-cutting, a night set aside and kept, without anyone troubling any longer to wonder aloud whether the keeping served any purpose at all.

## III. Of Ìde Grown Old

They sat their turn every year after that, as their household's place in the round came round to them, and every year Beathan sat his own turn near enough to theirs, by no arrangement anyone could point to, that the two watches came to be spoken of together, Beathan's and the young herding couple's, as though the valleys had quietly decided the four of them made one turn between them rather than two. Gilleonan filled out through his twenties into the broad, slow-spoken man his father had been before him, and lost two fingers of his left hand to a fall of stone clearing ground the third year of his marriage, and mended, and went on herding with the hand he had left, cursing it only on the coldest mornings; and Ìde bore him three children in the years the crack was watched, two who lived and one who did not, and buried the one who did not on the hillside above the burn with Beathan standing by, silent, at the digging, the way he stood by at every digging in that country, for it was known among the households, though never said to his face, that a grave dug with the king's grandson standing over it was a grave a family need not fear would be disturbed.

In the ninth winter of their marriage a hard season drove wolves down off the high ground closer to the fires than any household there had known them come in living memory, and a pack of them was heard about the shoulder of the hill on three nights running while Gilleonan's turn stood at the slab, near enough that Ìde kept the youngest child inside her plaid the whole night through rather than let him sleep the arm's length away he usually slept. Beathan, whose own turn fell two nights after theirs that round, walked up a day early with a spear he did not often trouble to carry, and sat the intervening nights himself so that Gilleonan's household need not; and when Gilleonan protested that the turn was his to keep and not another's to take from him, Beathan told him only that a spear that had once turned back worse than wolves without being thrown could turn back wolves easily enough, and that Gilleonan's children had more need of a living father than the crack had of a second watcher that season. The wolves came no nearer than the sound of them, in the end, and drew off with the thaw as they had come with the frost; but it was the nearest the watch ever came, in all the years Gilleonan's household kept it, to guarding against a thing that could be named and fought, and the valleys told it after as the one winter the watch had proved good for something, whatever they made of the rest.

Once, and once only, in the fourteenth year, a light was seen along the crack that none of the six households on watch that season could afterward agree on the colour of: two said it was no more than the fire's own glow caught oddly in frost-mist, and two said it ran along the white stones themselves rather than above them, low and brief, gone before a third watcher roused from dozing could open his eyes on it, and the last two said only that they had seen nothing and doubted anyone else truly had. Somhairle, told of it at the next Bealltainn, asked each of the six alone and apart from the others, the way he asked when a thing wanted testing rather than repeating, and set down in no telling that has come to us any conclusion beyond the plain fact that six watchers had seen five different things, or four, or none, depending which pair was asked; and the valleys, who had little patience for a wonder that told four tales at once, let the matter drop inside a year and never raised it again in Ìde's hearing, nor, so far as the Line keeps, in Beathan's.

By the twentieth winter of the watch Ìde's hair had begun to go the iron grey her own mother's had gone at the same age, and by the thirtieth it was white, and her hands, that had once threaded a needle by firelight without troubling to hold it close, now held their needlework at arm's length and squinted at it all the same; and Beathan, sitting his turn beside hers as he had sat it every year since their first married winter, looked across the low fire at her some nights and found himself unable to say, watching her face against the slab's grey bulk, whether thirty years had passed since he first knew her or three, for his own face in the water of the burn told him nothing that thirty years ought to have told a man, and hers told him everything.

She never asked him the thing every other soul in the valleys learned young enough not to ask. She had her own guess, and kept it, the way her household kept most of its guessing, close and unspoken; but she told her grandchildren once, in a winter she was still strong enough to sit her own turn, that she had sat thirty years beside a man who had not aged a season in all of them, and that the strangest part of the whole business was how little strange it had come, after the first few winters, to feel.

It was in the twentieth winter of the watch that Somhairle gave Beathan Sloinneadh a' Chlachair whole, the same season his own hair, which had held black far past the age when any other man's would have turned, began at last to silver at the temple, the first sign the valleys had seen that even a son born after the grove would grey in the end like other men, though slower than any of them. He gave it to his son the way it had been given to him, by the fire, twice through without a name out of place, and told him afterward, in the only words the Line keeps of that giving, that a thing carried this long by mouth alone had better be carried by more than one head before the head that held it went into the ground; and Beathan, who had by then sat more winters at the slab than any man then living except his father, took the Line the way he had taken the watch, without asking why it should fall to him and not another, only that it had. He said nothing of the giving to Gilleonan or to any other household of the round, holding, as his father held, that the Line was a matter for Clann na Ceiste alone and the slab a matter for whoever sat by it, and that the two, though they lived in the same valleys, need not be carried by the same conversation.

## IV. Of the Question Gilleonan Asked

By then every household in the round had its own guess, held loosely and traded at the Samhain fire the way a household trades any tale it does not quite believe and cannot quite let go of. The basket-weavers from lower in the glen held that the crack led down to wherever the coal itself had first come to rest, and that the stone had been laid over it by hands older than the Line, to keep the coal from being carried off whole by whoever might otherwise have found it. The shepherd's widow held, more darkly, that something of the sìth's own company lay under it, sleeping rather than dead, and that the watch was kept lest it wake unminded; and she would say no more of it than that, however pressed, holding that a thing said too often aloud grew truer for the saying whether or not it had been true to begin with. The two brothers who split their turns held no view at all beyond the wolves and the cold, and said so bluntly whenever the others fell to guessing, which did nothing to stop the guessing but gave it, each time, someone to argue against. Somhairle, asked more than once to settle the matter with whatever the Line might know that the households did not, always answered the same way: that his father had given him the Line entire and had never once, in all the tellings, given him a reason for the slab, and that a son did not improve on what a father had chosen not to say.

It was Gilleonan himself, old by then in the ordinary way, his beard gone the same white as his wife's hair and his bad hand stiffer every winter than the last, who asked the thing at last, in the thirty-ninth year of the watch, on a night colder than most, with the fire burned low on purpose against the frost and the two of them alone at the slab while Ìde kept the house with a grandchild too young yet to sit a turn.

"I have sat here since I was a young man with two hands," Gilleonan said, holding up the maimed one to the firelight without complaint in it, only a kind of tiredness that came from further back than the cold, "and my father thought the crack worth minding before ever I sat by it, though he never said against what. You have sat it longer than any of us, Beathan, longer than my grandfather was alive to sit anything. Tell me plainly, for I am old enough now to be told plainly if there is a plain thing to tell: what is it we are watching for?"

Beathan was a long while answering, not from any wish to keep the thing back, for he had turned the same question over in his own mind more nights than Gilleonan had years to have asked it in, but because the honest answer, when it came, was smaller than a man who had given forty winters to a watch deserved.

"I do not know," he said at last. "My father does not know, though he has asked his own father, and been given no more than a look for the asking. I have lived in these valleys since before your grandfather's grandfather, Gilleonan, and I have watched the same crack you have watched, and it has never widened, and it has never closed, and nothing has ever come out of it nor gone down into it that any of us here have seen with our own eyes. I sit because the sitting was agreed, and it seemed to me, when it was agreed, no worse a way to spend the dark half of a year than any other. If there is a thing under that stone worth watching for, I have not been shown it, and I will not pretend to you now, after what your hand has cost this watch and what your wife's hair has cost it, that I know a reason I do not have."

Gilleonan took that the way he took most things, without complaint and without much surprise, for he had half expected, asking it, that the answer would be no bigger than the one he got. "Then we watch for nothing," he said, "and call it something, because a fire kept for nothing is harder to keep than a fire kept for a reason, even a false one."

"We watch," Beathan said, "because the ground moved once where the coal's own stain lies, and because a household that has watched forty years does not like to be the household that stopped the year before the thing it watched for finally came. That is not nothing, Gilleonan, whatever else it is."

They said no more of it that night, nor, so far as the Line has ever kept, any other night after; but it is told that Gilleonan sat his turns the four winters he had left in him with no less care than he had given the first, and that he taught the asking, if not the answer, to his grandchildren, so that the households of Na Glinn Àrda came in time to hold it as a settled thing among them that the watch was kept without knowing why, and that the not-knowing was no shame to anyone who had sat it.

## V. Of the King's Night at the Slab

The king came up into Na Glinn Àrda once in those years, in the eleven hundred and sixtieth winter, a year to the season after Gilleonan had asked his question of Beathan at the low fire, riding alone as he rode when he rode at all by then, and found the turn that season fallen to Beathan's own household and to a family new to the round, and sat down among them at the slab with no more ceremony than any traveller taking a place at a fire not his own. He said nothing of why he had come, and the households, who had long since learned not to press him for reasons he did not offer, asked him nothing. He sat the whole night through, wrapped in a plaid a herding wife had lent him without knowing whose shoulders it went round, and watched the same grey stone and the same thin crack the valleys had watched for forty winters, and when the light came up grey over the shoulder of the hill he rose, and thanked the household for the fire, and rode back down toward Dùn ìseal without having said, in all those hours, a single word touching the thing that had brought him.

It is the only night Sloinneadh a' Chlachair keeps of the king sitting a watch he had not been asked to sit, in a place that was not his own hill, among people who owed him no turn and had not looked for him. Whatever he had come to watch for, or to see, or only to sit beside a while before riding back to a hill full of quarrels no one else could settle, the households of Na Glinn Àrda never learned; and it is remembered of that night, when it is remembered at all, for the plain fact of it and no more, the way the valleys had by then learned to keep most things that came to them without an answer attached: that he came, and sat, and said nothing, and went away again, and the crack beneath the stone lay as it had always lain, neither wider nor narrower for the king's own night beside it.

Word of it reached Gilleonan's household within the day, the way word of anything touching the slab travelled fast in those valleys whatever else travelled slow, and Gilleonan, hearing it, said only that a man who did not know the answer to a question and a king who would not give one amounted, between them, to much the same silence, and that he was glad, all the same, to have asked his while there was still a Beathan to ask and not merely a slab to ask nothing of. He died three winters after, in the ordinary way at last, of no more than the years finally catching a body that had outrun most men's a long while, with Beathan sitting the last night of it beside his bed as he had sat so many nights beside his fire; and Ìde, who kept the house and the watch some years longer, told her grandchildren at every Samhain that the question her husband had asked was the one true thing anyone had ever got out of that stone in all the years it had been sat by. It had been asked plainly and answered plainly, she said, and a plain asking and a plain answer were more than most things in this world could claim between them. She sat her own last turn the winter her legs at last refused the climb, carried up by a grandson on a sledge and set down beside Beathan at the fire she had first sat beside as a bride glad of any excuse to linger from her own cold hearth; and the round went on after her without either of them, household following household as it had followed for fifty years and would follow for a hundred more, the crack lying under its white stones exactly as it had always lain, and the slab grey and silent above it, and no one, by the time this telling closes, any nearer an answer than Gilleonan had been the night he asked for one.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of Salt for Wool

*GE 1,174 – 1,273*

*At the ford it is still said that the water remembers two men better than it remembers any king, though neither of them was one.*

## I. Of the Hill Without Salt

Raghnall Ceannfhionn was four hundred and fifteen years old the summer he first rode down to look at his grandfather's salt-kists and found three of the six empty and the other three going the same way, and he was, by the reckoning of Dùn ìseal, still a young man; his hair was the fair, pale colour that had given him his name from a boy, and it had not so much as dulled in all the years he had held the hill for the king, which by then was the better part of two hundred years, though no one troubled any longer to say when the holding had begun, only that it had, the way a river is said to run and not to have started running.

The hill in those years wanted for nothing that grass could grow. Dòmhnall Clachach's grandsons and Fearchar's, and Raghnall's own sons besides, had between them more sheep on the slopes above Dùn ìseal than any household could shear in a season without borrowed hands, and more wool piling in the byres each spring than the weavers could work before the next clip came down on top of it; a man could walk from the gate to the high pasture and never be out of sight of fleece, grey and black and the pale undyed white that the hill favoured, and think, if he had never travelled, that wool was the one thing the world was short of nowhere. What the hill did not have, and had never had in any quantity a household could keep a winter on, was salt. What little came up from the coast came dear, carried on the backs of traders who took as long over the hills as the weather let them and charged for every mile of it, and a bad autumn for the traders was a hungry spring for anyone who had salted less meat than the winter asked of him.

It was old Gormshuil's stores Raghnall had opened that morning, or what had once been hers and had passed, kist and key, through Dòmhnall and down to him with the rest of the holding, and it was the sight of them near empty, when he had thought there was salt enough laid by for two winters yet, that put the thing in his mind properly for the first time, though he had known the shape of it since he was a boy young enough to still be growing. He stood in the low stone room a long while with the lid up and the smell of brine gone stale in his nose, and thought less about the salt than about a five days' ride to the west, on the shore of the lake, there sat a hill that had salt in plenty from the pans of its own western shore, and sheared no wool worth the name, and that the two hills had sworn to the same king for close on nine hundred years and had never in all that time sent so much as a basket the one to the other.

He rode to Dùn ìseal's own gate the same week and put it to the king plainly, the way he had learned to put things to him, which was without wrapping. "An Cnoc Ruadh has salt it doesn't want and we have wool it does. Let me go and settle it. They are both yours; I will only be doing what you'd do yourself if you rode there."

The king was mending a bridle at the time, sitting on the low wall by the well with the leather across his knee and an awl in his hand, and he did not look up from it for the length of Raghnall's whole speech, which was simply how he attended to most things that were not directly in front of him, and no unkindness. When he did look up it was to say, "They are both mine. I will not do their talking." And then, before Raghnall could take that for a refusal and go, he added, in the same flat voice he used for everything, "You can do it, or it can go undone. It makes no difference to me which."

It was as close to a blessing as the king's kin had learned to expect from him on such matters, and Raghnall, who by four hundred years old had long since stopped waiting for a warmer one, took it as such and rode home to choose his company.

He had asked, before he left the well, whether the king would send word ahead of him, a name or a token An Cnoc Ruadh would know for the king's own, and the king had said no to that too, in the same flat way. "If they'll take wool from you for what it is, they'll take it. If they need my name on it first, it was never worth carrying." Raghnall had ridden away turning that over more than he turned over most of what the king said to him, for it seemed to him, on the road west, less a refusal than a kind of trust laid on him sideways, the way the king laid most things he meant to matter: never handed over outright, only left within reach of a man willing to pick it up and carry it himself. The hill was fifty-five miles from An Cnoc Ruadh by the straightest road a horse could keep to, and the ford lay some forty-three of those miles out, nearer the lake than the moor, at a crossing neither household had built and neither, so far as Raghnall could learn, had ever needed to ask the other's leave to use.

## II. Of the Wading at the Ford

He took nine men with him and no more, for a company of any greater size would have looked, on a road that had never in living memory carried the hill's spears anywhere near the lake shore, less like a settling of business than a raid got up in wool merchants' clothing, and Raghnall had no wish to be met at the water by men already counting his numbers against their own. It was a five days' journey by the shortest road he knew, west and a little south, over the moor where Dòmhnall's boundary stones still stood in their quarrelling rows and down through country the hill's shepherds walked every summer without ever once, so far as Raghnall could learn by asking, having spoken a word to the households on the far side of it. Word had gone ahead of him by a faster rider all the same, for An Cnoc Ruadh's own herders had eyes, and by the fourth day Raghnall's company was passing through country where children stood well back from the road to watch them go by and said nothing to anyone until they had passed.

They came down to the ford on an evening of early summer, the river low and clear over its stones the way it ran in that season before the autumn rains filled it, wide enough at that crossing that a man standing in the middle of it could not easily be reached from either bank without getting wet to do it, which was, Raghnall thought afterward, very likely why it had been chosen for whatever had been settled there before his own people ever came to it, though he never learned what that earlier use had been, if it had one. On the far bank, drawn up along the shingle in a loose line that was trying not to look like a line, stood a company near the size of his own, and at the front of it, alone a pace ahead of the rest, a broad, weathered man past his middle years whose name the reciters of neither hill, then or after, ever troubled to set down, though both lists kept the deed whole. Whether the omission was the man's own choosing, a holder who wanted the meeting remembered and not himself, or only an accident of two households each waiting for the other to ask first and neither ever doing it, no one now living could say, and it had not seemed, at the time, worth anybody's asking.

The two companies looked at each other across the water for longer than was comfortable, long enough that one of Raghnall's own men muttered that they might as well make camp and settle it in the morning, and it was the river, running loud enough over its stones to cover any silence a man cared to stand in, that made the waiting bearable at all. Then Raghnall walked his horse to the edge of the shingle, dismounted, handed the reins to the man beside him, and walked into the ford alone, without spear or shield, his cloak gathered up out of the water in one fist and the cold of it climbing his legs with every stride until it stood at his knees in the middle of the crossing, where he stopped.

He had thought, walking out, that he might have to stand there some while before the other made up his mind to answer it, and braced himself for the discomfort of the water without complaint, since a man who has asked another to trust him ought at least to be cold about it himself; but An Cnoc Ruadh's holder was already moving before Raghnall had properly settled his feet on the gravel, wading out with the unhurried step of a man crossing his own dooryard, no cloak held up, no ceremony made of the wet, until the two of them stood face to face in the middle of the river with the current pulling at both their legs and nine men on either bank watching close enough to see, though not to hear.

What passed between them the reciters give short, not, Raghnall thought later, because there was more to it that had been lost, but because there had truly been little enough said, the whole of it fitting easily inside the time it takes cold water to numb a man's shins past feeling them. The hill would send wool, come the autumn shearing and every autumn after, and take salt for it, measured out however the two households agreed a fair measure was; neither would bring spears to the ford again, not that year nor any year after, so long as both sides held to the bargain; and if either hill's people broke faith with the other over the trade itself, it was the two hills' own quarrel to mend and none of the king's, since he had said as much himself and meant it. An Cnoc Ruadh's holder put this last part to Raghnall almost as a question, watching his face for whether the king's own grandson would balk at being told his grandfather's word bound him, and Raghnall, who had heard the king say it to his own face not ten days before, only said that it did, and that he for one was glad of it, since a bargain a man had to keep because no one bigger would keep it for him was worth a great deal more to him than one he could run crying to the hill about. At that the older man laughed, once, short and surprised, as though he had not expected the king's blood to say a true thing about its own blood so readily, and put out his hand.

They clasped arms in the water, each man's grip made clumsier than it should have been by the current and the cold and by hands too numbed for a proper hold, and waded back each to his own bank without either of them once looking round to see whether the other made it, which struck Raghnall, drying his legs by a fire someone had got going with more speed than the evening strictly needed, as a kind of trust in its own right: that a man could turn his back on you in the middle of a river and not trouble to look and see you weren't drowning behind him.

## III. Of the Ground the Water Never Dried

The wool came that autumn as promised, and the salt in return, and if either side thought it had been cheated in the weighing neither said so loudly enough for it to reach the other hill's ears, and by the second year no one on either bank had troubled to ask whether they ought to meet again, only where and when, as though the question of whether had been settled for good in that one cold crossing and needed no further deciding. Raghnall did not go himself every year; there was a hill to hold and quarrels enough on his own side of the moor to keep a man from five days' travel each way whenever the wool was ready, and after the third meeting he sent his eldest son in his place more often than not, and after the sixth he sent whoever of his household happened to be free of other business, for the ford by then wanted less a king's grandson to stand in it than it wanted someone, anyone, of the hill's own blood or trust, to be there at the appointed time with the wool loaded and the scales honest.

It was the honesty of the scales, more than anything either holder had said in the water that first evening, that Raghnall came, as the years went on, to think had made the thing hold. A trade that cheats slowly dies slowly and no one troubles to mourn it; this one, weighed fair on both banks from the first autumn, grew instead the way a well-tended thing grows, without anyone deciding it should. By the fourth or fifth year traders who were no part of either household had begun coming down to the ford on the appointed days with flint from the eastern diggings and dried fish off Tràigh an t-Salainn and pots thrown by potters neither hill had ever heard of, setting their goods out on the shingle a little apart from the wool and the salt as though asking permission of a custom not yet old enough to have a name for what it permitted; and no one turned them away, for turning a man away from a bargain that cost the hill nothing to allow was not a thing either Raghnall or An Cnoc Ruadh's holder, nor after him his own son who took up the same watch, could see the sense of.

In the thirty-fourth year of the ford's meetings, which the reciters of Clann na Ceiste mark by counting back from a thing that happened rather later and is easier to fix a year to, a young man of the hill and a young woman of An Cnoc Ruadh's people, who had between them done no more over three or four autumns than stand near enough to each other at the weighing to be remarked on by both their mothers, were married on the trodden ground, with both banks' households standing for it and the river running past unconcerned a few strides off, and it was the first marriage the ford ever gave anyone, though the reciters differ, as reciters will, on whether it was also the least remarkable, since by then half the young people on either bank had begun finding reasons of their own to be at the crossing on the appointed days whether they had wool or salt to weigh or not. Raghnall was there for that one, an old custom of his own by then, to see the ford give something back besides trade; and standing a little apart from the crowd of both households mixed together on ground that had been nothing but shingle and cold water thirty-four years before, he found himself thinking, not for the first time and not for the last, that a thing agreed between two men standing waist-deep and shivering had somehow, without either of them meaning it to, become a thing that no longer needed either of them at all to keep it going.

There was one year, the eleventh or the twelfth of the meetings, that the wool came down thin and poorly washed, a bad clip after a wet shearing season, and An Cnoc Ruadh's people, who had weighed fair salt against fair wool every autumn before that one, said plainly at the ford that they would not weigh the same measure of salt against wool that stank of the fleece still on it. Raghnall was away in the north that year; his son stood on the hill's side of the scales and heard it, and who rode home afterward expecting, by his own later telling, to be sent straight back to the king to ask what was to be done about a bargain the west meant to break. Raghnall heard him out and asked only one thing in return, which was whether the wool truly was as poor as An Cnoc Ruadh said. His son allowed that it was. "Then they're not breaking the bargain," Raghnall told him. "They're keeping it exactly as it was made, which was fair wool for fair salt, and this year we brought them the wrong half of it." He sent his son back the following spring with a better clip and, besides it, enough extra fleece to make up what the thin year had shorted them, and said nothing to the king about any of it, there being nothing in it that wanted a king's settling; and An Cnoc Ruadh, for its part, never afterward pressed harder than a fair measure asked, nor did the hill ever again send down wool it had not first looked over with its own hands. It was the nearest the ford's custom ever came, in Raghnall's lifetime, to being tested, and it held by nothing written and nothing sworn beyond the two hills' own wish to keep being able to trust each other the following year, which Raghnall came in time to think was worth a good deal more than anything a law could have bound them to.

## IV. Of Murchadh Gearr on the Salt Road

An Cnoc Ruadh's holder who had waded out that first evening held it a further twenty years and some, and was followed by a son and then, the son dying young of no more than an ordinary fever, by a grandson who held it only a little while before the hill passed, by whatever reckoning the west kept of such things, to a kinsman of the old holder's line named Murchadh Gearr, a short, thick-set man with a laugh too big for the size of him, who came to the ford for his first weighing already known on both banks as a man who walked everywhere he might as easily have ridden, on the grounds, he said, that a holder folk could see coming a mile off on his own two feet was a holder they trusted more than one who appeared among them suddenly from horseback, as though he had something to hide in the arriving.

He took the habit further than any before him. Every year from the salt-pans of Baile ghorm down to the ford, the length of what the traders by then had begun to call Rathad an t-Salainn without any of them quite remembering who had first called it that, Murchadh Gearr walked it on his own feet in the weeks before the autumn meeting, stopping at every household along it whether they had wool or salt to send that year or not, eating what was set in front of him and asking after names he plainly already knew the answers to, so that by the time he came down to the water there was not a child on the road who could not say they had seen An Cnoc Ruadh's holder pass, on foot, in the flesh, with his own eyes. Some of the older folk of both hills said he did it only for the love of being seen doing it, which was likely true and no fault in a man; others said, and this too Raghnall came to think likely, that a holder who let the folk forget him between one autumn and the next was a holder whose word, when it came time to weigh salt against wool, carried less than a stranger's, and that Murchadh Gearr, whatever his vanity, had understood that plainly enough to walk fifty miles a year rather than risk it.

Raghnall himself, by the year Murchadh Gearr first walked the road, had held Dùn ìseal the better part of three hundred years, and looked, so far as anyone below sixty could judge such a thing by eye, no older than the fair-headed young man who had waded into the ford at four hundred and fifteen; his own children by then had children with grey coming into their hair, and those children in turn were bringing wool to the ford themselves without any memory of a time the crossing had not been kept, so that to them the ford was simply a thing the world had always had, the way a hill has always had a river running past it, and not a bargain their grandfather's grandfather had once stood shivering in cold water to strike. It was a strangeness Raghnall had grown used to without ever quite growing easy in it, watching a thing he remembered making pass, year on year, out of anyone's living memory of its making and into the kind of fact a child simply knows without being told when he first learned it.

## V. Of the Trodden Ground

He came down to the ford himself for the last time in his hundredth year past the wading, an old habit more than a needed one by then, since the meeting by that year ran on custom thick enough that neither hill's holder needed stand in it to see it kept faith. It was a cool morning with mist still lying along the water when he arrived, the shingle already crowded with more traders and more households than he could remember it holding even ten years before, wool and salt and flint and pots and dried fish all laid out in their long accustomed rows, children of both banks running between the stalls in a way that made no distinction any longer between the hill's side of the water and An Cnoc Ruadh's, and somewhere among the crowd, though Raghnall did not trouble to seek him out, Murchadh Gearr's big laugh sounding over the general noise the way it always did.

He stood a while on the bank, at the same stretch of shingle, near enough as made no difference, where he had stood before wading out the first time, and looked at the ground the ninety-nine autumns since had worn bare and hard of any grass, packed down by so many feet coming and going that it held, even in the wet of that morning, no mud to speak of, only a smooth dark path running down to the water's edge on both banks alike, wider now than any road the hill could show. It came to him, standing there, as an old thought finally said plainly, the way a thing known a long while sometimes waits years for its own saying, that the ground under his own feet would go on being trodden by feet that had never known his name and would not miss the knowing of it, long after the last of the people now crossing it had gone the way of everyone but him and the man mending a bridle by a well who had told him, on a morning near a hundred years gone, that the settling of it was Raghnall's to make or leave unmade and no business of his own either way. The king would outlast the ford, Raghnall thought, the way he had outlasted the grove and would outlast whatever came after the ford too; and Raghnall himself, four hundred and fifteen years old the day he first stood shivering in that water and near five hundred and fifteen the morning he stood dry-shod on its bank watching strangers weigh salt against wool without so much as a glance toward the old man who had once made the weighing possible, understood, with no particular grief attached to the understanding, that he would be gone from the ford a long while before the ford was done with anyone.

He did not say any of this to the men who had ridden down with him, nor to his own son, who found him some while after, still standing on the same stretch of shingle and asked, not unkindly, whether he meant to stand there all morning or come and see the year's weighing properly begun. Raghnall said that he was coming, and went, and put his hand once, briefly, to the packed dark earth of the trodden ground before he did, the way a man touches a doorpost on his way out of a house he does not expect to enter again by the same door; and the ford, which had by then long since stopped needing either hill's holder to keep faith with the other, took no more notice of the gesture than the river had taken, all those years before, of two men wading back to their own banks without once looking round to see whether the other had made it safely home.

# Part Three: The Far Shores and the Name

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Western Shore and the Amber Bead

*GE 1,274 – 1,440*


*At the western Seann Skell the amber-drillers still say a woman carried the finest stone any of them ever found the whole length of the island on foot, and gave it away before she had gone a mile back the way she had come.*

## I. Of the Bay of Hawks

In the twelve hundred and seventy-fourth year of the hill, three households that had grown too many mouths for the grazing above Baile ghorm took their cattle and their looms and their children and went west, over the spine of the island and down through country no hill family had settled before, until the ground fell away under them and they stood looking at open water for the first time in their lives. They built where a stream came down to a curve of grey sand under a headland thick with gorse, in the round manner of the hill, turf-roofed and set back a little from the tide, and they fished from the shore with lines and baskets and did not put out boats, for none of them had ever built one and none of them trusted the water enough to learn. The bay took its name, in the way places took names on that coast, from what a man first saw standing on the headland looking down at it: a pair of hawks working the updraught off the cliff face, hanging so long on one spot of air that the man who told of it afterward swore they had not moved a feather the whole time he watched.

It was the first hill household on that shore, though not, the old wrack-gatherers of the strand would tell you, the first household of any kind, for the low grassed-over shapes further round the headland had held roofs once, and the middens under them, when a spade turned one up, gave back shell and bone gone the colour of the ground itself. The three households let those middens lie. They had come down out of hill country too poor to bring more than they carried on their backs, and a heap of old bones was no poorer a neighbour than the wind. No one among them could say who had raised those roofs or why the roofs had come down, and no one asked twice, for the second asking got no more answer than the first and only put a chill on the fire it was asked beside.

The crossing itself was told for two generations after as its own small history, though it took the three households no more than nine days on foot with their beasts loaded and their children carried the last of it. They had gone by Rathad na Spor as far as it ran west, then off it along a drover's track that ran out into heather with no path left in it at all, over a spine of hill where the wind never once let up, day or night, and down at last through a birch wood into ground softer underfoot than any of them had walked since leaving the valley they were born in. The eldest of the three households, a woman near her ninetieth year named Beathag, walked the whole of it on her own two feet and would take no one's arm, and said, when they came out at last above the bay and saw the water, that she had not believed until that moment there was so much of it in the world, more than any river or loch she had ever heard sung of. She lived eleven years more on that shore and was the first hill-folk buried within sound of that particular tide.

Flòraidh was born into the second of those three households, eleven years after the crossing, in a winter when the sea froze white with salt-rime along the tideline and her mother said afterward that she had come squalling into a world already half turned to stone. She was a middle child among five, neither the eldest who would hold the house nor the youngest who would be petted for it, and she grew up the way middle children on a poor shore grow up, finding for herself the one thing in the house nobody else wanted and making it hers.

## II. Of the Amber and the Wrack

The thing nobody else wanted was the wrack line after a westerly gale, when every other child on the bay went straight for driftwood and the gulls' eggs in the gorse and left the weed itself, black and stinking and thigh-deep in places, for whoever cared to turn it over. Flòraidh turned it over from the time she could walk without falling, at first for nothing more than the shells and the drowned crabs a smaller child could carry home for the pot, and then, the summer she was nine, for a lump of something the colour of cold honey that her fingers found half buried in a raft of bladderwrack and would not let go of even when the tide came back for it.

Her mother knew the stuff at once, though she had never in her own life found a piece worth keeping. The old people of the bay called it sun-stone or sea-stone, and said, without much conviction, that it wept out of trees that had stood somewhere in the world before the world was as it now was; it warmed in the hand faster than any true stone should, and when rubbed hard against wool it would lift a hair or a scrap of down off the ground and hold it there, dancing, for longer than any child who tried it could sit still and watch. It washed up seldom and only after the worst weather, thrown loose from some bed the sea kept far out and gave up nothing about, and a lump the size of a thumb-joint was talked of on the bay for a season.

Flòraidh's find that ninth summer was the size of a hen's egg, the largest anyone on that shore had seen brought in whole, and her mother would not let her keep it raw. There was an old man three houses along, blind in one eye from a spark struck off a flint, who had learned from a trader out of the eastern hills how a hole could be worked through a piece of sea-stone with a flint point and wetted sand and more patience than most men owned, so that a cord could be run through it and the thing worn rather than merely kept in a pouch to be taken out and admired. He worked at Flòraidh's egg-sized lump through the better part of a winter, a little each evening by the fire, turning the drill between his palms while she sat and watched and learned, without being taught in any way she could have named afterward, the weight of hand that kept a flint point true and the weight that snapped a good stone in two for nothing. By the time the hole ran clean through, front to back, no wider than a strand of wool, she was old enough to hold the drill herself on the next piece, and old enough, too, to understand that she had been given a craft rather than a favour.

She grew up the length of that shore known for it: the girl who did not mind the stink of the wrack, who could tell by the smell of the weed alone, before her hand had touched a thing in it, whether a gale had brought anything worth the walk. Traders who came down Rathad na Spor with baskets of pots and strings of shell for the coast learned to ask for her by name rather than knock at any door at random, and went away with beads worked to a finish no other hand on that bay gave them, paying in salt or wool or, once, in a knife of southern flint that Flòraidh's father wore at his belt the rest of his life and was buried with.

Her elder sister, who would hold the house after their mother, thought the whole business beneath a grown woman's time, and said so at every hearth-telling until the saying wore smooth from repeating; her two younger brothers thought it a fine excuse to spend a morning at the tideline instead of at the byre, and were sent home more than once with nothing to show for it but wet feet and their sister's amusement, for the wrack did not give itself up to a boy hunting driftwood with half his mind on his supper. Only her father never asked why she troubled with it, holding, as he held of most things, that a craft which fed itself and asked nothing of the byre was a craft worth leaving be. He was a quiet man who had come west already grown, in the first crossing, and remembered the hill valleys of his own boyhood well enough to tell of them but never troubled to wish himself back among them; it was he who first walked the strand with her after the worst gales, saying little, carrying whatever she found until her own arms could not hold more, and it was from him, more than from the blind drill-master, that she learned the patience the work wanted.

There came a summer, the year she turned sixteen, when no gale worth the name touched that coast from Bealltainn to Samhain, and the wrack lay thin and ordinary the whole season through. Flòraidh took to walking further than she had ever walked before, past the headland and along strands no household of the bay had troubled to search, on the reasoning, which she could not have argued for aloud, that a sea too idle to throw anything ashore near home might yet have thrown something further off where no one thought to look. She found little enough for her trouble that year, a few small pieces no better than what any child brought in, but she came to know the whole coast within two days' walk of the bay by its own name, before and after that, by the shape of its rocks and the run of its currents, in a way that would matter to her later more than she then knew.

## III. Of the Bead and the Road

The finest piece she ever drew from the wrack came to her in the thirty-first year of the hill households on that shore, out of a storm that took the roof off two houses and left the whole strand for half a mile heaped with weed a man could have got lost in. It was larger than the egg of her ninth summer by half again, the colour of a full winter sun through cloud, with a cloudiness deep inside it like smoke caught the instant before it thins, and no crack anywhere in it that her eye, or the old drill-master's, now three years dead, could have found. She worked the hole through it herself over four evenings, slower than she had ever worked a stone before, and when it was done she strung it on nothing, for a while, only kept it wrapped in wool in the box where she kept her mother's few beads of shell, and did not know, or would not say, what she meant to do with it.

Her mother knew. There had been talk on the bay for some years, carried up Rathad na Spor and back down again by traders, of a meeting each summer at a ford far to the east, between the hill and the holders of a red rise of ground called only An Cnoc Ruadh, where salt from the southern pans was traded for wool and for everything else besides, and where, it was said, the king himself came and walked among the stalls, though what he did there nobody on that shore had ever heard told plainly, only that no one who had stood near him at it came away with quite the same telling as the man beside him.

"Carry it there," her mother said, turning the bead once in the firelight before she gave it back. "A stone that size, off this shore, should be seen where the whole of the hill can see it, and not sit in a box behind my loom until one of your own children breaks it playing."

The trading party that would carry her east was five years in the gathering, for no household bound so far went empty-handed and the bay's own wool and worked stone took that long to grow to a load worth the road; Flòraidh kept the bead wrapped through every one of those years rather than send it ahead with a smaller party she trusted less. She was five-and-twenty by the time the party was ready, and had never in all that waiting gone further from the bay than Rathad na Spor's first bend. She went with a trader's party that left the western Seann Skell at the turn of summer, six households' worth of wool and hides and worked stone loaded on eleven pack-beasts, and walked the length of the island in the company of people she had known a month, sleeping under whatever roof would have a trader's party or, twice, under no roof at all with the stars thick enough overhead that she lay awake past exhaustion only to look at them. The amber travelled wrapped in the same wool it had always known, in a pouch she kept against her body under her clothes rather than trust to any pack, and touched it through the cloth most nights before she slept, the way another woman might have touched a charm.

The road took them up through hill country greener and better watered than her own coast, past herds larger than the whole bay could have grazed in a lifetime and byres built four-square in a manner her father's people had never troubled to raise on the poor ground of the west. At a crossing where a swollen burn had to be forded waist-deep, the party lost a full pack of hides to the current before a young man travelling with them, a boat-mender's son bound the same way to sell his father's work, went in after it and came out grinning and blue with cold, holding the pack over his head and the hides inside it dry.
