Flòraidh thought little enough of him at the time beyond the ordinary gratitude of a woman whose own pack had ridden the same beast, though she would remember, years after, that he had laughed at the cold rather than cursed it, and that this had seemed to her, without her quite deciding why, worth remembering.

Twice the party fell in with other travellers bound the same way, once a family of An Cnoc Ruadh kin driving cattle down for the same gathering, and once a lone drover who said nothing of himself at all and left before dawn each morning ahead of everyone else, so that Flòraidh never learned so much as which coast he called home. By the third week the country had opened out flatter and busier than anything her eye had known, smoke rising from more hearths in a single valley than her whole bay held households, and on the last evening before the ford itself, from a rise in the road, she saw the fires of the gathering laid out below her like a second sky come down to rest on the ground, more lights together than she had ever in her life seen in one place.

## IV. Of the Ford and the Man Who Bought Nothing

She came down to the ford on the fourth day of the gathering, footsore and burned dark by three weeks of open road, into a noise and a press of people greater than anything the bay had ever shown her: pens of sheep bleating against the lowing of penned cattle, the knock of a flint-knapper's hammerstone somewhere behind a line of tents, salt stacked in baskets taller than a child, and everywhere the particular high chatter of people haggling in a dozen accents of the same tongue. She had thought, walking the last mile of the road, that she would know the king the moment she saw him, by some mark or blaze she could not have named; instead she stood a full morning at the edge of the trading ground before anyone told her that the tall man in plain wool, moving slowly along the line of stalls with his hands loose at his sides, was the one she had come to see.

He bought nothing. She watched him the better part of an hour, at first from a distance and then, drawn closer than she had meant to go, from near enough to have touched his sleeve. At a stall of southern pots he turned one over in his hands, weighed it, set it down exactly where it had stood. At a rack of worked flint he stopped longer, running a thumb along an edge without testing its keenness the way any other man on the ground would have. He asked the price of nothing, offered nothing, and yet the stallholders straightened when he came near and settled again, slower, when he had gone on, as though the ground had held its breath under him and only now let it go. His face gave his years away no more than a hearthstone gives the years of the fires it has carried, smooth and unlined as a man of five and twenty summers, though he had the stillness of someone who had stood in that exact spot, or one very like it, more times than he cared to count, and found each time something worth the standing. No torque, no dyed cloth marked him, nothing a poor household could not have put on its own back for a feast day, and yet the crowd gave way from him a full arm's length on either side without any of them seeming to notice they had moved, the way water gives way round a rock in a burn without the burn troubling to ask why.

A stallholder near her, an old salt-woman down from the pans with a face gone the colour and grain of driftwood, caught Flòraidh staring and leaned to say, low, that the king had walked that same ground every gathering since the ford was first agreed, and had never once, in all the tellings she knew, been seen to buy so much as a bannock off any stall on it. "Some say he has no need of what we sell," the woman said, "and some say he buys everything already, in some coin none of us would know how to weigh, and needs nothing more from us than the standing and the looking. I have sold salt on this ground thirty summers and I could not tell you which of the two is truer, and I have stopped asking."

Flòraidh had meant to lay the bead quietly in the old ground at the meeting-place, among the other small offerings that travellers left there without much ceremony, a scrap of ribbon or a worked bone tucked under a stone, and go home again with a tale to tell rather than a gift given by hand. Her nerve failed her for that and gave her something else instead. When the king passed within an arm's length of her, she found the pouch already open at her breast and the bead already out and held up on her flat palm before she had decided to do either.

He stopped. He looked at the bead a long moment, and then at her, in a way that made her feel, for the length of that look, entirely known, though she had never in her life stood before him. His hands did not come up to take it.

"Where does the sun-stone wash," he asked her, "on your shore?"

"After a westerly," she said, her voice steadier than she had thought it would be. "Only after a westerly, and only the worst of them."

He nodded, as though she had confirmed something rather than told him anything new, and looked once more at the bead without touching it. "Keep it," he said. "Lay it in the ground here yourself, with your own hand, where you meant to. A thing carried the length of the island should be laid by the one who carried it, not passed off to another hand at the last step of the road."

She did as she was told, kneeling at the old ground among the ribbons and the worked bones while he stood by and watched, and when she rose he was already three strides off among the stalls again, buying nothing, looking at everything, and no one near enough to her afterward could tell her with any certainty whether he had smiled before he turned.

She stayed three days more at the ford after that, sleeping in the trader's tent among the wool bales and walking the trading ground each morning half hoping and half dreading to see him again, though she never did; he was, the salt-woman told her, as likely to be seen at the far end of the ground haggling in spirit if not in coin over a beast he had no wish to own as he was to vanish entirely for the length of a day and be found again at dusk sitting alone by the river with his boots off, and no one on the ground troubled him either way. On the second of those three days the boat-mender's son sought her out where she sat mending a strap, and asked, plainly enough that she laughed before she answered, whether a woman who had spoken with the king himself had any words left over for an ordinary man; she found, turning the question over afterward on the long road home, that she had rather more than she had expected.

## V. Of the Years the Bay Was Told Of

She walked home by the same road she had come, in a trader's party bound the other way, and told the tale of the ford so many times over the following winter that her younger brother swore he could have told it in her voice without her in the room, down to the very words of the salt-woman she had spoken to only the once. The boat-mender's son followed her west the next summer with two of his father's finished boats loaded on a cart drawn by a beast he had traded three years' labour for, and asked her father for her outright, standing in the yard with his boots still crusted from the road, in a manner the bay found so forward that it was talked of nearly as much as the bead had been. She married him that autumn.

They raised three children on that shore over the years that followed, in a house built nearer the water than her mother's had been, for her husband held, as boat-menders will, that a house too far back from the tide was a house always walking to its work. None of the three ever brought home a stone from the wrack worth a telling of its own, though all three learned the drill at her knee exactly as she had learned it at the blind man's, turning the bow between their small palms under her eye until she judged the weight of their hand true; and her eldest daughter, in her own old age long after this telling closes, would teach the same craft in turn to a granddaughter of Flòraidh's who never once heard her grandmother's own voice. Flòraidh herself gathered the wrack every westerly gale of her life until her knees would no longer take the wet stones, and after that walked the strand anyway, some evenings, with a stick, looking rather than gathering, for she said the looking had always been half the pleasure and she saw no cause to give it up before the walking failed her too.

She died in her sixty-eighth year, in a mild autumn with the wrack lying quiet and unbroken along the whole strand, her husband four years dead before her and her children grown with households of their own up and down that coast. She was buried, at her own asking, facing the water rather than the headland, so that whatever came in on the tide would come in past her; and for a full year after, it is told, no household on that bay let a westerly gale pass without someone walking down at first light to see what it had brought, half in the old habit of the work and half, though none of them put it in so many words, in case it had brought something meant for her.

It is told on that shore, too, of other things of those years, carried back to it the way all news of the wider island came, by traders and by the boat-menders who took after her husband's trade and travelled further with it than he ever had.

The households at Cala nan Taighean Cruinne, near enough An Cnoc Ruadh to pay it salt, had begun in Flòraidh's own middle years to pay it and to be counted among An Cnoc Ruadh's households, as every household within a hard day's walk of a hill holding had by then come to do without any word from Dùn ìseal telling them to. No one could afterward point to the year it started or the household that started it; it was said only that one autumn the custom was new and the next it was old, the way a path across a field is new one season and worn the next without anyone marking the day the first foot crossed it.

Cattle were walked up Rathad na Spor itself, the length of it, into the north-west, to a green rise called Cnoc ghorm where until then the people had lived off seal and fish and deer and had never kept a beast on a tether in their lives. It took three summers of driving small herds up by stages, resting them at every burn the road crossed, before a herd stood there large enough to be called a herd rather than a curiosity; and the first calves born on that rise were watched over by the whole settlement in turn through their first winter, the way a stranger's child new to a household is watched, given the warmest corner of every byre and the first cut of every store, until they had proved themselves, calving in their turn and standing the cold as well as any beast bred to it, no stranger thing after all.

And in the north-west, on a rise above a firth wide enough to lose a fleet in, a long-house was raised the length of forty paces, byre and hall under the one roof, greater by half again than any roof the age had yet put up, timbered with wood carried down from Rathad na Spor's own hills and roofed with turf cut a whole season in advance and dried under cover so it would not sag with its own wet weight. Word of its raising travelled Rathad na Spor and down the coast within the year, and for a season it was spoken of on Flòraidh's own shore as the boat-menders spoke of a hull built beyond the ordinary run of hulls, admired by people who would never see it and never quite believed by all of them either.

It stood four winters before a spark from an untended hearth-fire took the thatch of the byre end in the small hours of a still night, and though every soul under that roof got out alive, the hall end burned with it before the byre's own beasts, driven out bawling into the dark, could be turned back to help beat down the flame. The household that had raised it raised it again on the same footing before the following winter closed in, for the ground, they said, had proved itself good ground, whatever the fire had proved about the roof; and it stood after that the way most things on that coast came, in the end, to stand: mended, and carrying its scorch mark where anyone who cared to look might see it, waiting, though none of that household would have said so aloud, for whatever the next spark might prove of it too.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Rope's End

*GE 1,441 – 1,540*

*At the moor of the eastern Toll-dubh the covering stone is still laid the same way it was laid in her father's father's day, and the household that lays it will tell a stranger only that it was Iseabail's way before it was theirs.*

## I. Of the Household at the Shaft's Mouth

The household that kept the eastern Toll-dubh had by then held it four generations without ever once finishing the work their own great-grandfathers had begun, for the shaft the old diggers had sunk into that level moor, straight and smooth-walled and reaching down past any depth a stone dropped from the lip would answer for, had long since stopped being a work in anyone's hands and become instead a thing only kept, the way a grave is kept, or a hearth that has not held a fire in a generation is kept swept all the same. The old plaited cords the first diggers had worn through hung yet inside the house's own door, two lengths of dark hide gone stiff with age, and a stranger coming to that threshold, seeing them hung where another household would have hung a net or a snare, learned soon enough not to ask after them twice, for the first asking got a plain enough answer and the second got only a look that closed the matter.

Iseabail was born into that household in the fourteen hundred and thirtieth year of the hill, the elder of two children, a dark, quiet, watchful girl who from her earliest years had a way of standing at the edge of any gathering with her arms folded and her eyes going from face to face that made the older women of the moor say, half in fondness and half in something nearer unease, that she watched a room the way her family's shaft watched the sky, taking everything in and giving nothing back. Her brother Eachann came five years after her, born loud where she was quiet, quick to laugh and quicker to dare, the kind of boy who could not pass a height without wanting to know what stood at the top of it nor a hole without wanting to know what lay at the bottom, and who by his tenth year had already been pulled twice from trouble a more careful child would never have found: once from a sea-cave the tide had near closed on him, and once from the roof-tree of the byre, where he had climbed to see, he said afterward, whether a man standing on it could see as far as Rathad na Spor.

Their father kept the shaft the way his own father had kept it before him, laying the flat covering stone loosely over its mouth at the first hard frost of every year and lifting it again when the days had lengthened past the shortest, a custom carried on with no more ceremony than swinging a byre door was carried on, and no more explaining given to a child who asked after it than the plain fact that the stone kept a wandering beast or a careless foot from the lip through the months no one went down to trouble it. He told his children, as his own father had told him, that the digging had stopped generations back when the lamp let down on its cord showed no more of the walls than a small patch no wider than two hands held apart, the rest of the depth standing dark above and below it alike, and that a stone let fall after that had given back no sound of striking anything at all, though a household had stood listening a long while to be sure of it. He told them, too, and told it more than once, for it was the one part of the telling he seemed to want driven in past all forgetting, that no one had gone down since, and that no one, so far as the household's own memory ran, had any cause to.

Eachann heard this the way he heard every closed door in his short life, which was as an invitation rather than a warning, though he was careful enough, even as a boy, not to let his father see the shine that came into his eye at the telling of it.

## II. Of the Boy Who Would Not Let It Be

The boy grew up circling that stone the way another boy might circle a girl he meant, in time, to speak to. He was forbidden the moor after dark from an early age, on no account explained to him beyond his mother's flat word that the moor at night was no place for anyone, and he kept, on the whole, to that forbidding, being fonder of his own bed than of any mystery enough to give it up entirely; but by day, through the years the covering stone stood lifted, he found reasons to be about the shaft's mouth that his elder sister, watching from a little way off with her arms folded in her old fashion, came to know for what they were without his ever once telling her plainly. He would lie flat on the moor grass with his head and shoulders out over the lip, calling down into the dark to hear how long his own voice took to come back to him, which by his own reckoning, kept in his head across three summers of trying it, was longer each year than the year before, though Iseabail told him more than once that a boy's memory of an echo was no more to be trusted than a boy's memory of a fish he had nearly caught. Every trader who came up the moor track he asked whether any other household, anywhere the trader had walked, kept a shaft like theirs, and grew quieter, not louder, each time the answer came back that none did, or that if any did the trader had never heard tell of it, as though the shaft's very rareness were argument enough for going down into it that his sister could see building in him long before he found the words to put it to their father plainly.

He put it to their father plainly in his fifteenth year, standing at the covering stone on a spring morning with his hands laced behind his back the way he stood when he wanted to seem more grown than his years, and asked to be let down on the old cord to see for himself what four generations of the household's own telling had never once claimed to know. Their father said no, without heat and without more explaining than he had ever given the shaft's own silence, and Eachann, to his credit and his sister's mild surprise, let the matter lie unspoken between them for the better part of two years after, though Iseabail, who watched him still the way she watched most things, never once believed the wanting in him had lain down with the asking.

Their father died in the fourteen hundred and fifty-first year, of no more than an ordinary fever that took three others on the moor that same wet spring, and the covering stone passed, along with the rest of the small holding, into the keeping of Iseabail and Eachann together, she twenty-two by then and he seventeen, both of them grown enough by the moor's own reckoning to be answerable for a household's custom without any elder standing over them to enforce it. It was the first winter the stone was laid by their own two hands alone, and Iseabail, laying it with her brother that first hard frost, felt him watching the dark gap it covered a moment longer than the laying asked for, and said nothing, for there was, by then, nothing left to say that had not already been said and let lie.

## III. Of the Rope's End

He asked her in the spring, when the stone had been lifted again and the moor had begun to green, not their father, who was a year in the ground by then and past asking anything of, and not any elder of the moor, for there was none left near enough to their holding to have the right of it, but Iseabail herself, standing at the shaft's mouth on a still morning with the old cord already coiled over one shoulder, the longer of the two hanging by the door, tested that same dawn for any rot the years might have worked into the hide and found, by his own report of the testing, sound. He did not ask leave so much as tell her plainly that he meant to go down, that the household's own cord was strong enough for it and had been proved so a hundred times over in the diggers' own day, and that a household which kept a wonder at its own door and never once looked into it was keeping, by his reckoning, nothing at all worth the keeping.

She told him no, in near enough her father's own words, and watched the telling glance off him the way it had glanced off their father two years before. What she had never told him plainly before, she told him then: that she had dreamed twice that winter of the shaft with no bottom to it at all, only dark going down forever, and had woken both times with her heart going hard enough to wake beside it; and Eachann, who loved his sister and did not, in the ordinary run of things, make light of what troubled her, said only that a dream was a dream and a shaft was a shaft, and that he would rather know, and be wrong to have looked, than spend the rest of his own life circling a stone the way he had circled it as a boy.

She held the rope in the end because there was no one else on the whole of that moor she would have trusted to hold it for him, and because she had long since understood, watching him these seven years and more, that a no from her would only send him down some day with no one holding it at all, which frightened her a good deal more than the holding did. The two of them went out on a clear morning in the fourteen hundred and fifty-second year, the two of them alone, with the cord looped twice about a stake her brother had driven the evening before into ground he had tested for its firmness with his own full weight, and a second cord besides, shorter, tied about Eachann himself under his arms in the manner the old telling said the first diggers had tied it, so that a fall would catch him rather than drop him clean.

He went down slowly at her paying-out, calling up to her at first in the old way he had called down as a boy, to test how long his voice took returning, and she answered him each time to know that the answer still reached him; but the calling grew further between as the cord ran out, and then stopped altogether a good while before the cord did, not through any fright in his voice, for the last of it she heard was steady enough, but simply because the distance, she thought after, had grown too great by then for a voice to carry either way without more shouting than either of them had thought, standing at the lip that morning, they would need. She stood alone at the stake with the cord running taut and cold through her two hands, feeling for its own small movements the way a fisher feels a line, and it seemed to her, though she never afterward could put a plain shape to the feeling nor swear to anyone that it was more than her own fright working on her, that the cord went, for a time near the very end of its length, curiously light in her hands, as though whatever hung on it had ceased, for those moments, to need the holding at all.

How long she stood there she could not have said, asked closely afterward, before the cord's weight came fully back into her hands and she felt, at last, the three short tugs he had promised her beforehand would mean he was ready to be drawn up. She drew him up alone, hand over hand at the stake, in a labour that left the skin of both her palms raw for a fortnight after, and did not stop nor rest the drawing once begun, for she had promised herself, standing at that lip with the cord gone light in her hands, that she would not let go of him for want of her own strength before she had seen with her own eyes what had come up out of the dark on the end of it.

He came up alive. He came up whole, with no mark on him beyond the ordinary chafing the cord had worked at his sides, and stood on the moor grass blinking in a morning light no brighter, by any telling, than the light he had gone down under, and said nothing at all for the length of time it took her own hands to stop their shaking. When at last he spoke it was only to ask, in a voice she did not at first know for his own, whether she was hurt from the drawing, and to take the raw of her palms into his own two hands and look at them a long while before he let them go.

She asked him, that same morning and every day for a long while after, what he had found at the rope's end. He never told her. He did not refuse her plainly, nor grow angry at the asking, nor once, in all the years the asking went on, give her cause to think he punished her with the silence for any fault of hers; he simply did not answer, turning the question aside each time with some small word about the cold down there, or the dark, or nothing worth the telling, in a manner so mild and so unshaken that she came, in time, to believe he had decided the not-telling before ever he was drawn back up, the way a man decides, going into deep water, how far out he means to swim before the water has told him anything of its own mind.

They laid the covering stone that same autumn and never lifted it again with any thought of going down after it. Within the year the household's own custom, which had stood four generations as a silence about a thing merely closed, hardened into something nearer a law that Iseabail herself set, without meaning to set anything so grand as a law, simply by telling every soul who asked after the shaft, traveller and neighbour and, in time, her own children, that the household went down into Toll-dubh no more, and would go down no more, and that whoever came after her might keep the stone or let it lie as their own conscience answered for, but that no cord of that house's plaiting would go over that lip again while she herself had breath to forbid it. No one on that moor, in all the years the telling of it ran, ever went down again.

## IV. Of the Question She Carried

She married, two years after, a man of a neighbouring holding who had courted her patiently through the very years the asking of her brother went unanswered, and who never once, in all the years of their own marriage, asked her to make her brother speak where she herself had failed; and she raised three children on that moor within sound of the same stone her father and his father had laid before her, teaching them, as she had been taught, to leave a thing closed that a household's own telling said was closed, though she taught it, her own children said, with a plainer weight in the telling than her father had ever put into it, as a woman teaches a lesson she has herself paid a full price to learn rather than one merely handed down.

Eachann never married. He lived on the moor within sight of his sister's own holding the whole of his life, keeping a small flock and mending the cords and creels of anyone on that stretch who asked him, a quiet, steady, well-liked man whom the moor came in time to call by no other name than Eachann Ròpa, the name settling onto him so gradually that neither he nor his sister could afterward have said which year it first was spoken to his face rather than only behind it. He bore the name without complaint and, so far as anyone on the moor ever saw, without any particular pride in it either, the way a man bears a scar got young that has long since stopped hurting and become simply a mark he answers to.

Iseabail asked him the question, in one shape or another, at every gathering of their two households across thirty years and more, at weddings and at burials and at the ordinary suppers a brother and sister keep between them when there is nothing pressing to say, and he turned it aside each time in the same mild way, until the asking itself became, between them, less a question in earnest than a kind of greeting the two of them kept up out of habit, the way another family keeps a joke worn smooth from telling; and yet she never, in all those years, stopped meaning it plainly beneath the habit, and he, she came to believe, never once mistook her meaning for less than it was, however lightly either of them wore the asking by then.

## V. Of the Hut and the Lake

There reached her, in the years her own children were growing, two tellings from other parts of the hill's country that she heard only as a traveller's news carried up the moor track, and neither of which she ever once, in her own telling of them after, set beside her brother's silence or asked to be read as answering it, for she had learned by then, better than most, how little good came of laying one unclosed thing over another for no better reason than that both were dark.

A herding family new to the hills where the shape called Marbh-bheò was oldest told of lit an open fire against the custom that country kept, being strangers to it and slow, as strangers often are, to weigh a neighbour's fear as heavily as their own comfort; and word came up the moor track, some years after, that the family's hut had been found standing with its fire still burning on the hearth and not a soul of the household anywhere about it, near or far, then or ever after, though every household within a day's walk had turned out to search the ground twice over. Iseabail heard the telling at a summer gathering, from a trader who swore he had it from a cousin who had helped in the searching, and thought of her brother's own silence not at all that evening, only of the hut standing open with its fire untended, and said, when her own children asked her plainly whether the two things were the same kind of dark, that she could not tell them so, not having stood at either mouth of it herself, and that a woman did well not to guess at a neighbour's mystery only for having one of her own.

The second telling came in the years her hair had begun to grey, of a scatter of platforms built out over the shallows of a lake far to the north-west, homes raised on stilts above the water by households that had kept them, by all report, three generations and more without trouble; and it was told that the platforms burned in a single night to the waterline, the charred piles left standing bare in the shallows after, with no household of that lake troubling, from that night forward, to build there again. This too reached Iseabail only as a tale carried by traders, and this too she kept apart in her own mind from anything of her brother's, though she noted, to herself and to no one else, that the island seemed in those years to be keeping a good many silences at once, each its own, none of them, so far as she could tell, speaking to the others.

## VI. Of Her Own Ending

She lived to see her own grandchildren grown and her brother's hair, like her own, gone entirely white, the two of them old together on the same stretch of moor they had been children on, the covering stone still lifted each spring and laid each autumn by hands that were, by then, mostly her own children's rather than hers or Eachann's. He died first, in the fourteen hundred and ninety-ninth year, in his own bed, of no more than the ordinary failing of a long life well spent, sixty-four years old and easy in his going, by every account his own household gave of it afterward; and Iseabail, sitting with him the last night, asked him once more, more for the old habit's sake than for any hope she still held of an answer, whether he meant to leave the moor with the question still hers alone to carry. He smiled at that, she told her own children after, in the way he had always smiled at the asking, and said only that some things were carried better than they were told, and that she had carried this one a long while now without it once breaking her, which was, he thought, answer enough to give her of what kind of thing it was, if not what the thing itself had been.

She never told her children, at the end, that she believed him, nor that she did not; only that she had stopped, some years before his dying, asking the question to be answered, and asked it after only to hear him turn it aside once more in the old familiar way, the way a woman keeps a worn path across a field long after the errand that first wore it has been forgotten. She died in the fifteen hundred and tenth year, eighty years old, in the same house her father had died in, with the covering stone lying undisturbed on the moor a little way off exactly as she had left it every autumn of her life, and was buried, at her own asking, within sight of it, so that whatever her own eyes had never been let see might, at the least, go on lying within her sight for as long as sight was any use to the buried.

The stone stands there yet, lifted every spring and laid every autumn by a household that keeps the custom now with no more reason given than that it was Iseabail's way before it was theirs, and no cord has gone over that lip from that day to this.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of Beitris and the Grey Winter

*GE 1,541 – 1,746*

*At Muileann leathan the weavers still leave one thread of the warp uncut at Bealltainn, and say only that it was Beitris's custom before it was theirs.*

## I. Of the Lamps, the Traps and the Standing Frame

In the fifteen hundred and sixty-second year of the hill, a household of Caol leathan set a hollowed stone on its hearth-ledge with seal oil in the hollow and a wick of moss laid along the rim, and lit it, and found that it gave a small steady flame that made almost no smoke and needed no wood at all. No one on that shore had lit anything but a hearth before. The stone was passed from hand to hand at the next gathering of the households, turned over, sniffed, held up and admired the way a new thing is admired before anyone has decided whether to trust it, and within three winters every house on that stretch of coast kept one burning through the dark months by its bed-place, where a hearth's heat would have been wasted and its light had never reached. The old people said the light was too small to be worth the oil it drank. The young people, who slept nearer the door where the hearth's glow had never quite reached them, said nothing at all and kept their lamps lit.

Down the coast at Caol fhiadhaich, in much the same years, the households of the river-mouth drove a fence of woven wattle out into the ebb where the salmon ran, angled so that a fish coming down on the falling tide was herded rather than caught, penned at last in water too shallow to turn in. The first fence took two households the better part of a season to stake and weave, and washed out twice before the third setting held; but the line of stake-holes it left in the mud, once cut, was used again every year after by whoever held that stretch of bank, so that a channel first fished by a man's grandmother was fished in the same channel, by the same worn holes, by his own grandchildren, and no one troubled to ask any more whether the holes could be moved to better water, for the fish, it seemed, had long since learned the fence was there and came down anyway.

It was at Muileann leathan, in the north, that the standing frame was first raised, some sixty years after Caol leathan lit its first lamp. Cloth on Dia-thìr had until then been twined by hand, a slow business worked in the lap or against a knee, a length grown a finger's width an evening if the light held and the worker's back did not give out first; the frame stood the warp upright instead, weighted at the foot with loops of fired clay so that the threads hung taut of their own weight rather than needing a hand to hold them so, and a worker could stand at it, pass the weft through with both hands free, and beat it home with a wooden sword faster than any lap-work had ever gone. The clay weights themselves, when a house burned or fell in, lay afterward in rows on the floor exactly as they had hung from the warp, and anyone digging into an old house-floor at Muileann leathan finds them still in their rows and know, without being told, that a loom had stood there and fallen straight down when the roof gave out above it.

There was, in those same years, a further thing begun that no teller has ever put a name or a face to. Someone, on some shore no reciter can point to first, began to cut a mark on a fixed rock at the line the highest tide reached, and to cut another beside it at the next high tide, and the next, until a row of marks ran up the rock face at intervals no fisherman's ordinary carefulness would have asked for; a fisherman need only know that the tide is coming or going, and does not, as a rule, care by how much more this month's flood beats last month's. Whoever began the cutting cared. The marks kept no other record than themselves, told no story a listener could follow, answered no question anyone thought to ask of them; and yet the habit spread, in the way a habit spreads on an island where everyone's business becomes everyone else's within a season, until more than one shore kept its own rock and its own count, and no household that kept one could have said, if asked, what it was counting toward.

These four things, the lamp, the fence, the frame and the mark on the rock, belong to no single teller and no single hearth; they are given here together because a chronicle that told each on its own night would tell four small things and miss the one large thing they say together, which is that in those years the hill-folk had begun, without any king's word and without any law, to make for themselves the ordinary furniture of a settled life: light apart from fire, food taken by cunning rather than by chasing, cloth grown fast enough to clothe a household without breaking the maker's back over it, and a way of setting a mark against the world's slow changes so that a change too slow for any one life to see could, all the same, be seen. None of the four made anyone rich. None of them was decreed. They simply were, one year, where they had not been the year before, the way the hill's whole way of living had come to be everywhere at once out of no single mouth's saying so.

## II. Of the Weaver

Beitris was born at Muileann leathan in the sixteen hundred and seventieth year of the hill, into the third household to raise a standing frame on that stretch of the northern stream, and she grew up under the shadow of her mother's loom the way another child grows up under a father's boat or a father's nets, knowing the smell of wet wool and hot stone before she knew much else. Her mother worked a frame with two others of the household in a shed built onto the north side of the house, out of the wind, and Beitris was set to carding before she could properly hold the comb, and to the spindle before she was tall enough to reach the frame's upper bar without a stool under her. By her twelfth year she could spin a thread even enough that her mother stopped checking it against her own; by her twentieth she had her own frame, raised in the same shed against the wall her mother's stood against, and a name on that stretch of the stream for cloth that lay flatter and held its dye better than any other hand's.

She was a tall woman, black-haired, with hands that by her thirtieth year had gone hard and quick at the knuckle the way a weaver's hands go, and a face that people who did not know her called plain and people who did know her called honest, which came, most who had dealt with her agreed, to much the same thing said two ways. She was not, in her own household's telling, a woman who went looking for anything beyond the shed and the stream and the yearly walk down to the salt gathering with the household's cloth loaded on two pack-beasts; she went because the household's cloth had to be carried somewhere to be traded, and she carried it herself rather than trust the carrying to a brother who could not tell a well-set warp from a badly one, and that was the whole of her reason, or so she told it afterward, more times than she can have believed it herself by the end of the telling.

Cruinneachadh an Àtha in those years drew households from every part of the hill's growing country, and the king walked it, as he had walked it since the first summer it was agreed, buying nothing that anyone at Muileann leathan could remember him buying, looking at everything with the same unhurried attention a man gives ground he means to farm rather than ground he is only passing through. Beitris had seen him at a distance twice before, in the ordinary way anyone who came to the ford enough summers running saw him, a tall plain-dressed man the crowd gave way from without seeming to notice it had moved; she had never spoken near him, had never particularly wished to, and would have said, asked beforehand, that a weaver's business at the ford was with the salt-traders and not with kings.

It was her cloth that brought him to her stall the summer she turned nineteen, not her face nor her name, which he did not yet know. He stopped at the length she had laid out on the trestle, a bolt dyed the deep blue-black that only the northern lichen gave, and ran two fingers along the selvedge the way he ran a thumb along a flint edge, testing nothing a stallholder could see him testing, and said, after a silence long enough that the woman at the next stall had time to nudge her neighbour and nod toward him, that he had not seen cloth lie so flat off a frame in longer than she would believe if he told her the number of years.

"It is the weights," Beitris said, because it was the truest answer and the only one she had ready. "Clay, fired hard, and hung even. A frame that is not weighted even pulls the warp crooked, and a crooked warp makes crooked cloth no matter how straight the hand that works it."

He asked her, then, whether she had made the weights herself, and she said she had, her mother having taught her the firing of them along with everything else the shed held; and he asked whether the shed at Muileann leathan could be found again by a man who did not know the stream well, and she said, drily, that a shed with three looms in it and the whole household's washing hung to dry beside it was not commonly mistaken for anything else on that stream, whoever was looking for it. It is the only exchange between them that any teller at Muileann leathan claims to have had whole from a witness who stood near enough to hear it, and the weavers of that stream have told it, ever since, near enough word for word, adding nothing and, they say, taking nothing away.

## III. Of the Wedding and the Grey Winter

He came to Muileann leathan himself the following spring, with no more company than two men leading spare horses, and stood in the shed a full morning watching Beitris work a frame while her mother, who had by then guessed a good deal more than her daughter had told her, kept the rest of the household well away from the door on one excuse and another. What passed between them in that morning no teller has ever claimed to know; what is told is that he left before noon, and that Beitris did not touch the frame again that day, and that within the year she had gone south to Dùn ìseal as his wife, in the sixteen hundred and ninetieth year of the hill, the household at Muileann leathan keeping her old frame standing in the shed against her return, which some of them, in the early years, still half expected.

She wove at Dùn ìseal as she had woven at Muileann leathan, raising a frame of her own in a shed built to her asking on the south side of the king's house, and the hill's women, who had twined their cloth by hand or worked smaller frames copied badly from travellers' tellings, came to her in twos and threes to learn the standing weights properly set, so that within a handful of years the craft had spread from her own shed to a dozen others on the hill without her troubling to teach it as a teaching, only as a woman teaches a neighbour who stands and watches long enough. She did not hold herself above the hill's other wives for being the king's; she held herself, if anything, rather below them in her own reckoning, being a weaver's daughter among households that could trace their blood, some of them, back to the six pots under the oaks, and she never once, in any telling that survives her, put on airs a weaver's daughter had no true right to.

In the tenth year of her marriage, in a winter that began no differently than any winter she had known on the hill, the king's hair went grey.

It went in a single season, not thinning first the way an ordinary man's hair thins toward grey over years of small changes no one notices until they are done, but all at once, dark to grey between one moon and the next, as though a frost had come down on him the way frost comes down on bracken, browning it all at one stroke rather than leaf by leaf. He said nothing of it, and no one at Dùn ìseal that winter was fool enough to ask him plainly what had brought it on, though it was noticed, and talked of low at every hearth on the hill, that he did not sit as still that winter as his custom was, and was seen more than once standing alone at the bank in weather no sensible man stood out in for pleasure. The grey did not go on. It came that one winter, took him entirely, and stopped, so that from that season to the end of any telling that reaches so far, he wore the one grey and no more of it, neither balding nor whitening further as an ordinary man's grey goes on to do, a man who had aged, once, exactly as far as one winter would carry him and then stood still again.

Beitris never asked him the cause of it either, not that winter nor after, though she was near enough to him, by then, that a lesser woman might have thought the asking her right. She told her own mother once, years later, on one of the two visits she ever paid back to Muileann leathan, that she had lain awake more nights that winter than she had lain awake in the whole of her life before it, though not from any fear of him, for she had none; only from a plain unwillingness to close her eyes on a man whose face had changed in his sleep once already and might, for all she then knew, change again before morning. It did not change again. By spring the grey had settled into him the way a colour settles into dyed wool, and the hill, which had talked of little else through the dark months, found other matters to talk of by Bealltainn and let this one rest, as a hill will.

Murchadh was born five years after, her only child by him and, as it happened, the only child either of them would raise together to see him grown, a black-haired boy from his first hour with his mother's hands already showing in the shape of his own small ones, quick fingers that closed round whatever was put into them and would not easily be made to let go. He was given his father's warmth from his first winter, though no one on the hill ever said so plainly in his hearing; the women who nursed him alongside their own children remarked only, low, that he ran hot for an infant and slept sound through cold that had other babies crying half the night, and left it at that, the way the hill had learned to leave a good many things at that.

## IV. Of the Rock at Ros dhomhain

In the eighteenth year of her marriage, with Murchadh not yet three and already walking further than his mother thought wise, the king took Beitris west with him, the two of them and the boy and a small household of the king's own choosing, to a harbour on a wide sea-loch called Ros dhomhain, where a fisher's household had lately begun to cut a mark against the tide on a boulder in the harbour mouth, in the same manner as the first mark cut, years before, on some rock further south whose keeper no one at Ros dhomhain had ever met. Word of the first rock's marks had travelled up the coast the way such word travelled, by trader and by kinsman visiting kinsman, and a young keeper at Ros dhomhain, hearing of it, had gone down to his own harbour mouth and begun a rock of his own, cutting the marks at what he judged, by ear and by memory of the telling, to be the same spacing as the first, though he had never seen the first rock with his own eyes and could not have said, pressed on it, how he knew the spacing to copy rather than invent his own.

The king stood before that second rock the better part of an afternoon, in much the same stillness Beitris remembered from the ford, running a finger down the row of cuts without pressing hard enough to mark the stone further, and said, when at last he turned from it, that whoever had carried the habit up this coast had carried a thing worth more than the fish it never counted. Beitris, standing by with Murchadh's small hand in hers, asked him plainly what he thought the marks were for, since no keeper of either rock had ever given her a straight answer to the question.

"For whoever comes after and wants to know how far the water has climbed," he said, "though I do not think the man who cut the first mark knew that was his reason, any more than the man who cut this one knows it now. A thing can be worth doing before anyone has worked out why."

It was, Beitris told her mother on the second of her two visits home, the longest single answer she ever had from him on any matter that was not a household's grazing or a stranger's quarrel, and she carried it the rest of her life the way another woman might have carried a gift he had given her outright. She watched the keeper's daughter, a girl not yet ten, standing at her father's elbow that same afternoon with the same unhurried attention the king himself gave the rock, and thought, though she said this to no one for years, that the habit of watching closely was its own kind of inheritance, passed from a father's hand to a child's eye with no more ceremony than the standing frame had passed from her own mother's shed to her own.

They stayed at Ros dhomhain the better part of a month, longer than the king's business at any one harbour commonly ran, and Beitris wove nothing the whole time she was there, content, for once, to sit on the harbour wall with Murchadh and watch the boats come in on the tide the rock had been cut to measure, the first true idleness, she said afterward, she had allowed herself since she was old enough to hold a comb. It did not last. Within the year she had a frame standing again, this time in a shed at Dùn ìseal built larger than the first to hold two more of the hill's women who had come, by then, to learn from her rather than merely to borrow her pattern of weights; and the harbour at Ros dhomhain kept its rock and its keeper's line long after the king and his household had ridden east again, the marks creeping upward summer on summer at a pace too slow for any one watcher to swear to, though every watcher who kept the count across two generations or more could point to the difference and say, plainly enough, that the water stood higher on the stone than it had at the first cutting.

## V. Of the Names She Was Given

Beitris aged as her own mother had aged, and her mother's mother before that, in the ordinary way of a woman born after the grove but not born of the king's own blood: slowly at first, so slowly that Murchadh, growing through his own first thirty years faster in every visible way than his mother grew old in any of them, did not remark it; and then, past her fiftieth year, more plainly, her black hair going the iron-grey of an ordinary long life rather than the single frost-stroke that had taken her husband's, her hands stiffening at the knuckle past what even a weaver's hard use could account for, her back bending a little at the frame where it had once stood straight through a full day's work without complaint. She kept the loom to the end, working shorter lengths in her last years and letting the younger women she had taught finish what her own hands could no longer hold taut, and she never once, in any telling the hill kept of her, spoke of the difference between her own slow going and her husband's stopped years as anything but the plain order of things, no more worth resenting than the tide is worth resenting for going out.

It was in her seventieth year, with Murchadh a grown man of thirty-five already spoken of on the hill for the north he meant one day to hold, that she asked him, on an ordinary evening with nothing in it to have prompted the question beyond her own long turning of it, whether he would forget her once she was gone the way a man forgets an old winter's cold once summer has come round again properly.

He did not answer at once, which was, by then, no more than his ordinary way with any question that mattered to him; and when he did answer, he gave her a name rather than any plain word either way. He said it quietly, the way a man says a name he has said to himself many times and rarely aloud, and then he said another, and then a third, and Beitris, listening, understood before the fourth name that he was giving her every wife he had had before her, in the order he had had them, going back further than any list the hill itself had ever troubled to keep whole.

She tried, at first, to hold the count on her fingers, the way she had counted threads on a warp her whole life without thinking about the counting; she lost it somewhere past the second hand, the names coming steadier and more quietly than she could keep pace with, some she half knew already from the hill's own old tellings, Muireall and Sorcha among the first of them, and others she had never once heard spoken in all her years on the hill, names that belonged, she understood as he went on, to wives the hill itself no longer kept any memory of at all, buried and mourned and forgotten by every mouth but his own. He did not hurry through them, and he did not slow for effect either; he said each one the way a man reads a tally he has read to himself so many times that the reading has stopped being an effort and become instead a kind of breathing. When he had done, he said nothing further, no word of what the naming meant or did not mean, and Beitris, who had asked the question hoping for comfort and had been given instead something closer to the truth than comfort commonly is, found that she no longer wanted an answer to the question she had actually asked. She had her answer. It was that he would not forget her, because he had not forgotten any of them, and that this was, for a man built as he was built, neither a kindness nor a cruelty but simply the shape of the thing, the way a warp holds every thread it was ever strung with whether the weaver remembers stringing each one or not.

She died four years after, in a mild autumn with the harvest well in and nothing wrong with her that any teller ever named beyond the plain wearing-out of a life lived its full ordinary length, in her seventy-fourth year and Murchadh's thirty-ninth, a black-haired man who looked, to any stranger who did not know his true years, no older than fifteen summers past his boyhood, standing at her graveside with a stillness that the hill, watching him, took at first for a young man's want of understanding and only slowly came to read as something nearer his father's own. The king buried her with his own hands, as he had buried Muireall and Sorcha before her and would bury few enough others after, and sat by the turned earth a night and a day, and spoke, in all that time, only once, low enough that only Murchadh, kneeling near, ever claimed to have heard it: that a warp holds what it is strung with, and that he had never yet had to learn a cloth again from the beginning. He said nothing further of her after that day to any ear the hill's tellings reach, any more than he had spoken again, in all the years since, the names of the wives who came before her.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of the Flint Road

*GE 1,747 – 1,892*

*At Cnoc àrsaidh the flint-pit keepers still let the first flake of a new working go free to whoever asks for it, and say only that it was a promise once made to a king's son.*

## I. Of the Road He Chose

For sixteen years after his mother was put into the ground at Dùn ìseal, Murchadh sat in the hall his father kept and watched the hearth-smoke go up through the same hole in the same roof it had gone up through every evening of his life, until, in his fifty-fifth year by his own true count, he found he could sit there no longer. No stranger meeting him on the road would have set him past a young man grown, and the hill had begun, in the way a hill will, to speak of him a little uneasily behind his back, careful of him the way people are careful of a thing they do not yet know how to hold. Beitris's only living son, and the only child either of his parents had raised to see grown, he was; and a hill that had buried one wife of the king after another without much trouble found it did not, after all, know quite what to do with a prince who showed no sign of being buried himself.

So he told his father he meant to go north with the flint-carriers, giving no better reason than that he wished to see the pit the grey flakes came out of, which was true as far as it went and left out the larger part of the truth, that he wished, for a season or two, to be a man doing a man's ordinary work among men who did not watch him for signs. His father heard him out standing at the door of the hall with the low warmth he carried with him into every room he stood in, and said only that a road was a road and Murchadh was free of it as any man was, and that he should mind, going north, that the households up there judged a stranger only by the work in his hands, whatever blood ran under it, which was, Murchadh understood even then, as near to a blessing as his father commonly gave.

He went out that summer with a train of carriers bound for Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only hill on Dia-thìr that gave good flint, a grey stone that flaked clean and held an edge no other stone on the island matched, and had been scraped at, by the time Murchadh first saw it, in shallow workings older than any single household's memory could account for; the deep pit was opened only in his twenty-first summer in the north, and he carried some of its first loads south himself. It was a wound in the hillside as much as a working, a hollow of raw earth and broken stone with years of chippings banked round its lip like the tide-wrack round a shore, and the men who worked it, stripped to the waist in all weathers, greeted the carriers with the particular rough courtesy of men who know their stone is wanted and mean to be paid fairly for the wanting. Murchadh took up a carrier's yoke among them without a word of who he was, and no one at Cnoc àrsaidh troubled to ask; a strong-backed stranger who worked a full day without complaint was welcome on that hill whoever had got him, and it was three seasons before the first man there learned, from a trader passing through, whose son he had been carrying flint beside.

On his way north that first summer he came down through Ros dhomhain, where his mother had once stood on the harbour wall with him small at her side and watched the boats come in on a tide the rock in the harbour mouth had been cut to measure. The rock stood where it had always stood, and the keeper's line of cuts had crept a hand's width further up the stone since he had last had it pointed out to him as a child, so slowly that no single year's mark could be told from the year before or the year after, and only the whole row together said plainly that the water climbed. He stood before it the better part of an hour, in a stillness the keeper's grandson, watching him from the harbour steps, took at the time for no more than a traveller resting his legs, and said nothing of what he thought there to any man on that coast.

The keeper himself, an old man by then and glad of company, came down at last to stand beside him and named the marks off one by one without being asked, this one cut in a hard winter, this one the year the salmon failed, this one the year his own father died and he had cut it crooked for grief and never straightened it. Murchadh asked him whether he minded that the sea seemed, by his own rock's telling, to be climbing toward his door a little further with every generation that kept the count.

"I'll not live to see it reach the door," the keeper said, "and my grandson's grandson can mind it then, if minding does any good by that time. A man keeps the rock he's given to keep. What the rock says is its own business." He looked at Murchadh a while longer than the words needed, as a man looks at a stranger he half-recognises and cannot place, and said no more, and Murchadh, who had not given his name at the harbour and did not give it then, thanked him and went on north before the light failed.

He walked the last stretch to Cnoc àrsaidh alone, by a hill road he had never travelled before, sleeping the two nights under nothing but his own cloak and a dry bank, and came down into the flint country on the third morning with his boots worn through at one heel and no coin on him beyond what a carrier travelled with, which he judged, rightly, to be the surest way of arriving anywhere on the island unremarked.

## II. Of the Flint Road and Ailig Spor

The road the carriers wore between Cnoc àrsaidh and Cruinneachadh an Àtha ran the length of the island's northern quarter and back, a season's walking each way with a laden yoke, and it was on that road, over years rather than seasons, that Murchadh, thirty years into his carrying, came to know Ailig Spor, born at a household by a shallow river-crossing in Rathad na Spor's northern flats and grown to a carrier himself before he was twenty. Ailig was a short thick-armed man with a laugh that carried further than his voice had any right to and a memory for a joke told once ten years before that he would produce again, word for word, at the one moment it would do the most damage to whoever it was aimed at; he took to Murchadh from the first season they walked together, not knowing or, once he did know, much caring who Murchadh's father was, and told him so plainly the first time another carrier tried to make something of it.

"A yoke doesn't care whose back it's on," Ailig said, "and neither do I. You carry your share or you don't, and so far you carry it."

It was, Murchadh told his father years later, the truest thing anyone outside the hall had ever said to him, and he kept Ailig's friendship the whole of the years the road gave them, walking the same stretches season after season until the track between Cnoc àrsaidh and that crossing, worn already by generations before either of them was born, sank a full yard below the level of the ground on either side of it, so that a man walking it in a low sun cast no shadow beyond its banks, and a stranger cresting the rise above it for the first time was, more than one carrier swore, apt to mistake the whole line of it for a dry ditch dug on purpose rather than a road worn by nothing but feet and yokes and the years. Murchadh and Ailig walked that sunken stretch together more times than either ever troubled to count, Ailig always a half-step ahead on the narrow going and always, without being asked, dropping back to walk level with Murchadh again once the road widened, a small courtesy neither of them ever spoke of and neither ever failed to keep.

It was on that same stretch, in a winter neither of them ever forgot, that a late storm came down off the sea with no more warning than an hour's dropping wind and caught their gang two days from any household with shelter enough for a full yoke-line. The snow came sidelong and did not let up through a whole night and the better part of the following day, and it was Ailig, not the eldest carrier of the gang nor the one who had walked the road longest, who thought to have every man dig into the sunken road's own bank rather than try the open ground above it, packing the yokes across the top of the cut for a roof and the men beneath them for warmth, so that the gang came through the storm with nothing worse than cold fingers and one man's frost-nipped ear, where an older carrier swore afterward they would have lost two or three had they tried to walk on through it. Murchadh dug beside him the whole of that night without once being told to, and it was there, packed shoulder to shoulder under the borrowed yokes with the snow hissing along the bank above their heads, that Ailig first asked him, not who his father was, for by then half the gang half-knew that already and said nothing of it out of the same rough courtesy that had first welcomed him, but only whether he meant to walk the road all his days or whether some other life was waiting on him somewhere further south.

"I don't know that any life is waiting on me anywhere," Murchadh said, "further south or otherwise."

"Then you're luckier than most of us," Ailig said, "and needn't tell me why, if you'd rather not," and turned over and slept, or seemed to, and Murchadh lay a long while after listening to the wind and thought that of all the answers he might have been pressed for on that road, that was the gentlest any man had ever let him off with.

It was on that same circuit, some years after, that an old keeper of the Cnoc àrsaidh pit-mouth, a man both of them had known the whole of their carrying lives, died in his own bed in the ordinary way of an old man whose work is done, and the two of them walked out from his burying together saying little, until Ailig, turning a half-charred stick in the embers of that night's fire rather than looking at Murchadh as he said it, spoke first.

"I've buried my own father," Ailig said, "and I'll own the ground took no more care over him than it took over that old keeper today, for all the years he gave the pit. A household forgets a man within three generations and calls the forgetting respect."

"Your father had a household to stand over him at the end," Murchadh said, "which is more than some are given."

"It is," Ailig said, "and I'll not say it isn't worth the having. I only say a man ought not to look for more from the ground than the ground has ever given anyone." He threw the stick into the fire whole and said nothing further, and Murchadh, who thought of his own mother's grave more often on that road than he ever told Ailig, found there was more truth in the saying than either of them was minded to sit with that night, and let the fire burn down without adding to it.

## III. Of the Years Between

The years went as years go on a road walked often enough that the road becomes its own kind of calendar, marked less by seasons than by which stretch had washed out that winter and needed re-cutting, which household along it had a new roof up since the carriers last passed, which old man at which hearth had died and which son now sat in his place at the door when the yoke-gang came through. Ailig married a woman of a household by that same crossing in his thirtieth year and brought two sons and a daughter up on flint-carrying wages, all three of them walking the near stretches of the road themselves before they were grown, and Murchadh stood godfather, in the plain way the hill kept such things, to the eldest of the three, a boy who grew, in his turn, to carry a yoke as unremarkably as his father had.

It did not escape the households along that road, in time, that Murchadh walked it decade upon decade with no more sign of the years on him than a carrier three seasons in shows on his first walking, and there were carriers, as the decades wore on, who would not share a fire with him for reasons they gave badly and mostly did not give at all; but Ailig never once, in all the years the road gave them, asked Murchadh the plain question every other man on that circuit sooner or later wanted to ask, and Murchadh, for his part, never once offered him an answer unasked, which both of them, without ever saying so to each other, understood to be the whole of the arrangement between them and the better part of why it held.

"You'll bury me on this road one day," Ailig said to him once, an ordinary evening with nothing in it to have prompted the saying, the two of them sitting out the last of a fire on the sunken stretch below Cnoc àrsaidh. "And you'll walk on with the next lot the season after, same as you walked with me."

"I'll bury you wherever your own people want you buried," Murchadh said, "and I'll walk the road a good while less easily after, whatever lot I walk it with."

Ailig laughed at that, the big carrying laugh that had first drawn Murchadh to him on a road neither of them had walked together yet, and said no more of it that night, and it was the only time in all their years that either of them came so near the question and let it lie unasked.

Murchadh's godson, the eldest of Ailig's three, grew from a boy who ran errands between the carriers' fires to a man walking a yoke of his own, married in his turn, and buried his own father's father, a keeper of that crossing whom Murchadh had known as a young man on his first summer north; and it was watching that ordinary chain of burying and marrying and being born again go round three and four times over on the one road that taught Murchadh, more plainly than any word his father had ever given him, what it was his father's own long life must look like from the far side of it, a single unmoving figure watching a whole hillside of households rise and fall around him like grass under a wind he himself never felt. He had not thought, going out with the carriers at fifty-five, that he was choosing his father's road as much as escaping his father's hall; by the time the thought came to him plainly, on a spring morning watching his godson's own son toddle after the yoke-gang with a play-yoke of bound sticks across his small shoulders, it had already been true a long while.

## IV. Of Ailig Spor's Death

Ailig aged as an ordinary man of the hill ages, slowly through his middle years and then, past his sixtieth, faster than either of them liked to remark on, his back bending under a yoke it had carried without complaint for forty years, his laugh coming a little shorter of breath each season though it lost none of its carrying power to the end. He gave up the road in his sixty-fourth year, handing his yoke to his youngest son and taking instead the lighter work of a keeper at the Cnoc àrsaidh pit-mouth, tallying what came out of the ground rather than carrying it away, and Murchadh, who could by then have claimed a dozen honest reasons to walk the far circuits instead, found himself somehow always coming back through Cnoc àrsaidh at the turn of a season, to sit an evening at the pit-mouth with a man grown grey and slow where he himself had not changed at all.

He was sixty-eight, and had been four years a keeper and not a carrier, when he did not wake one autumn morning, found by his own daughter with no mark of pain on his face and nothing in his last evening's talk, by her account, to say he had known it for his last. Murchadh was two days' walk south at the time, on the near stretch of the road with a fresh gang of young carriers who scarcely knew his name, and did not hear of it until a rider caught him up on the third day; he turned back at once, walking the two days north in one, and stood at the graveside among Ailig's grown children and grandchildren with a face the household, watching him, read for the first time as something nearer his own father's stillness at a grave than any young man's want of understanding, though none of them, then or after, ever said so to him plainly.

He stayed at Cnoc àrsaidh the better part of a month after the burying, walking the pit-mouth alone in the evenings where Ailig had sat tallying, and told the keeper who took Ailig's place that the pit should go on giving its first flake of any new working free to whoever asked for it, as it always had, and that he would see to it himself, from whatever he had, that the custom did not lapse for want of a man to keep it; which the pit-keepers of Cnoc àrsaidh have done, by their own telling, from that year to this, though most of them, asked why, can no longer say more than that it was a promise a carrier once made and that no one since has troubled to unmake it.

## V. Of the Bird Carved at Àth mhòr and the Wolves of Tobar fhiadhaich

He walked on alone after that, taking whatever gang would have him and giving no household of the north cause to remark on him beyond his usual steady carrying, and the years he walked without Ailig beside him seemed to him, though he never said as much to any living soul, longer than all the years he had walked with him put together. The road threw off paths of its own into every household that wanted flint, and it was on the longer of these circuits, far east of the pit, that he came, in his hundred and forty-eighth year, to Àth mhòr, where a young man of that household was cutting a hawk into the lintel over his father's door, wings closed and the head turned back over the shoulder as though it had heard something behind it and had not yet decided whether to fly. The carver worked at it through three evenings after the day's work was done, by firelight and by the little seal-oil lamps that had by then reached even that far corner of the north, and would say, when Murchadh asked him plainly why a hawk and not some other bird, only that the shape had come to him whole one night and would not leave him alone until he had cut it. It was, so far as any carrier ever heard tell afterward, the first bird cut into wood or stone on the whole of Dia-thìr, and Murchadh, standing in the doorway's shadow with a full yoke still on his shoulders, thought it a strange, small, patient thing to have watched come into the world, and wished, walking on, that Ailig had lived to see it, for it was the kind of small thing his friend had always had more patience for than most men gave him credit for.

At Tobar fhiadhaich, many years on, in his hundred and eighty-fifth year, he came upon a household burying a wolf. It lay on its side in a grave dug to a man's depth, its legs drawn up under it as a sleeping wolf draws them, and the household stood about the grave in the ordinary hush of a burying, an old woman among them saying over it words Murchadh did not know. He asked her, once the earth was turned in, why a wolf and no other beast was laid so, and she looked at him a long while before she answered, the way a person looks at a stranger deciding how much of the truth is worth the giving.

"The wolf keeps its own dead," she said. "We have found them at it, on the high ground, more times than I could tell you and told no other soul but the household. A creature that will not leave its own to the crows has earned better than the ditch from us, whatever a stranger thinks a wolf is owed."

Murchadh said nothing for the whole walk back down to the road, thinking of an old carrier put into ground that had taken no more care over him than it took over any other man, and of a friend of his own put into ground with more grief over him than either of them had ever let on to expect, and could not, that evening, have said with any certainty which of the two ways of being buried he thought the better bargain.

## VI. Of the Asking and the Refusal

He came south to Dùn ìseal the following spring, in his hundred and eighty-seventh year and looking, to any stranger's eye, no more than a well-set man in his middle life, and asked his father, plainly and without the long working-up to it that another man might have thought the asking deserved, for the north to hold as his own: the whole stretch of country Rathad na Spor ran through and beyond it, from Cnoc àrsaidh to Àth mhòr and Tobar fhiadhaich and the households between, which he had walked, by then, more times than any man living and knew, he said, better than any man living knew it.

His father heard him out in the same low warmth with which he heard every asking, standing at the same door of the same hall he had stood in the day Murchadh first told him he meant to go north with the carriers, and was a long while answering, long enough that Murchadh let himself believe the answer he wanted was coming.

"The north is Dòmhnall's to hold," his father said, "and has been these sixteen hundred years and more, by my giving and his own good keeping of it. I will not take a share from a man who has kept it well to give it to a son who has only walked it, however far he has walked."

"I have walked it further than Dòmhnall has ridden it," Murchadh said, and heard, saying it, how much of his mother's plain temper and how much of some other temper entirely had gone into the saying.

"That may be true," his father said, "and it changes nothing I have said. A share given is a share I do not take back for a better claim that comes after it, or no man on this hill would ever again trust a giving of mine to hold. Ask me for the north when Dòmhnall no longer holds it, and I will hear you as I heard him."

He gave no other reason, and Murchadh, who had walked half the length of the island more times than he could number without once being told by any keeper or carrier or grieving daughter that his asking was unwelcome, found in his father's plain refusal the first thing on the whole of that long road that had ever been flatly refused him. He stood a while longer at the door before he answered, and told it afterward as the hardest work he ever did to hold his voice as level as his father's own.

"Then I have walked it for nothing," he said.

"You have walked it for itself," his father said, "which is the only reason walking a road has ever been worth a man's while, and the only reason I ever gave you leave to go. If you went out looking for a hill at the end of it, that was your own asking of the road, and not mine, and not the road's."

Murchadh had no answer ready for that, and gave none, and his father did not press him for one, only stood a moment longer in the doorway with the same low warmth he had stood there with the day his son first went out, before turning back into the hall to whatever business the hall still held for a man who did not age. Murchadh said nothing further that evening, and rode out again within the week without asking a second time, north by the road he knew better than any road on the island, past the sunken stretch below Cnoc àrsaidh where a keeper's grandson still gave away, at Murchadh's own standing order, the first grey flake of every new working to whoever came asking for it; and it is told, by those few at Dùn ìseal who claimed afterward to have marked it, that he rode out that year with a face his father's household had not seen on him before, neither the young man's face he had worn going north the first time nor the stillness he had worn at Ailig Spor's grave, but something nearer pride than either, and, close under the pride, the first grievance the hill ever had cause to lay at a son of Ailean's own naming.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Hungry Years

*GE 1,893 – 2,020*

*At Dùn ìseal the grain-keepers still cut their tally by the count Sìleas Bhàn left them, and say so, though none now living remembers why the count runs the way it does.*

## I. Of the Store within the Bank

Sìleas Bhàn had held the hill the better part of four hundred years before the grazing failed her, and in all that time the list that kept her name had asked nothing more of her than that she go on holding it. She was of the king's blood, the eighth name in the list of those who had held Dùn ìseal, counting the king who took it first, and she had come to the hill already old enough in her own reckoning that the households below it had stopped remarking on her face and begun instead to measure their own lives by the fact that hers did not change; a woman married under her rule and buried under it still, and Sìleas no greyer for the burying.
