She was a plain holder, by every account the hill has kept of her: quarrels judged the way her father's father's fathers had judged them before her, a turn taken at Cruinneachadh an Àtha each summer, no law made and none broken. If any household asked what Sìleas Bhàn had done with her four hundred years, the honest answer, and the only one anyone at Dùn ìseal troubled to give, was that she had done what was asked and nothing more.

The store within the bank was not her own thing. It had stood since Dòmhnall's day, cut into the earthwork itself on the sheltered side, three pits lined with withies and clay against the damp, and it had been filled in good years and drawn down in poor ones for longer than any single holder's memory could account for by itself; but no one before Sìleas had ever emptied all three pits to the withies in a single winter, and no one, in the telling that came after, ever forgot that she was the one who did.

The winters before it had been ordinary winters, the summers ordinary summers, and no household on that ground, going into the spring of her three hundred and ninety-third year, had any reason to look at the sky over the high pastures with more than a farmer's usual wariness. The failure began in that spring, a spring so wet the high pastures would not dry enough to carry the flocks before Bealltainn, the rain coming in off the west for the better part of two months with hardly three dry days running between one soaking and the next, and by midsummer the grass that should have stood to a man's knee lay flattened and yellow, rotted at the root from standing water no one had seen the like of. Sìleas rode the near valleys herself that year, as she had never troubled to before, and found households already killing beasts they would ordinarily have kept through the winter, for want of anything to feed them; and she gave the order, without asking leave of anyone, that the store within the bank should be opened to every household of the hill's own ground by the count of mouths at its hearth, whatever the size of its herd.

Grain had come out of those pits before, in earlier lean years. This was the first time it had come out by that measure, and the households said so at the time, some of them with more thanks than others; a household with sixty beasts and four children found itself given no more than a household with four beasts and four children, and the man who had the sixty beasts rode up to the hill to say so to her face.

"You have taken from me and given it to a man who kept nothing," he said, standing in the yard with his hat still on, which was itself a kind of insult and both of them knew it.

"I have taken nothing from you," Sìleas said. "The grain in that pit was put there against a year like this one, by every household on this ground together, yours no less than his. It belongs to the year that made it needful, and to every hearth the year touches."

He kept his hat on to the end of it and did not ride up again, and by the second winter of the grazing's failure the households had begun, without any further order from her, to bring their own surplus to the pits before she asked for it, the way water finds the lowest ground without being told to.

The opening of the pits itself she never forgot, though nothing about it was remarkable to anyone who watched. Two men of the hill's own household went down into each pit in turn with baskets, working by the light let in through the mouth of it, and came up smelling of wet withy and old clay, a smell that clung to a man's clothes for a day afterward and that every household on that ground learned, that year, to know from a distance before the cart carrying the grain was near enough to see. Sìleas stood at the mouth of the first pit herself while it was opened, though there was no custom that asked it of her, and watched the level of grain in the baskets against what she remembered of the year it went in, saying nothing to the men below her, only counting.

By the second year the hunger had eased enough that a household or two began, on their own accord and without her leave, to bring back into the pits a little more than the pits had given them the winter before, a kind of paying-forward that no one had asked for and that Sìleas let stand without remark, for she judged, rightly as it turned out, that a custom left alone to grow its own root held firmer than one she might have ordered into being.

## II. Of Baile chrom

The grazing came back within three years, as such failures generally did on that ground, but the hunger it started did not stop at Dùn ìseal's own valleys, and the worst of it, when it came, came far off, on the north-western coast, at a scattering of hearths the hill-folk called Baile chrom for the crooked shore it sat on.

Word of it reached Sìleas the way word of most far things reached the hill in those years, slowly and by more than one mouth, each mouth a little more certain of what it had heard than the one before it: that the fish had failed there two seasons running, that the household stores had gone to bark and boiled seaweed before the second winter was out, that the dead were being laid in doubled rows because the ground could not be dug fast enough to keep pace with them, and that nothing so bad had ever, in any telling the coast itself kept, been tied to one place before.

The king rode north-west himself with the first grain that could be spared, in the last month of that same year, taking a road that had never carried him before and that the pack-horses found harder going than any road nearer the hill; he was gone the better part of a season, and no teller who rode with him ever said afterward what he found at Baile chrom when he came to it, only that he came back grey about the mouth in a way that had nothing to do with his hair, which had not changed, and that he gave no order when he returned beyond telling every hill of the kingdom to look to its own stores before the next storm season, and not to wait for hunger to ask first.

Sìleas did not go with him. She held the hill in his absence, as she had held it through every absence of every king before this one that the list remembered, and she sent after him what her own stores could spare, three cartloads of grain and a herd of goats too small to be missed from the near valleys, with instruction that they were to go wherever along that coast was worst served and not to Baile chrom alone, for she had heard, by then, that the crooked shore was not the only hearth burning low. The cartloads reached the coast a full month behind the king's own grain, and by every count that ever came back to the hill, they were not wasted.

The man who drove the foremost cart was still telling of it at Dùn ìseal's own hearths years afterward, an old carter by then and glad of an audience, and Sìleas herself sat through the telling more than once without saying she had heard it before. He told of hearths with no smoke over them that a passing man took at first for empty houses, until a dog came out from under one to bark at his horses, thinner than any dog he had ever driven cattle past; of a woman standing at her own door who would not take the grain into her hands until he had counted it out to her in front of her neighbours, for fear, she said, that a neighbour might call a full measure given behind a closed door a lie about by evening; of the grave-rows themselves, which he had seen from the road and would say no more about than that they ran two deep where at any other season they would have run one, and that he had made the sign against ill luck three times passing them and been glad of the horses' pace picking up of their own accord once the graves were behind. It was the doubled grave-rows of Baile chrom, more than anything the king himself said of that ride, that the hill-folk kept afterward as the measure of how bad a hunger could be tied to one place; and it is told that from that year forward, no household within a day's ride of Dùn ìseal let its own store run below a season's worth of grain again, whatever the grazing did, for fear of being asked one day what had become of it.

## III. Of Achadh shean

The eastern springs failed differently, and slower, and it took longer for anyone at Dùn ìseal to believe what the households of Achadh shean were telling them.

The first word came the year the wells there ran a hand lower than any digger's memory reached, which nobody thought worth a rider's time; the second came the year after, when the wells ran lower still and a shepherd's boy walked the whole way to the hill on his own two feet to say the upper field banks had cracked from the dryness, banks his own grandfather had raised and that had never once, in three generations of telling, cracked from anything but frost. The boy had walked the better part of three days to bring the word himself rather than send it by a rider who might, he said, get the shape of the cracking wrong in the telling, and he stood in the yard at Dùn ìseal with his feet raw through worn shoes and would not sit down to eat until he had said his piece through to the end. Sìleas had him fed and his feet looked to before she asked him anything further, and sent him home again on a borrowed pony rather than his own two feet, which the boy's household spoke of for longer, in the years after, than they spoke of the drought itself.

Sìleas sent no grain east that year, for there was, as yet, no hunger to send it against, only dry ground and a boy's report; but she sent a rider to look, and the rider came back saying the springs of Achadh shean had not merely run low, they had stopped, the whole visible flow of them, at a season when they had never in living telling stopped before.

By the third dry year the field banks east of the springs stood forsaken, the barley in them dead in the row and never cut, and the households that had worked that ground for longer than the list could reckon by name walked off it and cut new fields on another line, lower on the slope, where a smaller spring still ran thin but steady. They took nothing from the old banks with them but their own tools and the stones of their own hearths, and left the dead barley standing where a passing rider could see it for years after, going grey and then black with the weather, a field of dead grain kept upright by nothing but its own roots long after the households that had planted it were gone.

The moving itself took the best part of a month, one household at a time rather than all together, for no household would leave its own hearthstone cold a day longer than it had to before the new one was laid and lit; a woman of that ground, carrying her own infant on one hip and a bundle of tools on the other, was heard by more than one neighbour to say, passing the old banks for the last time, that the ground had given her mother's mother a living and given her nothing, and that she owed it no more grief over the leaving than a hall owed a guest who had stopped setting a place at the table. The saying went round the new fields for a season or two and then, as such sayings did, stopped being anyone's in particular and became simply a thing that was said of Achadh shean, by people who could no longer have told a stranger who had first said it.

Sìleas rode out to see it herself once, in the last year of the drought, and stood a while at the edge of the forsaken banks with the rider who had brought her the first word of it two years before, and neither of them said much. The rider asked her, at last, whether she meant to have the banks pulled down, since no one would work that ground again while the springs stayed dead.

"No," she said. "Let them stand. A bank tells a household what the ground once gave, and what it stopped giving. That is worth more standing than pulled down."

The banks stood. They are standing yet, by every account that has come down of that coast, grown over now with gorse and bramble in lines a stranger would take for nothing more than the shape of an old hedge, though the households of Achadh shean, cutting their new fields lower on the slope, have never once forgotten what the old lines mark.

## IV. Of the Deed and the List

It was in her five hundred and sixth year, with the drought at Achadh shean not yet a season closed and the grave-rows of Baile chrom forty winters behind her, that Sìleas Bhàn asked the king, at Cruinneachadh an Àtha of that summer, for a thing no holder of the hill before her had ever troubled to ask for.

The ford that summer ran low and clear over its stones, the way it always ran in a dry year, and the households had pitched their fires further back from the water than usual for want of the shade the willows gave closer in; salt and wool and dried fish changed hands as they always did, and a marriage or two was agreed on the trodden ground, and nothing about the day marked it out from any other gathering Sìleas had sat in her four hundred years, until the crowd thinned toward evening and the cook-fires began to smoke low and steady into a sky gone the colour of a hearth's own embers. She had watched the king greet the households at the river as he greeted them every summer, no different to look at than he had been the first year she herself came down to the ford as a girl of thirty, and when the crowd had thinned she asked leave to walk with him a way along the bank, which he gave her without asking why.

"Dòmhnall set the boundary stones," she said, when they were far enough from the fires that no one else could hear the shape of it. "Fearchar rode with the valleys and was lamed for it. Uisdean burned a palisade twice and built it a third time. Mòrag raided Tràigh an t-Salainn and kept the names of her dead. Iain Dubh died on the shingle for it. Raghnall waded the ford and made peace with An Cnoc Ruadh that has held ever since. Every one of them has a deed the list keeps by. I have held the hill through a bad spring, a coast's worth of hunger I could only watch from too far off to mend, and a drought I answered with a rider sent to look at dry ground. When the list comes to my name, what will it say I did?"

The king walked on a few paces before he answered her, his eyes on the water rather than on her face, in the way she had noticed, over four hundred years, that he looked at most things he meant to answer plainly.

"It will say you held," he said. "That is not nothing, Sìleas. Clachan Dhòmhnaill only moved the quarrels they were meant to end. Uisdean's palisade burned twice before it held once. Mòrag's raid cost seven lives to answer a want that a fair season would have answered for nothing. Every deed the list keeps was also a thing that might have gone the other way, and some of them did, before they went the way the list remembers. You gave grain by the mouth and not by the herd, and a man in a temper rode up to tell you so to your face, and the households have kept your measure since without being told to. Carts went a coast's width from your own ground to a hunger that was never yours to answer, and you did not wait to be thanked for sending them. A dead field stands at Achadh shean because you let it, so that a household two hundred years from now will know what its own ground once gave. That is the deed, Sìleas. Clachan Dhòmhnaill and Mòrag's raid were each one thing done once; yours was four hundred years of not failing, in a country where failing was always the easier road."

"That is a hard thing to put in a list," she said.

"Most true things are," he said. "The list is not troubled by that. It will put it in four words, the same four it has kept for every holder who did not fail: she held the hill. I have never asked the list for more than that of anyone, and I will not begin with you."

She said nothing further to him about it that evening, and the reciters, when the telling of that summer's gathering came down to Dùn ìseal, kept nothing of the walk along the bank at all; but it is told, in the hill's own keeping rather than the reciters', that Sìleas Bhàn never again asked what her deed would be, and that in the four years left to her holding, she gave out grain, judged quarrels, and rode to look at dry ground exactly as she had before, without troubling herself further over what the list would say of any of it.

## V. Of the Giving of the Hill

Sìleas gave the hill to Tormod Liath in her five hundred and tenth year, on a morning in early spring with the near valleys still carrying the last of that year's snow on their northern faces and the yard at Dùn ìseal churned to mud by every household on the ground that could send even one pair of feet to stand in it. The giving followed the shape every holder before her had given it who was not carried out of the hall feet first: standing before the assembled households, in the same plain wool she judged quarrels in, and saying that the hill was his to hold now, and that she would answer no more quarrels from that day, and that the store within the bank was to be counted before witnesses that same week so that the new holder took it up knowing to the basket what stood in it.

Tormod was a son of Iain Dubh, born in her own father's time, a broad quiet man of thirteen hundred and seventy years who had spent the better part of them at the hill's own margins rather than at its centre, minding cattle on the poorer ground to the north and asking the hill for nothing beyond what any household asked of it. He took the giving without ceremony beyond what the custom itself required, knelt to Sìleas in the mud of the yard though she waved him up again before his knee had properly settled, and told the households, in his first words as their holder, that he meant to change nothing about the store within the bank, for he had watched it feed two hungers in his own lifetime from the outside and saw no reason a new holder should improve on a measure that had already held. It was the longest speech anyone at Dùn ìseal had yet heard out of him, and the last of any length for some years after.

Sìleas did not go far. She took a house in the near valleys, within a morning's ride of the hill, and kept a small garden there that asked less of the ground than a herd would have, and more than once in the years that followed a household came to her own door rather than the hill's, out of old habit, to ask a judgement she no longer had any right to give; she sent them back to Tormod every time, and told no one, in all the years the sending went on, what it cost her to do it. She never told the households that the rule they kept about the grain-pits, the one about the mouth and not the herd, had been hers and no one else's before it was theirs; it did not occur to her that it mattered whose it had first been, once it was kept without her having to ask for it. When at last her own reciters set down what the list would carry of her holding, they gave her the four words the king had promised her at the ford, no more and no fewer: she held the hill. The withy-lined pits are cut to her measure in that country still, and the households that fill them and empty them by turns have long since stopped asking after the woman who first ordered it so.

# Chapter Twenty: Of the Eight Winds and Tormod the Grey

*GE 2,021 – 2,210*

*At Ceann leathan the boat-builders still touch the third stone from the landward end before they step aboard, and none of them, asked why that one, can tell you more than that it is always the third.*

## I. Of the Hill Given Over

Tormod was the son of Iain Dubh, who had died on the shingle at Baile ghorm with a salt-man's spear in him and been carried home to the cairn his own people raised. Tormod had been a boy of eighty-seven when that news came up from the coast, old enough to stand at the front of the crowd and young enough that the older men put their hands on his shoulders rather than asked anything of him, and he had grown to a man's full years, and then past them, on a hill that had already buried one holder younger than himself and gone on to a woman who was not of his line at all before it came round to him.

Sìleas Bhàn gave the hall over to him in the one thousand three hundred and seventieth year of his life, a great age for any man not of the king's own body, and yet the merest span beside hers, for she had held Dùn ìseal through years when the grazing failed two summers running and the store within the bank was opened to every household that had none of its own, and she had done it, the tellings say, with no deed to her name greater than that she had held and not let go. She did not die when she gave the hill over. She went to live among her own kin in the valley below the bank, and was there still, an old woman among older kin than herself, when Tormod's own hair began at last to go the colour it would keep for the rest of his days on the hill.

He came to the hall a man past a thousand years old and looking, those who saw him say, no more than forty, dark-haired still, broad through the shoulders as his father had been broad, and he took up the holding the way a man takes up a tool that has been left lying about for some time and finds, turning it over, that it still answers to the hand. The failed years were behind him. He set himself, in his first seasons, to putting right what the hunger had let go: the bank mended where two winters of neglect had let the ditch silt and the palisade lean, the boundary marks between the hill's own fields and the households' walked and set again where a season of each man taking what he could had blurred them past any two neighbours agreeing. He judged as his grandfather the king had judged, in a sentence, standing, and went back to his mending. It was the small, unglamorous work of a man putting a house in order rather than any deed fit for a telling, and the tellers of Dùn ìseal, pressed for a first act of Tormod's holding, will generally say only that the hill stopped losing ground and start their story somewhere further on.

## II. Of the Winds Given Names

It was in his thirty-seventh year on the hill, by the count his own household kept, that word came up from the coast of a thing done among the boat-crews that no one holding land had asked for and no one holding land could stop, being a thing of speech and not of law. Na h-Ochd Gaothan of the year, that every sailor from Bàgh an t-Seabhaig to the eastern cape had always known by their feel and their season without troubling to call them anything beyond "the one that blows off the ford" or "the one that brings the fish in," had been given names, all eight together, in one telling, by a man or a woman no one afterward could put a face to.

How it was done, and by whom, is not agreed between the coasts that tell it. At Tràigh an t-Salainn they say it was an old woman of no family, blown off course in an open boat and put ashore half-drowned, who named the winds one after another as she came to herself by the fire, the way a fevered person names the dead; that the fisherfolk who pulled her out were no reciters and wrote nothing of it down; yet every one of them who heard her went home with all eight names whole in his head and never afterward forgot one. At Ceann leathan they say there was no woman and no boat, only that the names had always been there, waiting under the tongue the way a word waits before a child is old enough to need it, and that all that happened in that year was that the whole coast began, on the same tides, to say them aloud where before they had only felt the winds without naming them. Tormod himself, asked once by a trader who wanted Na h-Ochd Gaothan' names written on a hide to carry inland, said that he did not know where they had come from and did not think it a question a landholder was fit to answer, the sea and its winds belonging to those who lived on it and not to those who held ground above the tideline.

What can be said plainly is this: before that year, Na h-Ochd Gaothan went unnamed on every coast of Dia-thìr that any telling reaches. After it, every coast used the same eight names, in the same order, for the same winds, and no coast since has changed one of them, though what the names themselves mean, if they ever meant anything beyond the wind each stands for, is dark even to the sailors who say them oftenest and could, any one of them, tell you at a glance which wind was rising and which was dying by the smell of the air alone.

A carrier of the hill's own salt, a man named Fearchar Gobha who ran the road between Dùn ìseal and the coast twice in every month of his working life, brought the eight names up to Tormod himself within the year, having heard them first at the fair from a crew he had never met before and never met again. He had gone down to the strand meaning only to trade, he told Tormod, and had come away with eight words in his mouth that he had not owned when he went down, said in an order he found he could not say them out of even when he tried it as a jest, the way a man cannot say the days of a week backward without stumbling. Tormod asked him to say them once more, standing in the hall with the fire between them, and Fearchar said them, and Tormod said nothing for a while after, and then only that a landholder had no business owning what belonged to the sea, and sent Fearchar back to his road with a measure of grain for his trouble and no more said on it. It is the one telling of that year that gives Tormod a voice at all in the matter of the naming, and it gives him, as the tellings of that hill are generally content to give him, very little.

## III. Of the Stones at Ceann leathan

The stones came after the names, and came, unlike the names, from a place and a hand that the tellings agree on. Ceann leathan stands on a point where the coast turns, a long low finger of rock run out into water that is calm on one side of it and broken on the other, and the boat-crews of that shore had always put out from the calm side and come home to it, so that the point itself was, before anything was set upon it, already a place where every crossing began and every crossing that went well was seen to end.

In the thirty-seventh year after the naming, the households of that point set eight standing stones in a ring on the seaward end of it, each a man's height or better, and gave one to each of the eight named winds, so that a sailor going out could lay a hand on the stone of the wind he wanted and, the telling has it, ask it for that wind and no other. Whether the wind ever came for the asking is not a thing any telling troubles to say either way; what is told is that the custom held from that year, and holds still on every coast that has heard of it, and that no sailor of Dia-thìr, however far past believing in the working of it he may claim to be over his own hearth, has ever been known to walk past the ring at Ceann leathan without laying a hand on one stone or another as he goes down to his boat.

The setting of the stones is remembered, unlike the naming, as the work of named hands: three brothers of the point, Aonghas, Dùghlas and Ailig mac Torcaill, who quarried the eight stones from a single outcrop above the landing rather than bring them from elsewhere, reasoning, Dùghlas is said to have said, that a stone that had always stood on that point would know its own wind better than a stone dragged in from a hill that had never felt sea air. It took the three of them the better part of two years to cut and drag and raise all eight, and the ring was not set true at the first standing: the stone of the wind that blows hardest off the open water was found, after one bad winter, to have settled crooked in ground softer than the rest, and had to be dug out and reset on a footing of smaller stones packed beneath it, which is why, of the eight, it alone stands markedly straighter and newer-looking than its fellows, a thing every boat-builder on that coast can point to and none of them, until told, ever thinks to ask the reason for.

The wind-names crossed water in their own time, forty years on. Eilean fhada, the long island that lies off the northern cape and takes the worst of every storm that comes down out of the grey mist to the north before the mainland feels it, kept no stones and had no point shaped for a ring of them, but its people cut the eight names as notches into the rock of its highest ground, one notch facing each way the wind could come from, so that a man caught on the height in weather too thick to see the coastline by could still lay his hand along the rock and find, by the run of the cuts under his fingers, which way he stood. The notches are there yet, cut deeper by every generation that has found them worn shallow and cut them again, and no one on that island now living remembers a time when the eight ways were reckoned by anything else.

## IV. Of the Heirs He Buried

Tormod had married in his three hundredth year, long before he held the hill, a woman of a household under the eastern shoulder of Dùn ìseal named for nothing that survives beyond her own children's naming of her as their mother, and she gave him three sons before she died an old woman in her own right, having lived out a full span and never seen any of the three grow older to look at than a young man.

That eldest son died first, in the thirtieth year of Tormod's holding, a man of eleven hundred years worn out at last by na Bliadhnachan Fada that had carried him further than any man not of the king's blood could go, and Tormod stood at the burying dark-haired still, and heard himself named by his own son's children as their grandfather's father, which none of them, being young, thought strange, not having any other grandfather's father living to measure it against.

The second son, who had never cared for the hill's holding and had spent his whole life on the western grazing with the sheep his brother thought beneath him, died sixty years after the first, an old man himself by then, and was buried, at his own asking made long before, on the slope where he had herded, with a cairn no larger than any shepherd's. Tormod rode out to see it raised and stood by it a long while, and was heard to say only that a man ought to be let choose his own ground if nothing else was left him to choose, which the tellings of the western slope have kept ever since as though it were a judgement, though it answered no dispute and settled no grazing; it was simply the thing he said, standing there, and it stuck to the place the way such things do.

The third, the youngest and the one Tormod had thought might outlast him if any of the three could, having been the strongest as a boy and the last to grey, died in the hundred and seventieth year of his father's holding, having lived to see his own grandchildren's children and having asked his father, near the end, propped up in the same bed he had been born in, whether it hurt, being left each time. Tormod sat with the old man's hand in his own hand, which the tellings note was by then the smoother of the two hands in that room by a very great margin, and told him no. It was the only lie the tellings ever charge against him, and they charge it gently, being of the opinion, most of them, that a man burying his third son has earned the right to one.

By the time the third son was in the ground, Tormod Liath had held Dùn ìseal longer than any holder before him whose length is remembered at all, and the hill had begun, without anyone deciding it should, to reckon its own age by how long Tormod had held it rather than by the year, the way a household with a very old grandmother will say "since before Granny's time" of anything far enough back, meaning nothing more precise than a long while.

## V. Of the Second Bank

It was in the year the hill's people count as his hundred and fifty-third that Tormod set the second bank, the one that still stands outside the first and gives Dùn ìseal the ground it needed once its granaries had grown past what the old ditch could shelter. He set it the way his father's brother Dòmhnall had set his boundary stones, walking it himself before he asked a spade of anyone else, pacing the line in the frost of two winters running until he was satisfied it took in the low ground by the spring without giving up the height that mattered for a watch-fire, and only then calling the households in to dig.

They dug through a spring and a summer, households that had never worked a spade together before finding, as households will, that the ones who talked least worked longest, and the bank went up doubling the hill's ground within it, so that Dùn ìseal from that year held near a hundred houses inside its earth where forty had stood before, with room, Tormod said when they asked him why so much more than they yet needed, for what would come after him, though he did not say, and none of them thought to ask, what he reckoned that to be.

## VI. Of the Grey

He went truly grey in the years the second bank was going up, not all at once as the king himself was said, in an older telling that had reached even that hill by then, to have gone grey in a single winter and no further, but slowly, the black going out of his hair the way colour goes out of cloth left too long in the weather, so slowly that no one household could have said which season it had happened in, only that a man they remembered dark was, some years on, a man they could not remember dark at all.

By his hundred and seventy-fifth year of holding he was grey through, brows and beard with the rest, and stooped a little at the shoulder where he had once stood straight, and the young of the hill, who had never known him any other way, took him for what he plainly appeared: the oldest man on Dùn ìseal, older, they said among themselves, than anyone could well remember, older than the second bank he had raised with his own hands, older, some of the very young said, than the hill itself. It did not trouble him to be thought so, and by the reckoning that matters to the tellings that keep this he was in fact the oldest living thing on that ground bar the oaks of the grove he had never once travelled north to see; he wore the age the young gave him the way a man wears a coat cut generously, room enough in it for a frame he had never quite grown into.

## VII. Of the King at the Gate

He was an old man by every mark anyone on the hill could read, in the hundred and ninety-third year of his holding, when the king came in at Dùn ìseal's gate one spring morning with no more than four of his household about him and no word sent ahead, as he did from time to time on no season anyone could predict, to see how a hill he had given into other hands was being kept.

Tormod came out from the hall to meet him bareheaded, as every holder of that hill had always come to meet him, and went down on one knee in the mud of the gateway the way his father Iain Dubh had gone down before him, and the king put a hand under his arm, as he always did, to raise him before the knee had fully bent, an old habit of his that the hill's people had long since stopped remarking on. It was only when Tormod was upright again, an old grey man more than fifteen hundred years old steadied by the arm of another, that the gathered household of the hill, watching from the gate and the bank above it, saw the two of them standing side by side in the one morning light: the king, grey-headed but unlined, no more than forty by the only measure any of them had ever been given to judge a man's years, and beside him the oldest man any of them had ever known, kneeling to him, and being raised by him, as a son might be raised by his father, though every soul on that hill knew, without anyone troubling to say it aloud, that it stood the other way about: that the unlined man had buried Tormod's father and the mother who bore Tormod, and had stood at every such gate on the island always the same age, while the sons and grandsons and great-grandsons he raised from the mud went grey and old and were carried to the cairn in their own turn.

One of the household who watched from the bank that morning was a girl of nine or ten, a granddaughter of Tormod's second son and so already three generations down from the old man in the gateway, and she is remembered, in the one telling that troubles to name a witness at all, as having asked her mother, in a voice not lowered as much as it should have been, why the young man was letting the old one call him nothing more than what a stranger might be called at a gate. Her mother said nothing there, in the crowd; she took the girl home and told her that evening, by the fire, what every household on that hill already knew and few of them said outright even to their own children until a child's own question forced the saying: that the young man was the king, that he did not age as other men aged, and that the old man he had raised out of the mud was the girl's own great-grandfather, who had held that hill longer than her mother's mother could remember any other holder of it.

None of the young who watched that morning had words ready for what they were looking at. It had been true of every holder before Tormod and would be true of every holder after him, and had been said, in one shape or another, at every gate on the island where the king had ever stood; but it is the tellings of Dùn ìseal in particular that keep the picture of that one spring morning, the old grey man on his feet again with the king's hand still under his arm a moment longer than it needed to be, because it was at Dùn ìseal, in the years just after, that the young first began to say aloud the thing their grandparents had only ever thought.

## VIII. Of the Name They Gave Themselves

By Tormod's hundred and ninety-first year of holding, the two thousand two hundred and first year of the hill, the children of that generation had begun, without any elder telling them to, calling themselves by a name none of their grandparents had used for themselves. Hill-folk was true enough of where they lived and said nothing of what they were. Clann nan Dè belonged by then to a handful of families near Na Glinn Àrda who traced their blood straight back to the grove and would not have thanked a Dùn ìseal fisherman's son for claiming it alongside them. The children took Dia-thìrich instead, the people of Dia-thìr, and gave the island the same name in the same breath, Dia-thìr and no other word.

No one now living, and no telling that reaches this far back with any confidence, can say whose mouth said it first, or whether it was said first at Dùn ìseal at all rather than carried there already made from An Cnoc Ruadh or the ford or some hearth further off that kept no memory of having coined it. What is agreed is only that it did not arrive as a law or a naming ordered by any holder, king or otherwise; it arrived the way the wind-names had arrived a hundred and fifty years before, all at once and everywhere, so that within a generation of children the old words for what they were had gone out of use among the young without ever being forbidden, and the elders who still said hill-folk out of habit found themselves, more and more, being gently corrected by their own grandchildren.

Tormod heard it first, the tellings say, from a boy of perhaps seven, one of the households settled along the new ground the second bank had opened, who told him plainly, when the old man asked what clan he belonged to, that he was Dia-thìreach, and that everyone was, and seemed puzzled that so old a man should need telling. Tormod, who was by then further past a thousand years of life than any of his own three dead sons had lived altogether, said only that it was a good enough name for a good enough island, and let the boy go back to his play; and that, so far as any telling of that hill preserves, is the whole of what the ninth of Rìghrean na Cloiche ever said, for or against, on the matter of what his people had decided, of their own accord and without asking him, that they were.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of the Forbidden Marriage and the Trench

*GE 2,211 – 2,327*

## I. Of Ealag and Torcall Tochlair

*This is told at Dùn ìseal by the hearths that still keep the shape of the old spring, though the two households that once stood there are long since gone into other names.*

Ealag was born in a household under the eastern shoulder of Dùn ìseal, the fourth of six, in a year when the hill's flocks did well and nobody troubled to remember which year that was by any other mark. Torcall was born two households over, the son of a man who gathered an gual dathach where it showed in the peat-banks and stream-cuts of the hills and was called Tochlair for it, the digger, a name that stuck to the boy before he had dug so much as a post-hole. The two families kept sheep on the same slope and drew water from the same spring, and the children of both ran together from as far back as either of them could afterward call to mind. Neither could say when it had started, only that it had always been so.

There is a telling, kept longer in that house than most of the rest, of the two of them as children no higher than the sheep-pen rail, caught out in a storm on the open hill with the flock scattered and no grown person near, and Torcall standing over Ealag with his own coat pulled off and held above her head against the rain until his father found them both wet through and laughing under it, the coat long since useless and neither of them minding. Whether it happened as the telling has it, or happened at all, no one now living can say; but it was told at both hearths for years afterward, by the mothers of the two children to each other, as proof of a thing neither household thought it needed proving.

They grew up counting each other's sheep by the ear-notch without being asked, and knowing which of the two spring paths the other would take of a morning by nothing more than habit, and by the time they were old enough to be spoken of for marrying, the whole slope had long since stopped thinking of them as two people who might or might not be joined and thought of them instead as a thing already joined, waiting only for its proper words.

By the time Ealag was grown enough to be spoken of for marrying, nobody on the hill thought to ask whether she and Torcall would be given to each other. It was taken for a settled thing, the way the path from the spring to the houses was taken for a settled thing, worn in by so many feet that no one remembered the first of them. Torcall asked her outright at the shearing in the year she turned sixteen, standing in wet wool to the elbows with the whole slope watching, and she laughed at him for asking what everyone already knew, and said yes in front of forty people, and that should have been the end of the matter and the start of another.

Word went between the two households in the old way, an elder of each sent to the other's hearth with a measure of salt, which is accepted or is not. Torcall's mother carried the salt across herself, being a woman who trusted nothing she had not done with her own hands, and she was not gone long. She came back with the salt still in its cloth and her face set in a way her son had not seen it set before, not at his father's dying, not at any hard winter.

"They will not have it," she said.

"Which of them said so?"

"All of them. The old man spoke for the rest, but I watched their faces, and none of them thought he spoke wrong."

Torcall went himself the next day, to hear it said to his own face rather than carried to him at second hand, and the elders of Ealag's household gathered in their doorway to tell him so, all of them together, as if one alone could not be trusted to hold the line against him. He asked why. He asked it plainly, the way a man asks the price of a thing before he buys it, expecting a plain answer back.

"It cannot be," said the eldest, a woman named Beathag who had held that household longer than Torcall had been alive.

"Cannot, or will not?"

"It cannot be," Beathag said again, as though the words themselves, said twice, were an answer, and turned back into the house.

He went to Ealag's father next, and her father would not meet his eye, and he went to two of her uncles, and they said the same three words between them and would say no more, and in the end he stood in the yard with the sheep moving round his legs and understood that no one on that hill was going to tell him why, because either none of them knew, or all of them had sworn not to say, and there was no way from where he stood to tell one from the other.

He tried the oldest woman of his own household too, thinking that if the refusal came of some old quarrel it might be known on his own side of it as well as the other, but his grandmother only shook her head at him and said that she had never heard the two families named together in any grievance in all her years, not over grazing, not over water, not over anything a person could point to, and that this was the strangest part of it to her: a refusal with no history behind it that she had ever been told of, standing as flat and as final as one with forty years of bad blood at its back.

Last of all he went to Ealag, at the spring, in the evening, when the water was the colour of the sky and there was nobody else to hear them.

"Do you know why?" he said.

"No," she said. "I asked my mother. She held my two hands in hers and told me it was not a thing I would ever be told, not by her, not by anyone living, and that I was to stop asking, because asking would not open it and might close other doors besides. Then she cried, which I have never seen her do, not once, not at any burying."

"That is not a reason."

"No," Ealag said. "It is not."

They stood a while at the spring without more to say, because there was nothing further to be got from either side of it, no thread that would not come away loose in the hand for the pulling. Of the true cause the households never spoke again in either of their lifetimes, and no telling that has come down from that hill has ever named it; it is set down here only as it stands, refused and unexplained, because that is how it stands in every version the reciters keep. Already, in those years, the Dia-thìrich had begun to order themselves by blood in ways that ran deeper than any one match or any one grudge, long before the vein gave them further cause to reckon who was kin to whom; and whatever lay beneath the refusal of Ealag and Torcall, it lay in that older ordering, and was not brought out into the light for either of them to see.

## II. Of the Marriage at the Ford

Ealag was given instead to a household of the ford, where salt had first been traded for wool in the days of Raghnall Ceannfhionn, and where households gathered every year for the fair in the same season the shearing had been held on the hill. Her husband was a fisher of the shallows there, a quiet man named Donnchadh who had asked for her honestly and without knowing, when he asked, that there had ever been another asking before his. She went to him in the year she turned seventeen, the two thousand two hundred and twenty-fourth year of the hill, the spring after the refusal.

She was married at the ford itself, in sight of the water, with the households of the ford standing about her on the bank in their fair-day cloaks and the salmon running so thick that season that two boys were sent to keep them from the shallows where the feet of the guests would trouble the fishing later. Donnchadh gave her a comb of horn he had carved himself through the winter evenings, clumsily, so that one tooth was shorter than the rest, and she wore it every fair-day after for the whole of her marriage, the short tooth catching on her hair in a way she never had mended. She did not weep at her own wedding, though she had wept twice in the week before it, alone, at the spring on the hill where no one from the ford could see her; and she came to her husband's house that evening dry-eyed and quiet, and was, by every account that survives of her, a good wife to him from the first night to the last, whatever else she carried that he did not ask after.

She did not tell him of Torcall Tochlair until they had been three years married, and when she told him he said only that it explained a look she sometimes had at fair-time, and never asked more, which she was grateful for the whole of her life after.

It was at that same fair, some years on, that she first heard a thing recited that had not been recited before. The ford had long drawn every kind of household to its yearly gathering, to trade salt for wool and wool for whatever the sea brought in, and it had always been a place where matches were spoken of and made, the elders of one hearth walking across to another with their measure of salt as Torcall's mother had once walked. But in that year, and it is remembered as the first year, before any match was spoken a household stood up and gave its line: the names of its dead, back seven generations, father to father and mother to mother, said aloud in the hearing of the whole fair, so that anyone who knew of a blood too close, or a blood forbidden for some reason nobody living could give, might speak before the salt was carried across. It began, so the telling goes, with a household that had been burned once already by a match no one had thought to question until it was too late to unmake, though whose household that was the tellers no longer agree.

Ealag stood in the crowd at the ford and heard the lines given, one after another, seven names back on each side, fathers answering fathers and mothers answering mothers, and she thought of Beathag in the doorway saying *it cannot be* and giving no seventh name, no sixth, no first, nothing a listener could have weighed. She thought that if such a reciting had stood between her and Torcall, the whole hill would have heard whatever it was that only the old people knew, said aloud where it could be judged, rather than kept behind four shut mouths. She said as much to Donnchadh that evening, and he said that a thing kept behind shut mouths might be kept there for good reason as easily as bad, and she said she supposed that was true, and neither of them believed it entirely.

The reciting at the ford held from that year on, and other fairs along the coast took it up after, until it was a common thing at any gathering where a match might be made: the households of the common people giving their lines aloud, seven names back, the same distance An Clachair's own line was said to keep, though no common household claimed kinship with that older line, only the same caution about it. It is the oldest tally of ordinary blood that the island keeps outside the king's, and no single telling of it has come down whole; each hearth kept its own seven names, and when a hearth failed the names failed with it.

## III. Of the Trench at the Black Hill

Torcall Tochlair did not marry. He gathered the coal as his father had, a few handfuls a season from the banks where it showed, and by all accounts he did it well and without complaint, but something in him had gone restless in a way that gathering what the hills let fall could not answer. He began to ask the older diggers, on the walk home from the peat-banks of an evening, whether the vein under the mountain was the only coal the island held, and the older diggers, who had asked the same question themselves in their own youth and had it answered by their own fathers' silence, told him what they had been told: that the vein chose where it lay, and had not chosen to lie twice.

Torcall was not a man the answer satisfied. He had a brother, Lachann, younger by five years and easier in his temper, who had never much minded being told a thing and made to let it stand, but who loved his brother more than he minded being talked into things, and when Torcall began to speak of a black hill in the east where the ground had a look about it he had heard described by traders from that coast, Lachann said he would go and look with him, if only to see him satisfied and brought home again.

Lachann had a wife of his own by then and a daughter not yet walking, and he told his wife he would be gone a season, no more, and was gone the better part of four years, coming back only twice in that time to see the child grow, once when she could stand and once when she could run from him laughing across the yard and had to be caught. He never complained of the distance in any telling that has come down, and the diggers who worked beside him at the black hill said afterward that he sang more than any of them at the trench face, old songs of the hill country sung in the wrong place, which made the other three laugh at him and made the work go easier for it.

They went east together in the dry season, with two other diggers who had grown as restless as Torcall on less cause, to the black hill, a rise of empty ground in the east, named already for the darkness of its soil before ever a pick touched it. They opened a trench along its shoulder with picks and fire-cracked stone, the same way a well is sunk, working by turns through the wet months and the dry, cutting down through soil the colour of char into rock that gave off no smell of coal and no shine of it either, only a grey stone that came away in slabs.

It was in the fourth year of the digging, in the two thousand two hundred and sixty-seventh year of the hill, that the trench wall gave. There had been rain enough that season to loosen what the diggers had already undercut more than they knew, and the fall came without any of the small warnings that a careful digger learns to read, no trickle of loose stone beforehand, no settling underfoot. Lachann was at the face with one of the other two men when the wall came down; Torcall was above, hauling a basket up on the rope, and heard it rather than saw it, a sound he said afterward he had no word for and never tried twice to find one. He dug with his hands until the others came running with tools, and dug after that too, long past when digging could do any good, and had to be pulled bodily away from the fall by three men before he would stop.

Lachann's wife came out to the black hill herself when word reached her, walking the whole distance with the child on her hip, and stood at the trench a long while without speaking to anyone, and went home again three days later with a handful of the char-black soil tied in a cloth, which she kept at her own hearth for the rest of her life and would let no one touch but herself. She did not blame Torcall to his face, then or ever, though it is told that she never again asked after him by name, and spoke of him only, when she spoke of him at all, as her daughter's uncle at the black hill.

Lachann was buried on the black hill, at the mouth of the trench he had died beside, because Torcall would not have him carried elsewhere, and the other man's people took him home to be buried among his own. Torcall did not go home. He built himself a turf shelter at the trench's edge and stayed there through the winter that followed, and when the diggers who had come with him packed their tools and went back west to the hills, he did not go with them. Word of it reached Ealag at the ford by way of a trader who had stopped at the black hill and seen him there, a man sitting alone by an open trench with his dead brother in the ground a few feet off, still saying, when anyone asked him why he stayed, that the coal was there to be found and he meant to find it.

## IV. Of the Stone That Would Not Break

He was not, in the end, the only one who tried. Word of the black hill's trench had gone about the island in the years it was being dug, as word of any strangeness does, and it woke in other places the same restlessness it had woken in Torcall: if coal could be looked for in the east, it could be looked for anywhere, and more than one household elsewhere on the island took up picks in those years with the same hope Torcall had carried east with him.

The largest of these second attempts was made some distance from the black hill, on rising ground the diggers judged as like to the mountain's own shoulder as any ground on the island could be, by folk who had heard of Torcall's trench but not of Lachann's death, or had heard of it and judged the risk worth taking regardless. They shored their trench with timber where Torcall's had gone unshored, having heard enough of the black hill by then to take that much warning at least, and they set watchers on the lip of the cutting in turns through every shift, and for all their care the ground gave them nothing to watch for. They dug two full seasons, deeper by the end than Torcall's own trench had gone, through soil and then through a bed of common grey stone that gave way at last to more of the same stone beneath it, unbroken, ordinary rock going down further than any of them had tools or patience to follow.

The leader of that digging, a man whose name has not come down with the rest of the telling, was said to have gone down into the cutting himself on the last day and struck the grey stone three times with his own pick before he would call the work done, as if the stone might yet answer a fourth household where it had refused three years of others; and when it did not, he climbed out, and told the rest to bank their fires, and the digging at that hill ended there. They struck at it a while longer out of stubbornness more than hope, and then they stopped, because there is only so long a household can feed itself on the hope of what a hillside has not shown it, and this hillside, in the end, showed them nothing at all.

It was from that failure, more than from Torcall's trench, which after all had found nothing but had not yet been called finished, that the saying began to travel the island: that the vein under the mountain was alone of its kind, that no second coal lay waiting anywhere else to be found by whoever dug hardest for it, and that the stone the second diggers had struck was proof of it, a stone that would not break because there was nothing under it to break for. Some said gual dubh itself had chosen its one place in the world the way na Seachd Guail of the old tellings were said to have chosen theirs, and that a stone unwilling to give up anything was simply the island's way of saying the choice had already been made and was not to be argued with by picks.

No one tried a third opening in that age. No elder of any hearth is remembered forbidding it outright; the will for it went out of the island unasked, the way the will for a bad match goes out of two families once the salt has been carried and refused, each hearth coming to the same mind alone and none of them saying so aloud.

## V. Of the Vein That Chooses

Torcall Tochlair stayed at the black hill for the rest of his years, and never took a wife, and never went back to the hills, though he sent word west now and then for tools he could not make himself. He kept the trench open well past the point any sensible digger would have let it fill with rain and go back to grass. Closing it, he told the few who still came to ask him, would mean agreeing that Lachann had died for nothing, and that he would not do. A small household grew up around him at the black hill's foot in his old age, folk who came for one reason or another and stayed because the ground was as good as any and the man at the trench asked nothing of them; by the time he was old it was Torcall's hill to those who lived near it, or Cnoc na Claise, which is the name the households about it keep.

Ealag lived out her years at the ford, and raised three children with Donnchadh the fisher, and grew old in a house within sound of the ford where the lines were recited every year at the fair, seven names back on either side, a custom that had not existed when she was a girl and that she had, in her own quiet way, watched into being. Her own children were given without trouble, in their turn, to households of the ford and the coast about it, their lines recited plainly and answered by no objection from anyone, and she stood in the crowd for each of their weddings with the same short-toothed comb in her hair that Donnchadh had carved her, worn nearly smooth by then with handling.

In her last years she would sometimes walk down to the ford at fair-time and stand at the edge of the crowd to hear the reciting, and those who knew her story, which by then was most of the ford's households, said she listened harder than anyone else there, though whether she was listening for Torcall's line, or for her own, or only for whatever answer the world had never given her, none of them could have said, and she never told them. She died at the ford in the two thousand three hundredth year of the hill, in her own bed, with her children about her, an old woman who had asked one honest question in her youth and had gone the whole of her life afterward without an answer to it.

Of Torcall it is told that he died at the black hill some years after her, in the two thousand three hundred and eighteenth year, and was buried beside his brother at the trench's mouth, and that the small household he had gathered kept the ground and did not fill the trench in even then, though nothing further was ever dug from it. What the two of them, Ealag and Torcall, might have made of each other's later lives, had the salt been carried and accepted instead of refused, is not a thing any telling of this age presumes to say. The reciters who keep the story end it always the same way, with the same words the elders of the two households were said to give and no others: that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choice was never anyone's to make but its own.

# Part Four: The Lot and the Saying

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Sharing before the Storms

*GE 2,328 – 2,390*


> *An làmh a roinneas, cha teirig i; an làmh a dh'fhalaicheas, falbhaidh i.*
> The hand that shares does not fail; the hand that hides must go.
>
> — said at Dùn ìseal after the sharing, and after nothing else

## I. Of the Custom that Had No Beginning

No one at Dùn ìseal could say who first brought grain to the bank before the storms, or in what year, or why. The telling only holds that in one year a household with more than it needed carried the surplus to the hall and set it down before the holder without being asked, and that the households with less were glad of it, and that the year after, another household did the same, unbidden, because the first had. By the time it was a custom no one living remembered it not being one.

It was not a law such as the reciters kept at the ford, cut into no stone and sworn to no name. It asked only this: that before the season of the black-wind storms, when the boats came in for good and the passes closed and a household's stores were what they would live on until the grass came back, whoever had more than enough should say so, and bring it in.

Tormod Liath, who held the hill in those years and had held it longer than any before him, let it be done in the open. At the gathering of Samhain the households brought their surplus within the bank: grain in skins, dried fish strung on rods, salted meat in its own fat. It was weighed by the count of mouths in each house and given back out, so that every hearth went into the dark months even. A household that brought little because it had little lost nothing by it. A household that brought little because it had kept more back lost the thing it had kept, once, and after that lost more.

It is told that in the third year of the custom a woman of the shore households, whose net had taken more mackerel than her family could eat or smoke before it turned, carried three baskets of it up to the bank herself rather than let it spoil unshared, and that Tormod came down from the hall to help her set them down, an old grey man carrying fish like any hand of the household. After that the custom needed no one to ask.

There was no cutter's mark for it, no knotted cord to count it by, and no word among the Dia-thìrich for the thing itself; it was known only as the sharing, or the bringing-in, or, among those who did it least willingly, the asking, though no one asked, and that was the whole of its strength. A household that gave more than its share got back no more than any other; a household that gave nothing because it had nothing was not shamed for it, and a holder who tried to shame such a household was, in the one telling that gives the case, made to bring his own surplus in double the next year by the plain silence of his neighbours, without a word said against him that any reciter kept.

For thirty years and more it went so, and the island beyond the hill knew little of it, for it belonged to Dùn ìseal and its valleys and had not yet gone out along the roads the way the lot and the cup would go out after it. Elsewhere households still hoarded against the storms as they had always done, burying what they could not eat, and thought no worse of themselves for it. A household that dug a floor-pit in those years did so as its grandfathers had, against wolves, against a bad neighbour, against nothing it could have named; it was only where the sharing had come first that a hidden pit became a different thing, without the digger changing a stone of it.

## II. Of the House at Àth shean

Àth shean stood where Rathad an t-Salainn forded the shallow river below the hill, a scatter of houses on the near bank with byres cut into the slope behind them, no different from a dozen fords like it save that its ground was good for barley in a wet year and bad in a dry one, and that its households answered to Dùn ìseal the way the near valleys did.

Beasag was born there in the household of a man whose name the hill's own telling does not keep, only that he was a careful man, close with what was his, and that his neighbours called him so without meaning it as praise. He had built his grain pit himself, lined with hurdles and roofed with turf, under the floor of the byre where the cattle stood over it in winter and no stranger would think to dig; and he had built it before ever the sharing custom came down the valley to Àth shean, in the years when a hidden store was only good sense and no one asked a man to open his floor to his neighbours.

By the time Beasag could walk, the sharing had come to Àth shean too, carried down by households that had seen it done at the hill and thought it good, and her father brought his share to the bank each year with the rest, a little less than his neighbours guessed he had, though none could have said by how much.

She grew up knowing the pit the way a child knows the shape of a house without being told its walls have a name. Her father lifted the third flagstone from the door on nights when the household ate better than its neighbours, and laid it back after; and long before Beasag had words for understanding it, she understood that this was not spoken of outside the walls.

She remembered it best as a smell before she remembered it as a thing: the byre at night smelled of cattle and old rushes and, on those nights, for a little while, of turned earth and grain-dust, and under it the tallow smoke of the one lamp her father allowed himself for the lifting. He never spoke while he did it. He knelt on the flag beside the third stone with a length of ash wood for a lever, and worked it up an inch at a time so that it made no more noise going than a cow shifting its feet, and he never once, in all the years she watched him from the loft ladder with her chin on the top rung, looked up to see whether she was there. She thought, when she was very small, that this was a game fathers played, a secret kept the way a secret is kept from younger children about a feast day; it was some years before she understood that it was kept from the ford as well as from her, and some years more before she understood what that meant.

"A careful man keeps his own counsel," he told her once, the only time he ever spoke of it to her directly. It was said, on that one occasion, of a neighbour who had asked him plainly, at the ford, whether his barley had come in as thin as everyone else's. "What a man has under his own floor is between him and his floor." She was young enough then to think it a kind of wisdom, the way a child takes most of what a parent says for wisdom until the day it stops sounding like any.

Her mother had died birthing the last of Beasag's brothers, three winters before this telling opens, and after that the house was her father's and his alone to keep as he judged fit; and what he judged fit was to keep more back each year, a little at a time, the way a man tests how far a rope will stretch before it breaks. He was not unkind to his children. He fed them well in years others went hungry, and thought, in his own reckoning, that this was the whole of what a father owed.

## III. Of the Lean Year

The storm season that came in the forty-ninth year after the custom began was the leanest Àth shean had known. The grazing had failed the summer before along the whole of the near valleys; the barley came in thin and short-headed; and the fishing boats, which in a poor year on land could always be sent out again for what the sea still gave, lost three weeks running to a wind that would not turn.

Beasag was seventeen that year, old enough to be sent to the bank at Dùn ìseal with the household's share and to see with her own eyes what a lean year looked like gathered in one place: baskets half the height of other years, byres led up with cattle too thin to slaughter, old people who came to stand by the bank and be counted though they had nothing to bring. She saw the division made by the count of mouths, saw a widow with four children carry home more than she had brought, saw a household of two old men carry home less; and she understood, watching it, what her father's floor held that these people did not have.

She saw one thing more that day that stayed with her longer than the counting itself. A boy not much younger than her own brother stood near the bank with an empty sack over his shoulder, waiting his household's turn, and when the measure was poured into it he stood a moment holding the weight of it in both arms, where the other children ran home with theirs at once, and laughed, once, at nothing anyone else could see; and an old woman beside Beasag said, not unkindly, that it was the boy's first winter with a full belly in it, and that he did not yet trust it to last the walk home. Beasag thought of her father's pit, deep and dry and dark under the byre floor, holding more than that boy's whole sack twice over, and said nothing, then, to the old woman or to anyone.

She said nothing that year. It was not in her, yet, to say it. She told herself, walking home behind her father and brother with the household's own thin share on her back, that it was not her floor and not her word to give, and that a daughter did not measure her father any more than a son did; and she went on telling herself so through the winter that followed, a winter in which Àth shean buried two of its old people and her own house ate meat twice a week and bread every day, and no one at her hearth asked why, because no one at her hearth wanted to know the answer badly enough to ask.

But the year had marked her, and she went home turning it over the way a stone is turned over in a pocket, worn smooth by handling before it is ever thrown. She began to watch her father's face when he counted the household's share into the skins for the bank, and to notice what he set aside first and did not put in, and to reckon, as well as a girl of seventeen could reckon, how many mouths at Àth shean had gone hungrier that winter than they need have, for the sake of what lay under three courses of turf beneath the byre floor.

Her elder brother, who slept in the loft above the byre and had grown a man's shoulders that year, knew of the pit as she did and had made his own peace with it long before; it was their father's floor, their father's grain, and a son did not measure his father. He told her so plainly enough, the once she tried to speak of it to him, and after that she did not try again with him.

## IV. Of the Telling

She told it at the ford rather than the hill, and to a woman mending net on the bank rather than to any holder, in the first mild days after the storms broke, when Àth shean's household came down to the water again to see what the winter had left of the boats. The woman's name is not kept in the hill's telling, only that she was old enough to have buried a husband and a son that same winter, and that she asked Beasag, in the way of an idle question between neighbours who have both come through a hard season, whether her father's byre had fared as thin as the rest of the ford's.

"No," Beasag said, before she had thought whether to answer at all, and then, because the one word sat badly on its own, "there's a pit under the floor. There has been since before the sharing came to us. He never brought it all in."

The woman went on with her mending for a moment as though she had not heard, the way people do when a thing is too large to take in at the speed it was given. Then she asked, quietly, whether Beasag was certain, and Beasag said she was, for she had watched her father lift the flag with her own eyes more winters than she could count; and the woman put down her net and looked at her a long while before she said anything more.

"You know what this will cost him."

"I know."

"And you still say it."

Beasag gave that one no answer. The hill's telling holds, in the one line it gives to the moment itself, that she stood on the bank with the wind off the water in her face and found, turning the words over once they were out, that she felt lighter for having said them than she had felt in a long time, and that this frightened her more than her father's anger would, when it came.

She did not tell it to bring trouble on her father. She told the truth of what she said afterward, when she was made to say it again before others, in a plainer way: that she had been asked, and that she had grown tired, some time in that lean winter without her quite marking the day it happened, of watching her neighbours go thin while her own house did not, and that once the word was out of her mouth she found she did not want it back.

The woman told her own household, as neighbours do, meaning no more harm by it than Beasag had meant in the telling; and from there it went the short way a thing goes in a scatter of houses at a ford, hearth to hearth, until it reached Àth shean's own holder, who sent word up to Dùn ìseal, because a matter under the sharing custom was not his to judge alone.

Tormod Liath was an old man by then, older than any who had held the hill before him, and it is told that he heard the matter out in silence and asked only one question of the men who came to lay it before him: whether the girl had told it of her own will, unbeaten and unbribed. When they said she had, he nodded once, as a man nods at something he expected, and sent them to open the floor.

They found the pit as she had said it would be, lined and roofed and dry, and in it grain enough to have fed two households through the lean winter that had just passed, kept whole while the hall counted out its shares by the mouth. Her father did not deny it when they brought him before the holder's man at Àth shean. He said only that it was his own pit, dug with his own hands before ever the custom came to the ford, and that a man's floor was his own to keep as he judged.

The holder's man told him that the pit was his, and always would be; the grain in it was the households' now, by the custom the ford had kept for fifty years, and the household that had hidden it from the sharing would keep nothing at Àth shean past the day. Until dark he might take from his own house what he and his children could carry on their backs, and no more, and be off the ford's ground by morning.

Before the man turned to go, Beasag's father asked who had told it, though he must already have guessed, for there was no one else in the house who had known where the pit lay and lived to speak of it besides his own children. The ford kept no custom of naming the teller to the one told on, for fear of what might follow such a naming in a house before it was even emptied, and he got no answer to it. But he looked at Beasag across the yard as the man spoke, once, and she did not look away from him, and it is told that this was answer enough for both of them, and that no more words passed between father and daughter on the matter, that day or any day after.

## V. Of the Road

Beasag walked out with her father and her brother and the two younger children in the last light of that day, each of them under as much as they could bear: a folded hide, a cooking pot, what grain had not gone into the pit, a spindle, a knife, the small things a household gathers in a generation and cannot leave behind though it can carry almost none of them. No one at Àth shean came out to see them go, though she felt, walking the lane between the houses, that every door had someone standing just inside it.

Her father did not speak to her on the road, that night or the next, and it is not told in the hill's own telling whether he ever did again as they had spoken before. Her brother walked beside her without a word either way, carrying more than his share and setting his own pace to hers when the youngest flagged, which was the only kindness either of them had it in him to give just then.

They slept the first night in the open, under a hedge-bank within sight of Àth shean's own smoke, because the youngest could go no further, and Beasag lay awake listening to her father's breathing on the far side of the fire and could not tell, in the dark, whether he slept or only lay still. In the morning he was up before any of them, and led them east without a word about which way, as though the road had always run only that one direction and none of them had ever thought otherwise.

They went east, the way households went who could not or would not hold ground close under the hill: past the near valleys, past the last of the bank-ditches Tormod's line had thrown up, out to where the vein under the mountain gave way to common rock and the king's blood held no hall and claimed no grazing. They walked eleven days by Beasag's later count, though she owned that she had lost the true tale of them somewhere past the sixth, footsore and thin-shod, sleeping under whatever bank or overhang the evening found them near, eating the grain they had carried at half what they would have eaten it at home, because none of them yet knew how far east they would need it to last. There were households there already, scattered and thin on ground poorer than Àth shean's, who had gone east a generation before for their own reasons and asked no questions of those who came after with the same look about them. Beasag's father built a house on a slope above a stream with no name that she was ever told, and did not build a pit under its floor, though whether that was shame or only that there was nothing left worth hiding, she never said, in all the years the ford afterward kept her name.
