It is told that she stayed east of the vein the whole of her life, and raised her own children in a house with no door to any stone, and that whenever travellers came through from the hill she would ask them, before any other news, how the sharing had gone that season, and whether any household had been found keeping back; and that she never once said why she asked, though everyone she asked already knew.

## VI. Of the Hill in Its Old Age

Tormod Liath held the hill twelve years more after the matter of Àth shean's pit, into the last winter of his life, by which time his hair and beard had gone the colour of the stone the reciters named him for and his hands shook at the cup though his judgment did not. He had outlived three heirs of his own body before that, and buried each one himself at the bank he had built, and it was said of him at the end that no one now living at Dùn ìseal remembered a holder of the hill who was not Tormod.

He died in his own hall, in his sleep, with no wound and no fever on him, in the three hundred and eightieth year of his holding, and the hill mourned him the length of a season, for there was scarcely a household on it whose grandfather he had not judged.

The holding of the hill passed, as the list gives it, to Eilidh Ghlas, of the king's own blood, who had lived three hundred and forty years in the valleys under Dùn ìseal without any thought, her own telling says, of ever holding anything but her own hearth. She took up the hill in the year of Tormod's death, and the sharing custom with it, and it is told that the first thing she did, before the bank was even swept for the season's grain, was to send to Àth shean and ask after the pit under the byre floor that everyone at the ford still called by the name of the man who had dug it, though he had been gone from the ford for twelve years and more.

She was answered that the pit stood empty, and had stood empty since the day it was opened, for no household at Àth shean since had cared to dig one of its own; and it is told that she said only that this was well, and asked nothing further about it, then or after.

Eilidh had come to the hill an old woman already in the world's reckoning, though young beside Tormod's long holding, and those who had known her in the valleys said she brought to the hall a plainer hand than his: she weighed the sharing herself in the first years rather than leave it to a steward, and stood at the bank through the whole of the counting even in wet weather, so that no household could say the hill judged them from indoors while they stood wet outside it. Of the man who had gone east with his children she asked nothing more than the one question, and the ford's telling, which watched her closely those first seasons the way a ford watches any new holder, set that down as neither harshness nor forgiveness, but only as the manner of a woman who had watched the custom work for sixty years before it was ever hers to keep, and saw no cause to remake it.

Under her the sharing went on as it had under Tormod, brought in and weighed and given back by the count of mouths, and no household at Dùn ìseal or Àth shean was ever again found keeping a floor that lied about what lay beneath it. The house east of the vein, and the woman who had opened her father's pit with a word at a riverbank, the hill's own telling does not follow further; that thread Àth shean kept for itself, and told, when it told it at all, in its own words and not the hill's.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of Eilidh the Grey and the Boy Who Went

*GE 2,391 – 2,402*

> *An gille a dh'fhalbh, cha tàinig e dhachaigh na aon fhear.*
> The boy who went did not come home the same man.
> — An Cnoc Ruadh's own telling, of a fosterling it never named

## I. Of Eilidh's Two Sons

Eilidh Ghlas had held the hill a year when her elder son was born to her a second time in the telling, though he was the elder by birth from the first: for a mother of the king's own blood counts a child twice, once for the bearing and once for the year the world takes notice of him, and the ford did not take notice of Calum Ciar until his mother stood at the bank in the first sharing of her own holding and he stood a pace behind her right shoulder, dark-haired and watchful, and someone said, low, that here was the next one. He had not chosen it, and his mother had not pointed him out; a boy standing where an heir stands is heir enough for a ford to see, and after that no one at Dùn ìseal thought to look for another when they spoke of who would hold the hill when Eilidh was gone from it, however many hundred years that might be.

He was close with his mother in the way of a first child who remembers, or believes he remembers, a time before any other claimed her hand. Calum Ciar rode with her on the counting days and lifted the grain-skins himself beside her; and Eilidh, who did the same herself through every wet season rather than leave the weighing to a steward, thought this a good likeness and said so to no one but her own held silence. Of her younger son there is less to be told, and what is told belongs less to him than to the household that raised him, which is the way of An Cnoc Ruadh's own list when it comes to speak of him at all.

He was born in the fourth year of his mother's holding, in a wet spring when the river at Àth shean ran high enough to float the ford-stones, and no reciter troubles to give the day, for no reciter of Dùn ìseal ever gave him a day for anything, first or last. He was smaller than his brother had been, and quieter, and grew, in the few years the hill's own telling allows him before it sends him from it, into a boy who watched more than he spoke and who followed the dogs about the yard more readily than he followed the men to the bank. Eilidh loved him, it is told, exactly as she loved his brother, for she had held enough seasons of counting by then to know that a hand which gives one child more takes something from the other that no gift repays. But she watched him, in the years he was old enough to be watched, with a plainer eye than she watched Calum Ciar, the way a holder watches a field that will not be sown this year and studies it all the same.

It was Eilidh's own mother, dead these many years before, who had first spoken of fosterage to her as a girl, in the valleys under the hill, long before either of them thought Eilidh would ever hold anything: that among the households of the near valleys, when a family had more than one son and land enough for only one to inherit, the younger was sometimes sent to kin at another hearth to be raised, so that he might grow up loved and useful in a house that was not waiting for him to die or go, and so that the house he left might have one less mouth counted against its portion and one less claim laid against its bank when the holder's time came. It was a custom of ordinary households, not of the hill, and Eilidh had turned it over in her mind through all the years of her own holding without doing anything about it, the way a woman turns over a thought she is not yet ready to act on, until the year her younger son was six years old and stood in the yard one evening watching his brother ride out with the men to see the boundary stones renewed, and did not ask to go, and did not seem to mind that he had not been asked.

She watched him from the hall door a long while that evening. It is told that she said to her steward, who stood by her, that a house with only one door out of it was no house for a second son, and that the steward, not understanding her, asked which door she meant, and she did not answer him.

She sent, in the spring of the following year, word to An Cnoc Ruadh.

There had been peace at the ford for longer than either hill now living could number by its own holding: the meeting first made between Raghnall Ceannfhionn and a nameless holder of the west had held through every holder after, salt and flint and wool changing hands where it had first changed hands, marriages agreed there that neither hill's own custom would have made alone. But peace between two hills that owe fealty to the same king and nothing to one another is a thing kept fresh each generation by an act, not by the mere absence of a quarrel, and it had occurred to Eilidh, turning the old custom of the valleys over in her mind, that no act keeps a peace so well as a child sent to be raised inside it. She did not put this to her steward, or to anyone at Dùn ìseal, as a matter of the kingdom; she put it, when she put it to anyone, as a mother's plain wish that her younger son should learn a trade that was not waiting for an inheritance to be idle in, and An Cnoc Ruadh's salt and its boats and its far sight of the western sea were as good a trade as any a boy of the king's blood had ever been given. Both things were true. The hill's own reciters, in the years after, chose to keep the second and let the first go, as reciters will when a mother's plain wish makes a better telling than a holder's policy, though no one now living can say which she weighed heavier the evening she sent the word west.

Calum Ciar, when he heard of it, asked his mother only whether he too would be sent somewhere, and was told no, that the hill was his and would stay his, and he was satisfied, or seemed to be, and never again in the hearing of the hill's own telling spoke of his brother's going before it happened or after. It is told, though not by the hill's own reciters, that on the morning his brother left he stood at the gate a long time after the party was out of sight down the valley road, and that when a groom asked him if he would come in out of the wind he said he was only counting how many days it would be fifty miles there and fifty back, which is a strange thing for a man of a hundred and fifty, who looked a youth of twenty, to trouble himself with unless he means, by counting, to make a thing feel nearer than it is.

Eilidh herself did not stand at the gate. She walked with the party as far as Àth shean, a morning's distance, and there, where the road turned west and her own road turned back to the hill, she knelt to her younger son's height the way Rìonach would kneel to it again four days later, and told him three things, which the hill's own reciters have kept whole, though nothing else of that parting: that he was not sent away for any wrong of his, that An Cnoc Ruadh would be as much his home as this one had been for as long as he needed it to be, and that she meant to see him grown, and did not doubt the years the king's blood was given would hold long enough for it. None of the household walking behind her ever said she had wept at the parting, and she did not look back down the road once she had turned her own horse toward the hill, though the steward riding beside her said afterward, to no one who ever troubled to repeat it further than his own hearth, that she was silent the whole ride home in a way he had not known her to be silent before or after.

## II. Of the Road West

The boy went with two of his mother's household, a man called Donnchadh who had walked Rathad an t-Salainn before and a woman called Rìonach who had kin at Àth shean and would turn off there, and he went on his own feet, for Eilidh had said that a boy fostered ought to arrive on the legs that would carry him the rest of his life at An Cnoc Ruadh and not on a horse he would have to send home again. It was fifty miles and more from Dùn ìseal to An Cnoc Ruadh by Rathad an t-Salainn, west by south along the shoulder of the near valleys and down through country he had never seen, and it took the three of them the better part of a week's walking, sleeping the first two nights at households of the near valleys that Donnchadh knew by name and the rest under whatever roof or bank offered shelter, for Rathad an t-Salainn in those years had shelters built along it at a day's walk apart, low stone huts with a hearth-place and nothing else, raised by no one household but kept swept by whoever passed last.

He carried the shape of that week with him more than its particular days: the valleys giving way by evening stages to country that ran flatter and wetter, reed beds where herons stood so still he took them for dead trees until one moved; a night at a shelter where rain came through a gap in the roof onto Rìonach's sleeping place and she only laughed and moved her blanket, saying a roof that never let rain through had never had a family under it; a day when Donnchadh, for no reason the boy could see, stopped on the road and looked a long while at a low green mound off to the south of it, and would not go nearer, and would not say why, only that it was older than the road and older than the salt trade and best left to whatever kept it. He asked Rìonach about it that evening and she said only that there were places on the island Seann-Dhaoine had left, and that a wise traveller let them lie the way he let a wasp's nest lie, out of no fear of any particular sting, only a plain sense that some things were not made for a man's curiosity to test.

Rìonach turned off for Àth shean on the fourth day, and it is told that she knelt to the boy's height before she went and told him that a household that took him in for a season, or a decade, or the rest of his growing, was not the household he had come from, and that this was a kind of doubling rather than a loss, the way a river that forks becomes two whole rivers, neither one lessened by the other; and that he would find, if he let himself, that he had two homes rather than half of one. He did not understand her then, or said he did not, though he remembered the saying well enough to repeat it, unprompted, many years and many miles from that road.

The land changed again on the fifth day: the reed country gave way to a wider sky and a smell the boy had never smelled before, which Donnchadh told him was the sea, though they were still some miles from any shore he could see, and told him also that what he was smelling under the sea was salt, and that where they were going the salt came from a lake and never from the sea at all, which the boy found so strange a thing to be told that he made Donnchadh say it twice.

They came down to the western lake shore on the sixth evening, with the light going long and gold across water that lay flat as a held breath, and a hill rising low and red-earthed on its far side with smoke standing straight up from it in the still air, and Donnchadh stopped where the road first showed it and said that was An Cnoc Ruadh, and that its line had held the lake shore before ever the king came down from the grove, and that the boy would do well to remember, walking in, that this was a hill with its own long life and its own long pride and no cause whatever to feel itself the lesser of the hill he had left.

## III. Of the Household of Lachlann Ruadh

Lachlann Ruadh held An Cnoc Ruadh in those years, a broad, red-bearded man not yet forty, who had come to the holding young by the death of an uncle with no children of his own and had held it since with a hand that Eilidh's own steward, hearing of him later, called plain in the same word he used of Eilidh, though the two had never met. He met the boy at the gate of the hill himself rather than sending a steward to do it, with his daughter Peigi at his side, a dark, quick-eyed girl some years the elder, who looked the fosterling over with the frank, unhurried attention of a child assessing a new dog brought into a yard she considered her own, and said, before her father could say anything, that he was thin for a king's son and she supposed they would have to feed him.

Lachlann laughed at that, a big sudden laugh, the sound, the boy soon learned, of the whole household settling, and said that Peigi was to be told he was no king's son and no king's grandson either, but a boy of the ford's people come to learn a trade, the same as she would tell any fosterling from any hearth, and that if she called him otherwise even once more he would hear of it. Peigi said nothing to that, which the boy learned soon enough was her way of agreeing to nothing and losing no ground by it, and took his one bundle from him without asking and carried it in herself.

The household he found within the gate was smaller than his mother's hall and louder, a red-earthed yard with byres on two sides and a hall low and long, full, in the evenings, of more voices at once than he had ever heard indoors. Lachlann kept no steward apart from himself for the small business of the hill, weighed the salt tallies with his own hand at the season's end the way Eilidh weighed the grain, and ate at the same board as his household rather than above it, a plain oak table scarred along one edge where, Peigi told him with some pride, her grandfather's grandmother had once split it testing whether it would take an axe blow without cracking through, and it had not cracked through, and the mark was kept.

They gave him work before they gave him a name for himself, which suited him, for he had never much wanted the one he had. He carried water the first weeks, and mucked the byres alongside boys his own age who did not know or greatly care whose son he was, and slept in the loft above the hall with three other fosterlings and two of the household's own younger sons, in a row of straw that Peigi ruled over, by common consent of the loft, as absolutely as her father ruled the hill below. She was not gentle with him, in those first months, in any way that a reciter would trouble to soften in the telling: she corrected his speech of An Cnoc Ruadh when it slipped into the hill-talk of Dùn ìseal, laughed without much mercy the first time he fell into the lake wading for reeds, and once, when he cried in the loft at night in the second week and thought the others asleep, said nothing at the time but the next morning set herself beside him at the water-carrying without being asked and stayed there the whole of that day and most days after, which was, in its way, the kinder of the two responses and the one he remembered longer.

By the second year he had stopped thinking of the loft as a strange bed and started thinking of his own hall at Dùn ìseal, when word of it reached him, as the place his mother was rather than the place he lived; and it is told, though only by An Cnoc Ruadh's own reciters and in a single line that the hill of Dùn ìseal has never troubled to dispute or confirm, that Lachlann Ruadh came to think of him, within a few years, less as a hostage of peace than as a son the sea had lent him, and treated him accordingly, teaching him himself the reading of weather off the lake and the working of the salt-rakes, skills he might as easily have left to a steward and did not.

Word travelled between the two hills that season and the next along Rathad an t-Salainn itself, carried in the mouths of the carriers who walked it, for no household of either hill troubled to send a letter where a spoken word would do as well and travel as far. The boy learned, in this way and no other, that his brother had been given the judging of the near valleys' boundary stones that year, a small trust but the first of its kind, and that Calum Ciar had settled a dispute between two herders over a shifted marker with a plainness their mother was said to have approved of; and Calum Ciar, in the same way and by the same road, learned that his brother had grown a hand's breadth since the spring and had been let out on the lake in a boat for the first time and had come back wet through and pleased with himself. Neither brother sent more than that. An Cnoc Ruadh's telling is careful to say this was no coldness between them; it was only that two brothers, the one a boy and the other long grown though he looked a youth, living fifty miles apart had, with each season, less to say that a carrier's memory could hold whole, and more that belonged only to the hearth where each now slept.

Eilidh herself came once, in the third year of the fostering, on no business but the seeing of him that she had promised at the ford, and stayed four days at An Cnoc Ruadh as Lachlann's guest rather than as any holder visiting another's ground, sitting at the same scarred board the household ate from and asking after the tallies and the weather no differently than she asked after her son. It is told that when she left, the boy walked with her as far as the lake's western point, the furthest edge of ground the household called its own, and that she told him there, out of Lachlann's hearing, that she did not intend to come again for some years, out of no want of missing him, only a plain knowledge that a boy who watched the road too often for his mother's coming would never quite finish becoming An Cnoc Ruadh's own; and he understood her, this time, without needing Rìonach's river to explain it to him, and did not watch the road after that, or not so that anyone at An Cnoc Ruadh ever caught him at it.

## IV. Of the Lake and the Name Not Kept

The salt of An Cnoc Ruadh did not come, as the boy had first thought when Donnchadh told him so on the road, from the sea at all, though the sea lay close enough to smell on any west wind; it came from the shallow western reach of the lake, where the water stood warm and still in the summer months and drew down in a dry year until its margin turned white with a crust that the household raked into baskets and carried up to dry on stone platforms above the shore. It was slower work than sea-salt and finer for it, prized on Rathad an t-Salainn of the ford above the coarser grey stuff of the tidal pans, and the raking of it was a skill An Cnoc Ruadh kept jealously among its own households and taught to no fosterling until it judged him ready, for a rake dragged wrong through the crust broke it into the mud beneath and lost a season's crust to nothing.

He was eight years old, in the third summer of his fostering, when Lachlann himself put a rake into his hands for the first time and stood behind him on the drying platform to show him the turn of the wrist that lifted the crust clean without breaking it into the black mud under it, a turn Lachlann said had come down in his own family longer than An Cnoc Ruadh's own list could count, mother's hand to daughter's hand and, where there was no daughter, father's hand to whatever child stood nearest and willing. The boy broke the first three strokes of crust into the mud as any beginner did, and Lachlann said nothing but only turned the rake a little in his own grip to show the angle again, and by the fourth stroke he had it, a full clean sheet of white lifted whole onto the rake's flat and held there, and Peigi, who had come down to watch with no pretence that she had come for any other reason, said that was better than she had managed her first year and she would not have believed it of him.

It is a small thing to be given the first time a boy rakes salt without breaking it, and no reciter of Dùn ìseal has ever thought it worth the keeping; but An Cnoc Ruadh kept it, in its own way, the way An Cnoc Ruadh kept most things that mattered to it and let the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche keep the rest. The peace of the ford held, those years, without a word said of it at either hall; Rathad an t-Salainn ran as it had always run; and if any at Dùn ìseal wondered, in the wet seasons when word came west and east along the road with the salt-carriers, whether the boy sent away at six was thriving where he had been sent, the answer that came back, carried in a salt-carrier's mouth rather than in any letter, was only that he was well, and growing, and had taken to the lake.

An Cnoc Ruadh's own list, in those years, began a habit it would keep the rest of Lachlann Ruadh's holding and after: when the reciters spoke of him, weighing his years against his father's and his father's father's, they had taken to adding, more often than not, a second name after the first, so that he was Lachlann Ruadh and, in near the same breath, Lachlann an Altraim, Lachlann of the fostering, until in time the second name outran the first in the mouths of those who had never known him by any other, and the list, kept by rote from reciter to reciter, began to give the one where it might once have given the other. No one at An Cnoc Ruadh could afterward have said the day the habit started, only that it had, sometime in those years the boy grew from six to eight and learned the turn of a salt-rake on the lake shore under Lachlann's own hand, and that once started it was never afterward unsaid.

Of the boy's own name in those same years, the hill's own telling, both the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche and An Cnoc Ruadh after it, keeps nothing at all. His mother's name for him was spoken daily by the household that raised him, kept whole in every hearing; it is only that neither list, in the long custom that grew up around the two of them, ever troubled to set it down, An Cnoc Ruadh because he was not yet its own and the hill of Dùn ìseal because he was, by then, no longer entirely theirs to claim. So he passed into both tellings, and out of them, as he had come, without one, called only the fosterling by the hearth that kept him and, more rarely as the years went on, the boy who went by the hearth that had sent him.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Oighrig's Lot and the Stone Cup

*GE 2,403 – 2,408*

> *Chan e mo làmh-sa a th' ann, ach làmh gach teallaich.*
> It is not my hand; it is the hand of every hearth.
>
> — Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, at the grinding of the cup, as the hearths of Tobar dhìreach keep it

## I. Of the Turns that Wore Thin

*This is told at Tobar dhìreach by whoever sits the night watch, and has been told so long that the telling has worn as smooth as the slab itself.*

For as long as anyone at Tobar dhìreach could reckon, the slab had been watched by households in their turn, one family a night, drawn from a list that the eldest of the hill kept in her head and nowhere else. It had begun, so the old ones said, in the dark of a Samhain so far back that even the list-keepers before this one could not put a year to it: a scatter of families who lived near the crack in the ground had taken, without any word said over it, to sitting by the stain in the stone a household at a time, watching for they knew not what. No one had ever seen the slab do anything. It lay grey and split-veined in its clearing, cold to the hand in every season, with the one dark stain at its lower edge that no rain had ever washed paler, and generation on generation had sat by it through the short nights and the long ones and gone home in the morning with nothing to tell.

By the year the families met to change the custom, the list had grown past what any one head could hold true. Thirty-one households stood on it, scattered from the near slopes to a full day's walk east, and the eldest who kept it, a woman named Beathag who had held the list eleven years and outlived two husbands doing it, had begun to lose the order of it the way a rope frays first at the place it is handled most. A household from the far end of the valley had come two nights running the summer before, thinking its turn was owed, and found no one else at the slab either night, the family before them having gone home a day early on the strength of a different memory of the order entirely. Nothing had come of the gap. Nothing ever came of any night at the slab, watched or not. But it sat wrong with the hill-folk that a thing so old should be let go untended even by accident, and it was Beathag herself, in the year of her own eldest son's death, who said at the Samhain gathering that she would keep no more lists, and that the hill had better find another way.

They met at the slab itself to talk it over, as such things were talked over on the hill, standing in the clearing in the last mild days before the dark half of the year, thirty-odd households or their heads, with children running at the clearing's edge and old men leaning on staffs and a wind coming down off Na Glinn Àrda that smelled already of the winter behind it. Some wanted the list kept by two heads instead of one, so that memory might check memory. Some wanted no watch at all, arguing, not for the first time and not to be the last, that a stone which had done nothing in a thousand years of watching was unlikely to begin now for want of a night's neglect. It was an old man near the front, whom the telling does not name, who said at last that if the trouble was that no head could hold thirty-one households fairly in order, then perhaps no head should try, and that the thing should be given to chance instead, the way a household chose which child herded the goats on a wet morning: by lot, one keeper at a time, until that keeper's own life gave the place up.

The hill settled such matters by silence, as it always had. The silence held long enough that the old man took it for agreement, and no one afterward said he had read it wrong. Before the light went that day it was settled between them, without any of them quite deciding when the deciding had happened, that a single keeper would be chosen from among all the households by lot, would keep the slab alone or with whatever kin wished to sit by her, and would go on keeping it until death or infirmity called for another lot to be drawn.

Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill stood near the back of the gathering that day with her shawl pulled over her head against the first spits of rain, three-and-thirty years old and thinking, so far as the telling lets her think anything at all in that hour, of nothing more than whether her own turn at the slab fell that week or the next. Her household was among the thirty-one. She had sat the night watch herself perhaps a dozen times since she was old enough to be trusted not to fall asleep against the stone, and had seen, on every one of those nights, exactly what every watcher before her had seen: a slab, a stain, a silence, and morning.

## II. Of the Lot

The lots were drawn a fortnight later, at the next full dark, because a fortnight seemed to the hill-folk long enough to be fair and not so long that anyone would forget the agreement had been made. A leather bag was found, old and much mended, that had once held a household's spindle-whorls and now held one white pebble marked with a single scratch and thirty small dark stones that were not. Beathag herself, freed at last of the list she had kept eleven years, held the bag closed in both hands until every household had sent forward the one member the lot would fall on, by whatever rule of age or standing each house kept for such things; Oighrig's father, a herder of the near slopes named Dòmhnall who owned no more of the hill than any other man of that name and was kin to none of the old kings, sent his daughter forward because she was neither his eldest nor his youngest and it had fallen to her by a rule of his own that he never explained to anyone, least of all to her.

It rained that night, a fine soft rain that put no one off standing in the clearing, and the slab shone black with it under the last light. Oighrig stood in the ring of thirty-one with her hood down around her shoulders because the hood caught the rain worse than her hair did, and watched each in turn go forward, put a hand into the bag Beathag held, and draw out a stone. She had counted, without meaning to, that she stood eleventh from the front, and had spent most of the wait working out from the rate the others drew and were disappointed that there was no way to know, from a stone already drawn, whether the white one had gone before her turn or not.

When her turn came she put her hand into the bag the way she had put it into every dark bag of grain or wool her whole life, without ceremony, and felt the stones knock cold against her knuckles, more of them than she had expected for how few households remained undrawn, and closed her fingers on the first one they found. She brought it out already knowing, from the shape of it under her thumb before she ever opened her hand, that it was not like the others; the mark ran deep enough to catch a nail.

It is told that she stood a moment with her fist closed and the rain running off her knuckles, and that the two women nearest her, who had already seen the white edge of it between her fingers, said nothing to hurry her, out of a courtesy the telling does not explain and does not need to. When she opened her hand at last, Beathag saw it first of anyone, and let the empty bag fall to her side, and said only, "That's it, then," in a voice with no more weight in it than if the matter had been who carried water that week.

No one cheered, for it was not a thing to cheer, and no one wept, for it was not yet a thing to weep over either. An old woman near her touched Oighrig's shoulder once, the way a hand is laid on a shoulder at a grave rather than a wedding, and stepped back into the ring. Oighrig looked at the pebble a long while in the failing light, turning it so the scratch caught what was left of the day, and then at the slab itself, grey and rain-black in the clearing where it had lain since before her grandmother's grandmother watched it, and put the stone into her belt, where the hill's own telling says she carried it the rest of her life.

She walked home behind her father that night without either of them saying much, and it was her father, not she, who broke the silence somewhere along the track, saying only that he had not looked to send a daughter of his to a stone for the rest of her days when he sent her forward that evening, and had not looked, either, to be asked by every stranger on Rathad an t-Salainn for the next forty years whether he was kin to the king because he shared a name with the king's own son who held the north. It was the first either of them had said aloud of a thing that would follow her the whole of her keeping: that hill-folk who did not know the near slopes heard "nic Dhòmhnaill" and thought at once of Dòmhnall Clachach, third of Rìghrean na Cloiche, who held the north those very years and was, by every account the reciters kept, no kin at all to a herder of Tobar dhìreach's low pastures. Oighrig herself had to say it plainly more times than she troubled to count, to travellers who came up the valley expecting to find the old king's blood keeping the slab and found instead a herder's daughter with wet feet and no patience for the question: her father was Dòmhnall the herder, no more and no less, and the name had never carried further than that.

## III. Of the House with the Door to the Slab

The families raised her a house before the year was out, on the clearing's edge where the ground rose just enough to keep it dry, of the same turf and stone as any hill house save that its door was set to face the slab and no other way, so that whoever slept in it woke each morning looking straight along the floor at the stone she had drawn for. It was, so far as anyone on the hill could say, the first building on all of Dia-thìr raised for no reason but to stand near the vein, and it stood so plainly for that one purpose that even children who had never been told so understood it at a glance, the way a child knows a byre from a house without being told which beasts live in which.

Oighrig moved into it in the first hard frost of that winter, and found the sitting harder alone than it had ever been in turn with her own household beside her. The nights of a shared watch had passed in low talk and the passing back and forth of a skin of buttermilk and the small complaints of people who would be gone home by morning regardless of what the night gave them. A keeper's nights, she found, ran differently. She sat them mostly by herself those first months, for though her own kin and any others were welcome to sit with her and often did in the early evenings, none of them slept there, and by full dark she was alone with the slab and whatever wind came down off Na Glinn Àrda, and no list to check the next night against, only the one long unbroken watch that had no end she could see from where she sat.

She was not unhappy in it, the telling is careful to say, though it does not say she was happy either. That first winter gave her time to notice things about the slab that thirty-one households taking turns for a thousand years had somehow not troubled to set down in any telling she had ever heard: that the stain at its lower edge was darkest in wet weather and paled, though it never wholly vanished, in a dry summer; that the stone held the day's warmth an hour or two longer than the ground around it in autumn and lost it faster in spring, as though its temper ran contrary to the world's; that a hare had made its form under the slab's overhanging lip and raised two litters there in the years Oighrig watched, undisturbed by whatever the stone was or was not. None of this, she told the few who asked her directly, amounted to an answer to anything. She had sat by the slab longer now than any single household of the old rota ever had at a stretch, and had seen, she said plainly to a traveller who pressed her on it one spring evening, no more of what the stone was for than the traveller himself had seen, standing in the clearing a single afternoon.

What she had begun to see, by the second year of her keeping, was a different trouble altogether, and one nearer her own hand to mend. The handful of coal that each household of the near valleys burned in its own custom, the small ration of the vein's an gual dathach that a family measured for itself against the cold, was measured by nothing more exact than the cup of whatever hand did the measuring that year, a mother's palm or a grandfather's or a growing son's, so that one household's handful ran near double another's without either house meaning to cheat its neighbour of anything. It had never much mattered while the custom was young and the vein plentiful and no keeper stood over the counting of it. It mattered more, Oighrig came slowly to think, sitting alone by the stone through the second dark half of her keeping, now that the slab had a single keeper whose word the hill was beginning, without quite meaning to, to ask after on other matters too.

## IV. Of the Cup Ground to Her Hand

She went to Niocol Snaidhear in the spring of her third year, a man of the near slopes some ten years older than herself who had worked stone since he was a boy old enough to hold a hammer without dropping it on his own foot, grinding querns and hearthstones and, once, a trough for a household too grand for a wooden one. He kept a low shed at the edge of his own ground with a bench worn white at one end from decades of the same motion, and Oighrig found him there of a wet afternoon with a half-finished quern between his knees and stone dust in the creases of his hands that no washing ever wholly got out.

She did not, by her own account afterward, come to him with much of a notion of what she wanted, only a trouble she had turned over enough nights by the slab to have worn its shape smooth. She set her own right hand on the bench before him, cupped as if to catch water poured from a height, and told him she wanted a cup ground of grey stone that would hold exactly what that hand held and no grain more, so that whatever household measured its handful against it would measure the same as every other household on the hill, and none would ever again burn double its neighbour's share by the accident of whose palm did the measuring.

Niocol looked at the hand a long while before he answered, turning it a little under the shed's poor light, and said at last that a hand was not a thing to copy in stone the way a quern's face was copied from another quern; a hand curled differently full than empty, and differently cold than warm, and he would need, he thought, more sittings of her than she would likely have patience for before he was done. She told him she had nothing but patience, now, and came back to the shed eleven times that summer and into the following one, each time setting her hand to the bench in the same attitude, cupped, fingers a little curled, while he worked a lump of the grey stone down with chisel and rubbing-stone and, in the last weeks, nothing but a wetted thumb and infinite slow patience of his own.

Two cups cracked in the grinding before the third one held. The first split along a vein no eye had seen in the raw stone, in the last week of shaping, and Niocol swept the pieces into a corner of the shed without a word Oighrig heard him say about it, and began again from a fresh block the following morning as though the loss cost him nothing, though she noted, and said later that she had noted, that his hands shook a little at the first cuts of the new stone in a way they had not shaken at the last cuts of the old one. The second held longer, near to finished, before a blow struck a shade too hard opened a hair-crack across its base that would have let the coal run out one grain at a time, worse than no measure at all; that one he kept on the bench through the whole of the third cup's grinding, turning to it now and then as a man turns to a mistake he means to learn the whole measure of before he lets it go.

The third cup he fitted to her hand again and again through that second summer, grinding a hair's width here, a hair's width there, until it sat in the hollow of her palm the way, so the telling says, an egg sits in a nest that has been shaped around it and no other. It was smaller than either of the two that had cracked, and darker in the stone, veined faintly white through its base, and cold in the hand even on a warm day the way all the vein's stone ran cold, and it held, when she filled it once with water to be sure, exactly what her one hand held cupped, and no more.

It is told, though the telling itself allows that no one but Oighrig could have known whether she truly said it or the words only settled onto her afterward the way words settle onto anyone whose life the hill comes to measure by, that she stood in the shed with the finished cup in her hand and said to Niocol, who had by then spent the better part of two years of his working life on the shape of her one hand, that the stone held the hand of every hearth on the near slopes, hers no more than any woman's who would ever fill it. Niocol, whom the telling gives no word of his own in reply, is said only to have gone back to his bench and begun, without being asked, on a second cup, meaning it from the first stroke to be a copy and not an original, for he had already understood, before she ever said as much to him plainly, that one keeper's cup in one keeper's house would settle nothing for households that could not walk to Tobar dhìreach and back inside a winter's day.

## V. Of the Copies

Word of the cup went out along the near valleys faster than any single teller could account for having carried it, the way word does travel when it answers a trouble every hearth already knew it had without having words for it. Within the year, stone-workers at three other places had heard enough of the shape and the reason to ask for cups of their own ground against it: a woman at Àth gharbh, where the ford crossed Rathad an t-Salainn and half the near valley's flint passed through on its way south; an old man at Achadh dhìreach, whose own hearthstone still bore, though few remembered why, a long-healed crack where a fire had once run colour under the king's own hand; and a household at Cnoc chaol, a full day's walk east of the slab, on ground poor enough that its people had less coal to measure than most and cared more than most, for that reason, that the measuring be exact.

Oighrig walked to each in turn over the space of a year, carrying the first cup wrapped in wool in a satchel she would let no one else carry for her. In the two years of its making she had grown into the habit of having it always at her own hand, and trusted no other hand to keep it safe on the road. At Àth gharbh the stone-worker ground her copy against Oighrig's own in three sittings, quicker than Niocol had managed the first, for she had his cup before her the whole time to measure against rather than a hand alone; at Achadh dhìreach the old man took longer, being slower now in his hands than he once was, but got there in the end with his grandson holding the light for him through the last evenings; at Cnoc chaol the household set two of its own young people to the grinding turn and turn about, and finished theirs inside a single season, being, as Oighrig said afterward with something that in a less careful woman might have been taken for pride, the quickest hands of the four though the last to begin.

Each copy she filled with water against the first before she would call it done, pouring from one to the other on a flat stone in the open air where any of the household could watch and see for themselves that the levels matched to a hair, and where they did not match she said so plainly and sent the worker back to the wheel, twice at Achadh dhìreach and once, to the grandson's very open disappointment, at Cnoc chaol. No cup left her hand called finished until it held water level with the first, and none of the three stone-workers, whatever else the telling says of them, is recorded arguing the point with her once she had shown them the difference with their own water and their own eyes.

## VI. Of the Meeting of the Cups

The four cups were brought together at last in the last mild days before the dark half of the year, on a stretch of open moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach where a spring rose clear and cold out of a bed of grey stone and ran a little way before losing itself again in the heather. It had no name before that day that any telling keeps. Oighrig had chosen it, so far as she chose anything about the meeting rather than let the four keepers of the cups choose it between them, because it lay roughly equal walking from all four places and because the spring gave water enough and to spare for whatever filling and comparing the day required, and because, she said to more than one who asked her why there and not somewhere nearer the slab, a measure that was to belong to no one house had no business being fixed on any one house's ground.

They came in the cold clear morning of a day the hill-folk would go on keeping, in one way or another, for as long as the custom of the coal lasted: the woman from Àth gharbh with her cup in a bag of oiled hide against the damp; the old man from Achadh dhìreach carried in a cart the last mile by his grandson, his own legs no longer equal to the walk though his hands had lost none of their sureness; the two young people from Cnoc chaol, who had walked through the night to be there by first light and showed it in the set of their shoulders; and Oighrig herself, with the first cup, the one that had cost Niocol two broken stones and the better part of two years, wrapped as always in its wool.

They set all four on a flat stone at the spring's edge, side by side in the low light, and filled each in turn from the same water, and passed each cup along the line of four for every hand there to weigh in turn, a courtesy none of them had been asked to keep, kept without discussion, as though the measure required the handling of every hand it would ever serve before it could be trusted to serve any one of them alone. The water stood level in all four to the eye of everyone who looked, and to the more careful eye of Niocol, who had walked up from his own ground to see the meeting though none of the day's work was left for him to do, and who said only, when asked, that he could find no fault in any of the four and would say so to anyone who doubted him.

It is that place the hill has called, from that morning on, Coinneachadh nan Cupan, though nothing marks it beyond the flat stone and the spring that still rises there for whoever comes to fill a fifth cup against the first four, should one ever need making, or a broken one ever need replacing against the whole line of them. The families of the near valleys and the far, from the slopes above Tobar dhìreach to the poor ground at Cnoc chaol, took the four cups home with them that evening each to its own place, and from that year the hill-folk measured the coal of their handfuls by one measure and not by the accident of whichever hand did the measuring, a thing so small in the telling of it and so large in the daily life of every hearth that touched it that the hill's own reciters, when they came at last to set the year down, gave it no more than a line: that in the years of Oighrig's keeping, the hills came to measure with one measure, and had not measured otherwise since.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Coal that Went Home

*GE 2,409 – 2,416*

> *Chaidh an gual dhachaigh.*
> The coal went home.
>
> — the households near the slab, of the coal Gilleasbuig took, as the hearths of Tobar dhìreach still say it

## I. Of Gilleasbuig's Turn

Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill kept the slab for the rest of her life, as the lot had given it her, and the rest of her life was shorter than anyone at the clearing had looked for. She came back from Coinneachadh nan Cupan on the moor in the dark of the year with a cough the wind had put into her on the walk, and would not lie down for it, and sat her nights at the stone as she had always sat them; and before the turn of the year she died in Taigh na Lice with the door open on the slab, as she had asked, and the first cup in her hand. The families buried her at the clearing's edge, the first keeper by lot to be buried by the stone she had kept, and said afterward that six years had been time enough for her to give the hill the one measure, and not a season more. But the bag of pebbles was filled again, one marked among the rest, and passed hand to hand among the households who stood the watch, and it was a man named Gilleasbuig Beag, of a family that had come to the near valley only in his father's time, whose hand came out holding the white stone.

Giorsal Bhàn stood in that ring with the rest of her household the day the lot fell to him, a young woman not yet thirty with a husband two years married and no child yet at her skirts, and she remembered after, though it meant nothing to her at the time, that Gilleasbuig had gone pale rather than glad when he opened his hand and saw what was in it, the way some men do at good news as readily as bad, and that his wife beside him had laughed once, sharply, and then put her hand over her own mouth as if the laugh had got out before she meant it to. He was a broad, quiet man who cut good hazel withies and mended a roof as well as any three men on the near slopes, and no one standing in the clearing that day would have named him first, or last, among those it might fall to. That was the whole of the custom's mercy and its whole danger both: that the stone did not choose by what a household already knew of a man.

He kept the watch as any keeper kept it, through that first winter and on into the summer, sitting the cold nights at the slab with whichever of his own kin cared to sit beside him, walking the clearing at first light to see that nothing lay disturbed, carrying water up from the spring for whoever came to fill a cup against Oighrig's. Giorsal's own household lived near enough the clearing that she saw him often in those years, going to and from his own door with an axe or a creel on his back like any other man of the hill, and she thought no more of him than she thought of any neighbour whose turn had fallen on him rather than her.

It was in the first summer of his keeping, a lean one on the near slopes with the grazing thin and the stores stretched further than any household liked to see them stretched, that a woman of Gilleasbuig's own kin, going into his house on some other errand while he was from home, found a basket set back under the bed-place with a cloth over it, and lifted the cloth thinking it food, and found instead a basket of an gual dathach, broken small, more than any hand could have gathered by accident and more, by a long way, than the handful any hearth was allowed. She did not touch it. She put the cloth back as she had found it and left the house and told no one that day, being kin to him and slow to believe her own eyes; but she told her husband before she slept, and by the third day it was known past any hope of its being unknown, the way such things always were on the near slopes, where one door stood close enough to the next that a secret kept in one house was a secret only until the wind carried a word of it as far as the well.

## II. Of the Judgement at the Slab

The families sent for Gilleasbuig to come to the clearing on a morning when the frost still lay white in the shadow of the stone and had not yet burned off the open ground where the sun reached it, and he came, and Giorsal, standing near the back of the gathering with her husband's arm through hers against the cold, thought afterward that she had never seen a man walk so far to reach so short a distance. He did not deny it when it was put to him. He stood with his hands loose at his sides, not folded, not fisted, and said only that the basket was his and the coal in it was his, taken by his own hand from the crack he was set to watch, and that he had meant, when he took it, to use it against a winter he could see coming a long way off, for a mother of his who was old and slept cold, and for nothing else that he would name.

No one at the clearing that morning doubted that this much was true. It was the *use* of the coal that shook them, not the greed of it, for there was no greed to be seen in a man who had taken it to warm an old woman's bones and not to sell it on any road; and it was for that reason, more than any other, that the judgement took as long as it did, the families standing in the cold arguing among themselves in low voices while Gilleasbuig waited in the middle of them and said nothing further, as if the matter had already left his hands the moment the cloth came off the basket.

It was an old woman of Cnoc chaol, who had walked the better part of a day to be at the judgement because her own household held one of the four cups and felt the matter touched her as nearly as it touched the slab's own valley, who said at last what none of the near families had quite been willing to say first: that the coal was not Gilleasbuig's to spend on any love, however true, because it had never once, since the crack was first watched, been any single household's to keep behind a cloth under a bed. The custom had never asked a keeper to love the vein less than his own kin. It had only ever asked him to hold nothing of it back from every hearth that had a claim on the handful, his own included, and take no more for one house's fire than the vein gave to any other's.

They sat him at last under judgement the way the hill had always judged such things when a household was put out for hoarding grain against the storm-sharing: by the silence that follows, once every voice in the clearing has said its piece and no voice rises after to say different. The silence held long enough that morning, with the frost gone from the open ground and the sun well up, that there was no mistaking it for anything but agreement. Gilleasbuig was told he would be rowed out to Eilean chrom, the low island that lay off the near coast with nothing on it a household could live from, and left there without a boat to bring himself back in; and the coal, the same voice went on, once the old woman of Cnoc chaol had named the island, would go neither to any fire nor back into any basket a living hand might carry home, but would be carried instead to the slab's own edge and given back to the ground it had come from.

Gilleasbuig said one thing more before they took him down to the shore, and it was the only thing Giorsal, standing near enough by then to hear it plainly, ever heard him say with any heat in his voice at all: that his mother would sleep cold that winter whichever way the judgement fell, whether the coal burned in her hearth or lay under a stone she would never see, and that he did not understand what the stone gained by having it back that the old woman did not lose by going without it. No one answered him. It was not, Giorsal thought afterward, a question the clearing had ever troubled to answer, and perhaps for that reason no one there was willing to invent one on the spot, with the man standing before them waiting to hear it.

## III. Of Eilean chrom

They rowed him out in the afternoon of that same day, three men of the near households taking one boat between them with Gilleasbuig sitting in the stern and saying nothing more the whole crossing, by the telling of the men who were there and told it after. Eilean chrom lay low and treeless a short pull off the coast, grazed once by nobody's sheep and fished by nobody's nets even before that day, a spit of grass and grey rock with a spring at its middle that never failed and nothing else on it a person could live from beyond what the tide gave up. They put him ashore on its lee side, where the landing was easiest, and pulled the boat back out into open water while he stood on the shingle and watched them go, and none of the three who told it afterward could agree on whether he had raised a hand to them or not, though all three agreed he had not called out.

Giorsal did not see the crossing herself. She heard it told twice over in the days after, once by one of the three oarsmen at his own door and once by his wife, who repeated it word for careful word as if the repeating were its own kind of keeping. But she saw the fire.

It stood on Eilean chrom's low rise that first night, small and steady against the dark water, and half the near coast came out to its own doors to look at it, some out of pity and some out of nothing kinder than the wanting to see a thing everyone else was seeing. It burned again the second night, smaller, Giorsal thought, though she could not have sworn to it across that distance and in that light. On the third night it was there again at dusk, no more than a coal's worth of red low down near the shingle, gone before the deepest part of the dark, and after that no one on the near coast, watching night after night through a week and then a month of watching, ever saw a fire on Eilean chrom again.

No boat went out to it. The judgement had left him there without one, and no household, whatever it felt in its own heart about the man or the coal, was willing to be the one to row out and learn for certain what three nights of fire and no fire after meant. Eilean chrom stood empty from that season on, ungrazed and unfished, the way it had stood before Gilleasbuig was put on it and the way, so far as Giorsal Bhàn ever lived to see, it went on standing after. Children on the near coast were told, in time, not to ask about the island with the spring on it, and most of them grew up asking anyway, the way children always did about the one thing they were told not to, and were given the same short answer each time: that a man had kept the watch there once, and did not keep it well, and that no one had gone near the island since, and no one would.

## IV. Of the Second Lot and the Basket Unburned

The basket itself came to the slab's own household before the month of the fires was out, carried by the same kin who had first lifted the cloth from it, set down just inside the door of Taigh na Lice the way a thing is set down that no one wants to be the one to have carried the whole way in and put where it belonged. It sat there through the rest of that season under its own cloth, and every household near the crack knew it was there, and not one of them, in all the low talk that ran up and down the near valley in those weeks, ever proposed that it should be burned. It had not been theirs to burn before Gilleasbuig took it, and his taking it had not made it burnable; if anything the judgement had settled, past any further arguing, that it never would be.

The lot for a new keeper was drawn within the same season, at the clearing, in the same bag of pebbles that had given the stone to Oighrig and then to Gilleasbuig, and this time it was Giorsal Bhàn's hand that came out of the bag holding the white stone. She had stood at enough of these drawings by then, her own household near enough the crack that she was seldom far from one, to know what was expected of whoever the lot found; what she had not known, until she felt the pebble cold against her palm and understood from the faces around her before she had properly opened her own hand what it was, was how little warning the stone gave before it changed a life. Her husband put his arm round her the way Gilleasbuig's wife had once nearly laughed; Giorsal did neither. She looked at the stone a while, the way Oighrig was said to have looked at hers years before, and then closed her hand on it and said she would keep it.

She moved into Taigh na Lice at Tobar dhìreach before the month was out, her husband and, before long, a first child with her, and took up the night-watches and the water-carrying and the weighing of cups against her own the way every keeper before her had taken them up. But the basket was hers now too, set inside the door under its cloth, and she found in the first weeks of her keeping that she could not walk past it without her eyes going to it, the way a sore tooth draws the tongue whether the tongue means to go there or not.

It was on a still evening near the year's turn, with the frost already down and the last of the light going grey over the clearing, that she lifted the cloth herself and looked at what was under it: broken coal, small pieces, no different to the eye from any handful any hearth on the near slopes was owed by right, and yet made wrong, entirely and past mending, by nothing more than whose hand had gathered it and how. She thought of Gilleasbuig's mother sleeping cold that winter regardless, as he had said she would; she thought of the fire on Eilean chrom, three nights and then none; and she understood, kneeling there with the basket open in front of her in the last of the light, that there was only the one place left on the whole island where that coal could go that would not make a liar of the judgement that had sent a man to an island without a boat over it.

## V. Of the Coal that Went Home

She carried the basket to the slab's own edge on the first clear morning after, kneeling on the same cold ground where she had knelt through half a year of night-watches by then, and set it down beside her, and began to lay the coal back under the stone's lower lip, piece by piece, pressing each fragment into the dark gap where the slab met the earth until her fingers found the give of the loosened soil and the piece would sit and hold. It was slower work than she had looked for. The gap ran narrow in places and wide in others, and more than once a piece she thought settled worked itself loose again when she reached for the next, so that she had to go back and press it in a second time, and a third, before it would keep. She worked through most of that morning and came back to finish it the next, the basket half empty and then near empty and then, on the second day, holding nothing at all.

No one had told her to do it that way, piece by piece with her own two hands rather than tipped out all at once the way a lazier keeper might have emptied it and called the matter closed. She did it slowly because it seemed to her, kneeling there with the cold coming up through the ground into her knees the way it must have come up through Oighrig's, that a thing taken wrongly, however small each piece of it, ought at least to be given back with the same care it had been taken with, if not more; and because, though she never said this to anyone in so many words, she wanted, when it was done, to be able to say truly that her own hand had put every last piece of it back where it belonged, and not merely that the basket had been emptied.

It is from that unhurried morning, and the second morning after it, that the hearths near the slab keep the four words that are still said of the whole matter, short enough that a child can carry them whole after hearing them once: that the coal went home. Giorsal Bhàn never claimed to have made the saying herself, and by her own telling, given late in her life to whoever asked her about those years, she could not afterward say for certain who had said it first, in her hearing or out of it; only that by the following summer it was already going round the near valley as if it had always been there, the way the truest sayings on the hill always seemed to arrive already old.

## VI. Of Calum Ciar and the Lot at Dùn ìseal

Word of the judgement, and of what the new keeper had done with the basket after, travelled Rathad an t-Salainn and Rathad na Spor both before that year was out, and reached Dùn ìseal in the mouth of some traveller or other long before any of the households near the slab thought to send it there on purpose, for the crack had never asked the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche for leave to judge its own. It was two summers later, by Giorsal's own reckoning, that Calum Ciar himself came up the valley to the clearing, the elder son of Eilidh Ghlas and eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, a broad grey-eyed man well past his hundred and fiftieth year who carried himself, even walking alone and unarmed among households that owed him no more than any household owed the hill, as a man used to being listened to.

He did not come, he said, standing where Gilleasbuig had once stood to hear his own judgement, to question what had been done to Gilleasbuig or where the coal had gone after; both, he allowed, had been done as the custom asked, and he had no quarrel with either. What he asked was smaller, and larger, both at once: that the next time the bag of pebbles was filled, it should be filled and drawn at Dùn ìseal, in his own sight, so that the hill that held the grazing and called the gatherings and answered to the king for both might see with its own eyes that the lot which decided who kept the vein was drawn as honestly as the lot which had once, in Oighrig's year, decided the same thing at the clearing.

Giorsal stood near enough that day to see his face while the families gave him their answer, and she thought, though she never said so where it might travel back to Dùn ìseal, that he had not looked for the answer he got. The households near the crack held their silence the way they had held it over Gilleasbuig, long enough and level enough that there was no mistaking it, and it was the same old woman of Cnoc chaol, grown older still, who said at last what the silence had already said: that the lot had been drawn at the slab since the custom first began, and would go on being drawn there, in the sight of whoever near the crack cared to stand and watch it, and that Dùn ìseal's sight, however honestly meant, was not a thing the vein had ever asked for or needed.

Calum Ciar heard it out and did not argue it there in the clearing, which Giorsal set down afterward, when she spoke of that day at all, as the one thing in his favour that she never forgot. He thanked the families for hearing him and went back down the valley the way he had come, and it was only later, from travellers again rather than from any word Dùn ìseal troubled to send the slab, that she learned he had carried the same question on to the king himself, at the ford that same summer where the two hills met each year over salt and wool.

## VII. Of the Unwritten Line

What passed between Calum Ciar and the king at the ford, Giorsal Bhàn never heard first-hand, and neither, so far as she ever learned, did anyone near the slab; it came to the near valley the way most things from the ford came to it, worn a little smoother with every mouth it passed through on the way. But the words that reached her, and that she went on repeating to whoever asked her of it in the years after, in nearly one shape from the first telling to the last, were these: that the king had heard Calum Ciar out as the families at the clearing had heard him out, without anger and without haste, and had said at the end of it only that the slab was older than the hill, and older than the grove where he himself had first been crowned, and that he would not overrule a thing that old for the asking of a man not two hundred years in the world.

Calum Ciar went home from the ford, the telling said, and asked nothing more of it. The lot went on being drawn at the slab, as it had been drawn for Oighrig and for Gilleasbuig and for Giorsal herself, and no household near the crack ever again heard Dùn ìseal ask to stand over the bag of pebbles while it was filled. The hill ruled the grazing in those years, and called the gatherings, and answered for both to the king; the keepers ruled the vein, and answered for it to no one the telling could name, not even, when it came to it, to the king himself. It was a line drawn nowhere on any stone and sworn to in no words either side troubled to write down, and it held, so far as Giorsal Bhàn lived to see it hold, for every year of her keeping after; and when she was old, and her own knees had begun to fail her on the path up from the spring, she told whoever sat with her at the last of her watches that she had never once, in all her years at the slab, seen a holder of Dùn ìseal come up the valley to ask it a second time.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of the Black Wind and the Five Fires

*GE 2,417 – 2,420*

> *Chunnaic mi an teine, is thàinig mi dhachaigh.*
> I saw the fire, and I came home.
>
> — said of the eastern fire at Cuan ruadh, by more than one who came home by it

## I. Of the Wind that Took the Thatch

It came up out of the south-east in the black hour before a morning that never properly broke, and the fisher-folk of Cuan ruadh, who had weathered every wind the sea sent them with names for most and respect for all, had no name ready for this one until it was gone and they needed one to speak of it by. It struck the coast in the first days of an Gearran, in weather that had given no more warning than a wrongness in the swell the evening before, a heave that ran against the wind rather than with it, which the older boats' captains read and put their craft up on the shingle a full tide early for no reason they could afterward explain better than that the sea had looked wrong to them.

By midday it had stripped the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar, a stretch of coast a long day's walk and more, and driven three boats that had not been hauled high enough onto the rocks below the headland, and flattened, in one household's near ruin, a drying-rack hung with the better part of a season's salted fish that the sea took back grain of salt and flake of flesh together before anyone could reach it. The wind did not merely blow; it took, the way the old tellings say a wolf takes and not merely eats, choosing what it wanted and leaving the rest broken in the road. Children were carried indoors and held there bodily by mothers who could not otherwise keep them from the doorway to watch it. An old woman of Ceann chiar, who had seen eighty winters on that coast and outlived two husbands lost to lesser storms than this one, said afterward that she had heard the wind speak, though she would not say in what tongue, and no one on that coast ever doubted she believed it, whatever the rest of them made of the claim.

It blew out by the second dusk, going as suddenly as it had come, and left behind it a coast without roofs enough to shelter half the households that had had them two days before, granaries opened to the sky, and boats that would need a full season's mending before they swam again. Of Cuan ruadh's own eleven boats, four were fit for nothing but firewood, and a fifth would need a new keel before it saw water. The fishing that fed the coast through the dark months, which had never in living memory failed outright, failed that winter before it had properly begun, for a coast with half its boats broken and half its granaries roofless could neither catch nor keep enough against the cold.

It was the eldest folk of that coast, remembering other winds with other names and no name for this, who first called it A' Ghaoth Dhubh, for the sky it left behind was the colour of a smoored hearth for three days after, ash-dark from horizon to horizon though not a cloud stood in it, the way a fire's smoke hangs low over a valley long after the flame that made it is out. No reciter of the hill ever came to set the name straighter, and the coast never asked for a straighter one. It has been A' Ghaoth Dhubh on every tongue that has spoken of it since, the eldest storm whose name the coast still keeps whole, and every wind that has struck that shore in all the years since has been measured against it and found lesser.

No one of that coast died in the wind itself, a mercy the tellings are careful to set down plainly, for a wind that could take a roof whole could as easily have taken a life, and every household on the shore has its own small telling of how it came to be spared: a door that held when a neighbour's did not, a child called in from the shingle a breath before the worst of it struck, a boat left one turn later than it should have been on a rota that no one afterward could say why it had fallen out that way. What the wind took instead, it took slowly, through the winter that followed and not in the day itself: a season's food, a season's shelter, and, for more than one household, the last of a fishing life that a lost boat and a maimed hand between them made too hard to carry on. It was the winter after the wind, and not the wind's own day, that the coast came to reckon as the harder half of what A' Ghaoth Dhubh cost it.

## II. Of the Winter the Custom Reached the Coast

What saved Cuan ruadh that winter, when its own granaries lay open to the weather and its own boats lay broken on the shingle, was a custom the coast had never troubled to take up on its own account, having never before needed it. The sharing had begun generations before at Dùn ìseal, in the valleys under the hill, a grain-year's surplus carried in at Samhain and given back out by the count of mouths so that no household went into the dark months harder than its neighbour; and it had gone out from the hill slowly, the way such things go, along the roads that carried salt and flint and wool between one valley and the next, taken up first by households that had seen it worked at the hill and thought it good, then by households that had only heard of it and thought it good enough to try.

By the year of A' Ghaoth Dhubh it had reached, by whatever crooked road a custom travels, the settlements of that same coast north and south of the worst of the wind, Ceann chiar among them, and the inland valleys a day and more west of Cuan ruadh, households that grew barley and kept cattle on ground the coast had none to spare for, and knew nothing of storms that struck from the sea because their own hills stood between them and the worst of the weather. Word of what the wind had done to the coast reached those valleys within the week, carried by a trader who had meant to buy salt fish at Cuan ruadh and found instead a shore of broken boats and bare roof-trees. It was those settlements and valleys, with no word sent down from Dùn ìseal at all, that first sent grain east to a coast most of their own households had never set eyes on.

It went first as a scatter of single acts, one household sending what it could spare because a neighbour had told it what the trader said, and another following because the first had; and it was only in the second month of that winter, when the scatter had grown too large for any one household to account for on its own, that the valleys' own holders sat down together and agreed, in words close enough to the hill's own custom that whoever named it first is not remembered, to send it on as the hill would have sent it, weighed by the count of mouths at Cuan ruadh and given without asking what any one household there had managed to save from the wreck of its own store. Grain came down on carts and on the backs of the valleys' own cattle, salted meat in skins, wool enough to card and weave new roofing against the winters still to come, and none of it came with any reckoning kept of who at Cuan ruadh had lost the most and who the least, for that was not how the custom had ever been kept at the hill, and the valleys, having taken it up, kept it whole.

No household of that coast is known to have starved that winter, and the tellings of Cuan ruadh, when they came at last to set the year down, gave the custom no grander name than the coast's own folk gave it: the bringing-in, as it was called wherever it went, or, among the plainer-spoken, only the help, without further word for what it was or where it had first been thought of. It is told that not every household on that coast learned the custom's name or its origin that winter or ever after; it is told that every household learned, before the spring tide, that the grain had come, and had been fair, and had been enough.

## III. Of Lìleas, Who Watched the Boats Come In

Lìleas of Cuan ruadh was one-and-twenty that winter, the second daughter of a household that fished the water off the headland in a boat her father had built with his own hands and lost, along with two fingers of his left hand taken by a line under strain, on the second day of A' Ghaoth Dhubh. She had grown up on that coast knowing the sea the way a hill-child knows weather, by the smell of it before it showed itself and by what her elders' faces did when they looked at it, and had spent every autumn of her life since she was old enough to be trusted on the shingle watching for the boats to come home before dark, a habit the whole coast kept without troubling to call it anything, because a coast that fishes for its living watches its own boats home as a matter of course.

That winter, with her father's hand still healing crooked and the household's boat six weeks from swimming again, she had less to watch for than she was used to, and more time on the shingle than the work of the house strictly needed of her; and it was in that idle watching, as she told whoever asked her how the thing began, that she first came to notice what the coast had never troubled to put into words before: that a boat coming home in failing light, even a boat whose captain knew every rock of that shore by feel, ran a different risk in the last stretch before the beach than in all the miles before it, because the land, once the sun was down, gave a returning boat nothing to steer by but memory and the sound of the surf.

She had heard, from a trader who had come through with grain that same winter, of a fire kept somewhere on a headland of the western coast, built for a purpose she did not then understand well enough to repeat correctly to her own household, and had turned the tale over more than once through that long, roofless, half-fed winter without doing anything about it beyond turning it over, for it was, she said afterward, a stranger's tale of a stranger's coast, and she saw no reason a headland of Cuan ruadh needed anything a western headland had thought worth doing.
