What changed her mind, so far as the telling of it can be trusted, was neither the trader's tale nor any single storm, but the ordinary run of that whole hard winter, watching boat after boat come in later than she liked in light that was worse than she liked, and reckoning, each time, how much of what she watched for on the shingle she could not in truth see at all once the light had gone, and how much she was only listening for and hoping. A coast that watched its boats home by daylight had never needed more than eyes for it. A coast whose boats, mended late and fished hard to make up a lost season, were coming home later and later into the dark as the days shortened toward midwinter, needed, she came slowly to think, something the eye alone no longer served.

## IV. Of the Fire She Kept on the Eastern Cape

She put it first to her own household, over a meal thin enough that winter that no one at the board had much appetite for argument, and her father, whose hand had healed crooked enough that he no longer trusted it fully on a line in rough water, was the first to say he saw no harm in it and perhaps some good, if she meant to do the work of keeping it herself and did not look to the rest of the household to carry wood up a headland on top of everything else the winter already asked of them. It was agreed, in the plain way such things were agreed on that coast, without any vote taken and without anyone troubling to write the agreement down anywhere but in the memory of the household that made it: Lìleas would keep a fire on the cape east of the village, in her own household's turn, and any other household that wished to share the carrying of wood, or the watching of it through a night, was welcome to, and none was asked to.

The cape stood a stiff climb above the village, a shoulder of bare rock with nothing on it before that winter but sea-birds and the low scrub that grew wherever the salt wind let anything grow at all, and it took her and her younger brother the better part of a month of short winter days to carry up enough driftwood and cut peat to keep even a modest fire burning through a single long night, let alone through the run of nights a whole storm season might ask for. She built the fire first in a shallow pit scraped into the bare rock, walled on the seaward side with stones carried up one and two at a time from the shingle below, so that the wind that would have scattered an open fire in an hour instead drove the flame and the smoke both out toward the water, where any boat looking for it would see it best.

The first nights she kept it alone, sitting by it through the dark with a skin of water and whatever her mother could spare from the household's own thin table, watching the black water below for a shape that did not come, for no boat of Cuan ruadh's own crippled fleet was out on the worst of those first nights to need finding by anything. She kept it anyway, through nights that gave her nothing back for the keeping but cold hands and a fire that burned down faster than she had reckoned it would, and it is told, though the telling allows this much may be kindness rather than plain memory, that more than one household of the village climbed the cape those first weeks with no boat of their own out at all, only to sit an hour with her and see for themselves what she was about, and went down again having seen nothing but a woman and a fire and the black sea giving back no more than its own darkness.

It was her brother, keeping the fire with her on a night neither of them afterward could put a precise date to, who first said aloud what neither had quite let themselves say before: that if the fire served no boat that winter, it would have cost them a month's wood and nothing more, and that a month's wood was a thing the household could bear to lose against the chance, however small that first winter made it look, of a night when it would not be wasted. Lìleas kept the fire the rest of that season on no better reasoning than her brother's, and no worse, and told anyone who asked her why she troubled with it exactly that: that it cost little enough to keep, and might cost the coast a boat and its crew if it were not there the one night it was needed.

## V. Of the Fires that Answered It

Word of the fire on Cuan ruadh's cape went along the coast roads that winter and the next the way word of any new thing travels among people who talk to strangers at every ford and market, faster and further than the fire's own small light could have carried it, and by the second winter after A' Ghaoth Dhubh, three other coasts had heard enough of it, and had troubled enough over their own boats in their own bad weather, to want fires of their own.

The northern point took to it first, where the coast turned hardest and the currents ran fastest against a boat trying to make the shore in the dark. The households there raised a fire on ground that had, without anyone quite planning it that way, already been scorched black for longer than living memory by shore-fires kept for other reasons in other ages; theirs burned steadier than Cuan ruadh's Teine a' Chlachair had, for they had Lìleas's own year of trial to learn from before they ever laid their own wood, and never once let it fail through a whole storm season once it was begun. The cape north-east of that, where the passage in toward the deeper water ran narrow enough that a boat astray by even a boat's length could find rock instead of channel, was next: a man named Seathan mac Pheadair took the fire's keeping on himself much as Lìleas had, alone at first and then with kin who came to share it, and cut, on a stone at the fire's edge, one stroke for every boat he ever saw pass safe by his flame, a tally that within a few years had grown longer than any one telling has troubled to count out in full.

Last of the four to be built, and by every account the surest of them, was the fire of the southern cape at Tobar dhearg, raised on a mound of stacked stone breast-high rather than a scraped pit as Cuan ruadh's first had been, so that the flame stood clear of the spray even in the roughest weather. The coast's own reciters were already saying, before the mound was finished, that with Cuan ruadh's fire and this one and the two between them, and the older fire that had burned so long on the Baile chrom headland in the north-west that no one living could say when it was first lit, the sea round the whole island now had five points of flame to answer it in the dark, cape answering cape the length of the coast, so that a boat lost in a storm off any shore of Dia-thìr had, for the first time within any telling's memory, a fire somewhere within its sight to steer toward. It was from that reckoning, made first by a reciter of Tobar dhearg who never troubled to give her own name to the saying, that the coast came to call them together the five fires, and has called them so on every telling since.

None of the four newer fires were kept the same way twice; each coast built its own to its own ground and its own weather, and none of the tellings that keep them troubles to say one was better tended than another, save that Cuan ruadh's was first, and Lìleas its first keeper, a fact the coast has never once let a traveller forget, whatever else about that hard winter has worn thin in the telling.

## VI. Of the Boat that Came Home by It

It was in the third winter of the fire's keeping, on a night that gave no more warning than A' Ghaoth Dhubh had given, that the fire did the one thing every night before had only promised it might. A boat out of a village two coasts north of Cuan ruadh, blown far off its own water by a wind that had turned three times in an afternoon and given its crew nothing steady to read, came upon full dark with a failing wind, a following sea it did not know, and a coastline it could no longer place by any mark its captain trusted.

Lìleas was on the cape that night with her brother and, for once, her father, whose hand had healed well enough by then to carry wood if no longer to trust a line, and it was her father who first saw, or thought he saw, a shape against the last grey of the water that was not quite the shape of a wave. He said nothing at first, for a fisherman who cries a boat where there is none costs his household nothing but a wasted watch, but he set more wood on the fire than the night's cold alone called for, and it burned up bright and high enough that within a little while none of the three of them any longer doubted there was a boat out there, low and struggling, working hard against a sea that wanted to put it onto rock rather than sand.

What the boat's own captain said afterward, to anyone who asked him in the villages he touched for the rest of his working life, was that he had given the coast up for lost an hour before, was steering by nothing better than the set of the wind against his face and a growing certainty that the next thing his keel touched would be stone, and had seen, low on the black land ahead of him, a single point of fire where he had expected nothing at all: no village lit for a feast, no house left burning by carelessness, nothing he could account for by any tale he knew of that shore, only a fire burning high and steady on a headland with no house near it that he could see. He steered for it because he had nothing better left to steer for, and found, coming in under it at last with his boat still whole and his crew all breathing, a beach he did not know and three figures on the cape above him who came down the path with torches to help him haul his boat clear of the tide before he had so much as told them his own name.

He told Lìleas, once he had breath enough to tell her anything, that he had not known the fire was kept for boats like his until he was already steering for it, and asked her, in the plain way of a man who has just been given his life back and does not yet know how to speak of the size of the gift, why a coast that had never seen him before would keep a fire burning all a hard winter's night for a boat that might never come. She told him, in words the coast has kept ever since as near to what she said as any telling of a moment like that can promise to be, that the fire was kept for whichever boat needed it, on whichever night it came, no more for him than for any other, and that this was the whole of the reason for it and had been from the first cold night she carried wood up the cape alone and found nothing there to answer her but her own fire and the dark. He slept that night, and three nights after while his boat was made fit to sail home in, in the household that had fed most of that coast through the winter of A' Ghaoth Dhubh and had lit, out of that same winter's need, the first of the five fires that now stood along every shore of Dia-thìr the sea could reach in the dark; and it is that fire, burning on the cape above Cuan ruadh through every storm season since, that the coast's own tellers point to first, of all the five, whenever they are asked which one began it.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of Anndra Breac

*GE 2,421 – 2,423*

> *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.*
> We did not come; we were here.
>
> — cut on Calbh Cnoc ghorm, and spoken at the ford from the year after Anndra Breac

## I. Of the Watch at Seann Skell

Four men kept the tower at Seann Skell that autumn, as four had kept it every autumn since the hill-folk first put a roof back on Seann-Dhaoine' old watch-stones and set a household there to mind the western water: the island had no enemy worth the name; a coast that watches its own sea is a coast that is never taken wholly by surprise, and the hill-folk had learned that much from every people whose ruin they had walked through on the way west. The tower stood at the northern shoulder of the bay, round-walled in stone older than any teller could put an age to, and from its top a watcher could see the whole reach of water from the last rocks of the point to the grey line where the sea gave up and the sky began.

It was Tormod Chaol who saw it first, in the last light of a day that had already turned the water the colour of a knife, and he did not at first believe what his own eyes told him, for a man does not, seeing such a thing for the first time, trust himself over the water he has watched every evening of his working life without seeing anything stranger than a whale or a drifting spar. What rose off the point, a long way out and low against the light, was a back, dark and wet and shining, longer by half than any whale he had ever helped haul ashore or heard sung of by men who had, and it came up slow, the way a thing comes up that has all the time in the world and no fear of anything the shore can do to it, and went under again without breaking the water into foam, as a stone goes under that is let down rather than thrown.

He called the other three up from the fire below, and by the time they had climbed the narrow stair and crowded the parapet the water had gone flat and grey and empty again, giving nothing back but the ordinary chop of an ordinary evening, and for a moment each of the four half hoped, in the private place a man keeps such hopes, that he alone had seen nothing and the others would say so. None of them said so. Each had seen enough, in the last of the light, to swear afterward to a length, a colour, a manner of going under, and no two of their four tellings agreed in every particular, as no two tellings of a fast and half-seen thing ever do; but all four agreed on the two matters that mattered, that the back was long as three boats laid end to end, and that whatever wore it was not a whale, for a whale blows before it goes down and this had made no sound at all, only the low hiss of water closing over something that did not choose to be heard.

Word of it went down to the households below before the four had so much as come down from the tower, carried by the youngest of them, who could not keep it to himself the length of the stair, and by the time the tale had gone twice round the bay it had grown a head and a neck that none of the four had sworn to and lost nothing of the length they had. The old women of Seann Skell, who kept between them more tellings of the western water than any four men had years to have heard, said only that the sea had shown itself before to watchers who had the luck or the misfortune to be looking at the right hour, and would show itself again to others after these four were dust, and that a wise household neither doubted the watchers nor put out a boat that evening on the strength of the doubting. It is the first sighting the tellers ever tied to a place a man could point to and a count of men who could be asked, and it went into no telling grander than the bay's own, until a man who had never climbed that tower came to hear of it the following spring, at a gathering fifty miles from any water Tormod Chaol had ever wetted his feet in.

Tormod Chaol himself kept, for the rest of that autumn, a shorter watch and a longer silence than the other three, climbing the tower each evening at the hour the light had caught the thing and standing at the parapet a while after his turn was properly done, though he never again saw anything the water gave back but the ordinary chop it had always shown him before that one evening. Asked, in his own old age, whether he wished he had never climbed the stair that night, he would say only that a man who has seen a thing the sea does not commonly show cannot afterward unsee it, and that he did not know whether that was a burden or a gift, and had stopped trying to decide which.

## II. Of the Planks on the Western Sand

It was that same season, before the tale of the tower had properly finished going round the bay, that the wrack along the coast south of Seann Skell began to give up planks the like of which no household there had cause to build or buy. They were narrow, shaped with a care no coracle or hide-boat of the island's own building troubled to spend on a plank that would be under water half its life anyway, and stitched rather than pegged, sinew or cord drawn through holes bored close along each edge in a line as even as a weaver's selvage, so that a length of two boards lashed together lay along the sand like something sewn rather than built. No two pieces that washed in over that season matched exactly, as though the sea had broken up more than one hull and scattered the wreckage of each the length of the shore before any of it came ashore, and no household along that coast, asked afterward, could say it had lost a boat of its own building answering to any of the pieces, nor lacked a man, woman or child it could not account for among its own dead and living both.

That last was the part the coast turned over longest, more even than the planks themselves. A wreck without a body is not, on that coast or any other the tellers knew of, an ordinary wreck; the sea that breaks a boat commonly keeps something of what was riding in it, a length of rope still knotted to a thwart, an oar with a hand's wear worn into the grip, or, in the worst weathers, worse than an oar. What came ashore that season was wood alone, stitched wood broken small, and not one scrap of anything that had ridden in the wood, no cord that was not ship's cord, no tool, no bone, nothing a household could grieve over or bury, only planks enough, gathered and laid out along one low wall by a fisherman with more curiosity than most, to account for at least two hulls and perhaps three, and no drowned man's face to put to any of them.

The fisherman's name was Micheil Beag, a name half the coast bore by then, and it was he who first thought to walk the whole stretch of shore a second time with the planks already laid out, matching what he found against what he already had, the way a man pieces a broken pot back together to see what shape it kept before it broke. He got, by the end of that walking, two lengths of hull curved enough to show him the shape of the boats they had come from, narrower and longer in the beam than anything built on that coast, built for open water rather than the close fishing the coast's own boats were cut for, and he said so to anyone who would listen, at the tower, at the shore households, and later, because he was a man who liked an audience more than most, to a teller who had come that way with nothing better to do that season than listen to whatever the western coast had to tell him.

The teller's name was Anndra Breac, and he listened to Micheil Beag's planks the way he had, by then, taken to listening to everything that coast had to offer him, turning it over for longer than the matter seemed at first to deserve.

## III. Of Anndra Breac, Who Made a Telling

Anndra Breac was three-and-forty that year, a teller by trade in the loose way the word was used on that coast, meaning a man who carried news and old tales both from household to household in exchange for his supper and a place by the fire, welcome everywhere and rooted nowhere, with no wife the tellings ever named and no household of his own beyond whichever one had last fed him. He had walked the western shore, on and off, for the better part of twenty years, and knew its households, its old wrecks, its half-forgotten burial mounds and its Seann-Dhaoine' ruins better than most men born to any one of them, for a man who belongs everywhere a little comes in time to know a coast the way its own people, each rooted to their one stretch of it, rarely trouble to learn the whole.

He had heard, over those twenty years, a great many tellings of where the hill-folk had come from, most of them agreeing on nothing beyond the plain fact that Ailean Mòr had walked out of a grove at Doire ghlas with a warmth in him no man before or since had carried, and had gone south to take a hill, and that everything else the coast's own households believed of their own beginnings before that grove was a scatter of half-tales that no two households told alike: that the hill-folk had always been on the island, as the elders of Cnoc ghorm held and had carved into a stone before any teller now living had learned his trade; that they had come up out of the bare ground in the first spring after the world was made; that they had walked dry-shod over a sea-floor since drowned, from a shore no one now living had seen. Anndra had carried all three tellings in his own head at different times without troubling to choose between them, the way a man carries several coins of different mintings without asking which is truest, for a teller's business, as he understood it, was to carry a tale, not to settle it.

What the planks on Micheil Beag's wall did, over the weeks Anndra spent going back to look at them, was give him a fourth telling he had never carried before, and one he found, turning it over by whatever fires would have him that autumn, that he could not afterward put down. A boat, he came to think, watching the low light catch the stitched seams Micheil Beag had laid out for him a third and a fourth time, is not a thing a people builds to walk out of the ground with, nor a thing a drowned road leaves behind it. A boat is a thing built by hands that already knew water, built to be lost on water, and two or three boats broken small enough to leave nothing whole but their planking, with not one body to grieve, argued to his mind a crossing rather than a wreck close to shore, made once, long before any telling now kept remembered it being made, over water wide enough that whatever the sea did to the hulls and the people both, it kept what it took and gave back only wood.

He did not, by his own account afterward, come to the thought all at once, nor with any confidence he was right; he came to it slowly, the way a man comes to trust a bridge he has crossed several times without it giving way, and he tried it out first on Micheil Beag himself, who heard it out, turned it over as long as Anndra had, and said at the end of it only that he did not know, which was, from a man who knew that shore's wrecks better than any other living soul, as near to agreement as Anndra was going to get from anyone that season. He tried it next on two or three households up and down the coast who had known him twenty years and would hear him out on the strength of that alone, and got from most of them the same careful not-knowing, and from one old woman of a household near Seann Skell, who had heard every telling the coast possessed and outlived most of the tellers who carried them, a long look and the single remark that a tale a man cannot leave alone is a tale worth telling somewhere it will be properly heard, whatever comes of the telling.

One household alone turned him from its door over the telling before he had carried it further than the shore, a fisherman near Caol bheag who kept the old carving of Cnoc ghorm's saying cut small into his own lintel, as a few households of that coast did, and who told Anndra plainly that a man who came to his hearth to say the hill-folk had crossed a sea from somewhere was a man who might as well tell him his own father was a stranger, and would find no meal and no bed under that roof for the saying. Anndra took the door shutting on him without argument, as he had, by his own account, taken every door shut on him in twenty years of walking for one telling or another, and thought no more of it than he thought of a wet night with no roof at all, until the same closing came at him from every door at once the following spring.

It was the watchers' back in the western water, more than the planks, that gave Anndra the shape the telling finally took, for a coast that had just seen, with its own four pairs of eyes, a thing long enough and strange enough to argue for a sea with room in it for things no teller had words ready for, was a coast that would hear a tale of a long crossing without laughing him off its threshold before he had finished the first sentence of it; and by the turn of that year Anndra Breac had a telling whole in his head, worked and reworked by a dozen firesides until the words came to him without his troubling to reach for them, in which the hill-folk had not always stood on the island nor come up out of its ground nor walked over a drowned sea-floor, but had crossed the sea in boats, once, out of some shore no living telling named, and had lost more of themselves to the crossing than any telling now kept remembered losing, and had come ashore few and had grown many.

## IV. Of the Ford

He carried the telling east that spring, the length of the island, to the yearly gathering at the ford, where the hill's own holder and An Cnoc Ruadh's met each year to settle what wanted settling between the two, and where, over the generations since Raghnall Ceannfhionn first waded that water to talk salt for wool, every kind of household on the island had come to bring its own business, its own goods, and, more than either, its own news, so that a teller with a telling worth hearing could be sure of a crowd there such as no single coast, however long he walked it, would ever give him.

He waited, as the custom of that gathering ran, until the business of the day was done and the fires of evening lit, when tellers of every kind took their turn by whichever fire would have them, and when his turn came he chose the largest fire he could get a footing by, well clear of the small fires at the edge of the crowd, close enough to the king's own fire that men of the hill and men of An Cnoc Ruadh both stood within easy hearing of him. The telling came out as he had shaped it through the winter, plainly and without apology: the crossing, the loss, the coming ashore of few where many had set out. By every account that has come down of that evening he told it well, with the ease of a man who has said a thing to himself so many times by so many firesides that the words no longer cost him anything to find.

The crowd did not hear him out to the end. It began, as such things begin, with one voice from somewhere near the back of the gathering, an old man of a hill household who called out that no teller with any claim to his trade told the households of Dia-thìr that they had come from anywhere, for they had not come, they had always been, and Calbh Cnoc ghorm said so in words cut there before any living grandfather was born; and where one voice led, in a crowd already restless with a full day's business behind it and drink enough in it to loosen tempers that might otherwise have kept their own counsel, others followed fast, until Anndra's own voice, still carrying the last of his telling, could no longer be heard over the shouting that had risen to drown it. He did not, by every account, raise his own voice to match theirs, nor try a second time to finish what he had begun; he stood where he was until it was plain to him and to everyone else that no more of the telling would be heard that night by anyone who wanted to hear it, and then he stepped back from the fire and left the crowd to its shouting.

What followed, in the way of such gatherings, was less a judgement than a driving-out that no one household troubled to claim as its own doing: households that had fed him gladly enough on his way east that spring would not have him at their fires that night nor the next morning, and by the time the gathering broke and the households went their own ways home, it was understood on every road out of the ford, without any one voice having said it in so many words, that Anndra Breac was not to be fed at a hill hearth again, nor given a place by any fire that called itself of Dia-thìr's own telling, for the rest of whatever years the sea or the road left him. No one struck him. No one needed to. A teller lives by welcome, and the ford that evening withdrew his, coast by coast, faster than any single household could have managed alone, and by the following spring there was not a hearth from the eastern cape to the western shore that would own to having fed him since.

## V. Of the King, Who Laughed and Then Was Quiet

The king had stood the length of the telling at his own fire, near enough to hear all of it before the shouting rose, and those who stood nearest him that evening told afterward, each in his own words but all agreeing on the shape of it, that he had laughed, once, short and low, at some point in Anndra's telling that none of them could afterward agree on exactly, a man's low private laugh rather than any mockery meant to carry, the kind a man gives a jest that has caught him by surprise rather than one he saw coming and braced against. He did not join the shouting when it rose, nor did he move to still it, standing where he was with the firelight on him while the crowd did the driving-out it did without any word from him one way or the other; and when it was done, and Anndra had stepped back from the largest fire to find no smaller one that would take him either, the king was seen to be quiet, in the particular way those who had watched him thirty years and more knew to read as more than ordinary silence, a stillness that sat on him the rest of that evening and did not lift with the fire's dying.

He said nothing of it that night to anyone who left a telling of what he said, and nothing the next day either, by any account that has come down; and it is told, though the telling allows this much may owe more to the shape a tale takes in the mouths that carry it than to any one witness's sworn word, that a woman of his own kin asked him once, some time after, plainly, whether the teller had spoken true, and that he answered her only that he had heard a great many tellings of where his own people came from in all his own years, and had never yet troubled to choose one over another, which she took, as she told it after, for neither a yes nor a no but a door he did not mean to open for her that day.

Whatever the laugh had been, and whatever the silence after it was, the king made no move that spring, nor any spring after, to call Anndra Breac back to a hearth, nor to still the coast that had driven him from one; and the households that had shouted him down took his silence, as households will, for the answer that suited each of them best.

## VI. Of the Saying Spoken at the Opening

The gathering that met at the ford the following spring opened, for the first time within any telling's memory, with a saying spoken aloud before any business of salt or wool or marriage was so much as raised: the words cut on Calbh Cnoc ghorm, which the people of that hill had kept by mouth across more generations than any one line could count, spoken now not as a thing believed quietly in each household's own heart but as a thing said together, aloud, at the start of the year's meeting, by whoever stood nearest the fire when the crowd had gathered and the business was ready to begin. We did not come; we were here. No one teller is remembered as the first to have said it that spring in place of any other opening; it is told only that it was said, and that it was said again the spring after, and every spring after that, until no household coming to the ford could remember a gathering that had opened any other way, and the saying that had stood carved on a stone at Cnoc ghorm for longer than any living telling could account for became, from that year, a thing spoken at the opening of every gathering the ford ever held, a rule of the telling and not only a belief held apart in each hearth's own quiet keeping.

Of Anndra Breac himself, after that first spring, little more is told with any certainty. He was seen that same year along the western shore south of Seann Skell, walking the strand below the tower where Micheil Beag's planks still lay against the wall he had stacked them on, though whether he stopped to look at them again no teller who saw him passing troubled to ask him, and none who saw him that day spoke to him or was spoken to, for the coast that had fed him gladly twenty years running had by then taken up, coast household by coast household, the same closed door the ford had shown him first. He walked on south along the strand and did not look back at the tower nor at the man who watched him go, and it is that walking, and no other end to it, that the western shore's own tellers kept of him: a man going on along an empty beach in the direction the tide was running, out past the last household that would have fed him and on toward whatever shore lay beyond the one the tellings could still follow him to. No teller of that coast, then or after, claimed to have fed him again, nor buried him, nor marked where he stopped walking; and none, asked why the coast let a man who had first given them their fourth telling of themselves go so unremembered afterward, ever gave an answer better than that a coast which will not keep a tale will not trouble long over the man who carried it.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Fosterling's Return

*GE 2,424 – 2,428*

> *Dh'fhalbh e 'na ghille; thàinig e dhachaigh 'na dhuine.*
> He went a boy; he came home a man.
> — the salt-road's own telling, of the fosterling never named

## I. Of the Paired Marks at Ros dhomhain

*This is told at the river-mouth below An Cnoc Ruadh, where the rock still stands and the marks are still read, though few now living can say which keeper cut which.*

He was thirty years old that spring and had raked salt on the lake shore since he was eight, and it did not occur to him, walking down to the river-mouth on an ordinary morning to see what Seònaid Mhòr had done to the tide-rock, that he was walking toward the last four years he would spend calling An Cnoc Ruadh his only home. Seònaid was his own age within a season, a broad, quiet woman who had kept the rock since her mother's hands grew too stiff for the chisel, and she had taken, that year, to a habit no keeper before her had troubled with: where every mark since the rock was first cut had recorded the one thing a keeper thought worth recording, the high water that crept a little further up the stone with every generation that watched it, Seònaid cut two strokes for every tide instead of one, a mark for the water's highest reach and, beside it, a shorter mark for its lowest ebb.

"One tells you the sea is rising," she said, when he asked her why, crouched at the rock with her chisel still in her hand and salt dust white on her knees. "It says nothing about how far it falls back. I want both told, so whoever reads this after me has the whole of it and not the half that frightens."

He turned that over as he walked back up to the drying platforms, the way he turned over most things Seònaid said, slowly and more than once. It was, he thought, a small enough change to a stone that had stood plain and single-stroked since before either of them was born, and yet it was the kind of change that An Cnoc Ruadh's own people, unlike the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche fifty miles east, seemed to make without asking leave of anyone: a woman decided a thing was worth doing more fully than it had been done, and did it, and the doing became, within a season or two, simply how it was done. Her pairs could be read that year and every year after; the keepers who came to the rock once she was gone went back, in time, to the single stroke, finding the doubled work more than the plain record needed, but no reciter of that shore ever troubled to say her pairs had been wrong to make. They were only, in the end, more than the custom wanted kept.

## II. Of the Third Rock at Inis thais

Word of the paired marks went along the coast road the way most things went along that coast, in a carrier's mouth rather than in any letter, and reached Inis thais, two days' walk to the south-west round the shoulder of the lake, before the season was out. He never learned who first told it there, or whether the telling that reached Inis thais even kept the doubling that made Seònaid's marks worth remarking on; what came back to Ros dhomhain, the following year, was only that the households of Inis thais's own harbour had begun cutting marks of their own on a rock at their own harbour mouth, at the same spacing Seònaid used, though none of them could say why that spacing and no other, since none of them had ever troubled to ask the keeper who had first thought of it or the reasons she gave for the width between one mark and the next.

It struck him, when the word came back, as a strange way for a thing to travel: not as an idea carried whole, with the mind that made it still attached, but as a bare fact of practice, a spacing on a stone, taken up by people who kept the habit and lost the reasoning behind it in the same crossing. Three rocks stood, by then, along that shore and the next, cut at the same interval and read by three different hands, and no one at any of the three harbours could have told a stranger why the interval was what it was, only that it had always, within any keeper's memory, been kept so. He said as much to Seònaid once, sitting with her at the river-mouth while she cut a mark he had watched her cut a hundred times before, and she only shrugged and said that most customs, if you dug down far enough under them, turned out to have started the same way: someone thought a thing worth doing, and enough people agreed without ever quite saying so aloud, and after that it was a custom and no longer a thought, which was, she said, the whole of how anything at An Cnoc Ruadh or anywhere else on the island ever came to be done at all.

## III. Of the Landing of Laid Stone

The river-mouth itself changed under his own hands that same year, more than the tide-rock ever had. An Cnoc Ruadh's boats had put out from an open shingle beach since before Lachlann Ruadh's grandmother's grandmother held the hill, hauled up above the tide-line each evening on rollers cut fresh from whatever driftwood came to hand, a way of landing that worked well enough in fair weather and cost a boat or a bruised shin in foul; and it was Peigi Dhubh, not her father, who first said aloud, at the household's board one wet autumn evening, that a hill whose whole wealth now travelled by water deserved better than a beach any winter tide could rearrange without asking.

Lachlann agreed readily enough, being by then a man past sixty who had grown willing to let his daughter's plans stand alongside his own, and the work went to every household of the hill that could spare a season's labour from the salt-rakes: stone carried down from the low quarry above the lake, laid course on course at the river-mouth where the fresh water of Loch chrom met the tide coming up from the sea, until by the second summer there stood a landing a boat could come alongside at any state of the water without a single hand needed to haul it clear of the mud. He worked the stone himself through most of that second summer, his hands grown hard with salt-rake work but new to the different ache of setting a course of laid stone true, and it was there, more than at any tide-rock or salt-pan, that he came to think of himself as a man of An Cnoc Ruadh's own building rather than a boy the hill had merely taken in.

It was the hill's first way onto open water that did not depend on a beach's mercy, and word of it travelled, as the marks had, along every road the salt-carriers walked: that An Cnoc Ruadh now had a landing of laid stone at its own river-mouth, and boats out of harbours further down the coast began, within a few years, to put in there themselves rather than carry on to the open beaches beyond, so that the houses that had stood scattered along that shore for longer than any list could number began, almost without anyone deciding it should be so, to draw in closer round the landing and the rock together, until the scatter had become, by the time he was thirty-four, something a stranger walking down from the high road might have called, without much argument from anyone who lived there, a town: some sixty houses, by the count Seònaid kept as carefully as she kept her tides, standing round the tide-rock and the stone landing both, its people fishing now from boats of their own building rather than working the shallows on foot as their grandparents had.

## IV. Of Lachlann's Dying

Lachlann Ruadh had held An Cnoc Ruadh only a little while when the boy first came to it at six, a broad man just past forty then, and he held it four-and-twenty years more after, through the boy's whole growing and the raking of a hundred seasons' salt, until the winter the stone landing's second course was laid, when a chill he took wading the shallows to set a boat right settled in his chest and would not lift with the spring. He was five-and-sixty years old, which the household reckoned, when they spoke of it at all, an age past complaint for a man of no king's blood who had spent his whole life wet to the knee in salt water and cold wind off the lake; but it came hard all the same, in the way any death comes hard to a household that has never known its holder any other way, and the fosterling, sitting with the rest of the hall through the last of it, found himself grieving a man not his own father with a plainness that surprised him more than the grief itself.

Lachlann said little, in his last days, that An Cnoc Ruadh's own reciters ever troubled to keep whole; what they did keep was a single evening near the end, when Peigi sat by him with the salt tallies still in her hand from the day's weighing, and he asked her, not for the first time that season, whether she meant to send the fosterling home once she held the hill in her own right, and she told him she had not yet decided, and he said, in words the hearth still repeats though no one now living heard them first-hand, that a fostering kept a season too long stopped being a kindness to either house and became only a habit no one had troubled to end, and that she should not let her own fondness for having him about the place be the reason the peace of the ford went one day longer without its proper marking. He died within the month, in the same red-earthed hall he had been born in, with Peigi's hand in his and the fosterling standing at the door among the rest of the household who had no closer claim on the bedside than the years they had given the hill.

## V. Of Peigi Dhubh's Holding

Peigi took the hill at forty years old, the same plain, dark, quick-eyed woman who had told him, at the gate on his first evening there, that he was thin for a king's son and she supposed they would have to feed him, grown now into a holder her father's own steward said kept the tallies straighter than Lachlann ever had and forgave a bad season's raking no more readily than he had. She held it the way she had done everything since childhood, without ceremony and without much patience for anyone who expected one; the household's own telling of her taking the hill runs to a single line, that she sat down at the board the morning after her father's burial and asked for the tallies before she asked for anything else, and no one at An Cnoc Ruadh ever thought to ask her to do it any other way.

It was the better part of a year before she said anything to him of what her father had asked her, on the last evening he had strength to ask it, and when she did she said it plainly, the way she said most things, walking with him along the new stone landing in the last light of an evening in his thirty-second year: that her father had been right, and that a fostering kept past its season served neither hill, and that she meant to send him home before the year turned, with as much salt as a household could carry as gift and not as trade, so that Dùn ìseal would know An Cnoc Ruadh sent him back with honour and not merely let a hostage of peace go once he had grown too old to trouble keeping. She watched his face while she said it, in the frank way she had watched him at the gate four-and-twenty years before, and told him afterward, though only once and never again in his hearing, that she had put off the saying of it longer than her father would have liked, because the hill had grown used to him in a way no one at An Cnoc Ruadh had troubled to put into words until the words were needed.

## VI. Of the Leaving of the Red Hill

He spent the last month before the train set out doing the ordinary work of the hill as though nothing were ending, raking salt at the drying platforms beside rakers he had taught himself, setting a last course of stone at the landing that he would not be there to see finished, for Peigi had said plainly that she wanted no long leave-taking made of it, that a man who knew he was leaving in a month worked worse in that month than a man who did not, and the hill had salt to rake whether or not one of its own was about to walk fifty miles east and not come back.

Seònaid came to him the evening before the train left, at the tide-rock rather than at the hall, and cut, while he watched, one more pair of marks on the stone, though the tide that evening called for none, a high stroke and a low stroke set close together at the rock's edge where no keeper after her would think to look for a reading. She told him, when he asked what they were for, that she had not decided, only that the rock had marked every tide of his years on that shore and she saw no reason it should not mark the last evening of them as well, whatever the water was actually doing. He did not know, walking away from the river-mouth that night, whether to call it a kindness or only Seònaid's own plain way of saying a thing she would not otherwise have troubled to say aloud, and decided, by the time he reached the hall, that it was likely both.

Peigi herself walked with the train no further than the gate, which surprised no one who had known her a season, and gave him, in place of any long farewell, the same flat, appraising look she had given him as a boy of six arriving thin and friendless at that same gate four-and-twenty years before. She told him the salt was weighed true and the beasts were sound and that An Cnoc Ruadh would hear, by whatever road word travelled, how he did; and then, because she had never in her life been a woman to let a silence do work a sentence could do better, she said that her father had been right to send him, and righter still to wait as long as he had waited, and that neither hill would ever trouble to thank her for either, which was, she said, exactly as holding a hill ought to go.

## VII. Of the Road East

He went with three of An Cnoc Ruadh's own household and a train of pack-beasts loaded with salt enough to weigh down a lesser hill's whole season's store, walking east along Rathad an t-Salainn, the road that had carried him west at six years old on his own two feet, and it struck him, somewhere on the second day, that he remembered almost nothing of that first crossing beyond the shape of it: a woman named Rìonach who had knelt to his height and spoken of forked rivers, a low green mound Donnchadh would not walk near, the smell of the sea reaching him before any sea he could see. He looked for the shelters along the road that Donnchadh had slept them under and found most of them standing still, kept swept, as they had always been kept, by whoever passed last, and slept in one of them himself on the third night with a strange, quiet satisfaction in finding the road had not changed while he had.

The near valleys came up on the fifth day, country he had crossed as a child without troubling to look at it closely, and he found himself now noticing what a fostered boy of six had had no eye to notice: the boundary stones his brother, he had heard, once judged a quarrel by; the households that sent their surplus east at Samhain and never asked what came back to them in a lean year; small plain customs, kept without law, that he had grown up thinking belonged only to An Cnoc Ruadh's own shore until he saw, walking through them himself, how far they ran. He came in sight of Dùn ìseal on the seventh evening, the hill standing up dark against a sky gone gold the way he had been told, twenty-four years before, that An Cnoc Ruadh would stand against its own western light, and found he did not know, walking up the last stretch of road, whether the hill ahead of him was the home he was coming back to or another hill he was only passing through on the way to some third place he had not yet found.

## VIII. Of the Brother Who Did Not Know Him

Calum Ciar met the party at the gate, for Eilidh, who had given the hill into his hands some years before, was at the far end of the valley that evening, and it fell to her elder son to greet whatever An Cnoc Ruadh sent east. He looked the fosterling over, salt-carriers and pack-beasts and all, with the plain courtesy a holder's son owed any train that came in under a gift-load, and asked, when the greetings were done, which of the household he might be, for a face burned dark by lake wind and a way of standing learned on An Cnoc Ruadh had left nothing in him that his brother's eye could fasten on as kin. It is told, and the hill's own reciters do not trouble to soften it, that the fosterling stood a long moment in the gate saying nothing at all, watching his own brother wait for an answer to a question that should never have needed asking, before he told him plainly who he was; and that Calum Ciar's face did something then that no one standing near enough to see it ever troubled to name, somewhere between shame at not knowing and a plainer grief at how completely a boy could be lost to a household that had never once stopped loving him.

Eilidh knew him before he had crossed half the yard. She came to the hall door when word reached her that An Cnoc Ruadh's train was in, and she looked at the man coming up from the gate, salt-dark and grown a head taller than the boy she had knelt to at Àth shean four-and-twenty years before, and said his name, the one name she had never stopped using though no reciter of either hill had ever troubled to write it down, before he had said a single word to tell her who he was. She wept then, which the hill's own telling allows her, being by that year past caring what a hall full of her own household thought of her weeping, and held him a long while at the door before she would let anyone, even her elder son, come near enough to greet him in turn.

## IX. Of the Songs Sung at the Pans

He stayed the winter at Dùn ìseal and rode down, before the spring turned, to see the salt-pans at Baile ghorm, for it was there, among rakers who worked salt the sea-shore way and had never learned the lake-shore turn of the wrist Lachlann taught him at eight years old, that he found himself, one evening at their fires, teaching what the household at Ros dhomhain had taught him without meaning to teach anything at all: a refrain An Cnoc Ruadh's own rakers sang at the crust, four short lines whose meaning even An Cnoc Ruadh's own eldest could no longer wholly give an account of, though every hand on that shore had sung it at the raking since before Seònaid's grandmother's grandmother kept the tide-rock. He sang it for the Baile ghorm rakers as Peigi's own household had sung it for him, and one of them, an old woman who had raked that shingle sixty years, wrote nothing down, for no one at Baile ghorm troubled to write a working song down, but she kept the four lines whole from that single hearing and taught them to her own daughter's daughter before she died, so that the song ran on at the sea-shore pans as it had always run at the lake, in a tongue near enough the island's own that a raker of Baile ghorm could sing it without knowing she sang words An Cnoc Ruadh itself could no longer wholly construe.

*Salann geal, an cuan dorcha,
Làmh a' snìomh 's a' cur air ais,
Dachaigh ann an gach gràinne,
Cha chaill an fhairge a càs.*

What could be made of it, An Cnoc Ruadh's own eldest said when he asked them, before he ever carried it east, was something of white salt and a dark sea, of a hand that turns and gives back what it takes, of a home held whole in every single grain; the fourth line no keeper of that shore, in all the years anyone could ask after, had ever managed to render the same way twice, and some said only that the sea does not lose what is its own, and others that the sea does not count the cost of its own losing, and no one thought either wrong enough to correct the other. It did not trouble him, singing it at Baile ghorm's fires with rakers who had never set foot on the western lake shore, that the song's own meaning had worn thinner than its tune; a thing four generations of hands had sung at the same work needed, he thought, no more warrant than that.

He was thirty-four years old that spring, and stayed at Dùn ìseal the rest of his mother's life and some while after, neither holding the hill nor troubling anyone with a wish to, a man of the king's own blood who had gone west at six and come home at thirty grown, by every account, more An Cnoc Ruadh's than his own mother's hill had ever managed to make him in the six years it held him first. Rìghrean na Cloiche' own list, when the reciters after Eilidh came to set down her reign and her sons in order, gave Calum Ciar his place among the holders as it gave every holder before him; of the one who had gone to An Cnoc Ruadh and come back with salt in his hands and a song no one could wholly construe, it set down nothing at all, no year of birth and no year of death, no reign and no deed with a date fixed to it, so that a stranger reading the list a hundred years after would have found no trace that Eilidh Ghlas had borne more than the one son. It was An Cnoc Ruadh's own telling, not the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche, that kept what little of him is kept at all: the boy who went, it says still, at every hearth that sings the salt refrain without knowing whose hands first carried it home, and did not come back the same man, and was never, by either hill's own reckoning, given a name.

# Part Five: The Great Gathering

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Panther Road and the Edge of the Woods

*GE 2,428 – 2,460*


> *Nuair a philleas na cait, philleas an cuideachd leotha.*
> When the cats turn back, wise hands turn back with them.
> — said of the passes, after Iain Buachaille

## I. Of the Bone Pipes and the Turning of the Cats

At the southern skirt of Cnoc àrsaidh, where Rathad na Spor ran down off the high ground and lost itself among the last of the birch before the grazing opened out, there lived that year a man named Gilleonan, who had no craft the households about him could put a plainer name to than the making of small useful things out of whatever came to his hand, and who that winter came to hand on a heap of hollow bird-bones left over from a winter's snaring and took a notion, turning them over by his own fire of an evening, to bore holes along the length of the longest of them and see what came out of blowing across the end. What came out, after a week of ruined bone and burnt fingers and more silence than sound, was a thin high note that carried further than any voice raised across an open field, and by the second week he had bored four holes rather than one and could raise and lower the note as he pleased, and by the third the children of every household near enough to hear him practising had taken to gathering at his door of an evening the way children gather at any door where something new and strange is being made. No one before him is remembered to have made a thing on Dia-thìr that could be played rather than merely blown, and the pipes he cut that winter out of hollow bird-bone are the oldest instruments the island's tellers count, and Gilleonan, asked in his own age how he had come to think of it, would say only that a bone with a hole through it already wants to sing, and a man with enough patience and enough ruined bone will find where the rest of the holes belong.

It was in that same season, while Gilleonan's thin note was still new enough to draw children from three households at a call, that the word came down from the passes above Cnoc àrsaidh that the great cats were turning back on Imrich nam Pantar before ever they reached the foothills. Every year of any household's memory the cats had come down out of the high ground with the last hard frost of the spring, in ones and twos and sometimes in a string of them following the same worn track a day or two apart, crossing the passes on their own road as they had crossed them since before any teller's grandfather had words for a beginning, and going on south to whatever ground held them through the cold months, and every year the herders of the hill households that lay along that road kept their beasts well clear of it while the crossing lasted, for a cat on the move wants nothing of a man or his cattle and will do neither harm if neither stands in its way, but a cat turned or crowded is another matter, and no household along Imrich nam Pantar needed telling twice why the custom stood as it stood. That year the cats came as far as the narrow throat of the highest pass and no further, three of them seen by different watchers on three different days, each pausing at the same turn in the rock, each looking down the long fall of ground toward the foothills a while before it swung about and went back the way it had come, and by the fourth such turning the households nearest the pass had stopped waiting to see whether a fourth cat would finish the crossing and had begun instead to ask each other what a cat knows about a coming winter that a man does not.

The old answer, given by every old woman and old man who had outlived enough winters to be asked, was that a cat which will not cross into ground it has crossed every year of its own life is a cat that already knows the ground it is leaving is the kinder ground that year, and that a household which reads the turning aright and lays in double against a winter no cat will risk crossing into does better than a household that waits for its own eyes to be sure. The households along Imrich nam Pantar that year laid in double: double the dried fish, double the stored roots, double the cut peat and the split wood, working through the whole of that summer and autumn at a pace that left little time for anything but the storing, so that by the time the first true frost came down off the high ground behind the cats that had not come, every hearth within a day's walk of the pass had more laid by than it had ever laid by before against a winter that had not yet shown its own face. The winter that followed was as hard as any teller then living had words to measure it by, snow lying on ground that commonly saw none, and the burns running thin and slow under rims of frost, and it is told, though no single teller claims to have counted it exactly, that not one household along Imrich nam Pantar that had laid in double against the cats' own reading of the season went hungry before the thaw, while further east, where the cats' turning had been heard of only as a tale carried late and thin, more than one household came near the end of its own stores before the ground softened again.

## II. Of Iain Buachaille and the Cattle in the Passes

Not every household along Imrich nam Pantar heeded the cats that year, and the households of Muileann bhàn, a scatter of byres and huts set along the last good grazing before the ground climbed into the passes proper, were among those that did not, or that heeded too late to matter. The grazing about Muileann bhàn had run thin that spring before ever the cats were seen turning, the winter before having left the lower slopes bare and slow to green, and the herders there had already begun, before the first cat was so much as spoken of, to eye the high meadows inside the passes themselves, ground no household of that stretch had grazed within living memory because it lay along the cats' own road and the custom forbade it for the length of the crossing season, whatever grass stood ungrazed there while the custom held.

Among those herders was Iain, son of Iseabail of Muileann bhàn, three-and-twenty that spring and already known along that stretch of the road for a temper that took slights to the household's grazing harder than most men took slights to themselves, a fault his own mother had despaired of curing in him and had mostly stopped trying to. When word came down that the cats had turned back a second time at the throat of the pass, Iain heard in it a chance too good to waste, for a road the cats have given up crossing, he said to whoever would listen at his own hearth and at two or three neighbouring ones, is a road with nothing left on it to fear, and grass standing ungrazed a day's drive above Muileann bhàn while his own household's beasts grew thin below was a waste no custom, in his reckoning, had any business asking a hungry household to keep. His mother told him plainly that a custom kept by every household along that road since before her own grandmother's day had not likely been kept so long for no reason at all, and that three turnings of the cats in one season meant, to her mind, a road with a fourth turning still owed it, not a road with nothing left on it to fear. Iain heard her out, as a son will hear out a mother he does not mean to obey, and two mornings after went up into the passes with four other men of the household and near forty head of the household's thinnest cattle, meaning to graze them a week on the high meadows and bring them down fattened before the cats' season was out.

They had the cattle up and grazing by the second day, on grass richer than any of the five men had seen standing anywhere below the passes that whole dry summer, and for three days more nothing troubled them but the cold, which came down harder each night than the last, and the wind off the high rock, which none of them had properly dressed against, having gone up in the light gear of men driving cattle a short way rather than men meaning to camp a week among stone. It was on the fourth night, with the fire burned low and two of the five men asleep and Iain himself keeping the first watch more from restlessness than any sense that watching was needed, that the panthers came down on the herd, a whole string of them together, the last and largest cats of that year's crossing, driven onto the road at last, the tellers say afterward, by a hunger of their own that the turning back had only put off and not ended. Iain heard the cattle before he saw anything, a sound no herder mistakes for any other sound cattle make, and had the other four on their feet and the fire built high before the first cat broke into the firelight after a beast at the edge of the huddled herd, and what followed, by Iain's own telling of it afterward, he could give no clean account of, for a night fight with cats among cattle in the dark leaves a man with pieces of what happened and no whole cloth to lay them in: a beast down and screaming, a shape low and fast crossing the firelight, his own spear thrown and lost, and then the ground going out from under him as he threw himself sideways from a claw he never afterward could say he truly saw coming, his leg twisting under him against a stone he had not known was there, and a white pain up through the hip that put him on the ground for the rest of that night no matter how the fight round him went.

By first light the cats were gone, south along their own road as though the night's killing had settled whatever debt they had come down to collect, and the five men counted, in the grey after, thirty head of the household's forty taken or scattered beyond finding, and Iain unable to stand on the leg that had gone from under him in the dark. They carried him down off the high ground on a hide slung between two spear-shafts, the other three driving what was left of the herd before them, and it was three days before any of the five was fit to speak much of what the night had cost, and longer than that before Iain's leg, set as well as the household's own healing hand could set it, showed any household at Muileann bhàn what it had truly cost him: a leg that healed crooked at the hip no matter how it was bound, that shortened against its fellow by the width of two fingers by the time the swelling was fully down, and that left him, from that winter on, a man who walked with a stick and a roll to one side for every step he took, in a household of herders where a man's legs are as much his living as his hands. His mother said nothing to him of the custom he had broken, then or ever after that she is remembered to have said, and Iain himself said little of that night to anyone for a long while, beyond the plain account any household along that road would ask of a man who had lost it thirty head, and it was left to the road, over the seasons that followed, to turn what had happened to him into the shorter saying it kept: that the cats had turned back three times that spring to tell every household along the road what one household had not troubled to hear the first time.

## III. Of the Gatepost Sign and the Boats Named for Wind

It was in the years just after, while Iain was learning to make a lame man's work of a whole man's trade, that the custom the households of Muileann bhàn had broken began, further south, to be kept in a new way that no household along Imrich nam Pantar had thought to keep it before. At Baile dhomhain, where the grazing lay well clear of the passes but where the crossing season still shaped the year as surely as it shaped it anywhere the cats' own road ran, the households took to cutting a mark into the gatepost of every byre and yard at the season's start, a short straight cut no deeper than a knife needs to make its point, and scraping it away again at the season's close, so that a man riding through Baile dhomhain in the crossing months could read at a glance, gate by gate, which households stood mindful of the season and which did not trouble, and a household whose gatepost went uncut two years running found itself, without any word said outright, asked fewer favours and lent fewer beasts than a household that kept the mark faithfully. No household before that is remembered to have cut a sign for a season rather than for an event, a birth or a death or a boundary settled, and the mark at Baile dhomhain, plain as it was, is counted the first the island kept for nothing more than the turning of the year.

Further north, where the coast ran along the mouth of the river the fishing households called simply the blue water, the households of Caol bheag came in those same years to a custom of their own that answered no cat's road but the same restless weather that governed every boat on that stretch of coast. Each household there had long since taken to naming its boats, as households everywhere name the things they build with their own hands and trust their lives to, but it was at Caol bheag that the naming first fixed on the winds a boat was built and blessed to fish in, so that a boat built for the wind out of the north bore a north wind's name and was held unlucky if put out under any other, and a boat that went down under its own true wind was never, by the custom that grew up there, given its name again, for a name once drowned was held to carry the drowning with it into whatever boat next wore it. The fishing households up and down that coast came in time to know each other's boats as much by name as by build, and a man newly wed into a household there learned the winds' names for boats before he learned much else of his wife's own kin, for a boat wrongly named, in the reckoning of that coast, was a debt a household paid for sooner or later, whatever the weather did or did not do to collect it.

## IV. Of the Wind-Stone and the Broken Grave

At Seann Chwen, midway along the same stretch of high ground Imrich nam Pantar crossed, there stood, older than any household near it could put a beginning to, a low grey boulder cut about with marks no living hand had made and no living eye could read whole, the same close, careful, patient marks Seann-Dhaoine had left on stones the length of the island wherever the ground stood high enough and bare enough to take a chisel, and it was on that stone, in the years after Iain's leg had set crooked, that a cutter of that household first set one of Na h-Ochd Gaothan' names beside the older marks, in the plainer, broader cuts the hill-folk's own chisels made, so that the boulder came to carry, on the one face, both a telling no living hand could read and a telling any household passing could read at a glance. Few stones on the island came to bear the marks of both peoples so close together, for the households that raised their own signs commonly chose ground Seann-Dhaoine had left bare, out of a wariness that had less to do with any harm believed to lie in the older marks than with a plain unwillingness to set a new thing hard against an old one nobody living could account for; the cutter at Seann Chwen, asked why he had chosen that stone over any bare boulder near it, said only that the wind-name wanted a stone already old, and the oldest stone he knew stood already there.

A day's walk south of Seann Chwen lay the old burial ground the households of that country had kept, in one fashion or another, longer than any single line among them could claim to have kept it alone, a wide low field thick with thorn and bramble where the dead of a dozen households lay under cairns of every age from freshly turned to grass-grown past finding, and it was in those same years that a family newly settled nearby, kin to none of the households that already had dead lying there, took on the clearing of the thorn from the older rows, cutting it back each spring so the cairns beneath could still be found and the paths between them still be walked, though they laid none of their own dead among the ones they tended, having none yet to lay, and meant, by their own account, only to keep a ground that plainly wanted keeping and had no one household whose plain business it was. They kept it faithfully enough that within a few years no household of that country thought to clear the thorn any longer, trusting the keeping to the family that had taken it up unasked, and it was diggers of that same family, cutting a new row further back than any row before it had reached, who broke one spring into a grave older than any they had themselves opened, lined on every side with cut slabs set close and true in a manner no household of that country built its own graves in, a manner the diggers knew at once, without needing to be told, for the manner of Seann-Dhaoine. They closed what they had opened as carefully as they had opened it, moving the new row a spear's length further off rather than cut any nearer, and no digger of that ground, then or after, is remembered to have tried that older grave a second time, the family's own reckoning being, as the eldest of them put it, that a ground kept for the dead does not want its keepers asking after graves it was never given to keep.

## V. Of the Pilgrims and the Child Lost at Cnoc bheag

East of Seann Chwen, where the ground fell away into woodland thick enough that no household had yet cleared more than its own edge, there stood a stretch of forest the hill-folk had long held sacred without any household near it being able to say plainly when the holding had begun or why that wood rather than any other had been set apart from the ordinary clearing and grazing every other stretch of woodland on the island was put to sooner or later. In the years after the wind-stone was cut at Seann Chwen, people from households that had never before troubled to walk so far began coming to the edge of that wood in small numbers, singly and in pairs, to sit through a single night at the line where the trees began without ever passing in among them, keeping a small fire that burned itself out before morning and going home again at first light with nothing to show for the walk but whatever the night had given them to carry back. No household could say who had begun the walking, nor what any single pilgrim hoped to find at the wood's edge that could not as well have been sought at his own hearth, and the pilgrims themselves, asked, gave answers as various as the households they came from, though most agreed on this much: that a night spent at the edge of that wood, awake and watchful and asking nothing of it, left a man quieter than the same night spent anywhere else was likely to leave him.

Further east again, past a stretch of country still mostly given over to grazing, lay another wood held sacred in the same fashion and for the same unremembered reasons, and it was at the edge of that wood, some years after the pilgrims had begun sitting at the first, that settlers newly come down from An Cnoc Ruadh raised the earliest house of what would grow, in the years that followed, into a small settlement of its own at Cnoc bheag, taking their timber, as the custom of that country already held for ground so near a sacred wood, only from the far side of the river that ran between the settlement and the trees, and never from the unclaimed wood, however near and however tempting its unfelled timber stood. The settlement grew slowly, a house and then two and then a handful more over several years, each household keeping, without needing to be told twice, the same line the first house had kept between its own clearing and the trees, a line marked at last, once enough households stood there to agree on marking it, by a row of unhewn stones set at the wood's edge from the river to the higher ground, a line no child of that settlement was raised without being told, before it was told much else, never to cross.

It was past that line, in the year the settlement had grown to six houses, that a child went missing, a boy not yet seven summers old, last seen by his own mother at play near the stones and next seen by no one at all, though the whole settlement and every household within reach of the news spent three days searching the wood as far in as any of them dared go, calling his name through undergrowth thick enough that a man three strides off could not always be seen, let alone a boy small enough to have gone to ground under any fallen branch or into any hollow the wood offered him. Iain, near six-and-forty that year and walking still with the stick and the roll to one side that the panthers had left him three-and-twenty years before, was among the searchers who came from Muileann bhàn and the country about it to help hunt a wood he had never before had cause to enter, a lame man's search being slower and shorter-ranged than a whole man's but no less willing for that, and it was Iain, by more than one account, who first said aloud what every searcher among them had by the third day begun privately to think, that a wood no household of that country would fell timber from nor build a house nearer than the far bank of its own river was not, whatever the boy's own mother might in her grief still hope, a wood that gave back what it had taken, and that a search which had by then gone three days past the line of stones without one sign of the child was a search that had done, and would go on doing, everything a search could rightly be asked to do. The searchers stopped at the line of stones on the evening of the third day, no one among them commanding it, each in his own time and by his own reckoning coming to the same stopping as Iain had spoken first, and the boy was never found, in that wood or any other, and no teller of that country, then or after, ever laid the stopping at the searchers' own door, for a wood held apart from every other wood on the island for reasons no living household could name was, in the plain reckoning of that country, no wood a man could be blamed for failing to bring a child safely out of.

## VI. Of the Warm Springs

Iain carried the leg the panthers had left him for seven-and-twenty years after that first night in the passes, through the raising of his own household and the burying of his mother and the long slow work of teaching younger men of Muileann bhàn a herder's trade he could no longer himself practise at more than half a whole man's pace, and in all that time he tried, as any man in his place tries, every cure his own household and every neighbouring one had ever heard spoken of: bindings of every plant the hill country grew that anyone claimed had ever eased a joint, a winter spent wrapping the leg each night in hide soaked warm from the fire, a season's walking on a crutch cut shorter than his stick to see whether the leg, forced to bear more of its own weight, might in time straighten, which it did not. By the year the boy was lost at Cnoc bheag he had stopped, by his own later account, expecting any cure at all, and had come to think of the leg the way a man comes in time to think of any hurt that has outlasted every hope of mending it, as simply the form his own life had settled into and would go on wearing until it wore him out.

It was four years after the search at Cnoc bheag, in a spring when the leg had begun to pain him worse than it had in a long while, the cold and the wet of that season finding every old crookedness in it that fair weather let him mostly forget, that a neighbour of his, back from a journey south for reasons of the neighbour's own, told him of a warm water that rose from under the mountain a long way off, ground his own kin had once passed through and camped a night beside, water that came up out of the rock already heated and pooled shallow enough for a man to sit in it, and that more than one traveller resting there had come away saying the water had eased an old hurt no ordinary washing ever touched. Iain heard the telling the way he had by then learned to hear most tellings of cures he had not himself tried, without much hope and without much unwillingness either, and said nothing of going for the better part of that year, until the leg's own pain, worse that spring than any spring before it, gave him less to lose by the walking than he had ever before reckoned he had.

He went that same summer, on the stick he had carried seven-and-twenty years, a journey of many days for a whole man and a great many more for a man who could put no real weight on one leg, staying at whatever households along the way would have a lame stranger by their fire a night, and came at last to the warm water on an evening when a handful of other travellers were already camped about it, some there, as he learned by their own telling round the shared fire that night, for the same hope that had brought him and some merely to rest a night on a long road elsewhere. At first light the next morning, before the others were properly stirring, he eased himself down into the water onto a shelf of rock the water covered to the waist, and sat there a long while, by his own account longer than he had meant to, the heat working into the crooked hip in a way no binding or wrapping he had ever tried had come near to matching, and when at last he rose to climb out he found, standing on the rock in the cool morning air with the water running off him, that the leg under him held its own weight in a way it had not held it in seven-and-twenty years, not straightened, for no water on the island could undo what a night of panthers had done to the bone, but eased past whatever had kept it locked and grinding at every step, so that he walked the length of the pool's edge and back again without once reaching for the stick he had set down on the rock beside him.
