He stayed three days more at the warm water, going into it each morning and each evening, and walked home to Muileann bhàn, by every teller's account of it since, on his own two legs and without the stick he had carried south, a journey that took him near half the days the same road had taken him going, a lame man's walk cut down, near enough, to a whole man's pace. His own household, seeing him come up the last rise toward the byres without the roll to one side they had watched him walk with for seven-and-twenty years, took him at first, more than one of them said after, for some other traveller entirely, a man of Iain's own build and no more, until he was near enough to call his own name across the yard and be known by his own mother's grandchildren, who had never in their own short lives seen him walk any other way. It is that walking, and not the water, that the tellers of that country kept as the whole of what happened at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh that year, a herder who came to them lame and walked home from them whole, and it stands, of every cure any teller of Dia-thìr has since claimed for that water, the oldest and the first, told wherever the springs themselves are told of, in words that have changed little from the plain shape Iain's own household first gave them: that he came lame, and he walked home.

## VII. Of the Hollow Man and the Covered Hearth

In the years just after, two herders of a household near the hills where Marbh-bheò was oldest told of, driving cattle home later than they had meant to and caught by full dark still some way off, saw a shape walk the ridge above them with no breath showing in the bitter cold, though every breath of their own hung white before their faces the whole way down, and neither of the two, by their own telling after, could say the shape had done anything at all beyond the walking, no word spoken, no hand raised, nothing but a going along the ridge line at a man's own ordinary pace until the dark or the ground took it out of their sight. They had lit no fire that evening, having pressed on for home rather than camp so near those hills after dark, and it was that, the telling holds, and no virtue of their own, that let them come home at all to tell of it, for every older telling of that shape agreed on the one plain rule any household near those hills kept without needing telling twice: that a fire lit on those slopes after dark was a fire Marbh-bheò came to, sooner or later, and a household that lit one did not always sit by it undisturbed until morning.

It was in those same years, spreading out from those same hills toward the settlements that lay nearer the eastern woods, that a new manner of hearth began to be built in household after household, a fire pit dug below the level of the floor and roofed over with a low stone lid that could be drawn across at need, so that a household could bank its coals for the night and cover them close, leaving no open flame nor rising smoke for anything abroad in the dark to be drawn toward, and wake in the morning to coals still live enough to be raked open and blown to flame again with no fresh striking of fire needed. The covered hearth spread faster among the households nearest those hills than anywhere else on the island, and it was there, before it was anywhere, that the custom hardened at last into something near a law that every household on those slopes kept whether or not it had ever seen anything walk a ridge in the dark: that no open fire was lit there after nightfall, coal-banked or covered or none at all, a rule no council had made and no holder had set his hand to, kept simply because every household near enough to those hills to be asked had, sooner or later, heard from some neighbour's own mouth a telling near enough to the two herders' to want no fire of its own left open to whatever the telling was a telling of.

Iain Buachaille lived on at Muileann bhàn many years after his own walk home from the warm water, on legs that carried him, to the end of his days, further and more evenly than any household there had thought, in na Bliadhnachan Fada of his lameness, he would ever walk again, and it was said of him along that stretch of Imrich nam Pantar, for as long as any household there kept the saying, that he alone among the men who had broken the custom that hard year had lived to be mended of what the breaking cost him, though no teller of that country ever claimed the mending answered the breaking, nor said the cats had given him back what they had taken, for a leg does not forget, whatever ease the warm water worked into it, the night it was first twisted under a man in the dark, and Iain himself, asked in his own old age whether he still felt the passes in bad weather, would say only that he did, and that a man who has walked home once from a hurt he had stopped hoping to be rid of does not, after that, trouble much over what a little weather still asks of him.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Rings under the Oaks

*GE 2,461 – 2,600*

> *Sheas an darach mus do sheas sinne; seasaidh e às ar dèidh.*
> The oak stood before we stood; it will stand after us.
> — said of the grove at Doire ghlas, as the households that ring it keep it still

## I. Of the Middens and the Strait

*This is told among Clann na Ceiste, who kept the years of the settling the way they kept everything: by mouth, in Somhairle's own words, passed down through his line long after his face had begun to change.*

Somhairle was two thousand four hundred and twenty-three years old in the spring the covered hearth reached the last households of the near valleys, and he had by then stopped counting his years in the ordinary way, the way Clann na Ceiste counted a herdsman's or a raker's, because a century for him had come to feel no longer than a season felt for them. He kept the Line whole in his own head, every name his father had given him and every name added since, and he kept, besides the Line, a habit that was his alone among the king's blood: he walked. Where Dòmhnall had ridden north to hold what was won, and Iain Dubh had ridden south to lose his life on a shingle beach, and the rest of his brothers and sisters had taken hills or given them up, Somhairle went on foot, slowly, from one new roof to the next, and looked, and said little, and was, by the time this telling begins, known at every threshold of the island as the king's son who came and sat by the fire and asked nothing and took no share.

It was on such a walk that he came first to Caol mhòr, on the narrow water where Seann-Dhaoine had once heaped their middens high along the strand, shell on shell for longer than any teller could reckon. The households that settled there in his two thousand four hundred and twenty-fourth year built their walls, when they built in stone at all, from the midden, prising loose what the tide had not already carried off; but they would not turn a stone that still showed a mark, whether cut by a hand or worn by nothing but weather, and set those aside in a low unmortared line along the shore instead, so that a stranger walking the strand a hundred years on would find two kinds of wall standing side by side, one raised by the living and one left standing by people who had chosen not to disturb what they did not understand. Somhairle asked an old woman there, raking limpets from among the shells, why they troubled to sort the marked stones from the plain ones when no one now living could read either. She said only that a mark was a mark, whoever cut it, and that a wall built careless of what it stood on had no business standing long; and Somhairle, who had heard Seann-Dhaoine' silence answered a hundred ways by a hundred different households in his four and twenty centuries of walking, thought hers as good an answer as any and better than most.

He went from there along the coast road to Baile chrom, where households out of Cnoc ghorm had come down some years before to work ground the older settlement had let lie fallow since a bad season none now remembered clearly, and found the resettling further along than the last word of it had told him: byres roofed, a well dug and lined, children old enough to be sent for water without a grown hand beside them. The headman there, a broad quiet man called Donnchadh Ruadh, walked him round the bounds himself and showed him where the old field-marks still stood under the new grass, half sunk, half grown over, and said that his own grandmother had told him whose hands first set those stones though she had never once said the name aloud, only that the ground remembered its first ploughing whether or not the people who ploughed it were remembered with it. Somhairle set nothing of that into the Line, for Clann na Ceiste kept the Line before every small saying that crossed a walker's path; he carried this one with him all the same, turning it over on the road the way a man turns a stone he means to look at again by better light.

## II. Of the Salt Road and the Rebuilt Wall

Rathad an t-Salainn that ran from the pans at Baile ghorm to the north-west had, by Somhairle's two thousand four hundred and thirtieth year, been walked so long and by so many feet that its last unbroken stand of scrub, a thicket of thorn and low birch that had turned every laden cart a half-day out of its way for as long as the road had run, was cut through at last by carriers weary of the going round it, and Muileann àrsaidh stood at the road's end after that a full day nearer the salt than it had ever been before. The millers there kept no count of who had swung the first axe into that thicket, for a dozen hands had reason to want it gone and none troubled to claim the doing of it alone; what they kept, and what Somhairle heard told at their own hearth, was that the thicket had stood since before the eldest living miller's grandfather's day, and that its going felt to some of the older households less like a road cleared than like a boundary taken down, though none of them could say clearly what had stood on either side of it worth calling a boundary.

Further east, on ground no household of the king's blood had ever held a share of, the settlers pushing toward the rising country raised the first turned bank east of the old workings, at Dùn thais, in the same year the millers cleared their thicket, digging a ditch and setting the spoil up behind it the way Rìghrean na Cloiche' own hill had long since taught every settling household to do, without any word sent from Dùn ìseal telling them to do so and without any word sent back once it was done. Somhairle stood on that bank himself, some years after, and found it a smaller, rougher thing than his father's hill, no more than a shoulder-high ring of earth round a scatter of low houses, but built, he thought, by people who had watched the king's hill from a distance long enough to know a bank kept a herd in and a raider out better than any number of dogs, and had built one of their own the first year they had hands enough to spare for it.

Fire did the clearing at Achadh chaol, where the ground lay heavy with scrub too old and too green to be cut by axe alone; the households there burned it back a field's width at a time across three dry summers, and ploughed the black ground while the ash was still warm in it, and got, the first year, a crop the older fields further west had not equalled in a generation. Cuan ruadh, on the eastern coast A' Ghaoth Dhubh had stripped bare not many years before, set the last course of its rebuilt wall the same season, stone laid to the eaves the whole circuit of the settlement, the first roofs on that coast built to stand against wind rather than merely to be raised again after it; and Cathair fhada, further south, opened a well within its own bank the same year, so that a siege of weather, if it came again as A' Ghaoth Dhubh had come, need not send the whole household down to the shore for water while the wind still had teeth in it. At Caol ruadh, on the narrow strait where the current ran strong enough to carry a badly set net clean out to open water, the fishers took to marking the deep channels with woven buoys tied to stones, a small thing, Somhairle thought when he heard of it, but the kind of small thing that spread from one strait to the next the way An Cnoc Ruadh's paired tide-marks had spread, carried in a carrier's mouth and taken up by people who never asked who had thought of it first.

He asked the folk of Caol ruadh, once, sitting with the fishers over their evening catch, who had first thought to tie the woven buoys over the deep water, and got the same answer he had grown used to hearing everywhere he asked such a question: no one could rightly say, only that a boy had tied the first one two or three summers back after losing a net to the current, and that the next household to lose a net had tied one too, and after that it was simply how a net was set on that strait, the way a boat was rowed with the current or against it, and not a thing anyone thought to credit to a single pair of hands. It struck Somhairle, hearing it, as much the same shape of story he had heard told of the paired marks on the tide-rock at Ros dhomhain, a custom that had spread the same way, from one keeper's trouble to every household's taking-up of it, and he began, walking on from Caol ruadh, to keep a private reckoning of his own of how many customs on the island had grown that way, out of one household's trouble and every household's willingness to take up what worked without asking who had thought of it first: more, he judged, before he had gone very much further, than his father had ever once had to command.

He walked among all of these in the years his brothers and sisters held or lost their hills, and he came, in time, to think of the island less as his father's kingdom, which the reciters at every gathering still called it, and more as a great many small kingdoms of one custom each, none of them written anywhere, all of them somehow agreed to by people who had never sat in council to agree to anything.

## III. Of the Word from the North

Word reached him at the slab, where he still kept his own turn among the households that sat out the dark half of the year with Beathan, that families out of the near valleys had begun that autumn to come down to Doire ghlas and build there, in the grove, under the very oaks his father had set the six pots beneath on the night of the seven fires. It was told to him plainly, by a herdsman's wife who had no notion what the grove meant to the man she was telling, that the new households liked the ground for its shelter and its old cleared paths, and that they had already begun marking timber for the first of the new byres.

Somhairle said nothing to her of what she had told him, and sat out the rest of his turn at the slab as he always did, but he left Na Glinn Àrda within the week, alone, on foot, walking north by the same road his father had walked south on with eleven of his kin behind him near two thousand five hundred years before, though the road had long since worn wider and straighter than the track Ailean had first taken. It was sixty-five miles from the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche to the grove, a walk of four days at the pace Somhairle kept, and he spent much of it turning over, as he had turned over Donnchadh Ruadh's word about the ground remembering its ploughing, whether he had any right at all to want the grove kept as it had stood on the one night that made it matter to him, when every field and every wall he had walked past for four and twenty centuries had been let become whatever the people living on it needed it to become.

## IV. Of the Road North

The road ran through country Somhairle had walked so many times that he no longer needed to look at it to know what lay round the next turning, and yet he found, walking it that autumn with a purpose he had not carried on any of his earlier crossings, that he saw it as if new: the boundary stones Dòmhnall had once set with his own hands, still standing where quarrels had been settled in Somhairle's own boyhood; the wide trodden ground where the salt-carriers rested their beasts each evening, worn bare of grass by feet that had crossed it for longer than any single generation could account for.

He slept the first night in a herder's shelter kept swept, as every shelter on that road was kept swept, by whoever had passed it last, and shared bread with a family driving cattle down from the high pastures before the weather turned, who took him, from his plain dress and his slow speech, for nothing more than an old walker of no particular house, and told him freely what they would not have told a man they knew for the king's own son: that they thought the settling gone further and faster than any of them liked, fields opened where their grandparents' grandparents had grazed without a fence between one household's beasts and the next, and no one, king or otherwise, troubling to say whether that was a good thing or a bad one. Somhairle said only that he had walked the same roads a long while and thought most changes looked worse from close by than they read afterward from a little distance, which was as near to an answer as he ever gave anyone who did not know who was giving it.

He came to Doire ghlas on the evening of the fourth day and found the households further along than the herdsman's wife's telling had prepared him for: a dozen houses already roofed, more staked out in a rough ring, and among the oaks, cut low into the bark of three of the oldest trunks in the grove, the fresh white marks that meant a tree was chosen for the axe.

## V. Of the Marks on the Old Bark

He stood a long while before the nearest of the three marked oaks, a tree with a girth no four men could have spanned with linked arms, its bark grey and split with age in a way that put him, though he did not say so to anyone that evening, in mind of nothing so much as his own father's hands, which had held their warmth through two thousand four hundred and seventy years without once showing a single line of age. The households working nearby knew him for the king's son who walked and asked nothing, and one of the settlers, a lean, quick-spoken man called Fearchar mac Ailig who had come down from the near valleys with the first families that autumn, walked over to see what held him so still and told him, when he asked, that the oldest trees gave the best timber for roof-beams, being straight-grained where the younger growth still twisted, and that the households meant no disrespect to the grove in cutting them, only good sense in building.

"It is a fair grove for building in," Fearchar said, "sheltered from three winds and with good water below it, and we are grateful for the finding of it, whoever cleared the paths through it before us." He did not know, and Somhairle did not tell him, whose hands those paths had first been trodden by, or what had stood in the ring of oaks he was measuring for beams on the one night that ring had ever held its full seven fires at once.

Somhairle asked him, then, plainly, whether the household would spare the three oldest trees and take their timber elsewhere, and gave, when Fearchar asked him why, the only reason that was wholly his own to give: that his father had set six pots under those particular trunks once, long before Fearchar's grandmother's grandmother was born, and that Somhairle, who asked nothing of any household on the whole island and took no share of anything the king held, asked this one thing of this one household, for this one grove, and would ask it of no other. He did not say the word grove meant to Clann na Ceiste, or name the seven fires, or tell Fearchar what the Line said had moved between the trunks on the eighth night; he gave the household the plainest telling he could make of a thing that was not, at its root, plain at all, and left the rest to whatever weight his own asking carried.

## VI. Of the Oaks Left Standing

Fearchar carried the asking to the rest of the household that same evening, and it is told at Doire ghlas still, in the plain way the settlement kept most of its own small history, that there was little argument over it: the three trunks were old enough that felling them would have cost more labour than younger growth close at hand, and a request from the king's own son, however oddly reasoned, was not a thing a settling household weighed lightly against a morning's easier cutting. The white marks were cut away from the bark within the week, and the beams for the first byres came instead from a stand of younger oak a short walk to the east, straighter in the grain and easier to the axe than Fearchar had first thought the older trees would be, so that the household lost, in the end, less by the sparing than it had feared to.

The three oaks stood after that at the centre of the new settlement rather than at its edge, for the houses went up in a rough ring around them the way the households had first laid out their stakes, and within a generation the ring had a name among the people who lived inside it, though not one that named the grove's older meaning: they called it, simply, the ring under the oaks, for the three trunks that stood taller than any roof raised near them and gave a shade in summer no roof could match. No teller at Doire ghlas, in all the years after, ever set down why those three trees and no others had been spared when every household around them cut freely; the reason lived only in Somhairle's own telling, kept by Clann na Ceiste the way they kept everything, by mouth, apart from anything the settlement itself kept of its own founding.

Somhairle stayed at Doire ghlas the better part of that autumn, sitting some evenings at Fearchar's own hearth and some at others, watching the ring of new roofs rise round the old ring of oaks, and it was there, more than at any slab in Na Glinn Àrda or any bank raised against a storm, that he came to think the settling of the island had worked out, without any law behind it, the very thing his father never troubled to write down for anyone: a thing worth keeping got kept, in the end, because enough people, asked plainly and given a reason that cost them little, found they had no strong wish to refuse it, though no king had ever told them they must.

## VII. Of the Lines in His Face

He was walking south again, back toward Na Glinn Àrda, in his two thousand four hundred and thirty-fifth year, when a woman selling cheese at a roadside stall in the near valleys looked at him a moment longer than a stranger usually troubled to and asked, not unkindly, whether he had been unwell that season, for there were lines about his eyes that had not been there, she thought, the last time he passed her stall. Somhairle had heard such things said before, in jest, by people who took his slow way of speaking for an old man's caution and forgot, a breath later, that they had ever thought it; but he stopped that day at a still pool a little further on and looked at his own reflection for longer than he had troubled to look at it in decades, and found, when he looked closely, that she had told him true. There were lines at the corners of his eyes that had not been there when Beathan was born, and the grey that had stood at his temples a thousand years unmoving creeping now into his beard, so that a stranger might, for the first time in two thousand four hundred and thirty-five years, have taken him for what he actually was: a man growing old, slowly, the way his father never would.

He told no one of it at first, not even Beathan, who still sat out his own turns by the slab in Na Glinn Àrda and had not, so far as Somhairle could tell, begun to age at all; but Beathan noticed it himself before the year was out, coming upon his father unexpectedly at the slab one evening and stopping in the doorway a moment before he crossed it, the way a man stops when a familiar face shows him something he was not looking for. Neither of them spoke of it that night, or for some while after, for Clann na Ceiste were not a people who troubled a thing with words before the thing had finished happening to them; but it is told, among the few who kept that particular winter's telling whole, that Somhairle sat later that season at the fire with a young cousin of Beathan's wife, newly come into the household, who did not know him and took him, from his grey beard and his slow way of sitting, for an old man of no particular importance among the king's blood, and that Somhairle let the mistake stand a full evening without correcting it, listening to her talk of the settling further north as though he had walked none of that ground, and finding in the listening a quiet he had not expected the ageing to bring him.

It was Beathan who finally asked him of it, the following spring, sitting together at the slab through a night neither of them was properly owed by the custom, the young households having gone home early with a storm coming on. "You are changing," Beathan said, plainly, the way his father had taught him to say most things. "I have watched every face in Na Glinn Àrda change, mother among them, and I never once thought to watch yours." Somhairle answered that he had not thought to watch it either, and that he did not know why it should begin now, in his two thousand four hundred and thirty-sixth year, when it had not begun in his first thousand, and that he supposed the not-knowing was itself a kind of answer, of the sort Clann na Ceiste had always been given and had always kept without asking for better. Beathan sat with that a long while, turning it the way his father turned most things, and said at last only that he was glad, whatever it meant, that his father would grow old among them rather than remain forever the one face at every hearth that time did not touch; and Somhairle, hearing it, thought it the truest thing either of them had said to the other in some decades.

He kept the Line whole in his own head still, every name his father had given him and every name added since Doire ghlas took its own new name, and he went on walking, in the years that followed, from settlement to settlement across the widening island, though a little more slowly each year, and a little more often now stopping, on a road he had walked a hundred times before, simply to sit a while and watch new roofs going up round trees his father's own hands had once passed under, unremembered by anyone building beneath them but the one man on the whole island whose own years were, at last, beginning to run out the ordinary way.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of Murchadh in the North

*GE 2,601 – 2,999*

> *Cha bhi cnoc aig neach ach fhad 's a their an Rìgh e.*
> No one holds a hill longer than the King says he does.
> — said in the northern plain, of every holder since Murchadh

## I. Of the Spring That Never Freezes

Murchadh was the ninth of the king's sons, and the one the king sent north to the plain with nothing more than his own name to hold it by, and he was eight hundred and ninety-six years old the spring he rode out of Dùn ìseal with sixty households at his back and a strip of the northern plain in his keeping that no one before him had troubled to settle beyond its edges. He had his mother's black hair still, and would keep it long after the households he led north had buried three generations of their own greying, for he was born after the grove like his father's other sons, though already, in that ninth century of his life, the first grey had begun to show at his temples, faint as frost on a north slope, so that the older men riding with him took it for a kind of promise, that whatever else he was he would not outlast them by so many lifetimes that they need never learn the shape of his death.

The ground he was given had one thing on it worth the naming, a spring on a low rise above the plain that ran clear and full through every winter the households there could remember, never once skinned with ice though the standing pools about it froze hard enough to bear a man's weight from Samhain to the first thaw. Murchadh had heard of it from a herdsman before he had ever seen it, and when he came to it at last, in the fifteenth year of his holding, he stood over it a long while without speaking, watching the water break the crust of frost at its lip and run on regardless, and it is told that he said only, to the men beside him, that a household built round a thing that did not freeze need never again reckon its water against its wood, and that this was worth more to men in that country than any wall.

He raised his own hall there that same year, timber and turf as every hall on the island still was raised, and called the place for its size before it had earned the name, Baile Mòr mhòr, the great big town, which the households about him took at first for a joke against the six poor roofs then standing and kept afterward without irony once the joke had come true under them. By the time Murchadh's own hair had gone properly grey, in the fourth century of his holding, Baile Mòr mhòr stood eighty houses about the spring, byres and workshops and a granary raised on stones against the damp, the largest place built in that generation anywhere north of An Cnoc Ruadh, and the households of the plain came to it at every gathering-tide the way lesser streams come down into a river, bringing wool and hides and the grey flint of Cnoc àrsaidh to trade against salt carried up from the shore.

He did not call himself a king there, nor one of Rìghrean na Cloiche, nor anything the households of the south would have known the word for. He called himself, when anyone asked, a man holding ground his father had given him, and left it at that, and the plain took to calling him the same, Murchadh a chumas am Blàr, Murchadh who holds the plain, until the longer telling wore down to the shorter one and he was simply Murchadh Mòr, the name his own great size and his father's habit of naming things large had between them settled on him before he was two hundred years into the holding.

## II. Of the Rough Ground and the Boar-Thickets

The plain did not fill all at once, and what filled it, in the years after Baile Mòr mhòr stood entire, filled it the way water finds the low ground first and the high ground after, household following household along whatever line of easy walking or standing water led them on.

North-east of Murchadh's spring the ground rose rough and stony, fit for little but sheep, and it was sheep the households there kept from the first year they broke ground, calling the place Baile gharbh for the roughness under it, and sending their wool south along the coast road to Cruinneachadh an Àtha every year rather than north to Murchadh's own granary, for the coast road was the shorter way and the ford took wool as readily as the plain did. West of the spring, along the coast where the old thickets still stood thick with thorn and rowan, the boars ran heavier and meaner than anywhere else the island's herders knew, and the households that settled there, at a place they called Baile fhiadhaich for the wildness of it, hung the tusks of the biggest boars over their doors the way other households hung a fox's brush, and ate boar at every feast the way the southern shore ate fish, until it was said, half in mockery and half in plain fact, that a man from Baile fhiadhaich could be known by his gait before he opened his mouth, from a lifetime of walking ground a boar might break from at any step.

Further round the coast, on a harbour the old maps of that country did not trouble to name, households took up an anchorage beside a stone landing built by hands none of them could put a name to, older than any wall standing near it, and used the landing as it stood without mending a stone of it, out of a caution common enough among the island's settlers wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stood, that a thing built by hands so long silent was better left as it was found than corrected by hands that did not understand it. They called the place Cuan shean, the old bay, for the landing rather than for themselves, and it grew slowly at first and then, once the fish proved good off that coast, faster than either Baile gharbh or Baile fhiadhaich, until within two centuries it had its own small fleet and its own small quarrel with Murchadh's granary over which of them the coast road properly served.

Murchadh rode the round of these three settlements once in every decade of his early holding, less often as the decades lengthened into centuries and the ride came to feel shorter to a man for whom a decade was no longer than a season had once been to the men riding beside him. He judged what needed judging, a boundary dispute at Baile gharbh over a well two households claimed by the same spring, a quarrel at Baile fhiadhaich over whose dogs had put up whose boar, and settled each the way his father settled such things at the ford, by hearing both sides through and giving the ground to whichever household had been longer on it, without troubling to write the judgment down anywhere but in the memory of the households who had heard it given.

## III. Of Eithne and of the Sons

In the hundred and second year of Murchadh's holding, in the north, word came south to Dùn ìseal that the king had another daughter, born to a wife of the near valleys whom the reciters afterward remembered chiefly for a quickness of tongue that her daughter kept whole. They named her Eithne, and she was born in the year the households of Dùn ìseal count as two thousand seven hundred and three of the grove, a hundred years after Murchadh had ridden north with his sixty households, so that by the time she was grown enough to be spoken of as anything but a child she was already a stranger to the plain her half-brother held, and knew him, when she did come to know him, chiefly by his size and by a certain slowness of speech that she took, in her own quickness, for stupidity, and was some centuries in unlearning.

Murchadh himself, in that same span of years, had begun a household of his own sons, eleven of them born to two wives over the better part of three centuries, the first in the hundred and nineteenth year of his holding and the last so long after the first that the eldest of the eleven had grey in his own beard before the youngest had his first tooth. He gave each of them, as they came of an age to want it, a corner of the plain to hold under him rather than a share of his own hall, for he had learned, watching his father give and take back the whole island by the same rule, that a son set to holding a corner of ground learns the weight of it faster than a son kept idle at his father's own hearth, and every one of the eleven, in his turn, learned it. The eldest, a broad, slow-spoken man the plain came to call Aonghas an Spuir for a spur of high ground he held above the river, held it so well and so long that his own son after him held it in turn without any word from Murchadh needed to confirm it, and it was that steady holding, more than any of the louder ones, that Murchadh, grown old himself in the holding, came to think the truest mark of a household settled for good.

Eithne, for her part, grew into a woman as quick as her mother had been and quicker than most of her father's blood troubled to be, and when she went out from Dùn ìseal at last, in her hundred and forty-fourth year, she rode west to the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a broken watch-tower Seann-Dhaoine had raised and long since let fall, where a scatter of households had lately settled and asked, having heard she was of the king's blood and quick with a judgment, that she stay among them a season and help them lay out their fields before the ploughing quarrels set in that every new settlement seemed heir to. She stayed the season, and then a decade, and then simply stayed, taking no stone from the ruin above the houses though it stood the nearest quarry to hand, out of the same caution the households of Cuan shean had shown their own old landing, and the place grew up round her the way Baile Mòr mhòr had grown up round Murchadh's spring, its own households naming it, within that first year and out of no more than hope for what it might become, Cathair mhòr, the great city, though it was then no more than a dozen roofs below a broken tower. It was hers in all but the naming even once the naming was done, and she held it, in her own right and without asking her half-brother's leave, for longer than either of them then reckoned that either of them had left to hold anything.

## IV. Of Dùn chrom and the Bank That Faced Two Ways

Midway between Murchadh's plain and the hills where the vein ran, on rising ground that looked one way toward An Cnoc Ruadh and the other toward the passes, households raised in the two hundredth year of Murchadh's holding a banked fort they called Dùn chrom, the bent fort, for the shape the ditch took following the ground rather than any straighter plan a surveyor might have set on it. It was built, from the first spade of earth turned, by two kinds of household at once, herders come up out of the plain who wanted the bank to face south against no threat any of them could name but old habit, and herders come down from the hills of the vein who wanted it to face north against the cold winds off the passes rather than against any enemy at all, and the two parties, neither willing to give way to the other and neither troubling, in that easy generation, to make a quarrel of it, simply raised the bank both ways, a long crooked earthwork that curved to answer both wants at once and satisfied neither party fully, so that the fort stood from its first year with a name that fit it in more ways than the households who gave it ever meant.

It stood so, its bank facing both ways and troubling no one, only a little while, until the second year of its standing, when the holder its households had by then settled on, a stone-faced man named Ruadhan Beag, fell into a quarrel with the holder of Dùn thais, the older bank a day's walk to the south, over which way a bank ought properly to face when the ground it stood on gave a household the choice, and neither man, once the quarrel was well begun, could remember afterward which of them had started it or over what actual grazing or water it had first been raised, only that it had grown, over two winters of hard words carried back and forth by herders neither man had sent as messengers but who carried the words all the same, into something large enough that both sent to Murchadh at Baile Mòr mhòr to settle it before it grew larger yet.

Murchadh rode to Dùn chrom himself, in his own one thousand and ninety-seventh year, a season he remembered afterward, by his own account to his sons, chiefly for the cold of it, and stood on the bank between the two holders and asked each in turn to show him what harm the other's bank had ever done him, and neither could show him any harm at all, only the discomfort of a ditch that answered a want its own household no longer entirely remembered wanting. He told them, at the end of a long morning's hearing, that a bank built to face two ways had stood its first winters without falling to either enemy the two builders had once feared, and that this seemed to him a better argument for the bank than either holder had yet made against it, and he left the ditch as it stood and rode home, and the quarrel, having been heard rather than settled, wore thin over the following year the way most such quarrels did on that plain. Neither side yielded it. It simply grew too old to feed, once a season had passed without blood in it, and neither holder could find the heart any longer to keep it warm.

## V. Of Beathan at the Slab

It was in the two hundred and third year of Murchadh's holding, while the quarrel of the banks was still fresh enough in the telling that herders carried it as news rather than as an old tale, that word reached the north of a death far to the south that touched Murchadh's own house not at all and yet was carried up the plain, from household to household, with a weight the quarrel of the banks never had.

Beathan, son of Somhairle, who had sat his nights among the herdsmen at the slab since before Murchadh was born and had grown old in the sitting the way none of the king's other blood then living had yet grown old, died that winter at Tobar dhìreach, in his own two thousand two hundred and thirteenth year, the oldest death any household on the island could then remember among the king's kin, and word of it went out from Na Glinn Àrda the way a stone dropped in still water sends its rings, further than any messenger could ever have travelled on his own legs. Murchadh had met him only twice in his own long life, both times briefly, at gatherings neither man had come to for the other's sake, and knew him chiefly by the Line he kept whole in his own head and by a certain slowness of speech the households of Na Glinn Àrda shared and the plain's own quicker talkers found strange in a man of the king's blood.

What the plain took from the death, more than the man himself, was the number, two thousand two hundred and thirteen years, said aloud at every hearth that winter the way a weight is said aloud when it is finally lifted and known, and the households of Baile Mòr mhòr, hearing it, looked at Murchadh, then not yet eleven hundred, and did their own reckoning under their breath, and some among the oldest of them began, that winter, to speak for the first time of what it might mean for a household to outlive not only its own holder but the holder's holder too, a thing none of them had yet seen done on the plain and all of them, without saying so aloud, understood they eventually would.

## VI. Of the Holy Hill, the Red Well and the Marsh Houses

Further south and east of Murchadh's own ground, in the years the plain came to call the settled years, three more places rose that the reciters afterward set beside Baile Mòr mhòr, Baile gharbh, Baile fhiadhaich, Cuan shean and Dùn chrom in the long telling of how the north filled.

On a hill whose spring the households that came to it found already good and whose name, Cnoc naomh, the holy hill, they found already given, by whom or for what reason none of them could learn from any teller then living, a settlement grew that kept the name and never troubled the why of it, taking the hill's own holiness, whatever its cause, as a fact of the ground the way they took its water and its grazing, without asking more of it than it gave. On the southern cape, where the keepers of a beacon fire had for generations kept watch over water thick with wrecking rocks, households built at last round a well whose water ran faintly reddish from the rock it rose through, and called the place Tobar dhearg for the well's own colour, and it grew, in time, into the greatest place on that whole coast, its beacon burning nightly for boats that had learned, by then, to look for it. And between Tobar dhearg and the older Seann Skell to its west, on ground too low and wet for any sensible household to choose first, a settlement rose whose first houses stood on driven piles over standing marsh water, moved afterward, once the piles proved the ground beneath them firmer than it looked, onto solid footing a spear's cast inland, and kept, even after the moving, the name the marsh had first given it, Muileann naomh.

None of these three troubled Murchadh's own holding directly, lying as they did beyond the edge of the plain he had been given, but the plain's own tellers folded them into the same telling all the same, for it was in those years, the reciters afterward agreed, that the whole northern half of the island passed from a scatter of households each alone on its own ground into something that could be spoken of, at last, as settled, place answering place along roads that had grown, without any single hand laying them out, from nothing more than the paths households wore between one hearth and the next.

## VII. Of the Valleys Given and Taken Back

In the two hundred and ninety-ninth year of Murchadh's holding, word came north from Dùn ìseal, this time carried by two riders sent for the purpose rather than by herders passing news from one household to the next. The message they carried, given to Murchadh in his own hall at Baile Mòr mhòr before the fire had properly warmed the men who bore it, was that the king was taking back the western valleys of the plain, the poorer, wetter ground toward the coast that Murchadh had held longest of all his father's gifts, and giving them instead to a young grandson of An Cnoc Ruadh's own line, a man Murchadh had met perhaps three times in his life and could not, that evening, entirely call to mind the face of.

He did not argue it. He asked the riders only whether his father had given a reason, and they told him, as plainly as they had been told to tell it, that the king had said no more than that the valleys had grown crowded enough to want a nearer hand than a hand at Baile Mòr mhòr could give them, and that this was reason enough, from that hand, for anyone on the island to accept without further asking. Murchadh sat with it a long while after the riders had eaten and gone to their beds, turning it the way his own father was said to turn most things, and told his eldest son, the broad quiet man who held the spur above the river, that he had held those valleys for the better part of three hundred years and felt, losing them, less the loss of the ground itself than the loss of the particular quiet they had given him, a corner of his holding he had never had to think hard about because it had never once given him trouble, and that this, he supposed, was as fair a payment as any holder on the island ever got for three hundred years of a thing going well.

His son asked him whether he would send word south asking the reason plainer, or asking to keep even a corner of the valleys for his own line's sake, and Murchadh told him no, that his father gave and took back by a rule none of his children had ever yet seen written down or heard spoken plainly, and that the rule, so far as twelve hundred years of watching it worked on his own household and on every household he had ever heard tell of, came to this: that a man held what he was given for exactly as long as the giving served, and no longer, and that arguing the rule had never once, in any telling Murchadh knew, changed what the king in the end did. The valleys passed to An Cnoc Ruadh's grandson before the season turned, and the plain, within a year, had stopped speaking of it at all, the way a wound stops being spoken of once the scar has set, and Murchadh's own household held what remained to it, the spring, the granary, the eleven sons each settled on his own corner, without any further word from the south for the better part of a century.

## VIII. Of the Summons

It was in his own one thousand two hundred and ninety-fourth year, so near the close of the settled years that the plain had by then almost forgotten there had ever been an unsettled time, that Murchadh received the second summons of his life to leave his own hall and ride south, the first having been the summons that sent him north to begin with, near four hundred years before.

The riders who brought it this time were of the king's own household, sent for the purpose, rather than herders carrying word between one household and another the way the quarrel of the banks had travelled. The word they carried was short and gave no more reason than the taking of the valleys had given: that the king would hold a gathering at the ford of the salt and the wool, in the coming year, greater than any gathering the ford had yet seen, and that every holder of every share of the island, near or far, was to come to it and bring what of his own blood cared to stand with him. Murchadh asked the riders, as he had asked the riders who brought the valleys' taking, whether his father had said why now and not some other year, and got, this time, no answer at all beyond a shrug that told him the riders knew no more of the why than he did.

He sent word that year to each of his eleven sons on their own corners of the plain, to Baile gharbh and Baile fhiadhaich and Cuan shean, to the holder now settled at Dùn chrom in Ruadhan Beag's place, and south to Eithne below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, that the king had called a gathering and that whoever of the north's blood meant to be counted in it should be ready to ride before the spring turned. Most answered that they would come. A few, the households furthest north whom five hundred years of settling had made, by slow degrees, more the plain's own people than the king's blood at all, sent back only that they would send what they could and stayed where they were, and Murchadh, hearing it, found in himself neither the will nor, he told his eldest son, quite the right to press them further, for a household that had held its own corner of ground for five generations without once needing the king's hand to settle anything on it had earned, he thought, the right to decide for itself how far south its own feet still owed the walking. He rode for the ford himself that spring with sixty of his own household behind him, the same number, though none of the same men, that had ridden north with him at the holding's beginning, and did not yet know, riding, how many of his own blood he would find waiting there before him, nor how far south the ford truly lay from a life spent, by then, four centuries in the same one plain and close on thirteen hundred years in the world.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Great Gathering at the Ford

*GE 3,000*

*At An Cnoc Ruadh this is kept as the old woman's own telling, carried down by her daughter's daughter to the reciters there, and by them to the reciters of the ford.*

## I. Of the Road Down

She was nine years old that summer, and she had never gone further from An Cnoc Ruadh than Ros dhomhain across the lake, where her mother traded cheese for grain twice in a year. So when her mother told her they would walk to the ford for An Cruinneachadh Mòr, and sell salt there for the length of three days, she thought at first that a great gathering must be a kind of market larger than the one at the mill, and nothing more.

They went down with six households of the lake shore, each with a cart or a laden pony, and the salt wrapped in sacking against the damp and packed so carefully that her mother would not let her sit near it, for fear a wriggling child might loosen a cord. The road ran fourteen miles from An Cnoc Ruadh to the ford, easy walking for anyone grown, and they did it in a day, resting once at noon by a stream where the ponies drank and the women unwrapped bread and dried fish and ate standing, watching the road both ways out of habit rather than fear. It was on that road, past the second bend from the lake, that she first understood the size of what she was walking toward. Other households were on the road too, coming down from the hills to the north of the lake shore with pigs on a string and dogs that would not stop barking at the pigs, and further on a family from the west went by driving two carts heaped with hides and coils of worked leather, seal-skins among them, and one old man walking beside the second cart who nodded to her mother without a word, as people did to strangers they expected to meet again before the week was out.

By the time the ford came in sight, in the low light of that evening, she had counted more strange faces on that one road than she had seen in her whole life at An Cnoc Ruadh, and she gave up counting after that, because the ground below her, where the river widened and shoaled between two long green banks, was already dark with people and fires, further than she could see in the dusk, and more were still coming in on every road that led to it.

Her mother took her wrist then, and did not let go of it again for three days.

The ground the salt-traders used lay downstream of the ford, a wide flat shelf of turf between the water and the alder scrub, and it was there her mother's people made their fire that first night, among others of the lake shore and the pans of the south coast who knew each household by its salt before they knew it by its name. Upstream, where the river ran faster over a bed of clean gravel, was a second ground the girl did not understand until later, kept clearer than the rest and walked over by fewer feet, as though the grass there knew something the grass downstream did not. Beyond that again, on the far side where the bank rose in a low shoulder before the trees began, lay a third ground given over to the northern households and the households of the west, who set their pig-pens and their leather-stalls in orderly rows the salt-traders never quite managed among themselves.

By the second morning the three grounds had run together at their edges until nobody rightly knew any longer which bank was whose, and a child sent to fetch water might come back an hour later having made two new friends and lost the path to her own fire twice over. The girl was sent for water twice that morning and came back late both times, and her mother did not scold her for it, being too busy with her own trading to notice how late was late.

That first full day, before ever the king came down, was market enough on its own to fill a child's head for a year. Potters from the north-west had carried down whole stacks of grey ware nested one inside another on a single cart, and a man from further west than the girl had ever heard named traded three strings of amber, worn smooth by the sea and drilled through for the wearing, for a winter's worth of salt her mother would not have parted with for less. Wool went from hand to hand in raw fleeces and in cloth already woven, flint from Cnoc àrsaidh changed owners twice before noon, and somewhere among the fires a family of Tràigh an t-Salainn sang the old four-line refrain of the pans, over and over, to nobody in particular, the way people sing a thing they have always sung rather than a thing meant to be listened to. Marriages were spoken of that day as freely as salt was, two households from opposite ends of the crowd sitting down together over a shared fire to weigh what a match between their children might be worth to each in a few years' time, in grazing or in grandchildren, and the girl heard more than one old woman remark, watching such a pair of households talk, that the ford had made more marriages than it had ever made kings.

It was toward evening of that first day that she heard the word said which she carried away more clearly than any other from the whole gathering, though she did not understand it then and was not sure she understood it fully even in her own old age. An old reciter of the hill, sitting with others of his kind at a fire near the upstream ground, said to those around him that this was the three thousandth year since the grove was lit, and that word of it had gone out along every road on the island that summer for that reason alone, so that people had come from coasts that had never troubled to send anyone to an ordinary gathering. The girl did not know what a grove had to do with a king, or what a thousand years was worth beside nine, and let the words go by her the way she let most talk of the reciters go by her; but she remembered, long after she had forgotten a great deal else that a child forgets, that the old men at that fire had spoken the number the way her own grandmother spoke the number of a bad winter, as a thing to be marked rather than a thing to be explained.

## II. Of the Man Who Came Like a Herdsman

It was on that second morning, with the sun not yet clear of the eastern trees, that a stillness went through the crowd on the upstream ground the way a wind goes through standing barley, bending it all one way before anyone has felt a breath of it themselves. The girl was standing with her mother at the edge of the salt-traders' ground, both of them for once not haggling over anything, and she saw the bending before she understood its cause: old men who had been sitting all morning got to their feet without being asked; a woman with an armful of wool let the wool fall and did not stoop for it; two boys wrestling in the mud stopped mid-throw and stood apart from each other, looking the same way.

He was coming down the hill road from the west with a handful of others, dressed as any herdsman dresses for a day's walking, in undyed wool with mud to the knee and a plain staff in his hand that he was using as a walking-stick and nothing more. The girl, craning past her mother's shoulder, was disappointed. She had heard the word king used all her nine years the way other children heard the word storm, as a thing that came from a distance and changed everything it touched, and she had built in her own mind a man taller than any man, crowned in something that caught the light. The man on the hill road was younger-looking than her own father, and no taller, and carried nothing that caught the light at all.

Then the crowd opened for him.

It opened the whole way down to the river, though nobody called out and nobody pushed, a channel opening through several thousand people before he reached it, the way standing water parts before the bow of a boat without any hand rowing the boat aside. The girl watched the faces as he passed rather than the man himself, because the faces told her more than he did: the old people, who she had thought nothing frightened, stepped back from that channel with their eyes down in a way she had never seen an old person step back from anything, and one old woman near her, whom she did not know, put both hands over her own mouth and said nothing at all, though her eyes were wet.

It was the faces that frightened the girl in the end, more than the man, and once she was frightened of him she found she could not look away from him for the rest of that day.

## III. Of the Hands Between His Hands

He went down through the channel the crowd had made and out into the middle of the ford, where the water came only to his knees though it ran fast there over clean stone, and he stood, and waited, with the herdsman's staff still in his hand as though he might yet have some flock to see to before the day was out.

The holder of the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche came out to him first, wading in from the upstream bank with his cloak gathered up over one arm, and put both his hands between the king's two hands, the way a man puts his hands into water he means to drink from cupped, and the king closed his own hands over them a moment and let them go, and spoke a few words to him the girl was too far off to hear. The holder waded back with the front of his clothes wet to the chest where the current had caught him despite the gathering of his cloak, and nobody on the bank laughed at him for it, though a boy near the girl started to and was stopped by his own mother's hand on his shoulder before the laugh was fully out of him.

After the hill's holder came the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, a young man the girl's own mother knew by sight and called out to once, softly, before catching herself, for such a day called for no shouting across the crowd. He was a smaller man than the hill's holder, narrow through the shoulder, and he went into the water more carefully, as though he did not trust the current the way the other had, and when he came out from the king's hands he looked, the girl thought, smaller still, though she could not afterward say what had made him look so.

Then came the holder of Tràigh an t-Salainn, an older woman with grey plaited into her hair, whom the girl's mother did know well, having traded salt with her own people for two summers running, and after her the holder who spoke for the northern plain, and after him the holder who spoke for the households of the west; and each one waded out in turn, put hands between the king's hands, and waded back soaked to the chest or higher, and stood afterward among their own people a little apart from everyone else, the way a person stands apart who has just come from somewhere the others have not been.

Five went out and five came back, and the girl counted them on her own fingers without meaning to, the way she counted anything that happened five times running, and thought when the fifth had waded back that the day's strangeness must surely be finished.

Her grandmother, who had come up beside her by then, told her the names of the five as they went, in the low running voice old people use for things they have watched happen many times before: the hill's own holder that year, a grave, careful man the list would keep no separate count of once his turn was done; An Cnoc Ruadh's young holder, new enough to his own hall that half the crowd still called him by his father's name before catching themselves; the woman of Tràigh an t-Salainn, whom the girl's mother traded with every summer and had never once, in all that trading, mentioned held anything grander than a stretch of clay pans; and the two who spoke, in their turn, for the households of the northern plain and of the west, neither known to the girl by more than the word holder. Her grandmother named none of the five by any longer telling, and the girl understood even then, young as she was, that these were people whose whole worth to the reciters lay in the one wading and no more, the way a stone's worth to a wall lies in its standing and not in where it was quarried.

It was not the day's strangeness, either, that was finished.

For a little while after the fifth holder had waded back to the bank, nothing more happened, and the crowd, which had gone still for the wading, began to find its voice again in low murmurs and the shuffling of feet, the way a gathering does when it senses more is coming and cannot say what. Someone near the girl asked whether that was the whole of it, and someone else answered, in the flat certain tone people use when they are guessing and do not want it known, that it could hardly be the whole of it, for the king himself had so far done no more than stand there and receive what was brought to him, and a gathering did not walk days from every coast of the island only to watch five strangers get their clothes wet. The girl's mother, close enough by then to hear this exchange, said nothing to it either way, but drew her daughter in against her side and kept both hands on her shoulders, the way she held her at the edge of deep water, or at a cattle-fair when the beasts were being driven through, as though she too expected more to come and wished to be sure of where her own child stood when it came.

## IV. Of the Rings in the River

They came down from the upstream ground where the grass grew clean and little walked-over, and the girl had thought until that morning that the upstream ground was kept clear for some purpose of the reciters', a place for their fires and their reckoning apart from the crowd. She understood only when they began to come down, more of them than she could easily count, and more behind those, that the upstream ground had been kept clear all along for this, and for nothing else.

They were not all of an age, and that was the second thing that struck her, once the first shock of their numbers had passed. Some among them looked old, bent a little at the shoulder and slow on their feet, and she took these at first for the eldest of the family, until her grandmother, standing near her by then with the rest of the household, told her low that it ran backward: that the oldest of the king's children looked the youngest of any of them, and the ones with grey in their beards and stiffness in their knees were commonly the youngest born, grandchildren and great-grandchildren counted in mere centuries rather than in the thousands the eldest carried. The girl could not fit this into her head all at once, and did not try very hard; she only watched.

They went into the river in rings around him, the way water rings out from a stone dropped into it, the nearest ring made up of faces she thought at first must be his brothers and sisters, for they stood closest and moved with the most ease, though her grandmother said afterward that these were his children, the ones born earliest, in the first centuries of his reign, and that one bent, dry-faced old man among them, who took his place at the king's left hand as though the place belonged to him by long custom, was in fact among his eldest living sons, older by the reckoning of years than any grandfather the girl had ever heard named, though he stood in the water no straighter than any old man stands. She learned afterward, from a woman of the ford who knew the lines by heart, that this was Somhairle, keeper of the lines among his own people in Na Glinn Àrda, two thousand nine hundred and sixty-two years old that summer and looking, by every account she ever heard after, every year of it.

Beyond that first ring stood a second, younger to look at and yet, her grandmother said, coming after in the order of birth rather than before, and among these a tall grey-haired man whom people on the bank pointed out to each other by name, Murchadh, who held the northern plain for his father and had eleven sons of his own scattered among the rings further out; he stood a head taller than most around him and looked, the girl thought, no older than her own uncle, though the woman who knew the lines said he had passed his twelve hundredth year that same season. Further out again, near the edge of the innermost crowd, was a young woman who laughed at a word said to her by the man beside her, no more than three hundred years old and looking a girl of twenty, whom the same woman named Eithne, and said she held ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and had a temper her father was said to find diverting rather than troublesome.

Ring beyond ring they went into the water, until the girl lost count of the rings themselves and could only see that the whole width of the ford between the two banks was full of them, standing thigh-deep and waist-deep according to where the river bed dipped, and that the water was piling up visibly behind their legs where so many bodies broke its running, so that the ford above them ran higher and slower than it had run all that summer, and below them ran lower and quicker, as though the whole river had been made to answer for a moment to the people standing in it rather than the other way about.

Somewhere in the middle of that long standing, a boy of her own age pushed in beside her at the bank's edge, a stranger to her, from one of the households of the west by his dress, and asked her, in the plain way children ask each other things at a gathering where every face is new, whether all of that in the water was truly one family. She said she did not know, though her grandmother had just told her so, because it did not feel to her like a thing that could be answered yes or no in a single word; and the boy, considering the rings a while longer himself, said only that his own father had eight brothers and sisters and he had thought that a great many until that morning, and after that the two of them stood together and watched without talking further, the way children will share a silence when a thing is too large for either of them to explain to the other.

The reciters on the near bank began then to say the names.

They said them in order, the eldest first, working outward ring by ring the way the family had gone into the water, and the girl heard names go by all that afternoon that meant nothing to her, sons and daughters and grandchildren and the grandchildren of grandchildren, some given a single word of what they held or had done and most given nothing but the bare name and the name of the parent before it. The sun crossed the whole sky while the reciters spoke, and still they were not through the rings nearest the far bank when the light began to go gold and then to go grey, and word came along the bank at last, passed mouth to mouth the way word travelled in that crowd, that the reciters had reckoned some four hundred of his blood standing in the water that day, and that they did not expect, when they began the telling again the next gathering, to be able to say the number had not grown since.

Watching him where he stood at the centre of it, unmoving while ring after ring of his own children and grandchildren stood in the cold water around him, the girl came slowly to a thought she never afterward heard put better by anyone older than she was that day: that he could not know all their names himself, any more than she could have named every pebble on the shore of the lake at home, and that this did not trouble him half so much as it seemed to trouble the reciters, who kept glancing toward him as though checking their work against some standard only he could set and would not.

Once, while the naming went on, she saw him turn his head and look a long while at a young woman standing in one of the outer rings, near the far bank, a woman no different to the girl's eye from a dozen others near her, dark-haired and quiet-faced and dressed as plainly as anyone in the water that day. He looked at her the way a man looks at a face he has met before and cannot place, turning it over, and the girl, young as she was, understood that look better than she understood anything else that happened at the ford that summer, for she had worn it herself more than once trying to place a face from Ros dhomhain among a crowd of strangers. The woman did not seem to notice him looking, or if she did, gave no sign of it, and after a while he turned back to the reciters and the look was gone from his face as though it had never crossed it.

## V. Of Those Who Did Not Come

It was some while into that afternoon, with the names still being said and the light not yet failing, that the girl heard her grandmother say to another woman of An Cnoc Ruadh, in the flat voice people use for a fact rather than a complaint, that no one had come that year from east of the vein.

The other woman said she had noticed the same, and that it was the second gathering running that the east had sent no one, and the two of them turned the matter over a little longer, wondering aloud whether the households there had trouble with their own harvest, or a grudge with some family of the northern plain, or simply no salt worth carrying so far when they had none of their own to trade for it. Neither of them arrived at an answer, and neither seemed troubled by the lack of one; and within the hour the girl heard the same two women laughing together over a joke a trader from the south had made about his own mule, the matter of the east's absence set down as easily as it had been picked up, the way a stone is set down that a walker has turned over once in passing and found nothing under.

The girl herself gave the matter no more thought than her grandmother had, being nine, and being far more taken up with the rings in the river and the names still being said than with anyone who had chosen to stay away from them. It was only in her own old age, telling this same gathering to her own daughter's daughter at An Cnoc Ruadh, that she found herself dwelling on that hour longer than the rest of the day's telling seemed to want, turning over what it might mean that a whole coast of the island had gone unremarked at the one gathering every other coast walked days to reach; and even then she came to no answer either, and told it to her granddaughter only as it had come to her, a fact set beside the rest of the facts, with the day fine and the crowd content and nobody at the ford, that year, troubled enough by an absence to spoil an afternoon over it.

She asked her grandmother once, years and years after, whether anyone had ever gone east of the vein to ask why its people kept away, and her grandmother, by then old and stooped herself, said only that she had never heard of anyone troubling to, for the households there owed nothing to the ford and the ford asked nothing of them, and a debt that runs neither way is rarely chased down by either side of it. It was as much of an answer as the girl ever had, and she gave it to her own granddaughter in turn exactly so, no fuller than she had received it.

## VI. Of the Warm Water

The light was nearly gone from the sky, and the reciters' voices had gone hoarse with the saying of names, when the king spoke a few words to those nearest him in the water, too low for the bank to hear, and the rings began at last to break apart and wade back to the shore, ring by ring in something like the order they had gone in, though by then the light was too poor for the girl to be sure of it. She watched the crowd of them come up out of the river and scatter along both banks to their own fires, laughing now some of them, and calling to children left behind on the grass, ordinary people again once they were out of the water, mothers wringing river-water from their children's clothes and grandfathers complaining of the cold in their old joints, until it was hard to believe, watching them settle to their suppers, that they had stood, not long before, in rings four hundred strong around a man who had buried wives by the score and did not age.

When the ford was empty at last of everyone but himself, he stood there alone a while in the dusk, in the middle of the river where the current still ran a little high from so many legs having broken it all day, and did not come out at once, the way a man lingers in a doorway after everyone else in the room has already gone to bed.

The girl's mother had let go of her wrist by then, caught up in some last trade of salt for wool with a woman of the northern plain before the light failed entirely, and the girl had wandered, without meaning to wander far, to the very edge of the downstream ground, where the bank sloped low enough that the water came almost to the toes of her shoes. She was the nearest person to him on that whole stretch of bank, closer by twenty paces than anyone else left out in the dusk, and she stood there and watched him standing in the river the way she might have watched a heron stand in shallow water at evening, still, waiting on nothing she could name.

Behind her the fires were being built up for the night, and somewhere among them she could hear the salt-song being sung again, the same four lines she had heard sung all that first day, and further off a man laughing at something his own child had said, and under all of it the ordinary evening noise of several thousand people settling to their suppers within call of a river; and she remembered afterward how strange it had seemed to her, even at nine, that so much ordinary noise could go on so close behind her while the one man in front of her stood as still in the water as if the whole gathering had already gone home and left him there alone on purpose.

The water going past her own feet, she found when she crouched to trail her fingers in it, was warm, warm as the bath water her mother heated over the fire on a winter evening, though the day had not been especially hot and the river above the ford ran cold enough at that season to numb a foot left in it too long. Downstream of him, where the current carried past the place he stood, a thin mist rose off the water in the last of the light, the way steam rises off a spring on a cold morning, and hung there over the ford a little while before the evening air took it.

Her feet never went in past the ankles. She was nine years old, and her mother would have called her back before her knees were wet, and besides, some part of her, young as she was, understood without being told that the warmth in that water was not a thing meant for wading in. She crouched instead at the very edge of it, in the last light, with her whole hand under the surface where it ran warmest, and stayed a long while after he had at last waded out on the far side and gone up into the dark among his own fires, watching the mist thin and vanish over water that was already, by the time her mother came looking for her, beginning to run cold again.

To the end of her own long life she told it exactly so: that the river that evening had been warm as a bath round the king standing in it, and that downstream of him, in the last of the light, it had smoked like a spring.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of Somhairle's Grave

*GE 3,001 – 3,030*

*Clann na Ceiste say the Line was given whole to one who was not of Somhairle's own blood only once in all the age, and that this was the once.*

## I. Of the Child Who Counted Names

Diorbhail was born at Tobar dhìreach some ten years before An Cruinneachadh Mòr, in a house two hundred paces below the slab, and she was not three years old before the households of Na Glinn Àrda had begun to remark on her the way a valley remarks on any child who does a thing early: she could say her own line, mother to grandmother to great-grandmother, four generations back, before she could reliably tie her own shoe, and she said it, her mother told the fire more than once, the way another child said a rhyme it liked the sound of, for the pleasure of the saying and not because anyone had asked her twice.

Somhairle heard of her the way he heard of most things in the valleys, late and sideways, from a herding woman who mentioned the child to him at a Bealltainn fire as an oddity worth a laugh, no more; and he might have let the matter lie there, as he had let a hundred smaller oddities lie in na Bliadhnachan Fada he had gone round those fires, had he not, some months after, sat an evening at the same house himself and heard the girl, then five, correct her own grandmother on the order of two cousins' births without being asked and without seeming to know she had done anything worth remarking. He watched her a while after that without saying why he watched, the way a man watches a colt in a field before he has decided whether it is worth the breaking, and he came to no such decision aloud for some years more.

She was seven when he first sat her down by the slab, on a morning her mother could never afterward say he had asked for in so many words, only that he had come to the door and said the child might walk up with him if her mother had no need of her that morning, and her mother, who like every household in the valleys had long since stopped questioning what Somhairle wanted with an hour of anyone's time, had let her go. He gave her nothing that first morning but the names of the slab, what it was and where its stain came from and why no household built a byre against it, told the way he told any child the same thing, in the plain voice of a man handing over a fact rather than a mystery; and he sent her home before noon with nothing more asked of her than that she come again if she cared to.

She cared to. She came again the next week, and the week after, walking up the two hundred paces on her own once her mother judged the path safe enough for a child that age, and by the time she was ten the valleys had begun to say of her, in the flat way they said such things, that she went to the slab the way another girl went to the burn for water, as an errand too ordinary to remark on twice.
