What passed between the old man and the child on those mornings was not, in those first years, the Line, for Somhairle held, as his own father was said to have held before him, that a thing given too soon to too young a head is a thing given badly; he gave her instead the small tellings that ringed the Line the way bark rings a tree, the tale of na Seachd Guail and how each was lit, the tale of the crack and its white stones, the names of the watch-households back three rounds, small enough matters that a wrong word in the telling cost nothing worse than his patient correction and a telling again.

## II. Of the Years Before the Fire

Beathan's son sat the watch those years as his father had sat it before him, and as his father's father had before that, a broad quiet man the valleys had stopped, long since, remarking on for anything but the ordinary steadiness of a household that kept its turn without complaint; and he watched the old man take up the girl the way a man watches a neighbour's matter, closely enough, but from outside the fence of it. It was known in the valleys, though never said outright at any fire Diorbhail sat by, that the watch and the reciting had always run in different hands, the one kept by whoever of Somhairle's own blood cared to sit it, the other given to whoever of Clann na Ceiste's wider households could carry it best; and if Beathan's son thought once or twice, in those years, that the reciting might in time have come to his own house rather than a stranger's, he gave the thought no more room than a man gives a draught under a door he has learned to live with, and sat his own turns at the slab with no less care for the not having it.

Diorbhail turned twelve, and then fifteen, growing tall and quick-tongued in the way of a child raised half by her own mother's hearth and half by an old man's patient repetitions, and Somhairle, who by then had begun himself to feel the years in his hands on the coldest mornings, though he said nothing of it to anyone, gave her, a little at a time, the outer branches of the Line: the households that had married into the king's blood and out of it again, the names the Line kept only because a marriage had once touched them and then let them go. She learned quickly, and corrected him twice in those years on a name he had himself begun to give wrong, both times a small slip of an ordering he had held the same way for centuries and had, without noticing, let time wear at like a stone worn at by the same running water; and both times he thanked her plainly and set the name right in his own next telling, without any shame in the setting right that she could ever afterward remember seeing on his face.

There was a boy of the basket-weavers' household, a cousin of hers by the shoulder of the hill and no relation at all by the Line, who went up with her twice that same year out of plain curiosity and came away both times saying he could make no more sense of it than of the crack under the slab, and would rather learn to weave a creel that held water than a string of names he could not use to catch so much as a fish; and Diorbhail, who liked him well enough at the ordinary fires, found she had no answer for him either, beyond that the names had never once, in all her going up, felt to her like a weight she was made to carry, only like a shape she already knew the feel of before she was given the words for it. He went back to the baskets, and neither of them thought the less of the other for the going, and it became, as such partings do in a small country, only one more fact of the valleys: that the slab took some and let others alone, and asked no household to explain which was which.

By her sixteenth year she had begun, without being told to, to test her own memory against the households' own telling of themselves at the ordinary fires, asking an old woman for her mother's mother's name before anyone had thought to volunteer it, and setting it beside what Somhairle had already given her to see that the two held together; and twice in that testing she found a small gap, a name a household kept differently from the way the Line kept it, and brought both tellings up to Somhairle rather than choose between them herself, for she had learned early that a gap brought to him whole was worth more than a gap already guessed shut. He heard her out both times without hurry, turned the two tellings over against what his own father had given him, and settled each in its turn, once for the household's telling and once for the Line's, explaining to her afterward, so that she would know the reason and not only the answer, why the one had held truer than the other.

It was in her eighteenth year that the valleys first heard him say, at a Samhain fire with the whole round of watch-households gathered close against the cold, that he did not know how many more Samhains he would sit among them, said in the plain voice he used for any fact and not as a thing wanting comfort in return; and the households, who had never in living memory heard him say such a thing, fell quiet round the fire the way a gathering falls quiet when an old man says a true thing nobody present is ready to hear said aloud. Diorbhail, sitting that night at the edge of the fire's light with the other young of the round, heard it and understood, better than most of the children beside her, what the saying meant for her own two hundred paces up the hill each week, though she said nothing of it that night to anyone, and went home and lay a long while awake before she slept.

## III. Of the Line Given Whole

He gave it to her whole in her twentieth year, on a night in the dark half of that year when the watch-household's fire was banked low against the slab's foot and Beathan's son sat that turn, close enough to hear what passed between them though he had not been asked to and did not ask afterward what he had heard. Somhairle had told her, some days before, only that she was to come up after dark and to eat well before she came, for the thing he meant to give her that night would want the whole of a night to give and take no shorter telling than that; and she had gone up her two hundred paces with her heart going harder than the climb alone accounted for, not from fear of the thing coming to her, for she had known for some years now what was coming to her, but from the plain weight of being the one it was coming to.

He began, as his own father had given it to him and as he had given it to Beathan before her, with the grove and Ailean at the fire that did not go into any other hand, and worked forward from there, generation on generation, wife on wife and child on child, the short lines and the long, the ones who had died before their fathers and the ones the Line kept only as a bare name and a bare year because no telling had come down with anything fuller; and he said it through once without a pause long enough to let her ask a question, the way it had always been given, twice through and no name out of place, and only at the second telling did he stop, here and there, to let her say a stretch of it back to him and hear for herself where her own memory had already caught it and where it had not.

The night ran long past the middle of its dark, and Beathan's son fed the fire twice more than his own turn usually asked of it, saying nothing, only watching the old man's mouth working through names that had, by his own reckoning, been said at that same slab longer than any watch-household's memory reached back; and when at last Somhairle came to the end of the second telling, to her own name set at the foot of it, he sat a while without speaking at all, his hands loose over his knees, and told her only, in a voice gone hoarse with the length of the saying, that she had it now the way he had had it, and that what she did with it from that night forward was hers to answer for and no longer his.

She walked home in the grey of the morning with the whole of it turning over in her own head, generation on generation, the way a person walks home turning over a weight they have only just learned they are strong enough to carry; and it is told, though the Line does not keep who first said it, that from that morning the households of Na Glinn Àrda began, without any of them quite deciding to, to bring their own children's names to Diorbhail at the fires rather than to Somhairle, the way a valley turns by degrees from an old well to a new one dug beside it, the old well no less good for the turning, only no longer the one a hand reaches for first.

## IV. Of the Withering

The years after that giving were kinder to no one's hands than the years before them, least of all to Somhairle's own. His face, which had held the same lines for so many centuries that the valleys had stopped remarking on it the way they had stopped remarking on Beathan's son's steadiness, began at last, in the seasons after the great giving, to fall in the way a fruit falls in that has been kept a season past its ripeness, the skin drawing close over the bone beneath it until an old woman of the watch-households, seeing him at a distance one Bealltainn, said to her own daughter, not unkindly, that he had come at last to look like nothing so much as a withered apple left too long on the sill; and the saying, once said, travelled the valleys the way such sayings do, and stuck to him the way a byname sticks to a face that has worn the same look too long to shed it, until the households spoke of him by it as easily as they spoke of the slab.

He kept coming to the fires all the same, though slower on the path than any of them had known him, leaning at last on a stick a herding boy had cut him from the hazel above the burn, and he sat still through whole tellings without correcting a word, listening to Diorbhail say back to him a branch of the Line he had given her years before, nodding when she had it right and saying nothing at all when, once or twice, a small thing had shifted in her keeping that had not been in his; for he had come, by then, to hold that a Line kept forward by a living mind was worth more than a Line kept exact by a dying one, and he let her small changes stand without troubling either of them with the correcting of them.

Beathan's son watched the old man fail with the plain grief of a household that has sat beside a fire so long it has stopped imagining any other arrangement, and did for him, in those last seasons, what no one asked him to and he never named aloud: walked up before each Samhain to see the path cleared of the season's first fallen branches so an old man's stick would not catch on one in the dark, and sat longer at the slab on the nights Somhairle came up to it than his own turn strictly asked of him, so that there would always be a fire built up and someone by it if the old man wanted company on the climb down.

It was in the last of those years that Somhairle told Diorbhail, at a fire with no one else near enough to hear it, the one thing his own father had never told him: that he did not know, himself, what waited for a man of the grove's own blood who had never taken a wife of the king's giving nor a share of the king's kingdom, once his own years ran out; that his brothers and sisters who had taken wives and shares had each, in their dying, been carried into some telling that named them by their hall or their household, and he had no hall and no household to be carried into, only the slab and the Line and the valleys that had let him sit their fires the better part of thirty centuries without once asking what he was to them beyond a teller of names. Diorbhail had no answer for that either, being twenty-eight by then and no wiser in such matters than he was, and she told him only that the valleys would know what to make of his going when it came, the way they had always known what to make of everything else that came to them without warning, and he laughed at that, the first time she had heard him laugh in some years, and said she had more of Clann na Ceiste in her than her own mother's line accounted for.

## V. Of the Grave

He died at Tobar dhìreach in her thirty-fifth year, in the season the valleys keep for turning peat, and it is told that Beathan's son found him at the slab in the grey of a morning, sitting against the stone the way he had sat against it a thousand mornings before, his stick fallen just out of reach of the hand that had held it, and no mark on him anywhere that anyone could point to, only the stillness of a man who had finished a long day's walking and sat down at last to rest from it. Word went down from the valleys before noon that same day, carried by a boy on the fastest pony the round could put under him, and it went, as such word had always gone in that country, straight to Dùn ìseal and to no other hall first. He had lived two thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven years, by Sloinneadh a' Chlachair's own counting, and died before his father all the same, as every child of the grove would in the end.

The king came up from the kingdom on the third day, on foot the last two miles of it though he had ridden the rest, and the old people of Clann na Ceiste stood about the grave they had by then already dug, close by the slab on the side away from its stain, and looked at the two of them, the father with his straight back and grey hair and the son laid out in his shroud with a face like a withered apple, and none of them, not even Somhairle's own reciters, could find a word worth saying into that silence. Diorbhail stood among them with the whole of the Line sitting in her own head the way it had sat there fifteen years now, and found that she too had nothing to say, though she had, an hour before, half believed there would be some line of the telling that would rise up in her and fit the moment; there was none, and she let the not-having-one stand rather than force a thing that did not want forcing.

The king put his son into the ground himself, kneeling at the grave's edge in the plain herdsman's clothes he had worn, by every telling that has ever come down of him, since long before Diorbhail's own grandmother was born, and he did the work with his own two hands the way any household buried its own dead in those valleys, taking no help offered him though three men of the watch-households stood ready to give it. Then he sat down on the turf beside the closed grave with his arms round his knees, like a boy, and stayed there. The households drifted back toward their own fires as the light went, one by one and then in twos, until only Beathan's son and Diorbhail were left standing near enough to see him, neither of them willing to be the one who went first, and it was full dark before one of the older reciters, sent up at last by the others waiting below, went to him and asked whether he would come in to the fire.

"I have buried a wife in every century," said Ailean Mòr, "and a son before this one; and I shall bury them all. That was the bargain. I did not know it was the bargain when I made it."

He said nothing further that the Line has kept, and after a while he rose of his own accord and came down to the fire the reciter had asked him to, and sat among the households of the round until the grey of the next morning, saying little, listening more than once to Diorbhail say back a stretch of the Line at another's asking, and once, when she came to Somhairle's own name set near its middle, closing his eyes a moment the way a man closes his eyes against a light too bright to look at straight, though the fire that night gave no more light than any other fire.

## VI. Of the Keeping

He went back down to the kingdom within the week, and the valleys of Na Glinn Àrda closed over the going the way water closes over a stone dropped into it, quickly on the surface and slower underneath, where the households went on for years after speaking of the old man's dying at odd hours, over a distaff or a half-turned peat, the way a household speaks of a thing it has not finished carrying yet. Beathan's son took up, without any household troubling to make it a formal thing, the watch at the slab as his own to keep entire, the way his father had kept it before Somhairle's giving had ever divided the watching from the reciting between two hands; and no one asked him whether he minded that the reciting had gone, these fifteen years past, to a household not his own, for by then it had long ceased to be a thing anyone in the valleys thought worth asking after.

Diorbhail kept the Line the way she had been given it, whole and by mouth, adding to its foot each year the names the fires brought her and setting nothing down on any leaf or hide that a fire or a flood might one day take from her, for that was the way it had always been kept and she had been given no reason, in all her years at Somhairle's own knee, to keep it any other way. She said it through, twice each Samhain as he had said it, to whichever of the watch-households cared to sit and hear the whole of it rather than only their own branch of it, and she took, from the households of Na Glinn Àrda and from Dùn ìseal both, no share of anything for the keeping, holding, as Somhairle had held before her and told her plainly enough in her twentieth year that she must go on holding, that a Line taken up for a share was a Line a household soon began to shape toward that share, and that the valleys had kept theirs unshaped this long only by keeping it, and its keepers, apart from any hall's giving.

By the year the reciters set at the close of that decade the households of Na Glinn Àrda had stopped, in their ordinary speech, calling her the girl who had learned it from Somhairle, and had begun instead to call her only the reciter, the way they had once called him only the keeper of the slab, a name worn down at last to the office and away from the person who had first worn it; and it is told that when a stranger came up the two hundred paces one Bealltainn some years after, asking whether the old man who kept Sloinneadh a' Chlachair might be found at the slab, Diorbhail answered him herself, in the same plain voice Somhairle had used for any fact worth handing over and no other, that the keeper he asked for had gone into the ground some years since, and that the Line he had kept was kept still, by her own mouth now, and by no hall's leave.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of the Stone at Ceann leathan

*GE 3,031 – 3,495*

*This is kept at Ceann leathan among the wrestlers themselves, passed hand to hand at the fires the night before the contests, and carried down to the ford by whichever of them walks there after.*

## I. Of the Southern Shores

In those years the south filled slowly, the way a shallow dish fills last from a jug poured too fast. Households came down to Ceann mhin within sight of Làrach an Dùin on its headland, and built their houses with their backs to it and their doors to the sea, and would not climb the path up to the broken walls even to gather the good stone lying loose there for the taking. An old woman of that shore was heard to say that a wall raised by hands other than one's own kept its own quarrel, and no one troubled to ask her whose quarrel she meant.

Further round the coast the south had its own old harbour, unnamed by Seann-Dhaoine who first laid its stones and unrenamed by the Dia-thìrich who took it up after them, so that it was known only as the southern Seann Skell, the old landing. Within a few generations of its resettling it was the busiest quay on that whole shore, boats going out with the tide and coming home heavy, and the hook-makers there shaped bone hooks faster than the fishing wore them out.

Achadh shean had stood empty since the long drought, its fields cracked and its old well silted to mud, and when households came back to it they did what the ones before had not: they sank a new well first, deep into the rock, before they broke a single furrow, and planted only after the water had held through a dry summer. The well did not fail them again in all the years of that age, and the households there told it as a lesson to their children long after the reason for the telling had gone out of most other memories: dig first, plant after.

On the eastern cliffs a scattering of houses grew up at Inis mhin, where the birds nested in their thousands on ledges no goat could reach, and the people there lived as much by egg and feather as by anything grown in the ground, and carried baskets of down and quill inland to trade for grain and salt. And on the high ground above the upper waters, where the rivers that fed half the south had their beginning, households settled at Muileann chaol around a fold built for cattle in bad weather, a low stone pen with a turf roof over one corner of it, nothing more. A cairn was raised there for each head of a household who died, on the slope above the fold, one stone laid at a time by whoever had known the dead, until by degrees the slope came to have as many small heaps of stone on it as the fold below had cattle in a good year.

East again, past the middens of an older ruin the settlers called Seann Dunn and never dug into, calling the ground around it empty though it plainly was not, Baile Mòr ruadh grew up in the shadow of nothing at all, a broad red-earthed rise with no history that its own people troubled to ask after. And inland from all of these, on the eastern hills, stood Làrach an Teampaill that no one built and no one claimed, which the Dia-thìrich of that country passed without stopping, taking no stone from it though its stone was as good as any other for a house wall, until a path had worn round it at a careful distance, as a stream wears round a rock it will not cross.

These were the years, too, in which the island lost the last of the king's first sons. Fearchar Bacach, who had held Dùn ìseal for the king long before and had gone lame in Cogaidhean nan Gleann so long before that no one living remembered him whole, died in his own bed in the year three thousand one hundred and forty of the grove, having carried his lameness near three thousand years and lived three thousand one hundred and thirty years in all. His house mourned him quietly, the way a fire is kept without anyone remarking that it is being kept.

His brother Dòmhnall Clachach, who had been sent north out of that same hill the year Fearchar took it, and had grown old in the north country among people who called him only the stone-cutter's son and did not trouble themselves with what he had once been, died there in the year three thousand three hundred and ten, at three thousand three hundred and eight years of age, the elder of the two brothers by eight years at birth and by a hundred and seventy-eight at death. Word of it came south slowly, as word from the north always did, and reached Dùn ìseal a full season after the burying, so that Fearchar's house heard of their kinsman's death only after they had already marked, without knowing it, the anniversary of it.

A boy of Inis mhin once climbed down past the ledges after eggs and did not come up again by dusk, and the whole small settlement went out along the cliff-path with torches half the night calling his name into the wind, until they found him wedged on a shelf below the highest nests, unhurt but too frightened to climb either way, and had to lower a rope woven that same hour out of whatever cord the households owned. After that the cliffs were never worked alone, by custom rather than any law laid down, two to a rope always, one above and one below, and the old woman who had led the search with the loudest voice that night was, for the rest of her life, asked her advice on every matter to do with the birds, whether or not it had anything to do with ropes.

At Làrach an Teampaill on the eastern hills a shepherd once let his flock wander too near the fallen stones while he slept in the sun, and woke to find every sheep standing stock still along the outer edge of the worn path, none of them grazing, none of them crying, simply standing, as though some line had been drawn there that even beasts without words for it knew better than to cross. He drove them home without letting them so much as put a hoof past the path's edge, and told it after as the day his sheep had more sense than he did, and few who heard it thought he was wrong to say so.

Between these two endings, in the south, a son was born to the king in the year three thousand two hundred and four, and named Ìomhar, and called Dearg for the colour that came into his hair as a boy, redder than his father's or any of his brothers'. He grew up about the southern shores and the eastern marches with no love of the hill and no patience for lists and lots, and was already, before he had lived his first century, known along that coast for asking, wherever he went, whether a man might not simply be given ground and left alone to hold it, without a share given him and taken back again by a father who never explained the giving.

## II. Of Alasdair, Son of Torradh

Among the households of the southern shore that came down to settle near Clachan nan Gaoth at Ceann leathan, there was a man named Torradh who had two daughters and, late in his life, one son, born in the year three thousand three hundred and eighty, whom he named Alasdair. The boy grew large from his first years, in the plain way some children do, not sickly and not clever with his hands at any trade his father tried to teach him, so that Torradh in the end gave up trying to make a potter or a net-mender of him and let him run with the cattle instead, where his size was no hindrance and his slowness with words no shame.

By the time he had seen twenty summers Alasdair stood a head above every man of that shore and most of the women too, and had the kind of strength that came without his seeking it, so that he broke more than one tool in his father's shed simply by using it as another man would, and had to be told, more than once, to set a thing down gently rather than merely set it down. He was not quick-tempered. If anything he was slow to anger past the point most men would have reached it, and slower still to use the strength he had against another person, having learned early, from the one time he had shoved a boy his own age in a boyhood quarrel and put him in the dirt six feet off, that his own arm did not know its own weight the way other men's did.

It was Clachan nan Gaoth that first gave him somewhere to put it. The eight stones stood in their ring on the point above the harbour, weathered and grey, said by the old people to mark Na h-Ochd Gaothan and set there before anyone now living could say by whom, and below the ring, on the flattest ground of the headland, was held every year a contest of falls and grips and the lifting of stones that drew men down from half the southern coast to try each other, and drew everyone else to watch them try. Alasdair went to it first as a boy at his father's heel, carrying water for the older men between falls, and went to it next as a competitor before he had grown his full height, and put three grown men in the dirt in his first year at it, to his own evident surprise and everyone else's.

His mother, who had thought her one son would follow his father into the boats like her own brothers, gave up any such hope the year he came home from the shore with a net he had meant to mend torn clean through where his own hands had pulled the cord too hard, and told him, not unkindly, that the sea would have no use for arms like his and he had best find somewhere that would. It was his father, in the end, who walked him up to Clachan nan Gaoth one autumn and stood him at the edge of the ring to watch the contests through from first light to last, more to give the boy somewhere to be than from any thought of what would come of it.

He lost some years too. He was thrown twice himself, once by a smaller man from the southern Seann Skell who knew a trick of the hip that Alasdair had never troubled to learn, and once by his own overreaching, catching his foot on a stone half-buried in the turf and going down under his own weight before his opponent had done more than raise his hands. But he won more often than he lost, and by the time he had seen his tenth gathering he was known the length of that coast simply as Alasdair Làidir, Alasdair the Strong, a name given him by other men rather than claimed by himself, which was, among wrestlers, accounted the only kind of name worth having.

## III. Of the Stone That Would Not Be Lifted

Every contests ended the same way, once the falls were done and the light had begun to go out of the day: with Clach a' Neirt. It lay at the point where the headland narrowed to a lip of bare rock over the sea, a black boulder half again as broad as a man was tall, smooth on every face as though the sea had shaped it, though the sea at that height had not touched it in the memory of anyone's grandfather. Every year, at the close of the contests, whoever had won the falls that day was given the first try at it, and after him whoever else cared to, and every year, for as long as the telling went, it did not move.

Men had strained at it until the veins stood in their necks. One, in the years before Alasdair was born, had put his back into it so hard that something in his back gave way before the stone did, and he never walked upright again after, and the stone was left alone for two whole gatherings out of respect for him before anyone tried it again. Torradh himself had put a shoulder to it once, as a young man, and told his son afterward that it had felt, for the length of one long breath, as though he had set his shoulder against the headland rather than against any stone lying on it.

In the year three thousand four hundred and three, Alasdair Làidir won the falls at three-and-twenty, the youngest man in memory to take every bout of the contests from first light to last, and by custom the first try at the stone was given him. He set his hands to it, braced his feet in the turf worn bare by every year's failed lifting before his, and heaved until the sky went dark at the edges of his sight and his own breath roared louder in his ears than the sea below him. The stone did not stir. He stepped back at last, his hands scraped raw, and said, to no one and to everyone, that he did not think any man born of a woman would ever lift it, and sat down hard on the turf to get his wind back.

It was then that a stranger came forward out of the crowd along the edge of the ring.

He was a big man, though not so big as Alasdair, grey through the hair and the short beard he wore, dressed as plainly as any herdsman of that coast and carrying nothing that marked him as anyone in particular, a stick in one hand that he set down in the grass before he came to the stone. No one on that headland knew his face, though a good half of every crowd at Ceann leathan was strangers from somewhere else on the coast, so his being unknown troubled no one at first. He looked at the stone a while, the way a man looks at a thing he means to lift rather than a thing he merely means to try, and then he set his hands to it much as Alasdair had, low and wide, and lifted it.

He did not strain as Alasdair had strained. The stone came up off the turf as though it had been waiting only to be asked properly, and he held it a moment at the height of his knees, black and dripping the loose soil of centuries from its underside, before he set it down again, not with the crash and grunt every failed heave before it had ended in, but gently, the way a man sets down a sleeping child he does not wish to wake, so that it settled into the print it had worn in the turf without so much as a thud.

The whole headland had gone silent. Even the sea below seemed, to more than one who told it after, to have gone quiet for that one breath.

Alasdair, still sitting where he had dropped to get his wind, found his own voice before anyone else's. "Who are you?" he said, or something near it, for by his own account afterward the words came out of him before he had decided to speak them at all.

The stranger looked at him, and there was nothing unkind in the look, nor anything proud in it either, only the plain regard one man gives another after a day's work shared rather than a contest won and lost. "A traveller," he said. "No more than that."

"You lifted it," Alasdair said, getting to his feet, though he came up more slowly than he had ever come up from anything in his life. "No one lifts it."

"It only wanted lifting properly," the stranger said, and there was, in that, the ghost of something that might have been dry humour in another man, though his face gave little enough away to be sure of it. "You had the strength for it yourself. You set your hands too high."

"Will you give your name to the reciters?" someone called from the crowd, for by custom whoever lifted the stone had his name taken down and carried to every gathering after, to be spoken before the falls began each year until another man matched him.

The stranger picked up his stick from the grass. "I have no name that would mean anything carried," he said, "and I would take it kindly if none of you troubled to carry one for me." And with that he turned and walked off the headland the way he had come, unhurried, and was lost among the fires and the crowd before anyone thought to follow him, though half a dozen young men swore afterward that they had tried.

Alasdair stood by the stone a long while after the stranger had gone, and put his own hand flat on the print it had left in the turf, which was, he said later, warm, though the day had been no warmer than any other autumn day on that coast and the stone itself, when he touched it, was cold as any stone taken from the sea.

## IV. Of the Years That Followed

The tale went along that coast quickly enough that first winter, told at every fire from Ceann leathan to Achadh shean and back, and for a season or two it was told much as it had happened, a grey stranger, a stone lifted and set down gently, a name refused. But tales worn between enough fires wear smooth the way Clach a' Neirt itself was smooth, and within a few years some tellers had made the stranger taller, some had him lift the stone one-handed, and one teller at the southern Seann Skell, drunk on someone else's beer, swore the stranger's hands had glowed like coals in a hearth while he held it, which no one who had stood on the headland that day would allow, least of all Alasdair, who took to correcting that particular embellishment wherever he heard it, more sharply each year he heard it repeated.

He did not lift the stone himself again after that year, though he tried twice more before he gave it up, telling his own sons, when he had them, that a man who has once seen a thing done properly does not care to go on failing at it in front of witnesses. He married a woman of Achadh shean, Mòr, whose people kept the new well, and had three children by her who lived and two who did not, and went on winning the falls at Ceann leathan on and off for another five-and-twenty years, until a younger man's hip-trick put him in the dirt for good and he took, after that, to carrying water at the edge of the ring the way he had once carried it for the men before him, an old joke he made of it himself before anyone else could.

His eldest son, born the summer after the stranger's visit and named Torradh for his grandfather, grew up hearing the tale so often at his own hearth that he could recite it in his father's voice before he had seen ten summers, and did once, to a fire full of his father's own friends, word for word down to the setting-down of the cup, until Alasdair laughed so hard at hearing himself mimicked that he could not finish his own supper, and told the boy afterward that he had got the throat-clearing wrong but the rest near enough right to trouble him. That son took no interest in the wrestling himself, having his mother's build rather than his father's, and went instead to keep bees on the ground above Achadh shean, but he told his father's tale to his own children in turn all the same, throat-clearing and all, long after the man who cleared it that way was in the ground.

He never stopped telling of the stranger, though. Younger men at the fires learned to recognize the particular way he set down his cup and cleared his throat before he began it, and some of them, as the years passed, took to finding some other fire to sit at when they saw him settling into the telling, having heard it enough times that they could have told it themselves, word for word, without being there at all.

## V. Of the Ford

In the year three thousand four hundred and fifty, old now and slow in the hip himself, Alasdair Làidir walked north from Ceann leathan to Cruinneachadh an Àtha for what he told his wife would likely be the last time his legs allowed him the road. The ford by then drew households from every coast of the island, its ground long since parted by custom into three, the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, and the flint people on the rise beyond the river, more crowded each year than the year before, so that a man could stand at its edge of an evening and hear a dozen different accents of the same tongue called across the water at once.

The ground he walked to reach it had changed since he had last made the journey as a younger man, houses standing now where he remembered only open pasture, and twice he lost his own bearings on a road he had walked a dozen times before, until a girl minding geese by the wayside set him right again, unable herself to say how long the new houses had stood there, having been born among them and knowing no other way of it.

He found a fire of strangers that first night, southern men mostly, a few of them young enough to have been born after the year of the stone, and when the talk turned, as talk at a fire will, to feats of strength and stones no one could lift, he told it as he always told it: the ring at Ceann leathan, his own failed heave, the grey stranger stepping out of the crowd, the stone set down gentle as a sleeping child, the name refused.

Most of the young men at that fire heard him out politely and said nothing after, in the particular silence people keep for an old man's tale they do not believe and do not care to argue with. One of them, bolder or drunker than the rest, asked him outright whether he was certain it was not merely a strong man he had seen, dressed plain and travelling light, and not any stranger worth remarking twice.

But an older woman at the same fire, grey herself and further travelled than any of the young men there, said she had heard the very same tale told at a fire near the southern Seann Skell thirty years before, near enough word for word as Alasdair told it now, from a different mouth entirely, a woman who swore she had stood on that same headland the very year it happened and seen the stone set down with her own eyes. She said this without taking a side in the matter one way or the other, only setting the fact down beside the doubt, the way a stone is set down that a walker has turned over once and found something curious under after all.

Alasdair said nothing further to the young man who had doubted him, only reached for a stick and settled the fire, the way a man does who has told a thing often enough to know that the telling itself is worth more to him, by then, than whoever happens to believe it. He sat a while longer at that fire, an old man among strangers at the edge of a river crowded with more people than he had ever seen in one place outside the ring at Ceann leathan, and watched the flames a long time before he went to his bed that night, thinking, he told his wife afterward, of nothing in particular, only of a stone set down gently on a headland forty-seven years gone, and of hands that had known, better than his own ever had, exactly how much weight they carried.

# Part Six: Catrìona Mhòr and the Ford

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Green Axes and the Moor

*GE 3,496 – 3,999*


> *Tuagh uaine, air uaigh; cha do bhuail i riamh, is cha bhuail i tuilleadh.*
> A green axe, on a grave; it never struck, and it will strike no more.
> — said of the axes, wherever one is laid

## I. Of the Axes That Were Never Swung

In those years there came out of the north-west a fashion the households of every other coast were slow to understand and quick to want: axes of a green stone, ground and polished until they held a shine no flint or common rock could hold, cut at a single quarry above Àth àrsaidh and carried from there in packs on men's backs, in baskets on ponies, in the bottoms of boats going the long way round by sea when the land road was closed with snow. They were beautiful, and they were nearly useless. A green axe would take an edge finer than any grey one, and lose it faster, chipping at the first knot in a green log, and every household that owned one soon learned to keep it from the woodpile and give it, instead, to the dead: laid whole across the chest in a grave, or set under the corner-stone of a new house where no floor would ever wear it, a thing too fine to spend on work and too dear to leave undone something with.

Ìomhar Dearg was two hundred and ninety-two years old the autumn he first held one, at a wake in the north where an old man of the household was given his green axe to carry into the ground with him, and Ìomhar, who had already buried more kin of his own than he cared to count on days when the wind sat wrong, turned the thing over in his two hands before it went under the turf and found himself, not for the first time in his life, wanting a use for a thing everyone else was content to spend on the dead. He was the king's own son, one of the youngest of them then living, and he had grown, in nearly three centuries of watching households rise and fall and rise again about him, into a man who liked a thing to earn its keep before it earned its grave. He asked the old man's son, plainly, whether he might have one cut for himself, to carry and use every day until it broke, since none of his own kin were close enough to burying to need it spent that way.

The son said he might ask at the quarry itself, and so Ìomhar did, walking the length of the north-west coast that same winter to stand at Àth àrsaidh among the chips lying knee-deep about the cutters' huts, green dust on every threshold and every child's bare foot for a mile round. The cutters heard him out, and one of them, an old woman who had worked the stone longer than anyone else living there, told him plainly that no axe of that green stone had ever been cut to be swung, only to be shown, and that a man who wanted an axe to fell a tree with had best go to any flint-knapper on any common coast and leave the green stone to the graves it was already promised to. Ìomhar did not press her further. He had asked, and been answered, and he was old enough in the ways of the island's small customs to know that a custom held by an entire quarry's worth of households was not one man's argument to win in an afternoon.

He took her advice all the same, and had a knapper of the ordinary grey stone shape him an axe before that same winter was out, plain-hafted and quick to dull, which he used and had reground and used again for the better part of forty years until the head cracked at last on a root he had misjudged, and he buried that one himself, when it broke, in the same ground he had first turned it, judging that a tool which had earned its whole life in use had earned, too, the same rest the green stone was given for having earned none of it at all.

## II. Of the Quarry Forsaken and the Moor That Came Down

The quarry at Àth àrsaidh did not last out his own lifetime's watching of it. Within fifty years of that winter the households who worked it, and traded in nothing else besides, found the seam of the true green stone running thinner year on year under their own cuts, whatever they tried of following it deeper or sideways along the hill, until the day came, in the year three thousand five hundred and forty-seven, that the last cutter of the old skill died without having taken an apprentice, his own sons having gone to herding rather than stone in a decade when the stone itself had stopped paying for the teaching of it. The chips lay knee-deep still, and would lie so for longer than any teller then living could foresee, but no new axe came out from among them after that year, and what had been made before it went on being buried, one grave and one corner-stone at a time, until the graves of the whole north-west coast held between them more of the green stone than the quarry itself had ever held ground still uncut.

It was in those same decades, the tellers of the north say, that the winters themselves began to lengthen, though no single year could be named as the one where it started. The oak that had stood since before any household's grandfather began, about Doire ghlas and the low ground north of it, to fall back from ground it had held without contest for longer than the reckoning went, and heather and birch and the soft grey moss of the bogs came up in its place, spreading south a little further with every generation that did not trouble to burn it back. The groves that gave the whole north its many names built on the word doire, the oak-grove, shrank to the sheltered valleys where the wind could not reach them, and stand there yet, and the households of that coast told it to their own children simply as the time the winters began to run longer than a man's memory could hold two of exactly the same length together.

Ìomhar passed through that country more than once in the years the moor was taking it, an old man to look at by then though his own years ran further than any household he passed could reckon, and remarked once, to a woman of Doire ghlas who gave him a night's shelter and asked nothing of his name in return, that a country changes its face the way a man does, slowly enough that no one living in it sees the day it happens, and only a stranger returning after a long absence can say plainly that the thing before him is not the thing he left. The woman answered that she had been born among the heather herself and had never seen an oak-grove larger than the one behind her own house, and did not know, until he told her, that the ground under her own byre had once stood thick with trees a man could not see through. Ìomhar said nothing further on it. He had learned, of the moor as of the green axes, that a change too slow for one life to feel is not a grief to the life living in the middle of it, whatever it might be to a life old enough to remember the ground before.

## III. Of the Stepping-Stones and the Drowning at the Ford

The households along Abhainn fhionn had for as long as anyone's telling went crossed the river where they could, at a shallow bend below the willow flats, wading it in low water and going the long way round by the upper shallows when the water ran high, and it was in this same stretch of years that a family of that stretch, tired of wet feet and lost baskets, began laying flat stones across the shallowest crossing, one at a time as each summer's low water allowed the laying, until within two generations a man could cross the whole width of the river dry-shod, stone to stone, in every season but true flood. It was the first crossing of any river on the island made by hand rather than found by wading, and households from three days' walk in either direction came to see it before they believed the telling of it, and went home to lay stones of their own wherever their own rivers ran shallow enough to try.

No such stones were ever laid at the fords of Abhainn chaol, further south, where the river ran narrower and the ground on either bank rose steep enough that no household troubled to build what the current would only carry off again at the first spring spate. It was at those same fords, in the year three thousand six hundred and eighty, that a party of twelve crossing with salt on their backs, bound for the upland households that paid well and asked no questions of a trader's route, were taken by a spate that came down without the warning a slower rise would have given them, rain having fallen three days running in hills the fords themselves could not see. Ìomhar was two days' walk south of the fords when word reached him, carried by a boy on a pony who had been sent, he said, to fetch anyone of standing who might know what should be done with twelve bodies and no household near enough to claim more than two or three of them as its own dead.

He came as fast as the road allowed, and it was not fast enough. By the time he stood on the bank of Abhainn chaol the water had dropped back to its ordinary height, running clear and shallow over stones that gave no sign at all of what they had carried through them three days before, and the households of both banks had already done what could be done: five bodies found and given to their own kin, four more found further downstream and given, since no one closer could be found to claim them, to the nearest household willing to dig, and three never found at all, the river having taken them wherever a river takes what it does not choose to give back.

He walked the bank a while before he would let himself be led to the graves, looking for some sign of the crossing itself, the salt-baskets, a length of rope, a shoe, and found nothing the river had troubled to give back beyond a single pack-strap caught on a root a half-mile down, empty, the buckle still fastened as though the shoulder it had crossed had simply stepped out from under it. A woman of the upland households, come down to claim one of the four unclaimed dead as near enough kin to bury properly, told him that the twelve had crossed at that ford every season of her own life and her mother's before her, and that she did not think any of them had so much as looked upstream at the sky before they went in, the rain of those three days having fallen on hills none of them could see from the water's edge. Ìomhar asked her whether the households of that ford had ever thought to watch the upper hills for exactly such a rain. She said they had not, until that year, and that they did now. Ìomhar stood at the water's edge a long while, an old man of the king's own blood who had come two days too late to be any use to the living or the dead, and said, to the household elder who had walked down with him, that he had crossed rivers enough in his own centuries to know that a ford is a debt every household pays sooner or later, and that the only mercy in it was that this one had been paid all at once rather than one drowned traveller at a time across a hundred years. The elder answered only that no household on either bank had crossed those fords in the wet season since, and none has crossed them so in any year told of after.

## IV. Of the Twenty-Two Marks, and the Ground That Would Not Sit Still

Further round the coast, at Ceann chiar, the households rebuilding after A' Ghaoth Dhubh that had scattered their roofs a generation before set, in the year three thousand seven hundred and twenty-six, a stone in the midst of their new-laid houses and cut on it a mark for every house the wind had taken: two-and-twenty marks, plain strokes in a plain row, no names beside them, for the households that raised the stone held that the dead of one wind were better counted together than singled out one from another, a wind having taken no more notice of who it took than a wave takes of which shell it turns. Ìomhar saw the stone some years after it was cut, on a journey east that had no other purpose than his own restlessness, and stood before it counting the marks himself, twice, as though a third count might make the number smaller than the first two had left it, which it did not.

It was a restless country in those years in more ways than the wind alone. A summer came, in that same stretch of seasons, when the rivers of the eastern plain ran so low that the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drove their cattle to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to drink rather than lose them to a stream too thin to serve a herd, and the surplus each household had kept against exactly such a year held long enough that not one death was counted for the thirst of it, which the households themselves accounted, once the rains came back, less a mercy of the weather than a debt the sharing custom had quietly paid on their behalf. The sea, too, came in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, a second wave lesser than the first the coast still told of, and found the new houses standing higher on the slope than the old ones had stood, so that this time the water took only empty byres and left every hearth it reached for standing dry above it. And further west the old crack in the ground that no household there had ever fully trusted moved again in its sleep, as the reciters of that coast liked to say of it, shifting the spring back uphill and breaking the line of white stones that marked the danger in two places, so that the households had to walk out with fresh stone and lay the line again exactly as their grandmothers had laid it the first time, no wiser for the moving than their grandmothers had been, only more patient.

At Cnoc bheag, on the bank of Abhainn ìseal, households settled that same generation a short walk from the standing stone the place had already borne a name for, and set their own houses, without any law telling them to, so that no door among them faced the stone directly, a custom no one could afterward say who had begun but that every household coming after kept without question, the way a custom of that kind is kept once the first house has set the pattern for every house built after it. And on the lower reaches of the same river, at Inis bhàn, the households that lived by the seal-rocks off the river mouth settled their own quarrel over them the plain way island custom settled most such things: one rock to a household, taken in its turn, and a rock taken out of turn was, by every teller's account of that stretch of coast, the commonest cause of hard words between neighbours who agreed, on every other matter, rather better than most. Ìomhar was shown the turn kept for it once, a tally of notched sticks held by whichever household's turn had last passed, and asked the man who showed it to him what was done when two households both swore, in good faith, that the turn stood with them. The man said that the elders of both households sat down together at the tally and counted the notches aloud from the first stick to the last, and that this had settled every such quarrel so far without needing anyone to raise a voice past the counting, which he offered, Ìomhar thought, with more quiet pride than the small matter seemed at first to deserve, until he considered how many quarrels on other coasts never came to a tally at all.

## V. Of Niall, Born to Raonaid

Ìomhar had a half-sister he loved better than any other of his father's many children, Raonaid nic Ailein, a daughter of the king born to a wife of the eastern shore a hundred years before Ìomhar himself, and married, long before this telling reaches her, to a man of the king's blood by the line of Fearchar Bacach, a quiet herder of the river-lands below Dùn ìseal whom the eastern shore knew better by his flocks than by his name. It was Raonaid's house, more than any house of his own, that Ìomhar came back to between his wanderings, and her hearth he sat longest at, for she had the gift, rare among the king's children, of asking a man where he had been without asking him why.

Her son Niall was born in the year three thousand seven hundred and three, in that house on the eastern shore, with the midwife's fire built up high against an autumn that had come in colder than the last three running, and Ìomhar, by then close on five hundred years old, held the boy the first evening of his life and told his sister afterward that he found in him more of her own quickness in the eyes than of anything he recognised from the long line on either side. Niall grew laughing from his first year onward, the kind of child who found the small mishaps of a household, a dropped pail, a goat loose in the wrong field, a neighbour's dog barking at nothing, funnier than most children found anything at all, and it was said of him even before he had seen ten summers that a fire with Niall at it was a fire that stayed lively past the hour it would otherwise have gone quiet. He was the king's grandson by his mother and of the king's blood again by his father, and he learned to say both lines before he could say much else; the household laughed to hear a child of five tell a stranger at the door that he was owed twice.

Ìomhar watched the boy grow with the particular attention of a man who had already watched a great many children grow and outlive him, and told Raonaid once, on an evening when Niall had run the length of the yard three times over some joke of his own making that no one else quite followed, that he did not know yet how long the boy's years would run, and that he had decided, for his own part, not to trouble himself asking it aloud where the boy might hear the asking and grow strange about it before he had any cause to. He had a son of his own by then, Dùghall, born to him in the year three thousand nine hundred by a wife of the river-lands whom the tellings do not name, a grave, red-haired child with none of his cousin's laughter in him; and it was Niall, not his own boy, that the eastern shore came to think of as Ìomhar's shadow on the road.

## VI. Of the Share Ìomhar Asked For

It was in the year three thousand nine hundred and sixty, Niall by then a young man of two hundred and fifty-seven years who looked a youth of twenty, and already known the length of the eastern shore for the same laugh he had carried since the yard, that Ìomhar went up to the king himself and asked, plainly, for a share of his own: not the wandering right his blood had always given him to sit at any hearth on the island and eat from any household's table, which he had used all his long life and never once needed to ask twice for, but ground with a hill on it, held in his own name and passed, when his own years ran out, to whichever of his children the custom favoured. He had never asked such a thing before, in nearly eight hundred years of watching households given their ground and their grazing and their rights of way while he himself held nothing but the wandering right that came to him by blood alone, and he told the king, standing before him on the hill with his sister's son Niall a little apart, laughing quietly with one of the king's own grandsons over some jest of the road, that a man who had buried strangers at fords he came too late to and counted marks on stones cut for other households' dead had come, in his own slow way, to want a piece of ground that answered to his own name before it answered to anyone else's.

The king heard him out the way he heard out most such askings, without haste and without the warmth some visitors expected of him and did not always get, and gave him, before the day was out, the river-grazing on the eastern marches, ground between the last settled households and the open country beyond them, thin soil but good grass along the water, and told him only that a share given was a share that could be taken back, as every share on the island had always been and would go on being, and that Ìomhar, of all the king's own blood, understood that condition better than most men his ground might have gone to instead. Ìomhar said he understood it, and thanked him, and took his household, with his sister's laughing son riding along for the pleasure of the road, and went east to see the ground for himself before the season turned.

He stood on the river-grazing at the end of that same day, the light going long and gold across the water the way it goes in the last hour before a clear autumn evening turns cold, and looked east along the river toward ground he had not yet walked and households he had not yet met, thin grass under his own two feet for the first time in nearly eight centuries of walking on ground that answered, always, to some other name than his. He did not know, standing there, what would come up that river out of the east in the years his own line had still to run, only that the ground he stood on faced that way and no other, and that he had asked for it himself, wanting a thing at last that would need his own name spoken over it before anyone else's blood could rightly claim it back.

The green axe he had turned over at a wake near five centuries before came back to him that evening, too fine to spend on any wood it might have cut and given, instead, to the ground. His own grey axe was long since buried too by then, worn to a stub and cracked at the haft, spent to the last year it had in it before he let it go. Standing on grass no one else yet held, he judged a share of ground a different order of thing from either: too plain to fear the wearing, too lasting to wear away in one man's using of it, a thing that would go on answering to a name, his own or his son's or a name not yet given, for as long as any household troubled to keep the custom that had granted it. That, he thought, was longer than any axe of any stone, green or grey, had ever been asked to last.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of Dùn dhearg

*GE 4,000 – 4,324*

*This is kept at Dùn dhearg's own hearths, east of the vein, as a plain account of how the double bank came to stand, and how, once only, its people carried salt home from a fire that was not their own.*

## I. Of the Fields East of the Vein

In those centuries the eastern country filled the way water fills a shallow pan set out in rain, from a hundred small runnings that no one troubled to trace to their source. At Achadh mhòr, under Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, a household cleared and banked the widest field any of that country had yet cut from the rough, and set the bank on the bones of an older wall whose builders none of them could name and none thought to ask after; the field grew wheat enough, in a good year, to feed three households where before there had been land for none. Down at the lake shore An Cnoc Ruadh's own people drew their boats up at Baile ghlas in sheds of stone and turf built low against the wind, and it became, before the eldest of that first crew were dead, the harbour An Cnoc Ruadh fished from oftener than its own strand. In the north, at Achadh naomh, the settlers led water round a spring in channels of their own digging rather than over it, and fenced the spring before they had raised a single house, so that a stranger coming on the place for the first time might have thought the water, and not the people, was what had been settled there.

Further east and north the coast was harder and the land behind it thinner, and the households that took it took to the sea instead. At Caol gharbh, on the rough strait, they went out in boats of skin stretched over bent wood, and buried their paddles beside their dead as other households buried a spindle or a hoe, so that a man might go into the ground with the one tool his hands had known best. Under the dark oaks of Doire chiar, a morning's walk inland, pigs ran loose in the wood all summer and were driven out to the fallen acorns each autumn by boys too young yet to be trusted with anything that could bite back, and the smoke of that place hung low and blue among the trunks from one year's end to the next. And where the Abhainn ìseal ran down past the black hill of the old trench toward the sea, a landing grew up at Caol shean that took in salt and fish and seal-skins from the coast and sent them on inland, into the keepers' country and beyond it, so that a thing caught in a net one morning off the northern skerries might lie, within the month, on a hearth three days' walk from any smell of salt water.

None of these households owed anything to the hill at Dùn ìseal, and few of them had ever seen the man who held it, though all of them had heard of him, the way a man far inland hears of the sea: as a fact rather than a sight. They were of Clann nan Dè, as every household on the island was, sprung of the same first fires as the king's own kin, and no less sure of it for having no drop of his blood in them. They kept the handful at Samhain as every hearth on Dia-thìr had come to keep it, low and dark and burned all at once by agreement rather than by any law, and they shared before the storm season as every coast did, mouth for mouth, without a written word behind either custom. What they did not do, east of the vein, was send anyone to be counted, and no one from Dùn ìseal came east to count them.

At Caol shean, in the years before the double bank went up, two households fell out over a stretch of the river landing that each claimed to have cleared first, and there being no lot to settle it and no keeper nearer than the slab in Na Glinn Àrda, three days' walk and more, the households of the landing sat down together and heard both sides out at one fire until the sky went grey, and gave the disputed ground at last to neither family outright but to the landing, to be used by whoever had a boat drawn up that day and no other claim on it. It held so ever after, and the two households that had quarrelled over it were, within two generations, so thoroughly mixed by marriage that no one at Caol shean could any longer have said where one family ended and the other began, which some of the older tellers held had been the landing's own quiet way of finishing what the quarrel had begun.

It was said among them, at fires from Caol shean to Doire chiar, that the coast beyond the vein had had rulers enough of its own, and that a ruler who did not grow old was no bargain merely for being strong. Travellers brought word west to east the way water finds its own low ground: of a hill held near four hundred years by one grey man who had outlived three heirs of his own house; of a hill-holder in the middle country who had wanted, before she died, some deed to set beside the holding, some mark or stone that said the land was hers past her own lifetime, and had been told, gently and finally, that the holding was the deed and there was no other; of grandmothers who governed their own great-grandmothers' grandmothers, looking, the whole while, no older than a woman of thirty summers. None of it was told as complaint exactly, for none of those tales touched Dùn dhearg's own people, who had never been ruled by any of them. It was told, rather, as a reason already half made before the reasoning began: that a bank raised by one's own hands, and held by whoever's hands raised it, answered to no list and needed none.

So it was that in the year four thousand two hundred and seventy-four of the Grove, the households east of the vein put up, without asking leave of anyone, a fort with a double bank at Dùn dhearg, on rising ground above the river, and dug its ditch deep enough that a man standing in it could not see over the rim, and set the second bank a spear's throw beyond the first so that an enemy who won the outer ditch had another to take before he had won anything at all. Rìghrean na Cloiche' own list, recited at the ford, gave the fort no holder's name, for it had none that any list would keep; it said only, of that whole country, that Dùn dhearg did not come to the gatherings.

## II. Of Ailis

Ailis was born at Dùn dhearg in the year four thousand two hundred and forty, thirty-four years before the double bank went up, into a household that had already made its choice about the hill at Dùn ìseal without troubling to say so aloud. Her father cut turf for the first bank with his own hands when she was still too small to carry water to the diggers, and she grew up knowing the ditch before she knew the sea, playing along its lip with the other children of that country until an elder cuffed them back from the edge for the dozenth time and told them, not unkindly, that a fort dug to keep other men out was no fit place to break a child's neck in.

She had heard the old tales as every child east of the vein heard them, at hearths where the telling passed from a grandmother's mouth to a granddaughter's before either of them had thought to ask who had told it first: of a king who did not grow old, west beyond the vein, who had buried a wife in every hundred years of his life and never once forgotten her name; of a gathering held once, so long past that it was already a thing out of an old song rather than a thing anyone living had seen, where the king's whole kin had stood in rings about him at a river ford and the reciters had gone from dusk to sunrise naming them. Nobody at Dùn dhearg could say how many years had gone over that gathering by the time Ailis was grown, only that it was a great many, and that no one now living, east of the vein or west of it, had stood at that ford as anything but a teller's word.

Once, when she was no more than ten, a trader out of the west came through Caol shean's landing with cloth to sell that no one east of the vein had woven, and sat by the household fire that night answering the children's questions until the older folk grew tired of listening and went to their beds. He had stood, he told them, at the very gate of the hill at Dùn ìseal, and had seen with his own eyes a man come in at it who looked no older than the trader's own son, and been told by everyone about the gate that this was the same man who had held that hill since before any wall now standing on it was built. Ailis asked him, before her mother could hush her, whether it did not frighten the man's own children to grow old beside a father who did not, and the trader said he supposed it must, though he had never troubled to ask any of them outright, not wanting, as he put it, to spoil a fair trade in cloth by putting a bad question to it. She turned the thought over for years after, that a household might be built and outlived by its own maker the way a house of turf is built by hands that will crumble before the turf does.

She married a net-mender of Caol shean when she was two-and-twenty, and went to live a season on the river landing before she and her husband came back inland to Dùn dhearg, where the fort's ditch by then had a bank on either side of it and houses growing up thick along the inner slope. Three of her children lived, and one did not; that one she buried, as her own mother had taught her, with a small cup of salt at its feet, for the road, though no one in that country could have said any longer where the custom had first been learned or from whom.

Her husband was a quiet man, better with a net than with words, who took some years to grow used to a wife more curious about a river she had never seen than about the one that ran past their own door, and who told her once, not unkindly, that a woman might spend a whole life wanting a thing and be none the worse for never getting it. She answered that she had noticed as much of other people's wanting, and saw no reason it should hold true of her own.

In her middle years she was known along that stretch of the eastern coast less for any one deed than for a kind of restlessness that her neighbours took, by turns, for wisdom and for a nuisance: she asked, of every trader who came through Caol shean's landing, what the ford was like now, and how far it lay, and whether the king still sat among his own kin at it as the old tellings said, and she went on asking whether anyone troubled to answer her or not.

## III. Of the Double Bank

The digging of the double bank was the largest work Dùn dhearg's people had ever done together, and it settled, without any law behind it, the shape their custom would take from then on. Every household that meant to live inside the banks sent hands to the digging in proportion to the mouths it meant to feed there, an old man of that country keeping the count on a knotted cord much as the salt-folk kept their counts at the ford, though no one at Dùn dhearg had ever seen a salt-folk's cord to copy it from. When the ditch was done and the inner bank raised and turfed, the ground within it was shared out the same way, by households and not by favour, and a household that had sent three grown hands to the digging took no more ground than one that had sent three, whatever its standing had been before the digging began.

Not every household came to the digging willingly. One family on the northern edge of that country, holding good grazing already and wanting no ditch across the middle of it, sent word that they would keep to their own ground and let the rest dig as they pleased. No one from Dùn dhearg rode out to make them, there being no one with the standing to ride out on any such errand; instead the households already committed to the digging simply left that family's ground outside the second bank when the time came to draw it, so that within a generation that family found itself living, by its own choice and no one else's law, outside the shelter its neighbours had raised, and quietly asked, at last, to be let in on the same terms as everyone else, hands sent late being reckoned, by the same rough justice, at somewhat less than hands sent early.

Ailis's own household took a strip along the eastern slope, above the spring that fed the fort's own well, and it was there her husband died at last, an old man by any island's reckoning though not by the reckoning of the hill west of the vein, and was carried out and laid on the slope above the houses among the others of that place, with his own net-needle set in the ground at his feet.

The fort held its handful at Samhain as every hearth in that country did, each household burning its own measure in the dark of the year, and Ailis, growing old herself now, was one of the elders who walked the ring of houses on that night to see that no fire was lit before its neighbour's, the way the custom asked, though no one east of the vein could have named the keeper who had first drawn that lot at the slab, so far off and so long ago had that custom been made. It struck her once, walking that ring with a torch in the cold, that Dùn dhearg kept every custom the hill folk kept and owed the hill nothing at all for keeping them, and she said as much to the elder walking beside her, who only grunted that a custom belonged to whoever kept it and not to whoever had thought of it first, and went on with the walking.

## IV. Of the Seal-Skins and the Ford

In her eighty-first year, in the year four thousand three hundred and twenty-one, Ailis told her eldest son that she meant to see the ford before she died, and would go herself if no one else would carry her.

She had said it before, at intervals, for the better part of sixty years, and her son had learned to let it pass him like weather. This time she did not let it pass. She had put by, over three winters, a store of seal-skins taken off the rocks below Caol gharbh, more than her own household needed and more than any one trader passing through Caol shean's landing had offered a fair price for, and she said now that she would carry them west herself, to the ford, and trade them there for salt, since the salt-folk's pans lay nearer the ford than any coast of her own, and since, she said, she had asked after that river long enough that she meant to stand in it once before her legs gave out under her for good.

Six went with her in the end: her son, two of his own grown children, and three others of that country curious enough, or fond enough of the old woman, to make the walk. They went the road west from Dùn dhearg past Caol shean and Doire chiar, over ground none of them had ever crossed before, sleeping at other households' hearths some nights and in the open on others, until on the fifth day they came down out of hill country into a valley crowded with more people and more fires than any of them had seen gathered in one place in their lives.

The road surprised them before the ford did. Twice in the first two days they were taken in by households who had never heard of Dùn dhearg and had to be told, at some length, that a country lay east of the vein at all, and that it kept its own bank and its own hearths and owed nothing to any hill; and once, on the third night, they slept at a house whose grandfather remembered, or said he remembered, a telling of An Cruinneachadh Mòr held in the three-thousandth year of the Grove, though he could not himself have been born within a thousand years of it, and had it, he admitted freely, from his own grandmother, who had had it from hers. Ailis's son found it a strange thing, that a tale should be handed down mouth to mouth for so many lifetimes among people with no long-lived blood in them at all, and said so to his mother; she told him only that a good tale outlasted whoever had first the wit to tell it, which was, she said, no different east of the vein than west of it.

By the fourth day the road had thickened with other travellers going the same way, salt-carriers and wool-carriers and once a whole household driving cattle before it, and Ailis's small party fell in among them without any of the strangers troubling to ask where they had come from, so that by the time they came down into the valley of the ford they were only one more thread in a great deal of foot traffic, unremarked, which suited the old woman, she said afterward, better than being remarked upon would have.

The ford itself was nothing like the ford of the old tellings, or it was exactly like it and larger than any telling had prepared them for; Ailis, standing at the edge of that crowd with her bundle of skins on her back, could not afterward have said which. The salt people held the ground downstream and the hill people the ground upstream, as the tellings said, and beyond the river the flint people had their own crowded rise, and among them all, moving without any mark to set him apart from another herdsman, was a big grey-haired man that half the crowd would not look at directly and the other half seemed not to notice at all. Ailis looked at him a long while from where she stood and said nothing of it to her son, who had not yet seen him and would not, for the whole of that gathering, quite believe which man among the crowd he had been.

They were taken, in the end, to a woman not much past two hundred years of age, young by the reckoning of that blood though old by any other, who was named to them at the fire as Catrìona, of the king's own line, though she did not yet hold the hill herself and would not for some years after. She heard Ailis out with more patience than the old woman had expected of anyone born to that blood, asking where Dùn dhearg lay and how the double bank had been raised and whether the fort answered to anyone at all, and Ailis told her, plainly, that it answered to no one, and had been raised for that reason among others.

It was there, at that same fire, that one of the king's own blood, a red-haired man more than a thousand years old who held river-grazing on the eastern marches, looked over the seal-skins Ailis had carried the length of the island on her own back and asked Catrìona, in a voice not troubling to be quiet, whether she meant to trouble over ground for people who would all be dead, every one of them, inside a single lifetime of his own.
