He did not say it unkindly so much as carelessly, the way a man remarks on weather he has stopped noticing, and called them, in that same breath, the short-lived, a name that went round the fires of that gathering for some years after among those of the blood, though never once, so far as the tellings east of the vein remember it, in Catrìona's own mouth.

Ailis's son, hearing it, opened his mouth to answer the red-haired man in kind, but his mother put a hand on his arm before he could, and it was she who spoke instead, telling the red-haired man, plainly and without heat, that she had walked five days to stand at that river and did not mean to spend any part of the little time she had left in it arguing with a man who would have five hundred years to be sorry in, should sorry ever occur to him. Some at the fire laughed at that. The red-haired man said nothing further to her, and turned his attention back to his own grazing and his own grievances, which, it was plain even to a stranger from the east, ran a good deal deeper than any quarrel over seal-skins.

Catrìona did not answer him directly. She looked at Ailis a moment longer, at the seal-skins and the old woman's hands and the six who had come with her, and said only that the far bank of the river had room enough on it for one more fire, and that Dùn dhearg's people might have ground there, this year and every year after, if they cared to come to it. No oath was asked of them in return, and none was offered.

## V. Of the Salt Carried Home

They traded the seal-skins for salt on the far bank through that same evening, more salt, by weight, than any household of Dùn dhearg had carried home in living memory, and slept that night on ground that was, for the first time, theirs by nothing but a woman's word and their own presence on it. Ailis walked down to the river before she slept, and stood in the shallows a while with her skirts held up out of the water, an old woman alone at the edge of a crowded ford in the dark, and told no one afterward what she had thought while she stood there, only that the water had been colder than she expected and that she had stood in it longer than she meant to all the same.

They went home the way they had come, six going out and six coming back, with salt enough on their backs to see three households through a hard winter and word enough to keep every hearth from Dùn dhearg to Caol shean talking through it. No oath had been asked of them at the ford and none had been given, and the elders of Dùn dhearg, hearing it told, agreed among themselves, without needing to say so twice, that this suited them exactly as it stood: ground held and no word owed for the holding of it, which was, when it came down to it, no more nor less than the double bank had been built to be.

Ailis lived three years more after that journey, long enough to tell it herself at her own hearth a good many times, adding, each time she told it, some small thing she had forgotten the time before: the weight of the seal-skins going west and the lightness of them coming back; the grey-haired man in the crowd whom half the gathering would not look at; the red-haired one's word for her own people, which she came, in the telling, to say without any bitterness in it at all, as if a name given in scorn by a stranger who would outlive her ten times over was no great matter to carry home, set beside a river stood in once and salt enough for the winter.

She died in her own house on the eastern slope of the double bank in the year four thousand three hundred and twenty-five, eighty-five years old, with her net-mender husband's needle already long in the ground above her and her own place made ready beside it. Her grandchildren, when they were old themselves, still told of the seal-skins and the ford and the woman of the king's blood who had given them ground without asking anything back for it, and some of them told, too, in a lower voice and less often, of the word the red-haired man had used, the short-lived, which stayed at Dùn dhearg's hearths long after the man himself and everyone who had heard him say it were gone into the ground the same way Ailis had gone: at their own pace, in their own time, owing nothing to anyone for the manner of it.

The double bank stood after her as it had stood before her, and the ground on the far side of the river stayed Dùn dhearg's, without oath, without law, and without any name of a holder for Rìghrean na Cloiche' own list to keep.

In the years after, when a trader passing through Caol shean's landing asked, as travellers will, whether the fort's people ever meant to send word to the hill and be reckoned among the king's own households at last, the answer given him, by more than one household and always in near enough the same words, was that Dùn dhearg had gone to the ford once, on its own feet and by an old woman's own wanting, and had come home again with salt and no master, and saw no cause to make the journey a second time on any other errand.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Two Lists and the Asking of the Nine

*GE 4,325 – 4,390*

*This is kept at Dùn ìseal's own hearth, by the reciters who took it from Eòin Beul-binn's own mouth before he died, as the telling of the last of Rìghrean na Cloiche.*

## I. Of the Last Fields and the Last Fords

In the years after Ailis of Dùn dhearg was laid on her own slope, the hills went on filling the way a cup fills that no one is watching: a household here, a ford crossed there, and no one able afterward to say which handful of years had done it. In the south-eastern hills, where wild cattle came down to drink at a stony crossing, a household settled by the ford and took the calves born on the near bank for its own, rearing them apart from the wild herd until, within three generations, the cattle of that ford were spoken of the length of the coast as the best in those hills; the ford came to be called for the cattle, Àth fhiadhaich, the ford of the wild kind. On the Abhainn fhionn, people out of An Cnoc Ruadh's own country found an old landing worn into the bank, stones set for a boat's keel by hands none living could name, and built their houses about it and called the place for what they had found, the ancient headland. In the damp north-west a household drained a hill with ditches dug by their own hands, and the ditches carry water still, though the diggers' own names are forgotten; and on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east, a household built its houses in two rows facing each other across a single trodden way, the first street any teller remembers on Dia-thìr, though none of them thought of it as a street, only as a convenient way to borrow fire from a neighbour without crossing open ground in the rain.

Further south a house was raised with its walls limed white from the burnt shell of the old middens along that coast, and the place took its name from the lime before the household that raised it had a name of its own; and on the far eastern shore, where the coast bent back on the sea and the geese came down in their season, a household settled the last ford of the age, the easternmost hearth then burning on the main island, and went out after the geese in boats no larger than a man could carry on his back.

None of this made a chapter in any list. Rìghrean na Cloiche' own roll, which named every household that came in to Dùn ìseal to be counted, gave no room to a ford where the cattle were good or a lime-white house on a southern plain; it named holders, and marriages, and deaths, and left the filling of the island to be told, if it was told at all, at the hearths that did the filling. It is only because those hearths went on telling it, generation on generation, long after the households had forgotten which of their own great-grandmothers had first driven a stake into that particular ground, that any of it is known now.

## II. Of Catrìona

Catrìona was born at Dùn ìseal in the year four thousand one hundred of the Grove, granddaughter's granddaughter of a granddaughter of the king, though by then no one at the hill troubled much to count the degrees; she was of the blood, and that was the whole of what anyone needed to know of her standing. She grew up on the hill in na Bliadhnachan Fada the list does not trouble to fill, when the king himself was oftener at it than any holder, and she was already an old woman by the reckoning of any hearth outside her own blood, and still young by the reckoning inside it, when the holding of Dùn ìseal came to her.

She had a memory that the hill-folk who came to be judged by her called, half in wonder and half in complaint, a curse to any man who hoped his grandmother's dealings had been forgotten. A household's line she could give back seven names without pausing to think, the marriages and the deaths and which strip of grazing had gone with which daughter, and she used the gift the way her grandfather's grandfather had used the water at the taking of the hill: not to threaten, only to be exact. A man came to her once complaining that his neighbour had moved a boundary stone in the night, and she told him, before he had finished the complaint, that the stone in question had already been moved twice before in his own grandfather's day, and each time by his own family, and asked him whether he wished the full account read out at the ford that summer or would rather let the stone lie where it now stood. He let it lie.

She took the hill formally in the year four thousand three hundred and forty-seven, in her two hundred and forty-seventh year, the twelfth to hold it of Rìghrean na Cloiche' line and, though none of them yet knew it, the last whose name would go into that roll at all. She did not think of herself as an ending; the tellings give her, in those early years, no thought beyond a woman with a great many households to keep straight in her head, and she set about doing it with the same flat patience she brought to everything else.

That same season, at An Cnoc Ruadh, a young man named Seumas took up the holding his own line had kept since the palisade first burned and burned again in Uilleam Faire's day; he was seven-and-twenty, the last name An Cnoc Ruadh's own spoken roll would carry, though he no more knew it than Catrìona knew hers. He and Catrìona had never met before that year. They would meet within it, across a fire at the ford, and neither of them, so far as anyone at either hill ever heard either of them say, thought anything of the meeting beyond the ordinary business of two neighbours who had never before had cause to sit down together.

## III. Of the Two Lists

It had never before been done, in all the years Cruinneachadh an Àtha had drawn the hill people and the salt people and the flint people together, that the whole roll of Rìghrean na Cloiche and the whole roll of An Cnoc Ruadh should be spoken out in the one place on the one night, first name to last, each list heard entire by ears that had heard the other list entire as well. Whether it was Catrìona's own wish, in her first summer of holding, to have her name set down properly beside the men and women who had held the hill before her, or whether it was only that the two rolls had grown long enough by then that the idea of hearing them side by side had occurred to more than one mind at once, the tellings do not agree, and no one troubled, at the time, to ask.

The reciter of Dùn ìseal stood first, a man called Eòin, whom the hill-folk knew for the sweetness of his voice long before they knew him for anything else, and he gave the roll from its beginning: Ailean Mòr and the bank he raised in the snow; Gormshuil at the gate, greying while her father came in each autumn no older than her own sons; Dòmhnall Clachach and his stones that only moved the quarrels they were meant to settle; down through Mòrag the Hard and Iain Dubh brought home from the shingle at Baile ghorm and Tormod Liath who went truly grey and Eilidh Ghlas who sent her younger son west unnamed, and Calum Ciar, who had asked that the lot be drawn in his own sight and been refused, the refusal spoken as plainly as the granting of anything else would have been. When Eòin came at last to Catrìona's own name he said it, once, and sat down, and she felt, sitting where every eye at that fire could find her, every face at the ford turn toward her at once, the way a field of standing barley turns all together when the wind changes.

Then a woman called Ùna stood for An Cnoc Ruadh, and gave that roll in its turn: Beathag Ruadh who had first held the red earth by the lake; Uisdean who rebuilt the palisade through a whole winter under the king's own eye; Seonag nic Uisdein, who weighed her pebble bag before the king and was set into the roll, as every holder of that line was set, "after her father"; Lachlann an Altraim, who took in a fosterling with no name and sent him home again grown; down to Seumas, who had taken the hill that same season and now sat across the fire from Catrìona listening to his own name spoken for the first time in a roll rather than merely in his own household. By the time Ùna had done, the sky over the river had gone the grey that comes before the true grey of morning, and the children of both crowds were long asleep in heaps against their mothers' knees, and no one now living could say, the tellings admit plainly, how many hours the two rolls together had taken, only that it was the whole of one night.

The king sat among the listeners the entire while, his cloak drawn round him against the river's damp, saying nothing and asked nothing, one more grey-haired man among a crowd of grey-haired men, until Eòin came to his own name in its place near the beginning of the roll and some of those nearest him, glancing sideways as a person will at a thing he is not sure he ought to be looking at, saw him smile. A man hearing his own name read out among four hundred others he had buried or begotten or both is, by any account, a small enough matter. It was told after, at more than one hearth, as though it had been a large one, and Catrìona, asked about it in her own middle years by one of her grandchildren, said only that she had seen it too, and that it was the one time in all her years of holding the hill that she had seen him smile at hearing anything said of himself.

## IV. Of the Cord and the Districts

It was in those same years that Catrìona set her own people to counting the households of the hills plainly, a knot to a hearth, on a cord kept at Dùn ìseal for that purpose and no other. She did it, she told those who asked, because she found she could no longer carry the whole tally in her own head as her grandmother's grandmother once had, the hills having grown past the reach of any one memory, however good; and having said so once, plainly, she never troubled to explain it further to anyone who asked twice. The cord grew through her years of holding until it bore, by the reckoning of those who came after and counted the knots themselves, some nine hundred of them, the largest count made on Dia-thìr in that whole age. The king's own kin were not upon it. There was no counting them any longer by then, the tellings say, and no one at Dùn ìseal thought to try.

In the same years Luchd-faire na Lice, who for generations past had been drawn by lot from the households nearest the crack in Na Glinn Àrda, began to be drawn instead from every part of the hills, a household of the far south or the eastern marches standing as good a chance of the lot as a household that had lived its whole life within a day's walk of Tobar dhìreach. Catrìona neither ordered this nor opposed it; it happened, the tellings say, the way water finds a wider bed when the narrow one has filled, and by the middle of her years the keepers had settled at nine, one drawn for each of nine districts of the hills that no one had ever formally marked out on the ground but that every household somehow knew the edges of, the way a family knows where its own dooryard ends without a stone to show it. The nine met at the slab only when one of their number died and a new lot had to be drawn, and at no other time; the rest of the year each kept the custom in their own country and answered to no one for it.

Tobar dhìreach, where Taigh na Lice stood over Somhairle's own grave, came in these years to be a place people walked to for its own sake and not only on the business of a lot, households arriving from country so far off that their own grandparents had never heard the crack under the slab so much as mentioned at a neighbour's hearth. What they came to see, when asked, none of them could very well say. They came, and stood a while, and went home again, and the keepers let them, asking nothing of them and offering nothing beyond the standing there.

## V. Of the Handful That All Burned Together

The measured handful of an gual dathach, kept since Anna nic Coinnich's own day at Achadh dhìreach, had by Catrìona's years spread to every hearth in the hills without ever once being written into a lot or a judgement; it was simply done, everywhere, in the dark turning of the year, each household burning its own small share, measured in a copy of the stone cup Niocol Snaidhear had shaped near two thousand years before, on the one night that every other household in reach of it also burned. No one had commanded that the nights should agree. They had come to agree the way neighbours come to rise at the same hour who have no bell between them but the same rising sun, each household watching for the first low dark flame on the nearest hill and lighting its own the moment it saw it, until across the whole breadth of the hills the fires went up within the same short hour of the same dark night, and stayed low, and went out together before the next dawn. That night had, by then, a name of its own among the hill-folk, Oidhche na Glaice, and it fell at Samhain, which has been Oidhche na Glaice ever since.

Only one household, in all the country the handful had come to reach, would not burn it at all. They were of the line of Torcall Tochlair, who had dug for another vein near the black hill in the east near two thousand years before Catrìona's own birth, and whose brother had been crushed there along with another digger when the ground gave; Torcall's own household had stayed by the open trench long after the vein was given up, holding the ground where the two men died as their own, and their descendants, asked why they would not burn the handful with the rest of the hills, gave no single answer twice. Some said the coal had already taken what it meant to take from that family and would get no more of it burned or unburned. Others said only that a household that had stayed where it was told to leave saw no reason to start keeping customs it had never been asked to keep in the first place. Catrìona, hearing of it, sent no one to compel them, and no one at the slab suggested that she should; the household went its own way in this as it had gone its own way over the trench, and the hills, having no law to press against it, let it.

## VI. Of the Column and the Old Middens

In the seventeenth year of her holding a hand went out from Catrìona's own hill to Cnoc ghorm, where Calbh Cnoc ghorm stood with its marks worn shallow by the weather of an age no one could number, and recut the grooves along their old lines so that the words should not be lost to the rain. Whoever the hand belonged to left no name behind, only the work; and some who came after, comparing the cut marks against tellings of how Calbh Cnoc ghorm had once run, held that a single stroke had changed in the recutting, though none of them could ever agree which stroke it was, or prove that any had changed at all. Calbh Cnoc ghorm stood after that as it had stood before, telling whoever could read it only that the people who raised it had always been there, in words that every gathering at the ford still spoke aloud at its opening.

Further east, at the household places about Seann Dunn, a family digging a new house-floor into the shoulder of an old midden struck, not two spans down, a row of flat stones each cut with a single stroke, set upright in the old refuse the way a hearthstone is set, and knew them at once, from tellings that had reached even that far corner of the hills, for the tally stones of the people who had once lived along that coast and counted their own dead upon them. They did not take the stones for their own use, nor break them up for the new floor, though it would have cost them less labour to do either. They set the stones back in the order they had found them lying, as near as memory and care could manage it, and built their house-floor a little further along the shoulder of the midden instead, losing a morning's digging for the sake of ground that had, by then, no living person left to claim it.

Along the south-eastern coast, in those same years, the custom grew of rowing the newly dead out to Eilean ìseal rather than burying them on the mainland shore, a custom no one at those hearths could say for certain they had learned from anyone rather than come to on their own; some held it was taken from the graves the old coast people had left on the low island across the strait, and others held that a low island surrounded by water was simply where any sensible coast puts what it does not wish disturbed, whether the thought had first come from a stranger's grave or from a fisherman's own good sense. Both might have been true at once, or neither; the tellings, for once, let the question stand without troubling to settle it.

And out past the same coast, on Eilean chrom where Gilleasbuig Beag had been rowed and left with no boat to bring him back, no household in all those years put out a boat to fish its waters, though the fishing there was said to be as good as anywhere on that shore. His fire had been seen three nights running from the mainland, the tellings say, in the first year after he was left, and then no more; and whether that had been a true fire or only three nights of a frightened coast seeing what it feared to see, no one now living could settle either, and the island stayed unfished, empty, and left alone.

## VII. Of the Asking of the Nine

In the twenty-ninth year of her holding, in the year four thousand three hundred and seventy-six, the nine of Luchd-faire na Lice came up together across the trodden ground of the ford while the gathering stood at its fullest, salt-carriers and wool-carriers and flint-carriers all about them, and stood before Catrìona where she sat among her own kin, and asked to be heard.

She knew them, all nine, before any of them had said a word; she had held their lines in her own memory since before any of the nine now standing there had been drawn by lot at all, and she named the eldest of them, who had come forward to speak for the rest, by his own line seven names back before he had finished bowing to her. He did not seem surprised by it. He had likely expected nothing less.

What they asked was this: that their charge over the slab, the lot, and the handful be declared before the whole gathering, spoken out as plainly as the two rolls had been spoken the year of her own taking, so that it should stand fixed past any doubt, and so that no king who came after her should ever again think, as Calum Ciar had thought once, that the slab was a thing to be reached for by anyone who held Dùn ìseal, or ask that the lot be drawn in his own sight as though the sight of a king could weigh upon a stone that had lain over the vein since before the grove was planted.

Catrìona looked at them a long while and said nothing at first, and the old keeper, mistaking the silence for a hearing not yet finished, opened his mouth to say more. She looked past the nine of them while she considered, out over the whole crowded ground of the gathering, the salt people on their own bank and the hill people on theirs and the flint people crowded on the rise beyond the river, every one of them, so far as she could tell from where she sat, waiting on nothing more urgent than the next trade or the next marriage to be agreed at that year's fires, none of them, she was fairly sure, aware that nine old men and women stood asking her, at that moment, to fix something that had never yet been fixed.

"Not this year," she said.

The old keeper's mouth, already open to press the matter, stopped where it was.

"Ask me again," Catrìona said.

She gave them, in the whole of it, neither a refusal nor a consent, and the nine went back across the trodden ground to their own fires by the slab's own country to wait, as keepers had waited on lots and on kings for longer than any of the nine then living could have told her, without complaint, and without any sign that they took her answer for anything other than exactly what it was: an answer given, and a door left standing as it had stood before, neither opened wider nor shut.

## VIII. Of Her Growing Years

She held the hill a long while after that night at the ford, longer than any single reign the hill-folk outside her own blood had known, though shorter, by a very great deal, than the reigns of the blood who had held it before her. Eòin, whose voice had carried the whole roll of Rìghrean na Cloiche across one long night at the ford, died in his eightieth year, an old man by any measure the hills themselves would use, and was carried to his own household's ground with no more ceremony than any other hill-folk death; and Ùna, who had answered him roll for roll out of An Cnoc Ruadh's own line, followed him within two years, in her seventy-third, so that within a short span both voices that had first spoken the two rolls whole were gone from the hills that had heard them, and the telling of that single night passed, from then on, at second hand.

Catrìona herself went on a good while past either of them, keeping her households in her head as she always had, judging a boundary stone here and a marriage there with the same flat exactness she had brought to it from her first year of holding. It was in her two hundred and eighty-ninth year that the sickness came on her that would not leave again, a slow failing that those about her on the hill first took for nothing more than the ordinary tiredness of a long-held office and then, watching it deepen through one whole turning of the seasons, could no longer mistake for anything but what it was. She kept her seat at Dùn ìseal through it as long as she was able, still hearing what was brought to her, still able, when a household came before her with some quarrel over a strip of grazing, to give its whole line back seven names without having to be reminded of a single one of them.

The nine keepers, hearing that she had grown ill, sent no word asking again. They had been told to ask her again, and an asking made of a woman too worn to answer it plainly would have been, in the reckoning of that country, no true asking at all; and so they waited still, by their own slab, in their own nine districts, keeping the custom she had neither fixed nor unfixed, exactly as they had kept it before she was ever asked, and exactly as they would go on keeping it after.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of the Shares Counted

*GE 4,391 – 4,549*

*This is told at Dùn ìseal, among the households that camped nearest the hill in those years, as Niall Òg was said to have told it himself in his own age, laughing, before he had any cause to stop laughing at it.*

## I. Of the Hill Left to No One

Niall Òg was six hundred and eighty-eight years old, and looked, by the reckoning of the ordinary households camped that season at the foot of the hill, no more than a young man come newly into his strength, when Catrìona Mhòr died at Dùn ìseal in her two hundred and ninety-first year and Rìghrean na Cloiche ended with her.

He had neither claim on the hill nor any close standing to bring one; he went up with his mother because every soul of the king's blood within three days' walk had come, and staying away would have drawn more remark than coming did. He remembered afterward how many of them there were: cousins he had met at a dozen gatherings and cousins he had never met at all, old ones bent nearly double and young ones who did not yet know how old they would live to be, every last one of them able to say the two names of the line they stood on, and the second of the two always Ailean's. They stood in a great loose ring below the hill's own bank while the households that served the hill went in and out with water and bread for whoever asked it, and the king sat on the turf inside the bank with his back very straight, as he had sat, the old tellings said, in the first winter of the hill, and heard every claim that was brought to him.

There were more claims than Niall could ever afterward number, try as he did, more than once, to make the count come out the same way twice. Some came with a line traced back seven generations and a piece of the hill's own turf held out on an open palm, as if the ground might speak for them on its own account. Some came with nothing but their own two names said plainly, trusting the two names to be claim enough. One old woman, whom Niall's mother pointed out to him under her breath as kin of Murchadh Mòr's line and therefore, by the fashion of the day, owed more courtesy than most, came leaning on two sticks and said only that she had outlived every rival claim she had ever had, and that this ought to count for something even if nothing else about her did. A man of Tràigh an t-Salainn's own cousinage, three lines removed but proud of every yard of the distance, brought his infant daughter up in his arms and held her out toward the king as his whole argument, saying nothing else at all. The king heard them all out with the same still face, and it was Niall's mother who named the trouble in it afterward: watching him hear any single claim, she said, no one standing near enough to see his face could tell whether it moved him, because his face gave the same account of a claim that moved him as of one that did not, and there was no reading behind it from the outside.

When the last of them had spoken and the light was going off the hill, the king stood up from the turf, and Niall's mother took his arm hard enough to hurt, though he did not understand until later that this was because she, too, did not know what was coming. The king said that he had heard every claim brought to him, and that he judged none of them better than another, because none of them was better than another; that Catrìona Mhòr had been the last of a line that had begun the day he himself first walked up that slope, and that a line was not a thing a man could hand from one stranger's palm to the next merely because the palm was open. He said he would give the hill to none of them. He said he would hold it himself, as he had held it before Gormshuil first took it up in his name, and that he would go on holding it for as long as it pleased him to.

Then he walked up into the hill's own house and did not come out again that evening, and the kin stood a while longer in the failing light not quite believing that this was the whole of what they had come to hear, and then began, in twos and threes, to go back to their own fires, and Niall's mother did not let go of his arm the whole way down.

"He has never done that before," she said, when they were far enough from the hill that she judged it safe to say anything at all. "Given nothing. Not to anyone."

"Perhaps there was no one worth giving it to," Niall said, because he was young enough still to say a true thing plainly without weighing first what it would cost him to have said it.

His mother looked at him a long moment in the dusk, the way a woman looks at a child who has said something cleverer than she expected of him and is not certain yet whether to be pleased or afraid. "Perhaps," she said. "Or perhaps he has looked at every one of us and found that giving is the one thing left he has not yet tried keeping back."

## II. Of the Marriages Made for a Share

Niall did not understand, for some years after, what his mother had meant by that, and by the time he did understand it he had come, without quite noticing the coming, to be a part of the thing.

It began, so far as anyone afterward could point to a beginning, with a marriage. In the fourth year after Catrìona Mhòr's death a young man of one of the smaller lines, whose own hold on the kingdom amounted to grazing on the northern skirts of nobody's particular attention, married a woman three lines removed from the king on her mother's side and two on her father's, a match that would have raised no eyebrow at all in an ordinary year, since the two of them had known each other since childhood and were, by every account, well suited. What raised the eyebrow was the manner of the asking: the young man's own father stood up at the betrothal fire and said, in so many words, that the marriage joined two claims that might one day be worth more joined than either was worth alone, should the king ever be brought to naming an heir after all, and that he for one meant his son's children to stand as near the front of that reckoning as five lines instead of three could put them.

No one had ever said such a thing aloud at a betrothal fire before. The thought was old; what was new was the saying of it, and the profit in the saying. There had always, before, been a king who might yet live another thousand years and give and take back shares as the fancy or the need took him, and little enough profit in marrying for what a man might never live to see given out at all. Now there was a king who had refused to give anything, and a hill held in a hand that no one could say would ever open again, and the old unspoken thought became, within that single season, a thing spoken plainly at every fire that had two unmarried children of the blood between them.

Niall watched three more such marriages made before he was two hundred years further into his own life, each one a little more openly reckoned than the last. The second joined a household holding good river-grazing to one that held none but had, on its own side, a claim traced through four generations of daughters rather than sons, which some of the elder kin said counted for less and some said counted for more, and no one on the hill that year could point to any custom, old or new, that settled the question either way. The third was broken off within the month, when the bride's own grandmother discovered a nearer claim on her groom's side that she judged would weigh the marriage's whole worth downward rather than up, and said so at the man's own hearth in words plain enough that the match did not survive the telling of them. By the time Niall was of an age to be thought of as a match himself, no one troubled any longer to pretend that a marriage among the king's own blood was made for anything but the shares it might one day gather in one house. He was asked, more than once, by aunts and great-aunts who meant it kindly, whether he had given thought to which of his cousins' lines ran nearest the front of the reckoning, and he laughed at every one of them, honestly at first and then, as the years went on, because laughing had become the answer expected of him and he had found no better one to give in its place.

It was in those same years that the first valley changed hands by the king's own word rather than by death or marriage: a household that had held good grazing on the western slopes for eleven generations was told, without explanation given beyond what the king himself troubled to give, which was none, that the grazing was wanted for another line, and that they would remove themselves and their herds to ground of equal size two valleys over before the winter closed the passes. They went. No one on the hill that year could say why that household and not another had been chosen to lose what it held, and the king, asked directly by the household's own eldest whether some fault of theirs lay behind it, said only that a share given was a share that could be taken back, and had always been so, and that nothing about the taking back was new even if the households had grown unused to seeing it done. It was the plainest word he gave on the whole matter in all the years Niall watched it unfold, and it satisfied no one, least of all the household that had lost the western slopes for reasons it never learned.

## III. Of Raonaid's Share Taken Back

Niall's own mother, Raonaid nic Ailein, held through those years a stretch of river-meadow below the hill that had come to her from the king's own giving so long before that not even she could always give the whole of its telling at one sitting. She was herself the king's daughter, though by then so many generations stood between the fact and the memory of it that most of the households camped near the hill knew her only as an old woman of the blood who kept good meadow and asked little of anyone, and it was a long while before Niall understood that his own claim, when the aunts spoke of reckonings and frontings, ran doubled through her and through his father both, a thing that made him, without his ever asking for it, one of the names spoken of at other households' own betrothal fires in the same careful voice his own father had once used of somebody else's son.

She died in her own house on the river-meadow in the year four thousand four hundred and eighty, having lived, by the count the reciters kept for her afterward, one thousand three hundred and eighty years. Not long before the end she told Niall that the span had simply come to be the shape her life had taken, the way a river takes the shape of the ground it is given and does not ask whether another ground might have made it run differently. She had stopped some centuries back, she said, asking whether it was a long life or a short one, since the question had no one left living to compare it against who had not asked her the same thing first.

The king came down to the river-meadow himself when word reached him that she was failing, and sat with her the better part of a day and a night, as the tellings said he had sat once with Gormshuil at the gate and once with Somhairle in Na Glinn Àrda. What passed between them in the house no one who was not in it ever learned; she died within the week and never spoke of it, and he never spoke of any of them once they were in the ground. Niall stood outside through most of that night with his own wife beside him, and neither of them went in. He said afterward that he had wanted to, once, badly enough to put his hand on the door, and had taken it away again unopened, judging without needing to say so to his wife that the room held a conversation a good deal older than anything he himself had a part in.

His mother spoke to him alone the following morning, when the king had gone back up to the hill and the house was quiet again but for the two of them. She told him she had asked her father, in the night just past, whether he grieved the same grief each time or whether it wore differently with practice, the way a callus forms where a tool is held often enough, and that he had answered only that he did not know, because he had never yet finished grieving any one of them before the next was laid on top of it. "He did not say it unkindly," she told Niall, "only plainly, the way he says everything. I asked him because I wanted to know whether I ought to be sorry for him as well as for myself, in whatever time I have left to be sorry for anyone. I could not get an answer out of him either way, and I have stopped minding that I could not."

Within the month of her burying the king sent word to the river-meadow that the grazing his daughter had held was wanted elsewhere, and that Niall, as her nearest of that line, should remove his own household from it before the next season's herds came down. He did not say where the grazing was wanted, or by whom, and Niall, standing before him at Dùn ìseal to hear the word given in person, found that his own mouth had only the one shape left in it after a hundred aunts had asked him the same question a hundred different ways: he laughed. The loss itself did not strike him as funny. Laughing had simply become, over so many years of the same reckoning put to him in so many forms, the only answer his own mouth still knew how to make in the king's presence, whatever the question happened to be that season. The king looked at him a moment with an expression Niall could not afterward name, and said only that he was glad someone in the family still found some of it amusing.

"Someone has to," Niall said, "or we should all of us have gone mad reckoning it long before now."

"Some of us have," the king said, and did not say which of them he meant, and turned to the next matter waiting for him, which was, that season, always another claim, another marriage, another valley wanted elsewhere.

## IV. Of Niall Sent East

It was some forty years after his mother's death, in the year four thousand five hundred and twenty, that the king called Niall to him at Dùn ìseal and gave him an errand that had nothing to do with any share at all, which was, Niall said afterward more than once, the first time in a great while that anyone of the king's own house had asked something of him that was not a reckoning of some kind.

"You will go east of the vein," the king said, "to the fort they have raised there, and tell its holder that I bid him and his households come in to me at last, as every other coast of this island has come in, in its own time and its own way."

Niall asked why he, among all the king's kin nearer the front of whatever reckoning was being made that season, should be the one sent on such an errand, and the king said, plainly, that he wanted a messenger the east would not mistake for a claim: that a man sent to ask for nothing more than the coming-in, and known through every fire on the hill for asking nothing of anyone on his own account beyond a laugh, was less likely to be taken for the leading edge of a conquest than a man who held ground and wanted more of it. Niall thought this a fair enough reckoning, and said so, and went.

He went east by the long road the king bade him take, round by the households of the eastern marches so that the whole country should know a messenger was riding, and crossed the vein on the third day of it, over ground that grew stonier and less kept the further east he rode, past the last of the households that answered to Dùn ìseal in anything but name and into a country whose hearths he did not know and whose faces did not know him. He slept the first of those eastern nights at a household that fed him without asking who he was or where he rode, and the second at another that asked at once, plainly, and fed him no worse for the asking, telling him only, when he had answered, that he was welcome at their fire but that the fire owed his errand nothing on its own account. Children ran out along the road to look at his horse, which was of a taller island stock than the east bred for itself, and one boy walked alongside him the better part of a morning asking whether it was true that a man of the king's own house never grew old, and whether Niall himself was such a man, and looked plainly disappointed to be told that Niall was not, though not so disappointed that he stopped walking beside the horse until his own mother called him in for his dinner.

He came, on the fifth day, to the double bank of Dùn dhearg standing on its rise above the river, its ditch cut deep enough that a man standing in it could not see over the rim, exactly as the tellings west of the vein described it and exactly as none of those tellings had prepared him to find it: larger, and better kept, and fuller of people going about their own business without the smallest sign of having heard that a messenger of the king's own house was riding up their own road to speak with them. He counted three separate knappers' floors busy within the outer bank alone before anyone troubled to ask his business, and a granary raised on stone legs against the damp that he judged, from the width of it, held grain enough to see the whole fort through two bad harvests running, and it came to him, riding in past all of it, that he had ridden east expecting to find a grievance nursed in poverty, and had found instead a country that wanted nothing from the hill because it had, by its own hands, gone some way toward needing nothing from anyone.

They brought him, without much ceremony and less delay, before a man named Fearghal Donn, who held the fort in those years and had held it, by his own account, since before he was old enough to have chosen the holding for himself, having had it laid on him the way a family's oldest son is laid with a family's oldest debts. Fearghal was forty years old that season, by his own country's ordinary count, a broad quiet man with a scar along one forearm that he did not offer to explain and Niall did not ask after. He heard Niall out standing in the open ground within the fort's own bank, with a good part of the household gathered near enough to hear every word of it, which Niall understood, before Fearghal had finished hearing him, to be no accident at all.

## V. Of the Word Sent Back

"Tell your king," Fearghal Donn said, when Niall had given the whole of his errand plainly, word for word as the king had given it to him, "that we have raised this bank with our own hands, on ground none of his own blood ever set foot on before we did, and that we have neither asked leave of Dùn ìseal to raise it nor owed anyone west of the vein so much as a handful of salt for the raising. Tell him we have heard, from every trader who ever crossed the vein either way, what it is to be one of his own kin: to marry for a share and count another man's years against your own and wait a thousand of them, if it comes to that, for a hill that is never given after all. We have no wish to be counted among you."

Niall said that he had come to ask a coming-in, not a submission, and that the king had put no oath into the errand at all, only the asking.

"Then tell him," Fearghal said, "that the asking is answered. We will not come in. We have our own bank and our own dead in it, and we mean to keep both without any man's leave, west of the vein or anywhere else."

There was more said between them that afternoon, none of it, by Niall's own account afterward, either angry or unkind; Fearghal Donn gave him food and a bed for the night as any household on the island would have given a traveller, king's messenger or none, and asked him, before he rode out the next morning, a good many plain questions about the hill and the king and the manner of life west of the vein, listening to the answers with the same close attention he had given the errand, so that Niall came away from Dùn dhearg less certain than he had ridden in that the man who held it thought ill of the king so much as he thought the whole arrangement not worth the joining. He rode home with nothing to carry but the bare word, and gave it to the king plainly, as he had been asked to give it, standing again on the turf below the hill's own bank where he had once stood as a boy of six hundred and eighty-eight to hear Catrìona Mhòr's claimants turned away one by one.

The king heard the word and said nothing for a long while, looking east past the vein toward ground Niall knew he had never in all his years troubled to cross himself, and then said only that he had not looked for any other answer, and thanked Niall for the carrying of it, and turned to the next matter waiting for him.

It was not the last word from the east, though it was the last the king troubled to ask for. Within a season word came west, by traders and not by any messenger sent for the purpose, that the households about Dùn dhearg had begun keeping their own spears closer to hand than they had ever kept them before. No quarrel had broken out among themselves to account for it, and the traders who carried the word could not say what quarrel, whose, the spears were being kept ready against; only that they were being kept ready, and that the keeping of them had become, in the space of that one season, a plain fact of the country the way the double bank was a plain fact, needing no more explaining than the bank did. Niall heard the word at Dùn ìseal among a dozen other pieces of news that season, a bad harvest on the northern plain, a marriage broken off over a reckoning gone sour, a fourth household removed from ground it had held a hundred years to make way for a fifth; and he found, turning it over afterward at his own hearth, that this was the one word among them all he could not laugh at, though he could not have said, if anyone had asked him that year, exactly why a gathering of spears at a fort three days' ride east should have struck him differently from anything else the kingdom had counted and recounted in the whole of his own long lifetime.

The king, so far as anyone at Dùn ìseal could see, did nothing about any of it: no word sent east again, no muster called west of the vein, no change at all in the plain round of a man who held a hill in his own hand and heard whatever claims and reckonings the day brought him. He sat on the turf as he had sat since Catrìona Mhòr's death, and the kin went on counting their shares and marrying for them around him, and the spears gathered, slowly, at Dùn dhearg, the way a river gathers behind a dam it does not yet know is a dam at all.

# Chapter Thirty-nine: Of the Tents in the Valley

*GE 4,550 – 4,603*

*This is kept in Na Glinn Àrda among Clann na Ceiste, who had it first from Gille-Brìde himself, in his own age, before he was old.*

## I. Of the Eve as It Stood

In the year four thousand five hundred and fifty the island stood as it had stood, by then, for longer than any one household could remember it standing otherwise. The handful was kept at every hearth from the northern capes to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, each burning its own small measure in the dark of the year and none troubling another with the manner of the burning. Luchd-faire na Lice were nine, as they had been nine since the lot was last drawn, and the sharing before the storms was kept on every coast that had a boat to share it from, and the saying cut long before on Calbh Cnoc ghorm was spoken aloud, plainly and without dispute, wherever two or three of the blood or of the common households came together at a fire: *we did not come; we were here.* None of it had been set down as law. No oath had been sworn over the vein, and no oath had been asked. The king held the hill in his own hand, as he had held it since Catrìona Mhòr's death took the last of Rìghrean na Cloiche' list out of the world, and his kin waited about him, patiently or less patiently as it suited each of them, for shares that were not yet given and could not yet be counted.

It was a few years before this, in the year four thousand five hundred and forty-three, that a son was born in Na Glinn Àrda to Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line. The child was called Ceallach, after no one that the mother could name, and he was a quiet child, slower to walk than others of that blood and slower still to run, though when he did at last run he ran, his father said, watching him cross the floor of the high valley on legs that had taken the better part of two years to trust themselves, as though he meant to make up in a single afternoon what he had been given late. It was told back afterward, when the boy was grown into whatever he grew into, that this had been the first sign anyone in Na Glinn Àrda troubled to remark on: that the years were coming down faster in him than they had in his father, and faster in his father than in the father before that, a shortening that no one in the valleys named aloud, because there was no cause yet to name it, and because the years a man had were his own business until the manner of his dying made them everyone's.

Gille-Brìde was by then the seventh of Somhairle's line after Beathan, a man past a hundred years of his own, a big quiet man who kept to Na Glinn Àrda among Clann na Ceiste and went down into the lower country only when the asking or the giving of some particular thing required it of him. He held no hill and claimed no share, and it was said of him, by those few of the king's blood who troubled to think of him at all, that he had got the family's patience and none of its hunger, which some of them meant as a compliment and most did not. His own father, an old man then in the second century of his life, came down from the upper valley to see the child that same autumn with a gift of worked flint in a bag on his back, and sat with the boy on his knee by a low fire while Gille-Brìde told him, in the flat voice of a man reciting a thing he had said to himself too many times already to feel much about it any longer, that the fever which had taken two of his own brothers young had not touched this one, and that the boy, if the years ran true, might see out the whole of whatever remained to the line before they ran out altogether.

"They will run out," the old man said. It was not a question.

"They will," said Gille-Brìde. "Not in me. Perhaps not in him. In someone."

Clann na Ceiste, who kept Na Glinn Àrda about the slab and had kept them since the keepers were first chosen by lot, took little account of the king's kin's counting of years, having little enough occasion to count their own beyond the ordinary span of a life and a death, and it was one of their number, an old woman who had sat that year's watch at the slab and walked down afterward to see the new child for herself, who said to Gille-Brìde what he came, in time, to think of as the truest word spoken over the boy in the whole of his infancy: that a child born short-lived among the long-lived would grow up knowing early a thing neither his father's people nor hers had ever needed to learn until late, how much of a life could be made to matter in however much of it a body was given. Gille-Brìde kept that word to himself and did not repeat it to his own father, judging that an old man newly certain his line was running out wanted no philosophy laid over the plain fact of it, however kindly meant.

He watched the boy grow through his first years, and found the child each season a little further from what he had expected and a little nearer to something he had no word for yet: quiet where Niall Òg's blood ran loud, careful where Ìomhar's ran quick to grievance, watching the fires of a hearth that was not his own the way a man watches a thing he has been told he will not keep for long, though no one, least of all the boy, had yet told him any such thing in so many words.

## II. Of the Father's Three Hundred and Eighth Year

Gille-Brìde's father died at Samhain in the year four thousand five hundred and ninety-nine, in his three hundred and eighth year, which was fewer years than his own father had had, and far fewer than the six hundred his grandfather had counted, and fewer by a long way than the plain thousand-odd of the generations further back still, whose names Na Glinn Àrda kept only as a list recited at a fire and not as men anyone living had known. He died as most of that line had learned, by then, to die: without illness, without a wound, simply slower each year at rising from his own hearthstone until one morning he did not rise from it at all, and the household found him sitting upright with his eyes shut and his hands folded as though he had meant, at the last, to make as little trouble of the thing as a man could.

Gille-Brìde stood at the burying, and it was there, standing over the turned earth with Ceallach a solemn boy of six-and-fifty years holding his hand, that he first heard the word going about the fires that the kin of the king's own blood were, at long last, coming down out of their scattered holdings to gather in the valley below Dùn ìseal, each with tents and a fire of its own and a steward set over its own people, to wait there upon whatever the king should say of the shares that had gone uncounted since Catrìona Mhòr's death. It was said as news, and said, too, with the particular relish that news of the king's kin always drew from households that were not of it: that after so long a waiting, some matter or other was at last to be settled, or at least to be waited for in one place instead of many.

"You should go down and see it," said an old woman of the burying party, who had no love for the king's blood and every love for a spectacle involving it. "It will not come again in your lifetime, whatever it comes to."

"It may not come to anything," Gille-Brìde said, "in my lifetime or another's."

But he thought of it walking back up into Na Glinn Àrda with the boy's small hand still cold in his from the graveside, and he found that the old woman's word had lodged in him in a way her spectacle had not: not the gathering itself, which he had little enough curiosity for, but the plain, strange fact that after so many hundreds of years of a hill held quietly by one old man who asked nothing of anyone, the kin should choose, now, to come down and sit under it and wait.

It was in that same season, though the news of it was slower reaching Na Glinn Àrda than most news of the king's own household, that word came of another death nearer the vein than the hill: Fearghal Donn, who had held Dùn dhearg since before Niall Òg was sent to him with a message and sent back with nothing, died in his own bed at the fort in the year four thousand five hundred and seventy, an old man by the reckoning of the common blood though he had never claimed any other, and left the fort and its long unsettled quarrel with the hill to a son grown to manhood inside that quarrel and knowing, by his own later account, no time before it. The households east of the vein buried Fearghal Donn as they had buried Ailis two generations before him, without word sent to Dùn ìseal and without any expecting one to come back, and his son Artair took up the holding of the fort in the same season with no more ceremony than his father had used to take it up before him, and was heard to say, at the burying itself, that he meant to hold what his father had held and ask nothing further of it until the day the hill asked something of him first.

## III. Of the Tents and the Steward to Each Line

They began coming down in the summer of the year four thousand six hundred and one, household by household and line by line, no single word sent out to call any of them, each deciding on its own that the waiting had gone on long enough to be done nearer the hill than far from it. Murchadh Mòr's people came from the northern plain in a column that took the better part of three days to pass any one point on the road, eleven sons' worth of grandsons and their own grown children driving cattle before them and carrying, some said, more tent-cloth on their backs than the valley below Dùn ìseal had ever seen brought to one place at once. Eithne's people came from the plain below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire with less show and no less certainty, her own knot-keeper walking at the head of them with the household's cord wound about his arm as though he meant to be seen keeping count of every soul who set foot on the new ground, which he did, from the first day to the last. Ìomhar Dearg came from the eastern marches with his own household and a grievance he had been nursing, by then, for the better part of a hundred years, over grazing along the river that he judged his by use if not yet by any word of the king's, and he pitched his tents nearer the vein than any other line thought wise, which was, everyone agreed, exactly like him.

Niall Òg came laughing, as he had come laughing to every gathering of his life, claiming through both his mother's blood and his father's a share no one else troubled to dispute with him in the open, though more than one household said behind its own hearth-smoke that a claim made through two lines at once was, by the same reckoning, no more than half a claim doubled, and worth exactly what a claim through one line was worth and not a grain more. An old white-haired daughter of the king's own body came too, older than Eithne by some centuries, and pitched her tent apart from the rest with a small household of her own, and was seen at no fire but her own for the better part of that first summer, which some read as grief for shares long since given and taken back, and others read as nothing more than an old woman's wish to be let alone in her own tent for once in a very long life of not being let alone in it.

And Sìne nan Snaidhm came down from the hill as the household's own knot-keeper, claiming no ground of her own, carrying Sreang nan Teallach that had counted every soul under the king's roof for longer than any single line's memory reached, and she walked the new valley in its first weeks the way she had always walked the hill, checking each new tent against the cord in her hands and each steward's tally against her own, so that within a season there was not a fire pitched in that valley, of the king's blood or of any household following it down, whose count she did not keep somewhere on the knots she carried.

A steward stood over every line by the second summer, a man or a woman set by each household, holding no ground the king had given and holding no lordship over any but its own, only charged to speak for it at the common fires and see that its own people did not go hungry or unhoused while the waiting went on, which by then had gone on long enough that the valley below Dùn ìseal had come to look, from any rise above it, less like a gathering that would soon disperse and more like a town that had simply forgotten, or declined, to raise walls around its own fires.

## IV. Of Gille-Brìde Come Down

Gille-Brìde came down himself in the last summer of it, the year four thousand six hundred and three, more out of the same plain curiosity the old woman at the burying had first put in him than out of any claim of his own, for he had none, and wanted none. He walked the two days out of Na Glinn Àrda with Ceallach beside him, a young man now of sixty years and already, though neither of them said it aloud, walking a little more slowly than a man of sixty of the older reckoning ought to have walked, and they came down over the last rise together at evening and stood a while looking at what the valley below Dùn ìseal had become.

He had not seen a gathering of that size in his life, and said so. Fires ran the whole length of the valley floor as far as the last light let him see, more of them than he could have counted in an evening's standing, and the smoke of them lay along the ground in the still air the way mist lay along a river at dawn, so that the tents seemed to rise straight out of it rather than to stand upon the grass. He found Murchadh Mòr first, an old grey giant of a man surrounded by sons and grandsons who all shared his own build about the shoulders, holding forth to a knot of them about grazing rights on the northern plain in a voice that carried the length of three tents in either direction without troubling to be raised for the purpose. He found Eithne after him, seated outside her own tent with her knot-keeper beside her going over the day's tally by firelight, and she greeted Gille-Brìde with the particular courtesy of a woman who had long since stopped expecting to be surprised by anything a gathering of her own kin might produce.

Ìomhar Dearg he found arguing, as he had somehow known before he found him that he would be arguing, with a steward of one of the common households over the exact reach of the river-grazing he claimed, a dispute that had, by the sound of it, been running since the first week of the gathering and showed no sign of any conclusion either man expected to reach that night or any other.

"It was given me by the king himself, six hundred years since," Ìomhar was saying, loud enough that half the fires nearest his own could follow the argument without troubling to walk to it, "and I have grazed it every year since without asking leave of any steward set over any household that came to this valley after I did."

"It was given you the near bank," the steward answered him, patient in the particular way of a man who has said the same thing many times before and expects to say it many times again, "and you graze the far one besides, and call the difference nothing because no one has yet troubled to measure it."

"Then measure it," said Ìomhar, "and we will see whose nothing it is." Neither man moved to fetch a rope or a rod to do any such measuring, and Gille-Brìde, passing on beyond the firelight, judged that neither man expected the other to, and that the dispute itself, rather than its settling, was what each of them had come down into the valley to keep alive.

Niall Òg he found laughing at someone else's fire, as ever, telling some tale of Rathad an t-Salainn to a ring of younger cousins who had not heard it before and would, by the look of them, be glad enough to hear it again; and when he saw Gille-Brìde standing at the fire's edge he broke off long enough to call across to him, cheerfully, that a man of Somhairle's line who came down into the valley with no claim to press was either the wisest soul in it or the only fool who had not yet worked out what he was owed, and that he, Niall, had not yet decided which, and would let Gille-Brìde know when he had. Gille-Brìde said only that he was content to be thought either, so long as no one troubled to settle the question that same evening, which made Niall Òg laugh again and turn back to his cousins and his tale.

The old white-haired daughter he saw once at a distance, sitting alone outside her own tent with her hands folded, and did not go to her, judging rightly, he thought, that she wanted no company that evening and would not thank a near-stranger for offering it.

It was Sìne nan Snaidhm who found him in the end, coming along the fires with her cord wound about her wrist as she went, and she stopped when she saw him and looked at him a long moment before she spoke, as a woman does who is putting a face to a name she has heard and not yet seen.

"You are of Somhairle's line," she said. "The one who keeps to Na Glinn Àrda."

"I am," he said.

"Your name is not on any cord I carry," she said, not unkindly, "because you have asked for no ground and no share, in all these years, from anyone who might have given you one."

"I have not," he agreed.

"Then you are the only soul in this valley tonight of whom that can be said," she told him, and went on with her counting, leaving him to think, as he stood there among the fires of a gathering he had wanted only to see, that she had not meant it as praise and had not meant it as blame either, only as the plainest fact she knew about him, set down the way she set down every other fact that came to her along the cord.

Word ran through the valley that same week, from fire to fire faster than any steward could carry it formally, that Sluagh an Ear had begun to move. It had been gathering at Dùn dhearg, by all the telling that reached the western fires, since the spring of that year, under Artair, the same son of Fearghal Donn who had taken up his father's holding thirty years and more before with the plain word that he would ask nothing of the hill until the hill asked something of him; and it was said, by those who claimed to know his mind and by those who only claimed to know his household, that the hill's own moving that summer, the king going down at last among his people after so long a stillness, was the very thing Artair had told himself, thirty years before, that he was waiting for. What Sluagh an Ear meant to do once it had gathered, no one in the valley below Dùn ìseal could say with any certainty, and the tellers who claimed to know said different things depending on which fire they sat at, so that by midsummer there were as many accounts of the east's intent going about the valley as there were fires to tell them at, and most of the households simply went on with their own waiting and let the accounts settle themselves, or fail to, as they would.

## V. Of the King's Answer

It was the king himself who settled the question of his own household's part in it, and he settled it, as he had settled most things in his very long life, without asking anyone's leave to do so and without troubling to explain himself past the plain fact of the doing. He came down from Dùn ìseal on a morning near the end of that same summer with a handful of his own people about him, no more than would fill three tents, and word went round the valley before he had gone a mile that the king was going to meet the east himself, and that every line camped along that valley floor meant, upon hearing it, to follow him within a day or two, once tents were struck and stewards set to keep the ground, once this or that last matter of a household's own was seen to.

Gille-Brìde stood at the edge of Murchadh Mòr's fire that morning and watched the king go down the valley on foot among his handful of household, a grey-headed man with a young man's face, walking at a pace that did not look, from where Gille-Brìde stood, like the pace of a man who expected to be followed soon or gladly. He went to the king before he had gone far, not knowing himself quite why he did it until he had already done it, and asked him plainly whether he, too, should come down to the ford with the rest.

The king stopped and looked at him a while, the way a man looks at something he has not troubled to look at closely before and finds, on the looking, not unfamiliar after all.

"You are Somhairle's," he said. It was not a question either.

"I am what is left of that line that still walks Na Glinn Àrda," Gille-Brìde said, "and asks nothing of anyone."

"Then go home to them," said the king. "Whatever comes of this, it will want telling afterward by someone who was not in it, and your people have always been better at the telling than the coming."

Gille-Brìde said nothing more to that, because there was nothing in it that asked for an answer, and the king went on down the valley among his handful of household, and did not look back, and every line behind him along that valley floor went on saying, at its own fire and in its own time, that it would follow him in a day or two, as each of them had been saying since the news of the east's moving first ran the length of the tents.

Murchadh Mòr said it that same evening, standing at the edge of his own fire with a grandson on either side of him, that he would bring his own people down within the week once the cattle were seen to; and Eithne said it more quietly to her knot-keeper, who set it down on the cord as though a word of intent were as good, for her purposes, as a soul already counted; and Ìomhar Dearg said it loudest of all, to no one steward in particular, that he would follow the king to the ford himself and see the matter of the river-grazing settled once and for all where it could be settled by more than argument, though which matter he meant by that, the grazing or the gathering of spears at Dùn dhearg, he did not trouble to say, and no one troubled to ask him. Niall Òg said it laughing, as he said everything, and the old white-haired daughter said nothing at all that anyone at any fire heard her say, and struck her own tent two days later to pitch it again in the upper camps, apart from the noise of the rest, and did not come down from them.

Sìne nan Snaidhm alone said nothing of following, because it was no part of her charge to follow the king anywhere; her charge was the cord, and the cord stayed at Dùn ìseal, in the hands of whichever household the king left behind him to keep the hill while he was gone, and she was seen, in the days after his going, walking the emptying rows of tents with the same care she had walked them full, as though a valley half-struck were no less hers to count than a valley pitched from end to end.

Gille-Brìde took the boy Ceallach by the arm that same afternoon and turned north, back up out of the valley of tents and its smoke lying low along the grass, toward Na Glinn Àrda where no ground was claimed and no share waited to be counted, and he did not look back either, though he thought, walking, that he would remember the smoke of that valley for whatever years were left to him, however many or few they proved to be against his father's three hundred and eight, and that someone, as the king had said, would have the telling of what came after, and that it would not, after all, be him who came to it, only him who walked away from where it was about to happen and carried the boy home.

# Chapter Forty: Of the Ford below Dùn dhearg

*GE 4,603*

*It is the tellers of the east themselves who give this best, for they had cause to remember it, and the telling that follows keeps closest to the account of a lad who stood in it, sixteen years old and the youngest spear of his household, whose own name the east never troubled to keep.*

## I. Of the Camp under Artair mac Fhearghail

They came down to the river in the last days of an Lùnastal, the whole strength of the country east of the vein, household by household, until the fires along the east bank ran for the better part of a mile and a boy standing at one end of them could not see the far end for smoke. Artair mac Fhearghail held Dùn dhearg that year, an old fort's holder grown grey in a country that had never sent a name to be recited at any ford, and it was under his word, more than any other's, that the households had come down at last, though he himself said afterward that no one word of his had done it: the thing had been three generations gathering, like water behind a bank nobody built on purpose, and he had only stood where the bank happened to break.

The lad's household came with the rest, twenty-some strong counting the old women who would not be left behind and the boys too young yet to carry a spear who came anyway to mind the fires. His father had cut turf on the second bank at Dùn dhearg the year it went up, and had told him since he could walk that no household east of the vein owed the hill at Dùn ìseal so much as a good morning, let alone a season's labour or a daughter in marriage; and the lad had grown up on that telling the way he had grown up on his mother's porridge, without ever once asking where the grain in it had come from.

Word had run down from the west all that summer, the way water finds its own low ground without anyone digging it a channel: that the king's own kin, greedy for the shares that would fall open when the old man went at last into the ground like other men, had begun to count each other's herds and each other's daughters with an eye that liked what it counted less each year; that the king held the hill at Dùn ìseal alone now, giving it to none of his blood, and sat on it the way a man sits on a coal he does not mean to hand to his neighbour's fire; that he had sent to Dùn dhearg once, some seasons back, bidding the households come in and be counted at last, and been sent an answer that owed him nothing and never would. Fearghal Donn had given that answer before his son was born, and Artair mac Fhearghail told it again at the fires the night the host came down, so that even those too young to remember the sending of it should know exactly what had been said and to whom.

"We told him we would keep our own bank," the old holder said, turning a coal over with a stick so that the good side of it faced up, "and that a hill across the vein was no more to us than a story is to a man with his own field to plough. That was the answer. It has not changed since, and I see no cause in eighty years to change it now."

Someone asked, from further back at the fire, whether it was true the king did not age, and whether that made him something other than a man that a host of ordinary spears might reasonably hope to bring down.

"He is flesh," Artair said, and did not raise his voice to say it, which was more frightening, the lad thought afterward, than if he had shouted it. "Whatever else he is, under the grey hair and the years, he is flesh, and flesh comes to an end somewhere. I have not lived sixty years east of the vein to tell my own grandchildren that a man cannot be met."

They had been told the king was coming east at last with his kin, meaning to hold the ford against whatever the east chose to do about it, or to be met at it and answered plainly one way or the other after three generations of silence; and the host had come down to the river in the dark before the first morning meaning to hold it first, on the strength of numbers alone, three thousand spears and more against however many the old man's kin thought fit to bring.

His mother had not come down with the rest of the household, being past the age for it and no fonder of rivers than her son's father was fond of words, but she had stood at the door of their house the morning they left and told him, plainly enough that he still had the whole of it by heart years after, that a fight three generations in the gathering was not a thing one lad's caution or one lad's daring would settle either way, and that his business in it was to come home again, and that she would hear no telling of the ford from him that did not end with him standing at that same door to give it. His father had said nothing to that, being a man who left the giving of instructions to his wife and the keeping of them to himself, but he had put his own hand once, briefly, on the back of the lad's neck before they took the road east to the river, which was as much as the lad had ever known him to say on any subject at all.

The lad slept badly that night, if he slept at all, between his father's back and the noise of a country's worth of neighbours settling their gear along a riverbank none of them had camped on before, and he remembers, of that whole night, mostly the cold that came up off the gravel through the ground and the sound, endless and low, of the river below the camp, which none of them yet knew to listen to.

## II. Of the Man Alone at the Ford

In the grey light before sunrise the lad woke to find the mist lifting off the water in ropes, and the west bank, which the host had gone to sleep expecting to see thick with the king's kin and their households and the spears of the hills mustered against them, empty.

There was one man on it.

He sat on a flat stone at the head of the ford with a spear laid across his knees, and there was no one else with him: no household, no fire, no line of spears drawn up at his back. The lad looked up and down the far bank for the rest of them, the way a man looks twice at a gate he expects to find shut and finds standing open, and found nothing but turf and the track going up from the ford toward the vein and toward Dùn ìseal beyond it, empty in the thinning mist.

Word went along the fires quicker than any man could carry it on his own two feet, the way such word always does: that the king had come ahead of his kin with a handful of his own household, and had sent that handful back up the road again in the night; that his kin, for all their coming in with tents and stewards two summers past, had not come to the ford at all, each house waiting on the others, each afraid that while its own spears stood at a river its cousins' spears would be settling accounts on its own hills behind its back.
