They had already begun, it was said, to quarrel over what the old man would leave, before he had left anything.

Nobody in the host of Dùn dhearg believed it at first. Then, all down the bank at once, as such things happen, everybody did, and a shout went up along the whole mile of fires that startled birds off the river a long way downstream.

The man on the stone stood.

The lad had heard all his life, at hearths from Caol shean to the double bank, how the king was said to be a big man, and found, looking across the water at him in the grey of that morning, that the king was not big as he had pictured him, and was bigger. He came down to the water's edge without hurrying and stood there with the spear held loose in one hand, and the grey of his hair was the only grey thing on that whole far bank of green turf and dark river-stone; and the lad, who had a spear of his own in his fist and three thousand spears at his back, felt something come across the water to him that he could only afterward liken to the warmth off a kiln a long way from the fire, and was afraid of it, and could not have said why he was afraid, since the man had not moved to threaten anyone and stood, if anything, unnaturally still.

Artair mac Fhearghail came down the bank to where the lad stood with his father, and looked a long while across the river before he spoke.

"He has left his kin behind him and come to the water alone," the old holder said, half to himself. "Either that is a great courage, or he does not believe we will come at him at all. We had best show him which of the two he has misjudged."

## III. Of the First Day

The first rush went into the ford at sunrise, before the mist was fully off the water. Two hundred went in together, or near it, with a roar that the lad felt in his chest before he heard it as words, and the shallow water broke white round their knees as they crossed; and the king went into the river to meet them without any haste that the lad could see, wading out from his stone until the water was at his thighs, and the front of the rush reached him about the middle of the ford, where the gravel drops and the current runs strongest.

The lad was young yet and had been kept back with the boys who minded the fires, so he watched the whole of it from the bank, and he said afterward, more than once, that he could not rightly tell what he had seen, only what came after it. The king did not fight the way the lad had watched men fight at a boundary quarrel or a cattle-raid, one man squared against another and then a third coming up behind the first. He fought, the lad said, the way a river fights a bank: one continuous taking-away of whatever came against him, no single blow answered by a single blow, so that spears went into the place where he had stood and found him already somewhere else, and men went down round him in a ring in the shallow water, and the ring did not close because there was no man left near enough to close it. The current below him ran red before the rush had been in the water the length of time it takes to say a short prayer, and the rush broke on him the way a wave breaks on a rock too old to be moved by any one tide, and what was left of it came back across the ford in worse order than it had gone in.

The king waded back to the west bank and sat down again on his stone, and did not seem, from that distance, so much as out of breath.

A cousin of the lad's mother, a big quiet man who had carried a spear at every boundary dispute the eastern country had seen in twenty years and never once come home from one with so much as a scratch to show for it, had gone in with the first rush and had not come out of the river at all, neither on his own two legs nor carried by anyone else's, and it was some while before anyone at the fires could say for certain into which of the several places a man might vanish in a press like that he had gone. His wife asked after him at every fire down the bank before noon, and was told, at each one, only that no one had seen him fall, which was not the same as being told he had not, and by evening she had stopped asking and sat instead with her children at her own fire, watching the water.

They came at him again before midday, in smaller lines this time, testing the water above and below the main crossing where the channel ran deep enough to swim a man off his feet, hoping to come at him from the side while the ford held his eye; and he was there before each line reached the bank, wherever there was, so that a household that had planned to cross unseen a spear's cast upstream found itself, instead, wading back through its own dead not a quarter of an hour after it had gone in dry-shod. By early afternoon they had begun throwing spears from the bank rather than closing with him at all, a whole season's work of the spear-makers spent inside two hours, and the lad heard men say, at the fires that dusk, that some of those throws had struck him true and did not seem, from what could be seen at that distance, to matter to him one way or the other.

At dusk the host drew back from the water to its own fires, as a beaten thing draws back to lick whatever can be licked, and counted its own losses, and did not care for the count. The king walked back to his stone in the last of the light and sat, and the lad, who had gone down near the water's edge with two other boys to fill a skin, saw him kneel at the river's lip and wash his hands in it before he went back to sitting, the way any man washes his hands after a day's hard work, and found that stranger than anything else he had watched that whole day.

## IV. Of the Second Day

By the second morning the dead had begun to dam the ford.

They lay so thick at the shallows below the crossing, where the current dropped them, that the water backed up behind them and spread wide over the gravel on either side, slow and red and warm where the day before it had run cold and clear; and the men of the east, coming down to the water that second morning, found they must climb over their own dead to reach any part of the river shallow enough to cross at all, which no household among them had ever had to do at any ford before, salt or fresh.

The lad went into the water on the second day, being older by one day and one night than he had been the first, and thought himself no longer a boy to be kept at the fires. He remembered afterward very little of it in order: the cold of the river round his legs and then, further out, a warmth in it he had not looked for, as though he waded into the outflow of a spring rather than the same current that had run cold past his own feet the evening before; a grey-browed face above him, closer than he had ever thought to stand to it, neither angry nor gentle, only still, the way a deep pool is still; and a hand taking the spear out of his two hands the way a mother takes a knife from a child too small yet to be trusted with the edge of it, without violence, almost without haste, as if the taking cost the hand nothing at all. After that he was on the east bank again, face down in trampled mud with the noise of the river in his ears, and it was some while before he understood that he was not among the dead damming it, only close to being.

He lay there the better part of that day, coming to himself in pieces, and heard the rushes go into the water without him, one after another, from before noon until the light began to fail, and heard them come back each time in smaller numbers than they had gone in with.

That second night the host of Dùn dhearg met at its fires, all of it that could still stand, and there was less shouting in that meeting than there had been the night before, and more silence. Men who had spoken loudest of holding the ford two nights before sat now with their eyes on the ground between their own feet, and one, a holder of grazing along the northern edge of that country who had lost two sons to the river in as many days, said outright that he did not care any longer what the king's kin did or did not do with their shares, and that he would take what was left of his own household home to bury its dead in its own ground rather than add a third son to the river's count.

Nobody answered him with anger, that being a grief no man at those fires could fairly grudge another. Artair mac Fhearghail let him finish, and let the silence that came after him sit a while before he spoke at all, which the lad thought afterward had been its own kind of answer.

Some others said, plainly, that the thing should be let go: that a river ford was no prize worth the whole strength of the east country, and that they should take what remained of their spears home to their own hills before there were none left to take home at all. It was Artair mac Fhearghail, sitting with his own spear laid across his knees the way the man on the far bank had laid his, who answered it at last with the only counsel anyone in that gathering had to set against it.

"No one man can hold a ford forever," the old holder said, and his voice did not rise for this any more than it had risen the morning before. "Whatever he is, under the years and the grey hair, he told me himself, before any of us came to this water, that he is flesh, and flesh comes to an end somewhere, the same as the sea comes to an end of a cliff, given water enough and time enough. We have given him two days of the one. Let every spear the east has go into that river together on the third day, and go on going in, and not draw back for anything short of his falling, and we will come, between us, to the end of him, because there is no other counsel here that does not end in going home with nothing, which I for one will not carry back to my own hearth while I have legs to stand at a ford on."

Nobody spoke against it after that, though a good few, the lad among them, said nothing for it either, only sat with their own thinking. It was, as Artair had said, the only counsel anyone had, and a host with nothing else to hold onto took it the way a drowning man takes whatever piece of wood comes past him, without asking first whether it will bear his weight.

## V. Of the Third Day

On the third day every spear the east country had went into the river together, at first light, before the mist was off the water, and did not come out of it again by twos and threes as they had the two days before, but stayed in, wave folding over wave the way the tide folds over a rock at the turn, however far back the rock throws each wave that reaches it.

The lad went in with the rest, being neither dead nor so wounded that his father's household would let him stay dry-shod while every other household sent its whole strength; and he found the water above his waist that morning where the dead of the two days before had dammed it higher than any ford on that river had ever stood, red through and through and warm as a bath left too long on the fire, and it stank in a way he never after smelled without the whole of that day coming back to him whole. He was far back in the press and saw the king himself only in glimpses, over the shoulders and between the spears of the men ahead of him: a grey head standing in the middle of a river with the whole strength of a country closing on it from three sides at once, and the strength breaking round that one head and closing again behind it the way a rising tide breaks round a sea-rock and closes behind, over and over, the whole day long, while the sun went from behind them to overhead to behind the west bank.

By the afternoon there was a light on the water where the king stood, low and close along the river's surface, of no colour the lad had a word for, dark and shining together the way no true fire is, so that where it touched the current the current gave off a kind of steam though the day was warm and windless; and men near enough to be within it, coming back afterward to the bank too spent to go in again, said among themselves, low, that they had seen in it every colour there was and none of them, and would say no more than that however they were pressed, then or after.

The king's kin did not come. Whatever else was true of that day, that was true of it entire: no household from Dùn ìseal, no spear of the hills, no rider on the western track. Twice that afternoon a cry went up along the host that dust had been seen on the road down from the vein, and twice men turned to look, some with hope of relief for the old man and some with dread of it, and both times the dust proved to be nothing but wind lifting the dry summer's dirt off a track that no one at all was riding down. The east had the ford and the river and the whole strength of the man in it entirely to answer for, and by the second false cry no one troubled any longer to turn and look.

At sunset he was still standing, in the middle of the ford, the host round him on every side and the dead round him higher than his own knees, and the river going over the dam of them in a low red fall where the shallows had been. He was not beaten. The lad, looking across at him in the last light with what strength he had left in his own legs, was as sure of that as he was sure of anything that whole day: that not one man of the whole east country had beaten him, and that no one man among them, not Artair mac Fhearghail himself with sixty years' grievance behind his arm, could have. It was only that there was no end to the men coming at him, and there was, somewhere in him however deep it was hidden, an end; and between those two facts, and nothing else, the whole of that third day turned.

## VI. Of the Fall

He fell in the dark of the third night, and no man afterward could say which spear had done it, or from which household it had come, and no household of the whole east country would let it be said, then or later, that the blow had been its own. It is told that when he went down the light went out of the river all at once, the way a coal goes out when a bucket of water is thrown square onto it, and that the water, which had run warm through three days no matter how cold the nights between them, ran cold from that hour, cold enough that men standing in it felt it turn under their own legs and cried out at the change before they understood what the cry was for.

The host stood a long while in the dark water after that, not knowing, for what felt the longest stretch of the whole three days, what it was that it had done, or what a man was meant to do next having done it; and some began to weep where they stood, waist-deep in a cold river in the dark, and could not afterward have said why they wept, since it was the very thing the whole east country had crossed three days of blood to bring about. Artair mac Fhearghail himself, who had spoken the counsel that sent them in on the third day and would carry that all his life whichever way the telling of it went, stood longest of any of them at the place where the king had gone down, saying nothing, until two of his own household came into the water after him and led him out by the arms as a man leads out an old horse that has stood too long in a flooded field and no longer trusts its own legs to find the bank.

They drew him out of the river at last onto the west bank, to the flat stone where he had sat the first grey morning of it, and laid him there. He lay on his back with his eyes open to the last of the stars going out overhead, and his face, when they brought a torch near enough to see it by, was the face of a young man, unlined, with nothing in it that had not been there, by every telling anyone could set against it, in the grove itself at the very beginning of things. Word went afterward, from those closest to Dùn ìseal, that the mason's own line, which keeps the years of its dead beside their names, gave his as four thousand six hundred and twenty-six; that he had been king since the grove and had never once given it up in all that span; and that no man now living, east of the vein or west of it, had taken it from him with his own single hand, however many hands together had done, between them, what no one of them alone could have.

Before the dawn a saying went along the whole east bank, fire to fire, the way such sayings do when a thing has happened too large for any one teller to carry alone:

*Cha do leag aon duine e; leag an sluagh uile e.*
No one man brought him down; the whole host brought him down.

## VII. Of the Fire on the East Bank

The lad had waded out of the river some while before that saying reached his own fire, and sat by it wrapped in a dead man's cloak because his own had gone into the water with him on the second day and never come out again, too spent to feel the cold he must have been sitting in, and too spent, for a long while, to speak at all.

The men about that fire had been three days at a ford that had cost the east country more of its own blood than any raid or any famine any of them could tell of, and they wanted, as men will after such a thing, to have some word of it from someone who had been close enough to bring one back; and since the lad was known to have gone into the river both on the second day and the third, and to have come out of it alive both times, they asked him, when he had got his breath and a little of the fire's warmth into him, what the king had been like, close to.

The lad did not answer at once. He turned the question over the way a man turns a coin he is not sure he has been given the right change in, weighing what there was to say against what there was no way of saying, three days and a whole country's dead against a boy of sixteen sitting at one fire among a mile of them.

"He was warm," the lad said at last, and that was all he said, and he looked into the fire rather than at any of the men who had asked him, and none of them pressed him further for more, that night or, so far as the east country's own telling goes, on any night after it.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years GE 1 – 250

- <a id="ev-I-0080b"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *The vigil and the crowning* (Doire ghlas). Ailean keeps watch by the seven fires for seven nights, fasting, a night for each coal. On the eighth night the coals are cold, and Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè about him. He names Ailean Rìgh Chlann nan Dè, king of the godkin, and puts into him the power that was in the coals. Of that power Ailean tells no one while he lives.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-1000"><em>Coinneach follows his brother north</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1001"><em>The camp beyond the oaks</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1002"><em>Voices heard on the fifth night</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1003"><em>The grove fills with light</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ○ Same place <a href="#ev-EII-1004"><em>The six pots left cold</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-1005"><em>Coinneach finds his brother warm at dawn</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-1006"><em>"They named me king"</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1000"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *Coinneach follows his brother north* (Doire ghlas). Coinneach mac Shuibhne, unable to wait out a year of silence, sets off after his brother with a sack of oatcake and a skin of buttermilk, following the roads he judges Ailean must have taken toward the grove of Doire ghlas.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1001"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *The camp beyond the oaks* (Doire ghlas). Coinneach comes within sight of the seven fires at Doire ghlas and finds he cannot cross into the ring of oaks. Coimhdeach na Fine allows him to camp at the tree-line and no nearer, and he keeps his own vigil there through the seven nights of his brother's watch.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1002"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *Voices heard on the fifth night* (Doire ghlas). On the fifth night of the vigil Coinneach hears, low under the sound of the fires, what he takes for voices, one of them shaped almost like his brother's speech though fallen into a rhythm Ailean never used. He never swears to more than that he heard something.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1003"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *The grove fills with light* (Doire ghlas). On the eighth night, when the seven fires go dark together, Coinneach watches the grove of Doire ghlas fill with a light that is not firelight, and sees shapes moving among the oaks. His feet will not carry him past the tree-line to follow them.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1004"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *The six pots left cold* (Doire ghlas). At dawn the six pots that carried Ailean's fires north are found lying empty on the leaves of Doire ghlas, their turf lids scattered, and the pale stone that held the seventh coal lies among them, giving no light but warm to the touch.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1005"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *Coinneach finds his brother warm at dawn* (Doire ghlas). Ailean walks out of the grove at morning and catches his stumbling brother by the arm. Coinneach feels a warmth in it like a hearthstone long after the fire is swept, and knows before any word is said that the night has changed his brother.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1006"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1** — *"They named me king"* (Doire ghlas). Ailean tells his brother only this much of the night in the grove: that he has been named king. He says nothing of who named him, of what a king might be king of, or of what was put into him, and Coinneach asks no further, having seen enough from outside the trees.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1007"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 1** — *The brothers turn south* (Doire ghlas). Ailean gathers the six empty pots onto his shoulder-pole, leaves the pale seventh stone lying uncovered among the leaves of Doire ghlas, and sets out south with his brother, never lighting the six fires again.
- <a id="ev-EII-1008"></a>**7 an Lùnastal, GE 1** — *Ailean passes Na Glinn Àrda*. Ailean walks south past the households of Clann na Ceiste in Na Glinn Àrda without turning aside to any hearth, though he has kin enough among them to be fed and questioned there.
- <a id="ev-EII-1009"></a>**8 an Lùnastal, GE 1** — *Eleven kin walk south with him*. Households of Clann na Ceiste near Na Glinn Àrda leave byre and field to follow Ailean south, eleven in all, none able afterward to give a better reason than a feeling not to be argued with. The king shares out Coinneach's sack among them on the road.
- <a id="ev-I-0081"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, GE 1** — *Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings* (Dùn ìseal). Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove, comes down to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and takes it, and brings the households of the valleys about it under his hand: the first kingdom of the godkin. How he won, none who stood against him could say. He throws up the hill's first ring of bank. He is king from that day until his death, and gives the kingship to no one. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche, which names those who held the hill; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1007"><em>The brothers turn south</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1008"><em>Ailean passes Na Glinn Àrda</em>, 7 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1009"><em>Eleven kin walk south with him</em>, 8 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1010"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, GE 1** — *The bare ring in the frost*. Twice on the road south the company sleeps in the open, and both mornings the frost that silvers the field leaves a bare, warm ring the size of a sleeping man where Ailean lay, as it did at his feet in the grove.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1011"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, GE 1** — *Coinneach keeps the first telling*. Walking south behind his brother, Coinneach turns over what little he saw from outside the ring of oaks and fits it into an account he is careful never to swell beyond what he truly witnessed, the seed of the telling Clann na Ceiste keep of the seven nights.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1012"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, GE 1** — *The lad who brought the water* (Dùn ìseal). The knapper's son of Dùn ìseal is sent to the hill's crown with water for the man who has just taken it unopposed, and is asked his name and whether the spear he carries is his father's best. Told to take it home and to tell his father the king will want a great many more.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1013"></a>**13 an t-Samhain, GE 1** — *The valleys come in to the hill* (Dùn ìseal). Through the first year the households of the valleys about Dùn ìseal come in to the king one after another, unsummoned, bringing hides, pots, and whatever else they judge fitting, and with their gifts their grazing and their old quarrels, for a telling to be held over them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1014"></a>**17 an t-Samhain, GE 1** — *The first judgement on the hill* (Dùn ìseal). Two households of Dùn ìseal bring before the king a strip of pasture each has claimed for a generation. He asks one question, of whose cattle grazed it before the boundary stone was last moved, and gives the strip back in a sentence. Neither household ever brings the matter before him again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1015"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 1** — *The king's order to the flint-pit* (Dùn ìseal). The flint-pit behind the houses of Dùn ìseal is set, on the king's own word, to cut spearheads by the score rather than as they are needed, the first order of its kind on the hill. The knapper's son is set to the work alongside his father before that year's leaves are down.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1016"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, GE 1** — *The warmth with no fire* (Dùn ìseal). In the first hard winter on the hill, a girl of Dùn ìseal stands near the king's own untended fire at night and finds herself warmed through though no flame burns close enough to account for it. She keeps the telling to herself for years before it is believed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1017"></a>**30 an Giblean, GE 2** — *The line of the bank pegged in the snow* (Dùn ìseal). In the depth of the same winter the king walks the crown of Dùn ìseal setting ash pegs with his own hand, marking a line that takes in the old byres and ground for houses not yet built. The households break the frozen turf along it through the worst of the frost.
- <a id="ev-EII-1018"></a>**29 an Cèitean, GE 2** — *Flint tools finish the bank's ditch* (Dùn ìseal). When the antler mattocks digging the new ditch at Dùn ìseal blunt faster than they can be sharpened in the frost, the flint-pit sends up scrapers of worked stone to finish the work, so that the hill's first bank is cut as much with flint as with iron.
- <a id="ev-EII-1019"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2** — *Muireall and Gormshuil brought to the hill* (Dùn ìseal). As the frost breaks a small company comes down from Na Glinn Àrda to Dùn ìseal: Muireall, the king's wife, and Gormshuil, his young daughter, with a few kin and hands beside them. The hill, which had thought the king had no household of his own, falls quiet to let them through the new gate.
- <a id="ev-EII-1020"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, GE 2** — *Dòmhnall born within the new bank* (Dùn ìseal). A son is born to Muireall inside the finished bank of Dùn ìseal, the first of the king's children to draw breath on ground he holds, and the hill takes it as a settled thing that the king has come to stay among them.
- <a id="ev-EII-1021"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, GE 2** — *A spearhead given for nothing* (Dùn ìseal). The knapper cuts a spearhead finer than any he has made that year, for no order and no payment, and sends it up to the king's fire on the birth of the king's son. He will not say why, only that the giving seemed owed.
- <a id="ev-I-0082"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, GE 9** — *The bank of Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1017"><em>The line of the bank pegged in the snow</em>, 30 an Giblean, GE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1018"><em>Flint tools finish the bank's ditch</em>, 29 an Cèitean, GE 2</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1022"><em>Gormshuil set to keep the gate</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, GE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1022"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, GE 9** — *Gormshuil set to keep the gate* (Dùn ìseal). A child of eight, Gormshuil is given the gate of the new bank to watch, and takes to naming every face and dog on the hill so her father will have someone to tell him at evening what the day brought. The habit holds her the rest of her life.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0082"><em>The bank of Dùn ìseal</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, GE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1023"></a>**4 an Cèitean, GE 10** — *Fearchar born on the hill* (Dùn ìseal). A second son is born to the king within the new bank of Dùn ìseal and named Fearchar; he is the first of the king's children to open his eyes on the hill itself, and will hold it for his father in his time.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0082"><em>The bank of Dùn ìseal</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, GE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0083"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, GE 18** — *Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1024"><em>Word of the red hill's woman</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1024"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, GE 18** — *Word of the red hill's woman* (Dùn ìseal). A salt-fish trader carries word up to Dùn ìseal of a woman holding a red hill on the shore of the great lake in her own right, answering to no king. Gormshuil asks her father whether it means trouble; he tells her trouble comes from nearer at hand.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0083"><em>Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1025"></a>**7 am Màrt, GE 24** — *Muireall's dying words* (Dùn ìseal). In her last two nights Muireall speaks to her daughter of small things, a comb, a debt owed, and warns that her youngest son Fearchar has a temper that will want watching before it finds him trouble he cannot talk his way out of.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1026"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 24** — *The king hears three cases the day Muireall is buried* (Dùn ìseal). Two days after Muireall is put in the ground the king comes in from the valleys, stands by the mound, then goes into the hearing-house and gives judgement on three waiting cases before dark. He does not speak her name again where any ear can catch it.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0084"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, GE 27** — *Gormshuil nic Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Ailein, the king's daughter, holds the hill of Dùn ìseal for her father while he rides beyond it, and the list names her second of the Stone Kings; she is the first woman named in any list on Dia-thìr. She was born before the grove, and has none of the long years. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1019"><em>Muireall and Gormshuil brought to the hill</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1027"></a>**21 am Màrt, GE 27** — *The drive to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh* (Dùn ìseal). With the hardest winter in living memory emptying the byres and the king three valleys off, Gormshuil drives the standing herds two days through drifted snow to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, walking the whole way herself so no beast's fodder is spent on a rider. She loses none.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1028"></a>**16 an t-Iuchar, GE 27** — *The two fingers that never bent again* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil comes off the winter drive with two fingers of her left hand frozen stiff, and wears a glove over them in company from that year to her death without ever speaking of how they were got.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1029"></a>**18 an Gearran, GE 30** — *The king weds Sorcha* (Dùn ìseal). Ailean takes a second wife, Sorcha, a woman of the valleys younger than his own eldest daughter, and the hill notes the matter and does not remark on it aloud, as it has grown used to doing with the king's household.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1030"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, GE 33** — *Coinneach's counsel on the bank* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil tells Coinneach that her father does not age while she has begun to grey. He tells her what he saw the night the fires went out in the grove, and counsels her to keep from asking her father what it cost him, as he has kept from asking these thirty years.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1031"></a>**25 an Dàmhair, GE 38** — *Somhairle born* (Dùn ìseal). Sorcha bears the king a son, Somhairle, in the thirty-eighth year after the grove, the first child of Sorcha's line to be counted among those got after the grove.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1032"></a>**20 am Faoilleach, GE 40** — *Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Ruadh, who held An Cnoc Ruadh by the lake before any of the valleys came in to the king, dies an old woman in her own hall, unsworn and unbeaten; her household keeps the palisade after her and the lake shore does not change its ways for her going.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0083"><em>Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1033"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, GE 45** — *Iain Dubh born* (Dùn ìseal). A second son of Sorcha's, Iain Dubh, is born to the king on the hill, the youngest of Ailean's children to be reckoned among Rìghrean na Cloiche in his turn.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1034"></a>**19 am Màrt, GE 55** — *Coinneach dies, Sloinneadh a' Chlachair passed whole* (Dùn ìseal). Coinneach mac Shuibhne dies an old man, the first teller of the king's deeds, having taught Gormshuil Sloinneadh a' Chlachair word for word as Coimhdeach na Fine gave it in the grove. She is, after her father, the second on the hill to carry the whole of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0080b"><em>The vigil and the crowning</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1035"></a>**18 an Gearran, GE 60** — *The grandchildren take the king for her son* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil's own grandchildren, seeing the king young at the gate each autumn beside a bent grey grandmother, take him for her son rather than her father, and she lets the mistake stand rather than make them carry a harder truth too young.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1036"></a>**7 am Màrt, GE 76** — *Gormshuil's deathbed question* (Dùn ìseal). On the second night of her dying Gormshuil asks her father whether it hurts to stay young. He does not answer her in words, and says her name once instead, the way a man says a name he does not expect to say again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1037"></a>**5 an Giblean, GE 76** — *Gormshuil dies* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Ailein dies an old woman of eighty-one, the king's eldest daughter and second of Rìghrean na Cloiche. He sits by her a night and a day and helps lift the turf over her with his own hands, as he did for no one since Muireall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1038"></a>**17 an Giblean, GE 76** — *The hill understands na Bliadhnachan Fada* (Dùn ìseal). Watching Gormshuil, who carried her father's stubbornness and stillness but not his years, put into the ground beside a father who looks her grandson's age, the hill understands at last that na Bliadhnachan Fada are the grove's alone, and pass to no child got before it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0084"><em>Gormshuil nic Ailein</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, GE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1039"></a>**16 an Cèitean, GE 76** — *Dòmhnall takes the hill* (Dùn ìseal). Dòmhnall Clachach, seventy-four and looking a young man still, takes up the hearing-house his half-sister held since the grove, and says he supposes he had better learn to count who comes and goes, since no one is left who learned it from the start as she did.
- <a id="ev-I-0085"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107** — *Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones* (Dùn ìseal). Dòmhnall Clachach, a son of the king and third of the Stone Kings, holds the hill after Gormshuil and sets marker stones along the valley below it to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1020"><em>Dòmhnall born within the new bank</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, GE 2</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1021"><em>A spearhead given for nothing</em>, 7 an t-Samhain, GE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1039"><em>Dòmhnall takes the hill</em>, 16 an Cèitean, GE 76</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1500"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107** — *The old men disagree at the setting of the stones* (Dùn ìseal). As Dòmhnall Clachach walks the eastern boundary with his stone-setters, the old men of neighbouring households cannot agree, standing on the very ground, where a line has always run, for the becks have shifted and their memories have not moved with them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0085"><em>Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1501"></a>**23 an Gearran, GE 115** — *A grazing quarrel judged by the stones* (Dùn ìseal). Two households dispute a marker on the eastern slope, each swearing it stands to the wrong side of the old line. Dòmhnall Clachach settles it from his own memory of the setting, and both sides go home certain, for the first time, that a stone remembers better than a grandfather.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0085"><em>Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1502"></a>**21 an Cèitean, GE 116** — *Dòmhnall doubts his own stones* (Dùn ìseal). Walking home from the judgement at the marker, Dòmhnall Clachach understands that he has settled the quarrel only because his own long memory outlasts any old man's, and that the stones, once he is gone from the hill, will have no one left to ask which story is true.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0085"><em>Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1503"></a>**22 an Giblean, GE 142** — *Griogar's household turns back the king's riders*. In a valley to the north-west a hard old man called Griogar meets two of the king's riders with spears and no parley, the first household in years to refuse the king's word outright rather than simply keep clear of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-1502"><em>Dòmhnall doubts his own stones</em>, 21 an Cèitean, GE 116</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0086"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, GE 147** — *The first named storm*. A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.
- <a id="ev-I-0087"></a>**28 an Gearran, GE 147** — *The shell road broken* (Seann Warr). The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.
- <a id="ev-EII-1504"></a>**8 an t-Sultain, GE 147** — *Storm damage within the bank of Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The first named storm strips the thatch from six houses of Dùn ìseal and levels a seventh to its footings. Dòmhnall Clachach spends the night holding roofs down with rope and his own weight, and the hill loses its summer hay and two sheds of the flint-pit, but no one within the bank.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0086"><em>The first named storm</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, GE 147</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1505"></a>**30 an Dàmhair, GE 148** — *Word of the broken causeway reaches Dùn ìseal* (Seann Warr). Traders driven from their usual road by flooded fords bring Dòmhnall Clachach word that the shell causeway of Seann Warr stands broken in three places, and that the Seann-Dhaoine have watched it stay broken through a winter without coming out to mend it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0087"><em>The shell road broken</em>, 28 an Gearran, GE 147</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1506"></a>**25 am Faoilleach, GE 160** — *Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence* (Dùn ìseal). Labhrainn, elder of an old household on the western slope, refuses the line his own father stood by at its setting, the first quarrel in Dòmhnall Clachach's time that is fought not over ground but over a settling that no longer needs an old man's word to stand.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0085"><em>Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, GE 107</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1507"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, GE 161** — *Dòmhnall sits an evening with Labhrainn* (Dùn ìseal). After judging against him, Dòmhnall Clachach rides out to Labhrainn's byre and sits a whole evening over the household's own brewing, asking not about the stone but the ground itself, and gives the old man back in listening something the stones had quietly taken from him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-1506"><em>Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence</em>, 25 am Faoilleach, GE 160</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1508"></a>**4 an Lùnastal, GE 189** — *Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley*. Riding with a dozen men against the household that turned back his riders, Ailean Mòr's son Fearchar takes a spear through the thigh that will not heal straight, though the wound should by any ordinary reckoning have killed him.
- <a id="ev-EII-1509"></a>**6 an t-Iuchar, GE 200** — *Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste*. Somhairle, a son of Ailean Mòr some hundred and sixty years old and looking fifteen, asks his father for no land and no herds, only leave to live among the households of Na Glinn Àrda and be counted a single mouth at a single hearth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-1508"><em>Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley</em>, 4 an Lùnastal, GE 189</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1510"></a>**8 an Giblean, GE 201** — *Somhairle tells Dòmhnall why he wants no share*. Visiting his brother in Na Glinn Àrda, Dòmhnall Clachach is told that Somhairle wants to be believed when he names whose son follows whose, once the kin have grown too many for any one hearth to hold the account, and that a man who holds land judges his own kin differently.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-1509"><em>Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste</em>, 6 an t-Iuchar, GE 200</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1511"></a>**7 an Cèitean, GE 210** — *The chair of woven birch is built for Fearchar* (Dùn ìseal). The household carpenters of Dùn ìseal build Fearchar Bacach a chair of woven birch with long carrying-poles, unasked, so that he need no longer hide the leg that never set straight, and he takes to being carried with something like relief.
- <a id="ev-EII-1512"></a>**9 an Gearran, GE 225** — *Uisdean born on An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). A son is born by the lake shore to a household of An Cnoc Ruadh's holding line and named Uisdean; the watch on the palisade marks his birth with a fire on the point, as it marks every birth in that hall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-1032"><em>Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh</em>, 20 am Faoilleach, GE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0088"></a>**27 an Giblean, GE 227** — *Fearchar Bacach* (Dùn ìseal). Fearchar Bacach, the lame, a son of the king lamed in his father's wars, holds Dùn ìseal under the king after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1508"><em>Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley</em>, 4 an Lùnastal, GE 189</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1511"><em>The chair of woven birch is built for Fearchar</em>, 7 an Cèitean, GE 210</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1513"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, GE 227** — *Dòmhnall asks his father for the north* (Dùn ìseal). At a gathering below Dùn ìseal, Dòmhnall Clachach asks Ailean Mòr for ground still unsettled rather than the hill he has held a hundred and fifty years. His father grants him the north and no guidance in how to keep it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0088"><em>Fearchar Bacach</em>, 27 an Giblean, GE 227</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1514"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 227** — *Fearchar Bacach holds Dùn ìseal as Dòmhnall rides north* (Dùn ìseal). Dòmhnall Clachach leaves Dùn ìseal with a company of twelve, and the hill takes his brother Fearchar, already sitting its judgements from the chair of birch, for its holder without a word of dispute.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0088"><em>Fearchar Bacach</em>, 27 an Giblean, GE 227</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1515"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, GE 250** — *Uisdean Mòr takes An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean, five-and-twenty, takes up the holding of An Cnoc Ruadh on the western lake shore after those before him, an old line owing nothing to Dùn ìseal or to any king of the hill-folk.

## The Years GE 251 – 500

- <a id="ev-EII-1516"></a>**5 an t-Ògmhios, GE 262** — *Uilleam Faire born on An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). A boatwright's son is born on the lake shore in the twelfth year of Uisdean's holding, and grows up believing, as every child of that hill does, that the water below it has always belonged to his own people alone.
- <a id="ev-EII-1517"></a>**25 am Màrt, GE 267** — *The households dig the ditch across the neck* (Cathair dhearg). Every household of An Cnoc Ruadh turns out to cut the ditch across the low saddle of ground where the hill's rise meets the land, and to raise the oak palisade on the spoil bank behind it.
- <a id="ev-I-0089"></a>**29 am Màrt, GE 267** — *Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1515"><em>Uisdean Mòr takes An Cnoc Ruadh</em>, 31 an Lùnastal, GE 250</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1516"><em>Uilleam Faire born on An Cnoc Ruadh</em>, 5 an t-Ògmhios, GE 262</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1517"><em>The households dig the ditch across the neck</em>, 25 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1518"></a>**19 an Lùnastal, GE 282** — *Uisdean tells the watch why the wall stands* (Cathair dhearg). Walking the palisade by night with the young Uilleam Faire, Uisdean speaks of na Bliadhnachan Fada of the king and of the valleys brought in to the south and east, and does not say whether An Cnoc Ruadh will swear when its turn comes.
- <a id="ev-EII-1519"></a>**19 an Lùnastal, GE 289** — *The king's company camps unannounced on the shore* (Cathair dhearg). The king comes west along the lake shore with some two hundred spears at the end of a summer, camps below the hill, and sends up no word of his business to Uisdean or to any of An Cnoc Ruadh's households.
- <a id="ev-EII-1520"></a>**17 an t-Sultain, GE 289** — *The first burning of the palisade* (Cathair dhearg). On the last watch before dawn the new palisade catches along its whole length at once in a low, dark, shining flame that no one on the wall can trace to any torch or spark. The hill beats it out by morning with lake water and green hides.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1521"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, GE 289** — *Uisdean rebuilds with green oak* (Cathair dhearg). Rather than wait out a season for seasoned timber, Uisdean sets the households to rebuilding the palisade at once with green oak cut from his own hill, against every carpenter's word of how badly it will burn.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1522"></a>**16 an Dàmhair, GE 289** — *The king's spearmen trade through the winter* (Cathair dhearg). Neither striking camp nor pressing nearer the wall, the king's company fishes the shallows and mends its gear through the winter, and trades salted fish and small goods with households of the hill who find it easier than the long carry round the lake.
- <a id="ev-EII-1523"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290** — *Reothadh an Rìgh* (Cathair dhearg). In the early days of an t-Ògmhios, when the year should long since have been past any frost, a single clear night puts a white rime on the whole shore. The hill's old women name it from that morning Reothadh an Rìgh.
- <a id="ev-I-0089a"></a>**7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290** — *The Red Hill bends the knee* (Cathair dhearg). Ailean Mòr comes west to the Red Hill, where the palisade of Uisdean Mòr has twice burned. Uisdean comes down to the lake shore and kneels to him. The Red Hill keeps its own holders and its own list, and swears to the king and not to Dùn ìseal; so neither list names the other.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1518"><em>Uisdean tells the watch why the wall stands</em>, 19 an Lùnastal, GE 282</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1519"><em>The king's company camps unannounced on the shore</em>, 19 an Lùnastal, GE 289</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1522"><em>The king's spearmen trade through the winter</em>, 16 an Dàmhair, GE 289</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1523"><em>Reothadh an Rìgh</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1524"></a>**20 an t-Iuchar, GE 290** — *The second burning of the palisade* (Cathair dhearg). On the night of Reothadh an Rìgh the green oak takes in the same low, dark flame as before, and burns in less time than seasoned wood had, leaving nothing standing for the households to save.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1525"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, GE 290** — *Uilleam throws the water and never learns whose fire it was* (Cathair dhearg). Uilleam Faire is first to the second fire with a hide-skin of water, and throws it into the worst of the blaze without saving a hand's-breadth of the wall. He carries the question of whose fire it was the rest of his life.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0089a"><em>The Red Hill bends the knee</em>, 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1526"></a>**20 an t-Sultain, GE 290** — *The king's company departs east* (Cathair dhearg). Within the month of Uisdean's swearing the king's company strikes its tents and goes back east the way it came, and does not return to the lake shore.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0089a"><em>The Red Hill bends the knee</em>, 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1527"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, GE 290** — *Dùghall first walks the whole road to the shore* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall, nine years old, is let walk the whole three days down to the Seann-Dhaoine's shore with his father for the first time, rather than being turned back with the pack-ponies at the last ridge. He learns the trade is carried by gesture alone, in silence kept on both sides.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1528"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, GE 290** — *Mòrag born to Dòmhnall Clachach*. A daughter is born to Dòmhnall Clachach in the north country he was given, and is named Mòrag; she is the first of the king's grandchildren to carry na Bliadhnachan Fada, and grows up hard-handed among people who call her father only the stone-cutter's son.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0089a"><em>The Red Hill bends the knee</em>, 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1529"></a>**25 an Giblean, GE 291** — *The palisade raised a third time in seasoned oak* (Cathair dhearg). With no company camped below to hurry the choosing of timber, An Cnoc Ruadh rebuilds its wall a third time in properly seasoned oak. It never burns again in Uilleam Faire's lifetime.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0089a"><em>The Red Hill bends the knee</em>, 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1530"></a>**7 an Cèitean, GE 291** — *Dùn ìseal's reciters tell the swearing fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own list* (Cathair dhearg). Word of Uisdean's kneeling reaches Dùn ìseal, whose reciters tell it with the fire, the frost and the shingle scene kept whole, fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own spare list ever names it. An Cnoc Ruadh never quarrels with their telling.<span class="fn fl">✦ Fulfils <a href="#ev-I-0089a"><em>The Red Hill bends the knee</em>, 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1531"></a>**24 an Cèitean, GE 296** — *Dùghall's father gives up asking* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall's father tells his son that he tried, once, as a young man, to learn a Seann-Dhaoine word for the goods they traded, and was met with a courtesy that would not be moved. He has not asked again in forty years, and tells Dùghall which questions the shore means to answer.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1532"></a>**22 an t-Ògmhios, GE 300** — *The road passes to Dùghall* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall's father, too heavy in the knees for the bog-causeway, hands the whole carrying road to his son. Dùghall walks it alone that year with a string of ponies his in all but the naming, three days down to the shore and three days back.
- <a id="ev-I-0090"></a>**31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308** — *Strokes on the midden stones* (Seann Chwen). The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1532"><em>The road passes to Dùghall</em>, 22 an t-Ògmhios, GE 300</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1533"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, GE 308** — *The strokes on the midden stones are first counted* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall, three-and-twenty, notices that the flat stones set at the edge of one household's midden carry cut strokes, one or two to a stone, and that their number has grown by a few since he first began to notice them. He can get no answer to what they are, by word or by gesture.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0090"><em>Strokes on the midden stones</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1534"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, GE 310** — *Dùghall carries the question home unanswered* (Dùn ìseal). Dùghall tells his father what he has seen at the midden's edge. His father says he saw the same stones himself, years before, and had already judged them a question the shore did not mean to answer, and had stopped asking it.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0090"><em>Strokes on the midden stones</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1535"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, GE 312** — *Uisdean Mòr dies on An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean dies in his own bed on the hill in his eighty-seventh year, two-and-twenty years after the swearing, having outlived the fire, the frost and the king's two hundred spears.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0089"><em>Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill</em>, 29 am Màrt, GE 267</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0091"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, GE 348** — *The counting of the dead begins*. The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Dia-thìrich to take up the custom.
- <a id="ev-EII-1536"></a>**5 an Dàmhair, GE 348** — *A household mourns behind a wall of turf* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall, come down to the shore in his sixty-seventh year, wakes in the night to low voices shaped like no ordinary talk, and to boats kept ashore past their hour. He does not go out while it lasts, having learned from the hill's own griefs not to.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0091"><em>The counting of the dead begins</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, GE 348</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1537"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, GE 348** — *A fresh stroke is cut beneath an old one* (Seann Chwen). The morning after the low voices, Dùghall finds a second stroke cut fresh beneath the single old one on the newest of the midden stones, and understands, all at once, that the Seann-Dhaoine mark the going of their own dead the way a hill household marks a grave.<span class="fn fl">↩ Answers <a href="#ev-I-0091"><em>The counting of the dead begins</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, GE 348</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1538"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, GE 348** — *Dùghall counts every ridge on the shore* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall walks the whole shore that morning and finds every household keeps its own ridge of stones the same way, some bearing a single stroke, some bearing more than he can easily count. He carries the understanding home and tells his father, who is glad, at the last, to have the answer he had stopped seeking.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0091"><em>The counting of the dead begins</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, GE 348</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1539"></a>**11 am Faoilleach, GE 349** — *Dùghall keeps the counting stones from his sons* (Dùn ìseal). Dùghall says nothing more of the midden stones to his sons as they take up the road at his shoulder, judging that each will come to the ridge himself in his own year, as he had. He judges rightly.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0091"><em>The counting of the dead begins</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, GE 348</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1540"></a>**4 an Dàmhair, GE 352** — *Dùghall takes his grandson down for the last time* (Seann Chwen). One-and-seventy, and carrying the road no more himself, Dùghall takes his eldest son's boy down to the shore, both understanding without saying so that it is his last going. He finds two houses fallen roofless and fewer threads of smoke than he has ever counted there before.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0090"><em>Strokes on the midden stones</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1541"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, GE 352** — *The grandson counts the ridge and loses the count* (Seann Chwen). Dùghall sets his grandson to count the stones of the oldest ridge, and the boy loses the count twice among stones fallen and half-sunk in the turf. Dùghall tells him it is no bad thing to meet a count a man cannot finish, if the count is an honest one.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0091"><em>The counting of the dead begins</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, GE 348</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1542"></a>**1 an Dùbhlachd, GE 352** — *Dùghall trades for less on his last shore* (Dùn ìseal). Dùghall trades what hides he carried for less than the same weight once brought, and walks the three days home with his grandson bearing, unknowing, the whole weight of what the old man had carried down that road alone for two-and-sixty years.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0090"><em>Strokes on the midden stones</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1543"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, GE 352** — *Dùghall dies on the hill* (Dùn ìseal). Dùghall Ceannaiche dies on the hill that winter, an old man by any hill reckoning, and it is his grandson who takes up the packs the next summer and walks south alone, counting the midden stones before he trades a single hide, as the old man had taught him.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0090"><em>Strokes on the midden stones</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, GE 308</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0092"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389** — *The tally wall of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1544"><em>The king rides east with Somhairle to Seann Warr</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1545"><em>Somhairle first sees Balla nan Stràc</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1546"><em>The king's stillness at the wall</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1544"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389** — *The king rides east with Somhairle to Seann Warr* (Dùn ìseal). The king summons his son down from Na Glinn Àrda and rides the coast road east to Seann Warr with a small company. Somhairle, three hundred and fifty-one years old and near two hundred years among Clann na Ceiste, sees the shore he has only ever heard recited.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0092"><em>The tally wall of Seann Warr</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1545"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389** — *Somhairle first sees Balla nan Stràc* (Seann Warr). At the midden's edge of Seann Warr, Somhairle walks the whole length of the counting stones with his father and finds them built into a wall past any easy counting, the oldest courses run together into a single grey weight of strokes.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0092"><em>The tally wall of Seann Warr</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1546"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389** — *The king's stillness at the wall* (Seann Warr). The king stands a long while at the oldest of the tally stones with his hand flat against it, and tells Somhairle only that the wall has stood longer than the bank at Dùn ìseal, and perhaps longer than the grove. He says no more of it that day.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0092"><em>The tally wall of Seann Warr</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1547"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, GE 389** — *Somhairle sets Balla nan Stràc in the Line* (Seann Warr). Somhairle adds his first telling of his own to Sloinneadh a' Chlachair: the wall at Seann Warr, some three thousand strokes, grown over many lifetimes. It is the first fact he ever sets down unaided, and he keeps it carefully all his life.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0092"><em>The tally wall of Seann Warr</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, GE 389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0093"></a>**2 an t-Iuchar, GE 428** — *The count at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1548"><em>Somhairle finds the house over the dead at Seann Tarr</em>, 2 an t-Iuchar, GE 428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1548"></a>**2 an t-Iuchar, GE 428** — *Somhairle finds the house over the dead at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Sent north on a grazing dispute, Somhairle walks down to Seann Tarr and finds a household living in a long low house whose floor is paved with dressed slabs cut with strokes in fives. He does not enter, and sets the custom down without asking after it.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0093"><em>The count at Seann Tarr</em>, 2 an t-Iuchar, GE 428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1549"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, GE 470** — *A carrier brings word the strokes run thick* (Seann Warr). A carrier of hides tells Somhairle at a ford, in passing, that the tally stones are cut thicker that year than any season he has known, and thicker at all three shores at once. Somhairle rides to Seann Warr and Seann Tarr within the month and finds it true.
- <a id="ev-I-0094"></a>**6 an Giblean, GE 470** — *The bad years in the counts* (Seann Warr). The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1549"><em>A carrier brings word the strokes run thick</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, GE 470</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1550"><em>The king's one visit to the wall</em>, 6 an Giblean, GE 470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1550"></a>**6 an Giblean, GE 470** — *The king's one visit to the wall* (Seann Warr). The king rides to Seann Warr with a small company and walks Balla nan Stràc alone, his hand against the newest stone for the better part of a morning. Asked by his son what he saw, he answers only, "A people counting," and speaks of it to no one again.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0094"><em>The bad years in the counts</em>, 6 an Giblean, GE 470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1551"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, GE 470** — *Somhairle sets the thickening in the Line* (Seann Warr). Somhairle records the king's visit to the wall in the fewest words the Line will bear: that the king stood long before it and, asked what he saw, said only that he had seen a people counting. He adds no explanation of his own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0094"><em>The bad years in the counts</em>, 6 an Giblean, GE 470</a>.</span>

## The Years GE 501 – 750

- <a id="ev-I-0095"></a>**5 an Cèitean, GE 510** — *The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.
- <a id="ev-EII-1552"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, GE 512** — *Somhairle finds Clach nan Dà Stràc at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). Word of an unfinished stone reaches Na Glinn Àrda, and Somhairle rides two days south to Seann Chwen, quieter than either shore he knew. He finds the newest tally stone left with two strokes finished and a third abandoned mid-groove, the chisel marks stopped clean.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0095"><em>The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen</em>, 5 an Cèitean, GE 510</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1553"></a>**27 an Lùnastal, GE 530** — *The last smoke seen at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The carrier who first brought word of the thickening finds Seann Tarr's house over the dead standing open and cold, its hearth unlit, the household gone without any sign of where. Somhairle rides down the following spring and finds the whole shore silent.
- <a id="ev-I-0096"></a>**7 an Gearran, GE 551** — *The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent*. After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1553"><em>The last smoke seen at Seann Tarr</em>, 27 an Lùnastal, GE 530</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1554"><em>Somhairle rides the three shores in one circuit</em>, 7 an Gearran, GE 551</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1554"></a>**7 an Gearran, GE 551** — *Somhairle rides the three shores in one circuit* (Seann Warr). In a single season, the first any reciter has made the round, Somhairle rides from Seann Warr to Seann Tarr and down to Seann Chwen and finds all three the same: middens grown over, boats rotted on their keels, turf houses softening back into the ground.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0096"><em>The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent</em>, 7 an Gearran, GE 551</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1555"></a>**25 an t-Sultain, GE 551** — *Somhairle sets down the Silence* (Dùn ìseal). Somhairle enters the shortest of his four tellings in the Line: that after Clach nan Dà Stràc no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated, their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and how they ended, the telling does not know.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0096"><em>The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent</em>, 7 an Gearran, GE 551</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1556"></a>**4 an Giblean, GE 560** — *The hill-folk find the coasts wholly empty* (Seann Warr). By this year no hill trader who once walked the three shores still finds a fire lit on any of them. The households who might have answered a knock are themselves gone, and carriers give the roads over to shores that no longer answer.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0096"><em>The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent</em>, 7 an Gearran, GE 551</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1557"></a>**3 an Cèitean, GE 580** — *Somhairle weds Cairistìona* (Dùn ìseal). Somhairle marries Cairistìona of Na Glinn Àrda, a shepherding household's daughter of no house of Clann na Ceiste, before both their fires at the turn of the year. He sets nothing of the wedding itself in the Line, judging it a thing that belongs to the man and not to the telling.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0081"><em>Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-1558"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, GE 591** — *Word of Beathan's birth reaches the river households* (Dùn ìseal). News that Somhairle and Cairistìona have a son, Beathan, and that the boy will be kept among Clann na Ceiste in the high pastures rather than brought to the hill, travels down every settled valley by the ordinary traffic of drovers and salt-carriers. It reaches Iain mac Fhearchair's household on the Abhainn naomh the same week as the shearing.
- <a id="ev-EII-1559"></a>**26 am Faoilleach, GE 591** — *The hill-folk of the upper Abhainn naomh first say Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Iain mac Fhearchair's generation on the river inherits, without ever deciding it as a household, the custom of naming the Seann-Dhaoine's old places with the plain word for old set before them. Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen and Seann Skell pass into ordinary speech as though no other names had ever been possible.
- <a id="ev-I-0097"></a>**8 am Màrt, GE 591** — *The old names kept* (Seann Skell). The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-1558"><em>Word of Beathan's birth reaches the river households</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, GE 591</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-1559"><em>The hill-folk of the upper Abhainn naomh first say Seann Skell</em>, 26 am Faoilleach, GE 591</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2000"></a>**18 an Cèitean, GE 595** — *Iain forbids his household the tower before any of them have seen it* (Seann Skell). Iain mac Fhearchair, recalling a single visit to the coast as a young man, tells his daughter Marsaili and the rest of his household that no good comes of taking up what the Seann-Dhaoine left lying, and names the tower at the harbour's mouth as a thing never to be entered, years before the household has any plan of settling near it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0097"><em>The old names kept</em>, 8 am Màrt, GE 591</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2001"></a>**19 an Giblean, GE 620** — *Three river households crowd one bend* (Dùn ìseal). Grazing on the middle Abhainn naomh, held by one household in Iain's father's day, now feeds three grown from it, and the quarrels over the bend grow more frequent than the grass allows for. Iain begins to speak of the empty coast as a way out of them.
- <a id="ev-EII-2002"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, GE 627** — *Iain calls the household to the coast* (Dùn ìseal). On a dark-half evening Iain mac Fhearchair tells his household plainly that he means to move it to the empty harbour at Seann Skell before another winter turns, judging a shore with good landing and no claimant better than another forty years of quarrelling over the river bend.
- <a id="ev-I-0098"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628** — *The old landings taken up* (Seann Skell). Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-2001"><em>Three river households crowd one bend</em>, 19 an Giblean, GE 620</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-2002"><em>Iain calls the household to the coast</em>, 15 an t-Iuchar, GE 627</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2003"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628** — *Eleven souls come down the Abhainn naomh* (Seann Skell). Iain mac Fhearchair's household, eleven souls with ox-carts and what beasts they can drive, follows the Abhainn naomh two days further than any of them has gone, and comes out above the tide to find the harbour at Seann Skell standing exactly as the traders had always described it: empty, the old mole running into the flood, the tower blind-walled by the water.<span class="fn fl">↩ Answers <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2004"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628** — *Iain marks the ground and forbids the tower again* (Seann Skell). Before the household sleeps its first night at the harbour, Iain walks the ground himself and sets a line of stones marking where a house may be built and where it must not, keeping every wall a household's length from the nearest standing Seann-Dhaoine wall and the whole camp further still from the tower.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2005"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628** — *The household mends the mole with stone it did not take* (Seann Skell). The household repairs the landward stretch of the old mole with stone gathered fresh from the shore, never lifting a stone already laid by the Seann-Dhaoine, a distinction Iain draws carefully and his children keep after him without ever quite putting into words.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2006"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, GE 629** — *A winter storm breaks the seaward mole* (Seann Skell). In the first days of an Fhaoilleach a storm out of the west drives the tide higher up the shingle than any of the household remembers from their river years, and breaks the oldest, untouched stretch of the mole, scattering its stones along the shore.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2007"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, GE 629** — *Iain refuses to build with the broken stone* (Seann Skell). Two of Iain's sons-in-law argue that stone the sea itself has thrown down is no longer bound by the household's rule against taking up Seann-Dhaoine work. Iain refuses them, holding that the storm's breaking gives the household no claim the storm did not also give, and the mole is mended instead with new-quarried stone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2008"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, GE 631** — *The mole stands whole again* (Seann Skell). After two summers of quarrying and hauling stone down from the higher ground, the mended mole stands sheltered end to end, and no household on that shore again seriously argues for lifting a Seann-Dhaoine stone to lay it elsewhere.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2009"></a>**15 am Faoilleach, GE 640** — *The first hill-folk boats put out from Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Tearlach mac Ghilleonain and two of Iain's grandsons build the first boats the harbour has held since it was last worked, small hide craft trusted for the first time to open tide, and Marsaili herself goes out in the first of them on a calm morning her father judges safe.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0098"><em>The old landings taken up</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, GE 628</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-2010"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, GE 640** — *Marsaili sees the mole's true shape from the water* (Seann Skell).
