The line is sworn to in no words either side writes down, and it holds.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0158"><em>The kings and the keepers</em>, 7 an Cèitean, GE 2,416</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0159"></a>**1 an Gearran, GE 2,417** — *A' Ghaoth Dhubh* (Cuan ruadh). A storm called A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept.
- <a id="ev-I-0160"></a>**8 an Giblean, GE 2,417** — *The sharing holds after the Black Wind* (Ceann chiar). The settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter out of their shared surplus. None on that coast is known to die of hunger that season.
- <a id="ev-EII-4500"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,417** — *A' Ghaoth Dhubh strips the east coast* (Cuan ruadh). A storm out of the south-east strikes before dawn with almost no warning, stripping the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar and driving three unhauled boats onto the rocks below the headland. No one of that coast dies in it, though many households lose stores, shelter and boats within a single day.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0159"><em>A' Ghaoth Dhubh</em>, 1 an Gearran, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4501"></a>**14 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,417** — *The coast's fishing fails before winter begins* (Cuan ruadh). Of Cuan ruadh's eleven boats, four are broken past mending and a fifth needs a new keel; granaries stand open to the sky along the whole stripped coast. A fishing that has never in memory failed outright fails that winter for want of boats and stores enough to work it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0159"><em>A' Ghaoth Dhubh</em>, 1 an Gearran, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4502"></a>**5 an t-Samhain, GE 2,417** — *The coast names the storm A' Ghaoth Dhubh* (Cuan ruadh). The eldest of that coast, having no name ready when the storm struck, name it afterward for the ash-dark sky it leaves behind for three days. No reciter of the hill amends the name; every storm to strike that shore since is measured against it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0159"><em>A' Ghaoth Dhubh</em>, 1 an Gearran, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4503"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, GE 2,417** — *Inland valleys hear of the coast's ruin* (Cuan ruadh). A trader who meant to buy salt fish at Cuan ruadh finds instead a shore of broken boats and bare roof-trees, and carries word of it a day and more west to valleys that had never before troubled themselves over that coast's weather.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0160"><em>The sharing holds after the Black Wind</em>, 8 an Giblean, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4504"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,417** — *The valleys send grain to Cuan ruadh unasked* (Cuan ruadh). Single households send what they can spare because a neighbour has already sent something, until the scatter of gifts grows too large for any one house to account for, and the valleys' holders agree to weigh and send it on by the count of mouths, as the sharing is kept at Dùn ìseal, though none there had been taught the custom directly.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0160"><em>The sharing holds after the Black Wind</em>, 8 an Giblean, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0161"></a>**2 am Màrt, GE 2,418** — *The beacon at Baile ìseal* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). A fire is built on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. It is lit to bring boats home in a storm, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.
- <a id="ev-EII-4505"></a>**10 an Cèitean, GE 2,418** — *The sharing reaches the east coast* (Cuan ruadh). Grain, salted meat and wool for roofing come down to Cuan ruadh through the winter on carts and cattle-backs, weighed by mouths and given without reckoning who at the coast has lost most. No household of that coast starves; the coast calls the custom only the bringing-in, or the help.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0160"><em>The sharing holds after the Black Wind</em>, 8 an Giblean, GE 2,417</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4506"></a>**20 an Dàmhair, GE 2,418** — *Lìleas begins to watch the dark return of the boats* (Cuan ruadh). One-and-twenty that hard winter, with her father's hand maimed and the household's boat unfit to swim, Lìleas of Cuan ruadh spends idle hours on the shingle and comes to notice what the coast has never put into words: that a boat coming home after dark has nothing to steer the last stretch by but memory and the sound of the surf.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0161"><em>The beacon at Baile ìseal</em>, 2 am Màrt, GE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4507"></a>**11 an t-Samhain, GE 2,418** — *Lìleas's household agrees to the fire* (Cuan ruadh). Lìleas puts the keeping of a fire on the cape east of the village to her own household over a thin meal; her father, no longer trusting his maimed hand on a line, sees no harm in it and asks only that she carry the work herself.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0161"><em>The beacon at Baile ìseal</em>, 2 am Màrt, GE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4508"></a>**20 an t-Samhain, GE 2,418** — *The eastern fire is first kept* (Cuan ruadh). Lìleas and her younger brother carry driftwood and peat up the cape through a month of short winter days and build the fire in a stone-walled pit, driving flame and smoke seaward. She keeps it alone through nights that find no boat needing it, and more than one household of the village climbs the cape only to sit an hour with her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0161"><em>The beacon at Baile ìseal</em>, 2 am Màrt, GE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0162"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, GE 2,419** — *The beacon at Muileann bheag* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. Under the tower the ash goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.
- <a id="ev-I-0163"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,419** — *The beacon at Àth dhearg* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral, and less worn.
- <a id="ev-EII-4509"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,419** — *Word of the eastern fire travels the coast roads* (Cuan ruadh). Traders and travellers carry word of the fire on Cuan ruadh's cape along the roads faster than its own light could reach, and coasts that have suffered their own bad weather begin to want fires of their own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-4508"><em>The eastern fire is first kept</em>, 20 an t-Samhain, GE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4510"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,419** — *A fire is raised on the northern point*. On ground already scorched black by older shore-fires, the households of the hardest-running coast raise a fire that burns steadier from its first season, having Lìleas's year of trial to learn by before laying their own wood.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0162"><em>The beacon at Muileann bheag</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, GE 2,419</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4511"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,419** — *Seathan mac Pheadair keeps the north-eastern fire*. On the cape where the passage to the deeper water runs narrowest, a man named Seathan mac Pheadair takes up the keeping of a fire much as Lìleas had, and cuts a stroke on a stone at its edge for every ship's light he sees pass safe by it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0163"><em>The beacon at Àth dhearg</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,419</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0164"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420** — *The beacon at Tobar dhearg* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). A fire is kept for the boats of the south coast on the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands. With Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg the coasts of the island are lit at five points.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-4512"><em>The southern cape completes the five fires</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-4513"><em>A reciter names them the five fires</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4512"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420** — *The southern cape completes the five fires* (Tobar dhearg). Last of the four new fires and by every account the surest, the households of the southern cape raise theirs on a mound of stacked stone breast-high, clear of the spray. With the older fire on the Baile chrom headland, the coasts of Dia-thìr are now lit at five points.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0164"><em>The beacon at Tobar dhearg</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4513"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420** — *A reciter names them the five fires* (Tobar dhearg). Before the southern mound is even finished, a reciter of that coast says that a boat lost off any shore of Dia-thìr now has a fire somewhere within its sight to steer toward, and names the five together the five fires, a name the coast keeps on every telling since.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0164"><em>The beacon at Tobar dhearg</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,420</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4514"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, GE 2,420** — *A boat is brought home to the eastern fire* (Cuan ruadh). Blown off its own water by a wind that will not hold steady, a boat out of a coast two villages north finds the coast of Dia-thìr only by Lìleas's fire, burning high on the cape with no house near it. The crew comes ashore whole, and Lìleas tells the captain the fire is kept for whichever boat needs it, no more for him than for any other.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0161"><em>The beacon at Baile ìseal</em>, 2 am Màrt, GE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0165"></a>**31 am Màrt, GE 2,421** — *The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell* (Uilebheist na Mara). Four watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell see a back as long as three boats rise and go under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher tied to a named place and a count of witnesses.
- <a id="ev-I-0166"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,421** — *Wreckage in the western water* (Spùinneadairean-mara). For a season planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up along the western shore below the waters where raiders are afterwards seen. No bodies come with them, and no settlement on that coast lacks a boat.
- <a id="ev-EII-4515"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,421** — *The watchers see the long back in the water* (Seann Skell). Four men keeping the tower at Seann Skell watch a back long as three boats rise off the point in the failing light and go under without a sound. Their four tellings differ in every small particular but agree on the length and the silence.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0165"><em>The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,421</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4516"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,421** — *Word of the sighting runs round the bay* (Seann Skell). The tale of the tower's watch grows a head and a neck by the time it has gone twice round the bay of Seann Skell, though the old women of that coast say only that the sea shows itself when it chooses and take no boat off the water for the telling.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0165"><em>The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,421</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4517"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,421** — *Stitched planks come ashore south of Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Through a season the wrack south of the tower gives up narrow stitched planks from more than one hull, shaped for open water and like nothing built on that coast, with not one scrap of cord, tool or bone to say what rode in them.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0166"><em>Wreckage in the western water</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,421</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4518"></a>**5 an t-Sultain, GE 2,421** — *No household will claim the wreck* (Seann Skell). Asked along the shore, no household admits to a boat of its own building broken among the planks, nor lacks a man, woman or child it cannot otherwise account for; the wreck stays a wreck with no name and no mourner.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0166"><em>Wreckage in the western water</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,421</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4519"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, GE 2,421** — *Micheil Beag lays the planks against his wall* (Seann Skell). A fisherman of that coast, Micheil Beag, gathers the stitched wood along one wall and pieces two curved lengths of hull back into shape, finding boats narrower and longer in the beam than any the coast builds for its own close fishing.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0166"><em>Wreckage in the western water</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,421</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4520"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, GE 2,421** — *Anndra Breac comes to the wall of planks* (Seann Skell). Anndra Breac, a teller who has walked the western shore twenty years and more without a household of his own, hears Micheil Beag out and returns to look at the planking again by firelight more than once before the season turns.
- <a id="ev-EII-4521"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, GE 2,421** — *Anndra shapes a fourth telling* (Seann Skell). Turning the planks and the tower's tale over through the winter, Anndra comes to think a boat lost whole but for its wood argues not a wreck close to shore but a crossing once made, long before any telling now kept remembers the making of it.
- <a id="ev-EII-4522"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,421** — *The coast hears him out without agreeing* (Seann Skell). Anndra tries the telling first on households that have fed him twenty years running; none of them denies it outright, and an old woman near Seann Skell tells him a tale a man cannot leave alone wants telling somewhere it will be properly heard.
- <a id="ev-I-0167"></a>**29 an Giblean, GE 2,422** — *Anndra Breac says 'we came'* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering Anndra Breac, a teller of the western coast, recites a telling in which the people came to Dia-thìr over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down, and he is put out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept; only the memory that he told it.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4520"><em>Anndra Breac comes to the wall of planks</em>, 23 an t-Samhain, GE 2,421</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4521"><em>Anndra shapes a fourth telling</em>, 30 an t-Samhain, GE 2,421</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4522"><em>The coast hears him out without agreeing</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,421</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-4523"><em>Anndra Breac tells the crossing at the ford</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-4524"><em>The crowd shouts him down</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4523"></a>**29 an Giblean, GE 2,422** — *Anndra Breac tells the crossing at the ford*. At the yearly gathering, by the largest fire he can get a footing at, Anndra Breac tells a telling in which the hill-folk crossed the sea in boats once and lost more of themselves to the crossing than any telling now remembers.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4524"></a>**29 an Giblean, GE 2,422** — *The crowd shouts him down*. An old man of a hill household calls out that no teller says the hill-folk came from anywhere, for they were always here, and others take up the shout until Anndra's own voice can no longer be heard over the fire.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4525"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, GE 2,422** — *Every hearth of Dia-thìr closes to him*. No household strikes him and none needs to; by the roads home from the ford it is already understood that Anndra Breac is not to be fed at a hill hearth again, and by the following spring not one has.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4526"></a>**19 an Dàmhair, GE 2,422** — *The king laughs once and falls quiet*. Standing near enough his own fire to hear the telling, the king laughs low at some point in it those nearest him cannot agree on afterward, does not join the shouting nor still it, and is seen quiet the rest of that evening in a way his own kin know to read.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4527"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, GE 2,422** — *The king will not choose between the tellings*. Asked afterward by a woman of his own kin whether the teller spoke true, the king answers only that he has heard many tellings of where his own people came from and has never troubled to choose one over another.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0168"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,423** — *The doctrine said at the column* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. From this time it is said as a rule, and not only held as a belief.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-4528"><em>The saying is spoken at the opening of the gathering</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,423</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4528"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,423** — *The saying is spoken at the opening of the gathering*. The gathering at the ford opens for the first time with the saying of Calbh Cnoc ghorm spoken aloud before any business begins, we did not come, we were here, a thing said together from that year rather than kept only in each hearth's own quiet belief.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0168"><em>The doctrine said at the column</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,423</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4529"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, GE 2,423** — *Anndra Breac walks south along the western strand* (Seann Skell). Seen once more below the tower at Seann Skell, walking the strand where the stitched planks still lie against Micheil Beag's wall, Anndra Breac walks on and does not look back; no teller of that coast claims to have fed, spoken to or buried him after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0167"><em>Anndra Breac says 'we came'</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0169"></a>**25 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,424** — *The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock* (Ros dhomhain). The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low. Her pairs can be read still. The keepers after her go back to single marks.
- <a id="ev-I-0170"></a>**20 an Dàmhair, GE 2,424** — *A third tide-rock at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the interval of Ros dhomhain. So three rocks are kept side by side. None tells why the interval is what it is.
- <a id="ev-EII-4530"></a>**19 an t-Samhain, GE 2,424** — *Seònaid Mhòr cuts paired marks at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The keeper of the Ros dhomhain tide-rock takes to cutting two strokes for every tide instead of one, a mark for the water's highest reach and a shorter mark beside it for its lowest ebb, so that whoever reads the rock after her has the whole of the water's motion and not only its rising.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0169"><em>The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock</em>, 25 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,424</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4531"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, GE 2,424** — *The spacing of the marks travels without its reasoning* (Inis thais). Households at Inis thais's own harbour, hearing only that Ros dhomhain's keeper cuts her marks at a certain interval, begin cutting their own high-water marks at that same spacing on a rock of their own, though none of them can say why that width and no other.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0170"><em>A third tide-rock at Inis thais</em>, 20 an Dàmhair, GE 2,424</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4532"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,424** — *Peigi Dhubh calls for a landing of laid stone* (Cathair dhearg). At the household's board, Lachlann Ruadh's daughter says plainly that a hill whose wealth now travels by water deserves better than an open shingle beach a winter tide can rearrange. Her father agrees, and the households of An Cnoc Ruadh give a season's labour to the work.
- <a id="ev-I-0171"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,425** — *Ros dhomhain grows* (Ros dhomhain). Ros dhomhain becomes the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish now from boats and not from the shore.
- <a id="ev-EII-4533"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,425** — *The stone landing is set at the river-mouth* (Cathair dhearg). Course on course of quarried stone is laid where the fresh water of the lake meets the tide from the sea, until a boat can come alongside at any state of the water without a hand needed to haul it clear of the mud: An Cnoc Ruadh's first way onto open water that does not depend on a beach's mercy.
- <a id="ev-EII-4534"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, GE 2,425** — *Lachlann Ruadh falls ill* (Cathair dhearg). A chill taken wading the shallows to right a boat settles in Lachlann an Altraim's chest and will not lift with the spring. He is five-and-sixty years old, an age An Cnoc Ruadh reckons past complaint for a man who has spent his whole life wet to the knee in cold water.
- <a id="ev-EII-4535"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, GE 2,425** — *Lachlann asks that the fostering be ended* (Cathair dhearg). On one of his last evenings Lachlann tells his daughter that a fostering kept a season too long stops being a kindness and becomes only a habit no one has ended, and asks her not to let her own fondness be the reason the peace of the ford goes one day longer without its proper marking.
- <a id="ev-EII-4536"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, GE 2,425** — *Lachlann Ruadh dies at five-and-sixty* (Cathair dhearg). He dies in the hall he was born in, his daughter's hand in his own, the household gathered at the door with no closer claim on the bedside than the years they gave the hill. He held An Cnoc Ruadh one-and-sixty years.
- <a id="ev-EII-4537"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, GE 2,425** — *Peigi Dhubh holds An Cnoc Ruadh at forty* (Cathair dhearg). She sits down at the board the morning after her father's burial and asks for the tallies before she asks for anything else. An Cnoc Ruadh's own steward says afterward that she keeps them straighter than her father ever did.
- <a id="ev-I-0172"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, GE 2,426** — *The Red Hill's harbour* (Cathair dhearg). The households of the Red Hill build a landing of laid stone at the river-mouth below the hill, where the harbour of Cathair dhearg is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4532"><em>Peigi Dhubh calls for a landing of laid stone</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,424</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4533"><em>The stone landing is set at the river-mouth</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,425</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0173"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,426** — *Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the peace of the ford holds a generation more.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4534"><em>Lachlann Ruadh falls ill</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, GE 2,425</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4535"><em>Lachlann asks that the fostering be ended</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, GE 2,425</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4536"><em>Lachlann Ruadh dies at five-and-sixty</em>, 23 an t-Samhain, GE 2,425</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-4537"><em>Peigi Dhubh holds An Cnoc Ruadh at forty</em>, 30 an t-Samhain, GE 2,425</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4538"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, GE 2,426** — *Houses draw in round the rock and the landing* (Ros dhomhain). Boats from harbours further down the coast begin putting in at the new landing rather than carrying on to open beaches, and the scattered houses of that shore draw in closer round the tide-rock and the stone together until some sixty stand there, their people fishing now from boats of their own building.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0171"><em>Ros dhomhain grows</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,425</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0174"></a>**31 am Màrt, GE 2,427** — *The foster-son returns* (Dùn ìseal). The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal, bringing the salt-songs of the west. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went.
- <a id="ev-EII-4539"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,427** — *Peigi tells the fosterling he is to go home* (Cathair dhearg). Walking the new stone landing with him in the last light of an evening, Peigi says her father was right, and that she means to send him home before the year turns, with salt enough for a household to carry as gift and not as trade, so the hill of Dùn ìseal will know he is sent back with honour.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0173"><em>Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,426</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-4540"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,427** — *Seònaid Mhòr cuts a last pair of marks for him* (Ros dhomhain). On the evening before the train leaves, the keeper of the tide-rock cuts one more pair of marks at the rock's edge, though the tide calls for none, and will not say plainly what they are for beyond that the rock has marked every tide of his years there and should mark the last of them too.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0169"><em>The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock</em>, 25 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,424</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0175"></a>**2 am Màrt, GE 2,428** — *The first songs kept* (Baile ghorm). The salt-songs of the south and west are sung at the raking of the pans. They are the oldest songs on Dia-thìr whose words are said to survive: a refrain of four lines, which no one can now wholly construe.
- <a id="ev-I-0176"></a>**14 am Màrt, GE 2,428** — *Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are made in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments of the island.
- <a id="ev-I-0177"></a>**29 an Giblean, GE 2,428** — *The panthers turn back* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills without crossing. The hill-folk read it for a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.
- <a id="ev-EII-5000"></a>**4 an Cèitean, GE 2,428** — *Gilleonan bores the first bone pipes* (Cnoc àrsaidh). At Cnoc àrsaidh, Gilleonan bores four holes along a hollow bird-bone and finds a note he can raise and lower at will; children of three households gather to hear him play, the first instrument the island's tellers count as more than a horn blown flat.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0176"><em>Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh</em>, 14 am Màrt, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5001"></a>**5 an Cèitean, GE 2,428** — *Three cats turn back at the pass*. Watchers along Imrich nam Pantar see three great cats, on three different days, halt at the throat of the highest pass and turn back south rather than finish the crossing every household's memory says they always finish.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0177"><em>The panthers turn back</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5002"></a>**14 an Cèitean, GE 2,428** — *The households along the road store double*. Reading the cats' turning for a kinder ground left behind and a harder winter ahead, the households nearest the pass lay in double against a season no cat that year would risk crossing into, and go short of nothing before the thaw.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0177"><em>The panthers turn back</em>, 29 an Giblean, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5003"></a>**23 an Cèitean, GE 2,428** — *Iain drives cattle onto Imrich nam Pantar* (Muileann bhàn). With the household's grazing run thin, Iain of Muileann bhàn takes four men and forty head of thin cattle up into the passes against the custom that keeps the crossing season's road clear of herds, meaning to bring them down fattened within the week.
- <a id="ev-I-0178"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,428** — *The cattle lost in the passes* (Muileann bhàn). Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night, and the herders come down with nothing.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5003"><em>Iain drives cattle onto Imrich nam Pantar</em>, 23 an Cèitean, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5004"></a>**18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,428** — *The foster-son of Dùn ìseal comes home* (Dùn ìseal). He walks Rathad an t-Salainn east with a train of laden pack-beasts and three of An Cnoc Ruadh's household, and comes in sight of the hill of Rìghrean na Cloiche on the seventh evening, four-and-twenty years after he first walked the same road west at six years old.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0174"><em>The foster-son returns</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,427</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5005"></a>**6 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,428** — *Calum Ciar does not know his own brother* (Dùn ìseal). Meeting An Cnoc Ruadh's train at the gate in his mother's stead, Calum Ciar asks the fosterling which of the household he might be, a lake wind and four-and-twenty years having left nothing in him his brother's eye could fasten on as kin.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0174"><em>The foster-son returns</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,427</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5006"></a>**4 an Lùnastal, GE 2,428** — *Eilidh Ghlas knows her son at the door* (Dùn ìseal). Carried out to the hall door, Eilidh speaks her younger son's name before he has said a word to tell her who he is, and weeps and holds him a long while before she lets even her elder son greet him in turn.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0174"><em>The foster-son returns</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,427</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5007"></a>**22 an Lùnastal, GE 2,428** — *The salt refrain is sung at the pans of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). At the fires of the salt-rakers he teaches, without meaning to teach anything, the four-line refrain sung at the crust on An Cnoc Ruadh's own lake shore. An old raker keeps it whole from a single hearing, and it runs on afterward at the sea-shore pans in words An Cnoc Ruadh itself can no longer wholly construe.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0175"><em>The first songs kept</em>, 2 am Màrt, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5008"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, GE 2,428** — *Rìghrean na Cloiche' list keeps him no name* (Dùn ìseal). When the reciters after Eilidh set down her reign and her sons, Calum Ciar takes his place among the holders as every holder before him; of the one who went to An Cnoc Ruadh and came home grown, no year, no reign and no deed is written, and the list stands as if she bore only the one son.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0174"><em>The foster-son returns</em>, 31 am Màrt, GE 2,427</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5009"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,428** — *The panthers take thirty head in the night*. On the fourth night a string of cats, the last and largest of that year's crossing, comes down on the herd; by first light thirty of the forty head are taken or scattered beyond finding.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0178"><em>The cattle lost in the passes</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5010"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,428** — *Iain is lamed in the dark*. Throwing himself clear of a claw he never clearly sees, Iain twists his leg under him against a hidden stone; it sets crooked at the hip, and he walks from that winter with a stick and a roll to one side.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0178"><em>The cattle lost in the passes</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,428</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5011"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, GE 2,431** — *Baile dhomhain cuts the first season's sign* (Baile dhomhain). The households of Baile dhomhain begin cutting a mark into every gatepost at the start of the crossing season and scraping it away at its close, the first mark the island's tellers know cut for a season rather than for any single event.
- <a id="ev-EII-5012"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,434** — *Caol bheag names its boats for the winds* (Caol bheag). The fishing households of Caol bheag fix the custom of naming each boat for the wind it is built to fish in, holding a boat unlucky under any other wind and never giving a drowned boat's name again.
- <a id="ev-EII-5013"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, GE 2,440** — *A wind-name is cut at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). A cutter of that household sets one of Na h-Ochd Gaothan' names beside Seann-Dhaoine' own marks on the great boulder at Seann Chwen, choosing that stone, by his own word, because the name wanted a stone already old.
- <a id="ev-EII-5014"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, GE 2,444** — *A family takes up the old burial ground unasked*. Kin new to that country begin clearing the thorn from the old burial ground's rows each spring though none of their own dead lie there, and within a few years every household near it has come to trust the keeping to them alone.
- <a id="ev-I-0179"></a>**15 am Faoilleach, GE 2,447** — *The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain* (Baile dhomhain). At Baile dhomhain in the south the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at its end. It is the first mark made on the island for a season.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5011"><em>Baile dhomhain cuts the first season's sign</em>, 5 am Faoilleach, GE 2,431</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0180"></a>**13 an Gearran, GE 2,447** — *The wind-stone at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Dia-thìreach manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. In few places do the marks of the two peoples touch.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5013"><em>A wind-name is cut at Seann Chwen</em>, 8 an t-Samhain, GE 2,440</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0181"></a>**14 an Gearran, GE 2,447** — *Boats named for the winds* (Caol bheag). The fishing households of Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is held unlucky, and the name of a boat that sinks is never given again.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5012"><em>Caol bheag names its boats for the winds</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,434</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0182"></a>**14 am Màrt, GE 2,447** — *The Tuam keepers* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A family dwelling by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of thorn from the old graves. They bury none of their own there. They only keep it.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5014"><em>A family takes up the old burial ground unasked</em>, 10 an Dàmhair, GE 2,444</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0183"></a>**12 an Giblean, GE 2,447** — *A grave at Tuam opened* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into a grave older than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. They close it and move the row, and none opens that grave again.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5015"><em>Diggers break into a slab-lined grave</em>, 12 an Giblean, GE 2,447</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5015"></a>**12 an Giblean, GE 2,447** — *Diggers break into a slab-lined grave*. Cutting a new row further back than any before it, the keepers' own diggers break into an older grave lined close with cut slabs in the manner of Seann-Dhaoine; they close it as carefully as they opened it and move the row a spear's length off.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0183"><em>A grave at Tuam opened</em>, 12 an Giblean, GE 2,447</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5016"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, GE 2,447** — *No digger tries the older grave again*. The keeping family's eldest holds that a ground kept for the dead does not want its keepers asking after graves it was never given to keep, and no digger of that ground troubles the older grave a second time.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0183"><em>A grave at Tuam opened</em>, 12 an Giblean, GE 2,447</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0184"></a>**11 an Cèitean, GE 2,449** — *Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Their small fires, each of a single night, lie all along the edge.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5017"><em>Pilgrims begin sitting at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar</em>, 11 an Cèitean, GE 2,449</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5017"></a>**11 an Cèitean, GE 2,449** — *Pilgrims begin sitting at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar). People from households that have never before walked so far begin coming singly and in pairs to sit a single night at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, keeping a small fire that burns out before morning, and go home saying only that the night leaves them quieter.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0184"><em>Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar</em>, 11 an Cèitean, GE 2,449</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5018"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,450** — *Settlers from An Cnoc Ruadh raise the first house at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Households come down from An Cnoc Ruadh to build at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, taking timber only from the river's far side and never from the unclaimed wood, a line later marked by a row of unhewn stones.
- <a id="ev-I-0185"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451** — *A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A child of the settlement at Cnoc bheag goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The searchers stop at the stones, and the telling does not blame them.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5019"><em>A child of Cnoc bheag is lost past the stones</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5020"><em>Iain among the searchers who stop at the stones</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5019"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451** — *A child of Cnoc bheag is lost past the stones*. A boy not yet seven goes missing near the line of stones at Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag's edge; the settlement and its neighbours search three days into the wood without one sign of him.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0185"><em>A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5020"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451** — *Iain among the searchers who stop at the stones*. Lame still from the passes, Iain of Muileann bhàn joins the search at Cnoc bheag and is the first to say aloud that a wood no household will fell or build nearer than its own river is not a wood that gives back what it takes; the searchers stop at the line of stones, and no teller lays the stopping at their door.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0185"><em>A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,451</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0186"></a>**8 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,453** — *The first house at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the edge of the forest. They take their timber from the far side of the river, and never from the unclaimed wood.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5018"><em>Settlers from An Cnoc Ruadh raise the first house at Cnoc bheag</em>, 16 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,450</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0187"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455** — *The spring at Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Pilgrims come in numbers to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and a ring of shelters is built there. Here is set the eldest healing-tale of Dia-thìr: a herder came lame and walked home.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5021"><em>Iain goes to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5022"><em>Iain walks home whole; the cure-tale is set</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5021"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455** — *Iain goes to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh*. Seven-and-twenty years lame, and told by a neighbour of a warm water under the mountain that has eased other travellers' old hurts, Iain walks south on his stick and sits in the pool at first light, the heat working into the crooked hip as no binding ever had.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0187"><em>The spring at Muileann ruadh</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5022"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455** — *Iain walks home whole; the cure-tale is set* (Muileann bhàn). Iain stays three days at the warm water and walks the road home to Muileann bhàn on his own two legs without the stick, in half the days the journey south had cost him; his own household, seeing him come up the rise, takes him at first for a stranger. The tale kept of it is the oldest cure the springs are told for: he came lame, and he walked home.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0187"><em>The spring at Muileann ruadh</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, GE 2,455</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0188"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,457** — *The Hollow Man seen again* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). Two herders passing the Doire uaine hills after dark see a figure walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and so, the telling says, they lived.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EII-5023"><em>Two herders see Marbh-bheò on the ridge</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,457</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5023"></a>**28 an Cèitean, GE 2,457** — *Two herders see Marbh-bheò on the ridge*. Caught by dark on the way home, two herders near Marbh-bheò's hills see a shape walk the ridge above them showing no breath in the bitter cold, though their own hangs white before them; they had lit no fire that evening, and so, the telling says, they lived.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0188"><em>The Hollow Man seen again</em>, 28 an Cèitean, GE 2,457</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0189"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,460** — *The covered hearth spreads* (Muileann chiar). The covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements about Muileann chiar. From this comes the later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.
- <a id="ev-EII-5024"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,460** — *Peigi Dhubh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi Dhubh, who laid the stone landing and kept the tallies straighter than her father, dies on An Cnoc Ruadh in her seventy-sixth year, having held it five-and-thirty years; her boats go out the morning after her burying as she asked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0173"><em>Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, GE 2,426</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5025"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, GE 2,460** — *The covered hearth spreads and the night rule hardens* (Muileann chiar). The pit-dug, stone-lidded hearth spreads from Marbh-bheò's hills toward the settlements nearer Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and it hardens there into a rule no council ever set: no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-I-0189"><em>The covered hearth spreads</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,460</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0190"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462** — *Settlers at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Dia-thìreach households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5026"><em>Caol mhòr's settlers set aside the marked midden stones</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5026"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462** — *Caol mhòr's settlers set aside the marked midden stones* (Caol mhòr). Households raising walls from Seann-Dhaoine' shell midden at Caol mhòr will not turn a stone that carries a mark, cut or worn, and lay those aside in an unmortared line along the shore, so that two kinds of wall stand side by side there ever after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0190"><em>Settlers at Caol mhòr</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5027"></a>**7 an Giblean, GE 2,463** — *Somhairle walks the ground at Baile chrom* (Baile chrom). Somhairle finds the resettled fields at Baile chrom already byred and welled, and Donnchadh Ruadh shows him the old field-marks still standing half sunk beneath the new grass, ploughed by hands no household there now names aloud.
- <a id="ev-I-0191"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464** — *Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west* (Baile chrom). Households from Cnoc ghorm settle again the ground at Baile chrom that the old hunger had emptied. They dig their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5027"><em>Somhairle walks the ground at Baile chrom</em>, 7 an Giblean, GE 2,463</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5028"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464** — *The last thicket on Rathad an t-Salainn is cut through* (Muileann àrsaidh). Carriers weary of the long way round cut through the last unbroken stand of thorn and birch on Rathad an t-Salainn to the north-west, so that Muileann àrsaidh stands a full day nearer the pans of Baile ghorm than it had ever stood before.
- <a id="ev-EII-5029"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, GE 2,465** — *The first bank is turned east of the old workings* (Dùn thais). Settlers pushing toward the rising country dig a ditch and raise the spoil behind it at Dùn thais, a ring of earth built without any word sent from Dùn ìseal and without any word sent back once it stood.
- <a id="ev-I-0192"></a>**3 an t-Samhain, GE 2,466** — *Muileann àrsaidh settled* (Muileann àrsaidh). Houses are built on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint comes from Cnoc àrsaidh, and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5028"><em>The last thicket on Rathad an t-Salainn is cut through</em>, 18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5030"></a>**4 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,466** — *Fire clears the heavy ground at Achadh chaol* (Achadh chaol). Across three dry summers the households of Achadh chaol burn back the old scrub a field's width at a time and plough the black ground while the ash still holds its warmth, taking the first year a crop the older fields to the west had not equalled in a generation.
- <a id="ev-EII-5031"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,466** — *The last course is set on Cuan ruadh's wall* (Cuan ruadh). The households of Cuan ruadh finish laying stone to the eaves the whole circuit of the settlement, the first roofs on that coast built to stand against wind rather than merely to be raised again once it has passed.
- <a id="ev-EII-5032"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, GE 2,467** — *A well is opened within Cathair fhada's bank* (Cathair fhada). Cathair fhada digs and lines a well inside its own earthwork, so that a household need not send its water-carriers down to the shore while a storm still has teeth in it.
- <a id="ev-I-0193"></a>**5 an Dàmhair, GE 2,468** — *The salt road to the north-west* (Muileann àrsaidh). A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford gathering to the north-west. At Muileann àrsaidh the salt costs three times its price at the pans, and is paid for in flint and seal-skins.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5028"><em>The last thicket on Rathad an t-Salainn is cut through</em>, 18 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5033"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,468** — *Caol ruadh's fishers mark the strait's channels* (Caol ruadh). The fishers of the narrow strait take to tying woven buoys over the deep channels where the current runs hardest, a small custom that spreads along the coast in a carrier's mouth the way the paired tide-marks spread before it.
- <a id="ev-I-0194"></a>**26 an Giblean, GE 2,470** — *Doire ghlas settled* (Doire ghlas). Households settle under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5034"><em>Households come down to Doire ghlas</em>, 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5035"><em>Somhairle asks the household to spare three oaks</em>, 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5034"></a>**26 an Giblean, GE 2,470** — *Households come down to Doire ghlas* (Doire ghlas). Families out of the near valleys settle in the grove where the king kept his seven nights, drawn by its shelter and its old cleared paths, and mark timber in the oaks themselves for the first of their new byres.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0194"><em>Doire ghlas settled</em>, 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5035"></a>**26 an Giblean, GE 2,470** — *Somhairle asks the household to spare three oaks* (Doire ghlas). Finding the three oldest trunks of the grove marked for the axe, Somhairle asks Fearchar mac Ailig's household to take their roof-beams elsewhere, giving no reason beyond that his father once set six pots beneath those particular trees.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0194"><em>Doire ghlas settled</em>, 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5036"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,471** — *The three oaks are spared* (Doire ghlas). The household cuts its beams instead from younger growth a short walk east and leaves the three old trunks standing at the centre of the new settlement, ringed within a generation by houses that call the place only the ring under the oaks.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0194"><em>Doire ghlas settled</em>, 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0195"></a>**28 am Màrt, GE 2,473** — *The east settled at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first stronghold of the Dia-thìrich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5029"><em>The first bank is turned east of the old workings</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, GE 2,465</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0196"></a>**27 an Gearran, GE 2,475** — *Achadh chaol cleared* (Achadh chaol). Fields are cleared at Achadh chaol in the east by fire and by picking stones. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields still.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5030"><em>Fire clears the heavy ground at Achadh chaol</em>, 4 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,466</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5037"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, GE 2,475** — *Somhairle finds grey in his beard*. A cheese-seller on the road through the near valleys remarks on the grey coming into Somhairle's beard, and he finds at a still pool that she has told him true: the first lines his face has shown in two thousand four hundred and thirty-five years.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5036"><em>The three oaks are spared</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,471</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5038"></a>**23 an Giblean, GE 2,476** — *Beathan sees his father's face has changed*. Coming on Somhairle unexpectedly at the slab, Beathan stops in the doorway before he crosses it, having seen in his father's face the beginning of an ageing neither of them has yet spoken of aloud.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5037"><em>Somhairle finds grey in his beard</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, GE 2,475</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0197"></a>**29 am Faoilleach, GE 2,477** — *Cuan ruadh rebuilt* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement of the east coast to build its walls against the wind and not only the cold.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5031"><em>The last course is set on Cuan ruadh's wall</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,466</a>.</span>

## The Years GE 2,501 – 2,750

- <a id="ev-I-0198"></a>**13 an Cèitean, GE 2,523** — *Cathair fhada on the south coast* (Cathair fhada). Cathair fhada is founded on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It draws its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug, and never speaks of where the well came from.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5032"><em>A well is opened within Cathair fhada's bank</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, GE 2,467</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0199"></a>**14 an Giblean, GE 2,570** — *Caol ruadh on the southern strait* (Caol ruadh). Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the cod of the strait on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast to hold more fish than shell.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5033"><em>Caol ruadh's fishers mark the strait's channels</em>, 10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,468</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5039"></a>**25 am Màrt, GE 2,601** — *Murchadh rides north to hold the plain*. The king sends his son Murchadh north with sixty households to hold the northern plain in his name, the first of the king's sons given ground beyond the settled valleys to keep rather than merely to pass through.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0199"><em>Caol ruadh on the southern strait</em>, 14 an Giblean, GE 2,570</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0200"></a>**13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616** — *Baile Mòr mhòr in the north* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain, round a spring that never freezes. At its height it has some eighty houses, a great place for the age.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5040"><em>Baile Mòr mhòr rises round the spring that never freezes</em>, 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5040"></a>**13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616** — *Baile Mòr mhòr rises round the spring that never freezes* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Murchadh raises his hall on a rise above a spring that runs clear through every winter, and the households of the plain name the place Baile Mòr mhòr before it has earned the size of the name; within four centuries it stands eighty houses, the largest place north of An Cnoc Ruadh.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0200"><em>Baile Mòr mhòr in the north</em>, 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5041"></a>**22 an Giblean, GE 2,635** — *Sheep-households settle Baile gharbh* (Baile gharbh). Households take up the stony ground north-east of Murchadh's spring, keep sheep where the land will bear nothing heavier, and send their wool south along the coast road to Cruinneachadh an Àtha rather than north to Murchadh's own granary.
- <a id="ev-EII-5042"></a>**21 an Cèitean, GE 2,655** — *Baile fhiadhaich settled among the boar-thickets* (Baile fhiadhaich). Settlers build on the western coast where the boars run heaviest, hang tusks over their doors, and take boar for their chief meat; the island comes to know a man of that place by his gait, from a lifetime of walking ground a boar might break from underfoot.
- <a id="ev-I-0201"></a>**15 an Lùnastal, GE 2,662** — *Baile gharbh in the north-east* (Baile gharbh). Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5041"><em>Sheep-households settle Baile gharbh</em>, 22 an Giblean, GE 2,635</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5043"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,670** — *Cuan shean settled beside the old landing* (Cuan shean). Households take up a harbour beside a stone landing built by hands none of them can name, older than any wall near it, and use it as they find it rather than mend it, out of the caution settlers keep wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stands.
- <a id="ev-EII-5044"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,703** — *Eithne nic Ailein is born*. A daughter is born to the king in the near valleys and named Eithne; she grows quicker of tongue than most of her father's blood troubles to be, and comes north, in time, to hold ground of her own rather than sit idle at any hearth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5043"><em>Cuan shean settled beside the old landing</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0202"></a>**17 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,709** — *Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast* (Baile fhiadhaich). Settlers build at Baile fhiadhaich on the western coast, where boars run in the thickets. They hang boar tusks over their doors, and boar is their chief meat for the rest of the age.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5042"><em>Baile fhiadhaich settled among the boar-thickets</em>, 21 an Cèitean, GE 2,655</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5045"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, GE 2,720** — *The first of Murchadh's eleven sons is born*. The eldest of eleven sons is born to Murchadh over the better part of three centuries; each, coming of an age to want it, is given a corner of the plain to hold under his father rather than a place idle at his hearth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5044"><em>Eithne nic Ailein is born</em>, 18 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,703</a>.</span>

## The Years GE 2,751 – 3,000

- <a id="ev-EII-5046"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, GE 2,751** — *Dùn chrom is raised with its bank facing two ways* (Dùn chrom). Herders wanting the bank to face south and quarrymen wanting it to face north raise, between them, a single crooked earthwork that answers both wants at once and satisfies neither fully, and the bent fort stands from its first year with a name that fits it more ways than its builders meant.
- <a id="ev-I-0203"></a>**18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755** — *Cuan shean settled* (Cuan shean). Dia-thìreach households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, beside an old landing of unknown builders, and use the landing without mending it.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5043"><em>Cuan shean settled beside the old landing</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,670</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5047"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, GE 2,780** — *Eilidh Ghlas dies* (Dùn ìseal). Eilidh Ghlas, who sent her younger son west to be raised and knew him at the door when he came home, dies in her seven hundred and thirtieth year; both her sons stand at her burying, and the list keeps only one of them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0149"><em>Eilidh Ghlas</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,400</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5048"></a>**11 an t-Samhain, GE 2,790** — *Tobar dhearg rises round the red well* (Tobar dhearg). The keepers of a beacon on the southern cape build at last round a well whose water runs faintly red from the rock, and their settlement grows into the greatest place on that coast, its fire burning nightly for ships that have learned to watch for it.
- <a id="ev-I-0204"></a>**7 am Faoilleach, GE 2,801** — *Dùn chrom raised* (Dùn chrom). A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the midst of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5046"><em>Dùn chrom is raised with its bank facing two ways</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, GE 2,751</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5049"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,802** — *The holders of Dùn chrom and Dùn thais quarrel over which way a bank should face* (Dùn chrom). Ruadhan Beag of Dùn chrom and the holder of Dùn thais fall into two winters of hard words over which way a bank ought to face, until Murchadh rides to hear them and leaves the ditch as it stands, finding a hundred years without an enemy a better argument than either holder makes against it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5048"><em>Tobar dhearg rises round the red well</em>, 11 an t-Samhain, GE 2,790</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5050"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, GE 2,804** — *Beathan mac Shomhairle dies at Tobar dhìreach*. Beathan, son of Somhairle, who sat his nights at the slab since before Murchadh was born, dies in his two thousand two hundred and thirteenth year, the oldest death yet counted among the king's kin; the households of the north, hearing the number, begin for the first time to reckon what it may mean to outlive a holder's holder.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5049"><em>The holders of Dùn chrom and Dùn thais quarrel over which way a bank should face</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,802</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0205"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847** — *Cathair mhòr below the old outpost* (Cathair mhòr). Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it is the nearest quarry.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5051"><em>Eithne's households name the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire Cathair mhòr</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5051"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847** — *Eithne's households name the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). Settlers below a broken watch-tower ask Eithne, then a hundred and forty-four years old, to lay out their fields, and she stays; her households name the place Cathair mhòr, the great city, out of hope rather than size, and take no stone from the ruin above them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0205"><em>Cathair mhòr below the old outpost</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5052"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,870** — *Households come to Cnoc naomh for its spring* (Cnoc naomh). Settlers take up a hill already called, by no teller then living able to say why, the holy hill, and keep its water and the fact of its holiness together without asking more of either.
- <a id="ev-EII-5053"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,890** — *Muileann naomh is founded on piles over the marsh* (Muileann naomh). The first houses of Muileann naomh stand on driven piles over standing marsh water between Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell, and are afterward moved to firm ground a bowshot inland once the piles prove the footing sound, keeping the name the marsh first gave them.
- <a id="ev-I-0206"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,894** — *Cnoc naomh* (Cnoc naomh). Households come to settle on a hill for its spring, and the hill is already called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill. Why, is not known.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5052"><em>Households come to Cnoc naomh for its spring</em>, 18 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,870</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5054"></a>**8 am Faoilleach, GE 2,900** — *The king takes back the western valleys from Murchadh*. After three hundred years in Murchadh's keeping, the king takes back the poorer western valleys of the northern plain and gives them to a grandson of An Cnoc Ruadh's line, saying only that the ground had grown crowded enough to want a nearer hand; Murchadh does not argue it, and the plain stops speaking of it within the year.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5053"><em>Muileann naomh is founded on piles over the marsh</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0207"></a>**12 an Dàmhair, GE 2,947** — *Tobar dhearg on the southern cape* (Tobar dhearg). The keepers of the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the greatest place on the south coast.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5048"><em>Tobar dhearg rises round the red well</em>, 11 an t-Samhain, GE 2,790</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5055"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,960** — *Calum Ciar dies at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Calum Ciar, eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, dies in his seven hundred and eleventh year, having asked the slab for its lot once and never asked again; the king buries him on the hill beside his mother.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0157"><em>Calum Ciar asks for the lot</em>, 4 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,412</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-I-0208"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, GE 2,986** — *Muileann naomh founded* (Muileann naomh). Muileann naomh is founded near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses stand on stilts over a marsh, and are afterwards moved to firm ground.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5053"><em>Muileann naomh is founded on piles over the marsh</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,890</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5056"></a>**11 an t-Samhain, GE 2,990** — *Diorbhail born at Tobar dhìreach* (Tobar dhìreach). A daughter is born to a household of the watch at Tobar dhìreach and named Diorbhail; she will say her own line back before she can tie a shoe, and carry Sloinneadh a' Chlachair after Somhairle.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208"><em>Muileann naomh founded</em>, 24 am Faoilleach, GE 2,986</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5057"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, GE 2,993** — *Diorbhail says her own line before she can tie a shoe* (Tobar dhìreach). A child of Tobar dhìreach not yet three years old says her line back four generations at her mother's fire, for the pleasure of the saying and not because she is asked, and the households of Na Glinn Àrda begin to remark on her the way a valley remarks on any child who does an ordinary thing early.
- <a id="ev-EII-5058"></a>**4 an Cèitean, GE 2,997** — *Somhairle first sits Diorbhail by the slab* (Tobar dhìreach). Somhairle takes the seven-year-old Diorbhail up to the slab for a morning, on no more of an asking than that her mother has no need of her, and gives her the small tellings that ring the Line rather than the Line itself, holding that a thing given too soon to too young a head is given badly.
- <a id="ev-EII-5059"></a>**5 an Giblean, GE 2,999** — *The summons to An Cruinneachadh Mòr reaches the north*. Riders of the king's own household bring word to Baile Mòr mhòr that every holder of every share of the island is to come to a gathering at the ford of salt and wool greater than any before it; Murchadh sends word to his sons and to Eithne, and rides south himself with sixty of his household.
- <a id="ev-EII-5060"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, GE 3,000** — *An Cnoc Ruadh's salt-traders walk to An Cruinneachadh Mòr* (Cathair dhearg). Word goes out along every road that Cruinneachadh an Àtha in the three thousandth year since the grove will be kept greater than any before it. Households of An Cnoc Ruadh's lake shore, among them An Cnoc Ruadh girl and her mother, walk the fourteen miles down with their salt wrapped against the damp.
- <a id="ev-I-0208a"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The great gathering at the ford* (Fèill Muileann òg). In the height of his days Ailean Mòr keeps a gathering at the ford of the salt and wool. The holders of the hill, the Red Hill, the salt shore, the north and the west set their hands in his. Some four hundred of his own blood stand about him, children and their children, more than the reciters can name in a night. Only the households east of the vein send no one.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5059"><em>The summons to An Cruinneachadh Mòr reaches the north</em>, 5 an Giblean, GE 2,999</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EII-5060"><em>An Cnoc Ruadh's salt-traders walk to An Cruinneachadh Mòr</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5500"><em>The three grounds of the ford run together</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5501"><em>Amber, pots and flint change hands at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5502"><em>The reciters mark the three thousandth year since the grove</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5503"><em>The crowd opens for the king unbidden</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5504"><em>An Cnoc Ruadh's new holder is still called by his father's name</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5505"><em>Somhairle stands nearest the king in the rings</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5506"><em>Murchadh is pointed out among the king's blood</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5507"><em>Eithne stands young-faced in the outer ring</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5508"><em>The reciters reckon four hundred of the king's blood</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5509"><em>A boy of the west asks whether it is one family</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5510"><em>The east's absence is remarked and let go</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EII-5511"><em>An Cnoc Ruadh girl trails her hand in the warm ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5500"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The three grounds of the ford run together*. More households come in than the ford's three grounds, downstream, upstream and the rise beyond the river, were ever laid out to hold, until by the second morning no one can any longer say which bank belongs to whom, and a child sent for water is an hour finding her way back.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5501"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *Amber, pots and flint change hands at the ford*. Potters of the north-west, a stranger from the far west with strings of drilled amber, and carriers of eastern flint trade the first day of An Cruinneachadh Mòr through, while households from opposite ends of the crowd sit down together to weigh what a marriage between their children might be worth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5502"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The reciters mark the three thousandth year since the grove*. An old reciter of the hill tells those at his fire that the year is the three thousandth since the grove was lit, and that word of the count has been carried out along every road that summer, drawing to the ford households who had never before troubled to send anyone to an ordinary gathering.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5503"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The crowd opens for the king unbidden*. On the second morning the king comes down the hill road dressed as any herdsman, and the whole crowd between the road and the river opens a way for him without a word called, old people stepping back from the path with their eyes down as from nothing else at the gathering.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5504"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *An Cnoc Ruadh's new holder is still called by his father's name* (Cathair dhearg). Among the five who wade out to put their hands between the king's, An Cnoc Ruadh's own holder is so newly come to his hall that half the crowd on the bank still names him for his father before catching themselves.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5505"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *Somhairle stands nearest the king in the rings*. Somhairle takes his place at the king's left hand in the river as the rings of the king's blood go in, two thousand nine hundred and sixty-two years old that summer and looking, those at the ford say afterward, every year of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5506"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *Murchadh is pointed out among the king's blood*. Murchadh, who holds the northern plain for his father and has by then eleven sons of his own scattered among the rings, is pointed out by name on the bank, a head taller than most beside him and looking, past his twelve hundredth year, no older than a young man.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5507"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *Eithne stands young-faced in the outer ring*. Eithne, not yet three hundred years old and looking a girl of twenty, stands laughing among the outer rings of the king's blood, named to the girl of An Cnoc Ruadh by a woman of the ford who knows the lines by heart.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5508"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The reciters reckon four hundred of the king's blood*. The naming of the king's children and their children runs from midday to sundown and is not finished when the light fails; word passes along the bank that the reciters have counted some four hundred of his blood standing in the river that day, more than at any gathering before it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5509"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *A boy of the west asks whether it is one family*. A boy of a western household, standing beside An Cnoc Ruadh girl at the bank while the naming goes on, asks her whether all of that in the water is truly one family, and neither child can find a plainer answer to give the other.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5510"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *The east's absence is remarked and let go*. Women of An Cnoc Ruadh note at the fire that no household from east of the vein has come to the gathering a second year running, turn the matter over a little while without an answer, and let it go with the fine weather, unremembered again within the hour.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5511"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000** — *An Cnoc Ruadh girl trails her hand in the warm ford*. When the gathering has gone back to its fires and the king stands alone a while in the emptied ford at dusk, An Cnoc Ruadh girl, nearest the water of anyone left on the bank, finds it warm as bath-water round his legs and sees it smoke downstream of him in the last light.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0208a"><em>The great gathering at the ford</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,000</a>.</span>

## The Years GE 3,001 – 3,250

- <a id="ev-EII-5512"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, GE 3,004** — *A basket-weavers' boy tries the slab and turns back to his creels* (Tobar dhìreach). A cousin of Diorbhail's goes up to the slab with her twice out of curiosity and finds he can make no sense of the names, choosing to learn the weaving of a creel that holds water instead. Neither thinks less of the other, and it stands as one more fact of the valleys: that the slab takes some and lets others alone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5058"><em>Somhairle first sits Diorbhail by the slab</em>, 4 an Cèitean, GE 2,997</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5513"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,006** — *Diorbhail catches a gap between two tellings* (Tobar dhìreach). Testing her own memory against a household's telling of itself at the ordinary fires, Diorbhail finds a name kept differently from the way the Line keeps it and brings both versions to Somhairle rather than choose between them, and he settles which telling holds truer and tells her the reason for it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5512"><em>A basket-weavers' boy tries the slab and turns back to his creels</em>, 10 an t-Samhain, GE 3,004</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5514"></a>**13 an t-Sultain, GE 3,008** — *Somhairle says at the fire he may not sit many more Samhains* (Tobar dhìreach). At a Samhain fire before the whole round of the watch-households, Somhairle says plainly that he does not know how many more such nights he will sit among them, and the gathering falls silent around him, having never before heard him say such a thing of himself.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5513"><em>Diorbhail catches a gap between two tellings</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,006</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5515"></a>**12 an Dàmhair, GE 3,010** — *Somhairle gives Diorbhail Sloinneadh a' Chlachair whole* (Tobar dhìreach). Over a single night at the watch-fire, with Beathan's son sitting the turn beside them, Somhairle says the whole Sloinneadh a' Chlachair through twice without a name out of place, the same way it was given to him and to Beathan before her, and sets her own name at its foot when he is done.
- <a id="ev-EII-5516"></a>**17 an t-Iuchar, GE 3,011** — *The valleys turn to Diorbhail's fire before Somhairle's* (Tobar dhìreach). After the giving, households of Na Glinn Àrda begin bringing their children's names to Diorbhail's fire rather than Somhairle's, the way a valley turns by degrees from an old well to a new one dug beside it, the old well no less good for the turning.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5515"><em>Somhairle gives Diorbhail Sloinneadh a' Chlachair whole</em>, 12 an Dàmhair, GE 3,010</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5517"></a>**15 an Lùnastal, GE 3,014** — *Somhairle's face is likened to a withered apple* (Tobar dhìreach). An old woman of the watch-households, seeing Somhairle at a distance one Bealltainn, says he has come to look like a withered apple left too long on the sill. The saying travels the valleys and sticks to him, so that in time the households speak of him by it as easily as by his own name.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5516"><em>The valleys turn to Diorbhail's fire before Somhairle's</em>, 17 an t-Iuchar, GE 3,011</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EII-5518"></a>**20 an Cèitean, GE 3,018** — *Somhairle asks Diorbhail what waits for a man with no hall* (Tobar dhìreach). At a fire with no one else near enough to hear, Somhairle tells Diorbhail the one thing his own father never told him: that he does not know what waits for one of the grove's blood who took no wife of the king's giving and no share of the kingdom, having no hall to be carried into when his years run out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EII-5517"><em>Somhairle's face is likened to a withered apple</em>, 15 an Lùnastal, GE 3,014</a>.</span>
