A net-mender's kinsman of Caol shean, twenty years unhurt at every boundary quarrel of the eastern country, goes into the first rush and is not seen to come out of the river; his wife asks after him at every fire down the bank until evening, then asks no more.
- <a id="ev-EII-6535"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, GE 4,603** — *The dead of the host begin to dam the ford* (Dùn dhearg). On the second day the drowned and the slain lie so thick at the shallows below the crossing that the river backs up over the gravel, running warm and red, and the men of Dùn dhearg must climb their own dead to reach water shallow enough to cross.
- <a id="ev-EII-6536"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, GE 4,603** — *The king draws a boy of Dùn dhearg from the river with his own hand* (Dùn dhearg). In the press of the second day the king takes the spear from the hands of a sixteen-year-old of the eastern host as a mother takes a knife from a child, and the boy is carried out alive on the east bank; the telling of that hand is kept by the east long after his name is forgotten.
- <a id="ev-EII-6537"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, GE 4,603** — *Artair mac Fhearghail counsels the host to go in together* (Dùn dhearg). On the second night, with some of the host ready to go home, Artair mac Fhearghail tells the fires that the king is flesh and must have an end, as a cliff has an end before the sea, and counsels every spear of the east to go into the river together on the third day and not draw back.
- <a id="ev-EII-6538"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, GE 4,603** — *The whole strength of the east goes into the river together* (Dùn dhearg). At first light on the third day every spear the east country has enters the ford at once and does not draw back, the host closing on the king from three sides the whole day long while the dead already in the water rise higher than the shallows had ever stood.
- <a id="ev-EII-6539"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, GE 4,603** — *A light is seen on the water around the king* (Dùn dhearg). In the afternoon of the third day men near the middle of the ford see a light low along the river's surface where the king stands, of no colour any of them had a word for, and say afterward only that they saw every colour in it and none, and would say no more.
- <a id="ev-EII-6540"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, GE 4,603** — *The king's kin fail to come to the ford* (Dùn dhearg). Through all three days at the ford below Dùn dhearg, no household of the king's own blood, and no spear of the hills, comes down the western track to stand with him; Sluagh an Ear has the river to itself the whole time.

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh chaol** (Achadh chaol). Founded 27 an Gearran, GE 2,475. A settlement in the east where, across three dry summers from the two thousand four hundred and sixty-sixth year, households burned back the old scrub a field's width at a time and ploughed the black ground while the ash still held its warmth, taking the first year a crop the older fields to the west had not equalled in a generation. The stones they picked from the new fields they laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields for the rest of the age. Known for fields cleared by fire and bounded by picked stone.

**Achadh dhìreach** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 16 an Cèitean, VE 303. The oldest hearths of Na Glinn Àrda stand at Achadh dhìreach. In the nine hundred and second year three brothers clearing a strip for barley turned up a hearth laid true and never lit, and the valley left the strip unploughed and covered the hearth with peat until no living person remembered where it lay. Anna nic Coinnich was born two fields from it and kept the full hand all her life. In the thousand and sixty-sixth year Eanraig Ruadh, old and cold, burned a whole basket of an gual dathach in one night, and his house went up in a flame of a colour no one had a word for, with his wife Beathag and a grandchild within; the hearthstone split and ran with colour until the king knelt and laid his hand across it and it greyed. The king named the full hand a good custom and made no law of it. Eanraig's son kept the grey stone for his new hearth, and one of the four stone cups was ground here in Oighrig's years. Known for the unlit hearth and the basket burning.

**Achadh mhòr** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, GE 4,000. A field country near Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in the east, where in the four thousand and eighth year a household cleared and banked the widest single field the eastern country had yet cut from the rough, the largest of the age. It laid its bank on the stones of an older wall whose builders none could name, and grew in a good year wheat enough for three households where before there had been land for none. Known for the widest field of the age.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, GE 4,091. A settlement in the north beside a spring held sacred, whose settlers led the water round in channels of their own digging and fenced the spring before a single wall was raised, so that a stranger coming on the place might take the water, and not the people, for what had been settled there. They watered their fields from the channels and would not build over the spring. Known for the spring fenced before any house.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 21 an Giblean, GE 3,125. An old field in the east whose wells fell a hand lower than any digger remembered in the two thousand and third year. A shepherd's boy walked three days to Dùn ìseal to say that the field banks his grandfather raised had cracked from dryness; the springs stopped outright, and the households walked off their old banks and cut new fields lower on the slope. Sìleas Bhàn refused to have the dead field pulled down, saying a bank tells a household what the ground once gave and what it stopped giving. The households came back in the three thousand one hundred and twenty-fifth year, cut new fields on the higher ground, and sank a deep well before they broke a furrow; the well did not fail again in the age. Known for the drought and the well dug first.

**An Cnoc Ruadh** (now Cathair dhearg) (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18. An Cnoc Ruadh stood above the western end of Loch chrom, a palisaded hall over salt-pans and boats, held by a line older than the king's crowning. Beathag Ruadh held it when the valleys came in to the king and did not come; Uisdean Mòr cut the ditch across the neck, and saw his palisade burned twice, and at last knelt in the ford to put his hands between the king's in the two hundred and ninetieth year. Seonag weighed the salt tallies before the king with a pebble bag; Murchadh Gearr walked Rathad an t-Salainn every autumn; Lachlann Ruadh took Eilidh Ghlas's younger son to foster and was called Lachlann an Altraim for it. Peigi Dhubh laid the stone landing at the river-mouth, and the harbour grew round it. The hill traded salt for Dùn ìseal's wool at the ford fourteen miles off, and its reciters kept their own roll, from Beathag Ruadh to Seumas Òg, which was spoken whole at the ford only once. Known for salt, the palisade, and the fosterling.

**Àth àrsaidh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an t-Samhain, GE 3,458. An ancient ford in the north-west near a quarry of green stone, whose polished axes were carried all over the island in the three thousand four hundred and ninety-sixth year, too fine for work, laid unused in graves and under house floors. Ìomhar Dearg asked the cutters for one to carry and use and was told no green axe was ever cut to be swung, only shown; he had a common grey axe made instead and used it forty years. The few households who worked the quarry traded in nothing else, and the chips about it lay knee-deep. The seam ran thin under every cut, and in the three thousand five hundred and forty-seventh year the last cutter who held the old skill died with no apprentice; the quarry was forsaken, and the axes ceased. Known for the green axes never swung.

**Àth bheag** (Àth bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean, GE 4,347. A small ford on the far eastern coast, settled in the four thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Its households went out in boats after the geese on the islands offshore and raked salt from the flats beside the ford. It sent its geese-feathers inland by the traders' road and knew the hill only by report. The households kept the sharing before the storms as the coast kept it, weighing their surplus by the count of mouths on the shingle, and they cut the eight wind-names on a driftwood post above the landing so that a boat going out after the geese might know which wind would bring it home. Known for the geese on the islands.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Àth fhiadhaich). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, GE 4,325. A stony crossing in the south-eastern hills where wild cattle came down to drink. Households settled it in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-fifth year and reared the calves born on the near bank apart from the wild herd, until within three generations that ford's cattle were spoken of the length of the coast as the best in the hills. The settlers came from the valleys under Dùn ìseal and kept the sharing before the storms, bringing calves as their surplus rather than grain. Their herds were driven to the ford in the autumns, and in the years of the waiting below the hill they sold beasts to the camps of the king's kin. Known for the wild cattle's ford.

**Àth gharbh** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 13 an Gearran, VE 4,424. A rough ford on the drovers' road through Na Glinn Àrda, where the beasts were rested and watered. In a hearth of peat ash here the valleys say an gual dathach was first burned by a household outside Clann a' Chlachair, one sliver at a time. The custom of the full hand is told as beginning among the few households of this ford, after a sick child was warmed too generously, and from here it spread to every hearth of Na Glinn Àrda within a few years. In Oighrig's keeping a woman of Àth gharbh ground the first of the copies of the stone cup, measuring against Niocol Snaidhear's cup throughout, and she finished it quickest of the three. Coinneachadh nan Cupan was held at a nameless spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, chosen because it lay equal walking from all four places. The drovers who rested there carried the custom of the full hand and the tidings of the cups the length of Na Glinn Àrda, and the ford's own households were among the first to sit a turn at the slab when the watch was drawn from every part of the hills. Known for the drovers' ford where the full hand began.

**Àth mhòr** (Àth mhòr). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, GE 1,847. A great ford of the north on the far eastern circuit of Rathad na Spor. In the thousand eight hundred and fifty-third year a young man of the ford cut a hawk into his father's door-lintel by firelight over three evenings, wings closed and the head turned back over the shoulder; he said only that the shape had come to him whole one night and would not leave him alone until he had cut it. Murchadh watched him cut it. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird, and the lintel was set again over every door the household built after. Known for the hawk lintel.

**Àth shean** (Àth shean). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,361. The old ford below Dùn ìseal where the road west crosses its river. A careful household of the ford dug a grain pit under its byre floor against nothing it could name, and brought nothing of it to the sharing; in the lean storm season of the two thousand three hundred and seventy-seventh year the daughter of the house, Beasag, saw the division made by the count of mouths and the next spring told a neighbour the truth of the pit. Tormod Liath asked only whether she had told it of her own will, and sent to open the floor. The household was given until dark to take what it could carry and be off the ford's ground: the first punishment under the sharing that is remembered. It settled east of the vein and dug no pit under its new floor. The pit kept the man's name for generations, and stood empty. Eilidh Ghlas knelt here to her younger son's height when he went west to be fostered. Known for the hidden pit, and the first punishment.

#### B

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464. A settlement on the far north-west coast where, after two failed fishing seasons in the nineteen hundred and sixty-sixth year, the stores went to bark and boiled seaweed and the graves were laid two deep for want of time to dig them singly; no older hunger on Dia-thìr is tied to a place. The king rode north-west with the first grain that could be spared, by a road that had never carried him, and Sìleas Bhàn sent carts after him for the whole coast. The ground lay empty for five hundred years. In the two thousand four hundred and sixty-fourth year households from Cnoc ghorm settled it again, and Somhairle found them already byred and welled, the old field-marks half sunk beneath the new grass. They dug their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast. Known for the hunger, and the deep pits.

**Baile dhomhain** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Samhain, GE 2,388. A settlement a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, across whose fields the panthers' road ran. In the two thousand four hundred and thirty-first year its households began cutting a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scraping it away at its close, the first mark the island's tellers know cut for a season rather than for any one event; by the two thousand four hundred and forty-seventh year the custom was kept at every gate. The households shut their stock in while the cats passed. Known for the gatepost sign of the crossing season.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,709. A settlement on the western coast where the boars ran heaviest in the thickets. Its settlers hung boar tusks over their doors and took boar for their chief meat for the rest of the age, and the island came to know a man of that place by his gait, from a lifetime of walking ground a boar might break from underfoot. Its households kept the sharing before the storms by bringing boar meat salted in An Cnoc Ruadh's salt, and it was said at the ford that no settlement of the west brought fatter shares or quarrelled longer over the weighing of them. Known for boar tusks over the doors.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 2,662. The stony ground north-east of Murchadh's spring, settled by households who kept sheep where the land would bear nothing heavier. They sent their wool south along the coast road to Cruinneachadh an Àtha rather than north to Murchadh's own granary, and the wool market they kept grew with the flocks of the moor settlements about them. The flocks were small and hardy, and the households cut the eight wind-names into their fold-posts, reading weather by the post that stood in the lee. Their wool came to the ford in bales tied with their own twisted rope, and was known there by it. Known for sheep and wool for the ford.

**Baile gheal** (Baile gheal). Founded 27 an Giblean, GE 4,347. A settlement founded on the south-western plain in the four thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, round a house whose walls were limed white. The lime was burned from the shells of Seann-Dhaoine' middens along the coast, which the settlers judged no one's any longer to keep; the households took their name from the house and kept its walls white every spring. It traded cloth and lime along the coast road and sent its people to the ford. The settlers came from the older harbours of the south-west, and the first of them to lime her walls white did so, the telling says, so that her husband could find the house from the sea in the dusk. Known for the white-limed house.

**Baile ghlas** (Baile ghlas). Founded 7 an Cèitean, GE 4,047. A harbour along the lake shore from An Cnoc Ruadh, where the hill's households drew up their boats in sheds of stone and turf. Within a generation of the first sheds the boats kept there put out oftener than from An Cnoc Ruadh's own strand, and in the four thousand and forty-seventh year it was An Cnoc Ruadh's fishing harbour in all but the reciters' naming. It was never banked or palisaded, trusting to the hill above it. Its boat-sheds were built long and low against the lake's winds, each shed holding two boats, and the households of the hill took turns at the drawing-up after every storm. Its fishers were among the first on the lake to cut the paired tide-marks on their own landing stones. Known for An Cnoc Ruadh's boat-sheds.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 622. Tràigh an t-Salainn of the south, where the salt-folk scraped the flats and dried the crust on the shingle. In the six hundred and seventy-second year Mòrag Chruaidh came down on it with eleven spears and took salt, losing seven of her own, whose names the hill kept at its fire. In the six hundred and eighty-third year they made shallow clay basins behind the shingle bar, the first salt-works of the island, and raised a bank behind the pans. Iain Dubh came down in the seven hundred and twenty-seventh year at dawn with more spears, and Tadhg Garbh's spear killed him on the clay. The next summer the king walked south alone; the salt-folk raised spears against him and lowered them, and old Mòr knelt on the wet shingle and gave him a double handful of salt, and from that day the shore was called the king's. The salt-folk built a cairn of their own with seven stones in it, and in the fosterling's day An Cnoc Ruadh's own salt refrain was sung at their pans in words An Cnoc Ruadh itself could no longer construe. Known for the salt-pans and the double handful.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616. A rise on the northern plain above a spring that ran clear through every winter, where Murchadh Mòr raised his hall in the two thousand six hundred and sixteenth year after the king sent him north with sixty households. The households of the plain named the place Baile Mòr mhòr before it had earned the size of the name; at its height it held some eighty houses, the largest place north of An Cnoc Ruadh. Murchadh's eleven sons, born over the better part of three centuries, were each given a corner of the plain to hold under their father. The king's summons to An Cruinneachadh Mòr reached it in the two thousand nine hundred and ninety-ninth year, and Murchadh rode south with sixty of his household. Known for Murchadh's hall by the spring that never froze.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 3,311. A broad red-earthed rise near the eastern Seann Dunn, settled in the middle of na Bliadhnachan Fada by households who called the ground around them empty though Seann-Dhaoine' middens lay a morning's walk away and plainly said otherwise. They dug into nothing of what lay there. The settlement grew into a place of some size by the three thousand three hundred and eleventh year, raising its houses of the red stone of the rise. Known for the empty ground beside the middens.

#### C

**Cala nan Taighean Cruinne**. Founded 3 an t-Sultain, GE 1,347. A harbour of round, turf-roofed houses at the deep-water side of the river mouth below Loch chrom, near enough An Cnoc Ruadh to pay it salt. The first houses were raised in the thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, where the king's blood had first come down to the sea, and within a season the households were paying their salt to An Cnoc Ruadh rather than keeping it among themselves, with no word sent from Dùn ìseal to start it. An Cnoc Ruadh's list counts them among its holder's households, and the harbour's boats carried salt up the lake to the ford in the autumns. Known for the round houses that paid An Cnoc Ruadh salt.

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 2,414. A river-mouth settlement of fishing households on the north coast, at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm. They fixed the custom of naming each boat for the wind it was built to fish in, held a boat unlucky under any other wind, and never gave a drowned boat's name again. The custom was settled by the two thousand four hundred and forty-seventh year and spread along the north coast with the wind-names themselves. Known for boats named for the winds.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,547. A river-mouth on a wild strait where, in the thousand five hundred and ninety-eighth year, households staked a fence of woven wattle out into the ebb to trap salmon on the falling tide. The fence washed out twice before the third setting held, and the same line of stake-holes was fished again every year after through the rest of the age. Its smoked salmon went to Cruinneachadh an Àtha and along the coast road. Known for the fish-fence and its stake-holes.

**Caol gharbh** (Caol gharbh). Founded 10 am Màrt, GE 4,128. A settlement on the rough strait of the north-east coast, taken up in the four thousand one hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who fished the strait in skin boats. They laid paddles beside their dead, and their boats were heavier in the beam than any on that coast, for the strait's sake. Its fishers named their boats for the winds as the north coast did, and gave no drowned boat's name again. In the lean years they brought dried fish inland to the sharing, and a household that kept its catch back found no boat willing to put out beside it the next season. Known for the paddles laid beside the dead.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach, GE 1,560. A settlement on the wide strait on the western coast where, in the thousand five hundred and sixty-second year, a household set a hollowed stone with seal oil and a wick of moss on its hearth-ledge and lit it: the first light on Dia-thìr that was not a hearth, giving little smoke. Within three winters every house on that stretch kept one burning through the dark months, and the lamps went along the coast with the seal-hunters. Known for the first seal-oil lamps.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462. The great strait in the north-west, where Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal and heaped their shell middens high along the strand. Hill-folk households settled here in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-second year and built on the middens, raising their walls, where they built in stone at all, from what the tide had not carried off. They would not turn a stone that carried a mark, cut or worn, and laid those aside in an unmortared line along the shore, so that two kinds of wall stood there side by side. Known for the marked stones laid aside.

**Caol ruadh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 14 an Giblean, GE 2,570. A fishing strait on the southern coast named for the red rock that watches it. Its fishers took to tying woven buoys over the deep channels where the current ran hardest, a custom that spread along the coast in carriers' mouths as the paired tide-marks had spread before it. The settlement was taken up in earnest in the two thousand five hundred and seventieth year, and it traded with the harbour of Seann Skell and the marsh settlement at Muileann naomh. Its households kept the sharing before the storms along the whole strait, and in A' Ghaoth Dhubh's winter sent dried fish north along the coast road with the grain from the valleys. Known for the buoys over the channels.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 4,196. An old river port on the narrows of the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein. In the four thousand and fifty-eighth year two households quarrelling over a stretch of the landing sat out a night together and gave the ground to the landing itself, for whoever had a boat drawn up there; within two generations they were thoroughly mixed by marriage. By the four thousand two hundred and twenty-eighth year it was the river landing of the hill households of the east, where salt, fish and seal-skins came up from the coast; a cloth-trader passing through told the child Ailis of the young-faced man at the gate of Dùn ìseal, and she married a net-mender of the landing. Known for the landing given to no one.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 13 an Cèitean, GE 2,523. A long ridge in the south between the valleys and the coast, where households settled in the middle centuries within an earth bank. It dug and lined a well inside its own earthwork in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-seventh year so that its water-carriers need not go down to the shore while a storm still had teeth in it, and the town was taken up in earnest a generation later. It traded south to the coast and north to the ford, and sent its people to An Cruinneachadh Mòr in the three thousandth year. Its households kept the handful by the cup and the sharing by the count of mouths, and in the lean years they opened their store within the bank to the coast below them as Dùn ìseal had opened its own. Known for the well within the bank.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt, GE 1,378. A rise above the firth on the far western coast, where a long-house forty paces long, byre and hall under one roof, was raised in the thousand four hundred and sixteenth year, timbered from Rathad na Spor's own hills and roofed with turf. It was the greatest building of the age in the north-west and was spoken of the length of the coast. A spark from an untended hearth caught the byre-end thatch four years later and the hall burned with the byre; the household raised it again on the same footing before the next winter, holding the ground proved good whatever the fire proved of the roof, and left its scorch mark for anyone to see. It burned and was raised again once more before the age was out. Known for the long-house burned twice.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847. Households settled on the ground below a broken watch-tower of Seann-Dhaoine in the two thousand eight hundred and forty-seventh year and asked Eithne nic Ailein, then a hundred and forty-four years old, to lay out their fields; she stayed. Her households named the place Cathair mhòr, the great city, out of hope rather than size, and took no stone from the ruin above them though it was the nearest quarry. Eithne's knot-keeper walked at the head of her household with its cord about his arm when she came down to the valley below Dùn ìseal in the last years. Known for Eithne's fields below the ruined tower.

**Ceann àrsaidh** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 17 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. A point on the Abhainn fhionn where households from An Cnoc Ruadh's country found an old river landing, its stones set for a boat's keel by hands none living could name, and built their houses about it in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year. They named the place for what they found, the ancient headland, and used the landing as they found it rather than mend it, as settlers did wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stood. The households came down from the lake shore by boat, and the landing took their boats at every state of the river as it had taken Seann-Dhaoine' boats. They kept An Cnoc Ruadh's roll at their fires as their own. Known for the old landing on the Abhainn fhionn.

**Ceann chiar** (Seann Tarr). Founded 10 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,404. A harbour on the eastern coast at the southern end of the shore A' Ghaoth Dhubh stripped. It fed the people of Cuan ruadh through the winter after the storm out of its shared surplus, and no one on that coast is known to have died of hunger that season. Rebuilding after A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the households set a stone in the midst of their houses and cut a plain stroke on it for every house the wind had taken, two-and-twenty marks in a row with no names beside them. Known for the stone of the twenty-two houses.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, GE 2,061. A broad headland on the gulf where, in the two thousand and seventy-sixth year, three brothers of the point, Aonghas, Dùghlas and Ailig mac Torcaill, quarried eight stones from an outcrop above the landing and raised them in a ring, one for each of the named winds, so a sailor might lay a hand on the stone of the wind he wanted before he put out. The stone of the hardest offshore wind settled crooked in a bad winter and was dug out and reset on a footing of smaller stones, standing straighter and newer than its seven fellows ever after. The yearly contests of strength were held below Clachan nan Gaoth, and it was here that Alasdair Làidir threw every man at three-and-twenty and a grey stranger lifted the black boulder to his knees and set it down gently. Known for Clachan nan Gaoth and the lifted boulder.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,028. A harbour on the south-eastern shore below Làrach an Dùin, the ruin of the old builders, settled by fishing households in the three thousand and twenty-eighth year. They built their houses with doors to the sea and backs to the broken walls, and would not go up to the ruin or carry off its dressed stone lying loose for the taking; an old woman of that shore said a wall raised by other hands keeps its own quarrel. The contests below Clachan nan Gaoth at Ceann leathan drew its young men every autumn, and it was a son of this shore's herders, Alasdair Làidir, who threw every man who stood against him at three-and-twenty. Known for the harbour under the ruin.

**Cnoc àrsaidh**. Founded 14 an t-Samhain, GE 2. The hill in the north-west where a pit was worked for the only good flint on Dia-thìr, its grey flakes carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other. The carriers' track ran from the pit-mouth south and east toward Cruinneachadh an Àtha, and by the thousand eight hundred and seventeenth year it was worn a yard deep. Murchadh, the king's son by Beitris, came here with the flint-carriers in the thousand seven hundred and sixtieth year and carried a yoke for three seasons before any man learned whose son he was; he walked the road with Ailig Spor for the whole of the years it gave them, and when Ailig took the lighter work of tallying at the pit-mouth Murchadh came back through at the turn of every season to sit an evening with him. After Ailig's burying Murchadh set it as a standing custom that the first flake of any new working be given free to whoever asked. Known for the flint-pit and the free first flake.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 11 am Màrt, GE 2,405. A southern settlement near Imrich nam Pantar, where Gilleonan bored four holes along a hollow bird-bone in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-eighth year and found a note he could raise and lower at will; children of three households gathered to hear him play. The bone pipes are the oldest instruments of the island. The households kept watch on the passes in the crossing season, and in that same spring three great cats were seen to turn back at the highest pass. Known for the bone pipes.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, GE 3,908. A settlement on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal a short walk from the old standing stone. The generation that settled it in the three thousand nine hundred and eighth year set its houses, by no law anyone could name, so that no door faced the stone, and every household built after kept the same pattern unquestioned. Known for no door facing the stone.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cill thais). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,453. A settlement at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, raised by households come down from An Cnoc Ruadh in the middle of the age. They took their timber only from the river's far side and never from the unclaimed wood, and marked the line with a row of unhewn stones. When a boy not yet seven was lost past the stones in the two thousand four hundred and fifty-first year, the settlement and its neighbours searched three days into the wood without one sign of him; Iain of Muileann bhàn, lame from the passes, said aloud that a wood no household would fell was not a wood that gave back what it took, and the searchers stopped at the stones. Known for the line of stones at the forest's edge.

**Cnoc chaol**. Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,648. A village of low houses on the south coast under a narrow hill, where the sea rose past every mark it had kept in the seven hundred and seventy-seventh year and came in over the houses in the night, taking twelve of the shore's people and leaving a hand's depth of grey sand over every hearth it did not carry away. Seasaidh, seven years old, was carried up the slope by her mother; her father was among the twelve. The survivors rebuilt higher on the slope and left the old ground unbuilt, and when a lesser wave came in the three thousand eight hundred and seventeenth year it found only empty byres below the new houses. The measure of the full hand was ground into a stone cup here, despite two false starts, in Oighrig's keeping. Known for the wave, and the houses on the slope.

**Cnoc chaol** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 22 an Cèitean, GE 2,404. A settlement on a narrow hill in the near valleys, on poor ground. One of the four stone cups was ground here in Oighrig's keeping, and the copy was begun fastest of the three despite two false starts; the cups were sent back to the wheel when their levels would not match, until at Coinneachadh nan Cupan the water stood level in all four. From that year its households measured their handful of coal by the one cup and its copies. An old woman of Cnoc chaol was the first to say at the slab, in the judgement of Gilleasbuig Beag, that the vein was never any one hearth's to keep behind a cloth. Known for one of the four cups.

**Cnoc fhionn** (Baile ruadh). Founded 25 an t-Samhain, VE 3,715. A fair hill of sheltered farms in the north-east, settled long before the grove and keeping its old ways through the whole of na Bliadhnachan Fada. The king's word reached it late and lightly, and it was never asked for spears. Its barley went down to Seann-Dhaoine' harbour at Seann Tarr while there were Seann-Dhaoine there to take it, and to the hill-folk who settled Seann Tarr after them. It sent its young to Cruinneachadh an Àtha from the time the gathering became yearly, and its ale went south with them. Known for barley, and the road to Seann Tarr.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, GE 1,362. A green rise in the north-west where the settlements lived on seal, fish and deer until the thousand three hundred and seventy-ninth year, when small herds driven up Rathad na Spor by stages over three summers brought cattle there for the first time. The first calves born on the rise were watched through their first winter by the whole settlement in turn. It became the farm town of the north-west, and its hides went south by Rathad na Spor. Known for the first cattle of the north-west.

**Cnoc na Claise**. Founded 5 an Dàmhair, GE 2. A black hill in the east where Torcall Tochlair, refused the marriage he was promised and restless at the coal-banks under the mountain, went with his brother Lachann and two other diggers to open a trench for a second vein. In the two thousand two hundred and sixty-seventh year the trench fell in on two of them, Lachann among them, and Torcall buried his brother at the trench's mouth and would not leave. He built a turf shelter at the trench's edge, and folk who came to the hill for one reason or another began to stay, since the ground was as good as any and the man who kept the trench asked nothing of them. He died there and was buried beside his brother. His household kept the ground, did not fill the trench in, and in Catrìona's years refused to burn its handful of coal with the rest of the hills, giving no single answer twice for it. Known for the open trench and the refused handful.

**Cnoc naomh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,894. A hill south of the valleys already called, by no teller then living able to say why, the holy hill. Households came to it for its spring in the two thousand eight hundred and seventieth year and settled it in earnest a generation later, keeping its water and the fact of its holiness together without asking more of either. The households cut the spring's channel no deeper than they found it, and lit no fire within sight of the source. In An Cruinneachadh Mòr of the three thousandth year they sent water from the holy spring to the ford in sealed pots, and it was poured into the river at dusk. Known for the spring of the holy hill.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. A damp hill in the north-west settled in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who drained it with ditches before they built, and grazed its wet slopes with sheep. The ditches carried water through the rest of the age, and the households traded with the mill-folk of Muileann àrsaidh below them. The ditches were cut to a line the eldest of the settlers paced out alone over a whole wet winter, and no household afterward moved a ditch without the others walking it first. They measured their coal by the cup like every hearth of the hills. Known for the drained hill.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, GE 2,387. The easternmost harbour of the island. In the two thousand four hundred and seventeenth year a storm out of the south-east stripped the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar and drove its boats onto the rocks below the headland; the coast named it A' Ghaoth Dhubh for the ash-dark sky it left behind. The valleys sent grain unasked, weighed by the count of mouths, and the coast called it only the bringing-in. The winter after, Lìleas, whose father's hand was maimed, kept a fire on the cape east of the village for boats coming home in the dark, the first of the five fires. Sixty years later the households laid stone to the eaves round the whole settlement, the first walls on that coast built against wind. Known for A' Ghaoth Dhubh, and Lìleas's fire.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755. A harbour on the west coast beside a stone landing built by hands none of its settlers could name, older than any wall near it. Households took it up in the two thousand six hundred and seventieth year and used the landing as they found it rather than mend it, out of the caution settlers kept wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stood; the harbour was fully settled by the two thousand seven hundred and fifty-fifth year and shipped the western grain along the coast. Known for the old landing used unmended.

#### D

**Doire chiar** (Doire chiar). Founded 8 an Giblean, GE 4,183. A settlement that grew up under the dark oaks in the north in the four thousand one hundred and eighty-third year. Its people penned pigs in the wood and drove them out to the acorns at the fall of the year, and felled no oak they could spare. The households of the dark oaks kept the full hand at their hearths like every settlement of the hills, and sent their measure to be tried against a copy of the stone cup when the lot for the slab came to be drawn from every part of the hills. Their pigs went to the ford in the autumns, driven the whole way on foot. Known for pigs driven to the acorns.

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470. The grey oak grove where the six pots of na Seachd Guail were set under the oldest trees and Ailean kept his seven nights, fasting, until Coimhdeach na Fine named him king. Coinneach, his brother, camped beyond the ring of oaks and could not cross it; he found his brother warm at dawn with the frost standing off him in a bare ring. For more than two thousand years no household built there, the grove being held the king's and Coimhdeach na Fine's and no one's else. In the two thousand four hundred and seventieth year households of the near valleys came down into its shelter and marked the old oaks for their byres; Somhairle asked Fearchar mac Ailig's household to spare the three oldest trunks, because his father had once set pots beneath them, and they cut their beams from younger growth. The houses ringed the three oaks within a generation, and the place was called the ring under the oaks. In the later centuries the moor crept up on it from the north, and the oaks drew back into the sheltered hollows. Known for the vigil and the three oaks left standing.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 695. An old oak grove on the south-west coast. In the seven hundred and fifth year pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires in the lee of the oaks, were first made here, and two of the first of them reached Dùn ìseal within the season. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore used them, and pots were among the first goods that strangers to both hills set out beside the wool and salt at the ford. The potters dug their clay from the same bank for generations and traded their wares down the drovers' roads. Known for the first pots.

**Dùn chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 7 am Faoilleach, GE 2,801. A banked hill-fort in the midst of the island, between An Cnoc Ruadh and the hills of the vein. Herders wanting the bank to face south and quarrymen wanting it to face north raised a single crooked earthwork that answered both wants at once and satisfied neither, and the fort stood from its first year with a name that fitted it more ways than its builders meant. Its holder Ruadhan Beag quarrelled two winters with the holder of Dùn thais over which way a bank ought to face, until Murchadh rode to hear them and left the ditch as it stood, finding a hundred years without an enemy a better argument than either holder made. Known for the bank that faced two ways.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 9 an Gearran, GE 4,274. A hill-fort east of the vein with a double bank, raised in the four thousand two hundred and seventy-fourth year by households who owed nothing to Dùn ìseal and asked leave of no one. They shared out the labour, and afterward the ground within, by households and not by standing; a family that sent no hands was left outside the second bank and asked within a generation to be let in on the same terms. Ailis carried seal-skins from here to the ford, and Catrìona of the king's blood gave the eastern households ground there asking no oath. In the four thousand five hundred and twentieth year the king sent Niall Òg to bid Dùn dhearg come in to him, and Fearghal Donn sent him back with nothing. From that year the spears of the east were gathered here, and under Artair mac Fhearghail the host mustered along the river below the fort in the last days of an Lùnastal, meaning to hold the crossing. Known for the double bank, and the refusal.

**Dùn ìseal** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1. The hill of the first kingdom. Ailean Mòr came to it from the grove in the first summer with eleven of his kin, sat under its lip through the first winter hearing the households of the valleys, and set the flint-pit to making spearheads for anyone who asked. The bank was pegged out in the snow of the second spring and raised in the ninth year, with antler picks and flint scrapers; Gormshuil kept its gate, and after her, Rìghrean na Cloiche held it for the king, twelve in all, from Dòmhnall Clachach to Catrìona Mhòr. Sìleas Bhàn cut grain-pits into the bank and opened them by the count of mouths; Tormod Liath paced out the second bank and doubled the ground within it to near a hundred houses. Here the sharing before the storms began, here Calum Ciar asked for the slab's lot, and here Catrìona's cord was knotted to nine hundred hearths. In the last years the valley below the hill filled with the tents of the king's kin, each line with its own fire and its own steward, waiting on shares the king would not give. Known for the king's hill, the bank and the store within it.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 28 am Màrt, GE 2,473. A hill above good grazing in the east, where settlers pushing toward the rising country dug a ditch and raised the spoil behind it in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-fifth year, a ring of earth built without any word sent from Dùn ìseal and without any word sent back once it stood. It was the first banked place of the hill-folk away from Dùn ìseal and An Cnoc Ruadh. Somhairle stood on the bank some years after and found it a smaller, rougher thing than his father's hill. Its holder quarrelled two winters with Ruadhan Beag of Dùn chrom over which way a bank ought to face, until Murchadh rode down and left both ditches as they stood. Known for the first bank east of the old workings.

#### G

**Gleann na Scoltaidh**. Founded 25 an Giblean, GE 2. A green valley walled by low scarps two days inland from the coast, where Seasaidh came as a bride with Pàl, a drover's son. In the eight hundred and twenty-seventh year the ground opened below Pàl's byre, a crack that ran along the valley and moved its spring to a new channel. The king walked the length of the crack and forbade nothing. Twenty years later Seasaidh, in her old age, carried white stones up from the stream bed and set them a stride back from the crack's edge, choosing them for their whiteness so a child running in poor light might see where the safe ground ended; the valley finished the line after her, and no house was raised within a stone's throw of the crack. In the three thousand eight hundred and sixty-third year the crack moved again and the spring shifted back uphill and broke the line in two places, and the households laid it again exactly as their grandmothers had. Known for the crack and the white stones.

#### I

**Inis bhàn** (Inis bhàn). Founded 16 an Giblean, GE 3,916. A settlement on the lower Abhainn ìseal by the skerries off the river mouth, where the households took seals by agreement, one household to a rock in its own turn, kept on notched sticks. A rock taken out of turn was the commonest quarrel of that coast, settled always by counting the tally aloud rather than by raised voices. Known for the seal-rocks taken in turn.

**Inis mhin** (Achadh naomh). Founded 20 an Cèitean, GE 3,172. A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway on the eastern coast, where a few households settled in the three thousand one hundred and seventy-second year to live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, trading feathers inland. A boy caught by dusk on a shelf below the highest nests was brought up by torchlight on a rope woven that same night, and from then no one of the settlement worked the cliffs alone: two to a rope, by custom rather than any law spoken. Its feathers went inland to the ford and to the valleys under Dùn ìseal, where they stuffed the bolsters of the king's kin in the waiting years. Known for the egg-cliffs and the two to a rope.

**Inis mhòr** (Inis mhòr). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, GE 4,328. A fishing settlement on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east, taken up in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who lived by the fish of its sheltered pools. They built their houses in two rows facing each other across a single trodden way, so that a neighbour's fire might be borrowed without crossing open ground in the rain: the oldest street any teller remembers on Dia-thìr. The two rows faced each other close enough for a word to cross between doors, and the settlement kept its sharing in the trodden way itself, each household setting out its surplus at its own door to be divided by the count of mouths before the storms. Known for the oldest street.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 2,408. A harbour of the south-west where, in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-fourth year, households hearing only that the Ros dhomhain keeper cut her marks at a certain interval began cutting their own high-water marks on the harbour rock at that same spacing, though none of them could say why that width and no other. So three tide-rocks were kept side by side on the island, and the interval travelled without its reasoning. Known for the third tide-rock.

#### M

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 3 an t-Samhain, GE 2,466. A settlement on a stream in the north-west, built in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-sixth year, after carriers weary of the long way round cut through the last unbroken thicket on Rathad an t-Salainn and brought the place a full day nearer the pans of Baile ghorm. Its flint came from Cnoc àrsaidh and its salt from the south, carried the length of the island by Cruinneachadh an Àtha; at the stream the salt cost three times its price at the pans and was paid for in flint and seal-skins. Known for the far end of Rathad an t-Salainn.

**Muileann bhàn** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 24 an Dàmhair, GE 2,378. A settlement of herders on the eastern plain, below the passes the panthers cross. In the two thousand four hundred and twenty-eighth year Iain of Muileann bhàn drove forty head of thin cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing, and the panthers took thirty head in a night; he came down lamed at the hip. Twenty-seven years later he walked south to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh on his stick, sat in the pool three days, and walked home whole. In the three thousand seven hundred and seventy-first year, when the rivers of the eastern plain ran low all summer, its households drove their cattle to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to drink, and the shared surplus held. Known for the cattle lost in the passes, and Iain's cure.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,218. A hill above the upper reaches of the rivers where, in the three thousand one hundred and third year, the kin of a settling household's head carried stones up the slope above the cattle-fold and raised the first cairn there, one stone laid at a time by whoever had known him. Within a lifetime the slope held as many small heaps of stone as the fold below held cattle in a good year. The households settled the hill fully in the three thousand two hundred and eighteenth year, round the cattle-fold. Known for the cairns above the cattle-fold.

**Muileann leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 24 an Giblean, GE 1,610. A settlement on a northern stream where cloth was first woven on standing frames, the warp held taut by weights of fired clay rather than by hand, in the thousand six hundred and twenty-eighth year; a worker stood free to pass the weft with both hands. Beitris was born into the third household to raise a frame here, and her blue-black cloth lay flatter and held its dye better than any other hand's. The king stopped at her stall at the ford, tested the weave with two fingers, and married her; she went south to Dùn ìseal and taught the standing weights to the hill's women until the craft had spread to a dozen sheds. The loom-weights lie in rows in the houses of the stream where they fell from the warp. Known for the standing looms, and Beitris.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, GE 2,986. A settlement near the south coast between Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell, whose first houses stood on driven piles over standing marsh water. They were moved to firm ground a bowshot inland once the piles had proved the footing sound, and kept the name the marsh first gave them. It was founded in earnest in the two thousand nine hundred and eighty-sixth year and traded with the fishers of the strait at Caol ruadh. The marsh gave the settlers eels and wildfowl in plenty, and the moving of the houses to firm ground was done over three summers, one row at a time, so that no household was ever without a roof while it was done. Known for the houses on piles over the marsh.

#### R

**Ros bheag** (Ros bheag). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, GE 1,274. The bay of hawks on the west coast, settled in the thousand two hundred and seventy-fourth year by three hill households too many for the grazing above Baile ghorm, the first hill-folk on that shore. They built round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fished with lines and baskets from the shore and not from boats. Beathag, eldest of the crossing, walked the nine days on her own feet and was the first buried within sound of that tide. Flòraidh was born here, found amber in the wrack at nine, learned the drill from a blind drill-master, and carried the finest bead of the western strand the length of the island to lay it at the ford at the king's word. She married the boat-mender's son who followed her west, and was buried facing the water. Known for amber, and Flòraidh's bead.

**Ros dhomhain** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,694. A settlement at the harbour mouth on Loch chrom, where in the thousand seven hundred and eighth year a young keeper cut marks for the high water on a boulder, at the interval of the first tide-rock, which he had never seen. The king stood before it with Beitris the better part of an afternoon and told her a thing can be worth doing before anyone has worked out why. The marks crept upward from keeper to keeper as the lake rose, a hand's width in a lifetime. Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, for high water and low, and cut a last pair for the fosterling on the evening before he went home. By the two thousand four hundred and twenty-fifth year some sixty houses stood round the rock and An Cnoc Ruadh's stone landing, the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, its people fishing from boats of their own building. Known for the tide-rock and its rising marks.

**Ros ruadh** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, VE 3,075. A red headland on the north-west coast where fishing households kept lines and hide boats long before the hill had a king. The king's word reached it late and lightly: it sent no spears to any quarrel of the valleys and was asked for none. In the hungry years, when the fishing failed along that whole coast and the graves at Baile chrom were laid two deep, Sìleas Bhàn's grain came up the shore to the headland in carts, and its households kept the custom of the store after, laying a season's fish by against the next bad year. Its boats went out further than most on that coast, and its people told the voyage of the first boats as their own. Its fishers cut the eight wind-names on the rock of the headland in the manner of Eilean fhada, a notch facing each way, and a boat that came home in the dark steered by the fire on the Baile chrom headland to the north once that fire was kept. Known for a headland of hide boats on the north-west coast.

#### S

**Seann Dunn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an Cèitean, VE 642. A town of Seann-Dhaoine on the Abhainn chaol a little above the river mouth, on footings no hill-folk laid. Its middens were Seann-Dhaoine' own, and its tally stones, each cut with a single stroke, stood upright in them. The hill-folk who came after them built along the middens' shoulder. In the four thousand three hundred and sixty-sixth year a family digging a house-floor struck a row of the tally stones, knew them for what they were, and set them back as they lay rather than break them; a year later the last of Seann-Dhaoine' middens here was disturbed, and the households closed it again. Known for the tally stones set back.

**Seann Skell** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 10 an Gearran, VE 1,404. A harbour of Seann-Dhaoine on the far north-west coast, with a tower on its point older than any telling. The hill-folk who came there kept Seann-Dhaoine' name for it and a watch in the tower. In the two thousand four hundred and twenty-first year four watchers saw a long back rise off the point in the failing light and go under without a sound; that season the wrack south of the tower gave up stitched planks from hulls built for open water, and no household would claim them. Micheil Beag laid the planks against his wall, and Anndra Breac, a teller of that shore, made from them a telling of a crossing that he carried to the ford and was shouted down for. He was last seen walking south along the strand below the tower. Known for the tower's watch and the stitched planks.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 29 am Faoilleach, GE 2,664. A harbour of Seann-Dhaoine on the southern coast, empty through the first two thousand years of the age and taken up again by fishing households in the long settling. Within a few generations of its resettling it was the busiest quay on that coast, boats going out on every tide and its hook-makers at work from first light beating out bone hooks faster than the fishing could wear them. The tale of the grey stranger who lifted the boulder at Ceann leathan grew hands like a smith's iron at a fire near here, an embellishment Alasdair Làidir spent the rest of his life correcting, and an old woman of this shore carried her own telling of the stone to the ford. Known for the busiest quay of the south.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. Seann-Dhaoine' river harbour on the Abhainn naomh, with a mole and a tower at its mouth. The hill-folk of the upper river were saying its old name before any of them had seen it, in the year Beathan was born. In the six hundred and twenty-eighth year Iain mac Fhearchair brought eleven souls of his household down the river to the empty harbour, marked the ground, and forbade the tower; the household used Seann-Dhaoine' mole as it found it, and when a winter storm broke the mole's oldest stretch Iain would not build with the broken stone. His daughter Marsaili held the household after him, went out in the first hide boats the harbour had held since Seann-Dhaoine, and chose how a household newly of the sea should bury the first one the sea took. Known for the mole, the tower, and Marsaili's boats.

#### T

**Tobar dhearg** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, GE 2,947. A southern cape where the households raised the last and surest of the five fires in the two thousand four hundred and twentieth year, on a mound of stacked stone breast-high, clear of the spray; a reciter of that coast named the five together before the mound was finished. The keepers of the fire built at last round a well whose water ran faintly red from the rock, and the settlement on the cape grew into the greatest place on the south coast, its fire burning nightly for boats that learned to watch for it. Known for the southern fire and the red well.

**Tobar dhìreach** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42. The well village of Na Glinn Àrda that keeps the slab laid over the mason's crack, the eldest of the three wells that claim it. In the thousand and seventy-first year a wet spring opened a crack below the slab's stain, and the households laid white stones along it. From the thousand one hundred and twentieth year the families nearest the crack sat the slab in turn through the dark half of every year, a household at a time; Beathan mac Shomhairle sat among the first six, and Gilleonan and Ìde kept their first turn the same winter. The king came up alone once and sat a night among them. In the two thousand four hundred and third year the families chose one keeper by lot, and Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill drew the white stone; a house was built for her with its door to the slab, and Niocol Snaidhear ground her a stone cup. Gilleasbuig Beag, who drew after her, was rowed to Eilean chrom for a basket of coal, and Giorsal Bhàn laid the coal back under the slab. Somhairle died against the slab in the three thousand and twenty-fifth year and is buried beside it; Diorbhail kept the Line after him. In Catrìona's years the lot was drawn from every part of the hills, the keepers were made nine, and Taigh na Lice became a place walked to for its own sake. Known for the slab, the lot and Taigh na Lice.

**Tobar fhiadhaich** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, GE 1,879. A wild spring on the moor whose herders walked the same paths through the whole of the age, and whose spring was said never to fail. The households of the spring buried wolves whole and with care, laid on their sides with their legs drawn up as in sleep, a care they spoke of to no one outside the household; an old woman told Murchadh, who came on a burying in the thousand eight hundred and ninetieth year, that the wolf kept its own dead on the high ground and had earned better than the ditch. No other beast was so buried in the age. Known for the wolves buried whole.

# Appendix A — The King, Rìghrean na Cloiche and An Cnoc Ruadh

An Aois Ailein had one king and many holders. Ailean Mòr mac Shuibhne was crowned in the grove at Doire ghlas in the first year and ruled the whole island until he fell at the ford below Dùn dhearg in the last days of the age, four thousand six hundred and three years later. Under him the hill of Dùn ìseal was held in his name by a line of his own blood that the reciters called Rìghrean na Cloiche, and An Cnoc Ruadh by the lake was held by a line that was not his blood at all and swore to him and not to Dùn ìseal. An Dà Chlàr were spoken, never written, in this age. They give each holder a name and a place in the order and say almost nothing of how long each held; where the years are known they are given here from the tellings, with each ruler's age at the taking of the holding and at death.

## The king

**Ailean Mòr mac Shuibhne**, Rìgh Chlann nan Dè. He was twenty-four when he kept the seven nights in the grove and was crowned on the eighth, and four thousand six hundred and twenty-six when he fell. He did not age after the grove: his hair went grey in a single winter in about his seventeen-hundredth year of kingship and changed no further. The king married several times; the tellings name Muireall, the mother of Gormshuil, who died in the twenty-fourth year of the hill; Sorcha, a woman of the valleys, the mother of Somhairle and Iain Dubh; and Beitris of Muileann leathan, the weaver, the mother of Murchadh. He named every wife before Beitris to her in order when she asked whether he would forget her. He heard judgements in person in the first years, gave the north to Dòmhnall Clachach, walked south alone to Tràigh an t-Salainn after Iain Dubh was killed there, and in the last age of his reign took back Dùn ìseal into his own hand when Catrìona Mhòr died, giving it to none of her kin.

## Rìghrean na Cloiche

Rìghrean na Cloiche, counts the king himself first and Catrìona Mhòr twelfth and last. Each holder after the king held Dùn ìseal under him, heard its judgements, called its gatherings and kept its bank. The list passes from one name to the next without saying how long each held or what came between.

| | Holder | Born | Held | Died | Age at death |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ailean Mòr mac Shuibhne | twenty-four years before the grove | from the first year | at the ford, the four thousand six hundred and third year | 4,626 |
| 2 | Gormshuil nic Ailein | before the grove | 27 – 76 | 76 | 81 |
| 3 | Dòmhnall Clachach | 2 | 76 – 227 | 3,310 | 3,308 |
| 4 | Fearchar Bacach | 10 | from 227 | 3,140 | 3,130 |
| 5 | Mòrag Chruaidh | 290 | to 719, holding in 672 | 1,610 | 1,320 |
| 6 | Iain Dubh | 45 | 719 – 727 | 727, slain | 682 |
| 7 | Raghnall Ceannfhionn | 760 | holding in 1,175 | 2,160 | 1,400 |
| 8 | Sìleas Bhàn | 1,500 | to 2,010, holding in 1,927 | 2,380 | 880 |
| 9 | Tormod Liath | 640 | 2,010 – 2,390 | 2,390 | 1,750 |
| 10 | Eilidh Ghlas | 2,050 | from 2,390 | 2,780 | 730 |
| 11 | Calum Ciar | 2,250 | holding in 2,412 | 2,960 | 710 |
| 12 | Catrìona Mhòr | 4,100 | holding in 4,321 and after | 4,391 | 291 |

Years are counted from the grove.

**Gormshuil nic Ailein**, the king's eldest daughter by Muireall, was born before the grove and had none of na Bliadhnachan Fada. She kept the gate of the hill from the ninth year and held it from her thirty-second year, and died at eighty-one beside a father who looked her grandson's age. It was at her grave that the hill understood na Bliadhnachan Fada were the grove's alone.

**Dòmhnall Clachach**, the first child born to the king after the grove, took the hill at seventy-four and set the boundary stones of the valleys in the hundred and seventh year. At two hundred and twenty-five he asked his father for unsettled ground and was given the north, and he grew old there among people who called him only the stone-cutter's son. He died at three thousand three hundred and eight.

**Fearchar Bacach**, lamed in Cogaidhean nan Gleann, took the hill at two hundred and seventeen when his brother rode north, and was carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch: the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt. He carried his lameness near three thousand years and died at three thousand one hundred and thirty.

**Mòrag Chruaidh**, Dòmhnall's daughter, the first of the king's grandchildren to carry na Bliadhnachan Fada, raided Tràigh an t-Salainn at Baile ghorm in her three hundred and eighty-second year and lost seven, whose names the hill kept at its fire. She rode to An Cnoc Ruadh, weighed Seonag's pebble bag against her own spears, and raised no raid again. She gave the hill to Iain Dubh at four hundred and twenty-nine and died at one thousand three hundred and twenty.

**Iain Dubh**, a son of the king by Sorcha, took the hill at six hundred and seventy-four and held it eight years. He went down to the salt-pans at dawn with more spears than Mòrag had taken and was killed on the clay by Tadhg Garbh, at six hundred and eighty-two. His son Tormod stood at his cairn.

**Raghnall Ceannfhionn**, Fearchar's son, found the hill's salt-kists near empty in his four hundred and fifteenth year and waded into the ford to meet the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, and the two hills agreed salt for wool. He died at one thousand four hundred.

**Sìleas Bhàn**, of the king's blood, held the hill through the hungry years, opened the store within the bank by the count of mouths, and was told by the king that four hundred years of not failing was itself the deed the list would keep. She gave the hill to Tormod Liath at five hundred and ten and died at eight hundred and eighty among her kin in the valley.

**Tormod Liath**, Iain Dubh's son, took the hill at one thousand three hundred and seventy, raised the second bank, outlived three sons, went grey through, and died in his own hall in the three hundred and eightieth year of his holding, at one thousand seven hundred and fifty.

**Eilidh Ghlas**, of the king's blood, took the hill at three hundred and forty. She sent her younger son to be fostered at An Cnoc Ruadh, the first fostering in either list, and knew him at the door when he came home. She died at seven hundred and thirty.

**Calum Ciar**, Eilidh's elder son, asked in his hundred and sixty-second year that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight, and was refused; the list sets the refusal down. He died at seven hundred and ten.

**Catrìona Mhòr**, of the king's blood, gave the households of Dùn dhearg ground at the ford at two hundred and twenty-one, took the hill formally at two hundred and forty-seven, knew every household of the hills by its line seven names back, and had the households counted on a cord of nine hundred knots. She answered the nine keepers "not this year; ask me again", and died at two hundred and ninety-one. With her the spoken list ends.

## The list of An Cnoc Ruadh

An Cnoc Ruadh kept its own holders and its own list, An Cnoc Ruadh's roll, and swore to the king from the two hundred and ninetieth year and never to Dùn ìseal. None of its holders had na Bliadhnachan Fada. The list sets every holder of Uisdean Mòr's line "after her father" or "after his father", whatever lay between.

| | Holder | Born | Held | Died | Age at death |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Beathag Ruadh | before the grove | named in 18 | 40 | 73 |
| 2 | Uisdean Mòr | 225 | 250 – 312 | 312 | 87 |
| 3 | Seonag nic Uisdein | 670 | holding in 694 | 741 | 71 |
| 4 | Murchadh Gearr | 1,215 | 1,240 – 1,280 | 1,280 | 65 |
| 5 | Lachlann Ruadh, Lachlann an Altraim | 2,360 | holding in 2,401 – 2,425 | 2,425 | 65 |
| 6 | Peigi Dhubh | 2,385 | 2,425 – 2,460 | 2,460 | 75 |
| 7 | Seumas Òg | 4,320 | holding in 4,347 | 4,390 | 70 |

**Beathag Ruadh** held the hill by the lake when the valleys came in to the king, and stayed away. She was fifty-one when the tellings first name her and died at seventy-three. **Uisdean Mòr** took the hill at twenty-five, cut the ditch across the neck, saw the palisade burn twice, and knelt to the king in the ford at sixty-five; he died at eighty-seven. **Seonag nic Uisdein** counted her people by pebbles in a bag and was twenty-four when Mòrag Chruaidh came to her; she died at seventy-one. **Murchadh Gearr** took the hill at twenty-five and walked Rathad an t-Salainn every autumn to be seen upon it; he died at sixty-five. **Lachlann Ruadh** took Eilidh Ghlas's younger son to foster at forty-one and was called Lachlann an Altraim for it; he died at sixty-five, asking that the fostering be ended. **Peigi Dhubh** took the hill at forty, sent the fosterling home with salt, and laid the stone landing; she died at seventy-five. **Seumas Òg** took the hill at twenty-seven and died at seventy; his is the last name An Cnoc Ruadh's spoken roll carries. Between the holders the list names, others held whose names it does not keep, among them the unnamed holder who waded to meet Raghnall Ceannfhionn and the new holder who stood in the river at An Cruinneachadh Mòr of the three thousandth year.

## The king's children and blood named in this volume

The king's children born after the grove had na Bliadhnachan Fada; each generation after them had fewer, and no child of the kin outlived its long-lived parent's span.
