Murchadh Mòr had eleven sons, born over the better part of three centuries, each given a corner of the northern plain; the four hundred of the king's blood reckoned standing in the river at An Cruinneachadh Mòr are not named one by one in any telling that survives.

## Sloinneadh a' Chlachair and Somhairle's line

Sloinneadh a' Chlachair, runs from Neachdan the mason to Ailean, and was given whole by Coinneach mac Shuibhne, the king's mortal brother and the first teller of his deeds, to Gormshuil before he died in the fifty-fifth year. Somhairle carried it after, among Clann na Ceiste in Na Glinn Àrda, and gave it whole to his son Beathan in the eleven hundred and fortieth year and to Diorbhail, a child of the watch at Tobar dhìreach, in the three thousand and tenth; Diorbhail kept it by mouth and took no share for it. Somhairle's own line held no share of the hill. It runs from Somhairle to Beathan, and from Beathan to the son who cleared the path for Somhairle's stick and kept the whole watch at the slab after him; the tellings name his descendants only as they come to Gille-Brìde, whose father died in his three hundred and eighth year, and to Gille-Brìde's son Ceallach, born in the four thousand five hundred and forty-third year, in whom the years were already coming down faster than in his father.

## Luchd-faire na Lice

The families near the crack sat the slab in turn, a household at a time, from the eleven hundred and twentieth year. From the two thousand four hundred and third year they drew one keeper by lot. **Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill**, a herder's daughter of three-and-thirty, drew the white stone first and kept the slab until she died in the winter after Coinneachadh nan Cupan. **Gilleasbuig Beag**, a roof-mender, drew after her and was rowed to Eilean chrom for a basket of coal. **Giorsal Bhàn** drew after him and laid the coal back under the slab. The tellings do not name the keepers after Giorsal one by one. In Catrìona Mhòr's years the lot was drawn from every part of the hills, and the keepers were made nine, one for each of nine districts no household ever marked on the ground.

## The holders of Dùn dhearg as the east names them

Rìghrean na Cloiche' list does not name the holders of Dùn dhearg; it says only that Dùn dhearg came not to the gatherings. The households east of the vein name two. **Fearghal Donn**, who held the double bank when the king sent Niall Òg in the four thousand five hundred and twentieth year, sent the messenger back with nothing and died an old man in his own bed in the four thousand five hundred and seventieth. **Artair mac Fhearghail**, his son, took up the holding with no more ceremony than his father had used and led Sluagh an Ear down to the ford below the fort in the last days of an Lùnastal of the four thousand six hundred and third year.

# Appendix B — The Reverence of the Hearths

An Aois Ailein had no priests, no temple and no god at the hearth. What it had was a set of customs about fire, coal, the dead and certain places, kept by households who could seldom say where a custom had begun and never troubled to write one down. This appendix gathers them as the tellings of the age give them: Aithris a' Chruthachaidh kept among Clann na Ceiste; the slab and those who watched it; the handful, the basket, the cup and Oidhche na Glaice; the sharing before the storms; the saying spoken at the ford; the unlit and the covered hearths; the holy woods; and the keeping of the dead.

## No god at the hearth

The hill-folk of this age made no offering at the hearth and named no one who lived in the fire. Coimhdeach na Fine, belonged to the grove and to Sloinneadh a' Chlachair, and the tellings put him in only two places: before Diarmad of that line in the oldest days, and in the grove on the eighth night, when he named Ailean king. No household of the age claimed to have seen him, and none set a place for him. No one prayed to the king himself. He was knelt to at gates and in fords, as a holder is knelt to, and he raised those who knelt with his own hand; the hill talked of his warmth and his unageing face in the way a valley talks of weather, and let the matter rest.

## The king's warmth

The one wonder the age took for granted was the king himself. A girl of Dùn ìseal stood near his untended fire in the first hard winter and was warmed through though no flame burned close enough to account for it; Coinneach found him warm at dawn after the vigil with the frost standing off him in a bare ring; the water of the ford ran warm round his legs at An Cruinneachadh Mòr and smoked downstream of him in the dusk. At Achadh dhìreach he laid his open hand across a hearthstone running with colour and it greyed under his palm. At An Cnoc Ruadh, in the summer Uisdean knelt, a frost came down out of a clear sky in an t-Ògmhios and put a white rime on the grass along the whole lake shore; the tellings call it Reothadh an Rìgh, and Uisdean's people could not say afterward whether it was his doing or the sky's. The hill spoke of these things in the way a valley speaks of weather, and made no rite of any of them. No one asked him for rain or a good calving. The hill asked him for judgements, and for grain in a hungry year, and he gave both.

## Aithris a' Chruthachaidh among Clann na Ceiste

The households of Na Glinn Àrda, Clann na Ceiste, kept Sloinneadh a' Chlachair and the tellings that ring it. Coinneach mac Shuibhne gave the Line whole to Gormshuil; Somhairle, who asked his father for no land and was counted a single mouth at a single hearth, carried it among Na Glinn Àrda for near three thousand years, gave it to Beathan and then to Diorbhail, and set in it what he saw on the three shores of Seann-Dhaoine. The keepers of the Line took no share from any hall for the keeping, and set none of it down on leaf or hide. It was said twice through without a name out of place when it was given, and after that each Samhain to any of the watch-households who would hear it, with the year's names added at its foot. Clann na Ceiste held that a thing given too soon to too young a head is given badly, and that a question the ground does not mean to answer is best let lie.

## The slab and its keepers

At Tobar dhìreach a slab lay over the mason's crack, stained where Teine a' Chlachair was said to have come up out of the vein. In the thousand and seventy-first year a crack opened in the turf below it and the households laid white stones along it. From the eleven hundred and twentieth year the families nearest the crack sat by the slab in turn, a household at a time, through the dark half of every year. What they watched for none ever said; Gilleonan, after forty years of sitting it, asked Beathan, and Beathan answered that he did not know and never had. The king sat one night among them and said nothing of why he came.

In the two thousand four hundred and third year the turns wore too thin for one memory to hold and the families agreed to choose one keeper by lot, from a bag of pebbles with one marked white. The first keeper had a house raised beside the slab with its door facing the stone, the first building on Dia-thìr made only to be near the vein. When a keeper was found with a basket of the vein's coal, the families judged him by a silence held past any voice rising to answer it and rowed him to Eilean chrom without a boat; the basket was set inside Taigh na Lice under its cloth and was neither burned nor kept, and the keeper after him laid the coal back under the slab piece by piece. The coal went home, the valleys said. Calum Ciar asked that the lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight and was refused, and the king would not overrule a thing older than the grove of his own crowning. From then the holders of the hill ruled the grazing and the gatherings, and the keepers ruled the vein, and the line between them was sworn to in no words either side wrote down. In Catrìona Mhòr's years the lot was drawn from every part of the hills, the keepers were made nine, and the nine asked to have their charge declared before the whole gathering. She told them to ask again.

## The handful, the cup and Oidhche na Glaice

An gual dathach of the vein was burned by the handful. The custom that no fire should have more of it than one cupped hand could hold took hold in all the hill settlements about the thousand and eleventh year, nowhere written and everywhere kept: làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh, a full hand and no more. The king named it a good custom at Achadh dhìreach after Eanraig Ruadh burned a whole basket in one night and his house went up in a flame of no colour anyone had a word for, and he made no law of it. Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill had a cup ground from grey stone to the size of a cupped hand so that no household's handful ran bigger than another's by the accident of whose palm measured it; its copies were tried against it with water at Coinneachadh nan Cupan, and from then the hills measured the coal with one measure. In Catrìona's years every household came to burn its handful on the same dark night, each watching for the first low flame on the nearest hill before lighting its own. One household only, Torcall Tochlair's at the black hill, refused to burn at all.

## The sharing before the storms

Any household with food to spare shared it before the storm season: this too was unwritten. At Dùn ìseal it was done in the open, every household bringing its surplus within the bank to be divided by the count of mouths and not by the size of a herd, as Sìleas Bhàn had opened the store in the hungry years. The first punishment under it that is remembered fell on a household of Àth shean that hid its grain in a pit under the byre floor; it was put out with what it could carry. After A' Ghaoth Dhubh the valleys sent grain to the east coast unasked, and the coast called the custom only the bringing-in, or the help.

## The saying

The hill-folk did not hold that they had come to Dia-thìr from anywhere. The saying cut on Calbh Cnoc ghorm, we did not come, we were here, was held at every hearth long before it was spoken aloud. When Anndra Breac told a telling at the ford in which the people crossed the sea, the crowd shouted him down and every hearth closed to him; from the next year the gathering opened with the saying spoken together before any business began. The words on Calbh Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, were recut in their old grooves by a hand from Catrìona's hill.

## The unlit hearth and the covered hearth

At Achadh dhìreach a hearth was laid true, with a slip of an gual dathach beside it, and never lit; the valley left it under peat and ploughed round the strip it lay in. In the hills where Marbh-bheò was told of, no open fire was lit after dark. A herding family new to that country lit one and was never found; two herders who had lit none saw Marbh-bheò walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold and lived. The covered hearth, pit-dug and lidded with stone, spread from those hills toward the settlements nearer Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and hardened there into a rule no council set. The platforms on Loch chrom burned to the waterline in one night, and no household built on the lake again in the age.

## Holy woods, holy ground and the places of Seann-Dhaoine

Some woods were not entered. At the edge of the forest at Cnoc bheag the settlers took their timber only from the river's far side and marked the line with unhewn stones; when a child went past the stones and was not found, the searchers stopped at them, and the telling did not blame them. At the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar people came singly and in pairs to sit one night by a small fire that burned out before morning, and went home quieter. Cnoc naomh was already called holy when households came to it for its spring, and they kept its water and its holiness together without asking more of either. Seann-Dhaoine' work was let stand wherever it stood: the tower at Seann Skell, Làrach an Dùin ruin above Ceann mhin, Làrach an Teampaill in the eastern hills with a path worn round it at a distance, the old landings used unmended, the marked stones of the middens laid aside, the tally stones set back as they lay.

## The dead

The hill buried its dead in the ground and raised cairns over those it meant to remember: Iain Dubh's on the hill, the salt-folk's own at Baile ghorm with seven stones for the seven of Mòrag's raid, and the slope of small cairns above the fold at Muileann chaol, one stone laid at a time by whoever had known the dead. Mòrag named her seven at the hill's fire on the night kept for the dead, and the naming went on at the same fire after her. At the old burial ground a family who buried none of their own there cleared its thorn each spring, and when diggers broke into an older grave lined with Seann-Dhaoine' slabs they closed it and moved the row a spear's length off. The households of the rough strait laid paddles beside their dead. At Tobar fhiadhaich wolves were buried whole, laid on their sides as people were. In the last centuries the households of the south-east coast began to row their dead out to Eilean ìseal, after the old manner of Seann-Dhaoine or of themselves; the tellings let the question stand.

# Appendix C — Reckoning: Years from the Grove, na Bliadhnachan Fada and the Turning Year

An Aois Ailein counted its years from the grove. Every telling of the age that gives a year gives it as a count from the night Ailean was crowned at Doire ghlas: the ninth year of the hill, the thousand and sixty-sixth year, the three thousandth year since the grove. The count needed no other beginning, for no one alive in the age remembered one, and the king, who did, never offered another. This appendix sets out how the age counted its years, its lists and its lives; how it divided the turning year; and the marks it cut to keep time on the coasts.

## The count from the grove

The reckoning was the king's own. In the first years the hill counted by the years of the hill, which were the grove's years under another name, for the king came to Dùn ìseal in the summer of his crowning; within a generation the reciters spoke only of the grove. The reciters of Dùn ìseal kept the count by mouth, and the households learned it from them at the gatherings. It was an unbroken count, never begun again at the taking of a holding: Sìleas Bhàn held the hill in the nineteen hundred and twenty-seventh year, not in her first. A thousandth year was marked as a thing worth travelling for. In the three thousandth year since the grove, word of the count was carried out along every road that summer, and it drew to the ford households who had never before troubled to send anyone to an ordinary gathering.

Ordinary households kept their own years less exactly. They counted by holders, by storms and by marriages: the winter A' Ghaoth Dhubh came, the year the second bank was dug, the summer the foster-son came home. Most tellings of the age give a year only for what touched the hill, and leave the rest to the order of events.

## Lists without lengths

The lists of the age are orders of names, not counts of years. Rìghrean na Cloiche gives twelve names from Ailean to Catrìona Mhòr; the list of An Cnoc Ruadh gives its own holders from Beathag Ruadh to Seumas Òg, and sets every holder of Uisdean Mòr's line "after his father" or "after her father" though Seonag was born more than three hundred years after Uisdean died. Neither list says how long any holder held, or what lay between one name and the next. The reciters held that the list keeps who and in what order, and that the length of a holding is the business of those who lived under it. When An Dà Chlàr were spoken one after the other at the ford in Catrìona's time, from dusk to the grey before morning, it was the first time either was heard whole, and the tellings count the hours of the night and not the years of the holders.

The households' own lines were orders of the same kind. At the ford, before any marriage was made, each household gave its line aloud seven names back on either side, so that a forbidden blood might be named before the salt was carried. Catrìona Mhòr could give any household's line back seven names without pausing to think.

## Na Bliadhnachan Fada

The power of the coals was Ailean's alone, and he did not age after the grove. His children born after it had na Bliadhnachan Fada, and every generation after them had fewer: the longest life in a generation was never longer than the longest in the one before, and no child of the kin outlived its long-lived parent's span. Those born before the grove, like Gormshuil, and those not of the king's blood, like every holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, had ordinary lives. The long-lived aged slowly and then, near the end, all at once: Tormod Liath went grey through in his hundred and seventy-fifth year of holding, and Somhairle found the first lines in his face in his two thousand four hundred and thirty-fifth year, and came in his last years to look, a woman of the watch-households said, like a withered apple left too long on the sill.

The kin reckoned their own ages in the ordinary way until the counting grew too long to be worth saying aloud. Ìomhar Dearg, near five hundred at his nephew's birth, had stopped troubling to count them; Somhairle had stopped counting in the ordinary way long before, as Clann na Ceiste counted, by Samhains sat and not by years. Ceallach, born to Gille-Brìde in the four thousand five hundred and forty-third year, was slower to walk and to run than the children before him, the first sign, told back afterward, that the years were coming down faster in him than in his father.

## The turning year

The year of the age was a year of two halves and Na Ceithir Fèilltean. The dark half began at Samhain, when the herds came down and the slab's watch began; the light half began at Bealltainn, when they went up. Between them lay the feast of the lambing in the cold and Lùnastal at the harvest. Samhain was the night the hill kept for its dead, when Mòrag's seven were named at the fire, and in Catrìona's years it was the night on which every household burned its handful of an gual dathach together, watching for the first low flame on the nearest hill. The gatherings of the valleys were held at the feasts, and Cruinneachadh an Àtha in the autumn after the shearing and the salt-raking. The months of the reckoning, from am Faoilleach to an Dùbhlachd, were used by the reciters of the hill for the days of the great deeds, and by few others.

The panthers kept a season of their own. Twice a year the great cats crossed the passes by the same road, and every household near the road knew the crossing season and kept its herds out of the passes while it lasted. At Baile dhomhain the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scraped it away at its end, the first mark on the island cut for a season. When three cats turned back at the highest pass in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-eighth year, the households read it for a hard winter and stored double, and the winter was hard.

## Na h-Ochd Gaothan

In the two thousand and forty-seventh year Na h-Ochd Gaothan of the year were given names all at once, by no one the coasts could afterward name, and every coast that told them used the same eight names in the same order from that year on. Their meaning was dark even to those who spoke them, and they were never changed. The brothers of Ceann leathan raised a ring of eight stones for them on the point; the people of Eilean fhada cut the names as notches into the rock of their highest ground, one facing each way, so a man lost in thick weather might find his bearing by touch; a cutter of Seann Chwen set one of the names beside Seann-Dhaoine' own marks on the great boulder there, because the name wanted a stone already old; and the fishers of Caol bheag named each boat for the wind it was built to fish in.

## The tide-rocks

In the sixteen hundred and seventy-first year an unnamed hand on an unnamed shore began to cut a mark on a fixed rock at each high tide's furthest reach, at intervals more even than any fisherman's need would ask. A young keeper at Ros dhomhain began a rock of his own in the seventeen hundred and eighth year at the spacing he judged by memory of the telling, and the households of Inis thais cut a third in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-fourth, at the Ros dhomhain interval, though none of them could say why that width and no other. Seònaid Mhòr of Ros dhomhain cut her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low; the keepers after her went back to single marks. On the Ros dhomhain rock the marks crept upward from keeper to keeper, so slowly that no one year's mark could be told from the next, until the lake stood a hand higher on the stone than at the first cut. The keepers went on cutting. The king told Beitris, standing before the rock, that a thing can be worth doing before anyone has worked out why.

## Tallies and counts

The age counted things more than it counted time. Seann-Dhaoine cut single strokes on flat stones at the edges of their middens, then counted their dead in fives, until their tally stones thickened together on three coasts and stopped. Seonag of An Cnoc Ruadh counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household. The seal-rock households of Inis bhàn kept their turns on notched sticks. The keeper of the tide-rock at Ros dhomhain cut a stroke for every tide, and Seathan mac Pheadair a stroke for every ship's light he saw pass safe by his fire. The greatest count of the age was Catrìona Mhòr's cord, a knot to a hearth, which grew to some nine hundred knots; Sìne nan Snaidhm kept its like for the whole valley of tents below Dùn ìseal in the last years, and the king's own kin were never upon it.

# Appendix D — Peoples: Seann-Dhaoine, the Hill-Folk and the East

Three peoples, or four, shared Dia-thìr in An Aois Ailein, and only one of them lasted the age. Seann-Dhaoine, whom the hill-folk called the Seann-Dhaoine, held the coasts when the king was crowned and were silent within six hundred years. The hill-folk, who called themselves Clann nan Dè and then Dia-thìrich, spread from the valleys under Dùn ìseal to every coast. Among them the salt-folk of the south and the lake-folk of An Cnoc Ruadh kept ways of their own long after they knelt to the king; and in the last centuries the households east of the vein grew into a people who owed the hill nothing and said so.

## The last centuries of Seann-Dhaoine

Seann-Dhaoine built harbours, towers, moles, a shell causeway at Seann Warr, fortresses whose ruins stood above Ceann mhin and Cathair mhòr, and a temple in the eastern hills. They had a script, cut on stone, that no hill-folk could read. The hill-folk traded with them at the shore by gesture, in silence kept on both sides: Dùghall Ceannaiche walked the road down to their shore for sixty-two years and never learned a word of their tongue, and his father, who had asked once, was met with a courtesy that would not be moved.

In the three hundred and eighth year Seann-Dhaoine began to cut single strokes on flat stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household, a mark and then another, simpler than their script. Forty years later they began to keep count of their dead. At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall, some three thousand strokes in all, and the king rode east with Somhairle to see it and stood before it a long while without speaking. At Seann Tarr the stones were cut in fives and set in the floor of a house that was lived in over its own dead. About the four hundred and seventieth year the stones thickened together on three coasts at once, more strokes to each stone and more stones to each course; death came on three coasts together, and what it was the strokes do not tell. At Seann Chwen the last tally stone was left half-cut in the five hundred and tenth year, two strokes finished and a third begun and forsaken, the chisel marks stopping in mid-groove. After it no work of Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stopped growing, their harbours silted, and their script was cut no more. Somhairle rode the three shores in one circuit and set the silence in the Line.

The hill-folk kept Seann-Dhaoine' place-names and set before them only their own word for old: Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell, Seann Warr, Seann Tarr. They turned nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names were not understood. For the rest of the age Seann-Dhaoine' work was let stand: the hill-folk took up their empty harbours and used the moles and landings unmended, built on their middens but laid the marked stones aside, set their tally stones back as they lay, took no stone from their ruins, closed their graves when they broke into them, and walked round the temple at a distance.

## The hill-folk and the name

The people of the grove called themselves Clann nan Dè, the children of the gods, and the king Rìgh Chlann nan Dè. Most of the age they were simply the hill-folk, the households of the valleys under Dùn ìseal and of Na Glinn Àrda, who spread down every river to every coast. In the two thousand two hundred and first year the children of Dùn ìseal began, unbidden by any elder, to call themselves Dia-thìrich and their island Dia-thìr, and within a generation the old words fell out of use among the young. A boy of seven told Tormod Liath that he was Dia-thìreach and that everyone was; Tormod answered that it was a good enough name for a good enough island. With the names went the belief of the saying on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: they did not come; they were here.

Clann na Ceiste, the households of Na Glinn Àrda, kept Sloinneadh a' Chlachair and the slab, took no share of any hall, and asked their questions of the ground and not of the king. Somhairle lived among them nearly three thousand years, counted a single mouth at a single hearth, and his line held no share of the hill after him.

## Lines and the forbidden marriage

The hill-folk ordered themselves by blood long before the coal gave them cause. In the two thousand two hundred and twenty-third year the match of Ealag and Torcall Tochlair, which two households who shared a slope and a spring had treated as settled, was refused, and every elder of Ealag's household gave the same three words, that it could not be, and no reason. Ealag was married to a fisher of the ford town and lived her whole life without the reason; Torcall went east to dig for a second vein. Twenty-four years later, at Cruinneachadh an Àtha, households began to give their lines aloud before any match was spoken, seven names back on either side, so that a forbidden blood might be named before the salt was carried: the first genealogies of the common households. Only Sloinneadh a' Chlachair is older. Of the king's own kin, in the last centuries every marriage among the blood came to be reckoned for the shares it brought nearer the front of a reckoning the king never made; the hill argued without settling whether a claim through daughters weighed more or less than one through sons.

## The king's kin

By the last centuries of the age the king's blood was a people within the people. It was reckoned at some four hundred at An Cruinneachadh Mòr of the three thousandth year, and it went on growing. The kin held grazing in every part of the island by the king's giving, and the king took shares back as freely as he gave them: Ìomhar Dearg's river-grazing, Raonaid's river-meadow within the month of her burying, a household's western slopes after eleven generations. When Catrìona Mhòr died and the king held the hill in his own hand, every soul of the blood within three days' walk came to press a claim, each able to say the two names of a line whose second name was always Ailean's. From then the kin married for shares. After the four thousand six hundredth year they came down out of their holdings, household by household and line by line, and camped in the valley below Dùn ìseal, each line with its own tents, its own fire and its own steward, until the valley looked less like a gathering than a town that never raised walls. Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line, who asked for no ground and no share, was the one soul in the valley whose name was on no cord.

## The salt-folk

The salt-folk of Baile ghorm scraped the flats of the south coast and dried the crust on the shingle, and in the six hundred and eighty-third year made shallow clay basins behind the shingle bar, the first salt-works of the island. They had no king and a hill without salt had none of theirs. Mòrag Chruaidh raided them and lost seven; Iain Dubh came down on them with more spears and was killed by Tadhg Garbh; and the king came down alone, and they raised spears and lowered them, and old Mòr knelt on the wet shingle and gave him a double handful of salt. The southern shore was his from that day, with no blood shed and none paid. The salt-folk raised a cairn of their own for Iain Dubh with seven stones in it for the seven of Mòrag's raid, having come to think of both raids as one account, and sang at the raking of the pans the four-line refrain the fosterling later brought them from An Cnoc Ruadh's lake shore, the oldest song on Dia-thìr whose words are said to survive.

## The lake-folk of An Cnoc Ruadh

An Cnoc Ruadh's people lived by salt and fish at the western end of Loch chrom, behind a palisade on the neck of their hill. They were not the king's blood and had none of na Bliadhnachan Fada. They swore to the king in the two hundred and ninetieth year when Uisdean Mòr knelt in the ford, but kept their own holders and their own list and never swore to Dùn ìseal. Salt went from their pans for the hill's wool at the ford from Raghnall Ceannfhionn's wading on, and married across the water at the ford within a generation. They settled Cala nan Taighean Cruinne, the landing of laid stone below the hill, the boat-sheds at Baile ghlas, Cnoc bheag at the forest's edge and the old landing at Ceann àrsaidh; their children, fostered or born, learned the salt-rake before the spear.

## The coasts

The households who took up the empty coasts after Seann-Dhaoine became peoples of their own by the middle of the age. The river-folk who came down the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell had never dwelt by the water before and learned from Marsaili how a household newly of the sea buries one the sea has taken. The west-coast households of the bay of hawks fished from the shore and not from boats and drilled amber from the wrack. The east-coast households lived through A' Ghaoth Dhubh on the sharing of the valleys and kept five fires for the boats. The south-coast harbours became the busiest quays of the island. Each coast kept the eight wind-names, the handful and the sharing as the valleys did, and each thought itself the valleys' equal.

## The east

East of the vein lay country the king's blood held no hall in and claimed no grazing on. Households went out into it a generation at a time for their own reasons, among them Beasag's household from Àth shean after the hidden pit was found, and they dug no pits under their new floors. In the four thousand two hundred and seventy-fourth year the eastern households raised a double bank at Dùn dhearg, owing nothing to Dùn ìseal and asking leave of no one, and shared out the labour and afterward the ground within it by households and not by standing. They came to the ford for the first time in Catrìona's day with seal-skins, and she gave them ground on the far bank asking no oath. Ìomhar Dearg called them the short-lived; Ailis of Dùn dhearg answered that she had five days' walking behind her and no wish to spend what time she had left arguing with a man who would have five centuries to be sorry in. When the king sent Niall Òg to bid them come in, Fearghal Donn answered that his people had raised their own bank and buried their own dead without any man's leave, and would not be counted among a kin who married for shares and waited a thousand years for a hill never given. From that year the spears of the east were gathered at Dùn dhearg.

# Appendix E — Land and Trade: the Ford, the Roads and the Weather

Dia-thìr in An Aois Ailein was an island of households, not of towns. At the grove there was one hill with a bank, one hill with a palisade by the lake, Seann-Dhaoine' empty harbours on every coast and the hearths of Na Glinn Àrda; by the close of the age there were banked places in the east, the north and the midlands, harbours on every coast, and a gathering at the ford that drew households from all of them. This appendix sets out the ford and its grounds, the roads that ran to it, the goods that went along them, the fires kept for the boats, and the weather, water and ground the age had to live with.

## Cruinneachadh an Àtha

The ford lies fourteen miles below An Cnoc Ruadh, where the lake-folk's salt and the hill's wool first met. In the thousand one hundred and seventy-fifth year Raghnall Ceannfhionn found his grandfather's salt-kists near empty, rode west with nine companions so that the company would not be taken for a raid, and waded into the ford to meet the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh in the water. They agreed salt for wool. Both hills were the king's, and neither was the other's; the king would not do their talking for them. The bargain held on nothing written, only on each side's wish to be trusted the year after: when An Cnoc Ruadh refused a thin, unwashed clip, Raghnall sent a better one the next spring with fleece besides, and neither hill pressed harder than a fair measure again.

Traders with no part in either household began to bring flint, dried fish and pots on the appointed days and set their wares apart, and no one afterward remembered deciding to let them stay. In the twelve hundred and eighth year the meeting became a yearly gathering, and the first marriage of the ford was made on the trodden ground with both banks' households standing for it. No meeting-place on the island was used longer without a break. By the twelve hundred and sixtieth year the children who ran between the stalls made no distinction between the hill's side of the water and An Cnoc Ruadh's.

The gathering had three grounds: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, and the flint people on the rise beyond the river. By the three thousand four hundred and fiftieth year it drew households from every coast. It was at the ford that the lines were first recited before a marriage, that Flòraidh laid her amber bead in the old ground among the ribbons and worked bones other travellers had left there, that Anndra Breac was shouted down, that the saying was first spoken at the opening, that An Dà Chlàr were heard whole in one night, and that Catrìona gave the households of Dùn dhearg ground of their own on the far bank.

In the three thousandth year since the grove the gathering was kept greater than any before it. More households came in than the three grounds were ever laid out to hold, until by the second morning no one could say which bank belonged to whom. The king came down the hill road dressed as any herdsman and the crowd opened a way for him without a word called; five holders waded out to put their hands between his; the rings of his blood went into the river, Somhairle at his left hand, Murchadh a head taller than most, Eithne laughing in the outer ring; and the reciters counted some four hundred of his blood standing in the water. No household from east of the vein came. When the gathering had gone back to its fires the king stood alone in the emptied ford at dusk, and a girl of An Cnoc Ruadh found the water warm as bath-water round his legs and saw it smoke downstream of him.

## The roads

**Rathad an t-Salainn** ran from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford to An Cnoc Ruadh and on to the north-west. Murchadh Gearr walked it every autumn to be seen upon it, and every household on it had seen An Cnoc Ruadh's holder pass in the flesh. In the two thousand four hundred and sixty-fourth year carriers cut through its last unbroken thicket, and Muileann àrsaidh stood a day nearer the pans; at the far end the salt cost three times its price at the pans and was paid for in flint and seal-skins. Eilidh Ghlas's younger son walked it west at six years old, fifty miles and more from Dùn ìseal to An Cnoc Ruadh, past a low green mound his guide would go no nearer to, and walked it east again twenty-four years later with a train of laden pack-beasts.

**Rathad na Spor** ran from the pit at Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west south and east toward Cruinneachadh an Àtha, worn by generations of carriers with yokes on their shoulders until, by the eighteen hundred and seventeenth year, it sank a full yard below the ground on either side and a stranger took it for a dry ditch dug on purpose. Carriers caught by storm dug into its banks and roofed themselves with their yokes. Cattle were walked up it to Cnoc ghorm in the north-west. Murchadh walked it for a hundred and thirty years and asked his father for the country it ran through, and was refused.

**The drovers' roads** of Na Glinn Àrda ran by fords like Àth gharbh, where the beasts were rested and the full hand began, and by Àth shean, the old crossing below Dùn ìseal. The coast road ran round the east and south, and carried grain to Cuan ruadh after A' Ghaoth Dhubh.

## The goods

**Salt** from An Cnoc Ruadh's pans on the lake shore and from the clay basins at Baile ghorm, raked from the crust without breaking it, went to every hearth that could pay in wool, fish or flint. **Wool** came down from the hill and from the sheep-households of Baile gharbh. **Flint** from the one good pit on the island went to hearths from one end of it to the other in grey flakes, and the first flake of every new working was given free to whoever asked. **Pots** of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, were first made at Doire shean in the seven hundred and fifth year, and within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore used them. **Amber** came out of the western wrack and was drilled with flint points by a few hands on the bay of hawks. **Cloth** was woven on standing frames with fired-clay weights at Muileann leathan from the sixteen hundred and twenty-eighth year, and Beitris taught the standing weights to the hill's women. **Light** came first from seal-oil lamps of hollowed stone at Caol leathan. **Salmon** came from the wattle fence at Caol fhiadhaich, **seal-skins** from the rocks of Inis bhàn and the east, **feathers** from the cliffs of Inis mhin, **boar** from Baile fhiadhaich, and **green axes** from the quarry at Àth àrsaidh, too fine for work, until the quarry was forsaken. The one thing no one traded was the vein's coal, which went by the handful to every hearth and was sold by none.

## The boats

The oldest boat on Dia-thìr known in its whole shape is a dug-out hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, sunk at a landing on the Abhainn uaine in the seven hundred and sixteenth year. The river-folk who came down to Seann Skell built small hide boats and trusted them to open tide for the first time in the six hundred and fortieth year. The first households of the west coast fished from the shore and not from boats. Stitched planks from hulls built for open water, like nothing built on any coast of the island, washed up south of Seann Skell in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-first year, and no household claimed them. Peigi Dhubh laid a landing of laid stone below An Cnoc Ruadh so a boat could come alongside at any state of the water, and the fishing households of Caol bheag named their boats for the winds.

## The five fires

After A' Ghaoth Dhubh a young woman of Cuan ruadh, Lìleas, kept a fire on the cape east of the village for boats coming home in the dark, in a stone-walled pit, driving flame and smoke seaward. Word of it travelled the coast roads faster than its light, and within two years there were fires on the northern point, on the north-eastern cape where Seathan mac Pheadair cut a stroke for every ship's light he saw pass safe, and on the southern cape on a mound of stacked stone breast-high. With the older fire on the Baile chrom headland, the coasts of Dia-thìr were lit at five points, and a reciter named them the five fires. They were lit to bring boats home, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.

## Weather, water and ground

**Storms.** The first storm the reciters of Dùn ìseal named came in the hundred and forty-seventh year; its name is lost, only the memory of the naming remains. It stripped Dùn ìseal's thatch and broke Seann-Dhaoine' shell causeway at Seann Warr in three places. A' Ghaoth Dhubh of the two thousand four hundred and seventeenth year stripped every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar, and it is the eldest storm whose name is kept. Cuan ruadh rebuilt in stone to the eaves, and Ceann chiar cut a mark for every house lost: twenty-two.

**Waves.** In the seven hundred and seventy-seventh year the sea came far inland over the village at Cnoc chaol and left a sheet of sand a hand thick on its hearths, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it; the village was not rebuilt on the same ground. When the sea came in again in the three thousand eight hundred and seventeenth year, less far, the new houses stood higher on the slope and none was lost.

**The crack.** In the eight hundred and twenty-seventh year a crack a man could fall into opened across a valley two days inland and moved its spring a hundred paces downhill. The king walked its length and forbade nothing; Seasaidh laid white stones a stride back from its edge, and no house was built within a stone's throw of it for the rest of the age. It moved again in the three thousand eight hundred and sixty-third year and broke the line in two places, and the line was laid again.

**Hunger and drought.** Two failed fishing seasons emptied Baile chrom in the nineteen hundred and sixty-sixth year, the oldest hunger on Dia-thìr tied to a place. The springs of Achadh shean ran dry forty years later and the field banks were forsaken. The rivers of the eastern plain ran low for a whole summer in the three thousand seven hundred and seventy-first year, and the cattle of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn were driven to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to drink. Each time the store within the bank and the sharing held.

**The lake and the moor.** The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock crept upward from keeper to keeper until Loch chrom stood a hand higher than at the first cut. In the north, about Doire ghlas, heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the oak ground in the three thousand five hundred and eighty-eighth year, and the groves that gave the north its many doire-names drew back into valleys the wind could not reach.

**The fords.** A spate on the Abhainn chaol took a party of twelve crossing with salt in the three thousand six hundred and eightieth year, and none crossed there in the wet season after. Stepping-stones were laid across the Abhainn fhionn at its shallows a stone at a time until a man might cross dry-shod in every season but true flood: the first made crossing of any river on the island.
